title: The Jaguar Type 01: a £150k gargantuan getaway vehicle utterly useless in the city | Jaguar Land Rover | The Guardian
description: Too costly for most, too large for UK car parks, and wheels bigger than a warlord’s pickup truck. But it does come in ‘London red’
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Too costly for most, too large for UK car parks, and wheels bigger than a warlord’s pickup truck. But it does come in ‘London red’
Content: The Jaguar Type 01 is 2 metres wide and 5.2 metres long – more tank than car.Photograph: Mark Fagelson/PRView image in fullscreenThe Jaguar Type 01 is 2 metres wide and 5.2 metres long – more tank than car.Photograph: Mark Fagelson/PRJaguar Land RoverReviewThe Jaguar Type 01: a £150k gargantuan getaway vehicle utterly useless in the cityToo costly for most, too large for UK car parks, and wheels bigger than a warlord’s pickup truck. But it does come in ‘London red’Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EVZoe WilliamsWed 7 Oct 2026 08.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cutting-edge car du jour, even while very few will ever buy one, is a good index of what the world’s coming to. It’s a dress-for-the-job-you-want principle, on wheels: drive for the world you want to inhabit.That’s why when Tesla launched the Model X with a bioweapon defence mode (2016!), we should have been much more worried than we were, and it’s why theJaguar Type 01 Grand TourerEV has a lot to say.“A new era,” the heritage carmaker calls it, and it’s not wrong. But having test-driven the era (just with my eyes and imagination, rather than the car itself), I would like to return it to the showroom and choose pretty much any other era.View image in fullscreenRawdon Glover, Jaguar’s MD, speaks during the big reveal in New York.Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for Jaguar Land RoverIts gigantic size alone makes it look as if it wants to wage war on the future. The whole point of the electrification revolution in motoring was that we could wean ourselves off energy profligacy and on to elegant sufficiency.If you counteract all that with a car too wide (2 metres) and too long (5.2 metres) to fit into any UK car parking space, whatever advances you’ve made with aerodynamics cannot overcome the fact that you are hulking around something that looks more like a tank than a car, the atmospherics underscored by the glassless tailgate and 23-inch wheels.To unpack that a bit, you can’t see into the back at all, the preference for all the other glass is blackout, and the wheels on a Toyota Hilux, the Chad warlord’s vehicle of choice, are between 16 and 18 inches.All the aluminium in the world (73%of the car’s makeup) can’t put a dent in the 2.5-plus-tonne weight, and they’ve bust their own balls to reduce the drag coefficient only to arrive at one (0.23) easilybested by any average electric saloon(0.21).The look it’s going for, according to the literature, is “monolithic”, but it’s a thin line, isn’t it, between an immutable colossus and a menace, so attempts have clearly been made in the design to introduce a note of friendliness.View image in fullscreenThe Type 01’s interior.Photograph: Jaguar Land Rover PRIt comes in peace, the Jaguar 01 GT; you can tell by the rounded nose, and the body design creating the visual illusion of a front-to-back taper. If it were in a cartoon, it would be driven by the heroes not the villains, but they’d be heroes with no domestic life who knew how to handle themselves. They wouldn’t be The Incredibles.Traditionally, the Jaguar was driven by a guy in his 50s, wanting to signal to the world that he could afford a car that cost roughly half his salary. That’s what the company is now trying to steer away from, preferring buyers who are “rich, urban, very design literate, very technology literate”, according to Rawdon Glover, Jaguar’s MD.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome texture on that 50-year-old of yesteryear, whose type I knew well: my uncle had a Jaguar. Its paintwork was maroon, its interior a buttery leather, which meant we all knew he was earning a tidy packet, and we weren’t allowed to bring our dog for Christmas in case he scratched it. That, in a nutshell, was the personality type, which – I posit – was bad enough.Jag Persona #0.1 is different: he doesn’t want your social admiration, he wants you to jump out of your skin and get your children indoors at his approach, which you’ll see before you hear and only fleetingly, as he races from 62mph to 112mph in four seconds.View image in fullscreenFlorence Pugh at the Jaguar Type 01 launch in New York.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicHe wants you to know he has 150 grand in spare change (ticket price is £120,000 but the extras make that unlikely), and “urban” my aunt Fanny, there is no city situation in which this is a useful car. Regular city driving would be unbearable, given its width, and its standout features of power and agility (three engines, one at the front, one on each rear wheel) are best conceived for a getaway vehicle. Considering its gargantuan size, it doesn’t even have much space – only four seats and boot space that a Skoda Octavia would look at and laugh.And yet, on the plus side, it comes in “London red”, inspired by our mansion blocks and doubledecker buses, our postboxes and room 32 of the National Gallery. These are all different reds, by the way, but then so are red trousers, yet their message is always the same: “I am the kind of person who would wear red trousers.” So if you see one, just think of that person and make them worse, times a thousand.Explore more on these topicsJaguar Land RoverAutomotive industryMotoringreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump
Content: A very interesting impression … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenA very interesting impression … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMoviesReviewThe Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet ZuckerbergJeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions TrumpPeter BradshawWed 7 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts. Sixteen years have gone by sinceThe Social Network, written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher; this was the addictive, obsessive-compulsive movie about the birth of Facebook in Harvard’s macho-competitive cauldron of student sexism and nerdy self-pity, starring Jesse Eisenberg as the fast-talking, arrogant, not-necessarily-evil genius Mark Zuckerberg. Now Sorkin is back with a sequel of sorts, directing his own script – and now Zuckerberg is basically evil, but also weirdly slow talking, as if all the zinging, smart-alecky Sorkinesque dialogue energy of the first film has been siphoned away in early middle age and dispersed among the insurgents in the new cast.Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?Read moreSorkin’s jittery, funny, syncopated style is unmistakable, as distinctive in its way as David Mamet, although he has one joke about “spatula” being a Yiddish word that hehas borrowed from Philip Roth’s Portnoy’s Complaint. It is the story of how in 2021, Zuckerberg’s Facebook empire was challenged bycourageous whistleblower-employee Frances Haugenand Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, who were on a mission to tell the world how Zuckerberg, scared by falling revenue, changed the algorithm so that engagement was supercharged by rage bait and hate speech, malice and envy. Facebook, moreover, didn’t factcheck political ads, thus driving a huge, nationwide surge in extremist groups and teen bullying and becoming a major player in the Capitol riots. (Having said that, this film does not say aloud the word “Trump” and rather cravenly declines to specify Maga activity.)Mikey Madison sympathetically plays the unhappy, principled, supersmart Haugen, who is dismissed as a “disrupter” – and Sorkin leaves it to us to notice that this in other circumstances is what oligarchs smugly call themselves.Jeremy Allen Whitedoes a capable, unflashy, unrisky job as Horwitz, a stolid performance that perhaps, in sync with the film, tells us about the diligent professionalism of old-school print journalism. And Zuckerberg? Well, we were all hoping and expecting it would be Jesse Eisenberg again. (You’ve heard of Richard Linklater’s Boyhood; this would be Aaron Sorkin’s Techbrohood.) But no: it is Jeremy Strong, who does a very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet, modifying the torpid sadness of his Kendall Roy in TV’s Succession, making this the unhurried contempt of someone simultaneously burdened and energised by knowing he’s richer and therefore smarter than everyone else. (A famous line in The Social Network was “A million dollars isn’t cool. You know what’s cool? A billion dollars.” This film starts by telling us that Facebook is worth a trillion dollars.)Zuckerberg, though, is almost a cameo, with no equals with whom he can exchange dialogue, only employees – although the film imagines one former investor-turned-critic called Charlie (Bill Burr) who heckles Zuckerberg’s practice performance before a confessional hearing, with Zuckerberg amusingly having to be told how to smile. Charlie is the angry, unheeded voice of conscience.View image in fullscreenRattles along at an entertaining clip … Jeremy Allen White as Jeff Horwitz and Mikey Madison as Frances Haugen in The Social Reckoning.The resulting drama rattles along at an entertaining clip, although there are false notes. When Frances has secret meetings with Horwitz in a hotel, the film has her wearing a slinky evening dress, supposedly as a kind of disguise, so that if recognised it would seem like she was out on a date. Hmm, really? Or is it so that the movie’s female lead has scenes where she looks glamorous? Later, Horwitz affectionately tells her to be less “mean”. But she is not “mean”. She just speaks Sorkinspeak. So does Horwitz. The ubiquity of Sorkinspeak effaces the difference between all the characters.The most disturbing scene comes at the very beginning, showing a drunk woman livestreaming her racist abuse of traffic cops; this is the woman whom Haugen recognises as an acquaintance of hers, radicalised byFacebook. Towards the end we glimpse her again, looking ambiguously appalled by what she has become. But would she be appalled in reality? Or is this just the film-makers’ wish fulfilment? The closing-credit titles – usually the platform for a film to promote and summarise its heroes’ achievements – concedes that Facebook still isn’t checking political ads. Plus, of course, the film is set at the start of the Trump interregnum of 2020-24, when it seemed as if the Capitol riots were the ultimate wake-up call and moderation had returned. Nowadays Trump and his tech bro courtiers are more vainglorious than ever, and the values of investigative journalism have been thrown out at the Washington Post by its owner Jeff Bezos. This is a film which doesn’t reckon with the future we’re living in.The Social Reckoning is out on 8 October in Australia, and 9 October in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFacebookMark ZuckerbergWall Street JournalAaron SorkinMikey MadisonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: All hail the Death Kult of Kemi – captain, coach and owner of the Conservatives | John Crace | The Guardian
description: The Tory leader is now too big for the party to allow her to fail, so everything she does is acclaimed a work of genius
Author: John Crace
Headline: The Tory leader is now too big for the party to allow her to fail, so everything she does is acclaimed a work of genius
Content: The Tories have no idea if Kemi is messiah or lemming, but they are happy to go over the cliff regardless.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Tories have no idea if Kemi is messiah or lemming, but they are happy to go over the cliff regardless.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesThe politics sketchConservativesAll hail the Death Kult of Kemi – captain, coach and owner of the ConservativesJohn CraceThe Tory leader is now too big for the party to allow her to fail, so everything she does is acclaimed a work of geniusWed 7 Oct 2026 12.26 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTShareWhere’s AI slop when you need it? It could all have been so much simpler. Just ask ChatGPT to write me a leader’s speech in the style ofKemi Badenoch. Make it an hour and 10 minutes long, so plenty of room for padding. Go heavy on the slogans, cliches and the obligatory crap politician jokes. Ones we’ve all heard many times before. Not least at this conference.Make the usual digs at Labour and put the boot in to Reform. The main aim of the speech is to try to reposition a party that is tanking in third place on 20% in the polls as the main opposition to the government.And just to give everyone a reason to go home with a feeling of mild optimism, chuck in a retail offer at the end. An uncosted tax cut for people who are rich but don’t feel quite rich enough. The new multimillionaire common-or-garden lower middle classes.Unfortunately, Kemi made the schoolgirl error of trying to write the speech for herself. And it was much the worse for it. What’s the point of having AI if you don’t use it? It was too long, too flabby. No real argument, just a collection of random thoughts. Andy Burnham in Liverpool it wasn’t.Parts of it even seemed to bore Kemi herself. As if she was going through the motions. Lazy, even. That it was still by far and away the best speech of the entire conference is not really the point. More of a reflection of how dire the others have been. Four days of the Tories in Birmingham is a trial for anyone remotely sentient.On the surface, the Tories have seemed a happy tribe this week. There has been a soporific tranquillity to the proceedings. Few members attending, nonexistent queues and above all no Robert Jenrick. Or even Liz Truss. How we miss her.But the unity feels very fragile. The Tories are now Kemi and Kemi is the Tories. The party has bet the bank on her.Kemi even now calls herself the captain, coach and owner of the Tories.Everyone else is an also-ran.This comes at a huge risk. Because Kemi has become almost too big for the Tories to allow her to fail. So they daren’t question her. Anything she does has to be acclaimed as a work of genius. Just walking on stage is enough to secure her a standing ovation. No one has ever quite walked like that before.View image in fullscreenDelegates applaud Kemi Badenoch’s speech.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAThe party has been captured by the Kult of Kemi. It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy that could lead them to oblivion. They have no idea if Kemi is messiah or lemming, but they are happy to go over the cliff regardless. They are out of other options.Just don’t stop to ask why nothing the Tories seem to do is cutting through. Why the polls are stubbornly flatlining. Why it’s odds-on that beyond the few hundred people in the hall, no one will pay a blind bit of attention to her speech. It will be forgotten within a day.Wednesday morning’s proceedings began with the Tory chair, Kevin Hollinrake. Kev’s dog got a bigger cheer than Kev. Next up was the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, a one-man cluster of antimatter. No man can suck the energy out of the room like Nick. The only thing that would cheer him up is a public execution.Then the Philpster. The UK’s self-proclaimed superhero.The vigilante who took on the French.Endearingly, he still thinks the French navy knows who he is. Chris, most of the UK don’t know who you are. Nor do they care.After this, things began to get surreal as each member of the shadow cabinet was announced and applauded as they took their seats. A bit like a third-rate talent show. The presenter still didn’t know who Nick Timothy was, despite having introduced him moments earlier. She also got Helen Whately’s name wrong. And there was one empty chair. Tom Tugendhat had invented an unmissable trip to India to get out of the embarrassment. Wise choice.A spot of Elgar and then it was Kemi. There was a fight for the soul of the country. There’s always a fight for the soul of the country as far as the Tories are concerned. They don’t seem to realise that it was them that ripped the soul out of it.“What a great conference we’ve had,” she said. It was hard to know if she was being ironic. Other than the fact that everyone has been wandering round in brain-dead surprise that the Tories still exist, it’s been a disaster.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTories delight as satirical tapestry pokes fun at ‘turncoat’ Robert JenrickRead moreAfter that things went weird. As if we were entering a weird dystopia. Being asked to believe the unbelievable. Like when she said that her shadow cabinet was a united team that listened to one another. This after Kemi had literally said she was the party and that anyone who disagreed with her could go fuck themselves. The whole point of Kemi is that she listens to no one.She also had a pop at Labour for putting all their faith in one man. Pots, kettles. As for Reform, she had nothing but contempt. You’d like to think that would rule out a possible coalition.The one moment when Kemi became truly passionate – believable even – was when she talked about race. This was Kemi at her best, talking about something she really cared about. Even if she did imagine there was no racism in football in the 1970s and 80s. But this bit was all too short and the speech began to feel like it was dragging into eternity. We’d still be trying to stay awake well into the afternoon.Finally the reveal – the inheritance tax reduction that would be funded by as-yet-unspecified welfare cuts. Therewould be no inheritance taxon anyone leaving their home to their children. With an extra million-quid freebie thrown in, in case you needed to do it up after your parents had let it get tatty. You could hear the cheers from the country’s stately homes echo around the hall.Here was a party that really got it. Which was prepared to do something about the cost of living for the mega-rich. Even as Kemi was speaking, millions of ordinary citizens were phoning their brokers to liquidate their stock market assets so they could upgrade their £1m homes to something far more palatial. The property market in mega-homes had just gone wild. The people’s earl, Charles Spencer, could breathe easy. Althorp was safe. Let them drink champagne.There was just time for Kemi to pay tribute to Jeffrey Archer – the Tories have a soft spot for a convicted conman who ruined several lives – and then came the extended standing ovations. An echo chamber is going to echo.On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. title: Cruel torment, depraved violence, evil turns: where did TV’s real baddies go?  | Television | The Guardian
description: From Carrie’s bullies to Cathy Ames, sympathetic backstories have made villains boring. It’s time to bring back truly awful villains – in all their deliciously sinful glory
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: From Carrie’s bullies to Cathy Ames, sympathetic backstories have made villains boring. It’s time to bring back truly awful villains – in all their deliciously sinful glory
Content: Not brutish enough? … Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames in East of Eden.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenNot brutish enough? … Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames in East of Eden.Photograph: NetflixTelevisionCruel torment, depraved violence, evil turns: where did TV’s real baddies go?From Carrie’s bullies to Cathy Ames, sympathetic backstories have made villains boring. It’s time to bring back truly awful villains – in all their deliciously sinful gloryRebecca NicholsonWed 7 Oct 2026 10.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe new Netflix adaptation ofEast of Edenlargely sticks to the plot of the John Steinbeck novel. There are tweaks – the introduction of a wedding photograph, for example, which becomes a significant item – but otherwise, it is faithful to the book. That is, in terms of the plot. There has already been some discussion about what it has done to Cathy Ames, played with considerable ferocity by Florence Pugh. Cathy, who later changes her name to Kate, kills her parents by burning down the family house. She shoots her husband, Adam, and leaves her baby sons wailing and alone. She slowly poisons the brothel madam Faye, a woman who acts as a mentor to her and treats her as a daughter, while simultaneously tricking her into leaving her everything in her will. In the book, Steinbeck lets Kate reflect on killing Faye. She finds that she has “no feeling” about it at all.She is a brilliant, brutal character, but on television, she becomes something else: complicated. Her cruelty remains intact, but Pugh and showrunner Zoe Kazan have fleshed her out and given reasons for her fury. They invent a scene that implies Cathy was abused as a child by two men in the woods, and when she takes her final bow, the series returns to this moment in flashback, suggesting that her campaign of destruction has been shaped by a life of trauma and pain. In Steinbeck’s hands, Cathy is cold and unfeeling. In the 2020s, Cathy is more sympathetic and less of a brute.View image in fullscreenKickass Kate … Pugh in East of Eden.Photograph: Geoffrey Short/NetflixBut Cathy isn’t the only character to be treated with softness. In the novel, Charles Trask, like Cathy, is violent and vicious. Early in the story, Charles beats his brother Adam almost to death, then returns with a hatchet with the intention of finishing the job. Adam survives only because he manages to roll his body into a ditch, where he hides until Charles gives up and goes away. On television, this scene, so chilling in the novel, is shortened to a beating, and a tearful Charles is shown to be full of remorse. He is lonely, lost and lovelorn. He is not really a brute either.It is strange that, in an era where hostility and anger feel par for the course, whether online or in public discourse, there is a need to soften fictional characters who might otherwise be treated as pure villains. It also happens inCarrie, the latest take on Stephen King’s first horror novel, which has been turned into an eight-part series by The Haunting of Hill House’s Mike Flanagan. While heartfelt and gracious, its two main baddies have been entirely defanged. Famously, Carrie is driven to take bloody revenge on her school bullies and her fanatical mother.View image in fullscreenVengeance is mine … Summer H Howell as Carrie.Photograph: Courtesy of PrimeIn Carrie, the 2026 edition, there is bullying, though it takes root on social media, and there is fanaticism, though this becomes a fixed belief in anti-government conspiracy theories. Here, Carrie’s main tormentor, Chris Hargensen, has been given a terrible home life and neglectful parents. Carrie’s mother is a formidable force driven by misguided morals but with a fierce love for her daughter. Both of them do bad things, but they are no longer allowed to be bad people. It is empathetic all round, but it lacks the snarl and bite of a horror classic.You can see it again in the recent glossy legal potboilerWar. It probably depends on the podcasts you prefer, but there are few people who would still see billionaires as anything other than Dr Evils with a Mars-colonising complex. Not so in War, where Dominic West plays an investment banker turned social media mogul called Morgan Henderson. Henderson is divorcing his movie star wife, Carla (Sienna Miller), whom he has cheated on in the past. But Henderson, a billionaire, just doesn’t seem all that bad. He made his fortune by building a “nice” social media platform. He hides his assets and allows his legal team to play dirty, but only because they told him to. He writes sad, heartfelt letters to his ex. By the end of the series – spoilers ahead – he realises that they don’t need the courts, because they can just work it out, fairly and amicably, between themselves, because they’re just not awful people.View image in fullscreenUnapologetically evil … Claire Danes with Matthew Rhys in The Beast in Me.Photograph: Courtesy of Netflix/APWar is highly entertaining, but it could have been even more entertaining if it had let rip. Instead, like Carrie, it is too open-hearted to be vicious, preferring instead to give everyone a shot at redemption. This is not a bad thing, of course. It suggests that we are more receptive to empathy and redemption, and more open to kindness, if only in the realms of fiction. But if this softer touch is the direction of travel, television might be getting that bit less fun. Matthew Rhys won one of his Emmys forThe Beast in Me, in which he plays an amoral, unrepentant sociopath. It might not have been one of the all-time greats, but it was deeply enjoyable, in part because Rhys’s character was so unapologetically evil. Sometimes, hate-watching is cathartic and necessary. Despising an antagonist who only behaves badly because they need more love in their life is less enjoyable. There’s no joy in rooting against a villain when you’re forced to feel bad about it.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and Niles | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: From a breathless tango to a kiss that sent fans wild, the pair crafted a sensational seven-year TV crush. The real-life best friends talk first impressions, Casablanca moments – and having hot husbands
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: From a breathless tango to a kiss that sent fans wild, the pair crafted a sensational seven-year TV crush. The real-life best friends talk first impressions, Casablanca moments – and having hot husbands
Content: ‘Our bodies must be in continuous contact!’ Daphne and Niles in the actors’ favourite scene.Photograph: NBC/NBCUniversal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Our bodies must be in continuous contact!’ Daphne and Niles in the actors’ favourite scene.Photograph: NBC/NBCUniversal/Getty ImagesMaking loveTelevision & radio‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and NilesFrom a breathless tango to a kiss that sent fans wild, the pair crafted a sensational seven-year TV crush. The real-life best friends talk first impressions, Casablanca moments – and having hot husbandsLesley Manville and Peter Mullan on their heart-melting TV romanceHollie RichardsonWed 7 Oct 2026 06.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Dr Crane, your glockenspiel has sprung to life!”It was a crush. An unexpected one. The psychiatrist Niles Crane (snooty, conflict-avoidant, married to a high-society wife with a fear of buffets) fell for his father’s physio, Daphne Moon (working class, Mancunian, reckons she’s a bit psychic)the moment he met herin his brother’s Seattle apartment.Across seven seasons of the mega-sitcomFrasier, the crush took hold. Daphne remained seemingly oblivious, but the pair built a friendship and a will-they-won’t-they story that fans loved to be teased with. It made for some cracking episodes: from the pair being holed up in Niles’ candlelit mansion during a rainstorm (with that broken glockenspiel) in the side-splitting A Mid-Winter Night’s Dream, to a passionate leg-in-the-air tango after Niles’ divorce in Moon Dance (“Oh mama, I’ve got it all!”).View image in fullscreenAnd the dish ran away with the spoon … Niles and Daphne in Frasier.Photograph: Getty ImagesDaphne finally learned the truth the night before her wedding to Donny. The next morning, in her white gown, she knocked on the Winnebago in which Niles (four days into a bad new marriage himself) was hiding and told him to drive.“Fasten your seatbelt, Daphne.”“Fasten yours, Niles.”It’s been 22 years since we last saw the pair on screen, but the stars Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce remain dear friends. Hyde Pierce attended – and had a near fatal car accident at – Leeves’ English wedding and he is godfather to her son. They are both in long-term marriages: Hyde Pierce and the writer-producer Brian Hargrove married in 2008 after 25 years together; Leeves and the TV executive Marshall Coben have been married for 30 years. In fact, John Mahoney, who played Marty Crane in Frasier, predicted Leeves’ relationship one day in the green room: “I always wanted kids and said to John: ‘I’m going to adopt,’” she remembers. “He said: ‘Do not do that now. Within a year, you will meet someone.’ And she did, at a Paramount party. “I don’t know how that happened.”View image in fullscreenIn the chair … Leeves and Hyde Pierce backstage on Frasier.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane Leeves“I love you doing this,” Leeves laughs from her Malibu kitchen, as Hyde Pierce joins from a study (which features a bookcase Niles would be proud of) in his New York home. He claims to have just had his hair done – endearingly, he’s a bit frazzled – before asking for reassurance that no one will see this video. They’re more than happy, though, to tell the story of Daphne and Niles.Do you remember meeting for the first time?Jane Leeves:I was on the set on the first day of the pilot and I saw David walking in and crossing the bleachers. I went racing up to him like a mad fan because I’d been watching [the Washington-DC-based sitcom] The Powers That Be, which was cancelled for some bizarre reason – it was brilliant and he played the most odd and fabulous character. I don’t think you really had any dialogue, did you?David Hyde Pierce:No, I played a suicidal congressman who only mumbled.JL:I thought there was a calmness, a kindness and an intellect that was devastatingly sexy, I have to say.DHP:Well, I thought: I can’t believe Paramount Studios doesn’t have security … No, I realised that I lucked out getting the best loon in the business.JL:A couple of lunatics.DHP:I knew her from Seinfeld and Murphy Brown – another show from the dark ages. And we just felt like kindred spirits. It’s safe to say that was true of the whole cast. They put a real family together.JL:It was extraordinary, because I was the only person at that first table read who had read with Kelsey [Grammer]. So the chemistry was unknown.View image in fullscreen‘You were pulling my tie and I liked it’ … David Hyde Pierce and Jane Leeves in Frasier.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyDHP:Also, we did a photoshoot before the pilot and I remember Jane saying something about how there could be just a little something between us, and we ended up leaning on each other.JL:I was pulling your tie.DHP:Yes, and I liked it.JL:The idea came into my head that they were polar opposites and it would be funny if he found her attractive – because she was also the opposite of Maris.What was your real relationship like off camera?JL:Contentious.DHP:A lot of sex.JL:I love David. He’s a true gentleman in every sense of the word and the finest human being you’ll ever meet.DHP:It was as it is now. We’re just best friends. Jane and her husband, Marshall, rented this wonderful shack near the ocean in Malibu. My husband and I, and our dog, would go over and stay. When they moved on, they talked to the landlord about us taking over the rental and we did that. We were very close.JL:John Mahoney was asking me for my parents’ address [in East Grinstead, West Sussex] one time – he wanted to send them a card – and I read it out. And David went: “Muffin-on-Poot?” and the whole room just fell apart.DHP:As a person from the US, everything is “something-upon-something” in the UK. That one just occurred to me and it seemed to stick. But it was with great affection.What do Daphne and Niles love about each other?DHP:For Niles, Daphne is far and above the most beautiful woman he’s ever seen in his life. Whatever aura she gives off just mesmerises him: her personality, the scent of her hair. He’s bewitched. He also thinks she’s completely beyond him, like a creature from another planet or from mythology or the woodlands or something. The fact that the relationship impossibly comes together is a beautiful surprise for him.JL:For Daphne, it’s the kindness and gentleness. He’s so different from any man she’s ever experienced. She came from a family with seven brothers, these brutes, so to find that a man could be kind, an intellectual … it’s the same thing for her, it’s this magical man in front of her.View image in fullscreenGroovy, baby … Daphne go-go dances her way into Niles’s dreams, wearing Donny’s mother’s old wedding dress.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane LeevesWe kept the suspense of the Niles attraction to Daphne going for years and people often ask me: “Why did she not know?” Yes, part of her thought that [he liked her], but the other part of her would say: “Oh, what are you talking about? He’s married and look where you come from and look who he is. He’s a doctor, for goodness sake.” And that voice in the back of her head is what made sense of that seven years of longing.DHP:The tango in Moon Dance was amazing.JL:We rehearsed at lightning speed for that. [The episode was written for the pair last minute as Grammer was on “blue flu” strike to negotiate his contract. Unusually, eight of the show’s writers each wrote a part of the script. Grammer returned in time to direct and appear in short scenes.] We had to rehearse with a choreographer. I remember going to David’s house, because we were loving it so much, to rehearse at the weekend. [The director] Jimmy Burrows would have been appalled.It takes two … the tango scene.DHP:Our late, great director was famous for not wanting people to rehearse because he had such a keen sense of the rehearsal timeframe of a situation comedy, which is not like rehearsing for a play that’s going to run for months. Even the dog [Moose, who played Eddie] suffered if he learned the trick too soon – it would be ruined and he wouldn’t be able to recreate it in front of the live audience. Jimmy was very big on: “Don’t think it out too much beforehand, because it will blossom at the right moment.”JL:I love the scene between us [in Mixed Doubles] when Daphne has been dating a Niles lookalike – he breaks up with her and runs off with Niles’ date – and Niles comes to tell Daphne. There’s a wonderful, sweet, gentle scene between them, like shades of Casablanca. [“If it’d been a different time in both our lives, we might actually have met. How do you suppose that would have gone?” Daphne asks him. “I would have said: ‘What are you doing for the rest of your life?’” he replies. They both, as friends, say they love each other.] It was such great writing – these writers were real romantics.Is there anything you wish Daphne and Niles had done differently?JL:Seven years is a long time and I think the audience was sort of begging to please bring this to a conclusion.DHP:I think we all felt we had played that “these two people didn’t think they deserved each other and didn’t believe that they could ever end up with each other” and there comes a point where you just stop believing that.View image in fullscreenA love story for the ages … Leeves and Hyde Pierce preparing on set.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane LeevesOne thing that the writers did very smartly: they got us together before people were tired of the suspense. I remember very well – speaking of moments that stick with me – when we kissed in front of the live audience. They lost their minds. That was the moment we finally came together. The creators also knew when to end the series; they ended it before any of us were ready. They didn’t want it to dribble off and have the network or the studio say: “Yeah, you’re done.” They wanted to be able to craft a final season. So I don’t know if there are things we wish they did, but I do think those two things were handled really well.JL:The only thing I wish had been handled differently was the hiding of my first pregnancy. But those were different times. [When Leeves came back from hiatus, she was pregnant with her first child. Her bump was hidden in the series and in later episodes she was given a weight-gain storyline and sent to a “fat camp”.] Daphne and Niles had just got together. I came back and I was pregnant – and they probably thought it was too early for Daphne to be pregnant and they wanted to explore this relationship. But then again, it might have been interesting if she was!DHP:I’ve never thought of that, Jane, that’s interesting, so off the rails: the idea that we see them run off together at the end of a season and when they come back they’re having a baby.When did you realise this was a love story for the ages?Love at first sight … Niles meets Daphne.DHP:I don’t know if I ever did think of it as a love story for the ages … love story for theagents?JL:There was an episode or two of Niles and Daphne every season. They were always such great fun. It wasn’t until season two that I realised this thing has legs. Niles’ reaction to Daphne in the room added another layer to Frasier’s apartment; there was this pushback between Niles, Frasier and their dad, and then Daphne comes in and there’s a whole other thing going on. But yeah, by season two, I realised that they were mining this.DHP:One of the cool things about it, too, was that it’s such sophisticated writing: knowing not to say anything when you have set up a dynamic between two characters. The whole audience knows, when Daphne walks into a room, exactly what Niles is thinking. And, eventually, vice versa. There could be comedy there, it could be poignant, it could be a million things – but it was not a show where it was a joke a minute, getting three jokes on the page. It was a different style. That’s between all the characters, in some ways. You got to know us so well.What does romance mean to you and how romantic are you in real life?JL:Oh my goodness. It’s friendship, it’s respect, it’s love. And admiration. I admire my husband, I admire his character. He’s my best friend. And he’s hot. That helps.DHP:Are you talking about my husband or your husband?JL:Oh, both of them, darling.‘I’m completely devoted to one person’: David Hyde Pierce on love, death and the Frasier rebootRead moreDHP:All of those things. I was thinking about both Niles and Daphne on the show, and me and Brian, or Jane and Marshall – what is romance? It’s a poetic thing. I think it’s possibility. Even having been together for ever, there’s just this air of possibility that the whole world has, because you are together.JL:I think I know what you’re saying: being with the right person seems to make everything possible.DHP:Yeah.View image in fullscreenHyde Pierce at the christening of Leeves’ son.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane LeevesJL:You’ve got a good one, too.DHP:I agree.What has been the most intense fan reaction to Daphne and Niles?JL:We’ve always had such respectful fans. I don’t know if there’s been a wild one!DHP: One of my favourite was in the States when the show first started to air. It was at a set time on a Thursday night or a Tuesday night: therefore, the people who wanted to watch Frasier watched it because they knew when it was on. But then there was a point where it went into syndication, which meant suddenly it was on reruns. I remember walking down the street in New York City. A garbage truck drove by and one of the guys hanging off the truck shouted: “Yo, Niles!” And I thought: oh, there’s a whole new audience getting to see the show.JL:I get the same thing in New York – New Yorkers are more open. But I always just get: “Hey, it’sthe virgin from Seinfeld.” It’s so bizarre. I’m like: “Not any more …”Did you keep anything from the set that reminds you of Daphne and Niles?JL:I kept Daphne’s wedding ring and engagement ring.DHP:The green room over the years became covered wall to wall with stills from every episode that our production photographer, Gail, took. At the end, we walked through and took pictures that were meaningful to us. [He turns his camera to a photo in his office.] It’s the three of us [him, Leeves and Grammer] at the piano. I’ve got a million more and they’re all around.View image in fullscreenThe famous Frasier green room.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane LeevesJL:We have millions. There’s a little gym upstairs and they cover the walls up there. That was the saddest thing for me, before the show was even over. We hadn’t even started rehearsing that week and people were taking those off the walls. I was like: “No, leave everything this way, I don’t need everything to change.”DHP: I think Marshall took a load of those [the photos in Leeves’ book]. Those are great.What can Daphne and Niles teach us about love?JL:To persevere. Don’t ever give up on the dream. It would have been so easy for Niles or Daphne to say: “Well, that’s just ridiculous.” But Niles never gave up that longing. And so many people were in his ear saying: “Niles, you fool, you’re sticking your knife in the toaster!”DHP:Love comes when you least expect it and it takes seven years.JL:But it’s worth it in the end.Daphne and Me by Jane Leeves with Isabella Kathryn Coben is published in the US on 20 October and in the UK on 5 November (HarperCollins, £22). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Labour Send changes at risk as parents rush to secure support, say experts | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Overhaul of special education in England could unravel, thinktank finds, because of ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Overhaul of special education in England could unravel, thinktank finds, because of ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic
Content: The IfG says the government’s plans may take longer to complete than the 2030 timeline.Photograph: Sydney Bourne/Getty Images/Image SourceView image in fullscreenThe IfG says the government’s plans may take longer to complete than the 2030 timeline.Photograph: Sydney Bourne/Getty Images/Image SourceSpecial educational needsLabour Send changes at risk as parents rush to secure support, say expertsOverhaul of special education in England could unravel, thinktank finds, because of ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamicRichard AdamsEducation editorWed 7 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour’s flagship changes to special education inEnglandare at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing tosecure support for their childrenbefore the system changes, new analysis has found.TheInstitute for Government (IfG) thinktanksays the government’s plans to largely replace education, health and care plans (EHCPs) in England with more widespread support in mainstream schools may be too optimistic and take longer to complete than its 2030 timeline.The thinktank’s report calls on the government to review the timetable for the changes. And it suggests that if ministers do not act they “risk basing both their reforms and spending plans on assumptions that the system cannot deliver”.The news will be seen as a sign that the government’s ambitious plans to overhaul the special education system did not reckon with the scale of worry among parents, many of whom appear to have acted to ensure support and avoid uncertainty in the future.Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for supportRead moreThe Guardian recently reported that councils and schools havereported a surge in applicationsfor EHCPs, with one school describing the level as “unreal” compared with previous years. Several councils are now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.Amber Dellar, the author of the IfG report out this week, said the long rollout of the changes created a “moral hazard” that encouraged parents to apply for EHCPs now rather than wait for the new system.“There’s a ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic, as schools and parents have an incentive to secure EHCPs before they are phased out, because there’s a lot of uncertainty about what these new specialist packages of support will contain and who will be eligible for them,” she said.Dellar said the government’s plans added new resources in order to reduce the need for families to seek EHCPs, the individualised packages of support agreed between parents and local authorities that can be enforced by specialist tribunals.But Dellar said budgets for the additional resources for special educational needs and disabilities (Send) would be eroded if demands for EHCPs shot above the government’s own forecasts, with councils saying they have to keep issuing EHCPs until the existing legislation is repealed.She said: “The government has a lot riding on the reforms taking effect before they fully kick in – its spending plans for the parliament have some assumptions about savings baked in that are based in particular on them being able to slow the growth or the trajectory of numbers of pupils with EHCPs.“It has a lot politically riding on it as well, and of course in terms of the wellbeing of the children and families involved.”View image in fullscreenThe changes would see mainstream schools given greater support for pupils with special needs.Photograph: Daniel Atkin/AlamyADepartment for Education(DfE) spokesperson said: “The figures in this report are speculative and there is no evidence that proposed reforms are driving additional EHCP demand.“We inherited a Send system with record numbers of EHCPs and families waiting months for support. We are already investing to change that, backing schools to improve inclusion, widening access to specialists and rolling out training for every teacher to better support children before needs escalate.“It is vital that we take the time needed to get this right, but we are completely committed to the implementation timelines set out in the schools white paper and will announce next steps soon.”The changesannounced in Februaryunder Keir Starmer’s administration promised to overhaul a system that parents have denounced for forcing them to seek EHCPs to secure specialist support or a place in a special school.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMany parents said the EHCP application process – introduced by the Conservatives in 2014 – required lengthy waits for NHS assessments for conditions such as ADHD or autism, or great expense for those who could afford private assessments. Families then face bureaucratic delays from schools and local authorities, or legal appeals to a specialist Send tribunal to override councils’ objections.Mark Franks, the director of welfare at the Nuffield Foundation, which funded the report, said: “While there is broad agreement that the current system is under strain, uncertainty and concern remain about whether future levels of investment and the nature of reform will be sufficient to provide high-quality support for all children and young people.”The IfG said the additional costs of Send provision could erode the extra funding being offered for state schools in England, saying it could absorb “around two-thirds of the generous schools funding uplift over this parliament”.The package of changes would see mainstream schools given greater support for pupils with special needs, including the creation of specialist bases, allowing pupils to attend local schools and reduce pressure on special schools.The DfE also wants individual support plans to replace many EHCPs, which would be retained for children with the most profound needs.The IfG said: “It is not clear exactly how the reforms will slow the growth in EHCPs before the new system is fully in place.”‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provisionRead moreDellar said: “The government is making investments now, in early intervention and in specialist bases. But the whole way the government is approaching these Send reforms is deliberately to take a slow, phased approach – largely because it knows that those investments are going to take a while to have an effect.“Its investments in early assessment are going to take a little time to bear fruit. It has not yet properly set out exactly what preventative support it wants schools to put in place. So until schools have that, it’s unclear that they will actually be able to start doing the work the government wants them to do.“On top of that, the system is tightly bound by existing legislation. Local authorities [LAs] in particular have quite strict guidelines, and tribunals suggest that there are often disputes over eligibility for EHCPs but LAs are likely to be pulled towards the law as it stands until the law changes.”Explore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsSchool fundingSchoolsEducation policyChildrenDisabilityDepartment for EducationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I reside in Monaco’: billionaire said to have quit UK over potential wealth tax had already left | Tax and spending | The Guardian
description: TaxWatch contradicts claims about David Reuben’s departure and questions stories of super-rich exodus
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: TaxWatch contradicts claims about David Reuben’s departure and questions stories of super-rich exodus
Content: David Reuben, right (seen in 2015), was said to have joined his brother Simon, left, full-time in Monaco because of potential taxes on wealth in the upcoming budget.Photograph: David M Benett/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDavid Reuben, right (seen in 2015), was said to have joined his brother Simon, left, full-time in Monaco because of potential taxes on wealth in the upcoming budget.Photograph: David M Benett/Getty ImagesTax and spending‘I reside in Monaco’: billionaire said to have quit UK over potential wealth tax had already leftTaxWatch contradicts claims about David Reuben’s departure and questions stories of super-rich exodusApparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playgroundHelena HortonWed 7 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the Sunday Times broke the news that David Reuben, one of the richest men in the UK, had apparently fled to the tax haven of Monaco, there was much pearl clutching. Reuben had moved from his Holland Park house in London to live full-time in the principality.Labour’s tax regime was blamed and there were said to be fears there would bea cascading effectacross the economy, with wealth draining from the UK. It was reported that he had probably left because of potential taxes on wealth in the upcoming budget.Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playgroundRead moreHowever,research by TaxWatchhas found that Reuben, 88, has been a tax resident in Monaco since at least 2014.A spokesperson for the Newcastle United shareholder, who with his brother Simon, 85, shares a combined estimated wealth of almost £28bn, confirmed this was the case.Simon Reuben has lived in Monaco for 40 years since moving on health grounds while having cancer.The principality is a popular place for those who do not wish to pay UK taxes as it does not impose income tax, capital gains tax or inheritance tax.In July 2019, when David became a director of the Reuben foundation, the paperwork filed at the UK company registry stated he was “usually resident” in Monaco.In 2024 he provided a signed declaration to a Los Angeles court stating: “I reside in Monaco. I have resided there for approximately 10 years.”It was reported that the Reuben brothers were“non-doms”, which allowed them to pay UK tax only on income generated in the UK. The then chancellor Rachel Reeves axed this system in April last year, prompting areported exodusof foreign super-rich individuals.View image in fullscreenThe Reuben brothers’ assets include Burlington Arcade in Mayfair …Photograph: John Kellerman/AlamyAsked whether Reuben would have been caught by changes to these rules if he had not decided to move out of his UK residence, a spokesperson said: “That’s an entirely hypothetical question to which it would be impossible to give an answer.”Mike Lewis, the director of TaxWatch, told the Guardian: “When we started looking into this, we were surprised that publicly available documents completely contradicted a major news story. Sadly, these kinds of stories dominate the UK’s public and political conversation about our tax system.“The autumn budget may see some of the biggest changes in years to how gains from wealth are taxed. Perhaps it’s time that our politicians, and our media, debate these changes based on public facts and verifiable numbers – not anecdotes and anonymous reports from billionaires and their spokespeople.”The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who campaigns for a wealth tax, said: “If you want to live in this country, being British, having access to the culture of London, people want that, and there are lots of billionaires and millionaires who do stay because of that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s instructive that there is a grouping of commentators who put on the scare tactics to say the wealthy are leaving this country. We can see that many of these billionaires don’t reside here anyway, many of them do stay here, and those who want to go, we can’t stop them anyway. This has always been the case.”View image in fullscreen… and Admiralty Arch between the Mall and Trafalgar Square, which is being developed into a luxury hotel.Photograph: Antony Nettle/AlamySome of the super-rich are leaving. Analysis of Bloomberg’sBillionaires Indexhas found that super-rich UK residents worth a combined £121bn have either left or loosened ties with the UK since the Labour government came to power in 2024. This represents more than half of all billionaire wealth.Among those who have left are the steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, the Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and the shipping magnate John Fredriksen.Inheritance tax changes in Reeves’s budget were also blamed for pushing the wealthy out, and it is thought capital gains tax may be increased this autumn.The Reuben brothers were born in Mumbai, moved to London in their teens, and went to a state school in Islington, leaving education aged 17 with no A-levels. They started businesses in metal trading and carpet importing. Since then, they have built a property empire.They own prestigious locations including Mayfair’s chandelier-festooned Burlington Arcade, Admiralty Arch, which is being developed into a five-star hotel, and Millbank Tower in Westminster.Explore more on these topicsTax and spendingThe super-richBudget 2026Inheritance taxCapital gains taxnewsShareReuse this content

title: WHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia following suspected plague death | World Health Organization | The Guardian
description: ‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency says
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: ‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency says
Content: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s director general, said he wanted clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed reports of ‘a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause’.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s director general, said he wanted clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed reports of ‘a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause’.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesWorld Health OrganizationWHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia following suspected plague death‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency saysLuke HardingSenior international correspondentWed 7 Oct 2026 16.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheWorld Health Organizationhas said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia following the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia.Darya Shipilovadied two days after falling ill with cold-like symptoms. She was an employee at the anti-plague research institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, with some reports suggesting she was infected after a workplace accident.The Russian authorities have denied a connection with the institute and say Shipilovadied from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable.At the same time, officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted.What do we know about death of anti-plague institute worker in Russia and is there a wider risk?Read moreOn Wednesday the WHO director general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event and we’re not able to conduct a full risk assessment.“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.”Tedros said he also wanted more clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed media reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”.“We assess any reporting from the community,” he said. “We asked Russia to respond to that. We’re waiting for an answer.”The WHO’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, Maria Van Kerkhove, said the agency still did not know how Shipilova became infected in the first place – and with what viral disease. If pneumonic plague was ruled out, “what did she actually die from?” Kerkhove asked.In an interview with local media, Shipilova’s 64-year-old mother, Svetlana, discounted the theory that her daughter had been infected after smashing a test tube. “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid friends who believe this. A test tube is unbreakable, even if you throw it against the wall,” she said.She described her daughter as a dedicated worker and “pure person” devoted to her job.Former classmates are also sceptical she was infected at her workplace. One reportedly said: “They’ve smeared a woman without properly investigating. Knowing how hard-working and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.”The Kremlin has sought to downplay the incident and has brushed aside an offer of assistance made earlier this week by Donald Trump, the US president. The White House has pressed Moscow for more details of the case, while stressing the risk to the US is very low.On Tuesday Trump said he would speak about the plague issue “very soon” with Vladimir Putin, who celebrated his 74th birthday on Wednesday. The Kremlin said no call had been arranged but could be quickly organised.According to theBaikal Medical Journal, health officials in Irkutsk have taken extensive measures to stop a potential outbreak from spreading. Neighbours said workers in white protective suits and gas masks disinfected the two-storey brick building where Shipilova lived several times after her death last Friday.“The smell was unbearable and very pungent,” a woman in her 40s said. “A woman knocked on our door. I said: ‘What are you treating here?’ I already knew about the plague rumours.“She said: ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t even have any cockroaches in our building. I saw her packing her overalls into a bag. I was like, ‘Well, I get it.’”Explore more on these topicsWorld Health OrganizationRussiaEuropeBubonic plagueInfectious diseasesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gene therapy can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers reveal | Blindness and visual impairment | The Guardian
description: Optogenetic therapy, based on Nobel prize-winning science, involves turning nerve cells on and off using light
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Optogenetic therapy, based on Nobel prize-winning science, involves turning nerve cells on and off using light
Content: The therapy was first shown to partly restore vision in a single blind person in 2021.Photograph: fig/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe therapy was first shown to partly restore vision in a single blind person in 2021.Photograph: fig/Getty ImagesBlindness and visual impairmentGene therapy can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers revealOptogenetic therapy, based on Nobel prize-winning science, involves turning nerve cells on and off using lightNicola DavisScience correspondentWed 7 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA type of gene therapy based on Nobel prize-winning science is safe and can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers have revealed.The approach, known as optogenetic therapy, harnesses the technique for turning nerve cells on and off using light that scoopedthe 2026 Nobel prize in physiology or medicine.It was first shown to partly restore vision ina single blind person in 2021. Now researchers have reported the results from a larger trial involving the original patient and a further nine people.“What we can say for sure is that the concept of optogenetics is valid for vision restoration,” said Prof Botond Roska, director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel and a lead author of the study.Roska added the aim is now to work towards restoring high-resolution vision, with the hope of achieving the goal in five to 10 years.All 10 of the trial participants had advanced retinitis pigmentosa – a group of genetic disorders thought to affect more than 1.5 million people worldwide.In these disorders, light-sensitive cells in the retina gradually lose their function. However, ganglion cells in the retina, which send visual information to the brain, deteriorate less quickly.“These cells are not the primary cells targeted by the disease, so that’s why they are good candidates for the therapy,” said Dr José-Alain Sahel, another lead author of the study from the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in the US.The gene therapy involves giving a single injection into the eye. This injection contains a harmless, synthethic virus that delivers the genetic instructions for producing a light-sensitive protein into a ring of surviving ganglion cells. As a result, these cells are made light-sensitive.Each patient then receives a pair of light-stimulating goggles. These capture images of the world around the patient and convert them into pulses of light of a single wavelength These pulses activate the ganglion cells that have been made light-sensitive, allowing the wearer to perceive a monochrome image.Crucially, the technique does not depend on the exact genetic cause of the patient’s sight loss.Writing in theNew England Journal of Medicine, the researchers report how for each patient they treated only the eye with the worst vision, adding participants’ outcomes were then followed for up to five years.Only one severe eye-related side-effect occurred, but this was resolved within minutes, while there were no side effects related to the therapy in the rest of the body.However, six of the 10 participants had clinically meaningful improvements in light sensitivity after the treatment.What’s more, some of the participants showed improvements in a range of tasks when wearing the light-stimulating goggles after the gene therapy – such as detecting, locating and touching a notebook, locating a door and walking on a line.The team added that participants who spent more time training with the goggles tended to do better on the tasks.However, the study has limitations.“[Patients] can detect objects, but they cannot yet detect faces,” said Roska. That, the team say, is down to the treated ganglion cells being in a ring-like arrangement around the fovea – the tiny pit in the retina responsible for sharp central vision.Mark Hankins, professor of VisualNeuroscienceat the University of Oxford, who was not involved in the work, welcomed the study, noting it provides reassurance on the safety of the approach and its application to people who still have some residual vision.“We’ve gone from one patient to 10 patients, we’ve seen improvement in their light sensitivity … and we’ve seen that we can give a stable restoration of some visual function, some light sensitivity, that lasts for four or five years in these patients,” he said. “They’re baby steps, but they’re critical.”Explore more on these topicsBlindness and visual impairmentMedical researchNeuroscienceHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Family of student who took his own life say university ‘will be held to account’ | Universities | The Guardian
description: Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of Glasgow
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of Glasgow
Content: Ethan Scott Brown died at the age of 23 on the day he should have been graduating.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenEthan Scott Brown died at the age of 23 on the day he should have been graduating.Photograph: Family handout/PAUniversitiesFamily of student who took his own life say university ‘will be held to account’Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of GlasgowNadeem BadshahWed 7 Oct 2026 17.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe family of a student who took his own life after beingwrongly told he would not be eligible to graduatehave said the University of Glasgow “will be held to account”.Ethan Scott Brown, 23, was due to graduate in December 2024 after studying geography.However, his family said that in September that year,the universitytold him he had not been awarded a grade for one course and would therefore not be eligible to graduate with an honours degree.His family said as a result, he took his own life on 13 December 2024, the day he should have been graduating.He was found dead in his bedroom by his mother, Tracy Scott, that morning.Scott, who collected her son’s degree posthumously, has called for a fatal accident inquiry to be held into his death.The university has said it is “profoundly sorry” and is implementing a series of recommendations after a review.The university’s internal inquiry found “systemic” errors in the way Brown’s degree had been graded, and that he had enough marks for a 2:1 honours degree. It also found that although Brown had told staff that he had concerns about his mental health, they had failed to offer him support.View image in fullscreenTracy Scott, pictured after a meeting with the Scottish education secretary on Wednesday.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAOn Tuesday it was reported that the family had settled a civil court action with the university. The sum of the settlement has not been disclosed.On Wednesday, the family met the Scottish education secretary, Màiri McAllan, at St Andrew’s House in Edinburgh.Speaking after the meeting, their solicitor Aamer Anwar said they had placed “the University ofGlasgowon notice that they will be held to account”.Anwar claimed that in its drive to become a global institution, the university had “forgotten its soul”.He added: “Their failures were catastrophic and systemic. They failed not just in their duty of care to Ethan, but to many other students over the years.“Today’s meeting with the minister was important and was welcomed. The minister offered to ask the QAA [Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education], who are investigating the university, to meet with the family.“The family welcomed the apology by Ms McAllan for her predecessor’s statement in September 2025 which implied an acceptance of the university’s position that Ethan’s case was an isolated incident.”Anwar added that the university’s governance process was “not fit for purpose”.View image in fullscreenThe family’s solicitor, Aamer Anwar, claimed that the University of Glasgow had ‘forgotten its soul’.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAA spokesperson for the University of Glasgow said: “The university is profoundly sorry that Ethan tragically took his own life and fully understands the deep distress this has caused his family. We repeat our sincere apology as well as our deepest sympathy.“Following an internal investigation into assessment regulations, the university self-referred to the Scottish Funding Council.“The Quality Assurance Agency subsequently carried out a targeted peer review, which resulted in a series of recommendations for action.“The university fully accepted the recommendations and is on track to implement them.”A spokesperson for the Crown Office said the circumstances of Brown’s death were being investigated by the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service, adding that the family would be kept updated on any developments.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisiscounselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsUniversitiesGlasgowStudentsScotlandHigher educationMental healthHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decades | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Convicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum terms
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Convicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum terms
Content: Luke Ings (left) and Liam Bennett were jailed as teenagers.Composite: ITV MeridianView image in fullscreenLuke Ings (left) and Liam Bennett were jailed as teenagers.Composite: ITV MeridianUK criminal justiceTwo men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decadesConvicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum termsRajeev SyalHome affairs editorWed 7 Oct 2026 15.16 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men jailed with indefinite sentences for public protection (IPPs) have been freed after each serving about two decades in custody despite receiving minimum terms of two years or less.A high court judge and a magistrate hearing an appeal after a review by theCriminal Cases Review Commission(CCRC) told Luke Ings and Liam Bennett they would be freed, and also replaced an indeterminate sentence given to a third man, James Ward.Ward, who was freed in 2017 after serving 10 years more than his one-year minimum and was later recalled to prison, was also in court, sitting in the public gallery to see his original sentence replaced.Relatives of Ings and Bennett hugged in the public gallery at Wolverhampton crown court on Wednesday as Mr Justice Choudhury told them the IPPs had been “cancelled”.Choudhury said Bennett would instead be sentenced to four years and 264 days, Ward to two years, and Ings to 42 months with a 30-month extended licence.All three men’s original sentences were quashed and replaced after they argued that judges had wrongly found them to be dangerous or had not considered alternative sentences.Choudhury, sitting with the magistrate Norma Grant, told the appellants: “You have already spent considerably longer than those [replacement] sentences in custody. The effect is that you, Mr Bennett, and you, Mr Ings, will be entitled to release without further supervision, and you, Mr Ward, will no longer be subject to supervision.”The ruling came after the CCRC referred the cases of the three men back to the crown court to review minimum terms imposed on them by judges in Wolverhampton, Reading and Leicester respectively in 2006 and 2007.Bennett and Ings, now both 38, were 17 when they committed offences that led to them being classed as dangerous offenders and given indeterminate sentences with respective minimum terms of 24 months and 21 months in 2007 and 2006.Bennett was originally sentenced at Wolverhampton crown court in May 2007 after being found guilty of reckless arson for setting fire to items in the loft space of an empty council property, and admitting criminal damage and burglary.Ings was sentenced to detention for public protection after appearing at East Berkshire youth court in March 2006 and admitting offences including a robbery in an underpass and an assault on a teenager in a fast food outlet.Ward, now 41, was 21 when he was given a one-year minimum sentence in 2006 at Leicester crown court for arson and criminal damage. He admitted arson – after setting fire to items in his prison cell while serving time for assault – and was released in 2017, but was later recalled to prison and remained in custody until August this year.Muin Boase, representing Bennett, successfully argued that the judge who sentenced him in 2007 did not give proper weight to his youth, lack of maturity and capacity to change after a difficult childhood.In its ruling, the appeal court said there had been no proper basis for the original finding of dangerousness.Detention for public protection and imprisonment for public protection (DPP and IPP) sentences were abolished in 2012, having been made available to tackle offenders considered a significant risk to the public in 2005.The law was changed to stop courts handing out IPP sentences after warnings that they were being applied too widely, but the abolition was not retrospective, meaning many prisoners serving such sentences are still behind bars.The government has faced calls to take action on IPP jail terms, with the former justice secretary Ken Clarke saying last month that ministers should not to be too cautious.His comments came a week after the current justice secretary, Alex Norris, told MPs that the government planned to bring forward legislation to end IPP sentences “once and for all” by the end of this parliament.More than 2,000 prisoners remain held indefinitely under IPP sentences, with 99% past their original tariff and 80% having served 10 years or more.Additional reporting by the Press AssociationExplore more on these topicsUK criminal justiceCriminal Cases Review CommissionSentencingnewsShareReuse this content

title: María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87 | Spain | The Guardian
description: Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis
Content: Maricarmen in Madrid in October 2025.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMaricarmen in Madrid in October 2025.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesSpainMaría del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis‘Now is the moment’: housing activists at Madrid encampment pin wary hopes on Spain’s early electionAshifa KassamandSam Jonesin MadridWed 7 Oct 2026 16.57 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaría del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died.News of her death came two weeks after Maricarmen, as she had come to be known across Spain,was evicted from the Madrid apartmentwhere she had lived for more than seven decades.The pensioner, whose apartment had been purchased by an investment firm who sought to hike her rent by 230%, swiftlybecame a symbolof the many left behind by Spain’s surging housing market.Scenes of the eviction, which saw police use rounds of teargas as they carried out the order, made headlines across Spain. The shocking images – showing Abascal being forcibly removed from her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police – swiftly crystallised into anger.About 10,000 people took to the streets of Madrid hours later, wielding signs such as “Shame” and “We’re all Maricarmen”. From Spain’s north to the south, people poured into plazas to protest the suffering wrought by rentsthat had soared80% in the span of a decade while house prices had climbed 63%.View image in fullscreenA flyer with an image of María del Carmen Abascal is seen at a vigil in Madrid on 7 October.Photograph: Thomas Coex/AFP/Getty ImagesFrom the hospital where she was being treated for severe exhaustion, Abascal cheered on the fledgling movement. “I would like to be there with you all,” she said in a video shot from her hospital bed. “But I’m not that lucky. So from here, I ask you all for courage and to fight and defend what is yours.”As encampments began springing up across the country, the investment firm that bought Abascal’s home said she could return.
