The deal did little to quell the anger that had boiled over in the wake of the eviction.This week the wave of outrage led the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez,to call a snap general electionafter rightwing and far-right parties voted down two emergency decrees his government had proposed to address the housing crisis.The Madrid tenants’ union said the solution had come too late for the octogenarian. “This was a completely preventable situation following an agonising ordeal,” it said in a statement announcing that Abascal had died in hospital,reportedly hoursbefore she was due to sign a new lease with the investment firm that had evicted her.“The events triggered by the injustice of her eviction undoubtedly mark a turning point in the history of this country: massive demonstrations, encampments in the squares, an early election, and the call for a general strike,” it added. “The housing debate is at the center of it all, but the cost of getting to this point has been too high.”Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”Spain’s health minister, Mónica García, said Abascal’s plight had “served to awaken awareness across all of Spain, lighting a fuse that cannot be put out”, and adding that her “dignity and courage” had shown the way.View image in fullscreenMaría del Carmen Abascal in Madrid on 2 June.Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesThe Podemos MEP and former equalities minister Irene Montero was more blunt. “This isn’t a death; it’s a murder,” she wrote on social media. “Such bloody anger. Thank you for fighting, Maricarmen.”Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP) – which voted against last week’s emergency housing measures – also offered his condolences.“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”Her death came a day after Sánchez’s cabinet approved two new housing decrees intended to “maintain the spirit” of the two previous decrees that were voted down in parliament last week by the PP, the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party.The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; regulating room rentals; imposing a new tax on seasonal rentals; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases; and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.With the lower and upper houses of parliament dissolved following the calling of the snap election, the decrees will be voted on by the permanent council of congress, a special council that operates when parliament is not in session.The body’s 69 members are distributed proportionally among the various parliamentary groups to reflect the composition of the lower chamber, meaning Sánchez will probably have enough support to get at least one of the decrees passed.In the heart of Madrid, where campaigners have set up agiant protest camp, news of Abascal’s death was met with a moment of silence. Soon after, hundreds marched from the camp to the country’s parliament chanting: “Maricarmen lives on, the fight continues.”Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropePedro SáncheznewsShareReuse this content

title: Bendy elm still standing against all odds crowned UK tree of the year | Trees and forests | The Guardian
description: Hundred-and-fifty-year-old Wych elm in Newcastle, Co Down has grown sideways owing to strong winds
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Hundred-and-fifty-year-old Wych elm in Newcastle, Co Down has grown sideways owing to strong winds
Content: The tree has somehow resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m elms.Photograph: Michael CooperView image in fullscreenThe tree has somehow resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m elms.Photograph: Michael CooperTrees and forestsBendy elm still standing against all odds crowned UK tree of the yearHundred-and-fifty-year-old Wych elm in Newcastle, Co Down has grown sideways owing to strong windsPippa NeillEnvironment reporterWed 7 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe “astonishing and bizarre” Bendy Tree inNorthern Irelandhas been crowned the winner of this year’s tree of the year competition.Half a million trees to be planted in England in three years, says governmentRead moreThe wych elm tree, located in Newcastle, County Down, owes its name to its near horizontal trunk, which has grown sideways owing to the strong seaside winds coming off the Irish Sea.The 150-year-old tree has resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m elms, making it a worthy winner of the competition’s “against the odds” theme.The tree was originally planted in the mid-19th century as part of a row of wych elms along the town’s promenade to shelter the main street from sea winds. Many of those trees were felled during redevelopments of the town, with the bendy tree now the last one standing.View image in fullscreenNewcastle’s bendy elm.Photograph:  Michael Cooper“When you look at this astonishing and bizarre tree, there’s no doubt about what it has endured,” said May Chemais, ancient tree inventory lead for the Woodland Trust, the charity that runs the annual competition.“We’ve all been through changes and hardships that have shaped who we are: I think that’s why the Bendy Tree has struck a chord with people,” she said.For John Martin, director of the Woodland Trust NI, it is the whimsical nature of the tree that makes it a worthy winner.Could you be an ‘autumn spotter’? Public asked to track changing colours of trees in EnglandRead moreHaving grown up visiting Newcastle as a child, Martin recalls seeing the tree out of the corner of his eye and being surprised to see a tree growing this way.“You expect nature to behave in a certain way and we would expect a tree, most of the time, to grow upwards, whereas this one has grown sideways,” he said. “I guess it gives people a bit of a smile on their day.”The tree’s unusual shape has also provided welcome shade to residents and visitors resting on the bench located beneath its branches.“Older trees like this one are providing our communities with so much – from shade, wellbeing and health benefits, to stories, culture and pride of place,” said Chemais.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCrowhurst Yew in Crowhurst, Surrey.Photograph: Lee CooperOther trees nominated in this year’s competition included the Crowhurst Yew in Crowhurst, Surrey, England. Villagers hollowed out the trunk in 1820 to create a parish meeting room within the tree. The roof of this room collapsed during a storm in 1845, but the tree lived on, with the wooden door to the secret room remaining to this day.Also in the top 10 shortlist was the Culmstock Yew in Culmstock, Devon, England. This tree is perched on top a 20-metre high church tower, with its existence pre-dating residents’ living memories.View image in fullscreenCulmstock Yew in Devon.Photograph: Lee CooperLast year’s honour went to a75ft ash treethat shades homes on one of Glasgow’s busiest roads.The Woodland Trust has this week launched its Igniting Innovation competition for anyone aged 16 to 25 to share their ideas for projects that could benefit nature and make life better for woods, trees and people.Three winners will receive £5,000 in funding and up to a year of expert mentoring to bring their projects to life.Explore more on these topicsTrees and forestsNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins | Gaza | The Guardian
description: People tell of lives changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent Israeli offensive
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: People tell of lives changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent Israeli offensive
Content: Palestinians describe daily routines full of challenges including shortages of water and nourishing food, disease, unemployment and the threat of death. Photograph: Ali Jadallah/Anadolu/GettyPeople tell of lives changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent Israeli offensiveBySeham Tanteshin Gaza andJason BurkeWed 7 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAhmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are cheap and plastic and battered, but they are among the 43-year-old driver and mechanic’s most valuable possessions.Ishtaiwi lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in centralGazawith his two daughters. Their former home is far to the north, in the now ruined town of Beit Lahiya, uninhabitable and impossible to reach.View image in fullscreenAhmed Ishtaiwi, 43, from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in southern Gaza.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAhmed Ishtaiwi’s chairs are among his most valuable possessions.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian“When I sit on those chairs, I remember sitting in the garden at home, having breakfast and drinking tea. They remind me of my life there,” he said last week.Wednesday is the anniversary of the raid on 7 October 2023 by Hamas militants into southernIsraelthat killed 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and triggered a relentless Israeli military offensive that killed 73,000 Palestinians, mostly civilians, wounded many more and reduced swathes of Gaza to rubble.When Layan al-Jbour, a 15-year-old from the southern city of Khan Younis, tries to bring some order to the crowded makeshift shelter she shares with her parents, brothers and sisters in al-Mawasi, a strip of coastline at the southernmost end of Gaza, she recalls life before the war.“When I tidy the tent, I remember our home and how I used to tidy it. I remember my room and how I used to make my bed. When I put a sheet over a table and arrange the bedding, the place looks like our old home,” al-Jbour said.View image in fullscreenLayan al-Jbour, 15, from Khan Younis holds up a cardiology report from a hospital. The only item she took with her was her schoolbag.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianFormer UN food agency official claims he was fired for highlighting hunger in GazaRead more“We hardly took anything with us from our home. We left everything behind, and the only thing I took was my schoolbag. It is the most precious thing I own now. It reminds me so much of my school days. I loved going to school and meeting my friends there.”Across Gaza, Palestinians describe daily routines full of challenges that nothing in their former lives prepared them for: shortages of water and of nourishing food, minimal healthcare, disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the continuing threat of death or injury.Despite a ceasefire a year ago, Israel’s airstrikes continue. Palestinians who have approached the “yellow line” that divides Gaza into zones controlled by the Israeli military and by Hamas have been shot dead. In the last year, the overall death tollhas risenby a further 1,400 people.In recent days, Israeli attacks have intensified, killing at least two Palestinians in Gaza on Tuesday, according to health officials. The Israeli military said the strikes targeted militants.On Wednesday, Gaza medics said at ​least two Palestinians were killed and others wounded in airstrikes in Beit Lahiya and Khan Younis.View image in fullscreenPalestinians gather at the site of an Israeli airstrike that killed a Palestinian in a camp in Khan Younis on Wednesday.Photograph: Tariq Mohammad/APAImages/Shutterstock“It is what we feared … a ceasefire that just isn’t a ceasefire,” said one international aid worker now based in Amman, Jordan, who worked in Gaza throughout much of the conflict. “Daily life is horrible. People aren’t hungry any more but they are still malnourished. Our local staff are telling us that this is just the next stage of the conflict.”Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told the UN security council last month that despite the increase in supplies entering Gaza, the health situation remained critical, with “infectious diseases … widespread amid overcrowded displacement sites and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions”.Inadequate funding for relief efforts exacerbated the “shortages of medical supplies, fuel and the overall humanitarian response”, Alakbarov said, while “restrictions on the entry of critical humanitarian items imposed by Israel” were slowing preparations for cold weather.Israeli authorities deny shortages and say adequate supplies are reaching Gaza,with more than 600 trucksentering the territory each day.View image in fullscreenSaleh Kilani, 70, from Beit Lahiya, lives in a camp in Deir al-Balah in southern Gaza.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianSaleh Kilani, 70, from Beit Lahiya, used to have a farm and olive trees before the war. “Around this time of year, I used to press about 60 containers of olive oil. But I lost all of that too. If I go to my home I may die, and if I go to my farm, I may die too. This is not a life. We are exhausted and we have lost hope.”Kilani said life before the conflict seemed very distant. “We never used to think twice about seeing orange and peach trees, green fields, grapes and figs. These things were simply part of our lives. Now when we see them, we are surprised,” he said.Hamas, which swiftly reimposed its authority over the 2.3 million Palestinians who live in the third of Gaza not under the control of the Israeli military, has rebuilt a rudimentary administration which provides patchy education, some healthcare services and limited policing based on deterrence through often arbitrary punishment.Donald Trump’s plan to definitively end the war in Gaza has stalled, with little progress towards disarming Hamas, securing the withdrawal of Israeli troops and beginning the vast job of reconstruction.“My biggest fear is that this situation will continue. We are living through a period that can be described as neither war nor peace,” said Kilani.The only time Esraa Abu Taiba recalls her prewar existence is when she gets to practise her former profession: beautician.View image in fullscreenEsraa Abu Taiba, 26, from Bani Suheila to the east of Khan Younis, used to work as a beautician in her former life.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianThe 26-year-old lived in Bani Suheila, a town to the east of Khan Younis and now within the zone controlled by Israel. Of her five brothers, two were killed in the conflict, two were wounded, and one is among themore than 1,500 Palestinians from Gazain detention in Israel.“Before the war my life was quiet and good,” she said. “I could go wherever I wanted without fear or restrictions. We lived in our own home. We had a washing machine, a tap and a garden. The house belonged to us and we lived there comfortably.“Now we live in a tent. Our lives depend on carrying water and getting food from the community kitchen. A water truck comes to the end of the street and … I go to collect it because my mother cannot carry it.”Like most Palestinians in Gaza, her family was displaced multiple times during the conflict, and they have lost everything from their former home – except a house key, which her mother keeps close.“The only thing I still do from my old life is some beauty work. I cut girls’ hair in the tents around us and do their makeup for weddings,” said Abu Taiba.“It takes me back to a beautiful and happy period of our lives, when we used to celebrate weddings and other happy occasions before the war. It takes me away from the misery we are living through, even if only for a little while.”Explore more on these topicsGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineIsraelIsrael-Gaza warInternally displaced peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: China’s succession crisis: a generation of entrepreneurs is retiring, but are their children ready to take over? | Asia Pacific | The Guardian
description: Family run private businesses helped power China’s economic miracle, but the next generation is finding it difficult to carry on the work of their parents
Author: Danny Vincent
Headline: Family run private businesses helped power China’s economic miracle, but the next generation is finding it difficult to carry on the work of their parents
Content: China’s younger generation appears unready to take on the businesses of their parents.Composite: Noel Celis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChina’s younger generation appears unready to take on the businesses of their parents.Composite: Noel Celis/AFP/Getty ImagesAsia PacificChina’s succession crisis: a generation of entrepreneurs is retiring, but are their children ready to take over?Family run private businesses helped power China’s economic miracle, but the next generation is finding it difficult to carry on the work of their parentsDanny Vincentin Hong KongWed 7 Oct 2026 19.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrowing up, Ayu would watch his parents put together hand made leather shoes on the ground floor of their three storey home in the Chinese city of Wenzhou. Their relatives in Europe would send photographs of designer products from Italy for the workers to base their designs on, and in the decades that followed, the tiny family-run workshop transformed into a 700 person factory.“The factory and the home were the same place. I watched them make shoes by hand, piece by piece, using small machines,” Ayu recalls of watching his parents work in the 1980’s.By the mid eighties, Chinese economists had a name for this type of bottom up economic growth story: the Wenzhou model. It was a system that saw small companies secure finances through family connections and operate underground factories to produce cheap goods that would end up on the busy streets ofChinaand beyond.Why am I obsessed with China’s ancient golden age? I took my daughter on a trip to find outRead moreBut now many of the family-run manufacturing businesses that helped to fuelChina’s economic successare facing a succession crisis, with the children of factory owners unable or unwilling to take them over.Ayu – who today runs an online e-commerce platform – says it’s not that his generation doesn’t want to take them over, but that the market is much more competitive than when their parents started, and the crucial institutional knowledge and commercial relationships that powered their success will be impossible to pass on.Personal relationships, experience and instincts are difficult to hand over to the next generation, says Hanqing Fang, an associate professor at Missouri University of Science and Technology.“Shares can be passed to a son or daughter overnight,” Fang says. “But the heir is being asked to take over something that looks like a company on paper but, in practice, is closer to the founder’s personal belongings.”View image in fullscreenAyu’s family shoe factory in Wenzhou, China.Photograph: Ayu“The network is very difficult to inherit,” Ayu says. “You have to build it yourself. In the end, some people inherit an empty shell. On paper they’re the boss, but the people underneath them have already begun to leave.“We inherited the wealth, but we couldn’t inherit the industry.”‘I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy’According to HSBC Life research, two-thirds of wealthy Chinese people have no legacy plan. In a study led by the University of Ningbo, just 10 out of 114 private companies surveyed said they were being managed by the families’ second generation.Many of China’s second generation business owners speak of a profound anxiety about taking over the family firm.“I really don’t want to take over because there are so many interpersonal relationships and financial connections that I’d have to handle and learn about,” says Wu, a graduate who works in marketing in Hong Kong.China’s graduate glut: millions enter a job market with little use for themRead moreHis family own a snack processing factory in the Chinese city of Shanwei, as well as dozens of stores in Shenzhen and Hong Kong. But he is reluctant to join the family business.“Most young people dream of getting rich overnight, but I know there’s no such thing. When inheriting a fortune, you also have to consider all the complicated paperwork and whether you really have the ability to handle those responsibilities,” Wu says.According to official estimates, China’s private sector accounts for more than half of thecountry’s tax revenue and 60% of its GDP. Economists say unsuccessful handovers can lead to firms losing value or even closing.Because family-run companies represent such a large percentage of China’s private sector, if they fail in their thousands it could threaten the country’s future growth.“The risk is not that these family firms simply disappear. It is that the capabilities embedded in the founder – including the knowhow, the supplier networks and the relationships – are lost in the handover,” Fang says.For Wu, the idea of one day taking control of the family business is not completely out of the question, but he concedes he still has a lot to learn.“I’d say that one day my parents’ company will be mine. But I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy,” Wu says.“If I could just have the money without any responsibilities, I’d take it without hesitation. But the thing is, it’s not that simple.”Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei*Given names only have been usedExplore more on these topicsAsia PacificChinafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image | Kemi Badenoch | The Guardian
description: At Conservative conference, some worry about becoming a one-woman party, while others say party should thank their lucky stars they have her
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: At Conservative conference, some worry about becoming a one-woman party, while others say party should thank their lucky stars they have her
Content: Kemi Badenoch: ‘There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.’Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch: ‘There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.’Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesKemi Badenoch‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her imageAt Conservative conference, some worry about becoming a one-woman party, while others say party should thank their lucky stars they have herPeter Walker,Pippa Crerar,Rowena MasonandJessica ElgotWed 7 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch has long said that theConservativeswere “under new management”, but in a TV interview to mark the end of a party conference at which she has been front and centre of more or less everything, she took the analogy further.“Your viewers will know that sometimes you have a football team that’s disappointing,” the Tory leader told GB News. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.”These are bold words even for a politician known to possess an iron-clad self-confidence. But they are no exaggeration. Badenoch is not only outperforming her party in polling terms, she is busy remaking it in her own image.The broad ideological direction was already set, with Badenochsaying explicitlyat the start of this year that centrist ideas were no longer wanted. Some more moderate figures remain in her shadow cabinet, but they are signed up to a right-leaning agenda, including oppositionto net zeroand a bonfire ofhuman rights protections.Those around Badenoch say, however, that her control goes further, with policy decisions such as the move to grant free childcareto peoplewith incomes above £100,000, announced on the eve of the conference, made simply because she believes they are the right thing to do.“With policies it’s not about chasing certain groups of voters,” one shadow cabinet minister said. “She focuses on what she thinks needs to be fixed, what she feels is wrong.”Talking her out of a policy decision, they said, was a tall order: “It’s not going to happen – it’s tablets of stone. She’s not going to change her mind. She knows what the policies have to be.”View image in fullscreenPhotographers and delegates clamour to get a picture of Badenoch.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesMany political parties are, to a greater or less extent, a cult based around the leader, but this is particularly the case for the 2026-period Conservatives, where MPs say Badenoch is talked about on the doorsteps with an admiration and respect not accorded to their party more widely.MPs recount how her name is raised unprompted. One said: “She’s brought up in a positive way. Crucially, in a world where most people couldn’t name more than a handful of politicians, they know who she is.”This starring role was obvious throughout the Conservatives’ conference in Birmingham, not least Badenoch’s arrival, which saw her greeted by a flag-waving crowd of activists chanting: “Kemi, Kemi.”Inside the venue, Badenoch was the heroic centrepiece ofthe party’s “Birmingham tapestry”, shown in mocked-up 12th-century form doing everything from chastising Wes Streeting to sitting in the turret of a tank.Such veneration is not just wishful thinking by a party eager to move on from a revolving door of previous leaders. While last year’s conferencewas viewed asmake-or-break for Badenoch, even with her party still bumping along at 20% or so in the polls her position is now seen as secure, with the Conservatives more unified than they have been for years.This is in part the result of some serial malcontents leaving for Reform UK, especiallyRobert Jenrick, as well as the party’s diminished size in the Commons, which as one shadow cabinet minister notes, is too small for factions: “We could just about fill a corner table in Pizza Express.”View image in fullscreenThe ‘Birmingham tapestry’ showing Badenoch ‘expelling’ Robert Jenrick, who defected to Reform UK.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThere are still private doubts, including Badenoch’s instinct to lean into culture wars rather than focus on the economy, which those around her believe is the party’s strongest electoral card.Some party figures also wonder if Badenoch is thinking about election strategy at all with her very personal suite of policy choices, which in Birmingham mainly consisted of giving tax breaks to wealthier people.This was capped in her end-of-conference speech withthe announcement thata Badenoch-led government would exempt people’s homes from inheritance tax, an idea which, given that the levy only begins on property worth more than £500,000, is a largely theoretical idea outside London and the south-east of England.While such policies could be appealing to prosperous home counties voters who defected to the Liberal Democrats in 2024, this does not seem to be the plan. During another TV interview, Badenoch chided her questioner for suggesting her tax cuts were aimed at bringing back such support.“I’m very sad that you’re looking at this in crude electoral terms,” she said. “That’s how we’ve all got into this problem where we keep thinking about winning elections rather than thinking about what works.”One former Tory strategist said there was a risk of incoherence: “I can’t understand what is being achieved with these announcements. Forget lots of the small ones, just use the money and do a big tax cut for middle earners.”There was, they added, little chance things would change: “People are scared of her, to be honest. I think a lot of her team don’t know how to say no to her.”However, much like football, politics is not a one-person game, and a star player or manager will only get you so far. And while Badenoch was at pains to praise colleagues in her speech, it is fair to say that the rest of the shadow cabinet is lagging.Andrew Griffith, Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor, was feted by his boss for his private sector business expertise. But on Monday he gave a speech widely seen asone of the worstdelivered to any conference in years.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch takes her shadow chancellor’s measurements.Photograph: Jack Taylor/Getty ImagesIt is a matter of profile as well as ability. While Badenoch is recognised by 90% of voters, according to YouGov polling, only 22% say they know who Griffith is. A number of his colleagues are on similar ratings, with pollsters saying even these are likely to be inflated by people who don’t want to admit ignorance.The experienced Tom Tugendhat, now in the foreign affairs brief, does slightly better, on 46%. Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, hits 50%, but this is because some people mistake her for the Olympic cyclist, now Laura Kenny, formerly of the same name.There was some unease in Birmingham about Badenoch blotting out everyone else. “Isn’t there a danger we are becoming a one-woman party?” one activist asked a fringe of shadow cabinet members.Others disagree. “It’s a normal dynamic for an opposition party that is unpopular,” said Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary. “It needs a strong popular leader that can pull it up and we should thank our lucky stars that we have her.”Either way, most Conservatives now accept that, for now, it is up to Badenoch to chart the Conservatives’ course, whatever it involves. One ally said: “We win elections on the economy but there’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything.”Explore more on these topicsKemi BadenochConservativesConservative conference 2026Conservative conferencefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ties are back in fashion, thanks to gen Z – should we all be smartening up?  | Men's fashion | The Guardian
description: Sales at one UK retailer are up 200%, thanks in part to young people rejecting the informal look adopted by their middle-aged bosses
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sales at one UK retailer are up 200%, thanks in part to young people rejecting the informal look adopted by their middle-aged bosses
Content: Photograph: Randy Faris/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Randy Faris/Getty ImagesPass notesMen's fashionTies are back in fashion, thanks to gen Z – should we all be smartening up?Sales at one UK retailer are up 200%, thanks in part to young people rejecting the informal look adopted by their middle-aged bossesWed 7 Oct 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Ties.Age:Originated in the early 17th century.Appearance:They’re back.Where did they go?The fashion for wearing a suit with an open-collar shirt, combined with a Covid-inspired trend for working from home, had driven neckties to the edge of extinction.And now they’ve been savedby some kind of selective breeding programme?They’ve been saved by a fashion-conscious younger generation returning to more formal codes of dress.Do you have any evidence to supportthis claim?According to the menswear retailer TM Lewin, year-on-year sales of ties increased by 200% this summer.I didn’t realise TM Lewin still existed.It’s also back from the brink: after closing all its physical stores during the pandemic, the company is beginning to reopen some sites.So ties are in?Not everywhere – news of the resurgence comes just weeks after the House of Lordsrelaxed its rulesto allow men to appear tieless in the chamber.TheLords out of step withfashion trends? How did this deplorable state of affairs come about?It’s hard to imagine, especially when all they had to do was nothing.How times have changed.Think of it as a generational backlash – the informal, open-collar look is now the preserve of well-off, middle-aged men. Young people don’t want to dress like the boss, so they dress up.Where do ties come from anyway?They have their origins in the cravats worn by – and named after – Croatian mercenaries who served in France during the thirty years’ war (1618-48).Nice story, but a cravat is not a tie.Fashionable neckwear evolved over the centuries, from the stock to the scarf to the neckerchief. The necktie we know today was patented in 1922 by a New York tailor called Jesse Langsdorf.So neckwear stopped evolvingmore than a century ago?What changed over time was the fashion for certain lengths, widths, patterns and knots: the four-in-hand in the mid-Victorian era, the windsor between the world wars, the half-windsor in the 1950s.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAre any other endangered formal accessories being resurrected byimpressionable young people, or is it just ties?Apparently, they’ve also forsaken trainers in favour of wearing leather loafers, oxfords and derbies to work.That cannot be.It’s true – sneaker sales in the US have stagnated. And Cruz and Romeo Beckham have been spotted wearing suits with trouser braces.What next? Top hats?Spats?Honestly, don’t give gen Z any ideas.Do say:“The once-shunned necktie has returned, with the retail menswear sector riding on its coattails.”Don’t say:“Can coattails be far behind?”Explore more on these topicsMen's fashionPass notesSocial trendsAccessoriesMenMen's suitsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Contact review – Jonny Donahoe delivers a heated reunion at a bonfire of family photos | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Blythe Duff and Mark Barrett are excellent as two people helplessly bound to each other in this bitter two-hander
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Blythe Duff and Mark Barrett are excellent as two people helplessly bound to each other in this bitter two-hander
Content: Fractured … Mark Barrett and Blythe Duff in Contact.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenFractured … Mark Barrett and Blythe Duff in Contact.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanTheatreReviewContact review – Jonny Donahoe delivers a heated reunion at a bonfire of family photosÒran Mór, GlasgowBlythe Duff and Mark Barrett are excellent as two people helplessly bound to each other in this bitter two-handerMark FisherWed 7 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe arrival of a first baby changes everything. It is not just the upheaval of fitting the child into your life: the shift is also psychological. Children become parents. Parents become grandparents. Responsibility and accountability move down a generation.That is why, inJonny Donahoe’s knotty, bitter two-hander, a man known only as Son (Mark Barrett) has called on Mother (Blythe Duff) after an eight-month gap. She is spikily indifferent to his appearance, here in her back garden where she is burning family photographs on a bonfire. Despite the frosty reception, he must persist.Son’s wife Alice (pronounced Malice, according to Mother) is expecting a Christmas baby. With that in mind, he is eager to end the resentment harboured by the older woman since he was six. He wants their relationship to be civil. She is having none of it.The damage is not in their surface chitchat. If you did not know better you could miss it. Duff captures the sparkle of Donahoe’s hard-bitten wit and can be waspishly funny. Barrett counters with low-status calm, avoiding confrontation. It could all be quite innocent.Whaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? review – when John Home outdid Stratford’s BardRead moreBut Mother’s lack of sentiment goes deep. Incapable of empathy, she has been brutalised by her past. “Not everything you feel has to be expressed,” she scolds her son, sounding ever more the sociopath. The shadow of Son’s abusive father looms over them, but their own personalities also play a part in a trauma that has left them stressed, depressed and trapped in a destructive cycle.With its short, fractured sentences, the play is a tad slow, but in Ben Standish’s lunchtime production for A Play, a Pie and a Pint (with the Traverse and OneRen), Duff and Barrett are excellent in their depiction of two people helplessly bound to each other, inflicting pain even when they try to do the opposite.At Òran Mór, Glasgow, until 10 October. Then touring until 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreParents and parentingFamilyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Crush-worthy photography, camp sci-fi and a centenarian’s florals: five free exhibitions to see  | Art and design | The Guardian
description: A little exhibition of Daidō Moriyama at his artiest and strangest, like Warhol with added filth, is among the best on show in London’s free-entry commercial galleries this week
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: A little exhibition of Daidō Moriyama at his artiest and strangest, like Warhol with added filth, is among the best on show in London’s free-entry commercial galleries this week
Content: Gets you blushing … Dadiō Moriyama, Untitled (Lip Nine Times), 2001.Photograph: © Daidō Moriyama/courtesy Hamiltons GalleryView image in fullscreenGets you blushing … Dadiō Moriyama, Untitled (Lip Nine Times), 2001.Photograph: © Daidō Moriyama/courtesy Hamiltons GalleryEddy Frankel's gallery crawlArt and designReviewCrush-worthy photography, camp sci-fi and a centenarian’s florals: five free exhibitions to seeA little exhibition of Daidō Moriyama at his artiest and strangest, like Warhol with added filth, is among the best on show in London’s free-entry commercial galleries this weekEddy FrankelWed 7 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDaidō Moriyama: Ink★★★★☆If it’s a crime to have a crush on an elderly avant garde Japanese street photographer then lock me up and throw away the key, because I have some seriously strong feelings forDaidō Moriyama. His ultra-confrontational, high contrast, aggressive take on photography just gets me blushing, what can I say.This little exhibition is Moriyama at his artiest and strangest. In the 1960s he discovered Warhol and became obsessed. The works here find him playing with repetition and silk screening, printing up ghostly, painterly, effervescent monochrome images of stacks of soft drinks, neon lit crosswalks and peep show adverts. This is the grim, gritty side of Japanese urbanity, but you can see American capitalism creeping in and taking hold, slowly suffocating the streets.He repeats an image of lips like Warhol’s Marilyn Monroe, duplicates a photo of people walking down a street, their bodies becoming indistinguishable from the adverts hanging from the high rises around them. Then he snaps a woman lifting her skirt, another stomping down the road in thigh-high boots. It’s like Warhol without the pretence, and with added filth.Hamiltons Gallery, London, until 30 OctoberJenkin van Zyl: Enclosure★★★★☆View image in fullscreenUnsettling, dystopian film … Enclosure by Jenkin van Zyl.Photograph: Jenkin van ZylJenkin van Zylis hellbent on cementing their place as English art’s ultimate hyper-camp weirdo, and their new show at Somerset House Studios is a pretty persuasive argument.The exhibition is centred on a speculative sci-fi movie about some bleak company where tourists can inhabit other people’s bodies. But when the central character, a starlet called Mercy, comes to end the lease on her body, the line between reality and fiction starts getting anxiously blurry. Who is the real Mercy, and who is the clone? Who controls your identity? Who has access to what makes youyou?Its grubby atmosphere is reinforced by an immersive installation that replicates the film set as you walk in, with broken automatons, flickering lights and piles of rubbish, all bathed in a pink glow. It’s an unsettling, uncomfortable, dirty, dystopian bit of art cinema – like an overblown, fetishistic take on Terry Gilliam’sBrazil. Van Zyl has a singular aesthetic, and this is pretty much as watchable as this kind of art film gets. It stays with you long after you’ve escaped its unnerving clutches.The gallery handout wants to make out like this is about technological advancement and ideas of authorship. But like all good sci-fi, this feels more obviously allegorical than that. It’s about identity, the versions of ourselves that we present and preserve online, or in public, and how easy it is to lose your grip on the true you. Like a lot of artists these days who grew up with the internet and reality TV turning their brain into gloop, Van Zyl is trying to make sense of a post-reality world, a place where identity can be constructed, but never fully controlled.Somerset House, London, until 29 NovemberGeorge Shaw: Albion Groans Part Two★★★★☆View image in fullscreenHardly green and pleasant … George Shaw, The Ancient Britons, 2026.Photograph: courtesy the artistThere’s nothing all that pleasant, or even particularly green, about the England of George Shaw’s paintings. There are no rolling hills or quiet pub afternoons here in this excellent show of small works by the 60-year-old artist. Instead, there are endless potholes, crumbling masonry, darkened alleys and damp, muddy, miserable, mid-winter landscapes. This is the England of council estates left to rot.His landscapes – always based on his native Coventry – are devoid of life. There are no humans here, only the places they’re desperate to escape. Every sky is overcast, every tree barren, every path sodden with puddles. A union jack has been left crumpled on the pavement near an empty bottle of booze in one, endless knobs have been crudely graffitied on garage doors in another. There’s a painting of a single cloud blighting a blue sky, another of a robin lying dead on its side. Suburbia has leached into the countryside like a toxic spill.They are gorgeously painted, especially the smaller works: sticky with enamel, glossy and horrifyingly alluring, like staring at a car crash.But the car crash here is England itself. Sure, Shaw has been painting the same views of the same bit of Coventry for 30 years, but in that time the country has continued to erode. His whole career is a living portrait of England’s slow collapse. This time it doesn’t just feel like perpetual decline – it’s terminal.Anthony Wilkinson Gallery, London, until 7 Novemberskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTanoa Sasraku: Tropical Ken★★★☆☆View image in fullscreenFaint impressions … Tanoa Sasraku, The Interior (I), 2026.Photograph: Lewis Ronald/© Tanoa Sasraku/courtesy of Vardaxoglou Gallery, LondonThe thing that’s so good about the main work in Tanoa Sasraku’s Turner prize installation – open now atMima in Middlesbrough– is how perfectly it marries image with idea. Sasraku’s collection of corporate paperweights from oil companies acts as a horrifying symbol of the greed of that vile industry. Perfect.Here at Vardaxoglou, Sasraku is showing works from another series, some of which are also on show at Mima, that don’t quite hit the same dopamine receptors. They’re all paper cut into the form of torsos, held together with clips. She places acetates of military camouflage on top of them and then pops them in a tanning bed, leaving behind the faintest impressions of the patterns.They’re meant to evoke warfare, weapons crates and fruit boxes, all while alluding to Ken dolls, but they just look a bit like tea-stained gilets. The gap between image and idea, between the concept and its ability to communicate itself visually, is just a bit too wide.Vardaxoglou, London, until 31 OctoberCe Roser: Running With the Sun, works 1961-2014★★★★☆View image in fullscreenCe Roser, Voyage Into Discovery, 1990.Photograph: © Ce Roser/courtesy VeneKlasen, New York and LondonYou’ve got to hope you turn out likeCe Roser. The 101-year-old American artist has only got better with age. They call her an abstract painter, but all the flower paintings here feel pretty figurative. The earlier, flowerier works from the 1960s are nice, fuzzy, dreamy things. But the stuff from the 1970s, and then the watercolours from the 2010s … that’s where it gets good. Her work gets sparser and more minimal, but no less pretty. Landscapes and flora burst apart and writhe across expanses of white – they have all the aesthetic warmth and floral calm of the earlier stuff, but pared back and made lighter. I’m definitely worse at everything now than I was in my 20s. Let’s hope things pick up when I hit 90.VeneKlasen, London, until 3 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designEddy Frankel's gallery crawlExhibitionsPaintingPhotographyArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: As You Like It review – there are no mere players in the RSC’s ravishing all-male escapade | Theatre | The Guardian
description: With a WWE-style wrestling match, playful eroticism and a fine cast including Hamilton’s Jonathan Groff, this is an exquisite production
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: With a WWE-style wrestling match, playful eroticism and a fine cast including Hamilton’s Jonathan Groff, this is an exquisite production
Content: Prowling with desire … Jonathan Groff and Elliot Barnes-Worrell in As You Like It.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenProwling with desire … Jonathan Groff and Elliot Barnes-Worrell in As You Like It.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewAs You Like It review – there are no mere players in the RSC’s ravishing all-male escapadeRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-AvonWith a WWE-style wrestling match, playful eroticism and a fine cast including Hamilton’s Jonathan Groff, this is an exquisite productionArifa AkbarWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘To liberty, and not to banishment,” exclaims Celia to Rosalind, the exile who finds freedom in her disguise as a man. It is a key statement in Shakespeare’s transformative, gender-bending pastoral comedy, just before the usurping Duke Frederick’s court is replaced by the romance of the Forest of Arden. That big reveal brought a prolonged technical difficulty on the opening night of director Daniel Evans’ all-male production, which was paused for well over an hour so it could be fixed. The technical hitch aside, it is a ravishing staging, with stunning visual effects.There is little comedy or light in the severe court, which contains an intimidating physicality to reflect Duke Frederick’s thuggery, with slaps, shoves and a magnificently constructed WWE-style wrestling match, complete with bunny girls keeping score. It is replaced by Arden’s verdant hills on Anisha Fields’ exquisite set, so beautiful they verge on the voluptuous. The black Elizabethan gowns of the court, Puritan-like but flecked with ornament, and designed by Colin Richmond, are stunning too, as is the chequered shadow-play of the early scenes, in Ryan Day’s lighting design. The breathtaking contrast of the switch between worlds is inevitably lost, following the long wait of the technical problem, but is nonetheless beautifully envisioned.Jonathan Groff, the US screen star who is also Broadway theatre royalty thanks in part to his performance as the king in Hamilton, makes a fun Rosalind, perhaps too declamatory at the start, but more textured and subtle later on. He instantly establishes chemistry with Fisayo Akinade’s Celia who is a runaway highlight of this show, performing femininity without caricature, and bringing an added charge to their relationship – a playful, same-sex eroticism which sees Celia straddling Rosalind at one point.View image in fullscreenRibald romance … Greg Haiste and Gareth Snook in As You Like It.Photograph: Marc BrennerThe all-male casting brings depth and subtlety of meaning, proving ingenious rather than gimmicky, simultaneously nostalgic and of the moment: a nod to the Elizabethan age when boys and men played female parts, yet now more queer and transgressive. The love between Orlando (Elliot Barnes-Worrell) and Rosalind’s disguised male alter ego, Ganymede, stays rather superficial, but the homoeroticism is more effective in their quieter moments, when Groff almost prowls with desire. He is at his best when he is overtly performative – a male actor playing a woman (Rosalind) who is playing a man (Ganymede) – and makes it work without resorting to outright camp.The comedy is light and frothy on the whole. Gary Wilmot, who is both Duke Frederick and the exiled Duke Senior, never overplays his lines. A fantastically prim Phoebe (Tim Preston) brings a kind of librarian comedy with her disdain for the shepherd, Silvius (Edward Judge), and her love-at-first-sight for Ganymede whose brute, masculine scolding seduces her. The ribald romance between Touchstone (Greg Haiste) and Audrey (Gareth Snook) is played for music-hall laughs, the latter is flamboyantly big-haired and archly bawdy, little short of a pantomime dame.Arden itself is rural Wales. Could this be a personal vision of an idyll from Welsh-born Evans? There is a lung-opening splendour to the set as it rolls downstage, over the darkness of the court, and Shakespeare’s songs are replaced by Welsh folk hymns (music composed, arranged and supervised by Theo Jamieson). It is preceded by massive alarms made beautiful by sound designer Paul Groothuis, combining with lighting to conjure musical claps of thunder and lightning. The court could be Prospero’s colonised island, full of strange noises.The only (other) glitch in the production is its pacing, which feels too slow in its latter stages, perhaps due to the big technical pause of the night. Yet the big reveal of Arden is still awesome, when it finally comes. Evans has created magic here.AtRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Shakespeare CompanyAs You Like ItComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Greens may yet win in Holborn and St Pancras – but what happened to the party set to ‘replace’ Labour? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: On the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political margins, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: On the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political margins, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Zack Polanski and Green party deputy leader, Mothin Ali, with supporters in Camden, north London, during the campaign for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, 26 September 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenZack Polanski and Green party deputy leader, Mothin Ali, with supporters in Camden, north London, during the campaign for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, 26 September 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionGreen partyThe Greens may yet win in Holborn and St Pancras – but what happened to the party set to ‘replace’ Labour?Andy BeckettOn the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political marginsWed 7 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.26 EDTShareOnly a few months ago, in the spring, there was a sense of giddy possibility about the Greens. Zack Polanski’s radical new leadership felt fresh and dynamic, especially compared with those of the other parties. Former Labour supporters, in particular, were switching tothe Greens in huge numbers, Green candidateswere winningacrossthe country, and the party wassecond behind Reform UKin some national polls.Like Reform, theGreen partypresented itself as a revolt against a failed status quo. Unlike Reform, the Greens’ urgent stance on the climate crisis gave them a potent moral authority: even many people who did not support them believed that the Greens were right about the most universal issue.After an unprecedentedly hot summer, some of that authority and momentum remains. Last week, at theparty’s bustling conferencein Brighton, impressive-sounding statistics about the party’s growth this year – along with modern icons of Green success,such as Hannah Spencer, victor of February’s Gorton and Denton byelection – were presented to determinedly cheering delegates in crammed halls.This week, in the high-profile London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras, wherePolanski hopes to succeed Keir Starmerin Thursday’s byelection, the usual cheery squads of Green activists have been striding back and forth between wealthy streets and council estates, distributing thick bundles of a party newspaper with the front-page headline “Greens close in!”. Given the party’s recent election record, Polanski’s populist appeal and the possibility that some of the many local leftwing voters may see the contest as a low-risk way to warn Andy Burnham not to follow Starmer’s premiership rightwards,a Green win is not impossible.But, even if it happens, the problems the party has accumulated since the spring will not have gone away. For some voters, the novelty of Polanski’s leadership has faded. For others his style, more radical and provocative than previous Green leaders, has allowed the party to shift to extreme positions, particularly on Israel, with the Brighton conference passing a motion (which the Jewish Polanski neither supported nor opposed) that “Zionism is racism”.Zack Polanski had the chance to show real leadership. He blew it | Rafael BehrRead moreMeanwhile, Burnham’s confident, sometimes iconoclastic start as prime minister has removed Polanski’s unique selling point as a good communicator who does not accept the usually conservative terms of British political debate.In his conference speech, Polanski admitted: “Now I get asked, isn’t your job done?”The idea that one of the Greens’ main purposes is to shiftLabourleftwards and towards bolder climate policies, and that that approach is yielding results, was everywhere at Brighton, from mutually encouraging chats between activists in the queues to upbeat contributions from the main stage.It’s not a role that should be dismissed as minor. The Greens’ influence over Labour – both undermining Starmer in record time by taking so many votes from his party and creating political space for Burnham’s coup and governmental refresh – has arguably been a sign of Britain belatedly catching up with other European democracies, such as Spain, where centre-left parties have long been forced to be bolder by more leftwing ones. After decades of Labour paying most attention to forces to its right, the Greens’ important place in Labour’s calculations makes a refreshing change.And yet, being an influence rather than a definite national rival – the Greens are now about20 points behind Labourin some polls – is undeniably a comedown. During Polanski’s first months as leader, he regularly said he wanted the Greens to“replace” Labour. Partly because of that apparent possibility, the Greens attracted respected leftwing strategists such asMichael ChessumandJames Meadway, who had worked under Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership and became disillusioned by Labour under Starmer.At some leftwing gatherings last spring, those who hadn’t switched to the Greens could feel a bit over-cautious and old-fashioned. It’s possible that the rightwing media even encouraged this shift, giving Polanski plenty of coverage, in order to divide the left and prevent Labour from ever holding sole power again.With Labour’s electoral future now looking more promising, one of the Greens’ leaflets in Holborn and St Pancras modestly presents Polanski as “a strong voice … tokeep Labour in check”. In his Brighton speech, Polanski said: “Vote Green and watch Labour move.” It’s a typically pithy and clever line: explaining the mechanics of politics to voters, and treating them like grownups, in ways that party leaders rarely do.But it may not be an inspiring line for more tribal Greens who decided decades ago that Labour, and alliances with Labour, were not for them. Another Green conference theme was “Real hope. Real change.” It sounded defensive, and too similar to Labour’s conference theme the previous week: “Hope again”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Greens do still hold the initiative on some issues: advocating rent controls, wealth taxes, an end to fiscal conservatism, and more radical climate policies, with Labour expected soon to allow alimited expansion of oil and gas drillingin the North Sea. There are also signs of the Greens positioning themselves as the party of the most disadvantaged, such as asylum seekers, benefits claimants and transgender people – groups that Burnham’s less judgmental government may treat better than Starmer’s did, yet probably within limits set by Labour’s considerable number of socially conservative supporters.“We will always stand with … everyone who is under attack,” said Polanski in Brighton, a statement that could be seen as too vague, impractical and idealistic. Yet if this country is to become a more truly representative democracy – a possible upside of the current political fragmentation – why shouldn’t the most vulnerable effectively have their own party? The most privileged have had the Tories for centuries.The astute political analystRob Ford suggeststhat the Greens’ poll decline “may not matter much” if the party still campaigns effectively and attracts strong support from the dozens of relatively youthful, highly educated and diverse urban constituencies. Thursday’s byelection will test that theory.Yet either way, there is something disturbing about a party with such a crucial cause having to face a reduction in status. The Greens’ drift back towards the political margins reflects not just their own mistakes, but the reluctance of many Britons to face up to climate realities. As withExtinction Rebellion, it’s more comfortable to call them extremists and ignore what they say.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Badenoch made the best of it – but the Tories still have a mountain to climb before any hope of No 10  | Henry Hill | The Guardian
description: Conference announcements on inheritance tax and childcare boosted the party’s mood, but the task is still holding off Reform, rather than any realistic bid for power, says the political editor of the Critic, Henry Hill
Author: Henry Hill
Headline: Conference announcements on inheritance tax and childcare boosted the party’s mood, but the task is still holding off Reform, rather than any realistic bid for power, says the political editor of the Critic, Henry Hill
Content: Kemi Badenoch shakes hands with delegates after her speech on the final day of the Conservative conference in Birmingham, 7 October 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch shakes hands with delegates after her speech on the final day of the Conservative conference in Birmingham, 7 October 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionConservative conference 2026Badenoch made the best of it – but the Tories still have a mountain to climb before any hope of No 10Henry HillConference announcements on inheritance tax and childcare boosted the party’s mood, but the task is still holding off Reform, rather than any realistic bid for powerWed 7 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTShareOn paper, the traditional role of the journalist at a British party conference boils down to some simple questions: what was the mood of the assembled activists? Did the leader give a good speech? In practice, the changing nature of conferences and the media makes this superficially simple task more complicated than it may initially appear.Any journalist covering the leader’s speech, for instance, will have watched it in full. But it will reach the vast majority of its intended audience in fragmentary form, through clips – and speeches are increasingly written with that reality in mind. The conference hall is not really the audience, or the full speech really the product. This adds a layer of complexity to the reviewer’s task.Likewise, it is less meaningful than once it was to talk about the mood of the conference. Thirty years ago, when our political parties were much more robust social institutions than they are today, millions of Britons were party members through thick and thin, and thousands attended annual conference whether they liked the leadership or not.It was this democratic culture that gave us the spectacular showdowns at Labour conferences in the 1980s, or Tory activists cheering Norman Tebbit’s excoriation of the European Union in the 1990s. But it is unthinkable now: most people disaffected with a party – especially theConservatives– are simply not members of it; they certainly don’t take time off work and spend several hundred pounds to attend conference.Even with that caveat, however, there is no doubt that the mood inside the Conservative party is considerably improved on last year’s. Manchester proved that Kemi Badenoch can makegood use of a spotlight, even in otherwise extremely challenging conditions, and her position has improved markedly since then. Her personal ratings are up, her party’s polling has recovered (a little), her only real rival for the leadership has defected to Reform UK, and Reform has its own problems.The policy side of things is helping, too. I was very critical of Badenoch’s decision to go as slowly as she did on policy, and do think that first year of near-radio silence did the Tories serious damage. But the eventual policy announcements have, so far, been generally well-considered; if they still tend to err too much on the side of caution, it is at least better than the alternative, the wild promises of an opposition which has abandoned all hope of office.1:37Andy Burnham clashes with Kemi Badenoch at his first PMQs - videoBirmingham has also confirmed that the Conservatives have recognised the need for a strategic pivot. Badenoch has come under fire from some quarters for returning to the party’s “comfort zone” ontax cuts and deregulation, rather than trying to reassemble Boris Johnson’s 2019 coalition and go blow-for-blow with Reform.But that analysis fundamentally misunderstands the current state of play. As much as the gladiatorial spectacle of the “fight on the right” appeals to journalists, so long as the Tories and Reform are polling where they are, they are not really each other’s primary opponent. Reform’s immediate frontlies through Labour; of the 98 seats where it placed second in 2024, 89 are held by a Labour MP.The Conservatives’ front, in contrast, is much more southern, affluent and Liberal Democrat-facing. Many commentators, both inside the party and out, too quickly assume this means “liberal”, because they assume such voters should be Tory by default. This ignores the fact that, by 2024, the Conservatives did not actually have an attractive economic pitch to those voters. Badenoch’s bet is that a substantial number of these voters – both those who defected to the Lib Dems and a large share who party strategists identify as simply having stopped voting – can be wooed back with a strong economic offer on things such aschildcare and inheritance tax.It remains to be seen whether she gets the polling bounce that is the traditional marker of a successful party conference. But based on what I saw over the past few days, I would say this was broadly a positive event for the Tories.I worry, however, that the party itself is over-reading it. Yes, its situation has improved – but that is clearing the extremely low bar set by two sets of catastrophic local elections in 2025 and 2026. Yes, Badenoch’s personal ratings have improved – but she remains in truth the second least unpopular leader, rather than a particularlypopularone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKemi Badenoch is the most rightwing leader in Tory history. Isn’t it time she got some actual scrutiny? | Owen JonesRead moreTory loyalists can be perhaps forgiven, meanwhile, for playing up the “Kemi bounce”, which has lifted their party from about 17.5% to about 20% inthe current polling average, while ignoring the “Kemi slump” that preceded it (she took the leadership when the party was at 26% on that same average). But you would not guess, reading the room in Birmingham, that the Conservatives are still several points shy of their disastrous vote share at the 2024 election.Yet perhaps this is again a problem of the chimerical nature of conference. The party strategists I spoke to seemed quite realistic about their task at the next election: avoid extinction and remain the largest rightwing party. But the party leadership could hardly make that their top line: it would simply demotivate their remaining troops and be severely punished by the press.It is therefore their difficult task to consistently strike an optimistic note without entirely falling for it themselves – and ours to try to work out if, or when, they have.Henry Hill is political editor of the CriticExplore more on these topicsConservative conference 2026OpinionKemi BadenochConservativesConservative conferencecommentShareReuse this content

title: Why do billionaires have so many children if they’re not prepared to parent them? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Kim Kardashian’s revelation that she has five nannies for four children has cause a ruckus. But the world of the ultra-wealthy throws up far more extreme examples of parenthood, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Kim Kardashian’s revelation that she has five nannies for four children has cause a ruckus. But the world of the ultra-wealthy throws up far more extreme examples of parenthood, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Kim Kardashian with her children North, Saint, Chicago and Psalm.Photograph: Instagram, Kim KardashianView image in fullscreenKim Kardashian with her children North, Saint, Chicago and Psalm.Photograph: Instagram, Kim KardashianOpinionKim KardashianWhy do billionaires have so many children if they’re not prepared to parent them?Arwa MahdawiKim Kardashian’s revelation that she has five nannies for four children caused a ruckus. But the world of the ultra-wealthy throws up far more extreme approaches to childcareWed 7 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTShare“I have the best advice for women in business,” Kim Kardashiantold Variety in 2022. “Get your fucking ass up and work. It seems like nobody wants to work these days.”The billionaire got a lot of flak for this comment but no one can accuse her of being a hypocrite. It takes serious graft to spin a sex tape into lasting fame and a business empire. That said, like many high-flyers who preach the importance of hard work, the Skims co-founder isn’t above outsourcing the less glamorous domestic labour. She has primary custody of the four kids she shares with her ex-husband, Kanye West, and, according to an interview withthe Sunday Times, employs five nannies to take care of them: “One nanny on duty, four on rotation,” she said. Despite having more nannies than kids, she apparently still does the school run. And I bet she doesn’t turn up at the school gate with yoghurt on her shirt like I do.The revelation about Kardashian’s numerous nannies has caused a bit of a ruckus. Largely because there’s nothing people love more than judging how a woman mothers while ignoring the dad. And I’ll admit I was a bit judgy at first. But, look, if I could afford to contract out all the boring bits of parenthood I would too. You’re not a better mother because you’re running yourself ragged doing absolutely everything.Back to being judgy though: while there’s nothing wrong with getting help, I don’t really understand the point of having four kids if you don’t have time to parent them all. Particularly as Kardashian’s kids weren’t oopsies: numbers three and four were born via a surrogate because of complications in her earlier pregnancies.But of course, four kids is rookie numbers compared with some other breeding-obsessed billionaires, many of whom seem keen on procreating but not parenting. The Russian-born tech mogul Pavel Durov has more than 100 biological children in 12 countries via sperm donation. The Chinese billionaire Xu Bo isreportedto have more than 100 children via surrogates. And obviously there’s Elon Musk, who has 14 known children.Meanwhile, for the rest of us it’s getting tougher to afford kids at all. A 2024Pew Research Center studyfound that, among adults under 50 who say they’re unlikely to have kids, 36% cited costs as a key factor. Having big families used to be associated with lower economic status. Butresearch showsthat’s gradually being flipped on its head. Having multiple kids, and a team of nannies to take care of them, has become the ultimate status symbol. Albeit the only status symbol that’s going to grow up demanding therapy.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future.
