title: Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its investors for £550m after sewage spills
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its investors for £550m after sewage spills
Content: South West Water’s Countess Wear sewage treatment works on the River Exe at Exeter in Devon, which treats wastewater from Exeter and Cranbrook.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyView image in fullscreenSouth West Water’s Countess Wear sewage treatment works on the River Exe at Exeter in Devon, which treats wastewater from Exeter and Cranbrook.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyNils Pratley on financeWater industryBurnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cashNils PratleyOwner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its investors for £550m after sewage spillsSouth West Water owner taps investors after sewage spillsWed 7 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.25 EDTShareWater is “a service where the shareholders never lose and the public never win,” Andy Burnham, the prime minister,told the Labour party conference last week, reflecting the popular feeling towards the industry in England.And, of course, his big-picture point is familiar: the £80bn, or thereabouts, that has been paid in dividends over the past 35 years represented over-the-top rewards for investors in many cases. It is easy to agree the public was taken for a ride.But the idea that shareholdersneverlose is not correct – and has been out of date for a while. For starters, the current owners ofThames Waterhave been wiped out. Their shares are worthless whatever the outcome of the interminable talks over whether to put the company into administration or opt for a recapitalisation by the creditors (who will get a sharp haircut on their debt in all circumstances).South West Water owner taps investors to fix infrastructure after sewage spillsRead moreMeanwhile, the owners of Southern Waterhave been obliged to shove in cashon dilutive terms. Now comes something similar at Pennon Group. The owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Wateris tapping its shareholders for £550m via a rights issueto fund, in effect, the cost of clearing up past failures.The new-ishPennonchief executive, Keith Haslett, outlined an extra £1bn of capital investment on top of the existing £2.6bn in the current five-year period. Of the new £1bn, only £400m represents spending on new infrastructure that can be charged to bills (an extra £10 a year for South West customers if Ofwat gives a thumbs up). The other £600m hits shareholders directly and is the catch-up cost of fixing things that should not have gone wrong in the first place.Reading between the lines, Haslett seems shocked by what he found. The rights issue document talked about sustained improvement requiring “a fundamental change in how we plan, deliver and maintain our assets” and how previous efforts have been “held back by the way accountability sits within the organisation and gaps in the capability”.Mr Fixit is not saying it’s an overnight job. All the biggies of water companies’ performance – pollution, leaks and supply interruptions – got a mention as items in need of improvement. The plan is merely to reduce regulatory penalties by 50% in the current period. Haslett’s hope is that, come 2030, Pennon will be closer to earning a few rewards via Ofwat’s incentive mechanism.The point is that none of this will feel like a case of “shareholders never losing” if you’re unfortunate enough to own Pennon’s shares. Anybody who bought at virtually any point in the past five years has lost a packet. The price was £13.30 in July 2021. Now it is 361p, down 20% on Wednesday with the rights issue to a 22-year low.For good measure, the dividend is being cut by 30% on a per-share basis to reflect the new equity issuance. Reality has arrived at Pennon. Burnham might reflect that private investors can have their uses: the capital has to come from somewhere and shareholders can sometimes be forced to swallow some financial medicine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne could take the view that those investors deserve something even sourer, such as outright nationalisation. It’s a point of view but, since Burnham has pretty much ruled it out for water as a blanket policy (we wait to see what happens at Thames), the argument feels academic at this point.If Burnham, despite it all, is going to live with a privatised system, he could do everybody a favour at this point by hurrying up and deciding what he means by his “public control” overlay. Keir Starmer’s water bill, based onSir Jon Cunliffe’s 2025 review of the water sectorand including a stronger regulator, would have been published about now. Instead, we’ll get Burnham’s “strengthened” version some time next spring, according to the Westminster whisper.Given that it could take 12 months to become law, that will be four years for the Labour government to reform the water sector. That is shockingly slow. As Pennon’s fundraising demonstrates, even the current rickety system is moving faster.Explore more on these topicsWater industryNils Pratley on financePennonUtilitiesAndy BurnhamCorporate governanceRights issuescommentShareReuse this content

title: Abide with me: English choral music is a living part of our cultural heritage – we should cherish it | Classical music | The Guardian
description: One hundred years since the BBC first broadcast choral evensong, MP and former chorister Jonathan Davies hymns a beautiful and empowering collective experience that we should praise – and protect
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: One hundred years since the BBC first broadcast choral evensong, MP and former chorister Jonathan Davies hymns a beautiful and empowering collective experience that we should praise – and protect
Content: ‘Singing in a choir taught me that you can achieve more through collaboration than you can alone’ … St Paul's Cathedral choristers.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Singing in a choir taught me that you can achieve more through collaboration than you can alone’ … St Paul's Cathedral choristers.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesClassical musicAbide with me: English choral music is a living part of our cultural heritage – we should cherish itJonathan DaviesOne hundred years since the BBC first broadcast choral evensong, MP and former chorister Jonathan Davies hymns a beautiful and empowering collective experience that we should praise – and protectWed 7 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTShareSome sounds seem to belong to Britain. The peal of church bells. The brass band on a village green. The roar of a football crowd. And, heard from a cathedral at the end of the day, the extraordinary sound of a choir singing evensong.This year marks the centenary of choral evensong on BBC radio. On 7 October 1926, when the BBC was in its infancy, listeners heard a live service broadcast from Westminster Abbey. A century later, evensong can still be heard onRadio 3every week from cathedrals, churches, chapels and abbeys across the country. It is the BBC’s longest running outside broadcast and reaches hundreds of thousands of people every week.For the listener at home, the radio can make a distant cathedral feel remarkably close. But we should not celebrate this simply as a remarkable broadcasting survival story. We should celebrate it because it represents something much bigger: a living part of our cultural heritage.double quotation markFor some, evensong is prayer,  for others contemplation, inspiration or simply a moment of peace.You do not have to be religious or particularly musical to understand the power of evensong. You do not even need to know what a Magnificat or an anthem is. There is something profoundly human about sitting quietly in a great building, hearing young and old voices combine in astonishingly beautiful music. Being given permission for 45 minutes of detachment from the frenetic pace of modern life. For some it is prayer, for others contemplation, inspiration or simply a moment of peace.That is culture at its best: not something kept behind closed doors, but a collective experience. And that is why we should care about what happens when the ecosystems that sustain this tradition come under pressure.View image in fullscreenCultural inheritance … a choir in Westminster Abbey in 1937.Photograph: Sueddeutsche Zeitung Photo/AlamyCathedral music is not simply about preserving an old repertoire. It is a living tradition, with newly written music sitting alongside pieces that have been passed down through generations. Around 3,000 children and young people currently sing as choristers in the UK’s cathedrals, churches and chapels, with thousands more taking part in youth and school choirs led by church musicians. Through these experiences they develop exceptional musical skills alongside confidence, discipline, teamwork and a sense of belonging to something much larger than themselves. Many take these skills into careers far beyond music.double quotation markSinging in a church choir as a child opened up worlds for meThere is also an important social mobility story here.A cathedral choir can give a child access to world-class musical training, extraordinary cultural experiences and educational opportunities that might otherwise be beyond their reach. But we also need to be honest about the barriers, too: affordability, access to music tuition and the unfamiliarity of cathedral culture can all restrict who gets through the door. Preserving this tradition cannot mean simply preserving the status quo. It must mean widening access to it.View image in fullscreenA tradition renewed by the children who sing it … Coventry Cathedral choristers.Photograph: David Jensen/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsSinging in a church choir as a child opened up worlds for me. Not just through the opportunity – asThomas Cranmerput it – to “read, mark, learn and inwardly digest” the most sacred of texts, illuminated by a wealth of the most enriching music humankind has created. It instilled an appreciation of routines and hard work, and it taught me that you can achieve more through collaboration than you can alone. It also taught me that success is sometimes built on of the insights of failure. Something of which I occasionally have to remind myself as a member of parliament.The charityCathedral Music Trustis working hard to ensure the continuation of these sorts of opportunities and is leading a campaign to secure Unesco status for English sacred choral music. Their submission forLiving Heritage statusseeks recognition not for a historical artefact, but for a vibrant and thriving art form, one continually renewed by the children who sing it, the composers who add to its repertoire and the communities who participate in it. Unesco recognition would send an important message worldwide: that this is deemed worthy of recognition, investment and protection, and remains a vital part of the UK’s national cultural inheritance.The UK rightly celebrates its great theatres, galleries and museums. We should be equally confident in celebrating a cultural and religious tradition that is performed every day, in buildings at the heart of communities, by musicians of extraordinary skill. A tradition that has reached so many people through the simple miracle of radio. We have a responsibility not simply to admire this wonderful tradition, but to protect it and to make sure that the next generation can claim it as their own.Jonathan Davies is MP for Mid DerbyshireExplore more on these topicsClassical musicChoral musicBBCRadioRadio 3commentShareReuse this content

title: From Bentley Pauncefoot to Yetts O’Muckhart, I’m obsessed with Britain’s weirdly named villages | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: I was stuck in traffic when a road sign set me dreaming. If the places on it were people, what would they be like? Could Leigh Delamere be anything but the glamorous heiress to a biscuit-making fortune, asks Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: I was stuck in traffic when a road sign set me dreaming. If the places on it were people, what would they be like? Could Leigh Delamere be anything but the glamorous heiress to a biscuit-making fortune, asks Adrian Chiles
Content: ‘There are countless Prestons.’Photograph: Yorkshire Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘There are countless Prestons.’Photograph: Yorkshire Pics/AlamyOpinionGeographyFrom Bentley Pauncefoot to Yetts O’Muckhart, I’m obsessed with Britain’s weirdly named villagesAdrian ChilesI was stuck in traffic when a road sign set me dreaming. If the places on it were people, what would they be like? Could Leigh Delamere be anything but the glamorous heiress to a biscuit-making fortune?Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTShareStuck in traffic in the Wiltshire town of Chippenham, I chanced upon a road sign to Christian Malford and Sutton Benger. Placenames that could be people are dotted across our green and pleasant land – it’s charmingly British, somehow. Waiting to escape Friday night rush hour, I found a persona for Christian Malford taking shape. I had him down as a child actor in one of the early Harry Potters. Sutton Benger was more of a stretch, but I settled on a precociously talented young footballer of Anglo-Norwegian heritage. He signed for Chelsea with great fanfare, but never really made the grade. Poor chap.The traffic moved on, but my mind didn’t. Once on the M4, I was soon passing Leigh Delamere, the glamorous heiress of an American biscuit-making fortune, now fallen on hard times.Back home, I dug out my late dad’s AA road atlas of Britain (2019 edition). How I loved scouring the index in search of more imaginary friends peopling our placenames. Fun for a feeble mind? Probably. Deeply satisfying? Certainly.First, a mention for the mononymous. Patrick on the Isle of Man, Paul in Cornwall – and then there’s Barry in the Vale of Glamorgan, as we all know. A warm wave as well to Kelly in Devon and, in the Highlands, to Kirk and, sweetly, Arabella. There are two Lees, in Devon and London, and Leighs aplenty. Countless Prestons, too. And Bradleys. I make it three Martins and four Hopes. I’m assuming, by the way, that Hope Bagot in Shropshire and Preston Bagot in Warwickshire are somehow related.Many of the first-second name combos are almost disappointingly mundane – no offence to George Green in Buckinghamshire, Roy Bridge in the Highlands or any of the three Rose Greens. By the way, these things can hide in plain sight – I lived next to a place called Hayley Green for most of my life without once realising it would make a perfectly charming girl’s name.Moving on to slightly more engaging names, there’s Ash Thomas and George Nympton, both residing in Devon. Also Nevill Holt in Leicestershire, Rodney Stoke in Somerset and Kirk Deighton in North Yorkshire, while I’ve developed a bit of a fancy for Edith Weston in Rutland. In Kent, we find Dean Bottom, who must have endured terrible stick when he was a kid.I must give an honourable mention to Sandy Balls. Sandy, sadly, doesn’t make the grade, as she/he is not a village, but an area of woodland in Hampshire. That said, there is a Sandy Balls holiday village. What exactly goes on there I haven’t dared to check.It’s in the more intriguing (that is to say unlikely) names that I’ve found the greatest joy: Clifford Chambers in Warwickshire, for example. Surely by now someone called Chambers should have moved there, begat a son called Cliff, raised him to be a lawyer and then opened a practice. “Hi, I’m Clifford Chambers of Clifford Chambers in Clifford Chambers …” C’mon, someone, do it!In neighbouring Worcestershire we find Chaddesley Corbett, surely a philanthropic 19th-century educationist, and Bentley Pauncefoot, the friendly but clueless youngest son of a local landowning noble, nicknamed Paunstar (obviously) by his chums at boarding school. Over the border in Shropshire we can go for an audience with Cleobury Mortimer, a big star in restoration comedy. Staying with arts and culture, North Yorkshire is in good shape with Burton Leonard, the handsome but troubled early 50s Hollywood heart-throb, and Ainderby Quernhow, a fantasy novelist, latterly doing good business with her well-received Olde English Book of Spelles.Elsewhere, there are many foppish-sounding coves. To name but three, Hertfordshire’s Furneux Pelham, Danby Wiske in North Yorkshire and, my personal favourite, Worcestershire’s Flyford Flavell. In sport, Buckinghamshire is strong. There’s the widely feared West Indian fast bowler Aston Clinton and the footballer Lee Clump, the holder of several non-league scoring records.I puzzled awhile over Quadring Eaudike in Lincolnshire, but concluded he had to be a pioneering mathematician. As for Huish Champflower in Somerset, Yetts O’Muckhart in Clackmannanshire and Zeal Monachorum in Devon, I’m afraid I’m stumped. I simply can’t find the characters to do these places justice.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Halloween is looming – this year, I’m ditching my cynicism and getting busy with the pumpkins | Iman Amrani | The Guardian
description: From Day of the Dead to Samhain, celebrating autumn is centuries old. Now, I want this to be a moment of magic and connection for my kids, says writer Iman Amrani
Author: Iman Amrani
Headline: From Day of the Dead to Samhain, celebrating autumn is centuries old. Now, I want this to be a moment of magic and connection for my kids, says writer Iman Amrani
Content: The pumpkin patch at Tulleys Farm, Crawley.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe pumpkin patch at Tulleys Farm, Crawley.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionHalloweenHalloween is looming – this year, I’m ditching my cynicism and getting busy with the pumpkinsIman AmraniFrom Day of the Dead to Samhain, celebrating autumn is centuries old. Now, I want this to be a moment of magic and connection for my kidsWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTShareDarker nights are drawing in, there’s a hint of a chill in the air and the supermarket’s seasonal aisles are groaning with spooky paraphernalia. Halloween is coming. Every year about now, I tell myself I’m going to get my hands on a pumpkin andbake a pielike the ones my mum would make with us when we were little.Halloween wasn’t a huge deal in our house, and neither was baking, but I hold warm memories of helping my mum go through the steps that led us to one delicious latticed pumpkin pie and one uglyjack o’lanternthat we would display in the window with pride.As I got older, Halloween became an excuse to ride around on my bike looking for trouble or going to parties wearing risque outfits under the guise of them being “costumes”. Now, along with that proliferation of Halloween tat in the shops – mountains of plastic ghosts and witches, destined for landfill – cafe chains try to exploit my olfactory memory by lacing their products with artificialpumpkin spiceflavouring. Simple magic has been lost, life has moved on and I realise I’ve never followed through on making that pie.Now I’m a mum to twin toddlers, which means my hands are full – as strangers constantly remind me in the street – but I’m finding myself inclined to create some magic around this dark time of the year, especially at this dark time in the world. Never one to miss an educational moment, my mum would teach us that Halloween wasn’t always an American celebration of commercial excess. One of itspredecessors was Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival still celebrated by some, which marked the end of the harvest season and the beginning of winter, and during which the veil between the physical and spiritual worlds grew thin. A time for reflection and drawing your loved ones close.View image in fullscreenPeople in costume at a Day of the Dead event, Mexico City, 30 October 2025.Photograph: José Méndez/EPALast year, my mother and I took the twins to a Dia de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) community event in Margate, led by local Mexicans. There was Mexican food and music, and even an altar where people could put pictures of lost family members and pets. It was a lovely cultural exchange that felt fun, meaningful and very much in the spirit of the season. Rather than just being about consumption, the event reminded me thatHalloween, Dia de los Muertos or Samhain can also be wonderful opportunities for storytelling – something that should not be underestimated.When I was five, my mother’s father died suddenly, and it concerned me to discover she didn’t hold all the answers about where he had gone. My questions multiplied and I’d sometimes stand in the playground watching other children running around and wonder why no one was talking about the fact that, one day, we were all going to die. The silence made it feel much more scary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStores are selling Halloween stuff in August. Time has lost all meaning | Dave SchillingRead moreI have a lot of bones to pick with Disney, but our family loves thefilm Coco, which is set in Mexico during Dia de los Muertos. Miguel, the protagonist, crosses over to the Land of the Dead in search of his ancestors. Watching it as an adult makes me realise how much I needed stories like this as a child, that could have helped me make sense of terrifying unknowns such as death. We are living through scary times on so many levels and a celebration now feels like as good a time as any to build strength and resilience through imagination and the exchange of stories.The twins are still small, but they have loved the books we got from the library with themes of witches and werewolves or yetis and fairies. I have paper Halloween decorations from last year stored with the Christmas ones and the twins have worn their bat costumes again to flap around the living room. These are moments that I treasure already.They are remembering things now too, which means we are in a memory-building era. I am not going to kill myself with an unrealistic Halloween to-do list, and I don’t want to contribute to unnecessary waste, but this year I’m adamant that we will go to a pumpkin patch together, so they can connect this time of year to harvest and nature. And I’m going to make that pie, although I might have to invite my mum over to help us. I’m still getting started on all of this but I’m going to embrace the celebration in the spirit that my mother did, and try to add my own details to the story. Just don’t expect anything from me at Easter.Iman Amrani is a freelance writer and producerExplore more on these topicsHalloweenOpinionAutumnChildrenPumpkinFamilyAutumn food and drinkcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Conservative conference: struggling to break out of the comfort zone | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Kemi Badenoch’s personal brand is not strong enough to revive a party that so thoroughly lost the trust of the British people
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Kemi Badenoch’s personal brand is not strong enough to revive a party that so thoroughly lost the trust of the British people
Content: ‘Kemi Badenoch thinks victory is available by attaching her personal brand to a classic Tory formula, unrevised for decades.’Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Kemi Badenoch thinks victory is available by attaching her personal brand to a classic Tory formula, unrevised for decades.’Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionConservative conference 2026The Guardian view on Conservative conference: struggling to break out of the comfort zoneEditorialKemi Badenoch’s  personal brand is not strong enough to revive a party that so thoroughly lost the trust of the British peopleWed 7 Oct 2026 14.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 19.27 EDTShareFor a party that keeps losing elections, the Conservatives have enjoyed a remarkably upbeat conference in Birmingham this week. A party with a strong regicidal impulse is united behind Kemi Badenoch. Opinion polls show the leader’s personal ratings, while not spectacular,outperformingthe wider Tory brand. Mrs Badenoch exuded confidence in her keynote speech on Wednesday, setting out what she believes is a path back to power.The strategic focus is the economy. The Conservative leader expects Andy Burnham’s honeymoon to come to an end when his chancellor delivers a painful budget later this month. A spending review will then compound the pain, forcing grim trade-offs on a prime minister who has a reputation for deferring hard choices.Mrs Badenoch presents herself as made of sterner stuff. By that she means she is prepared to say that an overgrown state does too much for too many people. What the Tory leader imagines to be fiscal courage is really ideological complacency pitched at her party’s comfort zone. The Conservative conference generated multiple commitments to cut taxes, mostly for upper-middle- and high-income families, alongside pledges to boost spending on defence and prison places, while also reducing the national debt. This is affordable, according to Mrs Badenoch, thanks to£70bn of “savings”the Conservatives claim to have identified in cuts to the civil service, regulators and working-age benefits.It is a phoney equation that doesn’t account for the increase in costs to government once the social consequences of austerity become apparent. But the proposed reallocation of resources from mythical undeserving benefit-claiming idlers to enterprising but overtaxed middle-class families is a trusted campaign device.Mrs Badenoch presents this agenda as “something for everyone”. In reality, she is trying to reach two particular audiences. The Tories need to attract voters in their former “blue wall” heartlands, now held by Liberal Democrats, and people who backed Boris Johnson in 2019 and then switched to Nigel Farage’sReform UK. These groups have very different attitudes, crudely represented by the polarised political identities that coalesced into leave and remain blocs – one nationalistic, the other more liberal – on the question of Brexit.Mrs Badenoch spent two years courting the former camp with hardline positions on immigration and hostility to net zero climate policy. She has belatedly noticed the existence of people who are appalled by Mr Farage’s agenda. A significant passage in her speech on Wednesdayrebuked Reform UKpoliticians who use a narrow ethnic definition of Englishness.But mostly the Conservative leader talked abouttax cuts, because she believes they appeal across the spectrum. That is often a reliable assumption, although the same plan didn’t help the Tories in 2024. Recklesspre-election giveawayssucceeded only in poisoning the fiscal well for Keir Starmer.The problem for theConservativesthen was that people didn’t trust them to govern responsibly or competently. This hasn’t changed. Mrs Badenoch thinks victory is available by attaching her personal brand to a classic Tory formula, unrevised for decades. Judging by the mood in Birmingham, her MPs and members agree. This is what happens when a party speaks to itself. A much harder test awaits when they have to speak to a country that remembers Conservative government well enough to be disinclined to listen.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency
Content: Supporters of James Talarico, the Democratic candidate leading the Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, in Eagle Pass on 13 July.Photograph: Bob Daemmrich/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSupporters of James Talarico, the Democratic candidate leading the Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, in Eagle Pass on 13 July.Photograph: Bob Daemmrich/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionUS midterm elections 2026The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy tooEditorialDonald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacencyWed 7 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.49 EDTShareFor once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president hasinstructed supporters. Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, theyhave reason to be upbeat. The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and thegerrymanderingof Republicans, but surveys give it a lead ofabout nine pointson the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates.Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. That wouldrequire flipping four seats, with 35 in play. Remarkably, Democrats are prospering in red states from Texas to Alaska. In Kansas – which Mr Trump carried by 16 points, and which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932 – the race is neck and neck.Even putting aside the ongoing questions about polling accuracy, there are very good reasons for caution. The first and most glaring is that the Democrats remainunpopular. Voters are being turned off the Republicans rather than drawn towards their rivals; pundits talk of ared undertowrather than a blue wave.Second, the picture is extremely patchy. Democrats’ striking progress in key races where few had favoured them is tied to standout candidates and especially unpopular opponents – notably in Texas, where the Christian pastor and economic populistJames Talaricois leading Ken Paxton, viewed unfavourably by a third of his own party’s supporters. Yet Democrats are struggling in some places where they initially had good reason for optimism, such asMaine. Third, the huge Republican spending advantage is now materialising – with$700m of advertisingbooked since the start of September.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesMr Trump, who has fared better than his party in elections, is hitting the campaign trail. He may make sure his base turns out. But candidates – including those who benefited from his endorsement – are increasinglydistancing themselvesfrom the president because he alienates others. He is visibly more energised by his construction projects than how his voters can pay their bills. His war on Iran looks not only reckless and ineffectual, but is pushing up prices. Strikingly, voters are now more likely to identify Republicans than Democrats as“elitist”. Latino voters who swung to him arechanging their minds, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement excesses contributing.Outrageously, Mr Trump has usedtaxpayer-funded advertsto laud his presidency. It goes without saying that he cannot be expected to respect the midterm results. The supreme court rejected his efforts torestrict mail-in voting– used by almost a third of the electorate – but he continues to smear it.Just as he disrupts the electoral process, in office he rejects the norms and restraints that his predecessors recognised, and relies more and more on executive orders – seeking to avoid checks on issues ranging from war to vaccines. But shouldDemocratsmanage to take both House and Senate, they would regain both legislative control and investigative powers. In these elections, most votes will be driven by economic stress rather than democratic peril. But their outcome will be critical to the defence of American democracy – or its continued erosion.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionDonald TrumpDemocratsUS politicseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Plan to cut disability support will harm young people | Welfare | The Guardian
description: Letters: Anna Bird and Rick Burgess respond to the government’s proposal to axe the health element from universal credit that disabled people under 25 receive
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Anna Bird and Rick Burgess respond to the government’s proposal to axe the health element from universal credit that disabled people under 25 receive
Content: ‘Disabled young people need opportunity and security. One cannot safely be traded for the other.’Photograph: RioPatuca/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Disabled young people need opportunity and security. One cannot safely be traded for the other.’Photograph: RioPatuca/AlamyWelfareLettersPlan to cut disability support will harm young peopleAnna BirdandRick Burgessrespond to the government’s proposal to axe the health element from universal credit that disabled people under 25 receiveWed 7 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareReports that the government is considering removing the universal credit health element for disabled people under 25 will be alarming for families (Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes, 1 October). For many, it raises serious concerns about how they will keep disabled young people supported and able to participate in everyday life.At Contact, we hear from families worried about universal credit and its impact on disabled family members. Some receiving the health element are studying, working part-time or volunteering; others have disabilities so significant that paid employment is impossible.We recently joined more than 40 charities urging ministers not to take financial support away from disabled young people. We share the government’s ambition for young people to work and thrive, but we do not believe removing financial security will create those opportunities. Ministers have said that those with the most severe disabilities will be protected. But worried families still don’t know what criteria would apply or how hard it would be to prove eligibility.Crucially, receiving the health element of universal credit does not mean a young person is not in education, employment or training (Neet). Before making such a fundamental change, ministers must publish the evidence. How many young people receiving the health element are actually Neet? And among those who are, how many cannot participate because of their disability or health condition?Disabled young people need opportunity and security. One cannot safely be traded for the other.Anna BirdCEO, ContactThis proposal to cut support for disabled young people rather than provide equal access to welfare sends a message to them that they matter less to society. Far from improving their independence or opportunities for work, such cuts would harm their health and push more people into poverty. It is careless to assume that employment support could fill the gap.Disability does not discriminate based on age; nor should the welfare system. A wheelchair, specialist equipment, transport or social care still costs the same whether you are 20 or 60. Young disabled people deserve a social security system that respects their human rights and dignity equally.Rick BurgessChair,Amnesty International UK’s DisabledPeople’s Human RightsNetworkHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Beware rightwing economic myths such as ‘maxing out the nation’s credit card’ | Economics | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article in which Larry Elliott argues that Andy Burnham must challenge neoliberal nostrums
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article in which Larry Elliott argues that Andy Burnham must challenge neoliberal nostrums
Content: ‘A government that issues sterling cannot run out of sterling to pay them. John Maynard Keynes  understood this.’Photograph: Tim Gidal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘A government that issues sterling cannot run out of sterling to pay them. John Maynard Keynes  understood this.’Photograph: Tim Gidal/Getty ImagesEconomicsLettersBeware rightwing economic myths such as ‘maxing out the nation’s credit card’Readers respond to an article in which Larry Elliott argues that Andy Burnham must challenge neoliberal nostrumsWed 7 Oct 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareLarry Elliott’s column on the rightwing economic myths constraining Andy Burnham’s government should be required reading beforeJohn Healey’s budget(Rightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes, 1 October).I spent 20 years trading bonds, and agree that the household budget analogy bears no relation to how the UK state finances itself. Parliament votes on the spending, the Treasury instructs theBank of England, and the Bank credits accounts in the private sector. Taxes withdraw money afterwards.The same accounting exposes the “black hole”: every pound of government borrowing ends up as a financial asset held by households, firms and pension funds. That money hasn’t disappeared into any hole, black or otherwise.The triple lock is debated as a question of whether Britain can afford its pensions, yet a government that issues sterling cannot run out of sterling to pay them. John Maynard Keynes and Clement Attlee understood this, and so did an unlikely ally. Asked in 2005 whether US pay-as-you-go pensions were secure, Alan Greenspan, then chair of the Federal Reserve,told Congressthat there was “nothing to prevent the federal government from creating as much money as it wants and paying it to somebody”.The same is true of sterling. The real question, he added, was whether the economy creates the real assets those pensions are used to buy. Deciding how to provide the care workers, homes and medicines is a political and moral question of the kind democracies exist to settle.Elliott warns that Burnham risks becoming the prime minister who asked the right questions without finding the answers.Ending Treasury-Induced Decline,a report that I co-wrote, sets out the institutional reforms he needs. He could start by dropping the wrong question: “How will we pay for it?”Vince GomezThe 99% OrganisationLarry Elliott is right: Burnham’s government needs to challenge neoliberal ideas, “the nostrums of the past four decades”, like the one about the government being like a household, if it is to repair the damage done to our social services by the Tories. There are others which Elliott didn’t mention.TheLaffer curvecannot be accepted by a government when chronically underfunded public services are crumbling, and therichest 1%in the UK own 36.5% of all financial assets, with a value of £1.8tn. We must reject arguments against equalising capital gains and income tax and imposing wealth taxes – and of course increasing income tax when fiscal rules allow – which use this old and long-disproved Tory economic myth.The same applies to the silly notion of trickle-down economics when tackling the excessive profits of banks and companies cashing in on the effects of war. That leads to the Bank of England’s inevitable blaming of wage increases for inflation, ignoring the relatively recent research in the US showing that that most price inflation comes from “companies seeking to maintain profit margins”.Bernie EvansLiverpoolGrateful thanks to Larry Elliott for demolishing the conditioned belief that we must not “max out the nation’s credit card”. Producing and spending is fundamentally important to the ultimate revival of the UK economy and the restoration of industrialisation. My late husband always insisted that we could afford what we needed to and I didn’t believe him. I do now.Val BynnerLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The US has backed Libya’s Haftar clan. The UK should not make the same mistake | Libya | The Guardian
description: Letter: Steven Kay says Britain should act independently and in a role consistent with its status as a member of the UN security council
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Steven Kay says Britain should act independently and in a role consistent with its status as a member of the UN security council
Content: The Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar in Athens, Greece, in 2020.Photograph: Aris Messinis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar in Athens, Greece, in 2020.Photograph: Aris Messinis/AFP/Getty ImagesLibyaLettersThe US has backed Libya’s Haftar clan. The UK should not make the same mistakeSteven Kaysays Britain should act independently and in a role consistent with its status as a member of the UN security councilWed 7 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTSharePatrick Wintour’s report (Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities, 3 October) should not surprise anyone concerned with the attempts to end conflict and seek the unification of Libya. Saddam Haftar, like his father, Khalifa, has been backed by the US to support its aims and ambitions in Libya. There is no logic, if democratic elections are the goal, to be backing a member of the Haftar clan for any role in the future of Libya.The Libyan population want nothing more than peace, security and to use constructively the wealth that could be generated from their extensive natural resources for the improvement of their society. Instead, their resources are being dissipated in corruption and conflict, a state of affairs that benefits only the warmongers.As a result of representations received from Libya set out in a 9BR Chambers report,Libya: The Voice of the Tribes, the UK’s present and previous governments and successive ambassadors to Libya have been offered a role in brokering a peace and unification conference in this country.All it required from the UK was to formally issue visas and invite the political leaders from east and west Libya, who would attend with the legitimate military commanders from both sides, rather than the bad actors. There has been no take-up by either Tory orLabourgovernments, with neither showing any confidence to do anything contrary to the policies of the US, which are doomed to failure.The benefits to the UK to be seen to be acting independently and in a role consistent with its status as a member of the UN security council would undermine the current perception of it being a declining power. It would also be an opportunity for the UK to assist in the reconstruction and development of an important economy with obvious benefits in its own search for trade.Steven Kay9BR ChambersHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Esther Rantzen’s Mama was a lifeline for new mums | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: Letter: Fiona Lindop says she will always be grateful to the TV presenter for establishing the Meet-a-Mum Association
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Fiona Lindop says she will always be grateful to the TV presenter for establishing the Meet-a-Mum Association
Content: ‘She was warm, welcoming and a true inspiration, demonstrating how important being there for her own family was while she was also busy trying to make the world a better place.’Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘She was warm, welcoming and a true inspiration, demonstrating how important being there for her own family was while she was also busy trying to make the world a better place.’Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianEsther RantzenLettersEsther Rantzen’s Mama was a lifeline for new mumsFiona Lindopsays she will always be grateful to the TV presenter for establishing the Meet-a-Mum AssociationWed 7 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareEsther Rantzen (Obituary, 1 October) is rightly remembered and honoured for her wide-ranging charity work, including establishing Childline and the Silver Line. One of the charities that she pioneered was the Meet-a-Mum Association (Mama), founded in 1979. Mama established a network of local groups offering friendship and support for new mothers.In 1984, I was a young mum with a toddler and a two-week-old baby, and had just moved to Hertfordshire from South Yorkshire. Mama was a lifeline that helped me become part of the new community with access to support, and I joined the local Mama committee soon after.Esther invited us to a meeting at the BBC studios in London to discuss the charity’s future. She was warm and a true inspiration, demonstrating how important being there for her own family was while she was also trying to make the world a better place. The meeting had to end promptly as she had to get to her daughter’s birthday party on time. I will always be grateful to Esther for establishing Mama and for the difference it made to my life and the lives of many others.Fiona LindopDuffield, DerbyshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Jon Rahm’s LIV exit set to trigger mass exodus of players from stricken tour | LIV Golf Series | The Guardian
description: Tyrrell Hatton and other big names are likely to follow Jon Rahm in abandoning LIV Golf, which faces a race against time if it is to continue
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Tyrrell Hatton and other big names are likely to follow Jon Rahm in abandoning LIV Golf, which faces a race against time if it is to continue
Content: Jon Rahm became LIV Golf’s highest-profile player when he joined in December 2023.Photograph: Michael Miller/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJon Rahm became LIV Golf’s highest-profile player when he joined in December 2023.Photograph: Michael Miller/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesLIV Golf SeriesJon Rahm’s LIV exit set to trigger mass exodus of players from stricken tourTyrrell Hatton and other big names likely to followTour filed for bankruptcy after Saudi funding withdrawnEwan MurrayWed 7 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConfirmation that Jon Rahm will play no part in LIVGolfin its post-Saudi Arabian form is likely to be only the start of a mass exodus from the breakaway circuit.A bankruptcy hearing on Wednesday heard Rahm’s lawyer say “unacceptable” terms proposed by LIV 2.0 mean the Spaniard will shortly walk away from a tour which has lingering hopes of continuing as a going concern. Rahm’s departure from LIV, which he joined in 2023, was inevitable, but still a significant blow and moment in time given his status in his sport.Phil Mickelson’s reps say he sought treatment for family trauma and addictionRead more“Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0,” the two-time major winner’s attorney, John Beck, said.The expectation from those with knowledge of the LIV situation is that a batch of other players including Tyrrell Hatton, Tom McKibbin, Cameron Smith, Joaquin Niemann and Adrian Meronk will also flee the scene when legalities permit. The initial habitat for those players, from the start of next season, is likely to be the DP World Tour. LIV faces a race against time to earn commitment from players of even average quality in its mission to continue with 75-man events into 2027.Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) abruptly confirmed in April it willend funding of LIV at the end of 2026. It is estimated the PIF spent more than $5bn (£3.8bn) in the project, which was intended to challenge golf’s established tours. LIVentered Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedingsin the US last month, which was always likely to facilitate the departure of big names such as Rahm. They had signed for LIV on multi-year, multi-million dollar contracts which had become unaffordable.Rahm’s representatives are “in advanced discussions for a consensual separation agreement” with LIV. Documents listing creditors had previously shown that Rahm had an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.7m).View image in fullscreenJon Rahm (left) and Sergio García both participated in the LIV Golf tour.Photograph: Erik S Lesser/EPAThe status of Bryson DeChambeau, LIV’s remaining marquee name, is unclear. DeChambeau is known to have little appetite to return to the PGA Tour in the US, with that sentiment thought to be mutual. DeChambeau’s preference has always been an elongated version of LIV but that competitive model remains open to much question.LIV Golf, along with BC Partners Credit, has been outwardly bullish about its future. “Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf’s emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season,” said Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, in a statement. An immediate winner from this mess is likely to be the DP World Tour. Golfers are expected to gravitate towards that circuit for 2027 as a means to potentially play their way back on to the PGA Tour.LIV has already cut ties with all but a skeleton staff.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLIV entered into a formal restructuring support agreement with BC Partners Credit on Tuesday. Full detail of that, including potentially $300m (£227m) financing, remains unclear. Scott O’Neil, LIV’s chief executive, said: “We believe deeply in the future of this league and in the opportunity to build something distinctive alongside our players. We’re delivering on our major milestones and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers.”Rahm withdrew from this week’s Spanish Open in Madrid in order to remain at home as his wife, Kelley, is expecting their fourth child. He previouslysettled a dispute with the DP World, formerly European, Tour which could have impacted his future Ryder Cup involvement.Explore more on these topicsLIV Golf SeriesGolfSaudi Arabia and sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: All aboard the Tuchel train? England camp has clear winners and losers | England | The Guardian
description: While it’s full steam ahead for Alex Scott, Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly, others look likely to be left behind
Author: David Hytner
Headline: While it’s full steam ahead for Alex Scott, Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly, others look likely to be left behind
Content: Myles Lewis-Skelly (centre) and Lewis Hall (right) were among those who impressed.Photograph: Michael Regan/The FA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMyles Lewis-Skelly (centre) and Lewis Hall (right) were among those who impressed.Photograph: Michael Regan/The FA/Getty ImagesEnglandAll aboard the Tuchel train? England camp has clear winners and losersWhile it’s full steam ahead for Alex Scott, Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly, others look likely to be left behindDavid HytnerWed 7 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel’s original idea had been for continuity. The England manager wanted to build on the positives from the World Cup and he was minded to stand by the vast majority of the players who had been a part of the journey to the semi-finals in North America over the summer. His squad for the four-matchNations Leaguewindow and the beginning of a new international cycle would not be defined by radical change. What was it about the best-laid plans?As Tuchel prepared to name his group in mid-September, he knew that he would be without a clutch of World Cup players because of injury. He then lost another handful after the announcement. Fast forward tothe Czechia game at Wembleyon Tuesday night – the final one of the quartet – and, after further withdrawals, Tuchel could count only 12 players who were available to him during the World Cup. He knows the train moves quickly in football, stopping for nobody. That flexibility is a prerequisite in his line of work. This felt like something else.England ready to level up and embrace ‘calculated risks’, claims TuchelRead moreTuchel and his staff were resolved to road-test an updated game model as they sought to move on from the devastation ofthe World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina. Again, nothing too radical because the principles were in place. They wanted to give the players greater freedom in terms of where they could roam on the pitch; encourage them to trust their instincts and take risks, all within a framework where covering for a teammate was fundamental. Tuchel would need some new players to execute it and, as he reflects on a positive window, in whichdefeat by Spainwas followed by three wins, two against Czechia either side ofthe 7-0 dismantling of Croatiain Rijeka, he will feel he has found them.There are always winners and losers from an international camp and maybe they are more pronounced on this occasion because of the timing; the sense of a fresh start, the desire to turn the page after Argentina. It was always going to be a tone-setter for the ultimate goal of Euro 2028 glory.The biggest winners were Alex Scott and Lewis Hall, with Myles Lewis-Skelly getting an honourable mention. James Trafford pushed his claim to supplant Jordan Pickford as the first-choice goalkeeper, and then there was Trent Alexander-Arnold, ever tantalising, ever nuanced.As for the losers, well, take your pick from those who were not present, with Tuchel making it clear that it would be harder for them. “It is always like this,” he said. “Everyone should be desperate to come because the train is rolling. Full credit to the players who bought in to that. We can only put our full energy into the camp and the players who are in camp. They make the camp special.”View image in fullscreenAlex Scott (centre) caught Thomas Tuchel’s eye before being forced to withdraw with injury.Photograph: Sebastian Frej/Getty ImagesTuchel described Scott and Hall as “really excellent”. In the case of the former, Tuchel cannot contain his excitement. He does not want to. Scott did well when he came on as a 70th-minute substitute for his debut against Czechia in Prague and was very good from the start against Croatia, catching the eye with his smoothness on the half turn, his dynamic surges.It was noticeable that when Tuchel’s assistant, Anthony Barry, spoke on Monday about fluid, hard-running midfielders to fit the team’s style, he name-checked three: Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson, who are well-established, and Scott. It is such a frustration thathe aggravated a thigh problem against Croatiaand is out for two months, which will rule him out of the matches in November against Croatia and Spain. Tuchel worked with Scott in November 2025 and at the pre-World Cup camp in Florida. “Alex came in here now and was on a completely new level,” Tuchel said. “He was super-strong.”Graphic showing minutes played for England in the international breakIt was a positive window for Lewis-Skelly, who Tuchel counted on as a midfielder rather than a left-back for the first time. The 20-year-old started three of the games and came on as a 79th-minute substitute against Croatia. The worry was how he picked up bookings in both matches against Czechia; he is now suspended for the home game against Croatia. “I wasn’t aware of the yellow card,” Tuchel said of Tuesday’s one at Wembley, rather surprisingly. He knows about the need to stay out of red card territory.Kobbie Mainoo is a potential loser from the emergence of Scott and Lewis-Skelly. Tuchel was at pains to sympathise with the Manchester United midfielder over the injury that forced his withdrawal, particularly after he did not play him for a single minute at the World Cup. But with Rice certain to return after an agreed rest this time this out, and James Garner in the frame, Mainoo has work to do. Ditto Jordan Henderson, who was not up to speed fitness‑wise after his broken arm at the World Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTrent Alexander-Arnold made his mark after being brought back into the fold.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesHall has taken his chance at left-back, stepping up after Nico O’Reilly played against Spain and was then forced to withdraw. Hall started in each of the subsequent games – “three top matches from him”, Tuchel said – and if he is plainly in possession of the shirt, he deserves to keep it in November. Which is bad news for O’Reilly and Djed Spence, who has not yet played this season.Did Alexander-Arnold do enough at right-backafter his surprise recall? He could not have done much more with his starting opportunities in both Czechia games. There was the lovely cross for Anthony Gordon’s breakthough goal in Prague and a driving, attack-minded performance at Wembley. Everybody knows what Alexander-Arnold can do; he showed it again and the argument remains that he must be included for his points of difference.Total Midweek Kane: England’s icon delivers a classic on his way to footballing ultimacy | Barney RonayRead moreOn the other hand, what does Tuchel do when Reece James, Tino Livramento and Spence are available? The manager has previously made it plain he considers all three to be ahead of Alexander-Arnold. He said he might have called up Ben White if he were fit and also has Jarell Quansah, even if the Bayer Leverkusen player would rather be considered in central defence. That was where Tuchel started him against Czechia at Wembley – ahead of Trevoh Chalobah and Jarrad Branthwaite.Cole Palmer has found himself under an unforgiving spotlight after his withdrawal, particularly after Tuchel questioned whether he wanted to play forEngland. It looks a long way back for the Chelsea No 10 and the same is true of Phil Foden. Both were overlooked when Tuchel gave a late call-up to Morgan Gibbs-White, and neither looks an easy fit for this team’s aggressive style. “I don’t know [if they are],” Tuchel said. “That is the honest answer. They were not here. This team took another step and it’s always about the guys who are here.”Tuchel has plenty to ponder before the November matches. He will hope to see John Stones recover his fitness and form at Inter. There is a belief that the centre-back’s move to Serie A, where the tempo is slower, can help him find his rhythm. Marcus Rashford will be expected to return; he has credit in the bank with Tuchel, even if Gordon has nailed down the starting spot on the left wing.Can Noni Madueke stage a comeback on the right after being dropped? And what of the strikers in the Saudi Pro League, Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney, who were also dropped? Tuchel now sees Jude Bellingham as the back-up No 9 to Harry Kane. He gave Dominic Calvert-Lewin only brief substitute appearances against Spain and Czechia at Wembley. The train hurtles on.Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelNations LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Eckert’s Spygate ban may be lenient, but no sane manager will try the same trick again | Southampton | The Guardian
description: Verdict has been a long time coming and the Southampton head coach has recaptured hearts and minds at St Mary’s
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Verdict has been a long time coming and the Southampton head coach has recaptured hearts and minds at St Mary’s
Content: A Middlesbrough fan with a pair of binoculars at the height of Spygate – before the first leg of the playoff semi-final against Southampton.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Middlesbrough fan with a pair of binoculars at the height of Spygate – before the first leg of the playoff semi-final against Southampton.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersSouthamptonEckert’s Spygate ban may be lenient, but no sane manager will try the same trick againVerdict has been a long time coming and the Southampton head coach has recaptured hearts and minds at St Mary’sLouise TaylorWed 7 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Hi Tonda, are you a cheat?” That simple, succinct, question cut to the heart of a matter that has vexed the Football Association all summer. It was posed by the Northern Echo’s Dominic Shaw afterSouthampton overcame Middlesbroughin the second leg of May’s Championship playoff semi‑final and proved the cue for Tonda Eckert to walk out of his press conference at St Mary’s.Although Southampton’s manager subsequently admitted to authorising spying on opponents, England’s football authorities struggled to decide what punishment best fitted an act some regard as heinous but which others fail to take seriously. Now, in autumn, we finally have an FA verdict, withEckert given a six-week bansuspended until the end of the 2027-28 season, a £28,000 fine and a reprimand.Southampton manager Tonda Eckert given six-week suspended ban for Spygate scandalRead moreDespite the apparent leniency of the sanction, one thing is clear: Eckert’s summer in purgatory surely dictates no sane England-based coach would contemplate engaging in espionage now.Eckert may wish he could turn back time to early May and rewrite history. On the eve of the playoff semi-final first leg on Teesside, William Salt, then an intern Southampton first-team analyst, was caught lurking awkwardly beside a tree while filming a Middlesbrough training session on his iPhone. Spygate was born and an independent disciplinary commission convened by the Football League (EFL)expelled Southamptonfrom the playoff final against Hull after their win against Boro across two legs. The governing body also decreed the Saints would begin the current Championship season on minus four points.View image in fullscreenTonda Eckert on the touchline at Middlesbrough’s Riverside Stadium during the first leg of Southampton’s playoff semi-final.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersBy then Southampton had also admitted to spying on Oxford and Ipswich training. There is a certain irony that Eckert’s team won none of the three games – albeit Middlesbrough were ultimately beaten on aggregate – involving covert surveillance. Yet the EFL independent disciplinary commission panel made plain its discomfort regarding the “particularly deplorable” pressure placed on a young worker hired on a temporary contract. Salt has since been given a staff job as an analyst in Southampton’s academy and is reportedly progressing well.With the EFL empowered to sanction clubs but not individuals in such cases, it was down to the FA to punish Eckert. The 33-year-old German issued a public apology in June but wasnot charged with misconduct by the FA until late July. A further hiatus ensued before a hearing at Wembley on 24 September.This extraordinary delay afforded Eckert ample time to regret dispatching Salt to Middlesbrough’s training ground adjacent to the luxury Rockliffe Hall Hotel and golf course just south of Darlington. Salt’s primary mission was to discover whether Hayden Hackney, Middlesbrough’s star midfielder and theChampionshipplayer of the season, was fit after injury. Unfortunately, clandestine manoeuvres were evidently not his strong suit. Salt soon found himself being chased into hotel toilets, and realised that using his bank card to buy a coffee at Rockliffe had not been the smartest move. That payment facilitated a search for his name on Southampton’s website. It was swiftly identified, enabling Steve Gibson, Middlesbrough’s owner, to make a formal complaint to the EFL regarding a breach of its anti-spying regulations.It is understood that, until this point, Southampton’s manager remained unaware of the Bev Priestman precedent. The former head coach of Canada Women wasbanned from all football activity for a yearby Fifa after being found guilty of initiating spying. During the 2024 Paris Olympics her staff secretly filmed a New Zealand training session using a drone and the former England women’s assistant manager paid a high price.It is unclear whether Eckert has since been in touch with the 40-year-old, now in charge of Wellington Phoenix. Priestman met such extreme hostility in previously welcoming Canada that she relocated her family to New Zealand. During ‘Spygate’, Eckert’s wife was heavily pregnant and based in Berlin, preparing for the birth of their first child. Back in Hampshire, her husband received death threats via LinkedIn.Southamptonsupplied the manager with protection while police advised him that driving his own car was unsafe and that he should restrict his movements.Plenty of people were extremely angry, with St Mary’s regulars polarised between those who believed the manager had shamed their club and should be sacked, and others who reflected that what is euphemistically called “training observation” of opponents is commonplace and largely unpunished across tracts of Europe. The second camp remembered that, seven years ago,Leeds were fined £200,000after the club’s then manager, Marcelo Bielsa, sent an analyst to monitor a Derby training session. Frank Lampard, then in charge of Derby, complained after spotting him perched up a tree.After that incident the EFL tightened its regulations regarding espionage appreciably. Nonetheless, Eckert’s advocates claim that, given he started last season as Southampton’s under-21s coach and became the manager afterWill Still’s sacking in November, he had missed the EFL’s annual managerial summer rules refresher course.View image in fullscreen‘I would lie if I said this summer’s been easy,’ Eckert said last month.Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PAEckert, who began his career as a Germany national team analyst before moving into coaching at Cologne, RB Salzburg, RB Leipzig, Bayern Munich, Barnsley and Genoa, was only half-joking when he recently told reporters that the EFL handbook was his staple bedside summer reading. He also made contact with Gareth Southgate and visited the former England and Middlesbrough, manager, with the pair discussing English football culture and its zero tolerance for spycraft at length.“I would lie if I said this summer’s been easy,” said Eckert last month. “I’ve asked the FA for forgiveness.” He has had unwavering support from Southampton’s board who made it clear they had no desire to sack him in the face of considerable dressing room hostility on the part offrom players who felt betrayed by ‘Spygate’.With first-team hearts and minds since seemingly recaptured by the coach who led them so close to promotion last season, Southampton have won four and drawn two of their opening eight Championship games. Next up on Sunday is the visit of Portsmouth. South-coast derbies are invariably tense but Eckert’s reprieve may ensure he cuts an unusually relaxed figure in the technical area.Explore more on these topicsSouthamptonFootball LeagueFootball politicsThe FAChampionshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mystery | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: Jorge Messi wanted his country to fall in love with his son. That ambition was fulfilled during a brilliant international career that ended this week
Author: Marcela Mora y Araujo
Headline: Jorge Messi wanted his country to fall in love with his son. That ambition was fulfilled during a brilliant international career that ended this week
Content: Lionel Messi and his Argentina teammates reflect on an emotional night against Benin.Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/ReutersView image in fullscreenLionel Messi and his Argentina teammates reflect on an emotional night against Benin.Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/ReutersLionel MessiLionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mysteryJorge Messi wanted his country to fall in love with his son. That ambition was fulfilled during a brilliant international career that ended this weekMarcela Mora y AraujoWed 7 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“What Argentina is doing in this World Cup is of a sacred order,” Brazilian writer Milly Lacombe posted at the height of the tide of anti-Argentinian sentiment during this year’s tournament. She was exploring the contradiction she felt around her support of Lionel Messi: “a player who is a God and a man who shakes Trump’s hand”.Lacombe highlighted the importance of acknowledging the complexities around Messi and the Argentinian team. How is it possible that Messi was not speaking out against the racist incidentswe all saw around the Argentina team, she asked. “That’s why it hurts so much to see someone with Messi’s power choosing to make himself small,” she wrote.Much was made of Messi’s silence at the time. Then again, much has been made of his visible discomfort with words throughout his epic career. Journalist John Carlin once said that having interviewed Messi twice, he would decline a third opportunity, such was the challenge of getting the little giant to say anything of consequence. In 2010, Juan Sebastián Verón said he had never seen Messi as nervous as when he had to address his teammates for the first time asArgentinacaptain. In terms of public speaking, perhaps Messi’s most famous outburst was at the 2022 World Cup when he told a Dutch player to “go away”.View image in fullscreenA giant number 10 shirt was displayed on the pitch before Messi’s farewell apperance.Photograph: Rodrigo Abd/APDespite this reticence, Messi has always meant something, even when he doesn’t speak. Messi and Argentina were treated as darlings when they won the World Cup in 2022. By the time the 2026 final ended in defeat to Spain, they had become villains.“That’s why it’s important to understand that when Messi, in the middle of a game that was lost, looks at the sky, and then after that he turns the game around and smashed it, there is something very mysterious there. Right? That we can’t explain. That we just feel,” Lacombe said after Argentina’s semi-final victory over England this summer. “I started supporting England but by the end of the match I was weeping, surrendered to the commitment, the passion, the love that I saw the Argentina team pour on to the pitch. It’s only in that moment of intense passion that we reach the sacred.”Not everyone surrendered to the sacred in the same way. The final against Spain lacked sublime power and opened the floodgates of vitriol from all corners of the globe. Argentinian fans were offended, hurt, defensive and aware they may have just seen Messi’s last appearance in an Argentina shirt. When he confirmed he would end his international career – his final appearance for Argentinacame against Benin on Tuesday– a wave of grief and gratitude swept the nation.View image in fullscreenAn 18 yr old Lionel Messi grapples with Hungary’s Vilmos Vanczák and is sent off after 44 seconds on his Argentina debut.Photograph: Michael Mayhew/Getty Images/AllstarMessi grew up in Barcelona’s youth system, and he was eligible to play for both Spain and Argentina. His debut for Argentina – in a youth match against Paraguay – set up a rush to ensure he pledged his allegiance to the country of his birth, before Spain could tempt him. He was already one of the Barcelona’s academy most promising stars, but he was little known in Argentina. His father, Jorge, wanted nothing more than for his son to represent Argentina, and sent videos to then-manager Marcelo Bielsa hoping to expedite the process. For years, Jorge endured an uphill struggle to consolidate the ties between Lionel and Argentina. Messi’s prowess, seemingly unstoppable in a well-oiled Barcelona system, did not come through at national level. For a long time, Jorge would ask his compatriots the same question. How can we get Argentina to love my son?Now, as we start to write Messi’s football obituary, some of the most grievous incidents against him are resurfacing. There was the time when a panel of pundits stood in a minute’s silence in protest against Messi’s performances for his country. He was criticised for not singing the national anthem. We learned that before Argentina matches he suffered bouts of vomiting and diarrhoea. Diego Maradona mocked him, saying he was no leader (although he would later make Messi Argentina’s captain). And when the campaign to win over the nation stepped up and he gave interviews, his discourse was shockingly basic and he gave little away.But Messi never gave up. He missed penalties, wept, and stood to take them again. “What characterized Messi in the national team is that he lost. He lost a lot. He’s constituted in defeat” Argentinian journalist Alejandro Wall says.View image in fullscreenAdoring fans cheer for Messi before the match against Benin.Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/ReutersBut the vitriol more often came from the press than the people. When hequit the national team in 2016, a spontaneous show of love and desire swept the nation, and he reversed his decision. From then on, the Argentinian Football Association’s main priority mirrored that of Jorge Messi: finding a coach who could adapt the entire system to Lionel. It wasn’t easy.Perhaps it was only after Maradona’s death in 2020 that the new Messi started to emerge. He walked taller, more confident and comfortable in his role as leader. In 2021, Argentina won the Copa América, and snippets of Messi’s pep talks to his teammates filtered out. He made simple statements in his unmistakable Rosario accent, aspiring the ‘s’ and not pronouncing most final consonants. His – and Argentina’s – achievements since then speak for themselves.Tuesday’s farewell at the Monumental Stadium – much like that first youth game against Paraguay – had a rushed, improvised air. The Argentinian FA struggled to secure opponents, not wanting to share box office with another footballing power. Benin were mocked by some as unworthy, and even Lionel Scaloni made reference to a desire to face bigger opponents than Bolivia and Burkina Faso, the other teams Argentina played this window. Burkina Faso ended up sending an Under-23 side who arrived a few hours before the match, and the stadium was not filled to capacity. Ticket prices were extortionate, and diehard fans refused to fall for what they called “a scam”.View image in fullscreenAn electric atmosphere at Estadio Monumental.Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/ReutersBut against Benin they turned up in numbers. Earlier, Messi had picked up an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires, in a small and shabby ceremony in a back office of the Argentinian FA. Delicately produced homages to No 10 were aired. Social media posts full of hyperbolic emotion appeared. “Like Scheherazade, he mocked destiny match by match, to gift the Argentina people another day of his magic. The thousand and one nights of Lionel Messi with the light blue and white come to their end,” read one post. “Whoah, hold it! It’s 9am. I can’t start weeping yet” came a swift reply.To paraphrase Wayne Rooney, the entertainment around the match was crap. There was a drawn out homage by Soledad Pastorutti, who sang the same number she had once performed with Maradona. A veteran of the Falklands/Malvinas War sang the national anthem, and thenclad himself in the same flagthat fell on the pitch in Atlanta. The terraces chanted against AFA president Chiqui Tapia in a beautiful chorus, which went some way to atoning for the drone show at the end, with adverts for an insurance company glittering in the sky.But football is about redemption, and the night was redeemed. Benin actually put up a fight, bookended by the team’s captain gifting Messi a statue of a Dahomey Agojie, the group of women who fought against French occupation. Messi set up three of his team’s three goals and took a penalty. He didn’t miss.View image in fullscreenLionel Messi salutes his adoring fans after his final match for Argentina.Photograph: Roberto Tuero/ZUMA/ShutterstockThe cameras zoomed in on weeping faces but the sounds from the concrete terraces were decisively celebratory, relentless, trembling. It was football through and through. And Messi loved it. You could tell. He picked up the microphone and launched into a speech so articulate and confident that it merits a dissertation studying its every word. He addressed conspiracy theories surrounding the World Cup final: “Nothing odd happened. The match against England wore us out at an emotional level”. He warned of hard times to come but said team unity is the way through.“We had the dream of fulfilling our dream,” he said, adding: “I don’t know, I’m talking more than ever. I don’t want to leave here. I love you”. And Argentina loves him back.As Lacombe said, when Messi looks at the sky, then turns a situation around and smashes it, there is mystery. There is something sacred.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiArgentina (Football)Argentina (World news)US sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Saracens’ Brendan Venter takes aim at ‘autocratic’ Prem over media duties | Saracens | The Guardian
description: Technical director held court at club’s training base, comparing rugby to winemaking and claiming interviews ‘steal my joy’
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Technical director held court at club’s training base, comparing rugby to winemaking and claiming interviews ‘steal my joy’
Content: Brendan Venter (right) speaks to the media alongside the Saracens head coach Joe Shaw. ‘I have the desire as a human being not to want to talk.’Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrendan Venter (right) speaks to the media alongside the Saracens head coach Joe Shaw. ‘I have the desire as a human being not to want to talk.’Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesSaracensSaracens’ Brendan Venter takes aim at ‘autocratic’ Prem over media dutiesTechnical director held court at club’s training base, comparing rugby to winemaking and claiming interviews ‘steal my joy’Gerard MeagherWed 7 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrendan Venter began his long-awaited public appearance with head bowed, uttering one‑word answers and with a general demeanour suggesting he would rather be anywhere else. By the end he had comparedPrem Rugbyto an “autocracy”, mentioned Ukraine and Gaza, and detailed an inspirational talk he recently gave at a school.
