Of course there was wine to talk, too.An audience with Saracens’ technical director and head of culture is rarely boring and the latest was worth the wait.To recap, it was announced in February that Venter would replace Mark McCall as director of rugby, returning to the position he left 15 years ago. He has been conspicuous by his absence at press engagements this season, however, and was fined by Prem Rugby.His job title was changed to head of rugby culture and wine consultant, which felt like a two‑fingered salute to the powers-that-be, and then changed again. The missed media appearances continued until he held court on Wednesday on a rainy afternoon at Saracens’ training base in St Albans.After some monosyllabic responses Venter finally opened up. “I have the desire as a human being not to want to talk, because it’s not supposed to be about me, it’s about a team, and I expressed that desire before I came.“And I’m not the director of rugby of this club. This club does not have a director of rugby. This club has an unbelievably competent head coach in Joe [Shaw]. And I ask really kindly, and eventually I bend over backwards to explain my situation and I’m expected again to come and do an interview.“Joe’s input is way more valuable than my input. And if we get obsessed and we get into an argument and we fine a club, that for me does not make sense. It sounds like something we do in an autocratic land, in a country, not in a democracy where people have got the right to say: ‘This is not what I want to do.’”Venter has history here, and found himself in disciplinary hot water for speaking his mind when previously in charge. Hence biscuit-gate and a bizarre interview when he offered the immortal line: “three cheers for Sireli Bobo”. That he has little time for post-match platitudes, means he has been determined to keep a low profile on his return to north London.“It stole my joy the previous time,” he added. “I wanted to have a low profile. That was my desire. I want to coach or help coach the rugby team. I do not want to be doing interviews. And it’s not because of you or anybody else.View image in fullscreenBrendan Venter claims he wants to have a low profile at Saracens.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty Images“It’s not because I’m mean or I think I’m better than other people. I think the input people can get is brilliant from the people that work with me. To be put over as an arrogant person that thinks he’s better than interviews, it’s not at all that. My motivation is completely different. It’s how do I just get on with my job and help coaching this rugby team. That is my desire.“I am going to be authentic. And then I am going to have to go to Dublin and sit in some hearing and get a €10,000 fine. So I just want to prevent that. At my age, we actually look at life and go – I call them joy givers and joy stealers. There are things that give me joy and I do more of them. There are things that steal my joy and I cut them out of my life. And that was one of the things that took my joy.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt all raises the question: why did Venter choose to come back? He had remained at the club in a consultancy role, while working as a GP in South Africa, but was persuaded to take the reins after McCall signalled it was time for him to step back.“I love coaching rugby, I love coaching, I love working with people,” he says. “I love working with the players. It is a privilege which we get as human beings to be in a position where we can influence things for the good and the bad. People in life really get that privilege. When I work as a doctor, I have that same privilege. I have people coming to ask me for an opinion and I can treat them in a good way.“Rugby is an amazing game because it is so complex and you don’t get to beat rugby. Rugby is always a step ahead of you. There are always more clever people than you. Rugby is very much like winemaking. When you get arrogant or you get too confident, you will not make a great wine. It is exactly the same as rugby.“We are privileged enough to be doing that on a daily basis. You know what? Nobody has died. That is an unbelievable privilege. That privilege normally happens in way more high-stakes environments like Ukraine or the Gaza Strip where people are actually dying when there are challenges. Yes, we have challenges and our body perceives it the same. It is a challenge and our ability to deal with it is a privilege. This is why I came back.”Explore more on these topicsSaracensPrem RugbyRugby unionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Verstappen’s victory in Sepang should serve as a warning to Red Bull’s rivals | Max Verstappen | The Guardian
description: Improvements to the car are paying off as the team look to lay the groundwork for renewed success next season
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Improvements to the car are paying off as the team look to lay the groundwork for renewed success next season
Content: Max Verstappen and the Red Bull team principal, Laurent Mekies, are soaked with energy drink after victory at the Bahrian Grand Prix in Malaysia.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersView image in fullscreenMax Verstappen and the Red Bull team principal, Laurent Mekies, are soaked with energy drink after victory at the Bahrian Grand Prix in Malaysia.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersMax VerstappenAnalysisVerstappen’s victory in Sepang should serve as a warning to Red Bull’s rivalsGiles RichardsImprovements to the car are paying off as the team look to lay the groundwork for renewed success next seasonWed 7 Oct 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 14.43 EDTShareThe importance for Max Verstappen ofemerging triumphant from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysiawas writ large in the Dutchman’s pleasure at finally being able to drive a competitive car. In a ride with which he was comfortable and able to take to a dominant victory for Red Bull, Verstappen was in his element. With it came a sense of what might have been had he not been long out of the championship fight, but also what might be to come next year.The transformation was so marked because for so long this season the car has been a handful – the reason Verstappen’s title hopes faded long ago. That the team have come back to deliver a win in such emphatic fashion was no little achievement.F1 looks amateurish and incompetent after farcical scenes in Sepang | Giles RichardsRead moreIn the opening period of the season, the RB22 was nowhere, deficient in almost every department. It lacked pace, balance, even consistency, and for all his skill Verstappen seemed powerless. He described it as feeling like a passenger in the car at times.The four-time world champion wrestled it to a couple of podiums in the first half of the season but it was a sisyphean task. “At the start of the season, I really had weekends where I would turn the steering wheel and strange things would happen,” he said. Which, a rather understated critique, belies the fact that the last place a driver wants to be is in a car where he is unsure which way it is going to jump.Red Bull,under Laurent Mekies, stuck at it and brought major upgrades to Miami and Austria. Yet the scale of what needed doing across so many facets of the car remained difficult to overcome. Only a month ago Verstappen could only qualify sixth at Monza, admittedly a power track where the relative paucity of their electrical energy deployment was a hindrance. It nonetheless suggested a win was as far away as ever.View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen pulls ahead of Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli in Sepang.Photograph: Vincent Thian/APYet there were indications that each incremental development was bringing a greater understanding of the car and how to coax the best out of it. In Madrid, Verstappen qualified just over a tenth of a second off pole and had real pace in the race, which might have delivered more on a track where overtaking was possible. At the next round in Baku, Red Bull brought their final upgrade, including a development to the floor. In qualifying Verstappen was unlucky with yellow flags to start from eighth but in the race the car was rapid. He flew through the field,chasing the winner, Mercedes’ George Russell, to the flag right on his gearbox.The car’s speed on the straights was noted by rivals, not least Mercedes, as Verstappen closed on Russell. Red Bull’s other driver, Isack Hadjar, who had spent three races out with a wrist injury, felt as if he had been given a new ride. “I definitely feel like I jumped in a car that’s way better than when I left it in Budapest,” he said.What followed in Sepang was validation that Red Bull really had got it right. Verstappen took pole and won with a drive that exemplified his car’s improvements. The RB22 was quicker in a straight line than the Mercedes and fast in the medium and high-speed corners, its achilles heel previously.On a track punishing to the tyres, the car was well-balanced, less damaging to the rubber, allowing better energy deployment. Having addressed problems which conflated with one another, the car coalesced into a more coherent whole. Verstappen described the process as having “pushed weaknesses out of the car”. It has taken them 16 meetings but on this form Red Bull are finally up with McLaren, Ferrari and Mercedes.Their progress stands as testament to a team working collectively to tremendous effect. It is an achievement that must be acknowledged alongside building their own engine for the first time and delivering a win; a feat that is recognised across the paddock as perhaps beyond expectations and which was far from guaranteed to be successful as Honda, with more experience, have demonstrated all too clearly this season.View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen driving ahead of Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and his Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar.Photograph: Clive Mason/Getty ImagesThere may have been an element of the win in Sepang being track-specific. The fact the Mercedes upgrades deployed there did not deliver at all was a factor, and they must contend with Russell starting the Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid following an engine change after a late retirement in Malaysia. But the Red Bull is a different car now and how it performs on the streets of Singapore this weekend will be telling.Verstappen will want more wins, but it is instructive how he and the team are viewing these final meetings. They want to end strongly and feed every possible piece of information into next year’s car. Hadjar said: “We have to try all the things, make all the mistakes now and do all the learning to arrive in 2027 ready to roll and start on high.” It is an ambition which will not be lost on their rivals, who know only too well how formidable Red Bull can be if they are quick out of the blocks.Explore more on these topicsMax VerstappenRed BullFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘I wanted to depart in the best way possible’: Kieran McKenna on Ipswich exit and future plans | Ipswich Town | The Guardian
description: In an exclusive interview, former Ipswich manager talks of his lasting affection for the club, savouring time out with family and friends and ideas for his next move
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: In an exclusive interview, former Ipswich manager talks of his lasting affection for the club, savouring time out with family and friends and ideas for his next move
Content: Kieran McKenna: ‘I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community.’Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKieran McKenna: ‘I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community.’Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesIpswich TownInterview‘I wanted to depart in the best way possible’: Kieran McKenna on Ipswich exit and future plansNick AmesIn an exclusive interview, former Ipswich manager talks of his lasting affection for the club, savouring time out with family and friends and ideas for his next moveWed 7 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was on the Portman Road pitch, bathed in bright early May light while immersed in the relief and joy of a third promotion in five years, that Kieran McKenna realised the moment was right. The thought had flickered earlier in the season that this might be his final campaign at Ipswich, only to be pushed into the subconscious by the Championship’s remorseless grind. “But standing out there, I felt this was probably time,” he says of those moments after QPR had been swept aside and areturn to the Premier Leagueassured. “Another big victory, a full stadium, in front of my family and the fans. It was an amazing way to go out on a high.”Five months later McKenna has no regrets about electing to cut things short while the going was so good. The golf bag lying outside his garage speaks of a man enjoying the break and, more pertinently, of something bigger. His son has recently become interested in the sport and sharing those moments with loved ones, whether out on the greens or spending part of the summer travelling along the East Anglian coastline in a camper van, were among the biggest reasons to pause a soaring career. At 40, McKenna had spent two decades immersed in coaching; it was time to appreciate life’s essentials while continuing professional development at his own speed.Next Generation 2026: 20 of the best talents at Premier League clubsRead moreHe had, as usual, been linked with moves away but the idea of a voluntary career break was hard for many to fathom when the decision wasfinalised in June. “For people on the outside it’s maybe a bit more difficult,” he says. “But those who know my path and my values, the ones closest to me who know me really well, I think they understood why I wanted to step out and what the benefits were of having a period like this.”Not everyone in football saw it that way: the phone has rung with proposals for his next move but McKenna says those overtures arrived “too soon, especially given the way I left Ipswich”. Leaving through the front door, a luxury rarely afforded, made him proud and there is no desperation to leap back into the fray. “I’m certainly in no rush,” he says. “I’m enjoying the time I’m having and hopefully an opportunity will come along that’s right. I have an idea what that would feel like but football doesn’t always follow your plan.”Since early September he has dipped his toe back in. That has involved tuning back into the process of watching and assessing games, while travelling to spend time with Bayern Munich, the Wigan Warriors rugby team and Colorado Rapids, who are managed by his friend Matt Wells. He has been working on foreign languages, topping up an already competent level of Spanish. This week he is visiting clubs in Spain and, next Wednesday, he will begin work as a technical observer for Uefa when Shakhtar Donetsk play AEK Athens at Stamford Bridge. “I wanted to give myself the best possibility to learn before taking on the next challenge,” he says.View image in fullscreenMcKenna basks in Ipswich’s promotion in May. ‘All we get is people coming up telling the story of how much the last few years have meant for them,’ he says.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersMore than once McKenna repeats an assertion he made after promotion in May: that 2025-26 was the hardest of his four-and-a-half seasons at Ipswich, during which he masterminded a dizzying rise from League One to the top flight that marked him among football’s hottest managerial properties. The pressure was heightened last season: Ipswich had gone down and were expected to bounce back, even though the remarkably close-knit core who had propelled them through the divisions were drifting away. In effect, he took two different teams to the top.“You can see how it could really have gone in two distinct directions,” he says, making a comparison with the fall Luton experienced after a brief reacquaintance with the elite. “We had the feeling internally that if we didn’t work really hard to pull everyone together then it could have gone in a negative way.”McKenna pulled them over the line and reached the end of his own journey. Along the way he had come close to departing more than once but jumping ship earlier would have jarred. “I had a lot of different opportunities to leave, could have left in many different circumstances really,” he says. “But I was always aware I wanted to depart in the best way possible, with the club on a high, back in the Premier League and with a great chance to build for what will hopefully be a really successful period.”The hardest aspect of his final day, he explains, was looking down a camera and addressing the supporters with a five-minute speech in which he did not attempt to suppress his emotion. He reels off a list of coaching staff and other colleagues with whom the goodbyes were touching, meaningful, joyful. Many of the friendships, particularly with members of the “really, really special team” that he led to those successive promotions, will be lifelong. The night before this interview, he spent most of a journey back from London speaking to one of them.View image in fullscreenKieran McKenna acclimatising to the Premier League in 2024.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersHe laughs off the idea he would have relished getting his hands on the £200m summer transfer spend – not to mention a new training ground whose design he influenced – that appears to have given his successor, Gary O’Neil, a better shot at survival. If anything, he suggests, it shows the club have begun their own new chapter. McKenna also emphasises the thought of potential reputational damage from a second relegation did not factor into his decision to quit. “It wasn’t about the thought of a worst-case scenario or what could go wrong,” he says.It was about prioritising life where we meet, in the family’s home a brisk half-hour walk from Portman Road. He and his wife chose to stay in Ipswich, where their two children attend school, having become more than mere itinerants passing through. It so happens Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson kept homes nearby after moving upwards. McKenna has hero status here too, in these unassuming yet football-crazed surroundings. Although he keeps a low profile and locations for socialising are chosen judiciously, the overwhelming affection of a town and county often rear up.“Everyone is respectful; all we get is people coming up telling the story of how much the last few years have meant for them, their family and their friends, and wishing me the best,” he says. “Moving down here together, going all in, making ourselves part of this community, it’s been another of the really positive things. It’s a little bit different living in the area where you were managing but it’s the right thing for us at this time.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHas muscle memory ever taken him on an early-morning drive to the training ground? “You’d think it might, but it’s just a different life. You’re not setting the alarm for 5.30am and driving there in the dark. You’re getting up with the kids and having breakfast with them, and you’re around when they go to bed. Although the geography is the same, the life is different.”He does not think such a heady half-decade, in which a talent honed at Tottenham and Manchester United blossomed gloriously, has changed a grounded personality honed in rural County Fermanagh. “I probably feel about 20 years older,” he says. “But my friends at home were telling me in the summer that I haven’t changed since I was 10. I couldn’t have arrived at Ipswich with a better background as a coach but, on the other hand, if you’d given me a list of the things I’d have to deal with in the next five years I really wouldn’t have believed it. After going through so many things you’re wiser for the experience.”Nonetheless the fact remains: taking a breather when the world is your oyster feels vanishingly rare in football management. Maybe everyone should do it. “But what’s right for me, after two decades coaching, might be different for a manager who only stopped playing three years ago,” he says. “It’s been a massive body of work. You leave United, pick your bags up, get in the car and five-and-a-half hours later you’re in Ipswich. At 35 you’re leaving your family behind, checking into a hotel 10 days before Christmas; you absolutely throw yourself into the job for the next four and a half years and the family do the same. I want to enjoy the time we have now, take this period to reflect and be in the best position I can for the next role.”View image in fullscreenMcKenna says his two decades in coaching have taken a toll.Photograph: Nick Potts/PASo what would that next iteration of McKenna’s career look like, in a perfect world? He has been linked with any potential vacancies at Celtic and his old employers Spurs; his name will be circling once the season’s sackings start, although Ipswich will be owed a sizeable fee for any role he takes this year.“I’m always going to want to be somewhere where I can improve players, play attacking football and win games,” he says. “But beyond that I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community, trying to build something memorable. It was a really special opportunity at Ipswich and you want to do that again in your career. But you have to be ready to come in somewhere and get some short-term success as well.”The chance will surely arise soon; it does not take a giant leap to imagine McKenna in a Champions League dugout in the next few years if the stars align. Until then the self-growth will continue and there will always be dispatches from Portman Road, where his brother and children are regulars. McKenna would rather look forward and will not beat that path for now. “I think that’ll be some way down the line,” he says. “They’re cracking on with the season. There’s nothing that can lessen my pride and love for everything we’ve been through. Hopefully I’ll be back in the stadium as an old hand, and some of the people will remember the times we had.”They are unlikely to forget; McKenna’s aim is that, by then, at least one other set of supporters will have felt the magic too.Explore more on these topicsIpswich TowninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal and Chelsea set to miss a month of next WSL season due to Club World Cup | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: The Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to by the Club World Cup
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to by the Club World Cup
Content: Arsenal’s victory in the 2025 Champions League final has guaranteed them a place in the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028.Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/ReutersView image in fullscreenArsenal’s victory in the 2025 Champions League final has guaranteed them a place in the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028.Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/ReutersWomen's Super LeagueArsenal and Chelsea set to miss a month of next WSL season due to Club World CupBack end of 2027-28 season likely to be ‘challenging’Fixture contestion a growing area of concernExclusive byMatt HughesWed 7 Oct 2026 05.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to the Club World Cup, with Arsenal and Chelsea likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month.The Guardian revealed last week that the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup isset to be awarded to the US, with transatlantic travel to cause additional problems for European sides, while the proposed dates of 5-30 January will clash directly with the WSL.Too nice: do Arsenal lack the grit and tenacity to end WSL title drought?Read moreFifa has yet to confirm the qualification criteria for the Club World Cup but the Guardian has learned Arsenal are guaranteed to be involved as 2025 Champions League winners and Chelsea are likely to join them, although they would lose their place if Manchester City win this season’s Champions League. Based on this season’s schedule, an extended run in the Club World Cup would mean the two English clubs missing up to four WSL match weeks plus the fourth round of the FA Cup, playing havoc with the fixture list and causing major congestion at the end of the season.Uefa will be granted places for six clubs: five to qualify automatically and one to take part in a six-team qualifier before the tournament, with the three highest-ranked clubs joining 13 automatic qualifiers to form a 16-team competition. While the process has still to be ratified by the Fifa council, it is understood Uefa’s spots will be given to the Champions League winners between 2024 and 2027 – currently Barcelona as the two-time champions and Arsenal, with this season’s title still up for grabs – topped up by the highest-ranked clubs in Uefa’s Champions League coefficient table.Chelsea are third in that table for the current four-year cycle, behind Barcelona and Lyon with a 17-point lead over fourth-placed Bayern Munich, and cannot be caught. Based on the current rankings, Bayern and Wolfsburg are next in line to qualify, although the latter have not qualified for this season’s Champions League and will not accumulate additional points, so are likely to be overhauled by Real Madrid or Paris Saint-Germain. Fifa plans to cap the number of participants from each country at two, so City winning the Champions League would cost Chelsea their place.The WSL declined to comment as it has yet to be told of Fifa’s plans for the tournament, but sources conceded its impact is likely to prove challenging. The WSL has a winter break, which is scheduled for 21 December to 10 January this season, and although that could be pushed back slightly, aligning it with the Club World Cup is not viewed as practical due to the congested calendar.As well as creating a lopsided ­season, moving the winter break would result in a backlog of WSL fixtures during the period when the Champions League knockout stage begins at the beginning of February. The issue of fixture congestion is a growing area of concern in the women’s game and 2028 will be particularly problematic due to the Olympic football tournament taking place in Los Angeles in August, just before the start of the European domestic season.The International Olympic Committee has expanded women’s football to 16 nations at the 2028 Games, and unlike the men’s version which is restricted to players under 23 with three overage exceptions, senior internationals are permitted to take part.Fifa’s imposition of the Club World Cup in the middle of the European season has exacerbated the problem, and last month European Leagues, a lobby group, extended its legal complaint to the European Commission about the world governing body’s alleged “abuse of power and dominant position” to include the women’s game.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballShareReuse this content

title: Pidcock ‘mad’ after two teammates collide with police motorcyclist in Italy | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Tom Pidcock revealed that he considered quitting the Tre Valli Varesine after two teammates crashed upon being hit by a police motorcyclist
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Tom Pidcock revealed that he considered quitting the Tre Valli Varesine after two teammates crashed upon being hit by a police motorcyclist
Content: Pinarello-Q36.5 rider Tom Pidcock says: ‘I was mad. I had guys riding in front of me – for me – and two of them were on the floor.’Photograph: Dario Belingheri/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPinarello-Q36.5 rider Tom Pidcock says: ‘I was mad. I had guys riding in front of me – for me – and two of them were on the floor.’Photograph: Dario Belingheri/Getty ImagesCyclingPidcock ‘mad’ after two teammates collide with police motorcyclist in ItalyPinarello-Q36.5’s Camprubí and Gloag floored in crash‘Things like this shouldn’t happen,’ says British riderJeremy WhittleWed 7 Oct 2026 05.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 14.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Pidcock has admitted he almost quit the Tre Valli Varesine in a rage after a police motorcyclist drove into the peloton and struck two of his Pinarello Q36.5 teammates.Speaking after the race in northern Italy, in which he finished second, Pidcock said: “A police motorbike was going the wrong way down the course and crashed into two of our guys.‘We are really different’: Matthew Brennan on ‘next Cavendish’ hype and his five-star Vuelta debutRead moreI wanted to stop racing myself. I was mad. The guys all riding in front of me – for me – and two of them on the floor.”The British rider’s teammate Thomas Gloag was forced to abandon the race while Marcel Camprubí, of Spain, was able to continue, but finished last.“Luckily Marcel was OK, he could continue,” Pidcock said. “Tom was also OK, in the end, but he stopped the race, and he has some stitches in the knee.”Camprubí posted images of his smashed bike on social media, with the caption: “Sad that you have to risk your life to race, one month after a tragic accident.”View image in fullscreenThomas Gloag receives medical attention after being involved in a crash with a police rider.Photograph: Dario Belingheri/Getty ImagesThe latest lapse in race security came just weeks after the Welsh riderFin Tarling was killed by a rogue vandriving against the direction of the peloton during the Volta a Portugal in August. The incident remains under police investigation.Pidcock dedicated his recent win in the World Cross Country Mountain Bike Championship to Tarling and his family.There have been a series of near-misses with non-race vehicles this season, although on Tuesday the police rider was part of the race convoy. All those driving “in-race” have to follow strict rules on safety and on positioning on the road. “Things like this shouldn’t happen,” Pidcock said.According to team sources, the police motorcyclist was riding ahead of the riders and entered a roundabout, then circled back into the path of the advancing peloton. Gloag, who was treated on site in an ambulance, was described as “pretty shocked”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRecent near-misses at races include one at the Sauerlandrundfahrt in Germany, when vehicles twice entered closed roads and almost hit riders. During the Tour of Britain Women, theAustralian rider Maeve Plouffe found herself racing amid trafficand was nearly hit by a car.Plouffe said: “While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down [behind the peloton] there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout.”In the aftermath of Tarling’s death, cycling’s governing body, the UCI, was heavily criticised for its response to safety concerns. Richard Plugge, manager of Jonas Vingegaard’s Visma-Lease a bike team, said: “Neither UCI president David Lappartient, nor anyone else, stands up and says: ‘Wait a minute, we really need to think about how we are going to prevent this from happening in the future.’”Last month, Plugge’s British rider Matthew Brennan, who won five stages in the Vuelta a España, criticised race organisers and said “nothing has changed” in the aftermath of Tarling’s death. “I really think that is disgraceful,” Brennan told the BBC.“Instead of someone somewhere in these organisations saying: ‘OK, this should never ever happen again’, it feels the world has moved on, nothing has changed and there’s events where cars have been on the course still.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: World must change way it produces food to avoid biodiversity collapse, says WWF | WWF | The Guardian
description: Recovery of tigers, tuna and green sea turtles show nature loss can be reversed when action taken, charity says
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Recovery of tigers, tuna and green sea turtles show nature loss can be reversed when action taken, charity says
Content: After conservation interventions, numbers of wild tigers have increased by more than 70% since 2010.Photograph: wesdotphotography/AlamyView image in fullscreenAfter conservation interventions, numbers of wild tigers have increased by more than 70% since 2010.Photograph: wesdotphotography/AlamyWWFWorld must change way it produces food to avoid biodiversity collapse, says WWFRecovery of tigers, tuna and green sea turtles show nature loss can be reversed when action taken, charity saysMatthew PearceWed 7 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConservation comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and green​ sea turtles prove that global nature loss can be reversed, ​scientists have said. ​But a report warns food production must be the next ​“positive tipping point​” if the world is to avert biodiversity collapse.The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) analysed nearly 36,000 animal populations and more than 5,000 species, producing the largest ever database of vertebrate wildlife. Scientists found populations had declined by an average of 73% since 1970, showing that “nature continues to be degraded at an alarming scale”, with “no sign of losses slowing”.Nature loss is no longer just an environmental challenge but a direct threat to the global economy, the report says, noting that about half of global GDP – roughly $58tn (£44tn) in 2023 – depends on nature and its ecosystem services. The authors write that species collapse now poses an “existential threat to economic stability, geopolitical security and human wellbeing”.Animal populations were found to be falling most sharply in tropical, biodiversity-rich regions, while trends in northern temperate parts of the world appeared much gentler.In Latin America and the Caribbean, land and freshwater wildlife populations fell by an average of 95% between 1970 and 2022, while the equivalent declines were 80% in Africa and 23% in Europe and Central Asia.Graph of living planet index, globally and in different regions.Freshwater wildlife suffered the sharpest losses across the world’s ecosystems, with monitored populations in rivers and lakes down by an average of 85%, compared with 69% for land species and 59% for marine species.Tanya Steele, the chief executive ofWWFUK, said: “Nature loss is not just a crisis for wildlife. It’s already sending us the bill through growing risks to our food security, water supplies, economy and resilience to climate shocks.“We stand at a fork in the road: either we continue paying the rising price of nature loss, or we invest in nature’s recovery and a future where people and wildlife can thrive together.”But despite the pattern of globalbiodiversitydecline, wild tigers, green sea turtles and bluefin tuna are recovering, the report said, showing that “it is still possible to reverse the global loss of nature when action is taken”.In 2010, about 3,200 wild tigers remained globally and the species was sliding toward extinction. After sustained and targeted conservation interventions, the population has grown to roughly 5,700, an increase of more than 70%.Becci Day, WWF UK’s tiger lead, said the remarkable comeback of wild tigers demonstrated the “science of hope” and proved that when climate and ecological action was taken, change was possible.The report said Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna populations, which were collapsing after decades of overfishing, had now recovered to the point where neither was now considered threatened.View image in fullscreenA green sea turtle off the coast of Demre, Turkey.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesLast year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever downlisted from endangered to “least concern” on the IUCN red list, reflecting 50 years of coordinated conservation work across about 80 countries.Dr Mike Barrett, the chief scientific adviser for WWF UK and a co-author of the report, said: “These are examples that show that nature can recover even when pushed right to the brink, and they provide us with inspiration. It’s also very clear that conservation alone cannot tackle the scale of threats facing nature.”He said nature would have no chance of recovery if “negativetipping points” – self-reinforcing, irreversible ecological changes that accelerate climate crisis – were passed. “The systems which drive nature’s loss have to be transformed. And that’s energy, food and finance,” he said.“Our report shows that we’ve already passed the tipping point in the energy sector with the take-up ofrenewable energy. That transition is now unstoppable. It’s not happening fast enough, but it is unstoppable.”Humanity must likewise adapt the way it produces food, he said. “Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and degradation and therefore the loss of biodiversity. It’s also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and so helps drive climate change, so you have that feedback.”Dr Steve Smith, a research fellow at Global Systems Institute and a co-author of the report, said: “The biggest prize for nature recovery would be a sustainable and healthy food system, but it’s currently the farthest away from positively tipping. For example, agricultural expansion drives almost 90% of deforestation worldwide.”Positive tipping pointsare thresholds beyond which a sustainable technology or practice becomes increasingly cheap, widespread or politically popular, allowing progress to become self-propelling.Explore more on these topicsWWFBiodiversityWildlifeMarine lifeEndangered speciesConservationFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Democrats sue to stop Trump from using taxpayer funds for self-promoting ads | Democrats | The Guardian
description: Ads promoting the president have cost more than $12m so far and Trump’s Super Pac has refused to reimburse taxpayers
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: Ads promoting the president have cost more than $12m so far and Trump’s Super Pac has refused to reimburse taxpayers
Content: A screenshot from a pro-Trump ad the US government paid to broadcast in 2026.Photograph: White HouseView image in fullscreenA screenshot from a pro-Trump ad the US government paid to broadcast in 2026.Photograph: White HouseDemocratsDemocrats sue to stop Trump from using taxpayer funds for self-promoting adsAds promoting the president have cost more than $12m and his Super Pac has refused to reimburse taxpayersSign up to The Stakes 2026: your weekly guide to the US midtermsRobert MackeyWed 7 Oct 2026 18.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 20.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Democratic National Committee sued theTrump administrationin federal court on Wednesday, asking a judge in Washington DC to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air aseries of adspromoting himself, arguing that the ads are illegal government-sponsoredpropaganda.The ads promotingDonald Trump, including onerecycledfrom his 2024 presidential campaign, have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.Ken Martin, the DNC chair, said in a statement that Trump was misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to saveRepublicansin November. Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes.”LA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump suggesting Iran bomb themRead moreAfter a bipartisan backlash to the use of public money to promote himself during the final month of themidtermcampaign season, Trumpclaimedon Monday that he would direct the Maga Inc Super Pac he controls to pay for the ads instead.The next day, however, the White HousesaidTrump’s political action committee would not reimburse taxpayers for the money it had already spent on the ads. Then, when the government unveiled a fifth ad in the series, celebrating Trump’s military intervention in Venezuela, it was also paid for by the US government.TheDNC complaint, filed in the US district court for the District of Columbia, alleges the ads violate federal law, including a ban on congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda”.“President Trump personally directed this illegal activity. The White House office crafted the partisan campaign. The office of management and budget shifted $20m to pay for it. And US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has carried it out. These unlawful actions are ultra vires and violate the Administrative Procedure Act (APA),” the complaint states.The suit also notes thefirst adin the series features an image of Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, awarding Trump the so-called “Fifa peace prize” to support its case that the ads all violate a prohibition on the use of taxpayer funds for “self-aggrandizement”.View image in fullscreenA screenshot from a White House ad for Donald Trump, showing him accepting the Fifa peace prize.Photograph: White HouseThe complaint also referencesnew polling from Reuters/Ipsosreleased on Tuesday which found that an overwhelming majority of Americans, 86%, ​called it inappropriate to use taxpayer funds for TV ads featuring the president around an election. The survey reported that about 80% of Republicans called the ads inappropriate, with only 17% of the president’s party approving of them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAccording to the suit, the ads have been broadcast on ABC, NBC, MS Now, CBS, CNN, Fox News and Newsmax, and appeared during popular NFL and college football games, and news and entertainment shows in which the president has been criticized, including Meet the Press, Jimmy Kimmel Live! and Saturday Night Live.The federal lawsuit also includes details of another eight ads that have already been prepared for broadcast and were found “in a Dropbox account controlled by LMD Agency Inc, the government contractor bringing the ads to air”.The ads ready to be broadcast include: one that celebrates the UFC fights staged at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June; one titled “God Made Trump”, a fan-created hymn of praise to Trump that was shown during the Republican midterm convention; one titled “Resilience”, which includes images of Trump announcing his candidacy for the presidency in 2015, then being charged in Fulton county, Georgia, in 2023 for conspiring to overturn the results of the 2020 election, and video of the assassination attempt on him during the 2024 election campaign; one titled “King of the Jungle”, which shows a lion hunting in the wild and disparages Trump’s political enemies, including former president Barack Obama. In February, Trumpshared a racist videoon social media that portrayed him as a lion and Barack and Michelle Obama as apes.According to CNN, which gained access to the Dropbox last week, another ad in the series features attacks on Joe Biden, including the mocking image of the former president as an autopen installed by Trump on an exterior wall of the White House.Explore more on these topicsDemocratsDonald TrumpUS midterm elections 2026Trump administrationUS politicsRepublicansSuper PacsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Patricia Krenwinkel, former Manson follower, granted parole for third time | California | The Guardian
description: The 78-year-old has spent nearly six decades in prison and California governor has overturned last two parole grants
Author: Sam Levin
Headline: The 78-year-old has spent nearly six decades in prison and California governor has overturned last two parole grants
Content: Patricia Krenwinkel listens to the ruling denying her parole on 20 January 2011.Photograph: Reed Saxon/APView image in fullscreenPatricia Krenwinkel listens to the ruling denying her parole on 20 January 2011.Photograph: Reed Saxon/APCaliforniaPatricia Krenwinkel, former Manson follower, granted parole for third timeThe 78-year-old has spent nearly six decades in prison and California governor has overturned last two parole grantsSam Levinin Los AngelesWed 7 Oct 2026 19.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatricia Krenwinkel, a formerCharles Mansonfollower, was granted parole on Tuesday after nearly six decades in prison for her role in the infamous Tate-LaBianca murders in Los Angeles.This is thethird timethat Krenwinkel, 78, has been approved for release by California’s board of parole hearings. After both of her last two parole grants, Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, reversed the parole board’s decisions anddenied her freedom, and Krenwinkel’s attorneys are now urging the Democrat to allow this latest ruling to stand.Krenwinkel, who was 21 at the time of the 1969 killings, has been imprisoned longer than any other woman inCalifornia, and the parole board has repeatedly acknowledged her record of rehabilitation over 57 years in prison, concluding she would not in her elderly age be a danger to society.She was convicted in 1971 for her role in the violent crime spree over two nights that claimed the lives of actor Sharon Tate, who was eight months pregnant, and her four friends, and grocery owner Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary. The killings were gruesome and became one of the most notorious crime stories in the US.Krenwinkel was 19 years old when she “fell under Charles Manson’s control” and was exploited and psychologically abused by the cult leader, her attorneys have said.“Reaching this moment has taken decades of hard, deliberate work to confront who she was, what she did, and the devastating harm she caused,” her longtime lawyer, Keith Wattley, said in a statement after the parole grant. “She fully accepts responsibility for her actions, everything she contributed to, and every life she destroyed in 1969. Pat does not excuse or minimize that harm.”Over her decades in prison, Krenwinkel has had a clean disciplinary record, and nine consecutive psychological evaluations in the past 40 years have found her to be a low public safety risk, according to Wattley, who has represented Krenwinkel for 16 years. He said she has participated in extensive therapy and group counseling, earned a college degree and trained service dogs for people with disabilities.“I have seen the depth of her remorse and the extraordinary work she has done to change her life. I firmly believe she is ready to return home,” Wattley added.Debra Tate, Sharon Tate’s sister, has repeatedlyobjectedto the release of Krenwinkel and other Manson followers.When Newsom denied Krenwinkel parole in 2022, after the board first found her suitable for release, the governoracknowledgedthat she had been a “victim of Mr Manson’s abuse” and said she had “matured in prison and engaged in commendable rehabilitative efforts”. But he argued she had “not developed sufficient insight into the causative factors of her crime and her triggers for antisocial thinking” and was still dangerous.When Newsom again denied her parole in 2025, he also acknowledged her “serious chronic medical conditions” had diminished her strength, but concluded she “must do additional work to deepen her insight before she can be safely released”.The governor is required to consider her elderly age and that she committed the crime as a youth in his review of her case.Krenwinkel’s attorneys and advocates have repeatedly argued the governor was caving to political pressures by denying parole to people convicted in high-profile cases. Newsom previously vetoed the release of Leslie van Houten, another former Manson follower, but an appeals court sided with her andgranted her freedom in 2023. Newsom also faced scrutiny foroverturning the parole grant of Sirhan Sirhan, convicted of assassinating Robert F Kennedy, even after two of Kennedy’s sons favored his release.The push for Krenwinkel’s release comes at a time of growing concern about the increasing number ofelderly people languishing in US prisonsafter decades of incarceration. Krenwinkel’s longtime friends from inside California’s women’s prisontold the Guardianlast year that she was a mentor and support system to others in the prison.Wattley, founder of UnCommon Law, a non-profit organization that represents people at parole hearings, urged Newsom to “uphold the law” and approve Krenwinkel’s freedom: “The parole process exists because people can change, rehabilitation matters, and public safety must be grounded in evidence. Pat’s case raises a fundamental question: if three parole grants don’t lead to release, what is the point of this process?”Spokespeople for Newsom did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Wednesday.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaCharles MansonWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christa Pike ‘angry, confused’ and unable to move arms after failed execution, lawyers say | Tennessee | The Guardian
description: Attorneys say Pike was set to be taken off life support before she woke up, as judge orders officials to preserve evidence
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: Attorneys say Pike was set to be taken off life support before she woke up, as judge orders officials to preserve evidence
Content: 1:43Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after waking from botched execution, says lawyer – videoTennesseeChrista Pike ‘angry, confused’ and unable to move arms after failed execution, lawyers sayAttorneys say Pike was set to be taken off life support before she woke up, as judge orders officials to preserve evidenceAdam GabbattandMaya YangWed 7 Oct 2026 17.34 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChrista Pike awoke “angry and confused” after surviving two lethal injections, her attorneys said on Wednesday, as a judge orderedTennesseestate officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.Pike, 50, was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber last Wednesday after two supposedly lethal doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital.She was declared brain dead on Monday, her attorneys said, and her team was informed of plans to remove her from life support the next day. “But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking,” Randy Spivey, one of her lawyers, said at a press conference on Wednesday. He was told her first words were “Where am I?” and “Who are you?”Pike remains hospitalized and shackled to her bed, despite pleas from medical staff for prison officials to remove her restraints, her lawyers said. She has pneumonia, a blood clot, and is unable to move either of her badly injured arms, they added.“There’s still a lot of cognitive confusion, and so I will say that she has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people,” Spivey said. “She’s asked about her team. She’s asked about the victim’s family … I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.”Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers sayRead moreThe update on Pike’s condition came after a contentious court hearing in Nashville, where judge I’Ashea Myles ordered the state to preserve “anything that was in the actual room” during the attempted execution a week ago.Pike’s legal team accused Tennessee officials of “secreting away” evidence. Attorney Luke Ihnen said items from the attempted execution could be key to future legal challenges by Pike, should the state attempt to kill her again.“The state has made no promises that Ms Pike will not be subject to a future execution, and the evidence that we are seeking to preserve now is relevant for any future challenge that she makes, because as we pled in January, the same thing is likely to happen,” Ihnen said.Pike, believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection, was injected withlarge doses of the sedative whenTennesseeofficials had attempted to put her to death, in a case that shocked many in the US and created headlines around the world.At the press conference on Wednesday, Spivey said it was unclear “what if any function” Pike would regain in her arms. “Her hands look like if you were to blow up a surgical glove,” Spivey said.Despite her condition, Pike was still being restrained, her team said, shackled to her hospital bed by her feet and right arm.“Based on our understanding, medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request [by theTennesseecorrection department],” he told Myles earlier. He added: “We would also amend our request and ask for that relief.”Witnesses to the attempted executionof Pike described how they heard her breathing raggedly after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her and was declared to be in critical condition.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the botched execution attempt, Spivey called the process“cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered.Christa Pike’s lawyers had warned execution would be ‘difficult and perhaps cruel’ due to her veinsRead moreHer lawyers had warnedbefore the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward.There is speculation from medical experts that perhaps some or a lot of the drug missed her vein and went into tissue, that one of her veins, which were problematic and this fact flagged by her lawyers months earlier – blew, or that the drug was faulty, or a combination.Pike was 18 and her then boyfriend 17 at the time when they killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in Tennessee in 1995.According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area, tortured and killed her.Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder but, because she was 18, she was sentenced to death and has been on death row, isolated, for 30 years.Explore more on these topicsTennesseeCapital punishmentUS justice systemUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: British billionaire warned Epstein was a ‘sexual deviant’ decades before FBI closed in on the abuser | Jeffrey Epstein | The Guardian
description: Sir James Goldsmith’s links to Hilton Head, South Carolina, add to mystery of Jane Doe 4, who claimed she was abused by Epstein in the 1980s
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sir James Goldsmith’s links to Hilton Head, South Carolina, add to mystery of Jane Doe 4, who claimed she was abused by Epstein in the 1980s
Content: Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/United States District CourtView image in fullscreenComposite: The Guardian/Getty Images/United States District CourtJeffrey EpsteinBritish billionaire warned Epstein was a ‘sexual deviant’ decades before FBI closed in on the abuserSir James Goldsmith’s links to Hilton Head, South Carolina, add to mystery of Jane Doe 4, who claimed she was abused by Epstein in the 1980sMarilyn W ThompsonWed 7 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForJeffrey Epstein, the billionaire Goldsmith family was a gateway to elite society and he wanted to be in their circle.The disgraced financier, who died in prison in 2019 facing sex-trafficking charges, longed for a billionaire’s lifestyle and cultivated the family’s friends, bankers, business associates and advisers.But Sir James Goldsmith, who was knighted by the Queen in 1976 and became a prominent British politician, remained wary of the American financier and even “despised” him, his daughter Jemima recently told the Guardian.Two decades before Epstein came under federal investigation, Goldsmith – who died in 1997–told a confidant that Epstein was a “sexual deviant” who was recruiting children for illicit activities.Goldsmith “told me not to have anything to do with him, that he was a pervert, and he didn’t want him near any of us. He had four daughters to protect,” recalled the famous French architect Robert Couturier, who designed opulent homes for Goldsmith in New York and Mexico.Goldsmith’s alleged warning came around 1987, years before complaints about Epstein’s solicitation of young girls for sex began filtering into federal law enforcement. Epstein’s network of pretty “girls” evolved into what authorities describe as a global sex-trafficking ring that catered to the ultra-rich and powerful.It would become a scandal that touched royals, politicians, businessmen, academics, foreign diplomats and celebrities around the world, and left more than 1,000 victims in its wake.“That is the pity of it all. It was all preventable,” Couturier told the Guardian. Epstein, born on Coney Island, had been on the radar of New York’s elite since he first surfaced at society events, often on the arm of heiresses, Couturier said.“He was a charmer and a talker. Lots of rich people are deeply gullible, as protected as they are from reality. No one did anything about it.”View image in fullscreenJeffrey Epstein in 1985.Photograph: TT News Agency/AlamyIn the mid-1980s, Sir James Goldsmith – known as “Jimmy” – announced he was making a shift in his US business operations. Goldsmith had hired a new chief executive who would open an office for him in Hilton Head, South Carolina, an emerging luxury resort.Goldsmith’s Hilton Head office is rarely mentioned in writings about his reign as the “lucky gambler”, as Time Magazine called him, an adviser to US presidents who became one of the world’s richest men by betting on undervalued companies. His conglomerate, with command centers in Paris and London, had its US headquarters in New York, close to his elegant Manhattan townhouse where Goldsmith entertained and where the young Epstein trolled for wealthy clients.Hilton Head at the time was undergoing a chaotic development boom that brought in a rush of speculators, shady operators and vacationers lured by star-studded golf tournaments and tennis matches. Its population, 11,000 in 1980, doubled in a decade. Its tiny airport was suddenly a busy landing strip for private jets, including a $10m Gulfstream owned by Goldsmith’s company that was parked there for quick hops.Epstein developed a lifelong fascination with Goldsmith, his family and fortune, an investigation by the Guardian found.Epstein’s connection to Goldsmith, and the presence of the billionaire’s company and his associates on a South Carolina sea island – which was attracting an infusion of investors – is potentially relevant because of an alleged sexual assault that is said to have occurred there in the 1980s. A woman known only as Jane Doe 4 claimed in four FBI interviews after Epstein’s 2019 arrest that he had assaulted her during his visits to the island in the 1980s, when she was still a teenager. She has also claimed the man she only knew as “Jeff” trafficked her to other men, includingDonald Trump.The White House has vehemently denied the allegation about the US president, calling it “completely baseless” and “backed by zero credible evidence”.The Guardian has been examining records, digging into archives and conducting interviews to explore intersections of Goldsmith and Epstein and try to understand if Epstein, with decades of secretive movements and a web of global financial ties, might have had reason to be on Hilton Head in the 1980s when those alleged assaults by Epstein occurred. This remains a mystery, but Epstein’s relationship with Goldsmith provides some additional clues.Those who dismiss the claim of Jane Doe 4 – including Epstein’s brother Mark – have cited the lack of a public record of his presence on the island as proof that her story is untrue. Mark Epstein told the Guardian he has “no knowledge of him being in Hilton Head”.Understanding how Epstein won and retained access to power and privilege throughout his life is important as criminal investigations of his sexual abuse and financial crimes continue around the globe. Federal prosecutors in New York haveopened an investigationinto the two overseers – Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn – of Epstein’s $577m estate, according to the Wall Street Journal. Both have denied they knew of Epstein’s criminal behavior. The Department of Justice has said that Epstein “harmed” over 1,000 people, including minors who were sexually abused.The justice department has released about 3.5m documents under the Epstein Disclosure Act, including reams of emails, letters and bank transactions. But the trove includes almost no records from the 1980s, leaving a large gap in the public’s understanding. Epstein’s alleged victims continue to accuse the justice department of a cover-up for holding back documents that might implicate Trump and other powerful men in Epstein’s exclusive circle. Trump has said he ended their friendship in 2004 after a real estate dispute and kicked Epstein out of his Mar-A-Lago club in 2007 for poaching employees.It is unclear whether Goldsmith’s concerns about Epstein stemmed from specific encounters, and there is no indication that Goldsmith ever reported his concerns to local or federal law enforcement.It took decades for the FBI to catch up with Epstein’s crimes. Federal investigators in Florida charged him in 2008 with soliciting sex from minors after a two-year investigation in which they interviewed young women, including some minors, who he paid for sexual encounters in his Palm Beach mansion. He served 13 months in jail under a lenient deal cut with federal prosecutors.View image in fullscreenEpstein abuse survivor Annie Farmer holds up a photo of her younger self with her sister Maria Farmer during a news conference with lawmakers on the Epstein Files Transparency Act outside the US Capitol on 18 November 2025.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesUntil now, the earliest warning about Epstein’s criminal behavior is believed to have come in 1996, when one alleged victim – an artist named Maria Farmer – claims she alerted authorities that she was sexually assaulted by Epstein, according to a lawsuit she has brought against the FBI. Farmer has also claimed that Epstein stole nude images she had of her two minor siblings, which she kept for her personal use in her artwork. The FBI has said in response to the ongoing litigation, which now includes 34 alleged victims, that agents do not have a duty to investigate “every single tip that comes across their desk”.A fascination with ‘Sir James’Since Epstein’s death, Goldsmith has been portrayed as an important influence in his early career.TheNew York Times last yeardescribed Sir James as a connection Epstein shrewdly calculated was “worth nurturing for the long haul”. It recounted a party scene at Goldsmith’s Upper East Side mansion where Epstein, trained in classical piano, serenaded guests with a piano solo from the grand entry hall.Goldsmith’s warnings about Epstein came just as Epstein signed one of his biggest clients, the Ohio retail magnate Les Wexner, the founder of Victoria’s Secret, who was then ranked by Forbes as the 10th richest person in the US. Wexner says he severed the relationship with Epstein in 2007 after discovering he had stolen funds from Wexner.Some questions about Epstein and Goldsmith may never be answered given the secrecy surrounding these events and the refusal of key sources to answer questions.View image in fullscreenPosters with photos of the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, with the words:  ‘Ask Todd Blanche about Epstein’ displayed along a street in Washington, on 17 July 2026.Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, the debate over the government’s release of the Epstein files rages on. Attorney general Todd Blanche has declined to release about2.5m Epstein documents he deemed duplicative. An independent journalist, Katie Phang, is suing Blanche to try to force their release, and Blanche recently quietly turned over some of the documents related to Jane Doe 4 to a federal judge, who is reviewing the documents in his chambers.Prominent figures caught up in the Epstein controversy include former US president Bill Clinton, former Prince Andrew, former Harvard president Larry Summers and billionaire investor Leon Black. Black was recentlyheld in contempt of Congressfor his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him by the House oversight committee in connection to its Epstein investigation.Epstein’s emails about the Goldsmiths sometimes suggested bruised feelings and revealed he was watching the family from afar. He was not among the dozens of invited guests in 1997 to Jemima Goldsmith’s grand wedding party to the cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan, who served as Pakistani prime minister, according to the guest list.Just before he finished his lenient 2008 sentence for sex crimes in Palm Beach, Epstein scolded a young Romanian admirer for turning down her exclusive invite to a swanky dinner at Jemima’s Oxfordshire estate.“That was a BIG mistake,” he wrote in an angry 2010 email.Epstein criticized daughter Jemima’s choice of husband, calling Khan – who is now divorced from Goldsmith andin jail on corruption charges– a “whacko”.View image in fullscreenDiana, Princess of Wales in Lahore, Pakistan, with Imran Khan and Jemima Khan, during her visit to the Shaukat Memorial hospital, on 21 May 1997.Photograph: Tim Graham Picture Library/Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty ImagesIn a 2018 text, Epstein wrote of Imran Khan: “makes donald look like einstein. incapable of truth. , devout islamisist . many nuclear weapons. ( not erdogan or khomeni). he was married to two friends of mine. one daughter of jimmy goldsmith.”After the family distanced itself from him, Epstein gathered gossip about James’s daughter Isabel’s haughty behavior and joked when a hurricane seemed destined to damage Las Alamandas, her posh Mexican resort.“hurricane will hit isabel goldsmith resort and bye bye,” he wrote to a friend in 2015.Epstein elevated his access to the British elite when, in 1990, he started datingGhislaine Maxwell, the daughter of a British media baron, who hobnobbed with British royals and enhanced Epstein’s standing among upper-crust families like the Goldsmiths. Maxwell became Epstein’s closest partner in recruiting young women, according to her federal indictment. She is serving a 20-year sentence.Three Goldsmith heirs told the Guardian in emails they never met Epstein and doubted their father had any business dealings with him. Isabel Goldsmith did not respond to messages.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Donald Trump and his girlfriend (and future wife), former model Melania Knauss, Jeffrey Epstein, and Ghislaine Maxwell at Mar-a-Lago club, in Florida, on 12 February 2000.Photograph: Davidoff Studios Photography/Getty Images“I’m not sure I had ever heard ofJeffrey Epsteinbefore he hit the news for the first time. So I’m presuming my father did not know him,” said Ben Goldsmith, an environmentalist and investor who was 16 when his father died.Zac Goldsmith, a conservative member of the House of Lords, said he never met Epstein and was not aware of his fascination with the family.Jemima Goldsmith Khan, who owns a London-based film production company, said she never met Epstein. “I heard that my father despised him – he was certainly not a friend of his,” she said.Sir James was a king of US corporate takeovers in a frenetic era of Wall Street deal-making, earning hundreds of millions by seizing control of vulnerable companies and cutting thousands of American jobs. Goldsmith sold his New York investments in 1987 and made a hasty exit back to London after correctly predicting the Black Monday stock market crash.Epstein was a takeover amateur who concocted his own deals while working as a consultant to a shady Manhattan debt collection company, Towers Financial, whose chief executive, Steven Hoffenberg, was later convicted of running a $450m Ponzi scheme. Before his death, Hoffenberg accused Epstein of masterminding the scheme. Epstein was never charged.Hoffenberg’s most ambitious effort was an attempted takeover of troubled Pan Am Airlines, the prestigious international carrier Epstein had fantasized as a boy about one day owning, according to an email from one of his friends.Working from its Hilton Head office, Goldsmith’s takeover team had already analyzed Pan Am’s books and backed off from making an offer. Developer Donald Trump also flirted with a takeover bid but never made it, media reports show.Couturier met Epstein through Isabel Goldsmith, the titan’s oldest daughter. Jet-setting Isabel became friendly – but not romantically involved – with Epstein, he said, and Isabel and Epstein both socialized in New York City’s nightlife scene. Epstein kept Isabel’s phone contacts at several addresses in his “little black book” later seized by the FBI as evidence.Couturier had grown close to James Goldsmith and his long-term girlfriend, who hired him in 1981 to renovate a mansion on East 80th Street. Goldsmith cut famous takeover deals around the dining room table, and his catered parties attracted the cream of Manhattan society.View image in fullscreenJemima Khan, right, and her sister Isabel Goldsmith at David Frost’s annual summer garden party in Chelsea on 25 June 1998.Photograph: Tom Wargacki/WireImageIsabel told Couturier that Epstein wanted to discuss hiring him for another renovation at a huge Upper East Side brownstone purchased by Wexner, he said. Epstein later moved into the restored mansion at 9 East 71st Street, about a half mile from Goldsmith’s, and decorated its dark wooded interior with his private art collection and gaudy fabrics. It became a center of his sexual misconduct, an address where the FBI in 2019 carried out boxes of photographs of alleged victims, massage tables and sex toys.Wexner also owned a dilapidated historic townhome next door at 11 East 71st Street that needed total renovation. The house was eventually bought through a trust by Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, who has said he hardly knew Epstein, his nextdoorneighbor.Under questioning by House investigators, Lutnick acknowledged visiting Epstein for lunch at the predator’s Caribbean island, Little Saint James.Couturier was approached and interviewed by the FBI in 2010, after Epstein’s first arrest. A record of the interview, which is included in the Epstein files, indicates that Epstein had approached Couturier for a high-paying project on Little Saint James Island, where he was asked to provide “decor and furniture appropriate for teenage girls, with pink furnishings and bunk beds”.Couturier told the Guardian he remembered Sir Jimmy’s earlier warning. He withdrew from the contract, leading to a legal dispute.View image in fullscreenThe British financier and businessman Sir James Goldsmith (1933 - 1997) with his family, left to right: Jemima, Sir James, Zac, Ben and his wife, Lady Annabel, on their estate in Marbella, Spain, circa 1987.Photograph: Peter Jordan/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesGoldsmith was hardly a prude, Couturier said, but he had no tolerance for inappropriate behavior with children. Goldsmith’s own domestic life was what his daughter Alixonce described as “unconventional”, with three wives, numerous girlfriends and eight children. Two children were born in New York to his longtime girlfriend, a French journalist who moved with him to the city.Another link between Epstein and Goldsmith was Bear Stearns, where Epstein was a junior broker until he was targeted in an internal investigation of his trading practices. He quit in 1981 with an indignant resignation letter that was included in the Epstein files.Goldsmith remained a major Bear Stearns client, and Epstein, who somehow remained on good terms with the brokerage top brass, invested his own and his clients’ money into the firm, which collapsed in 2008.Epstein always kept an air of mystery around his business deals. In the 1980s, he described himself to friends as a “bounty hunter” who traveled the world to recover stolen money for rich clients.He and Goldsmith knew many of the same influential people. The Saudi billionaire Adnan Khashoggi, an international arms dealer, hired Epstein in the 1980s for unspecified work, according to published reports. Khashoggi and Goldsmith were both trusted advisers to President Richard Nixon, who met with them after his 1974 resignation to discuss overseas income opportunities, according to a Nixon biographer.Epstein became friendly with a wealthy international investor, Jean “Johnny” Pigozzi, who was in Goldsmith’s circle of advisers and is one of the trustees of Goldsmith’s estate, according to published reports. At one point, Epstein’s girlfriend Maxwell emailed Pigozzi to get price estimates for his French estate and nature preserve in Panama, saying she had an interested potential buyer, the emails show.Pigozzi, an art collector and heir to an auto fortune, is best known in popular culture as the inventor of the “selfie” because of his candid photographs of the rich and famous, including Goldsmith. He did not respond to messages.View image in fullscreenBear Stearns brokerage firm in New York in 1998.Photograph: James Leynse/Corbis/Getty ImagesGoldsmith’s massive holding company, GOSL, had operations around the world and a corporate office in Manhattan run by his trusted team.But in 1985, GOSL filed papers with the state of South Carolina seeking authorization to do business in the state, the Guardian found. It opened an office in Hilton Head, the home of Al Dunlap, a notorious corporate raider Goldsmith was hiring to run his US operations.Dunlap had been living part-time on Hilton Head since the early 1980s when he was running a company that made paper cups. He was among the many corporate bigwigs who had discovered Hilton Head as a sanctuary for executives and government officials who needed privacy. Most exclusive neighborhoods were gated and developed on former rice plantations.Dunlap – who died in 2019 – had the Wall Street clout to ask investors to come to him. A newspaper account describes one session in 1985 at a new Marriott waterfront resort in Hilton Head where Dunlap pitched a Lily-Tulip stock offering backed by Wall Street firms to 70 out-of-town investors before leaving on a global capital-raising tour.View image in fullscreenAn image of Al Dunlap on Hilton Head island from a 1987 Island Packet newspaper article.Photograph: Island PacketSome locals say the atmosphere on the island was so frenetic, with investors and deal makers arriving for meetings, that anyone could slip in and out without notice.Goldsmith’s office in Hilton Head was tasked with selling millions of acres of forest land the company had acquired in takeovers of US paper companies. Its vast new holdings stretched from the Pacific north-west to the Adirondacks, making Goldsmith’s company one of the largest owners of undeveloped US land.The Guardian tracked down former GOSL executive Phil Lader, who was in charge of land sales, to ask if he recalled seeing Epstein in Hilton Head during the time GOSL had an office there. The short answer was “no”.Lader was a Hilton Head resident and former chief executive at Sea Pines. In 1981, he founded the prestigious Renaissance Weekends, which drew luminaries to the island for private invitation-only retreats. He was especially close to Bill Clinton, who was governor of Arkansas when he and his wife, Hillary, began coming to Lader’s exclusive gatherings. Other featured guests included Wall Street executives, university and government officials and leaders in the arts and sciences.View image in fullscreenBill Clinton is greeted by the Lader family after arriving in Hilton Head, South Carolina, for the annual intellectual retreat known as ‘renaissance weekend’ on 30 December 1996.Photograph: Wilfredo Lee/APGoldsmith hired Lader as a GOSL vice-president in 1986, just after he lost a Democratic party bid for the South Carolina governorship. Lader was appointed Clinton’s deputy White House chief of staff in 1993 and moved to London four years later when he was appointed ambassador to the court of Saint James’s.Lader said he never met Epstein and “never heard the name Jeffrey Epstein in my years on Hilton Head”. Epstein reportedly made 17 visits to the Clinton White House and later flew Clinton on his private jet.A partially redacted 2011 exchange in Epstein’s emailsshows he was aware of Renaissance Weekends, which are promoted on social media as gathering places for “thought-leaders”. An unnamed friend asked if Epstein had heard of the gatherings.“Of course,” Epstein wrote. Asked if it was “something i should do?”, Epstein wrote “yes”.Renaissance Weekends were held in Hilton Head for 20 years, then moved to Charleston. Similar programs are also held in other cities.The woman who would come to be known as Jane Doe 4 first called an FBI victim hotline to report her alleged abuse on 10 July 2019. It was four days after Epstein’s arrest at a New Jersey airport. The agent manning the phones recommended that she be interviewed in person, near her home in Vancouver, Washington. One of her close friends made a separate call to anonymously report Jane Doe 4’s abuse.Jane Doe 4’s federal class-action lawsuit, filed later in New York against the Epstein estate, alleges she met Epstein around 1984, when she was a teenager, and had sex with him for several years when he visited the island. She said he rented properties, including a villa at Sea Pines, from her mother’s realty firm.In four FBI interviews in 2019 she described her abuser’s specific sexual quirks – including his use of butt plugs. Several were seized when the FBI gathered evidence in Epstein’s home in 2019.Some details squared with accounts given by other young victims who came forward during the previous Florida investigation. She described how he allegedly asked her to recruit friends and took nude photographs of her, also part of a pattern, and repeatedly plied her with drugs and alcohol. The FBI seized thousands of photographs and videos depicting victims when it searched his various properties.The Marriott hotel on Hilton Head figures heavily in her allegations. She told the FBI about a pool party there with local teenage girls and older males. She claimed the older man she knew as “Jeff” made a brief appearance at the pool before taking her back to his rented villa. She also mentioned a neighbor she had talked with during the period of alleged abuse.Her local attorney told the Guardian he sat in on the FBI interview and interrupted when she began describing telling other girls about “Jeff”.
