The lawyer said he feared the FBI might accuse her of aiding her abuser in soliciting other minors.FBI notes in the case, which were first reported by the Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina, repeat the woman’s allegation that at one point, Epstein transported her to New York or New Jersey where she claims he introduced her to Trump, who forced her into a sex act. She estimated she was about 13-15 years old, which would place the dates between 1983 and 1985, butshe acknowledged a fuzzy memory. Trump said in a 2002 interview with New York magazine that he had known Epstein for 15 years, which would date their relationship to 1987. The White House has denied Jane Doe 4’s allegations.Jane Doe 4 also offered names ofsome of her high school friendswho might have seen her with Epstein.But there is no evidence the FBI ever followed up on the leads Jane Doe 4 gave investigators. Its interest in her case appears to have died abruptly when she asked agents what the point was of her continued cooperation and told them she intended to join a class-action lawsuit, filed by the Bloom Law Firm in December 2019.A relative of Jane Doe 4 told the Guardian that she had been scarred by “layers of trauma” as a young girl from family tragedies and upheavals. She had spent time in foster care and had just finished elementary school when the family made its way south.Jane Doe 4 declined to answer questions from the Guardian relayed through the relative, who considers her account “plausible” because she was often unsupervised in her early teens. Three friends contacted by the Guardian did not respond to messages.Jane Doe 4’s attorney at the Bloom Law Firm told the Post and Courier she ultimately reached a settlement with Epstein’s estate but declined to give an amount.Court records show a claim she filed with the Epstein victims’ compensation fund, a formal review panel funded by the estate, was denied. The dates of her alleged abuse are much earlier than most other victims who have come forward with claims.In response to lawmakers’ questions about whether Jane Doe 4 had received a settlement from the estate, an attorney for Epstein’s accountant, Richard Kahn, said he could not recall details of all 60 women who settled with the estate outside of the compensation fund.View image in fullscreenRichard Kahn, an accountant for convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, arrives for a House oversight committee deposition about Epstein, on 11 March 2026.Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesThe record is far from definitive about whether Epstein ever visited Hilton Head during this time. He did not own a private plane in the 1980s, so no travel logs are available. Epstein did have other real estate development interests at that time, including a long friendship with a developer who was building an oceanfront golf course on nearby Kiawah Island.Later records in the Epstein files show his plane landing at the nearby Savannah airport several times from 2013 to 2019, for unknown reasons. The emails show a redacted exchange in 2014 suggesting he was on Hilton Head for a March visit.Kenneth Lannon, a retired FBI expert in child sexual victimization who has trained hundreds of law enforcement agents to investigate abusers, said it was “highly likely” Epstein had victims pre-dating his Florida arrest and that he probably “started out slowly and just got better and better at it as time went on.The typical child sex abuser, he said, begins targeting and grooming potential victims soon after puberty, although they may come across as “nice guys” in regular social interactions. Money and the ability to travel freely make the crimes easier to pull off, he said.Child victims are often so starved for attention they become compliant and have more than one encounter with the abuser.Jane Doe 4 had a troubled life after leaving Hilton Head. She married several times and moved to the west coast. She returned to be with family in Georgia and was arrested in 2023 for stealing money from a dying man. She pleaded guilty and spent a year in jail. Her brothers were well educated; one worked for a few years as a Bear Stearns trader before the brokerage collapsed in 2008.A family member told the Guardian in June that Jane Doe 4 was “staying off the grid” and lived in fear of retaliation from the Trump administration amid the ongoing controversy over the handling of the case.Additional research by Sophie SullivanGet in touchContact the Guardian US investigations teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. When you're ready to send a message, select ‘Investigations (Guardian US)’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsJeffrey EpsteinGhislaine MaxwellDonald TrumpUS politicsUS CongressRape and sexual assaultJemima KhannewsShareReuse this content

title: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’ | Birds | The Guardian
description: Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisis
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisis
Content: Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt to climate disruption as they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences.Photograph: John Dickens/British Antarctic SurveyView image in fullscreenChinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt to climate disruption as they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences.Photograph: John Dickens/British Antarctic SurveyBirdsWorld’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisisJonathan WattsWed 7 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, astudyhas revealed.Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands inAntarctica, increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.Antarctica’s Zavodovski Island is home to the largest penguin super-colony in the world“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, Prof Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at theBritish Antarctic Survey.The Guardian revealed in 2020 thatchinstrap penguin populations were decreasingon Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem.View image in fullscreenA penguin colony below Mount Curry on Zavodovski. The island had the biggest colony in the world in 2011.Photograph: Nicole Richters/British Antarctic SurveyThe new study, published on Wednesday in Current Biology, indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird – which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek – may need to be classified as an endangered species.The island of Zavodovski had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic peninsula to 5C above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4C, about 20C above normal for the time of year – a margin thatscientists describedas “absolutely crazy”.View image in fullscreenChinstrap penguins are named for the black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek.Photograph: John Dickens/British Antarctic SurveyChinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the north-west of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30% – though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”View image in fullscreenMt Curry erupted in 2016, but this is not thought to have contributed to the penguin population decline.Photograph: Nicole Richters/British Antarctic SurveyThe scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “Penguin Pompeii hypothesis”of a sudden population fall, this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.Explore more on these topicsBirdsAntarcticaPolar regionsWildlifeBiodiversityClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tents, night-vision goggles, bear tracking kits – and even books: America’s first nature library opens | Libraries | The Guardian
description: As well as books, the new facility in Colorado offers hundreds of kits to connect people with the natural world. We asked five of the first visitors what they thought of it
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: As well as books, the new facility in Colorado offers hundreds of kits to connect people with the natural world. We asked five of the first visitors what they thought of it
Content: Visitors to the nature library can borrow thousands of books as well as 850 kits to discover nature, such as wildlife cameras, microscopes and garden tools. Image: compositeView image in fullscreenVisitors to the nature library can borrow thousands of books as well as 850 kits to discover nature, such as wildlife cameras, microscopes and garden tools. Image: compositeThe age of extinctionLibrariesTents, night-vision goggles, bear tracking kits – and even books: America’s first nature library opensAs well as books, the new facility in Colorado offers hundreds of kits to connect people with the natural world. We asked five of the first visitors what they thought of itSupported byAbout this contentDonna Ferguson. Photographs by Kevin MohattWed 7 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 08.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Fink knows exactly why he opened the first public nature library in the US. “There are a lot of barriers for people to access nature here. We want people to learn about the birds and the plants in their own back yard and to appreciate that you don’t need a three-day camping trip in the mountains to experience nature.”The library offers people in Colorado’s Adams county the opportunity to borrow books and equipment to help them to engage with the natural world – for free.While most of the 40,000 items in the library’s collection are books, members can also check out 850 nature-focused “try it” kits – anything from birdwatching equipment, gardening tools and wildlife cameras to hiking gear, microscopes and hammocks.“In the US, as more information has come out about climate change and global warming, there’s been a lot of pushback on those scientific studies and their validity,” says Fink. He is executive director ofAnythink Libraries, which opened the Nature Libraryin August and is funded by alocal property tax levy.“We want to let people make up their own minds. We want to provide opportunities for them to learn more about the climate, the human impact on the Earth and how we can help reduce climate change and make our environment more sustainable,” he says, adding that spending even 20 minutes in nature has physical and mental health benefits.In addition,research suggeststhat people who have more experience with nature are more likely to be inspired to help protect it.View image in fullscreenSome of the first visitors arrive at the Anythink Nature Library, the first public nature library in the US, in Thornton, Colorado, on 15 AugustBuilt using local stone, the library has 370 solar panels on the roof and a sustainable geothermal heating and cooling system. It sits on a 6-hectare (15-acre) site – a former ranch – with a hiking trail and eight different types of garden, including sensory and pollinator gardens, and two focusing on plants that thrive in Colorado and the nearby Rocky Mountains.Inside, children can play in a boulder field made up of rocks from a local quarry, plus there are free workshops to help people build their confidence in activities such as birdwatching, gardening and hiking.We asked five of the first people to visit the library what they thought of it.Paula Jensen, 64, visiting with her mother, Jeanette, 88I heard about the library on Facebook. I decided to take my mom.It’s hard for an 88-year-old to go up to the mountains and connect with nature. I work full-time – I’m a pharmaceutical shipping specialist – and although my mom’s pretty independent, she mostly stays home when I’m at work.View image in fullscreenPaula Jensen, centre right, gets assistance from library staff member, Ricardo CardenasThere was a peaceful little rock garden outside, and she was able to walk around in there with her walker. At her age, it’s very important to get out of the house and do that.Then we sat down by the mud pit. That was really cute to see – all these little children running through it and making mudcakes.My mom loves reading and doing puzzles, and she was surprised to discover she could borrow a wooden puzzle and a Danielle Steel book. She told me it would be too expensive. I said: “Mom, it’s a library.” It was such an impressive building and she couldn’t quite believe that everything was free. It made her so happy.View image in fullscreenJensen holds a wooden puzzle she borrowed from the libraryWe’re having a water shortage in Colorado, so when I go back, I’m planning to borrow a book about how to design a drought-friendly garden, like the one I saw there.Anna Amici, 36, visited with her husband, Prashant, and daughter Asha, twoI’m a scientist for a science education company – I write curriculum for college students, for labs. I love nature and I love libraries and thought a nature library sounded like a cool place to go, especially with a child.View image in fullscreenAnna Amici and Prashant with their two-year-old daughter AshaAsha is growing up in a world where we have to care about and protect our environment. And with the current people in power, it feels like we’re going backwards, and that’s scary. I think she’s going to be forced into making tough decisions to protect the natural world – I think we all are – and I would rather she do that from a love of nature than a sense of doom.What’s exciting about the library is that it makes nature more accessible to her. She can touch it and interact with it in ways that she can’t when we’re out elsewhere. Also, when I’ve had a stressful week, I want to be able to go outside where I can hear birds and touch grass.We’re thinking of replacing our lawn, which died over the summer, with plants that can support pollinators, so we borrowed a pollinator-garden planning kit and a couple of bird guides from the library. We live near a lake that the birds of the Rocky Mountains visit – if I can learn to identify them, I can teach Asha their names.The next time we go, I’d like to borrow a stargazing kit so we can take Asha up into the mountains and look at the stars together.View image in fullscreenChildren run through a mud pit play areaDuring our visit, Asha had a great time climbing on the boulders and playing in the mud pit. It was such a fun way for her to connect with nature on a very physical, sensory level and it made me realise that she doesn’t get many opportunities to actually touch some dirt in her everyday life.We’ve since created a little mud patch in our own garden, which she has really enjoyed playing in. Being in the library has made me recognise that this kind of activity is a good experience for her, it’s building the love of the natural world that I want to foster and nurture in her. It’s worth the mess.Nataliya Zasadko, 40, who visited with her son Marko, sevenI’m a freelance photographer, videographer and content creator, focusing on outdoor family adventures, so the Nature Library sparked my interest. Camping gear can be expensive and a lot of people don’t know if they want to invest in it. Having tents and hammocks available to borrow is a phenomenal idea.View image in fullscreenSeven-year-old Marko photographs flowers using a camera he borrowed from the libraryWe borrowed an outdoor camera with a macro lens, which encouraged my son to go out in nature and photograph bumblebees and flowers, and a GPS gadget. We used that to go on an adventure along a very scenic alpine trail, Santa Fe Peak. I didn’t have to convince my son to come with me – he was excited to go because of this gadget. He was able to use it to plan our route and guide me. We picked a spot we had never been to before and explored. It was a perfect all-day adventure.That gadget would have cost me $300 or $400, and the camera $500, so to be able to check them out without buying was brilliant.We also borrowed a digital wind-speed meter, and talked about that, too. We watched a whole YouTube series about windmills and wind-power plants, and how the energy is produced and stored.I think visiting a nature library is a good way to teach children about nature and encourage them to care about the environment and wildlife. Whether my son was climbing on the boulders or playing in the mud pit, time flew by. The trail around the library is also very beautiful and I noticed that in the garden, they have hoses so children can water the plants.View image in fullscreenThe library has a range of devices, from wildfire detectors to GPS navigators, that users can tryWe’ve gone back twice because there’s so much to do, and I’m excited for the winter when I’m thinking of borrowing some snowshoes and micro spikes, and going on hikes to test them out.In this economy, with families struggling, I love that people are able to go to this library for a few hours and share community resources that can help us build a better future and learn to explore the great outdoors.Alex Bueno, 30, visited with his wife, Monse, and their son Edgar, sixWe live in Nebraska and decided to go to the library while we were on a trip to the Rocky Mountains. My wife is an architecture designer, so she wanted to see the building and I love the idea of a nature library.The countryside in the US is beautiful. But I’m from Cuba and when you go into nature there, there is a feeling that it is wild and untouched. There are so many trees and so much wildlife. Here, by comparison, it is quite built up.View image in fullscreenAlex Bueno and Edgar solving wooden puzzles togetherMy son and I are interested in books about bugs at the moment and enjoyed reading about insects at the library, what they do, how they live and why they are important.We get a lot of insects in Nebraska and my son doesn’t always realise they aren’t dangerous, especially if they are big and buzzing around. Like every kid, sometimes he gets scared. I think if he knew more, he would probably just say “oh look at this”.I grew up much closer to nature in Cuba than he is growing up. I’d like to encourage him to go out and do more. I wish there was a nature library near us in Nebraska.Ricarose Roque, 42, visited with her son Miles, sevenI’m a professor at the University of Colorado in Boulder – I study kids, learning and technology. I do a lot of community engagement work with libraries and I decided to visit because I was curious about what it meant to have a nature library. I also grew up visiting libraries and want my son to do that.When we arrived, Miles gravitated towards the “try it” equipment and the natural disasters section – he has been interested in tornadoes, tsunamis, earthquakes and wildfires since he was about three.View image in fullscreenRicarose Roque, left, and Miles, talk to library staff member Laura Wilson about the different kits they can borrowHe grabbed a book on wildfires and decided to borrow a fire sensor. He thought it could sense fire, but actually it’s a tool that measures humidity, temperature and wind velocity and direction, so you can understand if there’s a risk of a wildfire nearby. But we decided that next time we will try to borrow night-vision binoculars and hike one of our favourite trails at twilight.A bonanza for fans of the natural world: the digital library sharing 64m pages of scientific knowledge with everyoneRead moreWe also borrowed a bird-watching book and a brochure about animals, insects and trees that can be seen here in Colorado.I was born in the Philippines, and emigrated to Los Angeles when I was young. I don’t know much about the wildlife of Colorado, although I’ve lived here for 10 years. Until we borrowed that book, I didn’t know what a Steller’s jay was. But because of that book, we were talking about it – and today I saw one. I can’t wait to tell Miles.We’re not a very outdoorsy family and as someone who grew up in a big city, I feel a bit intimidated by the idea of camping in the mountains. But Miles is always asking to go, and being able to borrow camping equipment from the library makes it easier for us to try it.I hope going to the library can help me and other transplants to Boulder to feel that the wild open spaces of Colorado are ours, too – that they are there for everyone and we all need to take care of them.View image in fullscreenWindows at the library have been designed with dots in the glass to deter birds from flying into themFind moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsLibrariesThe age of extinctionColoradoBirdwatchingClimate crisisAccess to green spaceWildlifeAstronomyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: French wine industry facing historic low harvest after extreme summer heat | Wine | The Guardian
description: This year’s harvest expected to be down 2% on mediocre yield in 2025, when production was lowest in nearly 70 years
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This year’s harvest expected to be down 2% on mediocre yield in 2025, when production was lowest in nearly 70 years
Content: Grapes affected by drought at a vineyard in Douzens, south-west France, last year.Photograph: Idriss Bigou-Gilles/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGrapes affected by drought at a vineyard in Douzens, south-west France, last year.Photograph: Idriss Bigou-Gilles/AFP/Getty ImagesWineFrench wine industry facing historic low harvest after extreme summer heatThis year’s harvest expected to be down 2% on mediocre yield in 2025, when production was lowest in nearly 70 yearsAFPWed 7 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance’s wine industry is facing a historic low harvest after the country was hit by a series of summer heatwaves.At about 35m hectolitres, the total harvest would be down 2% on a mediocre 2025 yield and 14% below the 2021-2025 average, according to estimates published on Wednesday by the ministry of agriculture.The International Organisation of Vine andWine, which tracks global statistics on wine production and consumption, said that last year France had recorded its lowest production since 1957.This latest decline is a result of hot weather, slightly mitigated by recent rain, and a reduction in cultivated areas, which were pared back by 1.9% in the past year.View image in fullscreenChâteau Malartic-Lagravière in Bordeaux, where wine production has risen on last year.Photograph: Régis Duvignau/ReutersSome southern areas, already battered by the heat in 2025, have nonetheless seen production rise this year. In Bordeaux, despite a 5% decrease in cultivated areas, production is expected to increase by 10% on 2025, though this is still 11% below the 2021-2025 average.For the south-west the rise is about 12%, essentially a return to the previous four-year average.The Champagne region fared less well as growers had to harvest exceptionally early after the extreme heat sped up sugar buildup and hence natural alcohol production.The harvest there wrapped up in September for the first time, with production down by half on last year and the five-year average.Claude Mandois, a producer in Champagne, reported harvesting three-quarters of an average yield in terms of volume but added: “In terms of quality visually and in terms of taste we had an exceptional harvest.”In Burgundy and the Beaujolais region, production is projected to be 30% lower than the five-year average.“It’s a level of heterogeneity I’ve never experienced before,” said Jérôme Despey, the chair of the wine advisory board at the public agency FranceAgriMer and a winegrower in the southern Hérault department.He said vines in the south had become more resilient to the climate, with previous intense heat spells causing growers to adapt vineyard management practices such as largely leaving leaves to protect the grapes. Southern regions also benefited from May rainfall.The ministry and the industry emphasised overall the “excellent health” of the harvest, which was free of fungi and other moisture-related diseases.Explore more on these topicsWineFranceExtreme heatFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: British Jewish groups hold London vigil for victims of 7 October attacks | UK news | The Guardian
description: Organisations honour those who died three years ago as Andy Burnham says government stands with British Jews
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Organisations honour those who died three years ago as Andy Burnham says government stands with British Jews
Content: People pay their respects at the vigil in central London on Wednesday afternoon.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople pay their respects at the vigil in central London on Wednesday afternoon.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianUK newsBritish Jewish groups hold London vigil for victims of 7 October attacksOrganisations honour those who died three years ago as Andy Burnham says government stands with British JewsChris OsuhWed 7 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish Jewish organisations gathered in central London on Wednesday for a vigil honouring victims of the 7 October attacks inIsrael, after a day of tributes from politicians and community leaders.The vigil took place at Richmond Terrace, opposite Downing Street. The Board of Deputies of British Jews said: “Three years ago, Hamas terrorists infiltrated Israel, murdering 1,200 men, women and children, injuring thousands and taking 251 people captive. May their memories for ever remain a blessing.”The Jewish Leadership Council said 7 October 2023 had been “the deadliest day for our people since the Holocaust”.The attacks were followed by Israel’s war in Gaza. The Palestinian death toll in the past three years exceeded 74,000 last month, according to Gaza’s health ministry.Andy Burnham assured British Jews “we stand with you” against antisemitism, in a statement marking the anniversary.However, the Israeli embassy said in a statement: “It is a source of deep sadness that in the years since 7 October the position of the British government towards Israel has changed so substantially from the solidarity expressed in those first days,” claiming “the atmosphere for Jewish people continues to worsen” in the UK.Last month the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband,announced an import banon goods from illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine.The Community Security Trust (CST), which monitors antisemitism, said its research showed there were 1,926 antisemitic incidents recorded across the UK from January to June 2026, up by a fifth on the first half of last year. It was the second highest total reported to the CST in the first six months of any year, exceeded only by the 2,019 incidents recorded in the first half of 2024.View image in fullscreenThe UK’s chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, and Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, at the vigil in central London.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesCelebrations of Jewish life have been continuing in public spaces. From 27 September to 2 October, the Jewish festival of Sukkot was celebrated in the heart of Manchester, with the Sukkah in the City event in Albert Square.In his statement, the prime minister described the rise in antisemitic behaviour in the UK since 2023 as “disturbing” and pledged that his government was “committed to protecting our citizens from vile hatred”.Burnham referenced an attack just over a year ago, on the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, by Jihad al-Shamie, 35, at Heaton Park Hebrew congregation synagogue in Manchester, which left two worshippers dead.Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from stab wounds and his fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors from Al-Shamie. Police shot al-Shamie dead during the attack.Burnham said: “Three years on from the 7 October attacks on Israel, we remember those who were senselessly killed by Hamas terrorists. The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day.“In the years since, we have seen a disturbing rise in antisemitic behaviour in the UK. I want Britain’s Jewish community to hear this from me directly: we stand with you. Abuse and violence against you, in any form, will not be tolerated. Not on our streets, not online, not in our schools or universities.“That’s why we are funding protection for synagogues, schools and community buildings, and why we will come down hard on antisemitism wherever it is found – in classrooms, on campuses and in neighbourhoods.”He continued: “At home, we are committed to protecting our citizens from vile hatred. Abroad, we continue to work towards a two-state solution, with Israelis and Palestinians living side-by-side in peace and security.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“An attack on Jewish people in Britain is an attack on all of us.Antisemitismhas no place in this country, and we will do everything we can to stamp it out.”View image in fullscreenProtesters outside the University of Edinburgh’s Main Library on Wednesday.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAMeanwhile, the Metropolitan police said they had “imposed stringent conditions” on those taking part in a pro-Palestine student march inLondonon Wednesday.Eleven people were arrested in the capital, including five on suspicion of inciting racial hatred at a protest outside the office of the Board of Deputies of British Jews in north London, the force said.It said the other arrests were made at pro-Palestinian student protests elsewhere in London.Pro-Palestine protesters also held demonstrations at Edinburgh and Glasgow universities.Hundreds of people gathered for a rally outside George Square in Edinburgh, outside the University of Edinburgh’s Main Library. From there they marched to the Bayes Centre, the university’s hub for data science and artificial intelligence, before finishing in the Old College quadrangle.A similar demonstration was held on Library Hill in Glasgow, outside the university library.Protesters at both rallies carried Palestinian flags and banners, many bearing slogans about the conflict in Gaza.Explore more on these topicsUK newsLondonJudaismIsraelAntisemitismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour could oversee worst parliament on record for living standards, study warns | UK cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: Energy and housing costs threaten biggest decline in modern times unless bold action taken, says thinktank
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Energy and housing costs threaten biggest decline in modern times unless bold action taken, says thinktank
Content: The Joseph Rowntree Foundation is warning of a ‘dire’ outlook for the cost of living in the UK without ‘bold policy action’.Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Joseph Rowntree Foundation is warning of a ‘dire’ outlook for the cost of living in the UK without ‘bold policy action’.Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyUK cost of living crisisLabour could oversee worst parliament on record for living standards, study warnsEnergy and housing costs threaten biggest decline in modern times unless bold action taken, says thinktankHeather StewartandJessica ElgotWed 7 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 14.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSoaring energy and housing costs meanLabouris on course to preside over the worst parliament for living standards in modern times, a stark analysis warns.Three weeks ahead of John Healey’s budget, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation said Britain faces a “dire” outlook unless the government takes “bold policy action”.The JRF predicts that, after housing costs, average household incomes will be between £440 and £770 lower in real terms in 2029-30 than when Labour came to power two years ago.John Healey backs growth but says Labour must be honest on spendingRead moreEven the lower end of that range would mark the biggest decline in living standards since modern records began in 1961, the thinktank said, and come on top of a tight squeeze in the last parliament.Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, has been tasked by Andy Burnham to lead the Cabinet Office cross-government taskforces, with two focusing on turning around living standards. One is looking at short-term cost of living measures to help on housing and energy, and the other at big structural interventions such as public control that might alleviate those pressures long term.Their work will eventually form part of the 10-year plan expected later this autumn, which Burnham began discussions about with cabinet ministers at a Chequers away day this week.Haigh has repeatedly told officials that there will have to be “trade offs” in order to prioritise alleviating the cost of living and public control.Annual figures for living standardsAt the budget, Burnham has promised to offer a “breathing space” to voters and Healey isexpected to offer £1bnin additional support to energy consumers; but there are concerns inside government about whether that goes far enough.Healey is minded to rebuff a call from the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether. The most likely solution is understood to be increasingthe warm homes discount– a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.The chancellor is understood to be considering raising this by £100, with the rise funded by taxpayers.The foundation’s living standards analysis used the Bank of England’s two projections for energy prices – a “central” and an “adverse” scenario.The thinktank has pointed out that since the Bank set these out in July, real-world events have tracked close to the adverse scenario, with oil prices surging back above $100 a barrel after hostilities resumed in the Middle East.By driving up the cost of energy, the renewed conflict has also increased expectations that the Bank will raise the base interest rate to tackle resurgent inflation. Markets are now betting on four quarter point increases to 4.75% by the end of next year.Borrowing costs for homebuyers have already jumped in response to the resulting turmoil in bond markets – withthe average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hitting 6% this weekfor the first time in three years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChris Belfield, the chief economist at the JRF, said: “Without bold policy action on living standards, families are set to be poorer than they were a decade ago. This is terrible both for families who are just treading water to get by and the more than 7 million families who are already routinely going without essentials like food and basic toiletries.”Some forecasts have suggested the typical household dual-fuel bill couldleap by 16% to the equivalent of £2,000 a yearin the first quarter of next year. Given the scale of the looming squeeze, the foundation has argued for a more ambitious package of measures on energy than Healey appears minded to offer.It would like to see a baseline level of energy offered to all households at a cheaper price, with those in greater need entitled to more of these cut-price units of gas and electricity.Other recommendations include making benefits more generous by relinking local housing allowance to average rents; and increasing universal credit, as the Conservatives did during the Covid pandemic. This could be paid for via changes such as increasing capital gains tax rates to match income tax, it argues.The JRF analysis of changes in living standards over time differs from those of the Office for Budget Responsibility andother thinktanks such as the Resolution Foundationbecause of different ways of accounting for housing costs.Despite Burnham’s promise to correct 40 years of economic missteps, Healey’s budget is expected to be relatively modest, with important decisions on tax and spending delayed until next year. These include when the UK will implement spending 3% of GDP on defence – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.In his 28 October statement, the chancellor is expected to focus on filling the gaps in the defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer’s government in June; and laying out how the Treasury will devolve some income tax revenue to regional mayors.A Treasury spokesperson said: “We know families are feeling the impact of higher prices, pushed up by conflicts overseas.“The chancellor is focused on giving households and businesses a bit of breathing space where we can. That’s why we have removed VAT from electricity bills, capped bus fares in England at £2 in 2027, extended the 5p fuel duty cut, and frozen rail fares and prescription charges.”Explore more on these topicsUK cost of living crisisLabourEconomic growth (GDP)ThinktanksBudgetJohn HealeyEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity | Ageing | The Guardian
description: DNA analysis of oldest living land animal reveal patterns on genes that appear to protect functioning of mitochondria
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: DNA analysis of oldest living land animal reveal patterns on genes that appear to protect functioning of mitochondria
Content: Jonathan the giant tortoise at home on the island of St Helena in the South Atlantic.Photograph: St Helena Government, Communications HubView image in fullscreenJonathan the giant tortoise at home on the island of St Helena in the South Atlantic.Photograph: St Helena Government, Communications HubAgeingJonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevityDNA analysis of oldest living land animal reveal patterns on genes that appear to protect functioning of mitochondriaIan SampleScience editorWed 7 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ancient quest to extend human lifespan has received a boost after scientists analysed the genetic code of the world’s oldest living land animal, a giant tortoise called Jonathan.The tortoise, which lives in the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the governor of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, is believed to be 194 years old, making him a contemporary of Queen Victoria and Charles Darwin.Analysis of the animal’s DNA revealed a host of genetic variants in most of the biological pathways for ageing that scientists have discovered. Together, they help organisms to survive by repairing damaged DNA, regulating their metabolism and fending off cancer.But more intriguing to the researchers were chemical patterns on Jonathan’s genes that appear to protect the healthy functioning of his mitochondria, the tiny battery-like structures that power biological cells.Ailing mitochondriahave been strongly linked to ageing and age-related diseases.“We’re still trying to work out how ageing occurs and Jonathan gives us a real window on to what happens over a long period of time,” said Stephen Clark, a senior researcher on the project at the non-profitKallel Foundation. “His mitochondria must be especially stable and that’s an insight into longevity in general. It’s important that the mitochondria are kept as pristine as possible.”Jonathan arrived on St Helena in 1882.Photograph: AL InneThe insight came when the international team, led by Benjamin Vaisvil, looked at chemical tags that attach to DNA, creating patterns that change over time. The tags, known as methyl groups, typically silence the genes they latch on to.Writing inScience Advances, the researchers describe how they compared the methylation patterns on Jonathan’s genes with those from other giant tortoises. The patterns on many of his genes were similar to those of other old tortoises, but the patterns on genes linked to mitochondrial function matched those from much younger animals.It is unclear whether, or how much, the chemical patterning contributes to Jonathan’s impressive lifespan. Clark said the team now needed to validate the finding. “How do we test this idea?” he said. “Is there a way that makes the mitochondria young, or can we replace the mitochondria and see if it extends longevity? That’s one of the next steps.”The former senior veterinary officer of Saint Helena, Joe Hollis, took over Jonathan’s care in 2009. He was not faring well at the time. Cataracts had left him blind, he had lost his sense of smell and his beak was soft and crumbly, making it hard to forage. Hollis began hand-feeding him and six months to a year later, the tortoise had regained weight and sported a hard, serrated beak.In April, Jonathan was caught up in aviral crypto death scamwhen a message from a fake X account posing as Hollis claimed the tortoise had died. The news spread around the world before the Guardian made contact with Nigel Phillips, the governor of Saint Helena, who interrupted his bedtime routine to check on Jonathan. He found him asleep under a tree but “very much alive”.Jonathan certainly appears to be enjoying life. A few months ago, he was found mating with Emma, who shares his paddock. Shortly afterwards, the wife of the governor, who is also called Emma, checked on Jonathan and found him upside down. “Emma [the tortoise] has a very semicircular shell,” said Hollis. “So if you slip sideways fast enough the momentum will flip you right over. It’s phenomenal though. He’s 194. You’re going to have an accident, aren’t you, at 194?”Explore more on these topicsAgeingGeneticsBiologyZoologyBiochemistry and molecular biologyChemistrynewsShareReuse this content

title: George Galloway contests London byelection without setting foot in UK | Holborn and St Pancras byelection | The Guardian
description: Veteran leftwinger has been ‘in exile in the east’ in Russia and not been to Holborn and St Pancras constituency since campaign began
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Veteran leftwinger has been ‘in exile in the east’ in Russia and not been to Holborn and St Pancras constituency since campaign began
Content: George Galloway in 2024. His most recent public appearance was in Cape Town on SaturdayPhotograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGeorge Galloway in 2024. His most recent public appearance was in Cape Town on SaturdayPhotograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHolborn and St Pancras byelectionGeorge Galloway contests London byelection without setting foot in UKVeteran leftwinger has been ‘in exile in the east’ in Russia and not been to Holborn and St Pancras constituency since campaign beganDan SabbaghWed 7 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorge Galloway has been elected seven times to parliament, but his attempt to succeed for an eighth this week, in the London seat formerly held by Keir Starmer, is undoubtedly his most curious effort yet.Since the byelection campaign began, the leader of theWorkers partyof Britain has yet to set foot in the UK, let alone the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, because he is in what he describes as “self-exile” after being questioned by counter-terrorism police at Gatwick airport a year ago.Prolific social media feeds show that the veteran leftwinger has spent the past few weeks on a speaking tour inSouth Africa, with his most recent public appearance on Saturday at a pro-Palestine rally in Cape Town, though posts in the last 24 hours suggest he is in Shanghai, China.Prior to that he was in Moscow, repeatedly making his hostility toUkraineand Nato as explicit as his support for Palestine and opposition to apartheid.“The biggest issue in the H&StP byelection is the path leading us to WW3 in Ukraine,”Galloway wrote on Xin the middle of September, an argument that has not gained much traction with voters, though he has chosen to repeat it online – the only way he can reach voters personally before Thursday’s byelection.Meanwhile, social media feeds show handfuls of Workers party activists campaigning in the constituency without their candidate, fighting a peripheral campaign in a byelection considered to be a battle betweenLabour’s Sagal Abdi-WaliandZack Polanski, standing for the Greens.“Sincere gratitude to my campaigners who are performing miracles on the ground in my enforced absence. Salute to the supporters they are encountering every day. We can win this. And me and my family can come home. Thank you,” Gallowayposted at the end of September.The campaign highlights an anomaly with Britain’s electoral law. Any British, Irish or qualifying Commonwealth citizen over 18 may stand for parliament – as long as they are not bankrupt or members of the police, armed forces, civil servants or judges. There is no requirement to be a registered elector or other residency requirement,according to the Electoral Commission.Last month, Galloway also revealed he had been “debanked” – his bank accounts suddenly closed – by the Lloyds-owned Bank of Scotland. “Thirty-nine years ago I opened a personal bank account with Bank of Scotland in Byres Rd Glasgow. Yesterday without explanation or notice they closed my accounts,” heposted on 4 September, threatening Lloyds with legal action.The bank said it would not comment on individual cases, though account closures are rare. A Bank of Scotland spokesperson added: “Our policy is not to close a customer’s account based on political or personal beliefs and we make customers aware if we make the decision to close an account.”View image in fullscreenGalloway and his wife, Putri Gayatri Pertiwi, seen here campaigning in Rochdale in February 2024, were stopped by police at Gatwick airport last year.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianGalloway chose to leave the UK after he and his wife, Putri Gayatri Pertiwi, were stopped for what he said was “a total of 11 hours” in September last year by “five armed police officers” after returning from the Russian city of Nizhny Novgorod and attending a World Youth Festival assembly.Last month, the former MP said the first question police asked him was: “Why do you admire Mr Lavrov?” They were referring to Russia’s long-serving foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov.Posting on X, Galloway attached a photo of Lavrov smoking and added: “I could have just shown him this picture!”Galloway told the broadcaster RT, the former Russia Today, in an interview in March this year that officers “took all our stuff and copied everything on our phones”, forcing them to miss a public meeting in London at which, his wife saidin a post on Instagram, “the Chinese ambassador [was] waiting for us”.Neither Galloway nor his wife were subject to any further legal action in a stop that took place under schedule 3 of the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019. This allows police to detain people to determine if they have been engaged in hostile activity, considered by investigators to be a low bar.The former MP had appeared on a discussion panel with Lavrov in Moscow in June 2025, at the Forum of the Future,an event described as “far-right”by the Moscow Times, where Elon Musk’s father, Errol, and Alex Jones, the rightwing founder of Infowars, were also speaking.In Galloway’sMarch interview with RT, where he had hosted a talkshow for nine years until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he said he was “now in exile in the east, and I must say that Moscow in the spring is quite the place to be”.He was in Moscow in late April,speaking at the inaugural conference of Sovintern, an international pro-Soviet socialist network led by the opposition A Just Russia party, where a welcome address from the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, was read out.In early September, Galloway released a video promoting his online talkshow,filmed from Moscow’s Red Squarewhere he also said he would appear at a roundtable event on security at the city’s “prestigious university”.On 13 September he participated ina public Sovintern discussionwith Zakhar Prilepin, a leading pro-war author and propagandist who has fought in Ukraine and called for “the return of Kyiv to Russia”.A day later, Galloway was selected as the Workers party candidate, and he shortly afterwards went to South Africa for aspeaking and fundraising tourwith the leftwing activist and former journalist Yvonne Ridley. He continued to post on social media from South Africa, frequently on international affairs.He places a particular emphasis on Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this month Galloway posted an anti-Andy Burnham image, withthe prime minister dressed in blue and yellow, the colours of Ukraine. “I want you to die for Ukraine. Conscription coming soon!” the caption read.Particular criticism has also been reserved for Polanski, his most obvious rival for political support. On 25 September,Galloway posted: “I am with Russia Zack is with NATO. I am with an end to the war in Ukraine Zack is with Zelensky and risking WW3.”Galloway and the Workers party were approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsHolborn and St Pancras byelectionGeorge GallowayWorkers partyLondonByelectionsZack PolanskiRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while trying to repair campaign sign | Arizona | The Guardian
description: Bernadette Greene-Placentia says she is sharing her story in order to fight for victims of sexual assault
Author: Sam Levin
Headline: Bernadette Greene-Placentia says she is sharing her story in order to fight for victims of sexual assault
Content: Bernadette Greene-Placentia in Scottsdale, Arizona on 27 August 2026.Photograph: Diannie Chavez/The Republic/USA TODAY Network/Reuters ConnectView image in fullscreenBernadette Greene-Placentia in Scottsdale, Arizona on 27 August 2026.Photograph: Diannie Chavez/The Republic/USA TODAY Network/Reuters ConnectArizonaArizona congressional candidate says she was raped while trying to repair campaign signBernadette Greene-Placentia says she is sharing her story in order to fight for victims of sexual assaultSam Levinin Los AngelesWed 7 Oct 2026 16.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis article contains graphic descriptions of sexual assault.A congressional candidate inArizonasays she was attacked and raped in August while trying to repair one of her damaged campaign signs.Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a trucker and small-business owner, shared her account with thePhoenix New Times, a local publication. The assault took place on 14 August, according to the campaign.The Democratic candidate, running in a district that includes parts of Phoenix, told the newspaper that she was walking across a parking lot just after 2am to fix a campaign sign when an attacker smashed her over the head, causing her to black out.Greene-Placentia told the newspaper that she awoke to find a man on top of her and discovered he was raping her. She recalled another man coming over and pushing her leg, at which point she said she swung her foot at him. The man said, “Not even worth it”, and the two attackers left, leaving her face down in the parking lot, she recalled.The candidate said her memory of the incident and its aftermath was hazy, telling the newspaper she did not remember picking herself off the pavement or returning home.“It’s just these little tiny flashes of things that I do remember,” Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times. “As much as I don’t want to remember, I’ve tried very, very hard to remember more stuff. But that’s where I’m at.”She said she may have had a concussion as a result of the attack and that her body was covered in bruises. She said she initially wanted to forget what had happened and felt “embarrassed”, at first choosing not to report the assault. But she told the paper that on the campaign trail, she often spoke about fighting for Arizonans, “and I didn’t feel like I could keep saying that if I weren’t also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault”.Greene-Placentia told her campaign staff and husband about the assault days after it happened and reported it to the Maricopa county sheriff’s office two weeks later, according to the Phoenix New Times. The newspaper interviewed Greene-Placentia’s relatives, friends, campaign staff and landlord about the aftermath of the assault.“Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette,” a campaign spokesperson told the Guardian on Wednesday after the Phoenix New Times story was published. “She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone.”The spokesperson added: “She hopes the focus remains on supporting survivors and making sure people who have experienced sexual violence know they are seen, heard and supported.”“I need to let women know that it’s OK to talk about it,” Greene-Placentia told the newspaper.Stephanie Simacek, a state representative and friend of Greene-Placentia, said the congressional candidate told her of the assault in early September, telling the Phoenix New Times, “I felt sick to my stomach, and it was extremely disturbing. It was a big wake-up call for me. I think oftentimes, as candidates and electeds, we think that it’s not going to happen to us.”A Maricopa county sheriff’s spokesperson declined to comment, saying the investigation was ongoing.Greene-Placentia is running against an incumbent Republican member of Congress, Abraham Hamadeh.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsArizonaRape and sexual assaultUS crimeViolence against women and girlsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west Yemen | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land
Content: Several pro-Houthi men take part in a rally to recruit new fighters for the group in Sanaa on Wednesday.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSeveral pro-Houthi men take part in a rally to recruit new fighters for the group in Sanaa on Wednesday.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenHouthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west YemenGroup’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to landPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorWed 7 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-westYemen, approaching the city of Taiz and firing a missile and an explosive towards the airport in Aden, the chief international hub of the Saudi-backed government.The explosive hit the key airport moments before a plane was due to land. The British ambassador toYemen, Abda Sharif, said the attack could have endangered thousands of people. It forced the flight – from Cairo – to be diverted to Jeddah and led to a review about the safety of flights in Aden.Independent observers said there was a danger that the Houthis were on course to capture Yemen’s third city of Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure Aden. Saudi warplanes had been using their air superiority to try to hit any Houthi accumulation of forces near the city, especially to the west.View image in fullscreenA Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighter is seen purportedly firing at a Houthi position near Dhubab in Taiz.Photograph: Southern Giants Brigades/ReutersHouthi forces also claimed that they had fired missiles towards two airports in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Saudi authorities initially said the attacks had been repelled, but then said three people had been killed and 36 people wounded.The Institute for the Study of War said it was adjusting its previous assessment that Houthi forces on the coastal plain were collapsing “in light of evidence in the last 24 hours indicating that theHouthishave stopped Yemeni government-aligned advances”.Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?Read moreThere has been widespread criticism on social media of some of the claims aboutYemeni government advancesissued at the beginning of the week.Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, gave a lengthy address marking the third anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel, and singled out the Qatari-owned Al Jazeera for criticism of its coverage of the Yemen war. Trying to link the various conflicts in the Middle East, he urged Yemenis to investigate the Saudi role in the Palestinian cause, “stressing that whoever searches will only find it stabbing the nation in the back”, and said the formal positions taken by the Saudi regime did not in reality benefit the Palestinian people.The Houthi leader also stressed that the Saudi government was not content with complicity in Gaza, but played a key role in conspiring against the Islamic resistance in Lebanon, where it incited everyone against Hezbollah in a single front with the US and Israel.Southern Giants forces – a pro-government militia in Yemen – are still leading efforts to recapture the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea that had been the first target of an offensive launched by the Yemen government on Monday. The group is now positioned in the military airport sector in the Dhubab district near the Bab al-Mandab strait.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricaSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: FBI says it thwarted terrorist attack in Minnesota by an 18-year-old it supplied with an AK-47  | FBI | The Guardian
description: Authorities say they arrested an 18-year-old who was planning a shooting attack at the Mall of America
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Authorities say they arrested an 18-year-old who was planning a shooting attack at the Mall of America
Content: Shoppers walk through and shop at Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota, on 14 October 2018.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShoppers walk through and shop at Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota, on 14 October 2018.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesFBIFBI says it thwarted terrorist attack in Minnesota by an 18-year-old it supplied with an AK-47Authorities say they arrested an 18-year-old who was planning a shooting attack at the Mall of AmericaAuzzy Byrdsell and agenciesWed 7 Oct 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFBI officials stopped a potential terrorist attack on the Mall of America in Bloomington,Minnesota, authorities announced Wednesday. An 18-year-old was arrested on one count of obtaining a firearm to carry out an act of terrorism.Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud had been investigated over the last nearly two years by the FBI. He was arrested Tuesday in a public park after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of theIslamic Statefor an AK-47 and 200 rounds of ammunition, according to the criminal complaint.His messages with a confidential informant revealed Mohamud expressed intent to join terrorist organizations overseas but those plans soon became a planned attack in Minnesota when those plans failed. The messages date back as far as December 2024.Mohamud was seen on the mall’s security cameras walking around “nonchalantly” and eventually robbing a Lids store at gunpoint before being apprehended, according to Minnesota police.“I wanna get martyred inshallah,” he said in the messages with the informant.“That’s why I wanna save up to go to another country or…get a gun here and just start killing a bunch of white ppl.”Daniel Rosen, a US attorney, said Mohamud “needed to be watched”.It’s unclear what initially promoted the FBI’s investigation. According to Rosen, agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people, as we allege in far greater detail in the complaint”.The potential shooting at the mall comes after two recent shootings by Somali teens as victims and suspects, including agang-related shootingin Bloomington where more than 100 rounds of ammunition were fired.As terrorism and violence are an increasing concern in Minnesota, some in law enforcement are calling for a regional taskforce to address more harm in the state.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsFBIMinnesotaUS crimeIslamic StatenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil | Brazil | The Guardian
description: After a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian project
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: After a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian project
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro 45, goes into the 25 October runoff as favourite after a first-round win against Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday.Photograph: André Borges/EPAView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro 45, goes into the 25 October runoff as favourite after a first-round win against Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday.Photograph: André Borges/EPABrazil‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ BrazilAfter a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian projectFlávio’s surprise first-round win highlights rapid rise of Brazil’s House of BolsonaroTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroWed 7 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlávio Bolsonaro, the far-rightfrontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, increasing fears about a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power.Brazil was re-democratised in the 1980s after a brutal 21-year dictatorship that Flávio’s father, the disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro,has long praised.Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent LulaRead moreLast year,Jair Bolsonaro, a former soldier who served under that military regime, was jailed for 27 years for trying to engineer a coup after he lost the 2022 election to the current leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, in Sunday’s presidential election first round and goes into the runoff on 25 October as favourite. On Tuesday, the rightwinger vowed to capitalise on the hugely increased far-right presence in congress after the election to change the constitution and “re-democratise this country”.“The only thing standing in the way of Brazil becoming a barbarity is calledFlávio Bolsonaroas president,” he claimed at a campaign event in Goiânia, a city near the capital, Brasília.The incendiary comments caused outrage among historians and opponents of Bolsonaro’s radical populist movement, who have accused him of co-opting the language of democracy to disguise an illiberal shift.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro with the former presidential candidate Ronaldo Caiado (left) and the São Paulo governor, Tarcisio de Freitas, during a rally in Goiania.Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty ImagesTalíria Petrone, the leftwing congresswoman, wrote on X: “This is the announcement of a coup.”Marcelo Freixo, a newly elected congressman from Lula’s Workers’ party (PT), said: “Brazil was re-democratised in 1988. The person who tried to undo this was his father, who was convicted of an attempted coup. What they want, once again, is a coup.”Bolsonaro did not spell out what he meant by “re-democratising” Brazil, a vibrant if polarised multiparty democracy that the Sweden-based V-Dem instituteranks 28th on its liberal democracy index, two places ahead of the UK and 23 ahead of the US.But Jair Bolsonaro, who haspraised authoritarian leadersincluding Chile’s former dictator Augusto Pinochet, has long hankered for a return to military rule.Last September, the supreme court found Jair Bolsonaro guilty of trying toconvince military chiefs to help him cling to powerat the end of his 2018-22 presidency. The conspiracy culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, a far-right insurrection seemingly inspired by the 6 January 2021 storming of the US Capitol.Writing in O Globo newspaper, Míriam Leitão, a prominent political and economic journalist, warned that if Bolsonaro won, Brazil faced “theextreme and concrete dangerof … another coup d’état attempt”.“Flávio follows the same ideas as his father and has already said that an intervention in the institutions is necessary,” Leitão wrote. “If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, he will have more tools at his disposal to carry out his father’s authoritarian project: robust caucuses in the lower house and senate, a weakened supreme court, and the support of the Donald Trump administration.“Political science shows that it’s in the second term that an autocrat doubles down on their plan. Look at the case of Donald Trump. The risk isn’t of the son repeating the father, it’s that he surpasses him.”View image in fullscreenSupporters of Flávio Bolsonaro at a rally before the presidential election runoff.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersMiguel Lago, a political scientist, said Sunday’s far-right election triumph – in which Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) secured the senate’s largest caucus, with 28 of its 81 seats – would permit radical changes, including the impeachment of supreme court ministers considered enemies of the Bolsonarismo movement.Jair Bolsonaro and his jailed co-conspirators are likely to be freed if his son wins, with the former president expected to become an influential minister able to select the new heads of the armed forces.“It’s better than a coup d’état … it’s almost like a coup d’état with the support of the majority of the population,” Lago said.Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, has been accused of “killing” democracy by using control over the country’s congress and institutions to approve sweeping constitutional changes, includingscrapping presidential term limitsso he can seek indefinite re-election.Flávio Bolsonaro recently met Bukele’s security minister, Gustavo Villatoro, in São Paulo, hailing the Central American country’s hardline security policies under which thousands have been jailed during a state of exception that has lasted nearly five years.Bolsonaro told reporters that during their conversation, Villatoro “stressed the importance” of using control of congress to make the “necessary legal changes”.2:54Lula admits Brazil election result ‘unexpected’ as Bolsonaro leads first round – videoCelso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist, said he believed that by using the word “re-democratise”, Flávio Bolsonaro sought “to smuggle his authoritarian purposes into acceptable language”.Barros said Bolsonaro, unlike his father who always seemed to favour an “old school barracks uprising” to seize power, appeared to be part of “a new generation of authoritarians” who sought to dismantle democracy from within by undermining and occupying the institutions.“Then you don’t need to break any laws to achieve authoritarianism … because you are the law,” Barros added, citing Hungary’s former far-right prime minister Viktor Orbán as an example. “Clearly, Flávio’s plan is a corrosion of democracy so [Brazil] becomes a Hungary or Bukele-style system.”Danilo Araújo Marques, a historian, said the word “democracy” had been co-opted before in Brazil by undemocratic forces, when the military men and politicians behind the 1964 coup called their actions “an intervention to democratise the country”.“They all talked about democracy … [but] democracy has a different meaning in the mouth of a coup-monger,” said Marques, who is from a research unit at the Federal University of Minas Gerais called Projeto República.Marques noted that during the campaign, Bolsonaro had claimed his octogenarian opponent, Lula, represented the past while he was selling the future. “But this future means going back to what [Brazil] was before,” Marques said. “It’s a ‘future’ that is based on the order prior to the 1988 constitution, which is precisely the military dictatorship.”Asked to clarify his plans on Wednesday, Bolsonaro rejected speculation he was seeking to finish “what his father didn’t do”. “Let’s stop lying. Let’s touch down in the real world,” he told reporters, adding: “Brazil needs to go back to normal, that’s all.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilFlávio BolsonaroJair BolsonaroThe far rightAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada’s Weston family buys Boots for $8.9bn | Boots | The Guardian
description: Former Selfridges owners buy UK high street institution from long-term backer Stefano Pessina
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Former Selfridges owners buy UK high street institution from long-term backer Stefano Pessina
Content: Wittington Investments, the holding company of the Weston family that controls the Loblaws grocery chain and Drugmart pharmacies in Canada, will own Boots’ UK and Irish retail operations and opticians chain.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWittington Investments, the holding company of the Weston family that controls the Loblaws grocery chain and Drugmart pharmacies in Canada, will own Boots’ UK and Irish retail operations and opticians chain.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Getty ImagesBootsCanada’s Weston family buys Boots for $8.9bnFormer Selfridges owners buy UK high street institution from long-term backer Stefano PessinaSarah ButlerWed 7 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Canadian family that once owned Selfridges department store has bought the UK pharmacy and beauty retailerBootsfor $8.9bn (£6.74bn).Wittington Investments, the holding company of the Weston family that controls the Loblaws grocery chain and Shoppers Drug Mart pharmacy outlets in Canada, will own Boots’ UK and Irish retail operations and opticians chain, the No7 beauty brand and a franchise arm in Thailand.The acquisition of the Nottingham-headquartered chain, which has 1,800 stores across the UK and employs 50,000 people, is also being backed by the investment firm Fairfax, which owns The Sporting Life Group and Sleep Country, Canada’s largest mattress retailer, which owns Simba Sleep in the UK.Galen Weston, the chair of Wittington, who is likely to become chair of Boots, said: “Boots is one of Britain’s most enduring businesses, with a rich heritage, a trusted name and a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland.“We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come.”The transaction, which sees the exit of Boots’ long-term backer Stefano Pessina and his latest backer, the financial firm Sycamore Partners, is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027.In 2022, the US pharmacy group Walgreens put Boots up for sale with a suggested price tag of up to £10bn, but it later dropped the plans as potential buyers, including Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, the US private equity investor Apollo Global Management and Asda’s owners TDR Capital,struggled to raise funds. Aplan to float the businessat a valuation of about £7bn was dropped in 2024.“Boots is an iconic brand and a British institution,” said Pessina, whotook Boots privatewith the backing of the investment firm KKR in 2007. He has since kept a stake under different private equity owners and merged and demerged it from Walgreens.“It has been one of the privileges of my and [my wife] Ornella’s life to have been so closely associated with Boots over the last 20 years. We are delighted to be passing on a thriving Boots to strong and reliable owners who understand the value of its great heritage.”Pessina will retain ownership of Boots’ interests in the Farmacias Benavides pharmacy chain in Mexico and the Alliance Healthcare Deutschland, a German drug distributor.The acquisition of Boots marks the return of the Weston family’s Canadian branch to the UK high street, after the family sold off the Selfridges department store chainfor £4bnin 2022.The separate UK branch of the family’s company is known for holding a majority stake in Primark through the parent company Associated British Foods, which is led by family member George Weston.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham pledges extra £210m towards regenerating boarded-up high streetsRead moreRichard Hyman, the veteran retail analyst, said the Weston family were “the most encouraging ownership of Boots for many, many years”.He said: “For years, watching Boots has been a bit like watching corporate pass the parcel. Its ownership has changed with extraordinary frequency and each owner has stripped a bit more out of it.”Hyman said Boots had an opportunity to make more of its vast loyalty scheme and to offer more services through its network of stores across the UK, many of which had seen little modernisation in recent decades.Boots has closed more than 300 outlets in recent years. It is unclear whether its new owners plan to close more shops, but they are likely to take a close look given the rising costs of high street retail, the shift of trade to online, and competition from discounters such as Savers, Lidl and Home Bargains.Hyman said: “Boots needs and deserves owners that will show it a bit of love, and history shows the Westons take a longer view.”Explore more on these topicsBootsRetail industryMergers and acquisitionsPrivate equitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ex-Barclays traders jailed for rigging interest rates have convictions quashed | Banking | The Guardian
description: Acquittals of five former bankers come year after supreme court overturned ruling against City trader Tom Hayes
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Acquittals of five former bankers come year after supreme court overturned ruling against City trader Tom Hayes
