Content: Colin Bermingham (third from left) and Alex Pabon (fourth from right) with supporters including David Davis MP outside the Royal Courts of Justice on Wednesday.Photograph: Jack Hudson/PAView image in fullscreenColin Bermingham (third from left) and Alex Pabon (fourth from right) with supporters including David Davis MP outside the Royal Courts of Justice on Wednesday.Photograph: Jack Hudson/PABankingEx-Barclays traders jailed for rigging interest rates have convictions quashedAcquittals of five former bankers come year after supreme court overturned ruling against City trader Tom HayesJoanna PartridgeWed 7 Oct 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive more former traders who were jailed for rigging interest rates have had their convictions quashed by the court of appeal in London, after a long battle to clear their names.The court overturned the convictions of Jay Vijay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham – all of whom worked atBarclays.Their acquittals on Wednesday came just over a year after the UK supreme courtoverturned a decade-old rulingagainst the former UBS and Citigroup trader Tom Hayes.The five former Barclays traders were jailed between 2016 and 2019 on charges of manipulating the euro interbank offered rate (Euribor) or the now-defunct London interbank offered rate (Libor).The Euribor and Libor rates affected the value of ordinary people’s pensions, mortgages and savings, as well as hundreds of trillions of pounds and euros worth of financial products around the world. Nine bankers accused of rigging the rates were given fraud convictions.View image in fullscreenJay Merchant leaves Southwark crown court in London during his trial in 2016.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesThe five former Barclays traders applied to clear their names after Hayes, thefirst banker jailed for Libor-rigging in 2015, had his name cleared. Carlo Palombo, a former Barclays trader sentenced to four years in prison in 2019 for rigging Euribor, also had his conviction quashed on the same day in July 2025.The supreme court overturned the convictions of Hayes and Palombo after finding faults in the original trials, ruling that had ultimately “deprived” them of a fair trial. They found trial judges had given “inaccurate and unfair” instructions to the juries that found the former traders guilty.The cases of the American Pabon; Calcutta-born Merchant; Britons Bermingham and Mathew; and French national Moryoussef werereferred back to the court of appealby the Criminal Cases Review Commission in January.View image in fullscreenTom Hayes (right) and Carlo Palombo outside the supreme court in London after their convictions were quashed.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAThe move came after the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original charges against the men,found their convictions“may be considered unsafe” after the supreme court ruling in the cases of Hayes and Palombo. The SFO did not contest the appeals.Mathew said: “For the last 10 years, the stain of a criminal conviction has been a burden I have carried every minute of every day.”View image in fullscreenJonathan Mathew, pictured in 2014, said: ‘For the last 10 years, the stain of a criminal conviction has been a burden I have carried every minute of every day.’Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersHe added: “Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it’s about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a statement, Pabon, thanked Hayes, who he said “refused to let it go and pushed this through for all of us”.Tom Bushnell, a partner at the law firm Hickman & Rose, which represented Merchant, Mathew and Moryoussef, said: “In Jay Merchant and Jon Mathew’s case, it took over a decade for this wrong to be righted. In Philippe Moryoussef’s case, over eight years.“Their lives have been turned upside down as a result. All involved in the criminal justice system should now ask themselves not only how this error came to be made and repeated, but also why it took so long to correct.”Wednesday’s ruling marks a further blow for the SFO, with the unravelling of more of its high-profile prosecutions. It said: “After carefully considering this judgment and the full circumstances, ​we do not oppose the appeals ​of five individuals convicted by juries in relation ​to Libor and Euribor.”The agency reiterated in a statement that the supreme court had “found that there was ample evidence on which a properly directed jury could have convicted Tom Hayes and Carlo Palombo”.Jason Williams, the head of division at the SFO, added that it was not deemed in the public interest to seek retrials of Hayes and Palombo.A further attempted appeal by Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader who pleaded guilty in 2018, is expected to be heard on Friday. His case is the only one being contested by the SFO, which argues his conviction was safe.Explore more on these topicsBankingLiborCourt of appealSerious Fraud OfficeCriminal Cases Review CommissionUK criminal justiceBarclaysnewsShareReuse this content

title: South West Water owner taps investors to fix infrastructure after sewage spills | Pennon | The Guardian
description: Pennon slashes dividend and launches £550m cash call ‘to drive improved outcomes for customers and communities’
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Pennon slashes dividend and launches £550m cash call ‘to drive improved outcomes for customers and communities’
Content: A South West Water sewage treatment works in Devon.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyView image in fullscreenA South West Water sewage treatment works in Devon.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyPennonSouth West Water owner taps investors to fix infrastructure after sewage spillsPennon slashes dividend and launches £550m cash call ‘to drive improved outcomes for customers and communities’Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their usesJoanna PartridgeWed 7 Oct 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe owner of embattled South West Water has slashed its dividend and launched a cash call to investors as it attempts to fund infrastructure investment, days after it was hit by arecord £7.9m finefor hundreds of sewage spills.London-listedPennonsaid on Wednesday it would tap investors for £550m, as part of a £1bn investment “to drive improved outcomes for customers and communities”.Shares in the utility company, which supplies water to about 3.5 million customers across the south-west of England, as well as 380,000 business customers around the UK, tumbled in response to the announcement, making Pennon the biggest faller on the FTSE 250 index.Pennon’s new chief executive, Keith Haslett, who was appointed in April, said he had conducted a comprehensive review of the business and had identified areas for improvement, including customer service and the company’s environmental performance.Last month, a judge issued South WestWaterwith the largest fine for environmental offences in the region, at nearly £8m, and said the company’s conduct amounted to reckless failures in management systems and response to known risks. The fine will be paid by shareholders rather than through bill increases.The company wasfined after hundreds of sewage spillsduring a six-year period at popular bathing spots including the coastal village of Harlyn in north Cornwall and in sensitive habitats, such as the River Camel, which is home to otters and Atlantic salmon and popular with birdwatchers and sailors.In June, South West Water wasfined £1.85mby a judge in a separate case. The company pleaded guilty to the criminal offence of supplying water unfit for human consumption, after a 2024 parasite outbreak in Brixham, Devon, made hundreds of people sick and forced thousands of households to boil their water.Pennon said on Wednesday it would also slash its shareholder dividend by about 30%, including the impact of the equity raise, as part of its “operational reset”.Shares in Pennon, which also owns Bristol Water and SES Water, slumped by as much as 22% on Wednesday after the company’s announcement, named “project Proteus”, after a sea god in Greek mythology.Haslett told reporters the reaction to the company’s plans had been mixed, saying: “Investment is needed to achieve improvements – we’re funding the plans in the right way.”He added this would not be funded by further increases to customers’ bills and said he was also bringing some critical roles back in-house, including leakage teams that were previously outsourced.In its recent results for the year to 31 March, Pennon revealed it had incurred outcome delivery incentives from the water regulator for England and Wales, Ofwat, of about £42m for its water and wastewater performance. It said it had faced operational pressures from “exceptional storms and sustained rainfall coupled with a step up in targets and penalty rates”.The company anticipates it will continue to incur the penalties until 2030 but is aiming to reduce them by at least 50% a year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Tuesday, South West Waterapplied for a banon non-essential water use for some businesses across parts of Devon and west Dorset, after a lack of significant rainfall after the hot, dry summer. The proposed ban would restrict activities such as vehicle washing, the cleaning of buildings and the filling of non-domestic swimming pools and ponds.Customers of South West Water arealready seeing their bills riseto fuel £2.5bn of investment in infrastructure in the years to 2030.The number of customer complaints received by South West Water more than doubled over the past year, according to the latest figures from aconsumer watchdog. The Consumer Council for Water found complaints to the company soared by 153%, and rated South West Water and Thames Water “poor” for the number of complaints received and how they handled them.In recent weeks, Andy Burnham hascome under further pressurefrom a cross-party group of MPs to take control of indebtedThames Water.The MPs are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds that are effectively running the company and to consider emergency legislation to take charge of Thames’ financial affairs.However, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, has previously suggested a special administration regime – effectively temporary public control –could not be triggeredfor Thames Water and would require a change in the law.Explore more on these topicsPennonWater industryUtilitiesWaterInfrastructureCorporate governanceRegulatorsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Royal Mail to cut up to 2,500 jobs amid restructure and fall in letter deliveries | Royal Mail | The Guardian
description: Postal service says cuts will focus on head office and ‘support function roles’
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Postal service says cuts will focus on head office and ‘support function roles’
Content: Royal Mail says there will be no reduction in operational frontline roles in delivery and processing.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRoyal Mail says there will be no reduction in operational frontline roles in delivery and processing.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianRoyal MailRoyal Mail to cut up to 2,500 jobs amid restructure and fall in letter deliveriesPostal service says cuts will focus on head office and ‘support function roles’Mark SweneyWed 7 Oct 2026 07.23 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoyal Mail is to cut up to 2,500 jobs as the embattled company seeks to restructure its business amid intense competition and the continuing decline in letter deliveries.The postal service, which has been fined a total of£37m since 2023for missing delivery targets set by the regulator Ofcom, said the job cuts would focus on head office and “support function roles” with the restructure to be completed by the end of next year.Pointing out that the volume of letter deliveries had declined more than 70% since their peak in the mid-00s, Royal Mail said the cuts would be achieved through “natural attrition” and a voluntary exit programme with no compulsory redundancies.The company said there would be no reduction in operational frontline roles in delivery and processing, including the number of postal workers and drivers it employs. The cuts amount to less than 2% of Royal Mail’s workforce of more than 131,000.However, the Communications Workers Union (CWU), which represents frontline staff, said about 200 members with jobs in administration and revenue protection would be affected.“We will be meeting management to discuss this announcement, which is further evidence of a company that is demoralising staff and failing to deliver for customers and the wider community,” said Martin Walsh, a deputy general secretary of the CWU. “We urge the government to confront the reality of a collapsing Royal Mail and intervene to save this national institution.”The cuts are the first to be made since thecompletion of the £3.6bn takeoverof Royal Mail’s parent company, International Distribution Services, by theCzech billionaireDaniel Křetínský’s EP Group last year.Royal Mail last made abig round of cuts in 2022when it said it was looking to eliminate up to 10,000 roles, including 6,000 full-time frontline jobs.“We have been working hard to reduce costs and simplify processes across all areas of the business as we transform to win in a very competitive market,” said Alistair Cochrane, the chief executive of Royal Mail. “These proposed changes remove duplication and allow us to invest further in the service we deliver for our customers.“The proposed changes will not be easy, but they are an important part of building a stronger, simpler and future-ready Royal Mail for our customers and colleagues.”The union Unite said further job cuts were likely unless the government and the regulatorOfcomaddressed a number of issues facing Royal Mail, most notably high competition from rivals that operated “gig economy postal services”.“These devastating job losses have been directly caused by years of inaction, without urgent action, this will happen again,” said Sharon Graham, Unite’s general secretary. “More jobs will be lost, employment standards will continue to fall and customers will continue to be let down.“The answer cannot simply be another round of job cuts. Unite is now supporting our affected members at Royal Mail during this very difficult time and is committed to fighting this decision every step of the way.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast week, the company announced it was to hire 22,000 temporary workers – in roles including sorting, delivery and collection and HGV and MGV drivers – to cover the seasonal jump in mail volumes, including online purchases over Black Friday and Cyber Monday in November, and Christmas deliveries.In June, the postal regulatorlaunched an investigation into Royal Mailfor once again missing its annual delivery targets, with almost a quarter of first-class mail arriving late. Royal Mail has not hit its Ofcom-mandated delivery target for first-class post since 2017, or for second-class mail since 2020.In April, Royal Mailfaced criticismfor raising the price of a first-class stamp by 10p, or 6%, to £1.80. The cost of a first-class stamp has more than doubled since 2020.The cost of the second-class service rose by 4p, or 5%, to 91p. Royal Mail blamed the need for price increases on the “continued rise in the cost of delivery for every letter”.Last July, Ofcomgave IDS permission to loosenRoyal Mail’s universal service obligation, ending second-class post on Saturdays and reducing the service to alternate weekdays from Monday to Friday.A decade ago Royal Mail was delivering 20bn letters a year, but that has shrunk to 6.7bn and could drop to 4bn within four years. Over the same timeframe the number of addresses it serves has risen by 4m.Explore more on these topicsRoyal MailPostal serviceJob lossesOfcomnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anne Carson and Can Xue favourites to win Nobel prize in literature | Books | The Guardian
description: The Canadian poet and Chinese experiment writer are the bookmakers’ favourites to win, with Haruki Murakami, Gerald Murnane and Margaret Atwood also in the mix
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: The Canadian poet and Chinese experiment writer are the bookmakers’ favourites to win, with Haruki Murakami, Gerald Murnane and Margaret Atwood also in the mix
Content: Favourites … Anne Carson and Can Xue.Composite: PR, AlamyView image in fullscreenFavourites … Anne Carson and Can Xue.Composite: PR, AlamyBooksAnne Carson and Can Xue favourites to win Nobel prize in literatureThe Canadian poet and Chinese experimental writer are the bookmakers’ favourites to win, with Haruki Murakami, Gerald Murnane and Margaret Atwood also in the mixElla CreamerWed 7 Oct 2026 09.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanadian poet Anne Carson and Chinese experimental writer Can Xue are the bookies’ favourites to win this year’sNobel prize in literature, set to be announced Thursday.The frontrunners both have 10/1 odds of taking home the world’s most prestigious literary prize, this year worth 12m Swedish Krona (approximately £900,000), according to Ladbrokes.The 76-year-old Carson is known for her hybrid style, mixing poetry and prose, and combining contemporary stories with ancient myth. Among her best-known works is her 1998 verse novel Autobiography of Red, a queer coming-of-age story that reworks a Greek poem about Heracles.Can Xue has been a favourite for several years running. The 73-year-old, whose real name is Deng Xiaohua, has twice been longlisted for the International Booker for the novel Love in the New Millennium – translated by Annelise Finegan Wasmoen – and for her short story collection I Live in the Slums, translated by Karen Gernant and Chen Zeping.Coming in behind Carson and Can Xue is Haruki Murakami with odds of 14/1. The Japanese writer is one of the biggest international sellers among the favourites, known for works including Norwegian Wood and Kafka on the Shore.Ladbrokes also have Australian avant garde writer Gerald Murnane in the mix, along with American postmodern novelist Thomas Pynchon, both with odds of 16/1.And at 20/1 odds are seven writers: Margaret Atwood, Cristina Rivera Garza, Enrique Vila-Matas, Jamaica Kincaid, Lídia Jorge, Lyudmila Ulitskaya and Michel Houellebecq.Canadian novelist Atwood, author of The Handmaid’s Tale, already has many of literature’s biggest prizes under her belt, including the Booker and the Giller prize.Meanwhile, Mexican author Rivera Garza won the Pulitzer prize in 2024 for Liliana’s Invincible Summer, a memoir about her 20-year-old sister, who was murdered by a former boyfriend.Vila-Matas is one of Spain’s most prominent novelists, known for blending fiction with essay. In 2020, he was longlisted for the International Booker prize for his metafictional novel Mac and His Problem, translated by Margaret Jull Costa and Sophie Hughes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKincaid is an Antiguan-American writer, best known for books including Annie John, A Small Place and Lucy, which often explore family relationships and colonialism’s destructiveness. Kincaid “is a writer you don’t just read; she is a writer that takes you back to yourself”,wrote the poetJackie Kay in 2022.At longer odds are Karl Ove Knausgård, Alexis Wright, Colm Tóibín, César Aira, Deborah Levy, Don DeLillo, Emmanuel Carrère, Leila Aboulela, Michael Ondaatje, Mircea Cărtărescu and Salman Rushdie.The winner will be announced at 12pm UK time (1pm CEST) on Thursday.Last year’s recipientwas the Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai. Other recent winners include Han Kang, Jon Fosse, Annie Ernaux and Abdulrazak Gurnah.Explore more on these topicsBooksNobel prize in literatureAnne CarsonAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘In the wake of death, Courtney Love was giving it her all’: Hole’s Melissa auf der Maur on her best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘This is Courtney doing her makeup on the ’95 Lollapalooza tour. I was documenting my generation being hijacked by corporate greed – and destroyed following the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘This is Courtney doing her makeup on the ’95 Lollapalooza tour. I was documenting my generation being hijacked by corporate greed – and destroyed following the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain’
Content: ‘When the wild alternative freaks crossed into the mainstream’ … Self-Portrait with Hole, Lollapalooza, 1995.Photograph: Melissa Auf der Maur, courtesy DelMonico Books/AGO TorontoView image in fullscreen‘When the wild alternative freaks crossed into the mainstream’ … Self-Portrait with Hole, Lollapalooza, 1995.Photograph: Melissa Auf der Maur, courtesy DelMonico Books/AGO TorontoMy best shotArt and design‘In the wake of death, Courtney Love was giving it her all’: Hole’s Melissa auf der Maur on her best photograph‘This is Courtney doing her makeup on the ’95 Lollapalooza tour. I was documenting my generation being hijacked by corporate greed – and destroyed following the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain’Interview by Zoe WhitfieldWed 7 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was going through the archives for my rock photo book, I came across my first ever self-portrait, at Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris, in front of Jim Morrison’s grave. I am a 13-year-old on an awkward trip with my cool father. He had no respect or interest in Jim Morrison, and that photo is like every photo I’ve taken from that moment on – I’m trying to take agency over what is happening. Photography was the absolute first thing that gave me a feeling of having my own say. It became a way of creating my own universe, one that I could trust. It was absolutely my first love.I was sidetracked into music in a beautiful way by these radical women and a countercultural movement, so the subject of my photographs just changed. It was me within this environment, on stage with Hole, backstage with these luminary, wild people, travelling across the world. My photography followed and morphed with me, and my camera documented my generation being hijacked by corporate greed and destroyed in the wake of the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain. It was a generational call to document the Lollapalooza ’95 tour, where this photo was taken, for us to understand later. It was also when the wild alternative freaks crossed into the mainstream.double quotation markShe trusted me to be her bass player and right-hand woman. My camera got to just drink that inBass players are natural wallflowers and I always had a camera with me, just like everyone has a phone now. In terms of my duty as a female photographer in Hole – not a girlfriend, not an outside male photographer – I was able to glean the essence of that band through that misunderstood and wildly celebrated, but also dismantled queen, Courtney. What I love about the photos of her, and in this photo where she’s just doing her makeup, getting ready to go on stage, is she trusted me so implicitly. She either didn’t notice the camera, or she gave herself to the camera, so I was able to capture her true essence, in the same way that she trusted me to be her bass player and right-hand woman. My camera and I got to just drink that in.Courtney had been asked to do a tour diary of Lollapalooza for Spin magazine, so it was natural they asked me to take the photos. It felt really grown up for a 23-year-old. I was capturing the humanity, mystery and happiness – as much reality as possible to unpack later, understanding that time and distance would give me perspective. I had bought a new camera for the road, a Nikon point-and-shoot, because my manual camera was not cutting it on tour. It was a camera that could adapt to the subject changing quickly, and shit was happening quick. The wide-angle lens was a revelation, because my little hand could get the giant ocean of crowd, and I could also fit four people in a frame.This photo captures the spirit of the people who were central to this story in a very particular way, which is kind of how it landed on the cover of this book. It was near the end of the three-week tour; I have a whole roll that I took this day. I would always photograph us right before going on stage, unless shit was bad, so the fact I have half a roll of that moment means we were obviously feeling very strong that night. That is rare in a band that was living in the wake of death, with the struggles of addiction and with enemies on the tour. The fact I was confident enough to take our photo so much makes me think it was a very happy day on what should have been a very happy time in our band. We were at the peak of our alternative power, co-headlining with Sonic Youth, and Courtney was giving her all. Her life was an absolute nightmare – and there was a rivalry with Sonic Youth, who were the gatekeepers of cool at that moment – but she was giving her all on this tour.My life in the band was the defining role of that decade for me. Yes, I was later in the Smashing Pumpkins, and yes, I was an art photographer too, but my life in Hole defined me spiritually, emotionally, musically, and also publicly. Courtney, obviously, is infamous and misunderstood, but my portraits of her in this book are loving and true.Melissa Auf der Maur: My ’90s Rock Photographs is published byDelMonico Books. It accompanies the exhibition atArt Gallery of Ontario, until 6 June 2027.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Norman Jean Roy/Courtesy of the ArtistMelissa Auf der Maur’s CVBorn:Montreal, 1972High point:My 21st-century midlife resurrection as a photographer, out of the wild flames of the 90s rock life that defined me. It’s a very exciting way to use the past as a barometer, and as a way finder for the futureTop tip:The problem with our digital reality now is this abundance – I loved that, in the pre-digital film era, there was a limitation. So now it’s work within limitations and with intention, and then find your signature storytellingExplore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotCourtney LovefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Uprising review – Paul Greengrass turns revolutionary rage into a Robin Hood origin myth | Movies | The Guardian
description: Andrew Garfield’s fictional ploughman joins the historical heroes of the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt in a dirt-caked, docudrama-style film with disconcertingly silly moments
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Andrew Garfield’s fictional ploughman joins the historical heroes of the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt in a dirt-caked, docudrama-style film with disconcertingly silly moments
Content: Sickened by greed … Andrew Garfield as the Ploughman in The Uprising.Photograph: Betina La Plante/courtesy of Entertainment Film DistributorsView image in fullscreenSickened by greed … Andrew Garfield as the Ploughman in The Uprising.Photograph: Betina La Plante/courtesy of Entertainment Film DistributorsMoviesReviewThe Uprising review – Paul Greengrass turns revolutionary rage into a Robin Hood origin mythAndrew Garfield’s fictional ploughman joins the historical heroes of the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt in a dirt-caked, docudrama-style film with disconcertingly silly momentsPeter BradshawWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaul Greengrass has in fact already made his “uprising” film:United 93, the gut-wrenching 2006 masterpiece about the passengers onboard United Airlines flight 93 who rose up against the 9/11 hijackers and prevented them from hitting their destination and causing fatalities – except, that is, for those onboard the plane. Greengrass’s new movie, shot in his distinctive handheld, docu-reportage style, is notionally about the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, in which Wat Tyler and John Ball became legendary for leading an insurrection against the cruel poll tax of Richard II. Or at least … it sort of is. Because the film, in a disconcertingly silly way, imagines the uprising as an origin myth for Robin Hood, or at least someone who’s supposed to be more or less Robin Hood – because that’s not what he’s called and the dates don’t quite match up.Ex-soldier Tyler and radical preacher Ball, capably played by Cosmo Jarvis and Jamie Bell, are joined by a third fictional hero, apparently destined later to canter through the forest with a wealth-redistribution plan. He is a ploughman, known simply as “Ploughman”, played by Andrew Garfield; grieving the loss of his wife and children to the plague and sickened by the tax collectors’ greed and brutality, he instigates an insurrection that soon merges into other outbreaks of revolutionary rage. This involves rivers of smudgy-faced folk in rough clothes descending on the capital from all directions, to demand concessions from the king to whom they are still loyal and believe to have been misled by advisers.Marketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood?Read moreThe appearance of the well-bathed royal overlords themselves may remind you ofthe immortal line from Monty Python and the Holy Grailabout how to tell if someone is a king. Tom Hollander gives a very enjoyable performance as his majesty’s evil adviser Sir Robert Hales, and Katherine Waterston is typically stylish and composed as Joan of Kent, the king’s mother, while Woody Norman has a sinister moon-faced blankness as the young Richard II himself. There are moments to enjoy in all the overclass performances, and indeed to respect in those of the doomed uprisers, whose heroism nonetheless is supposed to create a historic legacy of fighting against bullies and tyrants.That, it seems, is the point of it all. Which brings us to the coda; I wondered if Greengrass would boldly hit us with an immersive scene from London’s 1990 poll tax riots. But no. It’s Garfield emerging from the dense forest with his un-merry men like a gag-free episode of Blackadder, and being oddly lenient with the ermine-clad VIPs that they catch. It’s a bit of letdown.The Uprising is in UK and Irish cinemas from 9 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmPeriod and historical filmsPaul GreengrassAndrew GarfieldCosmo JarvisJamie BellTom HollanderreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gnomes review – Asa Butterfield takes on murderous garden ornaments in pulpy horror-comedy | Australian television | The Guardian
description: Rightly described as ‘Gremlins meets Hot Fuzz’, this fun series has the high-spirit and gusto one hopes for in a show about evil killer gnomes
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: Rightly described as ‘Gremlins meets Hot Fuzz’, this fun series has the high-spirit and gusto one hopes for in a show about evil killer gnomes
Content: Sex Education’s Asa Butterfield has the ‘right amount of phoney bravado’ in six-part horror-comedy TV series Gnomes.Photograph: Narelle Portanier/StanView image in fullscreenSex Education’s Asa Butterfield has the ‘right amount of phoney bravado’ in six-part horror-comedy TV series Gnomes.Photograph: Narelle Portanier/StanAustralian TV reviewAustralian televisionReviewGnomes review – Asa Butterfield takes on murderous garden ornaments in pulpy horror-comedyRightly described as ‘Gremlins meets Hot Fuzz’, this fun series has the high-spirit and gusto one hopes for in a show about evil killer gnomesLuke BuckmasterWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne can never trust marketing materials to accurately describe a movie or TV series, but I’m pleased to report that Gnomes’ official synopsis gets its tone right: “Gremlins meets Hot Fuzz.” This six-part horror-comedy series indeed feels like the kind of rambunctious, high-spirited production that’d be right up the alley of Joe Dante and Edgar Wright, directors of the aforementioned films. Particularly in its air of barely controlled chaos, staged with a slight wink to the audience but never too self-consciously.It’s also – without a doubt – the greatest television series ever made about murderous garden gnomes awakened by an ancient evil.View image in fullscreenGarden gnomes get ‘very stabby-stabby, very killy-killy’.Photograph: Narelle Portanier/StanIn the small town of Nompton, there is – to paraphrase a line from anothertonally comparable production– something strange in the neighbourhood. Not ghostsper se, but activated garden gnomes who get very stabby-stabby, very killy-killy just as the community is gearing up for a special “Gnome-a-Palooza” festival. Mayor Lachlan Morrison (the always entertaining Darren Gilshenan) insists – like the mayor in Jaws before him – that the town stay open, no matter the risk. Though in his defence, Morrison isn’t fully across the whole “possessed inanimate objects going gnome-icidal” thing.From the start, Gnomes – created by Joel Kohn and written by Tegan Higginbotham and Paul F Verhoeven – has the kind of fun, pulpy tone one hopes for in a series about a gnome apocalypse. It opens with a William Castle-esque horror-homaging prologue, set in a castle on a dark and stormy night – with an eye patch-wearing Nazi to boot, before jumping forward and settling into Nompton.Key players include senior constable Arnold Kipps (Asa Butterfield, best known as Otis fromSex Education) and fellow constables Josie Leeds (Higginbotham) and Devon Raki (Matt Okine). The team doesn’t have much actual policing to do, attending kids’ parties and faffing about. And the powers that be have cottoned on, sending Kipps’ ex-partner, constable Ellie McKay (Megan Smart), to relay the news that all but one of them will lose their jobs due to a dramatic downsizing.When shit hits the fan, of course, it’s all hands on deck, with the death of poor old Luke McGregor’s DVD-shop proprietor signalling the crossing of a narrative threshold. Early on, Morrison informs Kipps that locating the missing “Gnome Queen” is hugely important, because he spent all the council’s money acquiring it from a museum. Later, this quest becomes significant for a different reason: get the queen and you take out the hive. A group of teenagers (Leigh Lule, George Rayias, Oliver Edis and Mila Hourmouzis) also help out, their presence feeding into the show’s slightly retro tone, 1980s horror-comedies (Gremlins, The Monster Squad, The Lost Boys, for instance) often putting youngsters at the centre of the action.View image in fullscreen‘The cast do a good job keeping a straight-ish face while recognising the silliness of it.’Photograph: Narelle Portanier/StanYou have to wait a few episodes for the real mayhem, though each is a punchy half-hour and the show is consistently entertaining during its buildup – which is often a good acid test, a sign the essential elements are in place. A fairly average zinger delivered at one point by Okine (“you don’t break the rules, the rules break you”) made me wonder if the script could’ve done with some better one-liners, and whether a “get off my lawn!” gag was ever on the cards. The cast do a good job keeping a straight-ish face while recognising the silliness of it – particularly Butterfield, who walks around with the right amount of phoney bravado: just enough to communicate he’s in on the joke.It’s energetically directed–by Matthias Hoene, Sian Davies and Kohn–and given a midnight-movie look by cinematographer Matthew Temple, who recently shot Colin and Cameron Cairnes’ instant classicLate Night with the Devil. The team understands that with this type of production, you can be many things – over the top, outrageous, etcetera – but you should never be boring. This inevitably requires telling a fun story, with characters you either like or want to see spectacularly dispatched to that great big garden bed in the sky. Gnomes pulls it off with pulpy gusto.Gnomes is on Stan in Australia now, and on Disney+ in the UK from 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsAustralian televisionAustralian TV reviewAsa ButterfieldHorror (TV)TV comedyStanTelevisionDisney+reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Goodbye Warner, hello Skydance: how will the major merger really impact Hollywood? | Warner Bros | The Guardian
description: After a windier road than expected, Paramount and Warners are now one, under the banner of Skydance, and the film industry is set for a shake-up
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: After a windier road than expected, Paramount and Warners are now one, under the banner of Skydance, and the film industry is set for a shake-up
Content: A billboard displaying the logos of Skydance, Warner Bros and Paramount on the Paramount Global offices in New York.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenA billboard displaying the logos of Skydance, Warner Bros and Paramount on the Paramount Global offices in New York.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersWarner BrosGoodbye Warner, hello Skydance: how will the major merger really impact Hollywood?After a windier road than expected, Paramount and Warner are now one, under the banner of Skydance, and the film industry is set for a shake-upJesse HassengerWed 7 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 07.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHollywood’s big five have officially become the big four. Following a twist-filled saga that saw the century-old studio Warner Bros nearly acquired by the streaming giant Netflix, only to be outbid by Paramount owners Skydance, the company led by billionaire scion David Ellison. After facing legal opposition that ultimately crumbled, Warner Bros and Paramount areofficially under the same corporate roof. They are divisions of Skydance, which joins Sony, Disney and Universal as the remaining major-studio players in Hollywood.Paramount completes $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros to form new media empire SkydanceRead moreThe merger goes beyond film production. Eventually, the streaming services HBO Max and Paramount+ will merge into a single entity, though a timeline has not been disclosed. The television channels HBO, Showtime, CBS, MTV, Comedy Central, Cartoon Network, Nickelodeon, TNT, TBS and CNN are among many now owned by a single corporation. The presence of CNN on that list has brought particular scrutiny, given the post-Skydance meddling with the once-respected CBS News, resulting in a rocky stewardship from Bari Weiss, who has overseen a dip in both ratings and prestige for the flagship program 60 Minutes. Weiss isn’t expected to add CNN to her purview;current chair Mark Thompson will remain in place for now, and Skydance has insisted that CNN will remain editorially independent. But given Ellison’s chumminess with Donald Trump, who has long ranted incoherently about CNN’s supposed biases, the presence of an oversight board with Ellison appointees has been cold comfort.That oversight board is one of a few concessions for a group of state attorneys general dropping their lawsuit attempting to block the merger. Many of these points amount to maintaining business as usual for certain elements of the companies: negotiations for pay TV rights and channel fees charged to cable companies, for example, will have to be negotiated separately, as if Warner and Paramount haven’t merged. And one of Hollywood’s great fears about the merger, unaddressed by the agreement – the inevitable layoffs that come with consolidation – may not make much immediate difference in casual media consumers’ lives (though the people actually working in the entertainment industry will feel plenty of impact, direct and indirect, none of it good).So what will be most noticeable from the consumer’s vantage, in the coming months and years? In terms of their wallets, streaming prices will jump again, though that’s less a change than an acceleration ofcurrent conditions. Paramount+ is one of the cheaper streaming services at the moment, but HBO Max is one of the pricier options; it’s hard to imagine a combined version would fetch much less than $25 a month, and that’s just for starters; it could easily go much higher (though, again, that fusion of services probably won’t be immediate, and will probably look like business as usual in the short term). This might eventually lead to a streaming landscape less dependent on viewers buying a seemingly infinite number of $20 monthly subscriptions. But consolidation isn’t exactly great for competition, either.View image in fullscreenDavid Ellison.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersThe bigger creative changes will eventually be seen on the movie side of the business. Skydance already nixed Warner movie studio co-chairs Pam Abdy and Mike De Luca, who noted upon their departure, with a hint of snark, that they’re leaving the studio with 39 movies – meaning that any real successes from Warner in the next few years will be owed to their development slate, not whoever at Skydance claims credit. Not all of those 39 movies are locked and loaded for release, of course, but there probably won’t be major, immediate changes to the Warner release schedule – especially not for 2026, which will probably still close out with the DC Comics-based horror movie Clayface, the animated Seuss adaptation The Cat in the Hat, and the sci-fi blockbuster-in-waiting Dune 3.Further ahead, the Warner movies already well into production for 2027 look financially and sometimes even creatively promising: new movies in the Superman, Ocean’s, Minecraft and Godzilla/Kong series, plus original projects from M Night Shyamalan (in collaboration with Nicholas Sparks) and JJ Abrams. Paramount, meanwhile, has new movies in the Sonic the Hedgehog, Paranormal Activity and Quiet Place series, plus a remake of the artier horror movie Possession and an adaptation of the bestseller Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow.But the movies that already have release dates plotted out a year or two ahead of time tend to be the bigger-budget, brand-name and/or franchise fare that defines most major studios these days. Less clear is how the combined studio will meet their self-selected benchmark for number of new releases a year, and whether that might include non-branded movies. That’s a theoretical bright spot of the merger, also owed to that mostly watered-downdecreefrom the attorney generals: Skydance must make good on its seemingly far-fetched promise that consolidating these companies would not reduce film production, and in fact would result in a total of 30 new releases a year, the equivalent of robust years for two different studios.The AG agreement codifies that number for five years: 30 each year for two years, then 32 each year for the following three. There are additional terms about how many of these need to be wide releases and/or independent films, as well as some deeply dispiriting definitions of what constitutes the latter (“independent” is defined as, essentially, a movie that’s not a big-budget IP play). The agreement also lays out some consequences of highly questionable utility. A sample wrist-slap: for failing to meet these standards, the company would be forced to divest from ... Miramax?! This seems about as punishing as insisting that Skydance misbehaves, they must absolutely, positively part ways with VH1.In theory, though, Skydance has committed to releasing 156 movies in the next five years, which should make theatrical exhibitors happy, and seems to be the main reason some Hollywood figures like Tom Cruise and James Cameron have championed the merger. As for the specifics, the combined planned Warner/Paramount output for 2027 is more or less on track to hit 30 films; 2028 would need another 10 movies or so to meet it, and Paramount’s post-Ellison sensibility hasn’t exactly been informed by the variety of genres and budgets that once defined big studios. These days, Paramount mostly makes big-budget sequels and cheaper horror movies.That’s where executives like the departed De Luca and Abdy would have come in handy. Their tenure at Warner was characterized by both risks and variety befitting one of Hollywood’s most recognizable and prestigious movie studios. They greenlit two beloved smash-hit horror movies with Sinners and Weapons. The studio won a best picture Oscar – their first in over a decade – with Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another. They let indie talents play in a big-studio sandbox with movies like Wuthering Heights and The End of Oak Street. Even their franchise films, like the Dune sequels, Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga, Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, and Superman had the clear creative imprint of individual creators.View image in fullscreenLeonardo DiCaprio in One Battle After Another.Photograph: APThis also meant that Warner released some major flops during the last few years, including The Bride!, Supergirl and the recent Digger, which may have sealed their fate in Ellison’s eyes. (As the producer of sequels to Top Gun and Days of Thunder, he likes his Tom Cruise in big, rumbly vehicles, not addressing the climate crisis!) 2026 was a particularly bleak year for Warner at the box office. More than half their titles were outgrossed by Coyote vs. Acme, a project that CEO David Zaslav wanted binned completely before it was finally sold off to a smaller distributor.A greater volume of releases should theoretically offset those kinds of big-money misses – and ensure that finished movies aren’t scrapped as tax write-offs, something that another possible penalty ($30m a movie that falls short of the benchmark) seems likely to hold off. But, again, Paramount’s current tastes for non-blockbusters only seem to extend as far as horror cheapies, with an added dose of shameless “apolitical” inspirational junk; Ellison doesn’t have a track record of delivering a diverse array of comedies, dramas and thrillers that might appeal to adults. That’s what ultimately feels so dispiriting about the merger, even as it shows a heartening bullishness over the theatrical business.Warner Bros, a corporate studio with plenty of ups and downs but an overall legacy of cinema history, is being absorbed by Skydance, a company that still treats the movie business – even one that has seen major recent hits like Obsession, The Odyssey and Project Hail Mary – like it can be tentpoled up to the moon.The nightmare scenario is a 30-movie theatrical slate that looks more like a streaming service’s lineup of assembly-line “content”, only minus the kinds of passion projects that Netflix and Apple have been known to finance as a lure, and maybe plus a whole lot of AI designed to cut costs. After all, Ellison has indicated that he wants Skydance to serve as atech companyas much as an old-fashioned media monopoly – a dystopian fusion that leaves little room for creative or consumer upside. It’s hard not to wonder if the most successful outcome at this point would be failure - which isn’t off the table with $80bn of debt that needs immediate attention. In the meantime, moviegoers might have to comfort themselves with one surprising takeaway: that the ego and greed driving endless entertainment-industry mergers still somehow includes making movies for theaters, at least for now.Explore more on these topicsWarner BrosParamount PicturesFilm industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carrie review – the teenage hell-raiser’s glorious return couldn’t come at a better time | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: This witty, smart remake takes bullying and telekinetic violence to new extremes. Even the shower scene is more excruciating than the original
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This witty, smart remake takes bullying and telekinetic violence to new extremes. Even the shower scene is more excruciating than the original
Content: Darker than Stephen King could ever have imagined … Summer H Howell as Carrie.Photograph: Courtesy of PrimeView image in fullscreenDarker than Stephen King could ever have imagined … Summer H Howell as Carrie.Photograph: Courtesy of PrimeTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewCarrie review – the teenage hell-raiser’s glorious return couldn’t come at a better timeThis witty, smart remake takes bullying and telekinetic violence to new extremes. Even the shower scene is more excruciating than the originalLucy ManganWed 7 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe automatic response to the news that a stone-cold classic of any genre is to be remade is: “Why?” In an accompanying letter to critics, the creator of the new TV series Carrie, Mike Flanagan, promises us that this was the first question he asked himself too when he was approached about the project. Why mess with perfection – in this case, the Brian De Palma horror film, based on and nearly eclipsing in terms of cultural currency Stephen King’s debut novel about a telekinetic teen, that has been gloriously shocking audiences for half a century?But it’s a far less necessary question than usual. Why remake Carrie, a story of teenage bullying, alienation and the vengeful violence they can fuel, for the modern age? Babe, look around! We’ve got the internet now. We’ve taken teenage bullying, alienation and the fuelling of vengeful violence to levels that De Palma and King, with all their vaunted capacity for darkness, could never have imagined! We are, to use a construction popular among the very youth of whom we are speaking, Carriemaxxing these days. The question is not why remake but quite why it has taken this long.De Palma’s masterpiece is a lean, mean thing, taking just 98 minutes to move from opening credits to high-school mass barbecue. Flanagan’s is an eight-hour series (and there are signs of seeds being sown for a second season already), so much in the way of plot and characters has been added. But the new Carrie has not fallen victim to the streamer’s curse of bloating. Almost everything and everyone is there for a reason, and if the whole plays more like a teen drama with extra bite than a straight up, blood-soaked horror event that is no matter when the former is clearly what it was designed to be. It’s also kinder than the film – perhaps intentionally, perhaps as a byproduct of having to flesh out the “baddies” who cannot remain elemental villains over such a long period if we are to stay interested in the story and their fates – but again, in an increasingly unforgiving world, this feels welcome and right.View image in fullscreenAll about the phones … from left: Alison Thornton, Summer H Howell and Siena Agudong in Carrie.Photograph: Courtesy of PrimeThe new Carrie starts by paying due homage. It opens with the high school gym on fire and frantic 911 calls playing over scenes of the inferno, as it consumes the rest of the school then spreads through the town. The calls segue into reports of 200 deaths, and the flames fade into interviews with survivors and students who knew Carrie. “Shy,” one calls her. “A bully,” says another. “A victim.” “Quiet … genuinely kind.” “A monster.”We then spool backward and get our introduction to Carrie (Summer H Howell) herself. She is found hiding in the “prayer closet” with her mother Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) as the police enter their home. Carrie’s father has been killed at work. None of his co-workers were aware he had a family. Carrie has been home-schooled and never been allowed to venture past the garden walls but she is not the terrified, damaged figure we expect. She is – heartbreakingly, given what is to come – open, curious and keen to experience whatever this new paterfamilias-free life, in which she must go to school and Margaret to work, has to offer. Howell does a wonderful job of playing an essentially good and optimistic character that could easily have become more Anne-of-Green-Gables-with-PMT than a potential hell-raiser driven beyond endurance.Nor is Margaret the religious zealot of the film or its source material. Conservative Christianity is definitely her thing, and she has evidently been influenced by her beloved husband’s controlling character and conspiracist bent, but in Flanagan’s version (and the mesmerising Sloyan brings out every note), this is mixed with real and profound love and fear for her daughter’s safety. She is forced out into the world at the same time as Carrie, and the effects it has on her are as carefully and almost tenderly explored by the series as her daughter’s are. It makes the endeavour noticeably richer and more compelling.Similarly, Carrie’s great tormentor Chris (Alison Thornton) is given reasons – not excuses – for her growing savagery, Sue (Siena Agudong) wrestles with her conscience from the beginning, and the dynamics between them, Carrie and the other friends/acolytes are nicely detailed.But the bullying is the thing. The supernatural powers it unleashes are not quite an afterthought, but they do almost take second place – especially in the early episodes – to the horrors unleashed by Chris and her gang on the new girl. The famous period-in-the-shower scene is of course filmed on mobiles and ends up online via a malevolent Gossip Girl-style account, and countless other cruelties are likewise compounded.Of course this Carrie doesn’t have the raw power of the film. But it has intelligence, wit and things to say about the fathomless potential for good and ill in the teenage heart – and how impossible it is to teach them which way to go.Carrie is on Prime Video nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Only connect: two composers who put humans at the heart of their music, and the conductor who didn’t | Classical music | The Guardian
description: This week, from Reich to Kendall and Celibidache, three musicians who prove there is no such thing as “pure music”, whether we’re talking about a technique, a mode of musical expression or a musician’s legacy.
Author: Tom Service
Headline: This week, from Reich to Kendall and Celibidache, three musicians who prove there is no such thing as “pure music”, whether we’re talking about a technique, a mode of musical expression or a musician’s legacy.
Content: The Paraorchestra perform Steve Reich's Music for 18 Musicians in the Southbank Centre, September 2026.Photograph: Siân O’ConnorView image in fullscreenThe Paraorchestra perform Steve Reich's Music for 18 Musicians in the Southbank Centre, September 2026.Photograph: Siân O’ConnorTom Service on musicClassical musicOnly connect: two composers who put humans at the heart of their music, and the conductor who didn’tTom ServiceThis week, from Reich to Kendall and Celibidache, three musicians who prove there is no such thing as “pure music”, whether we’re talking about a technique, a mode of musical expression or a musician’s legacy.Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.20 EDTShareSteve Reichturned 90 on Saturday, and I’ve been thinking about his early tape pieces from the mid-1960s, It’s Gonna Rain and Come Out. They’re such vital works not only because they opened his imagination to what could happen if you made a micro-canon – playing the same material slightly faster or slower – which is what happened when one of his tape machines slipped out of sync with the other: it’s that these are human voices that Reich is setting.It’s Gonna Rainis made from the voice of Brother Walter, a Pentecostal street preacher in San Francisco, whose warning of apocalypse in 1965 Reich recorded and looped against itself, over and over, so that Brother Walter’s voice becomes a wall and wail of sound, a sonic realisation of the sublime inundation he’s announcing.Come Outwas made in 1966 with the voice of Daniel Hamm, one of theHarlem Six, six black men wrongly convicted of first-degree murder in New York. Reich’s piece was commissioned for a benefit event for their legal costs as “background music for passing the hat”.These pieces don’t just set words, Reich says they “set human beings”, using the vocal recordings not only as musical material but political inspiration and emotional expression. Techniques that are seemingly all about narrowly musical processes – looping, canon-ing, fugue-ing – are embedded in the facts of where they were made and how, and whose voices are being represented by whom.View image in fullscreenConnecting … Hannah KendallPhotograph: Chris AlexanderThat terrain of historical consciousness is essential toHannah Kendall’s music. She is inspired by the idea of the “plantation machine”, Cuban writer Antonio Benítez-Rojo’s phrase, which sums up the industrial processes and global networks of dehumanising capital that powered the slave trade, which are still echoed, for Kendall, by all of today’s machinery of capitalism, from environmental destruction to technological control.These are fascinating and provocative ideas, but it’s how Kendall turns them into visceral musical experience in the way she reworks the sound of ensembles and orchestras that counts. As Kendall puts it, she “creolises” the orchestra, putting dreadlock cuffs on the string instruments to change, mute and distort the sounds they make; her compositions includesound sources and instrumentssuch as walkie-talkies, music boxes, harmonicas and kettles. These reference historical and musical contexts, from the blues to Kendall’s imagination of the music made by enslaved people, including prayers and songs spoken and sung into kettles, to be out of earshot of the plantation owners.Listen toShouting Forever Into the Receiveror her recentBuilding a Burning House, which will be part of theBarbican’s Always, Already Therefestival later this month, followed a few days later by the world premiere of her I Have Discovered the Secret of Death with theLondon Symphony Orchestra, also at the Barbican.Kendall’s music remakes the orchestra to interrogate the histories of trade, slavery, and globalisation that were the machines that made civilisations such as ours function, and to which the instruments, halls, and institutional fabric of the western orchestra are indebted. Her compositions tangibly connect musical culture with the reality of these complex and impure histories.Sergiu Celibidache, meanwhile, is at the forefront of musical minds this week as a biopic of the conductor,The Yellow Tieopens in UK cinemas. The movie – themost watched Romanian film of 2025– tells of his pursuit of music in the face of his father’s fierce opposition, his appointment to the Berlin Philharmonic age 33 and how his single-minded and – supposedly – purist approach to music was born: his belief that any audio recording of a piece of music was a soul-stealing lie that could not represent the reality of live performance. (Although, hundreds of recordings of his work, especially in his later years, were released after his death in 1996.)But here’s another film worth watching, that tells a story about the conductor not told. Abbie Conant: A Solo Among Men.At 25, Conant was appointed Munich Philharmonic’s principal trombone in 1980 after a blind audition, but wasn’t allowed ever meaningfully to take up her job. As Celibidache, the orchestra’s principal conductor, told her: “We need a man for the solo trombone”. He couldn’t really tell her why, Conant relates, but she was demoted to second trombone and her life was made a misery. She was paid less than her male colleagues, she was openly bullied by Celibidache, and when she initiated legal proceedings against the City of Munich (the Philharmonic’s owner) alleging discrimination,she was forced to undergo humiliating medical and physical tests to prove her stamina, lung capacity and ability to play under pressure. It’s a story of multidimensional misogyny. Conant won her case even though it took her over 12 years, and left the orchestra of her own accord in 1993.View image in fullscreenPioneering and brave trombonist Abbie Conant.Photograph: www.osborne-conant.orgMuch of Celibidache’s reputation hangs on the revelations and transcendence of his performances with the Munich Philharmonic, above all, ofBruckner’s symphonies. But hisexcessively slow performances, sonically beautiful, but expressively one-dimensional, often feel to me like a Brucknerian bad joke. Calcifying these symphonies with a one-dimensional monumentalism does the expressive power and contradictions of Bruckner’s music no favours. (Even more of a nadir is Celibidache’s so-slow-it’s-barely-alive performance ofBach’s Mass in B Minor: the opening fugue is a masochistic trial of patience – try it, if you dare.)But whatever you think Celibidache did or didn’t do with the music he conducted: as Conant’s experience shows, if you lose yourself to the revelations of his performances, you have to ignore the human cost they clearly came at. “Purity”, as always, is no such thing, and comes at an inevitably impure price. Reich, like Kendall, understands this and composed and made music with empathy and understanding, rather than following an ideology that would rather pretend that the goal of transcendence is worth subjugating the human.This week, Tom has been listening to:Kristian Bezuidenhout’s latest, thrilling, volume ofMozart’s piano concertos, playing fortepiano with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra. I can’t get enough of these records, and the way that Bezuidenhout plunges you right into the cauldron of the drama he and the players make in the D minor Concerto, or the joy of the D major concerto K175.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicSteve ReichcommentShareReuse this content

title: The 80-year-old market trader who became a Chilean music star | Chile | The Guardian
description: Born and raised in Valparaíso, JM is seen as one of the last of a golden generation after a late foray
Author: John Bartlett
Headline: Born and raised in Valparaíso, JM is seen as one of the last of a golden generation after a late foray
Content: Luis Gómez, known as JM, sings with Los Cracks del Puerto at the SCD Hall in Santiago, Chile. Photograph: Tamara Merino/The GuardianBorn and raised in Valparaíso, JM is seen as one of the last of a golden generation after a late forayByJohn Bartlettin ValparaísoWed 7 Oct 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt a concert hall in the Chilean capital, Santiago, an 80-year-old man edges unsteadily down a steep staircase. With one hand he grips the metal bannister, in the other he carries a mug of hot water with a slice of lemon, as if heading to bed.But when the red stage curtain is pulled aside for him, Luis Gómez, or JM as he is universally known, transforms in an instant. He skips on to the stage to a roar from the crowd and launches into a bolero, punctuated by hip thrusts and shuffling two-steps.JM is the frontman of Los Crack del Puerto, and one of the last remaining voices of a golden generation.Born and raised in Valparaíso, Chile’s vibrant second city, JM’s late foray into music has taken him all around the country, as well as to Mexico, the UK, Argentina and France.View image in fullscreenLuis Gómez was raised in Valparaíso, Chile’s vibrant second city.Photograph: Delphotos/AlamyBut things could – and probably should – have worked out very differently.At 65, he was still hawking vegetables at the market he had worked at since the age of eight.This May, Los Crack del Puerto released their fourth record, Lo Mucho Que Nos Queda (So Much Yet to Come), as a cassette – to great acclaim.“Singing has always been my release,” JM says in a wavering voice, in contrast to his confident onstage vocals.The father of two speaks with captivating enthusiasm about his life, often leaping to his feet to re-enact minor scenes. Scattered with bursts of song, most conversations return to his mostly tongue-in-cheek fear of his wife of 55 years, his penchant for sports clothing, or the market on Avenida Argentina in Valparaíso.View image in fullscreenLuis Gómez, known locally as JM, sings at La Quinta de los Núñez in Valparaíso, Chile.Photograph: Tamara Merino/The GuardianJM was born in the O’Higgins neighbourhood of Valparaíso in 1945, the youngest of five children. He was three years old when his father died, and 10 when he lost his mother. For a time, he would sleep out on the street between parked cars, until his aunt and uncle took him in and laid down the law, insisting that he was home by 10pm each night.“JM” was a cheeky nickname bestowed upon him by the family – the initials of a childhood friend, Juan Muñoz, with whom they said he spent too much time. The moniker has long since replaced his full name.Valparaíso then, as it is now, was defined by its music. As in many ports, cultures and ideas have long arrived in the city and been woven into its fabric; but the musical styles of its 20th-century heyday, from boleros to waltzes, tango to cueca, Chile’s official national dance, have barely changed in generations.“The same songs that were sung before are still the ones they sing now,” says JM decisively. Many now form Los Crack del Puerto’s repertoire.View image in fullscreenJM is one of the most recognised voices of Valparaíso’s traditional music scene.Photograph: Tamara Merino/The GuardianOne of his cousins, Juan Navarro, known simply as Juanín, would bring friends home and play his guitar for them, and the younger JM would come sing along.The cousins remained lifelong friends while Juanín pursued a career in the police and JM sold vegetables at the market.“That’s still what I am – a market trader,” he says.Through middle age, the self-taught double act entertained crowds in Valparaíso’s bars – JM the entertaining foil to his more serious older cousin, who would perch on a stool to play his guitar, always in an immaculate pressed suit.View image in fullscreenJM and Juanín began to take their music more seriously and formed a band with a group of local musicians in 2017.Photograph: Tamara Merino/The Guardian“Sometimes Juanín would just invent chords,” says Los Crack del Puerto’s manager, Juan Nuñez. “The rest of the band would stop and ask him what chord he’d just played, and he’d just shrug.”“JM was the entertainer, he can make anyone laugh,” Nuñez adds.But the dynamic worked. In 2017, JM and Juanín began taking their music more seriously, forming the band with a group of talented local musicians.“That generation is an intangible cultural heritage. They’re a living legacy,” says 33-year-old musician Felipe Riveros, who has played with JM as a guitarist.“He’s charismatic. People go mad when he comes on stage. He and Juanín are the archetypes of the oldporteño.”Juanín died in 2025 at the age of 87.“For three or four months, I missed him so much, I couldn’t bring myself to get back on stage,” says JM of his cousin. “People would request Juanín’s songs, but they were his, I didn’t feel like we could play them.”Now, as JM approaches his 81st birthday, the royalty cheques that supplement his miserly state pension are of little consequence to him.“I never planned any of this, and I’d be happy still working at the market,” he says quietly during a break between songs at the Quinta de los Nuñez, a hillside restaurant where he sings every Sunday for an adoring crowd.“But I suppose it’s never too late to give something a try.”Explore more on these topicsChileAmericasFolk musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Men are a scam!’ The trials of Danielle Ponder, the lawyer turned singer rooting for a better world | Music | The Guardian
description: After representing society’s dispossessed, Ponder started a music career in her 40s – then faced miscarriage, anxiety and more. She explains her survival instinct
Author: Iman Amrani
Headline: After representing society’s dispossessed, Ponder started a music career in her 40s – then faced miscarriage, anxiety and more. She explains her survival instinct
Content: ‘I have faith in my ability to survive’ … Danielle Ponder.Photograph: Faith JoyvonView image in fullscreen‘I have faith in my ability to survive’ … Danielle Ponder.Photograph: Faith JoyvonMusicInterview‘Men are a scam!’ The trials of Danielle Ponder, the lawyer turned singer rooting for a better worldIman AmraniAfter representing society’s dispossessed, Ponder started a music career in her 40s – then faced miscarriage, anxiety and more. She explains her survival instinctWed 7 Oct 2026 06.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“You can get everything you dreamed of career-wise, and your life can still crumble, and that is what happened to me,” says US singer-songwriter Danielle Ponder.Five years ago, and five days before her 40th birthday, Ponder left her job as a public defender – a lawyer for those without the means to pay for one – to pursue music full-time. Ponder’s rich, church-reared voice and resonant music quickly lent themselves to cinematic moments: she wrote and performed the theme song for Apple TV+’s Manhunt and her trip-hop-infused track Roll the Credits has been used by adverts, TV shows and video games. Several comments on the YouTube video come from viewers who searched for it thinking she was Nina Simone. Her debut album, Some of Us Are Brave, came out in 2022 and was warmly received by critics, and she appeared on Seth Meyers’ talkshow. Her gamble had paid off. “But personally,” she says, “it felt like everything around me was falling apart”.Ponder had become a public defender in her native Rochester in northern New York state, after watching her brother receive a 20-year prison sentence for a robbery in which nobody was physically harmed. She was 16 at the time. “Because of where I grew up and the experiences my family had, I was very familiar with injustice in the system,” she says. “Being a public defender just confirmed that.” She’s seen a teenage boy in a cell for not having a bell on his bike, watched a 76-year-old man on dialysis sent to prison for driving on a suspended license and witnessed women – predominantly Black women – lose access to their children, “not for abuse, but for things that are considered as neglect, which is actually poverty”.View image in fullscreen‘I’m trying to embody the divinity of being a woman’ … Danielle Ponder.Photograph: Faith JoyvonWhat she saw in her job reinforced her family’s experience of prisons being “breeding grounds for violence” that don’t address the root causes around poverty and crime. “We’ve created a billion-dollar criminal justice industry, a billion-dollar nonprofit industry, to police and ‘nurse’ the community as opposed to looking at living wages, affordable housing, reparations.” She sighs wearily. “It’s a dying culture, a sick culture, that I’m at the end of my ropes with.”Ponder poured themes of race, injustice and heartbreak into her songs, but the transition from the legal system into the music industry wasn’t smooth. She took every detail of the process as seriously as she had as a lawyer: “I had so much anxiety because I was approaching it like I was approaching someone going to prison.” And as she was starting again in her 40s – “I do feel very sensitive to time” – Ponder struggled with the pressure she put on herself: “I ruined relationships. I got consumed by my pain and my grief. I couldn’t focus, couldn’t write.”The title of her new album, Everything Has Changed, refers to how her life crumbled after her initial success: her brother-in-law died, her father deteriorated with dementia, and she had a miscarriage. A new song, Blues, documents her compound sadness, including stark imagery of her miscarriage: “Crimson colour covered me / buried bones where there were seeds.” It’s offset by God of You, a full-bodied ballad complete with horns and Ponder belting out lyrics to a man with feet of clay – even screaming at him. “That’s a real fucking scream,” she says. “The shit I went through” – the relationship and miscarriage – “ended up being a nightmare.”The miscarriage happened two weeks before the deadline of a song that she was working on with Adrian Quesada from blues and soul outfit Black Pumas. “I just ended up saying I had a personal loss, and I just can’t complete the song right now. Why couldn’t I say I had a miscarriage?” Ponder was battling feelings of shame. “When your grief feels shameful, then the community can’t really offer you the love that you need,” she says. And if you’re in a difficult relationship like hers, it can be that you feel “really out here by yourself”.Ponder has also spilled candid thoughts on to her Substack newsletter, including about the patriarchal ways women are conditioned to relinquish power to men in relationships and religion. She was raised by a pastor who forbade secular music at home but she speaks lovingly of his influence on her, of “wanting people to leave feeling better than they did when they came in”. I ask her head-on if she is a woman of faith. She pauses for a while. “I have faith in my ability to survive. As women, we fail to acknowledge the power within us. As Christians or religious people, we fail to acknowledge that power, and we give it to a man.”She says this album is the last time she wants to speak about bad relationships with men; she doesn’t explicitly swear off them, but she’s more interested in pouring her power into friendships with women. “This is where unconditional love comes from,” she says. “Men are a scam!” Just as in her songwriting, though, these strong feelings are offset with reflection. “Men are actually very emotional and emotionally fragile,” Ponder says: afraid of, and submissive to, religion, the military and Trump. “It would be a service to them for the truth to be revealed,” that they are indeed submissive and afraid. “They could stop trying to pretend so much.”‘I’m an ever-changing vessel’: Erykah Badu on defying definition, life as a birth and death doula and her first album in 11 yearsRead moreBut after her years of strife, there’s a hint at Ponder’s current mindset in her latest music videos, all shot in Dakar, Senegal. She first went there on a life-changing school trip aged 17, and she finds it to be much less restrictive than the US in terms of art; less tainted by capitalism or a drive to go viral. “It just feels like hip-hop in the 80s,” she says. The videos feature Ponder radiating in opulent outfits, looking like a goddess among beautiful models and dancers. “I’m really trying to embody the divinity of being a woman,” she says – another way of saying she has faith in herself.Everything Has Changedis released 9 October via Dead OceansExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockSoulMiscarriageWomenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Blockers by Michael Lewis review – the quiet heroes who tried to stop Doge | Politics books | The Guardian
description: The author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusade
Author: Sam Freedman
Headline: The author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusade
Content: Elon Musk at the CPAC conference in 2025.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreenElon Musk at the CPAC conference in 2025.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersBook of the dayPolitics booksReviewBlockers by Michael Lewis review – the quiet heroes who tried to stop DogeThe author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusadeSam FreedmanWed 7 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 03.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American government are slowly disintegrating.It is harder to get people to focus on the machinery of the state because the effects are often slow and hard to pin down. Outbreaks of disease – such as the recent wave ofexplosive diarrhoeaacross the US – might have happened anyway, but were probably made worse by lay-offs at the Centers for Disease Control. Likewise, Trump is not directly responsible for natural disasters, but response times in the past year may have been hampered by mass redundancies at the National Weather Service. Cuts to tax collection also seem to have reduced revenue by multiple billions, though we cannot be sure of the causal relationship.The other problem is that bureaucracies are hard to make interesting. Their work is technical and complicated, and most officials are taught to avoid saying anything engaging in public. By the time a journalist has explained what an agency does and why it is important, the reader may well have clicked on to the next thing.So there are few better suited to the challenge of telling this story than Michael Lewis, one of the world’s bestselling nonfiction writers, who has a knack for finding an angle that cuts through the complexity. After a career spent getting readers excited about credit default swaps (The Big Short) and sabermetrics (Moneyball) he has decided to try to help people understand the importance of civil servants.double quotation markMusk’s overweening arrogance, glibness and total lack of preparation have seriously harmed the case for proper reformBlockers is a loose sequel to the The Fifth Risk, in which Lewis focused on the transition from the Obama to the Trump administration and the disruption caused by the new team’s almost complete lack of interest in their jobs. It focused heavily on what different departments and agencies do and why they matter. This time around the problem is not indifference but malicious intent to destroy. The “blockers” are the dedicated officials who try to stop the wanton and often illegal destruction of their life’s work by Elon Musk’s Doge or other agents of chaos. They range from a researcher working on preventing wildfires to a security guard trying to block Musk’s goons from entering his building, and a lawyer attempting to keep personal tax data from being used to deport undocumented migrants.In truth, they don’t do much blocking – since they all either end up resigning when they’re asked to do something illegal, or are fired. The title refers more to the assumption by Musk and his fellow travellers that these are the people who are stopping progress and need removing. Much of the book is taken up with descriptions of the valuable work they did before being turfed out.It would have been good to have a bit more on the villains, whose motivations for participating in Doge are varied. They range from the addled young coders with limited social skills deployed by Musk, to turncoat bureaucrats looking for any easy life, and some very strange characters such as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, with his bizarre obsession with dead animal parts.
