Trump’s absurd commerce secretary Howard Lutnick also makes a brief cameo, deciding he needs to personally sign off any cheque for more than $100,000. It feels as if there is more to say about the personal journeys that lead people to behave this way.This is the particularly true of the boss baddie Russell Vought, the Republican operative central to developing the Project 2025 plans for Trump’s second term. Musk causes havoc, but quickly gets bored of Doge and heads back to Silicon Valley. Vought is the real deal, quietly and systematically deconstructing the state while keeping out of the spotlight and getting others to do his dirty work for him.He appears in one of the book’s most engaging chapters, which zooms in on Francis Collins, a scientist who helped discover a successful treatment for cystic fibrosis, allowing those with the condition to live much longer. Collins ended up at the head of the National Institutes of Health under Obama, continued through Trump’s first term and part of Biden’s, before stepping down to run an NIH research lab. After Trump’s re-election he was effectively forced out, saying that his position had become “untenable”. Lewis runs through a series of possible culprits, of which Vought’s cost-cutting is one. What makes this particularly remarkable is that Vought’s own daughter has cystic fibrosis. Ideology is a powerful drug.But perhaps the most interesting character of all is Sahil Lavingia. A successful software engineer, he bought into Musk’s vision and went to work for Doge in the Department of Veterans Affairs. He only lasted 55 days before giving an on-the-record interview in which he noted that “it’s kind of fine – because the government works. It’s not as inefficient as I was expecting, to be honest. I was hoping for more easy wins.” This was not on-message and he was shown the door.A few months later, though, once Doge had fallen apart, he was invited back by one of the few survivors, who had stayed on at the Treasury department. Lavingia was tasked with improving the Internal Revenue Service’s computer systems, and despite not needing the money, seems genuinely committed to the task of making things work better. Through Lavingia, Lewis gives us a taste of what serious work to enhance the state might have looked like.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are real problems with the way the government operates, both in the UK and the US, caused by poor resourcing, dysfunctional systems, or low pay for technical staff compared with the private sector. Alongside Lewis’s star civil servants, there are people who have checked out or become institutionalised. Lavingia’s lengthy battle to get a water cooler replaced reminded me of how difficult it was to get the lifts working when I was at the Department for Education.One of the most irritating aspects of Doge’s brief existence was the stream of op-eds from people who really should have known better celebrating that someone was finally trying to enact reform, even if was being done in a clumsy and aggressive manner. In reality, Musk’s overweening arrogance, glibness and total lack of preparation have seriously harmed the case for proper reform. Not just due to the mess he and the likes of Vought caused, but also because they brought the very idea of making the state more efficient into disrepute.Lewis is great at finding incredible civil servants and telling their stories. But agencies and departments should not have to rely on unsung heroes, battling failing systems, and doing 90-hour weeks for little money because of their intense devotion to public service. Most people employed by large organisations are not like that. Effective government needs processes that work when used by a regular person doing a nine-to-five job. Rather than trying to replicate the “blockers”, we need to understand what these superstars are doing and embed it in the fabric of our institutions.Sam Freedman is a former special adviser and author of Failed State (Macmillan). title: Other Worlds Than These by Stephen King and Peter Straub review – a self-indulgent finale to the Talisman trilogy | Stephen King | The Guardian
description: There are moments of shivering joy as the protagonist of two enduring classics, Jack Sawyer, returns – but this time his journey feels endlessly repetitive
Author: Alison Flood
Headline: There are moments of shivering joy as the protagonist of two enduring classics, Jack Sawyer, returns – but this time his journey feels endlessly repetitive
Content: Moments of true horror … Stephen King.Photograph: Ulf Andersen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMoments of true horror … Stephen King.Photograph: Ulf Andersen/Getty ImagesStephen KingReviewOther Worlds Than These by Stephen King and Peter Straub review – a self-indulgent finale to the Talisman trilogyThere are moments of shivering joy as the protagonist of two enduring classics, Jack Sawyer, returns – but this time his journey feels endlessly repetitiveAlison FloodWed 7 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBear with me, because there is some backstory to get through before we can talk about the book I am actually here to review. Back in 1984, Stephen King and Peter Straub collaborated on the fantasy novel The Talisman. Like all the best King stories, it follows a young boy: in this case Jack Sawyer, 12, whose mother, Lily, is dying. Jack learns that a magical object called the Talisman might save her – if he can find it in a parallel world known as the Territories. Straub and King followed this up in 2001 withBlack House, in which an adult Jack investigates a series of child murders that turn out to have disturbing links to the Territories.The books are very different: one a coming-of-age cross-country quest, in which Jack flips back and forth between two versions of the US; the other a fantastical and horror-inflected murder mystery. Both are brilliant and enduring classics which will always have a place on my bookshelves – I reread both of them, all 1,800-odd pages, to prepare for Other Worlds Than These and was as swept away and delighted as the first time round.double quotation markI cannot recommend that anyone who is not a Constant Reader embark on this 800-plus-page tomeSo: in 2013 Straub had an idea for a final volume in the Talisman trilogy, drawing as Black House does from a real-life series of murders, and returning Jack (previously left on a bit of a cliffhanger) to the fray. King didn’t pick up on it back then, and Straubdied in 2022. Now King is 79, and, as he writes in a somewhat valedictory afterword, “it’s time to think about tidying up, as much as such things are possible for a writer whose mind is still crammed with cool ideas”. So he went back to that old idea – the original email lost, but the concept of a “series of motiveless, brutal crimes” in the Far West of the Territories, as Straub put it, at the story’s heart.Jack, “his tide … going out”, is now 57. An aimless, lonely émigré to the Territories, he is sent on a mission by the two-bit despot he now depressingly reports to. He’s to travel through the toxic Blasted Lands to gather information on the Great Gorge, a mysterious area of “growing danger” that Governor Youngblood wants to know more about. Flipping back and forth between “America-side” and the Territories, Jack learns that an old policeman friend has gone missing on the trail of a pair of “murderin’ kids” who have been leaving a swathe of bodies in their wake in Nebraska. These kids are, he’s told, “infested” by demons – and the infestation is spreading to the children of the Territories.For the true King fan (the “Constant Reader”, as he puts it), there are moments of shivering joy in Other Worlds Than These – not least in the title, which draws from a key scene in King’s The Gunslinger. I could never not find pleasure in a billy-bumbler (a dog-like creature), or in memories of Wolf, a wonderful creation from The Talisman, or in references to chief gunslinger Roland Deschain from the Dark Tower series. As befits King, there are moments of true horror too, and good ones, as the teenage infection spreads across the Territories.But I cannot recommend that anyone who is not a Constant Reader embark on this 800-plus-page tome. For one, it would be pointless to read it without previously having read The Talisman and Black House (and if I’m honest, probably the seven-volume Dark Tower sequence too). And even for the Constant Reader, this is really not vintage King. I would have said that I’d follow Jack Sawyer anywhere, but as Ole Travellin’ Jack crisscrossed his way across the dry desert land of the Territories, his journey started to feel endless, and endlessly repetitive. As Jack’s crew are gearing up to cross yet another rickety bridge over yet another gaping chasm, one character even makes this point when they spot it. “Oh God … talk about repetition.” I hear you, fella! Jack himself does it: “Another echo. They’re becoming tiresome,” he says, in a rather too on-the-nose comment about the eerie (not so eerie the nth time they’re mentioned) similarities between the US and the Territories.Is this deliberate? Yes, undoubtedly: “ka [destiny] is a wheel”, as we’ve been told (more than once); Jack, as Roland did before him, is treading the path laid out for him in an endless cycle. But this time round, it all gets a little portentous, self-referential and self-indulgent – and, dare I say it, boring.I still thinkStephen Kingis a genius. I still think The Talisman is the perfect coming-of-age dark fantasy novel. So thank you for the endless hours of reading pleasure, Mr King. But unlike its predecessors, Other Worlds Than These will not be going on my reread shelf.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Content: An investment … Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenAn investment … Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection.Photograph: Rockstar GamesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Pushing Buttons newsletterGamesWhat the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gamingThe launch of a collector’s box hints at a new reality: the kinds of games I grew up with are becoming a luxury item, locked behind a forbidding spending barrierDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a parent (and partner) to a habitual collector, I do feel like an unwelcome portion of my life is occupied by an endless war against stuff. Surfaces in my home ceaselessly accumulate piles of random objects: a JoyCon wrist strap, a sticker sheet, an unidentifiable plastic piece of a toy or gizmo, an Xbox 360 controller with no batteries, cases for Switch cartridges lost down the side of the sofa … Stuff encroaches everywhere, especially in a gaming household. Much as I regret theimminent disappearance of physical games, I do not regret the extra space I have in my attic as a result of switching almost entirely to downloaded games over the last decade or so.Speaking of the imminent disappearance of physical games: Rockstar recently announced a £350 ($400) “collector’s box” of Grand Theft Auto 6 goodies … that doesn’t include the game itself. Not even a download code. The Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection, to give it its full and unwieldy name, contains a hat, a bag, a pair of sunglasses, a figurine, a poster and more, including a mirror and a “swizzle spoon” that looks, unambigiously, like a cocaine spoon. The game retails at £70, so if you want something to play alongside all your stuff, you’re looking at an outlay of £420.I’m not about to rag on this box of merch. People love this kind of stuff, and as a lifelong collector of Japanese gatcha and blind-box toys, I am in no position to judge how people spend their money. I have a few video game special editions that I cherish – the statue that came with my copy of The Last Guardian is still on my shelf – though I also have many more that are relegated to various cupboards. But it is unusual, however, for them to be this expensive. Usually with gaming special editions, we’re talking an extra £20-50 for a statue, or a steelbook, maybe a booklet and a keyring. 2009’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s “prestige edition”came with night vision gogglesfor $150. In 2015, Fallout 4’s $120 collector’s edition shipped with aplastic Pip Boywrist unit (I had one; alas, it was flimsy and disappointing).There have been some infamously expensive gaming special editions down the years, some of which were PR stunts (see Saints Row IV’smillion-dollar pack, which included a Lamborghini and cosmetic surgery – nobody bought it). But in the 2020s high-priced video game merchandise has become more common, from a Balenciaga PlayStation tie-in line to£580 for Pokémon Lego.View image in fullscreenPriced out … expensive video games and merch have now become a luxury item.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesWhat’s behind this is a troubling sense that video games as we once conceived of them – console games, played at home, perhaps on a nice 4K TV – have become a luxury item. People who can afford to spendup to £790for a console and games are perhaps now people who can afford an extra £350 for a box of merch.Continual price-risesfrom Xbox and PlayStation suggest that video game companies do not seem particularly worried about pricing people out. Super-expensive merch and special editions like GTA 6’s form part of the same upward trend.This stratification of the gaming world has been happening for years, ever since the first smartphones. The vast majority of the world’s players – about 80%, according toNewzoo– play for free, or at low cost, on mobile phones. The remaining 20% of players account for a disproportionate share of spending on the high-end gaming market on consoles and PC. With merch boxes like this, games companies are really going after that 20% for all they’ve got.I’m saddened by the idea of gaming becoming even more of a luxury hobby. On the one hand, games in the broadest sense are more accessible than ever – you’re three taps away from playing Monopoly Go on a phone at any moment. But the kinds of games I grew up with and love to write about, games that feel like worlds rather than temporary diversions, are now increasingly locked behind a spending barrier. With the increasing scarcity of physical discs and cartridges, you can’t even reliably buy them second hand any more.I guess there’s one advantage to the increasing cost of collector’s editions: the price has removed any lingering temptation to buy them. God knows I donotneed more stuff.What to playView image in fullscreenA game to sit back and wallow in … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17Keith has been playing Silver Pines, a neo-noir detective drama with point-and-click adventure sensibilities. “As I played, I discovered countless references to 80s and 90s neo-noir culture – from Blue Velvet to Twin Peaks,” he writesin our review.“It was a pleasure to explore every broken-down movie theatre, oily car garage and sweat-stinking interrogation room, collecting weird trinkets and working out how they’d all fit together – then exploring them again (and again) when the answers failed to show up. Silver Pines is a game to sit back and wallow in, like a private eye, kicking off his wingtip shoes and pulling that bottle of bourbon from the bottom drawer as rain trickles down the window and sodium street lights paint the walls a sickly shade of yellow.”Available on:PC, PS5, Switch 2Estimated playtime:12 hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenFarewell, Ninja Theory … Hellblade 2.Photograph: Ninja TheoryAward-winningUK studio Ninja Theoryhasreportedlybegun laying off staff. The creator of Hellblade was one of the developers affected byMicrosoft’s programme of lay-offsand studio closures in July, and according to Xbox COO Matt Booty two agreements to keep the studio running have failed. It is a sad end to one of the UK’s most interesting development houses.Meanwhile, Windows Centralobtained the transcriptto a recent in-house meeting held for Xbox staff by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. In it, Sharma refers to the next generation Xbox platform currently known asProject Helixas “a family of devices” rather than a single console. “There is not one device that fits all,” she stated. “We will certainly have a great console first, but we also know that many players will be on the go.” Could the ROG Xbox Ally, launched in partnership with Asus last year, have just been a beta test for a fully fledged handheld Xbox?The news site GamesIndustry.Biz hasan interesting featureonZach Cregger’s Resident Evil movieand how it has affected the Resident Evil games. Although the film led to a modest uptick in sales, the real value of movie and TV tie-ins, according to industry analysts, is that they keep those franchises in the minds of gamers so that subsequent titles benefit from the exposure. As game development cycles continue to widen, it looks like we can expect a lot more movies and TV shows to fill in the gaps.What to clickFrom Super Bowl champ to master architect: Mike Tomlin’s sprawling Minecraft city is magnificentGears of War: E-Day – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenGet cozy … Flame, Forest and Flood.Photograph: Fairy Mount GamesA question from my friendDavidvia email:“I keep hearing that game publishers are avoiding the whole of November because of GTA 6– will there really be NO choice for those of us who don’t want to shoot stuff and run people over?”Thankfully, it’s only the big western publishers who are staying clear of the GTA 6 launch window – lots of other developers are diving in regardless. Cozy strategy gameFlame, Forest and Flood(try saying that three times) is launching on the same day as GTA, offering a delightful tactical alternative, set in a hex-based woodland idyl. Staying on a rural theme, the purposefully rage-inducing “precision platformer”Trees Hate Youis a woodland hiking game, where you are attacked by nature. Alternatively,Football Manager 2027is arriving on 10 November, so instead of leading a gang of drug dealers into a bloody turf war, you could lead Plymouth Argyle into the Premier League. I’m not sure which scenario is more challenging.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Robert Ryman review – can your brain handle a show that only has white paintings? | Painting | The Guardian
description: What seem at first indistinguishable canvases offer challenges, revelations and transcendental effects – but only if you can give yourself over to them
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: What seem at first indistinguishable canvases offer challenges, revelations and transcendental effects – but only if you can give yourself over to them
Content: Bare-bones … Surface Veil, 1970 by Robert Ryman.Photograph: Robert Ryman / DACS, London. Photo: Bill Jacobson Studio, © The Greenwich Collection, New York.View image in fullscreenBare-bones … Surface Veil, 1970 by Robert Ryman.Photograph: Robert Ryman / DACS, London. Photo: Bill Jacobson Studio, © The Greenwich Collection, New York.PaintingReviewRobert Ryman review – can your brain handle a show that only has white paintings?Barbican Art Gallery, LondonWhat seem at first indistinguishable canvases offer challenges, revelations and transcendental effects – but only if you can give yourself over to themBen EasthamWed 7 Oct 2026 10.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWriting about painting is a futile exercise at the best of times. This is especially the case when, as with Robert Ryman, the paintings in question are variations on the theme of white. If that sounds pretentious – or like a tired joke – then it might also be understood as a reaction against the dependence of so much art on language (which is also to say, bullshit). Because these bare-bones paintings – white paint, a flat surface, wall fixtures – are the “real thing” in the most literal way: they are not trying to tell you a story, they do not require you to be familiar with any abstruse theories. There is just you and the materials, how the paint lies, how it scatters the light. So the question is: how much do you like looking at paint?Happily for me, given that it is a non-negotiable part of my job, I really like looking at paint. If you also like looking at paint, then there is much in this exhibition that will take your breath away. Take ThePaintingof the Mysterious Shadow from the mid-60s, after Ryman had left his job as a guard at MoMA, having given up on a career as a jazz musician, and settled into the project that would occupy the rest of his life. Six thick white stripes run horizontally across the canvas, as close to each other as can be managed by a steady hand without overlapping. The fabric is stretched over a deep wooden frame, meaning that its surface sits about three inches off the wall, and casts a thin shadow upon it. That’s your lot.View image in fullscreenThere is much that will take your breath away … The Real Thing installation view, Barbican Art Gallery.Photograph: © Thomas Adank/ Barbican CentreAnd it is a lot, if you are willing to go with it. Under this diffuse light, and against the warmer white of the walls, the surface of the painting comes to look grey-bluish. Because the eye adjusts the intensity of a colour by reference to those surrounding it, the previously imperceptible difference between those two shades of paint comes to seem dramatic. When I opened up my notebook to record this effect, I found that its pages, which had been white, were now a ghastly yellow-brown. This is exemplary of how Ryman’s intense focus on a narrow band of perception opens up worlds within it. And if you can sustain the same level of attention through the show, it will offer up revelations.Because Ryman could do it all, within his tightly circumscribed field. His use of different white paints allows you to focus on how his handling of the material, by turns delicate and heavy handed, rough and precise, changes its effects. The gorgeous scuff of white cloud looks like it would lift the work titled Concert to the ceiling, were it not for the four screws fixing its fibreglass surface so conspicuously to the wall; an untitled 1958 work is slathered in a bilious yellow-white that, in combination with Ryman’s cartoonish signature, conjures a welcome energy. The numinous Surface Veil II stages the meeting of some lavender-tinted atmospherics with a cold front on a monumental scale. Most remarkable of all is the 13-part suite Standard, here installed as an immersive environment that stays just the right side of the forced transcendentalism that so dates the work of some of his peers.View image in fullscreenRyman could do it all … Untitled, 1962.Photograph: Robert Ryman / DACS, London. Photo: Bill Jacobson Studio, © The Greenwich Collection, New York.These effects are made possible by the Barbican’s intelligent installation. Recognising that this is a demanding show even for true believers, benches direct viewers to the works most likely to open up under the pressure of their gaze. Refreshingly clear and intelligent texts are removed from the immaculate walls to a well-designed pamphlet. And yet, even as my eye adjusted to the point that I could identify (even revel in) the fractional discrepancies of white that animate these works, the law of diminishing returns began to take effect. And the question at the back of my mind returned to the front: does any of this matter? Is all of this just an exercise in academic connoisseurship?In defences against that claim, Ryman’s work is vulnerable to what you might call the emperor’s new clothes inverted: namely, that if you present an art historian with a plain piece of white fabric, they will tell you that they have discovered the emperor beneath it. Ryman was not interested in justifying his paintings by grandiose theories, and neither am I. Instead, he chased after an indefinable “wellbeing and rightness” that might be understood as a harmonious arrangement of homogenous elements. Because Ryman’s unframed paintings bleed into the white walls, this rightness comes to be a function of the architectural environment. The gallery resembles heaven as imagined by a 1950s melodrama.It might be that I am not ready for heaven. Because I came to feel trapped in this controlled space, so thoroughly insulated from the outside world. Neither the crises through which Ryman lived (as the literature notes) nor those of the present can penetrate it. His intense focus on a narrow band of colour might provide a momentary refuge from the stories that are crowding in on our lives. But there is no neutral colour, and no neutral space. In our historical moment, this show feels more like an escape from reality than a confrontation with it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRobert Ryman: The Real Thing is at Barbican Art Gallery, London, from 8 October to 28 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsPaintingArtBarbicanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Hungry Ghost review – this sexy, juicily spooky romcom is a scream | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Mei Leng Yew’s smart play veers between humour and horror as a young woman ignores her mum’s warning about big life changes during a ghost festival
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Mei Leng Yew’s smart play veers between humour and horror as a young woman ignores her mum’s warning about big life changes during a ghost festival
Content: Deliciously vile … Mei Mac as Girl in The Hungry Ghost.Photograph: Corinne CummingView image in fullscreenDeliciously vile … Mei Mac as Girl in The Hungry Ghost.Photograph: Corinne CummingTheatreReviewThe Hungry Ghost review – this sexy, juicily spooky romcom is a screamBush theatre, LondonMei Leng Yew’s play veers between humour and horror as a young woman ignores her mum’s warning about big life changes during a ghost festivalKate WyverWed 7 Oct 2026 07.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith shapeshifting performances and smart, heartfelt writing, Mei Leng Yew’s juicily spooky romcom is a seductively assured debut about second-generation family dynamics, the all-in nature of a new relationship, and the internal battles of a young woman trying to work out what she wants.You must not make any big decisions during the traditional Chinese Ghost festival, our protagonist’s mum warns, or else the hungry ghosts will get you. But Girl (My Neighbour Totoro’s Mei Mac) already has her bags packed to move in with her secret girlfriend of three months and nothing is as powerful as lesbians ready to U-Haul. Except perhaps a third-wheeling ghost with severe attachment issues, played giddily by Bridgerton’s Isabella Wei.As the excitable ghost climbs into Girl’s body, everything is new and tasty to her (except porridge, she realises with tongue-scraping disgust). Ailin Conant’s sensuous direction has Wei following then dragging Mac, manipulating Girl’s body and voice and capacity for consumption until she is a bottomless pit of need. Yimei Zhao’s sly set enables charming stage trickery as meals and shrines and escape-hatch windows appear. When food spills across the stage, it becomes a knees-on-the floor, arms-scooping, mouth-open-wide affair – but still not enough to fill up the hungry ghost.View image in fullscreenFood for thought … Mei Mac and Isabella Wei in The Hungry Ghost.Photograph: Corinne CummingMac and Wei are gorgeous together, twisting across the stage as they vie for space in Girl’s skin (movement direction by Jasmine Chiu), with Cantonese gliding alongside English as the ghost escalates Girl’s sense of being pulled in opposing directions. As the situation escalates, the show veers between bright comedy and grotesque horror. A tongue, in particular, serves up a deliciously vile moment for the squeamish to look away.‘Like swapping a Bentley for a Ferrari’: can the Harry Potter stage show survive being chopped in half?Read moreMac slips out of herself to play everyone else in the story: her bubbly girlfriend, her concerned mother, the disinterested officer called to the scene when the ghost’s hunger disrupts the fruit aisle at Sainsbury’s. The stage smells of incense sticks and oranges as the girl discovers she can collide the scattered parts of herself rather than be torn apart by them; this isn’t the kind of horror to leave everyone dead on stage. A late ghostly subplot earns less of your attention, but this dark, sexy, comic production is a treat for the taste buds.AtBush theatre, London, until 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreBush theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Thatcherism via the Walkman: Stuart Hall’s British cultural studies preserved online  | Stuart Hall | The Guardian
description: Project lead says it celebrates ‘incredible contributions’ Jamaica-born sociologist made to Britain’s culture
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Project lead says it celebrates ‘incredible contributions’ Jamaica-born sociologist made to Britain’s culture
Content: Stuart Hall in 2007. He used the Sony Walkman as a case study of how social, cultural and economic life can be expressed through a single technology.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverView image in fullscreenStuart Hall in 2007. He used the Sony Walkman as a case study of how social, cultural and economic life can be expressed through a single technology.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverStuart HallThatcherism via the Walkman: Stuart Hall’s British cultural studies preserved onlineProject lead says it celebrates ‘incredible contributions’ Jamaica-born sociologist made to Britain’s cultureChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentWed 7 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhether it was Thatcherism, populism or the story of the Sony Walkman, Stuart Hall was a public intellectual famed for defining the times. Now a majordigital archiveof his previously unpublished papers, notebooks, recordings and videos has been launched.When the Jamaica-born sociologist and seminal figure in postwar Black British history died in 2014 aged 82, hisobituaryin the Guardian said he had been “among the first to identify key questions of the age”. Hall coined the term Thatcherism and in 1985 warned of the dangers of “authoritarian populism”.TheUniversity of Birmingham, where Hall developed the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies, has digitised and released more than 3,100 items donated by his widow, the historian Catherine Hall.They include notebooks, index cards, his abandoned doctoral thesis and hours of previously inaccessible audio and video tracing the evolution of cultural studies, all within an interactive database.View image in fullscreenHall’s notes, charting the development of cultural studies, have been preserved in the archive.Photograph: University of BirminghamAlso released are his “Origins of the new left” lecture, notebooks on “race and moral panics”, andEncoding/Decoding Cybernetics, a research project exploring Hall’s impact on the architecture of large language models.In response to the era of artificial intelligence, and the questions it raises about culture, copyright and corporate power, the academics behind theStuart Hall Archive Projecthave barred AI bots from accessing the data.The Cadbury Research Library, which has catalogued the original papers, has run the digital archive through a programme that “poisons the data” for bots.The project lead, Dr Rebecca Roach, working with Helen Fisher and Dr Katherine Parson, said they did not create the archive “just for AI to scrape” and commercialise. She said the platform was built to ensure “it doesn’t replicate the exploitation of people of colour and their cultural heritage that technology has historically enabled”.View image in fullscreenA notebook with the handwritten title After Columbus.Photograph: University of Birmingham“One of the things that was really central to us developing theStuart Halldigital site was to think about what can we learn from Hall’s ideas – and how can we apply that to our current moment with machine learning,” Roach said.Hall died before the AI era fully arrived, but he left a body of work with which to interpret it. His theory of representation – examining how media builds meaning through language, symbols and cultural codes – remains relevant amid concerns aboutalgorithmic bias. Doing Cultural Studies, a textbook he co-authored, used theWalkmanas a case study of how social, cultural and economic life could be expressed through a single technology.Roach said it was important to celebrate Black British intellectuals who had made “incredible contributions” to British culture, and noted that while scholars had sometimes been “a bit sniffy” about popular culture, Hall was at its forefront. She called him “a guiding figure for making the world better”.Alongside the archive, Roach has produced learning materials for primary schoolchildren, while the art collective Vivid Projects has made a zine called Dear Stuart.University of Birmingham students have created Walking with Hall, a virtual tour of campus landmarks, raising questions about what it meant for the academic to walk in the shadow of Joseph Chamberlain, the imperialist statesman who founded the university.Classically educated in Jamaica, Hall came to Britain in 1951 on a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, became the founding editor of New Left Review, and worked as a supply teacher in Brixton before pursuing his academic career.View image in fullscreenHall is considered a seminal figure in postwar Black British history.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianHe met Catherine on an anti-nuclear march in 1963; they moved to Birmingham, where their two children were born and where he made his university department a beacon for debate on media, race, politics, Marxism and critical theory.From 1997 to 2000 he served on the Runnymede Trust’s commission on the future of multi-ethnic Britain, going on to collaborate with young artists and film-makers, and in 2005 he was made a fellow of the British Academy.Calling the archive “an extraordinary resource”, Prof Daniel McNeil, the Stuart Hall interdisciplinary chair at Birmingham University, said Hall “transformed how we think about culture, identity, power and belonging”.Explore more on these topicsStuart HallUniversity of BirminghamAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Eva Marie Saint obituary | Movies | The Guardian
description: Oscar-winning actor celebrated for her outstanding performances in On the Waterfront and North By Northwest
Author: Ronald Bergan
Headline: Oscar-winning actor celebrated for her outstanding performances in On the Waterfront and North By Northwest
Content: Eva Marie Saint with Cary Grant in the 1959 film North By Northwest, directed by Alfred Hitchcock.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenEva Marie Saint with Cary Grant in the 1959 film North By Northwest, directed by Alfred Hitchcock.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyMoviesObituaryEva Marie Saint obituaryOscar-winning actor celebrated for her outstanding performances in On the Waterfront and North By NorthwestRonald BerganWed 7 Oct 2026 08.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEva Marie Saint, who has died aged 102, made a lasting impression in two outstanding American films: as Edie Doyle, the wholesome, sensitive, Catholic girl who befriends the docker Terry Malloy (Marlon Brando) inElia Kazan’sOn the Waterfront (1954); and as Eve Kendall, the intriguing beauty helping and hindering the pursued advertising executive (Cary Grant) in Alfred Hitchcock’s North By Northwest (1959).In the latter, Saint, the coolest and wittiest of the “Hitchcock blondes”, was lit so beautifully that her fair skin looked like porcelain. In the scene when they first meet in the dining car of a Chicago-bound train, Saint and Grant deliver the double-edged banter with supreme style. Assessing him, she says, “Good taste in clothes. Good taste in food.” He continues, “Good taste in women – I like your flavour.”The celebrated final sequence has Grant rescuing her while hanging precipitously over the side of Mount Rushmore, then dissolves to the Pullman car on the train where he is helping her up into his upper berth.View image in fullscreenSaint as Edie Doyle with Marlon Brando as Terry Malloy in a scene from On the Waterfront, 1954 – her poignant performance gained her the best supporting actress Oscar.Photograph: Ronald GrantVariety noted that Saint had emerged as “a glamorous charmer”. If only her movie career had continued to be as shimmering. It started brilliantly with On the Waterfront, which gained her the best supporting actress Oscar, though, perversely, she was the female lead. It was a poignant performance in which Edie fights her love for Malloy, the brother of the man she believes killed her brother. “I didn’t say I didn’t love you,” she tells him. “I said stay away from me.”Saint was born in New Jersey, the younger daughter of Quaker parents, John Merle Saint, a businessman, and his wife, Eva Marie (nee Rice), a former schoolteacher, and grew up in Delmar, New York. She claimed her inspiration came from her mother. “She was very strong, and self-sufficient. She made everything we ever wore ... Today she could have been a designer.”Eva meant to become a teacher but, while studying at Bowling Green State University in Ohio, she became involved in dramatics. After college, she moved to New York City, soon establishing herself as a radio actor (she had a honeyed voice) and then in a number of television plays, one of which wasHorton Foote’sThe Trip to Bountiful (1953) as the young friend and confidante of a browbeaten widow (Lillian Gish).The play transferred to Broadway the same year, with almost the same cast, and because of Saint’s refreshing performance she was signed for On the Waterfront two weeks into the short run.After her triumph in that film, she returned to television for two plays, Yellow Jack, with Broderick Crawford, and Our Town, with the unknownPaul Newman, just before his film debut. She was hardly stretched in her second big screen role as the ex-wife of a cartoonist (Bob Hope), now engaged to a cad (George Sanders), in the pleasant but forgettable romantic comedy That Certain Feeling (1956). Nevertheless, it proved she had some sass and sophistication, not seen again until Hitchcock brought it out three years later.View image in fullscreenSaint, centre, with Angela Lansbury, Karl Malden, Warren Beatty and Brandon de Wilde in All Fall Down, 1962.Photograph: Ronald GrantIn the meantime, she had to be content with being wan and insipid in Raintree County (1957), in which she was unfairly pitted against a southern belle (Elizabeth Taylor) for the love of her beau (Montgomery Clift). Allowing her to pull out a few more stops was Fred Zinnemann’s A Hatful of Rain (also 1957), in which she played the pregnant wife of a heroin-addicted Korean war veteran (Don Murray).Saint, who had married one of her television directors, Jeffrey Hayden, in 1951, was pregnant at the time and lost out to Joanne Woodward for a part opposite Newman again in The Long Hot Summer. However, she co-starred with Newman in Exodus (1960), Otto Preminger’s lengthy epic on the birth of the state of Israel. Saint was cast as a widowed US nurse who falls for the blue eyes and cause of the ship’s captain, played by Newman.InJohn Frankenheimer’sAll Fall Down (1962) she was Echo O’Brien, the lodger who seduces a younger man (Warren Beatty). She was rather wasted in the absorbing thriller 36 Hours (1964) and accepted the thankless role of the steadfast wife of an adulterous pastor (Richard Burton) in Vincente Minnelli’s The Sandpiper (1965) only because she got equal star billing with Burton and Taylor – again as Saint’s voluptuous rival – and one-tenth of Burton’s half-million-dollar fee.View image in fullscreenSaint with James Garner in Grand Prix, 1966.Photograph: MGM/Sportsphoto/AllstarIn Frankenheimer’s Grand Prix (1966), billed as “the story of four drivers, the women behind them, the cars beneath them”, she was a fashion editor. There was more substance in The Stalking Moon (1969) as a white woman held captive for 10 years by Native Americans, who gives birth to a mixed-race son. But after playing another deceived wife, this time oppositeGeorge Segalin Loving (1970), and appearing with Hope again in the best-forgotten Cancel My Reservation (1972), she returned to more challenging parts in the theatre.Among the plays were Tennessee Williams’s Summer and Smoke (1973), The First Monday in October (1979) withHenry Fonda, both in touring companies, and Duet for One (1982) in Chicago and New York, in which she took on the difficult role of the violinist with multiple sclerosis, directed by Hayden, her husband.But it was in TV films, some worthy, some worthwhile, that she was most visible in the latter part of her career. She explained that many of them could not be big feature films because, “How could they compete with all the special effects that movies have these days?” In the 1980s, she was convincingly cast as the mother of the model-turned-sleuth Maddie Hayes (Cybill Shepherd) in the successful TV seriesMoonlighting.The only feature film she made in the 80s wasGarry Marshall’s Nothing in Common (1986), in which she was impressive as the bitter and lonely mother of a yuppie (Tom Hanks). Saint returned to the big screen again a decade later in Time to Say Goodbye? (1997) as a woman coming to terms with her husband’s Alzheimer’s disease. One of her last films was the fantasyA New York Winter’s Tale(2014) in which, according to one critic, her appearance as a newspaper tycoon was “a beautiful reminder of her stature in American films. Her presence almost justifies the film’s existence. Almost.”View image in fullscreenSaint arriving at the Oscars awards ceremony at the Dolby theatre in Los Angeles, 2018.Photograph: Jordan Strauss/APTelevision occupied most of her late career, and she was nominated for a number of Emmys. Yet Saint once remarked that “I never wanted to be in a sitcom because I never wanted to have an imaginary family. I had everything I needed from my real one.”Hayden died in 2016. Saint is survived by their son, Darrell, and daughter, Laurette, four grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.Eva Marie Saint, actor, born 4 July 1924; died 6 October 2026Ronald Bergandied in 2020Explore more on these topicsFilmTelevisionAlfred HitchcockCary GrantMarlon BrandoEva Marie SaintobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Celia Imrie | Celia Imrie | The Guardian
description: From Miss Babs in Acorn Antiques to Calendar Girls, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel and her infamous appearance on The Celebrity Traitors, it’s hard to know where to begin
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: From Miss Babs in Acorn Antiques to Calendar Girls, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel and her infamous appearance on The Celebrity Traitors, it’s hard to know where to begin
Content: Gift of the Babs … Celia ImriePhotograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGift of the Babs … Celia ImriePhotograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianFilm & Music reader interviewCelia ImriePost your questions for Celia ImrieFrom Miss Babs in Acorn Antiques to Calendar Girls, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel and her infamous appearance on The Celebrity Traitors, it’s hard to know where to beginRich PelleyWed 7 Oct 2026 05.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 05.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCelia Imrie has had such a varied career, it’s hard to know where you might know her best from. Maybe it’s as Miss Babs, the permanently flustered antiques-shop owner in Victoria Wood’s Acorn Antiques, or as Philippa Moorcroft, Dinnerladies’ spectacularly uptight HR manager. Perhaps it’s as Bridget Jones’s family friend Una Alconbury, or from Calendar Girls,The Best Exotic Marigold Hotelfilms, Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again.Everybody’s favourite manic pixie dream aunt: Celia Imrie’s 20 best films – ranked!Read moreMaybe you know her as Mrs Quickly, the ghastly would-be stepmother in Nanny McPhee. Or maybe you first encountered her in Upstairs, Downstairs, To the Manor Born, Bergerac, Lovejoy or The Darling Buds of May, or as Claudia Bing, the magnificently awful PR rival of Jennifer Saunders’ Edina in Absolutely Fabulous.More recently, she returned as Una in Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy; joined Helen Mirren, Pierce Brosnan and Ben Kingsley in The Thursday Murder Club; and popped up in The Diplomat. Then, of course, there was The Celebrity Traitors. Imrie entered the castle as a Faithful, survived being chained up in a wooden cabin, and accidentally farted while doing so – instantly producingthe Guardian’s No 2 TV moment of the year– and eventually got murdered in plain sight by Alan Carr.Now she’s back as in (yes, it’s nearly that time already) MerryChristmasAubrey Flint, alongside John Bradley as a Christmas-hating model-soldier painter sentenced to community service at a struggling retirement home, where he somehow ends up directing a chaotic production of A Christmas Carol. Richard E Grant and Jim Broadbent are along for the festive ride, too.So, from flogging dodgy antiques with Victoria Wood to meddling in Bridget Jones’s love life, retiring to India with Judi Dench to committing Celebrity Traitors flatulence on national television – plus the really important matter of what on earth she’s getting Richard E Grant for Christmas – what would you like to askCelia Imrie? title: Freddie Jackson, romantic US singer with 10 R&B chart-toppers, dies aged 70 | Music | The Guardian
description: Celebrated for his earnest, dextrous voice, Jackson crossed into the pop charts with the hits Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake) and You Are My Lady
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Celebrated for his earnest, dextrous voice, Jackson crossed into the pop charts with the hits Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake) and You Are My Lady
Content: Freddie Jackson pictured in 2016.Photograph: Evan Agostini/APView image in fullscreenFreddie Jackson pictured in 2016.Photograph: Evan Agostini/APMusicFreddie Jackson, romantic US singer with 10 R&B chart-toppers, dies aged 70Celebrated for his earnest, dextrous voice, Jackson crossed into the pop charts with the hits Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake) and You Are My LadyBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 7 Oct 2026 07.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 07.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFreddie Jackson, the US singer whose smooth and romantic take on R&B found a huge audience in the 1980s, has died aged 70.A statement from his family on social media reads: “Freddie was more than a legendary voice. He was a kind, generous soul who loved his fans, his family, his friends and his music with everything he had. For decades he gave us the songs that became the soundtrack to our love stories, our celebrations and our most treasured memories. That gift will live on for ever.” No cause of death was given.Blessed with a dextrous and technically brilliant voice that could flip from playful flirtation to earnest entreaties to crushed lamentations across the space of a single album, Jackson became a mainstay in the US R&B scene, earning 10 No 1 singles and four back to back No 1 albums on the country’s R&B charts. He also twice hit the main pop chart Top 20, with 1985’s Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake) and You Are My Lady. The latter song also earned him two Grammy nominations.Born in 1956, Jackson was raised in Harlem by a single mother, “eating collard greens and fried chicken”, he later said. “That’s not learned soul, it’s not acquired in some singing school or from copying what you hear on records. I live soul.”He was first grounded in gospel music, performing at a local Baptist church, before expanding his musical remit outwards, establishing himself in New York’s music scene before moving to Los Angeles where he became the vocalist of dancefloor-focused soul group Mystic Merlin, recording their third album, Full Moon, with them.After a spell as a backing singer for Melba Moore, eventually he was signed as a solo artist, modelling himself on “Black singers who were able to cross over to the pop market without selling out – Marvin Gaye, Sam Cooke, Al Green”. He released debut album Rock Me Tonight in 1985, which, containing the aforementioned hit singles, became a platinum seller and reached the US Top 10. Follow-up Just Like the First Time was also certified platinum, and four of its tracks – including a duet with Moore, A Little Bit More – hit R&B No 1.His unabashed sensuality meant he was marketed with a “lover man” image, but he was careful not to let it define him. “I’m fortunate that a lot of ladies have liked the record and gone out and bought it,” he said. “But didn’t go to Capitol and say, ‘I’m a ladies man and I want to make a ladies man record.’ I don’t want to stereotype myself and my music. I don’t want to alienate anybody.”Jackson was still topping at the R&B chart as late as 1991, but as the genre modernised and hip-hop emerged, Jackson’s style became less fashionable and his chart success waned. He nevertheless remained a familiar voice on R&B radio and continued to release new music, eventually putting out 15 studio albums.In 2024, he announced he was living with kidney disease. “This journey has had its challenges but I’ve decided to face it with openness and resilience,” he said.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockR&BSoulnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: how to wear a leather jacket so it doesn’t wear you | Women's coats and jackets | The Guardian
description: There’s a lot of Brando badboy baggage attached to this classic outerwear – here’s how to look chic rather than stompy
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: There’s a lot of Brando badboy baggage attached to this classic outerwear – here’s how to look chic rather than stompy
Content: Video: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Melanie WilkinsonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley on fashionWomen's coats and jacketsJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: how to wear a leather jacket so it doesn’t wear youThere’s a lot of Brando badboy baggage attached to this classic outerwear – here’s how to look chic rather than stompyJess Cartner-MorleyWed 7 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn lots of ways, the arrival of autumn makes getting dressed easier. Not having to shave above your knees. Enough pockets to make a handbag optional. But it’s not all plain sailing. For instance, I don’t think we talk enough about how hard it is to carry off a leather jacket.I thought maybe it was just me. And then I came across Lucinda Chambers – Vogue fashion director for 25 years, now co-curator ofgorgeous platform of desirables Collagerie– remarking that she found leather jackets tricky. Lucinda is without a doubt one of the best-dressed women in London, always rocking a strong look – colour, stripes, great jewellery, unexpected shoes – so I was amazed and a bit gratified to find even she struggles.The trouble with leather jackets is they tend to wear you, rather than you wearing them. They sort of cannibalise your personality. And while they are very cool and chic, I don’t want to look like a walking coat.double quotation markLeather has a more physical presence than most fabrics. It enters the room several seconds before you doFashion is insistent about leather jackets this autumn. Ideally a funnel-necked one, generously proportioned, zipped or buttoned high around the neck, sometimes almost to the chin. This jacket can be traced directly back toPhoebe Philo, who made dramatic funnel-neck outerwear a signature of the first collection from her own label in 2023. Since then, it has spread everywhere, from Khaite to Cos.The leather jacket is not a problem for Philo herself, obviously, because Phoebe could wear a sleeping bag and somehow make everyone else feel horribly un-chic. The rest of us need to work a little harder. Leather has a more physical presence than most fabrics. It enters the room several seconds before you do. The stiffness means the jacket tends to hold its own silhouette rather than adapting itself politely to yours. The sheer bulky expanse of it means a lot of visual real estate. You wear it because you want to feel a bit tough, but you end up feeling like a fire door.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The GuardianCounterintuitively, given that it adds yet more jacket, a high funnel neck makes the whole thing feel more elegant. A biker jacket has cultural baggage: Marlon Brando, motorbikes, the open road. A funnel neck has less attitude, more line. The vertical sweep towards the face is clean and graceful, a rock’n’roll Audrey Hepburn.Also counterintuitively: a generous cut is less overwhelming than a tight one. You might imagine a neat, cropped leather jacket would be an easier option to wear, but a loose fit looks more feminine and luxurious. There should be room for air to circulate between you and your jacket – so you don’t look vacuum-packed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: pair a little skirt with a chunky jumper for the perfect balancing actRead moreSome other questions to consider. Hair first, because nothing works if your hair looks rubbish. Long hair tends not to sit well outside a leather jacket, because unless you are blessed with lustrous ropes, the bulk of the jacket will make your locks look puny. The hair tuck, where you catch your hair inside the collar, is pleasingly Philo-coded (she invented it), but you do risk looking as if you accidentally zipped yourself into your jacket. A ponytail or messy bun is our safest bet.What to wear on the bottom half? I’d swerve a leather skirt or trousers, unless you are either Rihanna or on your way to commit a daring jewellery heist. You are getting dressed, not upholstered. Controversially, jeans wouldn’t be my first choice either. Jeans and a leather jacket sounds like a classic combination, but it tracks a bit too rugged. Some element of softness – a skirt, a soft trouser – is key.If you are still nervous, consider avoiding black. Burgundy or chocolate still goes with everything, and the softer the colour, the less likely the jacket will swallow you whole. What it comes down to is this: don’t let your leather jacket boss you around. Yes, it seems to demand stompy boots and a tough attitude, but you can resist its attempt to dictate terms. Put it on over a stripy jumper and go to the garden centre. A leather jacket, like a toddler, needs to know who is in charge.Styling: Melanie Wilkinson. Model: Imogen May at Milk.
