title: ‘Green, red, yellow, blue’? Beneath the surface, diaspora language is anything but Black and white | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Black communities across the globe have large and complex vocabularies to describe race, shaped by their specific cultures and histories
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Black communities across the globe have large and complex vocabularies to describe race, shaped by their specific cultures and histories
Content: Tone-dependent … the descriptors are unlikely to map neatly onto Western notions of racism.Illustration: Diana Ejaita/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTone-dependent … the descriptors are unlikely to map neatly onto Western notions of racism.Illustration: Diana Ejaita/The GuardianThe Long WaveLife and style‘Green, red, yellow, blue’? Beneath the surface, diaspora language is anything but Black and whiteBlack communities across the globe have large and complex vocabularies to describe race, shaped by their specific cultures and historiesDon’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNesrine MalikWed 7 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne thing you might not know about this newsletter is how much it is shaped by behind-the-scenes chat. The Long Wave team, and its broader family at the Guardian, is a mini-diaspora in and of itself – one that is constantly in conversation. Often, during our meetings, someone will mention what was assumed to be a quirk of their specific background, only to discover that it is replicated almost entirely across the board. This week, we spoke about the fact that in many of our cultures, there is not just one word for “Black”.View image in fullscreenCultural depth … the words denoting complexion in Sudan are grounded in a specific culture.Illustration: Jonathan Knowles/Getty Images“Green”, “red”, “yellow”, “blue”, “wheat”. These are some of the words many tribes in parts of Sudan use to describe complexion. There is no “Black”. I tripped over my words trying to explain to colleagues what these colours denoted – each category is infused with so much cultural depth. In fact, in some cases, they are not even descriptions of complexion, but of features, of broad ethnic background, and even of attractiveness. “Green” means dark, but also implies a sort of uniformity of colour, an even hue, and therefore almost a comeliness. Yellow is lighter, and comes with an unstated connotation of beauty. Blue is the darkest, and is sometimes pejorative, but other times just a description. “Wheat” is the one most likely to be a compliment, a shade that does not diverge too sharply into light or dark.But honestly, I am on slightly thin ice here in trying to assign a clear definition to any of these colours. Their meanings are dependent on context and tone. They are also grounded in a specific culture – one that merges Arab and African histories and encompasses complex prejudices that do not map neatly on to western notions of racism.Language that is hard to translateView image in fullscreenBehemoth of nuances … descriptors like ‘ripe plantain’ are notoriously hard to translate to outsiders.Photograph: Roger Yebuah/Getty ImagesMorgan Ofori, Guardian reporter and subeditor for The Long Wave, chimed in with Ghana’s numerous words for Blackness.Ameyibɔ or ameyibɔr but Yibɔɔ, uttered with prolonged emphasis in the Ewe language, describes someone considered to be “beautifully darker-skinned”. Someone with a lighter complexion (whether or not of mixed heritage) is referred to asKɔkɔɔin Twi, which directly translates to “red” but also “ripe plantain”, connecting those individuals to the starchy fruit’s red-yellow hue. In Morgan’s opinion, these categories are by and large neutral descriptors; however, being of lighter skin is nonetheless seen as a class differentiator.Another colleague Sundus Abdi points to similar descriptors of red and green in Somali, withmaariinbeing used to describe deep brown skin, while white is used to refer to lighter skin.This handful of words is nothing compared to the racial vocabulary found in Brazil, a behemoth of nuances. There are,according to a 1976 survey, a staggering 136 shades and variations in how Brazilians described their skin colour. They include “burnt yellow”, “sea blue”, “thistle” and “disappearing donkey” – a word used humorously to describe people whose colour is difficult to define. This is likely related to Brazil’s project of “racial whitening” or“Branqueamento”after abolition, contributing to the country’s heavily mixed present-day population.Despite being separated by geography and history, there are curious similarities between these vocabularies – many of which use colours as metaphors or approximations. I’m also struck by how difficult it is to translate them to outsiders, who don’t understand the context or connotations. Another similarity appears to be that these descriptions are crucially distinct from racial slurs, despite sometimes having racial implications.What about in majority-white countries?View image in fullscreenDefined against the imperial core … being racialised can narrow the way in which Blackness is perceived.Photograph: The Print Collector/AlamyThis vast array of descriptors vanishes in contexts where Black people are a racialised minority. In the US, for example, even very light-skinned people are often simply racialised as “Black” by a majority-white society. This identity is a political one, shaped by the use of theone-drop ruleas a means of racial classification during slavery.Globally, there is also a conception of Blackness that has come to shape a post-colonial identity, defined against the imperial core. Micha Frazer-Carroll, The Long Wave’s editor and assistant writer, grew up in the UK in the 90s with a clear sense of being “mixed race” (the predominant term of the era), but later realised that white British people simply identified her as Black. “This was partly to do with the local social context,” she tells me, “but I also think it was shaped by the cultural influence of the US and the ‘one drop rule’.”But in her Caribbean family, her sister was described as being “red skin”, and Micha herself as “coolie” – a word used to describe the Indian indentured labourers who settled in Jamaica after the abolition of slavery (in some countries and contexts, it is considered aslur, in others, a neutral descriptor). “I now see both of these terms as being fraught with histories of racism and colonialism,” she says, “but they were also used light-heartedly and jokingly.”For the Black diaspora, one’s Blackness as a political notion, grounded in campaigns for equality and enfranchisement, sits alongside a more layered and less fraught identity that is, as Micha says, at times almost playful. This is not to romanticise these descriptors – many of which cannot be separated from histories of colourism. These categorisations and differences can become sharpened and even turn deadly when civil conflict erupts along ethnic lines, and colour becomes a crude signifier of who is friend and who is foe.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDescribing Blackness on its own termsView image in fullscreenNot the entire reality … terms for Blackness originate from wit and innovations of language.Illustration: Diana Ejaita/The GuardianBut what broadly distinguishes these colour charts, for better or for worse, is that they are not exclusively defined by whiteness as a hegemonic political centre. Have standards of what is desirable been shaped by colonialism? Sure, one only has to look at the ubiquity of skin lightening creams and potions across the world. But colonialism is only one feature of many power dynamics that created this large colour palette. Class, immigration, religion, Arab and South Asian influences across Africa and theCaribbeanall play a part in these colour categorisations.In our conversations, what emerges is an important hesitation and nuance: these differing, humorous and even poetic descriptions are not necessarily an indication of benign expansive rainbow nations. Rather, they are a reality of Black life that is rarely reflected in global Black diaspora discourse, which is often situated in the context of oppression and activism. This is perhaps the natural result of Euro-American cultural and political projection and right wing resurgence.But this is not the entire reality–there is more space to think of Blackness on its own terms. Sometimes, it is an identity that is political, economic, and related to power disparities, and legacies of colonialism. But at other times, it is something also rooted in longer histories, in wit, in innovations of language, and in universal experiences of relating to each other that, as our conversations revealed, exist across distance and difference.To receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Tap inWhat culturally-specific words do you use to describe your identity or complexion? What do they mean to you? Tell us by replying to this, or emailing us atthelongwave@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Cartoon |Sarah Akinterinwaon Black History MonthView image in fullscreenThe classroom experience … an educator grapples with a deluge of US-influenced Black history material.Illustration: Sarah Akinterinwa/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Long WaveAfricaCaribbeanAmericasBlack British cultureBeautyColonialismnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Put down the pumpkin! How to create a cosy home this autumn – without the cliches | Interiors | The Guardian
description: From tactile textures to softer lighting, these expert-approved updates bring all the warmth of autumn while steering clear of Sleepy Hollow vibes
Author: Aimee Robinson
Headline: From tactile textures to softer lighting, these expert-approved updates bring all the warmth of autumn while steering clear of Sleepy Hollow vibes
Content: Autumnal, and not a gourd in sight …Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenAutumnal, and not a gourd in sight …Photograph: GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterInteriorsPut down the pumpkin! How to create a cosy home this autumn – without the clichesFrom tactile textures to softer lighting, these expert-approved updates bring all the warmth of autumn while steering clear of Sleepy Hollow vibesProfessional organisers’ tips for a tidy homeAimee RobinsonWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a long, hot summer, the autumn chill is creeping in and, according to social media, that means one thing: cosy season. I’m all for a blanket, a candle and those gorgeous amber and russet shades, but I’m less convinced that welcoming autumn requires turning your home into Sleepy Hollow.Pumpkins, faux foliage and Jack Skellington-shaped everything might be some people’s idea of heaven, but I’d rather bring in the season without needing to overhaul my lounge by December. As interior designer Lia Gold, winner of BBC’s Interior Design Masters, puts it: “There are so many ways to make your home feel cosier without it having to smell like pumpkin spice.”So, with a little help from interior experts, I’ve hunted down pieces that feel suitably toasty for autumn, but will work just as well for the rest of the year.How to make your home cosy for autumn and beyondLayer up with throwsThe “easiest and most affordable way” to welcome autumn is to change the colours of your cushions and throws, says Gold. She also recommends leaning towards fabrics such as wool in a herringbone weave, which feels particularly cosy. This John Lewis blanket ticks all the boxes, especially in autumnal burnt orange.View image in fullscreenJohn Lewis herringbone Shetlandlamb’s woolthrow£95 at John LewisOne of my favourite rituals when the weather turns is retreating to the sofa and cocooning in a blanket. I was given this Dunelm teddy fleece blanket one Christmas, and it’s so soft that, thanks to its versatile neutral shade, it’s stayed in my lounge year-round.View image in fullscreenDunelm teddy bear throwFrom £8 at DunelmFor more, read our guide to thebest heated throws and electric blanketsAdd colour with cushionsColour is undoubtedly a defining part of the season. Tash Bradley, director of interior design at home decor brand Lick, describes autumn’s palette as “almost like opening your spice cupboard: saffron, turmeric, cinnamon and paprika”.But don’t go overboard. “I think it’s important that an autumn palette doesn’t simply look like you’ve recreated an autumnal walk inside your house,” says Bradley. That’s where colours such as teal and blue can offer a welcome contrast. “They bring a different energy to those earthy shades,” she says, “evoking the sea, an open sky, a favourite coastal walk or somewhere they’ve travelled.”Cushions are an easy way to introduce new tones, and I love M&S’s affordable velvet options in shades of spice, chestnut and caramel, alongside a pretty, dusty blue.Mix cushion sizes and shapes, says Gold. “I recommend odd numbers, so think threes or fives. Start with a larger cushion at the back, like a 50cm by 50cm, then work towards the centre with smaller rectangles and a lumbar cushion to top it off.”View image in fullscreenM&S velvet cushion£20 at M&SIf you prefer a little more pattern, this art nouveau botanical cushion introduces rich colour with a subtle nod to changing foliage. The velvet and intricate print feel suitably sophisticated, rather than tipping into kitsch. Of course, at £195, it’s an investment, but this is the kind of cushion you can keep for years and make the centrepiece of a display. Pair it with brighter hues in summer, then swap for deeper tones come autumn and winter.View image in fullscreenLiberty Eustacia velvet-fringed cushion£195 at LibertyCreate warmth and textureI bought a Zara Home rug last year, and it immediately made my living room feel cosier. This vintage-effect cotton-blend design has an ornamental pattern, earthy tones, and comes in several sizes to suit all kinds of rooms.“Patterned rugs are practical, too – they are more forgiving than something pale and plain,” says Bradley.Size is another important consideration. “Go larger than you think you need. A rug should help zone a space and bring all of the furniture together, rather than feeling like a separate little island in the middle of the room.” In living rooms and bedrooms, she recommends having furniture sit on the rug (not around it) to keep the room grounded and connected.View image in fullscreenZara Home vintage-effect rugFrom £159.99 at Zara HomeTexture can add warmth to a room, but don’t feel limited to blankets or rugs. “Sheepskins are brilliant because they’re so tactile,” says Bradley. “Place one beside the bed so it’s the first thing your feet touch in the morning or throw one over a dining chair or bench.” Sheepskins can also add a lovely layer of texture to a sofa, draped over the arm or back. Ikea’s £45 sheepskin is a versatile option that won’t break the bank.View image in fullscreenIkea Ullerslev sheepskin, off-whiteFrom £35 at IkeaIs there anything more inviting as the cold weather sets in than your bed? Piglet in Bed’s breathable cotton percale bedding works year-round – pair it with a 13.5 tog winter duvet for extra insulation. I’d choose this fig and blush pink gingham for its toasty tones.View image in fullscreenPiglet in Bed gingham washed cotton bedding, double£99 at M&S£99 at John LewisFor more, read our roundup ofthe best duvets for every season and sleeperShine a lightAs nights draw in, a good table lamp becomes essential. Habitat’s mango wood base has beautiful natural grain, while its sculptural shape gives a hint of quiet luxury, despite being just £50.View image in fullscreenHabitat Emir Totum mango wood table lamp base£50 at ArgosIt may sound like a small detail, but the right lightbulb can make all the difference to a room’s atmosphere. Gold recommends swapping in spiral or straight LED filament bulbs for a softer, less glaring glow.She also suggests looking for one around 2,200K (kelvins). Kelvins measure the colour temperature of a bulb, and this rating provides a warm, amber-toned light that should feel inviting as those darker evenings arrive.View image in fullscreenVintage LED lightbulbs, pair£13.99 at AmazonSwitching the lampshade can quickly bring deeper tones into a room. I particularly love this red silk design from Morris & Co and Pooky. The heritage print was first produced in 1876 and nods subtly to foliage but doesn’t feel overly tied to the time of year.View image in fullscreenPooky x Morris & Co20cm scalloped empire shade£70 at PookyOne of my favourite candle brands this time of year is Bath & Body Works. I tend to avoid the usual pumpkin spice, so I love its more unusual scents, particularly Leaves, inspired by falling foliage with hints of red apple and golden nectar.View image in fullscreenBath & Body WorksLeaves candle£29.50 at Bath & Body WorksCandlesticks have been enjoying a revival in recent years. As well as providing the glow of candlelight, they make decorative accents in their own right, whether arranged on a dining table, sideboard or shelf. I particularly like the oxblood colour of this Heal’s + Aylesford hand-thrown holder, which works now but is versatile year-round.Have a bit of fun with the colour of the tapered candles, switching them up as your decorating mood changes. Ferm Living sells packs of four in various colour combinations for £15, andthe Whimsical setof cream, maroon, pale pink and pale blue would work particularly well with the oxblood holder.View image in fullscreenHeal’s + Aylesford clay loop candleholder£18 at Heal’sAutumn in the airIf scented candles aren’t your thing, an oil burner is another way to bring seasonal scents home. I like this hand-thrown one by Rebecca Proctor, made in Cornwall as part of a small batch. Its ochre glaze and simple design work year-round.View image in fullscreenRebecca Proctor oil burner£44 at ToastA diffuser can also introduce scent into a room without lighting a candle. “I start gravitating towards muskier scents, such as bergamot and cedarwood,” says Gold. I like the simple glass vessel of this White Company diffuser as it would happily sit with any decor.View image in fullscreenThe White Company bergamot and cedar diffuserskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£28 at the White CompanyStyle your surfacesVases are essentials in my house, and deeper-toned glass can shift a room’s mood. I like this chunky, textured design for its 70s-inspired shape and colour palette that doesn’t veer into seasonal schmaltz. It’s made from 30% recycled glass.The rich colours would look lovely with a seasonal arrangement, too. “Autumn is one of the most beautiful times to simply go outside and gather branches, twigs and foliage and arrange them in a big vase to create something sculptural,” says Bradley.View image in fullscreenH&M textured glass vase£34.99 at H&MIf you prefer something with more purpose, this hand-thrown slipware jug by Penzance-based potter Mollie Milton would work beautifully on the kitchen table, with or without flowers. The terracotta and cream pattern feels warm, and the wonky handmade finish makes it look more like something you’ve collected than simply bought to fill a space.View image in fullscreenMollie Milton slipware jug£65 at Toast“There’s something incredibly cosy about dark wood glowing in candlelight,” says Gold. This mango wood tray from Habitat has rounded edges and makes a subtle statement on a coffee or dressing table while doubling as a useful catch-all.View image in fullscreenHabitat dark mango wood tray£12 at ArgosCoffee-table books can add colour and dimension, as well as something to flick through over a cuppa. This cottagecore book pairs gorgeous photography with stories from charming homes, whisking you away to the quiet of the countryside.View image in fullscreenCottagecore: New Countryside Living£32.59 at World of Books£32.45 at AmazonBring the room to lifeOne little treat I like to buy myself, whatever the time of year, is flowers, which can instantly brighten a room. Gold recommends sticking to seasonal blooms such as protea, amaranthus and eucalyptus. While supermarkets have plenty of affordable options, M&S is one of my go-tos for occasions or last-minute deliveries, even if it’s simply a gift for yourself, with nominated and next-day delivery available. The protea and eucalyptus bouquet is a particularly lovely option, plus the flowers can be dried and kept for weeks or even months.View image in fullscreenM&S protea & eucalyptus bouquet£35 at M&SView image in fullscreenFreddie’s Flowers Autumn’s BountyFrom £29 at Freddie’s FlowersWe’ve also rounded up thebest flower delivery for every budgetSwapping artwork can provide a quick refresh, and I particularly like Desenio for affordable pieces you can rotate without guilt. This Paris-inspired canvas brings depth through brown, red and beige, with hints of green and blue, yet would feel just as right in summer.View image in fullscreenOlga BoznańskaMotif from Paris canvas printFrom £49 at DesenioServe up the seasonA good casserole dish is an autumn essential. Opt for Le Creuset’s classic cast-iron round casserole in forest green: a subtle nod to the time of year that won’t look out of place come spring. As Gold says: “Green gives you so much without ever feeling like a fleeting trend.”Plenty more affordable alternatives that capture the same look are also available. Habitat has a 6.7-litre cast-iron pot in forest green for £56, suitable for all hob types as well as hot plates. ProCook’s 4.7-litre cast-iron casserole is another option at £65 in a thyme green shade. It’s suitable for all hobs, including induction, and oven-safe to 260C.View image in fullscreenLe Creuset cast-iron casserole dish£265 at Le CreusetView image in fullscreenHabitat cast-iron casserole dish£56 at ArgosView image in fullscreenProCook cast-iron casserole dish£65 at ProCookFor more, read our guide to thebest casserole dishes for stews and saucesH&M Home is one of my go-tos for affordable pieces with a Scandinavian feel. I love this footed rattan bowl, which keeps those deeper wood tones while adding texture with its woven finish. It would make a lovely fruit bowl, but could just as easily work as a centrepiece or bread basket when friends come over for dinner.View image in fullscreenH&M footed rattan bowl£34.99 at H&MAs the temperature drops, my tea consumption rises, so I’m considering Emma Bridgewater’s splatter-effect mug. Its playful glaze doesn’t steer into the cutesy witches of the Halloween range, and would look good on a shelf, too.View image in fullscreenEmma Bridgewater Autumn Splatter 1/2 pint mug£30 at Emma BridgewaterA softer touchOne of the easiest ways to bring the season into your bathroom is to swap your towels for a new colour. M&S is great for soft, long-lasting towels, and these Egyptian cotton ones come in shades including chestnut, fern, amber and burgundy.View image in fullscreenEgyptian cotton towelFrom £4 at M&SA friend of mine has a Tekla bath mat, and I’ve lusted after it every time I’ve visited – not just because it looks good, but because it feels so lovely underfoot, too. title: Tom Hunt’s recipe for fridge-raid minestrone, UK-style | Food | The Guardian
description: A creative way to use up the bits you already have around, all while getting in a healthy mixture of vegetables and whole grains
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: A creative way to use up the bits you already have around, all while getting in a healthy mixture of vegetables and whole grains
Content: Tom Hunt’s zero-waste fridge-raid 'minestrone'.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s zero-waste fridge-raid 'minestrone'.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodTom Hunt’s recipe for fridge-raid minestrone, UK-styleA creative way to use up the bits you already have around, all while getting in a healthy mixture of vegetables and whole grainsTom HuntWed 7 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis hearty dish is inspired by the diets ofthe Blue Zones, or those regions of the world where people live the longest, including Sardinia, where minestrone is a staple.Dan Buettner, who studied these communities, found that their diets are generally rich in beans, whole grains and seasonal vegetables. I’ve generalised ingredients into groups such as alliums, rather than simply suggesting the standard onion base, to inspire you to use up whatever you have in the house and what’s in season; I’d of course also encourage further diversification with the addition of other vegetables and subtle spices.Fridge-raid “minestrone”This is a hodge-podge minestrone-of-sorts, inspired by the Sardinian classic and adapted for the British larder. I’ve used a grain and pulse soup, or broth mix, because it’s widely available in British supermarkets, and includes a nourishing blend of split peas, lentils, barley and spelt; however, any lentils, soaked dried beans or grains will also work well, as do canned beans, though add those (and their tin liquid, or aquafaba) only towards the end of the cooking process. Instead of the fennel in Beuttner’s recipe, I’ve used leafy greens, mainly to make the most of the greens in my fridge, which in this instance featured beetroot leaves, chard and cauliflower leaves. I like to batch-cook this soup and keep the excess in the fridge for another meal.Serves44 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil150g diced alliums– onions, leeks, spring onions2 medium carrots, peeled and chopped (about 100g net)2 medium celery stalks, chopped (optional)1 tsp fennel seeds, or coriander seeds4 garlic cloves, peeled and minced1400g tin chopped tomatoes200g dried grain and pulse soup mix(pearl barley, yellow split peas, green split peas, spelt, and red lentils) or pearl barley or another grain400groot vegetables– celeriac, turnip, potatoes150g chopped greens– spinach, or beetroot or cauliflower leaves20g flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped from stalk to leaf20gbunch fresh basil100g small mixed pasta shapes– broken spaghetti, ditalini, orzo50g grated pecorino, or parmesan, to serveWarm three tablespoons of the oil in a large soup pot on a medium heat. Add the diced alliums, carrot and celery, if using, then stir in the fennel seeds and saute for five minutes, until soft but not coloured. Stir in the minced garlic and saute for 30 seconds more, until fragrant.Add the chopped tinned tomatoes, followed by the grain and pulse soup mix (or pearl barley), root vegetables, chopped greens, chopped flat-leaf parsley, and the finely chopped stalks from the bunch of basil (save the leaves to finish). Pour in enough water to submerge everything by 2½cm (you’ll need about one and a half litres), then bring to a boil. Turn down the heat and leave to simmer uncovered for an hour, adding more water as needed. Finely stir in the mixed pasta shapes, add up to 500ml more water, if need be, then simmer for 10 minutes until tender.Season to taste, then divide between four bowls and serve topped with the reserved basil leaves, grated pecorino and a generous drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteAutumn food and drinkSoupItalian food and drinkBritish food and drinkMain coursefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Roast chicken, congee and cookies: Ravinder Bhogal’s autumn squash recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Nutty in flavour and creamy in texture, autumn’s bounty of squash and pumpkin has many uses, both sweet and savoury
Author: Ravinder Bhogal
Headline: Nutty in flavour and creamy in texture, autumn’s bounty of squash and pumpkin has many uses, both sweet and savoury
Content: Ravinder Bhogal’s pumpkin and miso congee with chilli oil.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.View image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s pumpkin and miso congee with chilli oil.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.FoodRoast chicken, congee and cookies: Ravinder Bhogal’s autumn squash recipesNutty in flavour and creamy in texture, autumn’s bounty of squash and pumpkin has many uses, both sweet and savouryRavinder BhogalWed 7 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe shops are heaving with pumpkins and squash, and though there are so many different varieties to choose from, most of them are interchangeable. My favourites are kabocha, crown prince and delicata, for their deeply nutty flavour and creamy texture, plus they hold their shape well when roasted or braised. And if you’re carving a pumpkin forHalloweenover the coming weeks, don’t waste the flesh: chop it up and throw into a risotto. It’s hard to imagine that such deliciousness could come from such a ghoulish grimace.Pumpkin and miso congee with chilli oil (pictured above)Congee is a favourite comfort food that is eaten across Asia, often for breakfast. This version isn’t particularly traditional, but it makes the most of pumpkin season. I love this with a drizzle of chilli oil as a contrast to the delicata’s natural sweetness.Prep15 minCook50 minServes6600gdelicata pumpkin, peeled and chopped into bite-size chunks, plus 6 wedges3tbsp avocado oil, or neutral oilSea salt and black pepper1 heapedtbsp white miso2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped1tbsp crushed ginger200g short-grain white rice1 piece kombu1 bunch spring onions, trimmed and sliced on the diagonalFor the garnish3tbsp toasted pumpkin seedsA few drops of sesame oilChilli oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Lay out the pumpkin on a baking sheet, drizzle over one tablespoon of oil and season. Roast for 30-40 minutes, until very soft and caramelised, then remove and leave to cool. Set aside the squash wedges, then puree the remaining chunks in a food processor with a splash of water.In a large saucepan, heat the remaining oil on a medium heat, add the miso and cook, stirring, until lightly caramelised. Add the garlic and ginger, and stir until fragrant.Add the rice, kombu and 1.8 litres of water and bring to a boil on medium-high heat. Partially cover, turn down the heat to a low simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, for 25-30 minutes, until the liquid has reduced and the rice is plump and has turned into a porridge. Stir in the pumpkin puree and half the sliced spring onions.Divide the congee between six bowls and top each portion with a wedge of roast squash. Garnish with the remaining spring onions, then finish with toasted pumpkin seeds, a drizzle of sesame oil and your favourite chilli oil.Chicken with kabocha squash and sageView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s pot-roasted chicken with kabocha squash and sage.This makes for a wonderful alternative autumnal Sunday roast, with minimal washing-up because it’s all cooked in one pan.Prep10 minCook1 hr 20 minServes4Sea salt and black pepper1 whole chicken(about 1½kg)1 whole garlic bulb, cut in half horizontally1 unwaxed lemon,halved1 bunchsage2 bay leaves2tbsp olive oil½tsp dried chilli flakes1tsp ground cinnamon1 small kabocha squash(about 750g), unpeeled and cut into wedges150ml dry white wine800ml chicken stock50mldouble creamSeason the chicken generously inside and out, then stuff the cavity with one of the garlic halves, both lemon halves, half the sage and the bay leaves.Put the oil in a large, deep casserole over a medium heat and, once it’s hot, brown the chicken all over – take your time to do this properly, because it really makes a difference to the overall taste. Once browned, set aside the chicken for the time being.In the oil left over from browning the chicken, fry the remaining garlic and sage with the chilli and cinnamon, then, once the mix is smelling fragrant, stir in the squash wedges to coat them in the aromatic oil. Cook for two minutes, then pour in the wine and leave to bubble away until reduced by half.Push the squash to the sides of the pan, then nestle the chicken in the middle. Pour in the stock,cover and leave to cook on a gentle heat for 50 minutes to an hour. Once cooked, stir in the cream, season if need be, and serve.Fudgy pumpkin pie cookiesView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s fudgy pumpkin pie cookies.No tricks, just treats. These are perfect for a little Halloween indulgence.Prep10 minChill40 minCook1 hr, plus coolingMakesAbout 20For the pumpkin puree200g red kurior kabochasquash, halved, deseeded, peeled and cut into 2cm cubes50g granulated sugar1tsp ground cinnamon½tsp ground gingerA pinch of ground clovesA good grating of nutmegFor the cookies225g plain flour1tsp cinnamon½tsp ground gingerA pinch of clovesA good grating of nutmeg½tsp baking powder½tsp bicarbonate of sodaSalt225g light brown sugar175g unsalted butter2 egg yolks1tsp vanilla extractStart by making the pumpkin puree. Put the pumpkin in a microwave-safe container and microwave on high for five minutes. Remove, toss, then microwave on high again for another five minutes. Keep repeating this process until the pumpkin is soft and mashable – the timing will depend on your microwave, but mine took 15 minutes. Once soft, puree in a food processor (or mash well with a fork) until smooth, then leave to cool.In a small bowl, mix the sugar and spices. In medium bowl, mix the flour, spices, baking powder, bicarb and half a teaspoon of salt. In a stand mixer, cream the brown sugar and butter until light and fluffy. Add the egg yolks and vanilla, whisk again until pale and fluffy, then stir in the pumpkin puree until well combined. Fold in the dry ingredients, then chill in the fridge for 40 minutes, until firm.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and line two baking sheets with greaseproof paper. Scoop out two tablespoons of the cookie mixture and roll them into loose balls. Roll these in the spiced sugar mix and place on the baking sheets spaced well apart. Repeat with the remaining cookie mix, then bake for 12 minutes, until golden brown.Remove and leave to cool on the baking sheet for five minutes, then transfer to a rack to cool completely.Explore more on these topicsFoodAutumn food and drinkMain courseVegetablesChickenMeatSnacksrecipesShareReuse this content

title: UK house prices flatline as rising mortgage costs weigh on market | Housing market | The Guardian
description: Average cost of home in September was £298,441, says Lloyds – about the same as year earlier and in August
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Average cost of home in September was £298,441, says Lloyds – about the same as year earlier and in August
Content: Economists had predicted a 0.1% monthly rise in prices in September.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/AlamyView image in fullscreenEconomists had predicted a 0.1% monthly rise in prices in September.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/AlamyHousing marketUK house prices flatline as rising mortgage costs weigh on marketAverage cost of home in September was £298,441, says Lloyds – about the same as year earlier and in AugustBusiness live – latest updatesJoanna PartridgeWed 7 Oct 2026 03.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 04.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK house prices flatlined in September, according to a leading index, asrising mortgage costsstarted to weigh on the market.The average cost of a home was £298,441, roughly the same as it was a year earlier and in the previous month, according to the tracker from Lloyds previously known as the Halifax HPI.Economists polled by Reuters had predicted a 0.1% monthly rise in prices, according to the median forecast, as well as a 0.2% annual increase.‘People are deserting it’: why are London mansions struggling to sell?Read moreIt came after house pricesfell by 0.3% in August, the first decline in three years, as prospective buyers were hit by geopolitical uncertainty, combined with higher mortgage rates and stretched affordability.In recent weeks most big banks and building societieshave put prices upas a result of turmoil in the global bond markets, even though there has not been a change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year.Andrew Asaam, the mortgages director at Lloyds, said: “While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of base rate.”On Monday the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgagereached 6% for the first time in three years. Rising mortgage rates are bad news for borrowers whose fixed-rate deals are ending, as well as prospective buyers who are hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a home and the sellers who want the best price from them.It also adds to the squeeze facing consumers as a result ofhigher energy bills, linked to the Iran war, while rising prices elsewhere are raising concerns of anew cost of living crisis.Asaam said: “While higher mortgage rates and wider economic uncertainty are encouraging some people to take a more measured approach, new inquiries from prospective buyers are now at their highest since February.”He added that any movement in house prices was likely to remain modest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTom Bill, the head of UK residential research at the estate agent Knight Frank, said: “This year has been a story of rising energy prices and stalling house prices, as the unpredictable Middle East conflict unfolds and drives borrowing costs higher. This month’s budget adds to the uncertainty as buyers and sellers wonder which of the recurring tax rumours proves to be true.”The number of people applying for a mortgage to buy a property fell between July and September, as higher borrowing costs continued to affect prospective housebuyers’ budgets, according to quarterly figures from Stonebridge, one of the UK’s largest independent mortgage and protection networks.Mortgage applications for home purchases fell by 18.2% in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, Stonebridge found, while applications from first-time buyers slumped 18.6% over the same period.However, rising numbers of applications for remortgaging helped to slow the decline in overall mortgage activity.Explore more on these topicsHousing marketHouse pricesPropertyLloyds Banking GroupMortgagesMortgage ratesReal estatenewsShareReuse this content

title: The generation raised on sugar rations – and what their health reveals 70 years later | Sugar | The Guardian
description: From blood pressure to ageing, research suggests the first 1,000 days of sugar exposure could leave a decades-long mark on health
Author: Linda Geddes
Headline: From blood pressure to ageing, research suggests the first 1,000 days of sugar exposure could leave a decades-long mark on health
Content: Three children enjoy a portable, healthy snack – a carrot on a stick – amid wartime rationing in July 1941. Photograph: Ashwood/Getty ImagesFrom blood pressure to ageing, research suggests the first 1,000 days of sugar exposure could leave a decades-long mark on healthByLinda GeddesWed 7 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey were born into a Britain still recovering from the hardships of war. Though the air-raid sirens had fallen silent, many everyday foods remained rationed, including sugar. Adults were restricted to about 3 tablespoons (40g) a day to stretch between cups of tea, baking and desserts; children were limited to less than a tablespoon. Babies and very young children were expected to have little or no added sugar.Then, in 1953, the brakes came off. Separate restrictions on sweets and chocolate were lifted in February, followed by sugar in September. By the second half of 1954, average sugar consumption had almost doubled.View image in fullscreenA London shopkeeper puts up a sign announcing the new price of sugar, as announced in the budget in September 1939. The price has risen by a penny a pound.Photograph: Fox Photos/Getty ImagesThe lifting of postwar sugar rationing inadvertently created a natural experiment, whose consequences scientists are only beginning to unpick. A flurry of recent studies suggests that spending the first 1,000 days of life under sugar rationing may have left traces on people’s health more than seven decades later.“What makes the end of sugar rationing particularly interesting is the nature of the exposure,” said Dr Jiazhen Zheng at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in Guangzhou, China, who worked on several of the recent studies. “In September 1953, sugar availability changed quite abruptly at the population level, largely because of policy rather than individual choice. In a sense, history created an experiment that we could never deliberately run over a human lifetime.”The first of this recent wave of sugar rationing studies was published in the journalSciencetwo years ago. Dr Tadeja Gračner at the University of Southern California and her colleagues used data from theUK Biobankto compare the health of people born shortly before and after sugar rationing ended in the UK. Some had been exposed to this low sugar environment only during their time in the womb; others remained exposed for months or years, while those conceived once rationing ended were not exposed at all.Gračner found that the longer people had spent under rationing, the lower their risk of developing type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure in mid- to later life: those exposed throughout their first 1,000 days had a 35% lower risk of type 2 diabetes and a 20% lower risk of high blood pressure than those who had never experienced rationing.The findings prompted Zheng and others to wonder whether these effects might extend to other organ systems. Over the past few months, further studies drawing on UK Biobank data by his group and others have linked reduced sugar exposure to lower risks of a growing list of health conditions.View image in fullscreenA group of boys and a woman queuing outside a sweet shop in 1953.Photograph: Grace Robertson/Source: Hulton-Deutsch Collection/Corbis/Getty Images“I have been more struck by the consistency across different organ systems than by any single effect estimate,” Zheng said. “In our work, we have seen associations with cardiovascular disease, liver disease, respiratory health, dementia and, more recently, broader measures of ageing. Ourageing study, for example, found a lower overall incidence of diseases linked to the hallmarks of ageing and modestly younger biological and organ ages among people exposed to rationing early in life.”Gračner is not entirely surprised. “Many of these outcomes are connected,” she said. “Diabetes, hypertension and obesity are major risk factors for cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline and several other conditions, so if early-life sugar restriction affects those upstream risks, associations across a broad set of related outcomes are what one would expect.”Perhaps more surprising is the suggestion that the effects could extend beyond physical health. In August, Prof Nophar Geifman at the University of Surrey and her colleagues reported that people who had spent the full first 1,000 days of life under sugar rationing had a33% lower risk of being diagnosed with anxietythan those born after rationing ended.They were also less likely to report a preference for sweet foods decades later. “Despite increased sugar consumption after rationing, early nutritional environments appear to have lasting relevance for mental health,” Geifman said.How such a relatively brief difference in sugar exposure might leave traces detectable many decades later remains uncertain. Gračner said:“We can show that growing up with less sugar was protective decades later, but not how: whether through sugar itself, through taste preferences formed early, or through a metabolic response set in early life.”View image in fullscreenA confectionery ad from 1942.Photograph: John Frost Newspapers/AlamyHer team’slatest research, now under peer review, suggests that growing up under rationing may weaken the influence of genes that predispose people to a higher body weight.“Importantly, while we observe that people exposed to rationing do consume less free sugar in adulthood, we find that dietary difference is similar across genetic-risk groups,” Gračner said. “That points to a response that is not purely behavioural: early nutrition may act on physiological pathways such as metabolic programming, insulin sensitivity, appetite and satiety regulation, or adipose-tissue [fat tissue] development.”Explaining the anxiety finding is slightly trickier. Geifman says the brain undergoes rapid development in the womb and during the first few years of life, which could make it particularly sensitive to its nutritional environment. High-sugar diets have also been linked to inflammation and an altered gut microbiome – both possible routes through which sugar could affect brain function.View image in fullscreenA busy shop in April 1953 after rationing ended. Five months later, sugar availability changed quite abruptly at the population level.Photograph: Grace Robertson/Getty ImagesZheng’sageing studyoffers another potential clue. It found that people exposed to rationing scored about a year younger on several measures of biological age. The researchers also detected differences in proteins involved in pathways that help cells respond to nutrients and have been implicated in ageing. “I therefore see biological ageing as a possible shared upstream pathway, rather than necessarily a completely separate phenomenon,” Zheng said.The idea that early-life nutrition can have lasting effects is not new. Since the 1970s, researchers have used famines as natural experiments to investigate the consequences of severe nutritional deprivation early in life.Much of this research has focused on the Dutch “hunger winter” of 1944-45, when German restrictions on food transport left millions in the western Netherlands facing severe shortages. Because this famine began and ended abruptly in a previously well-nourished population, and because food rations were recorded and detailed birth records survived, researchers have been able to compare those exposed during different stages of pregnancy with those born before the famine or conceived after it ended.“The most reliable findings are an increased risk of overweight, obesity and type 2 diabetes,” said Prof LH Lumey, an emeritus professor of epidemiology at Columbia Mailman School of PublicHealthin New York. “People are likely to be more overweight starting from when they are 20 or 30, and they are more likely to have diabetes at age 50 or 60.”View image in fullscreenA woman shopping in wartime London has coupons removed from her ration book after buying a week’s supply of butter and sugar, circa 1942.Photograph: Chris Ware/Getty ImagesAlthough the British rationing studies might appear to point in the opposite direction, the conditions were very different. “British sugar rationing was not famine, and it did not involve severe overall caloric deprivation. Rather, it selectively constrained sugar intake while the broader diet remained relatively adequate,” Zheng said.The lesson, then, is not simply that less nutrition is better. “It suggests that the quality and timing of nutrition during early development can have consequences that extend across the life course,” Zheng said.So where does this leave us? Fascinating as the findings are, they don’t prove that differences in early-life sugar consumption caused the later health differences. “There’s no causality implied,” Geifman said. “It is an association.”View image in fullscreenA woman registers her family with a grocer for rations of bacon, ham, butter and sugar, circa 1939.Photograph: Fox Photos/Getty ImagesMany of the recent studies also draw on overlapping groups of UK Biobank participants, meaning they cannot be regarded as independent replications. “The strongest evidence will ultimately come from triangulation across independent datasets and research designs,” Gračner said.Lumey said the findings represented “a great first step, not the final word. They should be further examined, not to answer the question: is there an association or not? But is the risk really 30% higher or 50% higher, and does it relate to the first 1,000 days, or only the period in gestation?”Even if the associations eventually prove causal, these current studies cannot tell parents exactly how much sugar is too much. Nor can they pinpoint a single critical window. The evidence so far suggests that exposure during pregnancy matters, but some associations become stronger when rationing continued beyond about six months of age – around the time babies begin eating solid foods.View image in fullscreenA Mars bar ad in a magazine in 1943.Photograph: John Frost Newspapers/Alamy“The emerging picture is that the whole first 1,000 days may matter, with pregnancy and the transition to solid foods representing potentially important windows,” Zheng said. “While these findings support existing recommendations to limit unnecessary free or added sugars, they should not be interpreted as evidence that severe dietary restriction is beneficial.”Yet, this postwar experiment may be less divorced from modern life than it first seems. Sugar consumption under rationing was broadly comparable to levels recommended bycurrent UK guidelines,which state that free sugars – those added to foods and drinks, or naturally present in honey, syrups, smoothies and fruit juices – should not exceed 30g a day for adults and children aged 11 and over, with lower amounts for younger children. “Sugars should not be added to food or drinks given to babies,” NHS guidance says.In practice,average UK consumptionis roughly twice the recommended level.The question raised by these studies is not, therefore, whether today’s infants should experience wartime deprivation, but whether keeping sugar intake closer to already recommended levels may have benefits that extend much further into later life than previously recognised.This article was amended on 7 October 2026. An earlier version of the picture caption accompanying an image of a group of boys and a woman queuing outside a sweet shop was said to be in 1945; it was taken in 1953.Explore more on these topicsSugar (Society)Sugar (Business)Second world warHealthNutrition (Science)Nutrition (Life and style)ShareReuse this content

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: loose powders have had a glow up  | Makeup | The Guardian
description: No longer messy and cumbersome, a new generation of powders blurs, sets and mattifies without the faff
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: No longer messy and cumbersome, a new generation of powders blurs, sets and mattifies without the faff
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Sali Hughes on beautyMakeupSali Hughes on beauty: loose powders have had a glow upNo longer messy and cumbersome, a new generation of powders blurs, sets and mattifies without the faffSali HughesWed 7 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIcan’t remember the last time I wrote about loose powder because, honestly, there’s been little point. Pressed compact powders have become so sophisticated in formulation, so finely milled in production, that most of us rely on those to keep shiny bits matte and makeup looking fresh past lunchtime. Loose powders – messy, cumbersome and barely improved in decades – seemed trapped in the past. But there have always been times when one absolutely does benefit from a proper dusting.A fine coating of loose powder locks down foundation and concealer like nothing else can – no bridal or TV makeup artist, dancer or performer would be without it. Now, seemingly all at once, a flurry of new generation powders are offering way more for your trouble.double quotation markThe word ‘blur’ is exactly right here – everything is softer, hazier, and it looks terrific on cameraCharlotte Tilbury’s newAirbrush Flawless Blur Loose Powder(£40) is so good that I think she’ll revive the entire category. Its finish is ultra smooth, refined and flattering, and the packaging dispenses with everything that’s annoying about loose powder – no shaking messily from plastic sieves into lids here. The weightless powder sits neatly under a fine gauge mesh and you simply roll over your puff (included) to pick up exactly the right amount, then press on to the skin – even under eyes, where it sets concealer without caking or creasing.The word “blur” is thrown around like confetti these days, but here it’s exactly right – everything is softer and hazier. It also looks terrifically natural on camera.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: a shortcut to glass skin? Try these one-step moisturisersRead moreKosas makes one of my favourite pressed powders,Cloud Set(£35), and now they’ve smashed the translation to loose. This is a loose powder for the nervous, in that it’s doing precisely what it should, only without really showing its workings. This is not overly mattifying – even dry skin still looks radiant, only without the “faux” glow of shimmer or glitter.As with the Tilbury, powder particles are microscopic and diaphanous, allowing for creases around the nose to be coated without build-up or caking. The shades are realistic and approachable, too.Staying power on both is very good, but if longevity is your primary goal try MaybellineFit Me Loose Powder(£9.99). I feel certain you could wear this in a wind tunnel and it would still hold tight. As with all the high street powders I tried and rated, though, the range of shades is woeful in the UK (more inclusive in the US), so if you’re lucky enough to find one that works for you, snap it up.Explore more on these topicsMakeupSali Hughes on beautySkincareBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nicolas Ghesquière takes us into the future for Louis Vuitton show in Paris | Louis Vuitton | The Guardian
description: Models walk runway at the Louvre with flying cars hovering above as designer envisions city life in a warming world
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Models walk runway at the Louvre with flying cars hovering above as designer envisions city life in a warming world
Content: A model walks the runway for the Louis Vuitton show at the Louvre, which was illuminated with lights from hovercars.Photograph: Lou Benoist/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA model walks the runway for the Louis Vuitton show at the Louvre, which was illuminated with lights from hovercars.Photograph: Lou Benoist/AFP/Getty ImagesLouis VuittonNicolas Ghesquière takes us into the future for Louis Vuitton show in ParisModels walk runway at the Louvre with flying cars hovering above as designer envisions city life in a warming worldJess Cartner-Morleyin ParisWed 7 Oct 2026 03.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn silk slip dresses, breezy vented tunics and gossamer layers of chiffon, the models on Louis Vuitton’s catwalk were perfectly dressed for an unseasonably warm October evening in Paris. As the show began at sunset it was still 24C.This summer’s record temperatures were on designer Nicolas Ghesquiière’s mind. “The world is getting warmer, this definitely had a strong influence” he said.The show was staged in an inner courtyard of the Louvre, the catwalk illuminated by the tail lights of a fleet of 34 flying cars in Vuitton’s signature Damier check raised on stilts above the catwalk.View image in fullscreenModels on the runway.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni / WWD / Getty ImagesThe contrast between the futuristic set and the historic buildings was an elegant echo of the centrepiece of the Louvre, where IM Pei’s glass pyramid stands amid the French classical architecture.View image in fullscreenNicolas Ghesquière.Photograph: Lou Benoist/AFP/Getty ImagesThe future is always on Ghesquière’s mind – his science fiction bent showed up in the models’ beaded silver fringes that were somewhere between space-age hair extensions and sun visors – and this season, he was thinking about life in the cities of the future, his models as pedestrians among flying cars. “I was thinking about a woman walking through traffic, and how in the urban environment we sometimes feel vulnerable and sometimes feel strong.”The featherlight fabrics and free-floating silhouettes were a departure from the angular, ornate looks which are his signature. “I am a specialist in a kind of fashion that is like armour, fashion with strong architecture, but this summer I think we all felt like we needed a different wardrobe. The world is getting warmer. We need to think differently, for clothes to be relevant today and in the future.”Zendaya wore a ruffled organza jacket last seen on her Odyssey press tour and the Rivals actor Bella Maclean was in sleek black tailoring. Ghesquière took his bow casually dressed in jeans – but then, the show was only his second most important moment ofParis fashion week. Louis Vuitton is the flagship brand of luxury giant LVMH, which contributes about 1% to French GDP, placing it close to the core of economic and cultural power in Paris.View image in fullscreenZendaya she arrives for the Louis Vuitton show.Photograph: Lou Benoist/AFP/Getty ImagesOn Friday Ghesquière, who has led Vuitton for a decade, was knighted by President Emmanuel Macron for his contribution to French creative industries, at a ceremony at the Élysée Palace.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe first lady, Brigitte Macron, has a longstanding close collaboration with Ghesquière, attending his shows and wearing custom looks for state occasions. President Macron began his speech joking that “it feels strange to be decorating someone tonight who is used to looking at my wife from every angle … she just told me you are the second man in her life.”View image in fullscreenA model on the Louis Vuitton runway.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesGuests at the ceremony reflected the broad reach of Louis Vuitton, with Catherine Deneuve and the British designer Phoebe Philo alongside K-pop star Felix of Stray Kids. Ghesquière wore a striking double-breasted Louis Vuitton black suit, with a single button fastening and no lapel. Pinning the red ribboned medallion to his chest, Macron said: “This evening … it is the Republic itself that is adding a new element to your wardrobe.”Explore more on these topicsLouis VuittonParis fashion weekFashion weeksNicolas GhesquièreFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s hard to imagine the fires of July’: a bike ride through the Cairngorms in Scotland | Travel | The Guardian
description: Wildfires raged through the national park this summer, but much of the landscape remains untouched – and autumn is the perfect time to go
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: Wildfires raged through the national park this summer, but much of the landscape remains untouched – and autumn is the perfect time to go
Content: Much of the burned area is far from the roads. All photographs: Markus StitzView image in fullscreenMuch of the burned area is far from the roads. All photographs: Markus StitzTravel‘It’s hard to imagine the fires of July’: a bike ride through the Cairngorms in ScotlandWildfires raged through the national park this summer, but much of the landscape remains untouched – and autumn is the perfect time to goAilsa SheldonWed 7 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 02.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the Cairngorms national park, the bracken is changing from dark green to russet and umber. Birch leaves are lined with gold, while the Scots pines remain proudly green. Autumn is arriving with a little sigh of relief here, after a summer few will forget.The wildfire that began near Glenmore and Abernethy on 15 July burned more than 33 sq km (13 sq miles) of moorland and forest. More than 500 firefighters were involved; homes and businesses were evacuated; and the emergency response lasted over a month. Visiting now, it’s hard to see, or even imagine, the damage. Much of the burned area is high on the hill and far from the roads. It’s a huge loss but, in a national park stretching 4,528 sq km (1,748 sq miles), surprisingly easy to miss.I have come with a gravel bike to retest new bikepacking routes with Kees Wouters and Yannick Ferbeek fromLegendary Rides, which offers self-guided tours, and Bikepacking Scotland founder Markus Stitz, who helped develop the routes.View image in fullscreenAilsa Sheldon on the trailI arrive in Aviemore from Edinburgh on an electric Ember bus, which allows bikes to be booked on board, a welcome development in Scottish public transport. Soon I’m heading out of town through heather and Scots pines, my bike bags stuffed with everything I need for the next few days.The original route would have taken us through Glenmore, past Loch Morlich and Ryvoan bothy, but there are still path closures. Instead, we take a new line towards Nethy Bridge. Sunlight falls through birch and rowan and the track is soft with pine needles. At Loch Garten, where ospreys nest in spring and summer, it is hard to imagine the smoke and helicopters of July.Graham Niven lives in Nethy Bridge with his wife, Amy, and runs the self-catering businessArbor Nethybeside the forest. He joined the local volunteer firefighting effort coordinated by the RSPB, part of a huge community response. “We see the forest as an extension of our home,” Graham says. The Abernethy forest is ecologically rich, filled with ancient Caledonian pine trees that are hundreds of years old. “It’s a unique and special habitat, and it’s very fragile. We were all just grieving for the forest,” he tells me.View image in fullscreenCycling by the River AvonThe news cycle has long moved on, but locals are still dealing with the effects of the wildfire. “Only in the last few weeks have we been able to look back on it as something that’s come to an end,” Graham says. Peat smouldered underground for months, meaning firefighters had to keep returning to hotspots.While business has largely returned to usual, Graham has noticed a dip in bookings for photography workshops and holiday lets. “What is less measurable is people’s confidence in booking or coming back. The buzzwords were ‘apocalyptic fire’ and Abernethy and Nethy Bridge, Cairngorms, and that does stick in people’s minds. People think of Abernethy and say: ‘Oh, it’s been burned down.’ I think it’s less than 10% of the old forest affected.” Nearby, Polly Cameron atThe Dell of Abernethyhas seen the same effect: “Bookings wise, we certainly experienced a dip, and October has still been much slower to fill.” That matters in a landscape where tourism is a vital part of the local economy.double quotation markThe Cairngorms change character as you head east: forests give way to sheep, grouse moors, abandoned crofts and long gravel roadsWe ride on along the Speyside Way, following the river through woods and farmland. Then the landscape opens. The Cairngorms change character as you head east: deep forests give way to sheep, grouse moors, abandoned crofts and long gravel roads. This is whisky country too, and we ride through the grounds of Glenlivet Distillery. It’s after hours, or the smell of malted barley would have tempted me to stop.By late afternoon the hills have turned heather-purple. We started late and by the time we reachHotel Squarein Tomintoul, darkness has settled. Our bikes go into a storage room and, happily, hot curry and cold beer are still available.The next day is shorter but steeper, taking us on to sections of the old military roads built in the 18th century after the Jacobite risings. I’m reminded of that history later atCorgarff, a white fortress on the crest of a hill. Built in the 16th century and later converted into a barracks, it was used to suppress Jacobite sympathisers and, later, the illicit whisky trade.View image in fullscreenCairngorm Bothies near BallaterWe spend the second night atCairngorm Bothies, off-grid cabins surrounded by Scots pines. In each, there’s a little nature journal and I leaf through pages of children’s handwriting with tales of red squirrels and deer. When the rain starts, any disappointment about missing out on seeing the dark skies is replaced by relief not to be camping.With a flexible route we stop often, for photos, snacks and whenever the fancy takes us. We walk through woodland to visit Burn O’Vat, a huge glacial pothole in the Muir of Dinnet national nature reserve. At Ballater we stop for coffee and morning rolls atThe Bothywhile one of our group gets a quick bike repair. The route is deliberately forgiving, and Legendary Rides provides shorter alternatives for challenging weather or tired legs, with prebooked accommodation, a personalised plan, GPX routes and WhatsApp support. “It allows you to relax and just enjoy the ride,” says Yannick.double quotation markAutumn is an ideal time for this kind of journey. The midges have retreated, the roads are emptier and there is still plenty of golden lightFrom Ballater we wind towards Loch Muick, through the Balmoral estate. After a long, winding ascent over Capel Mounth the riding becomes rougher, with a rocky descent. The gentle undulating roads that follow to Glen Clova are a welcome contrast as we roll to Alyth.I’ve visited the Cairngorms region often in the past, but this trip broadens my awareness of the diversity of landscapes it holds. To mountain peaks and forest trails I add river valleys, whisky country, high moorland, farmland and roads so empty that the only sound is the freewheel of a bicycle.View image in fullscreenA waterfall at Burn O’VatBut this is not untouched wilderness. We cross private estates managed for deer stalking and grouse shooting, as well as national nature reserves. Debates over the right ways to manage this land span centuries, with wildfire prevention now a key part of that conversation. Scotland’s right to responsible access allows us to pass through this landscape, provided we leave no trace, close gates and avoid disturbing livestock and wildlife.Autumn is an ideal time for this kind of journey. The midges have retreated, the roads are emptier and there is still plenty of golden light in the days.Cyclingthrough the area helps to support local cafes, shops and accommodation providers, and there’s never been a better time to do so. “We want people to know we’re still here, we’re still awesome,” says Graham.My tired legs power me to a final Pitlochry cafe stop before my Ember bus back to Edinburgh.The trip was provided byLegendary RidesandBikepacking Scotland. title: A moment that changed me: I was heading for disaster on the Greek version of Strictly. Then instinct kicked in | Dance | The Guardian
description: I was gripped by fear, aching all over – and still recovering from cancer treatment. But Dancing With the Stars was a joyous celebration of survival
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I was gripped by fear, aching all over – and still recovering from cancer treatment. But Dancing With the Stars was a joyous celebration of survival
Content: ‘I forgot almost every move’ … Hislop with her dance partner, Tilemachos Fatsis, on Greek TV’s Dancing With the Stars in 2021.View image in fullscreen‘I forgot almost every move’ … Hislop with her dance partner, Tilemachos Fatsis, on Greek TV’s Dancing With the Stars in 2021.A moment that changed meDanceA moment that changed me: I was heading for disaster on the Greek version of Strictly. Then instinct kicked inI was gripped by fear, aching all over – and still recovering from cancer treatment. But Dancing With the Stars was a joyous celebration of survivalVictoria HislopWed 7 Oct 2026 01.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was an invitation I accepted in a moment of madness – and, over the next three months, regretted many times a day. I was in over my head, often with my heels literally over my head: I’d signed up to appear on the Greek version of Strictly Come Dancing.Dancing With the Stars, as it is called inGreece, follows the same format as its UK counterpart, with an identical studio, a matching shiny floor, even many of the same costumes that are hired out and circulated among the 70 or more international versions of the BBC show. Of course, it’s all in Greek – and in the season I took part in, Covid restrictions had been imposed, which intensified its strangeness.I am British, but by the time of my appearance on Dancing With the Stars I had become a bestselling author in Greece. In 2010, my first novel, The Island, was adapted for a 26-part series, which achieved the country’s highest-ever ratings for a TV drama. In 2020, I was granted honorary citizenship by the Greek prime minister. All of this had made me a minor celebrity.I never imagined the competition would be easy. The only woman older than me out of the dozen or so contestants was Bessy Argyraki, who had been aEurovision entrantin 1977, while I was still at school. In the first week, when we found each other weeping in the ladies’, we became best friends. All the other women could do the splits, but we were still struggling to remember basic steps.View image in fullscreen‘My mind was left behind – along with my anxiety.’There were six weeks of training and preparation and we were in the rehearsal room every day – except one, when I practised at home using a video I had recorded on my phone. I was exhausted, bruised, living on painkillers and suffering intense aches and pains – side-effects not just of my new dance regime, but also of a drug I was taking after cancer treatment six months earlier. If I had wanted a challenge, to celebrate survival, I had found it. And more.The fear of the first “live” show was beyond anything I could have imagined. I couldn’t eat for two days before and during the rehearsal I forgot almost every move. The director was unimpressed, the choreographer was disappointed and my partner was furious. The dress rehearsal was even worse. Meanwhile, the other contestants – lithe Olympic athletes, glamorous TV presenters, models and media superstars – effortlessly glided their way through their dances.I knew all my Greek friends would be watching. The Sunday night slot was a popular one and Star Channel was one of the most highly rated commercial stations.I watched from the wings as one couple after another scored almost top marks, then I went to get my hair done, which involved an industrial can of spray to stiffen it into a solid helmet. One of my fake eyelashes had to be re-glued to my eyelid.I retired to my dressing room, popped some painkillers and watched the video of my dance over and over again, still trying to get it into my head. Then there was a sharp knock at my door. I pushed my bunioned feet into some pointy ballroom shoes and followed the production assistant towards what felt like the gallows. The props for our dance (an airport arrivals scenario) were being shunted into position. Suddenly, I heard the opening bars of our tune. This wasit.View image in fullscreenEuphoric … Victoria Hislop in Greece.Photograph: Harry Mavrogenis“Break a leg,” I said under my breath to my partner. “Skata,” I thought I heard him say back, which is the Greek “good luck” equivalent and literally translated means “shit”. Yes, I thought, it probably will be.Almost suffocating in my body-hugging frothy tulle costume, I floated out across the stage. There was a warm ripple of applause and my mind was left behind – along with all the anxiety I had been holding. Muscle memory kicked in and my body had no need for instructions; it followed its own instincts, its own paths, taking me through a routine that I wasn’t even sure I had memorised.My brain was quiet in those minutes. If for a second I had allowed myself to think: “What comes next?” all would have been lost. In my whole life, I had never abandoned the rational and allowed pure instinct to tell me what to do. It was a transcendental moment.The euphoria arrived with the final note of the music. I was in a state of joyous disbelief. We had been step-perfect. We stood in front of the judges to listen to their compliments, but I took hardly anything in. Had that person they were referring to been me?In the following weeks, there were a few more times when I was gripped by instinct and nothing else. Eventually, although I had technically become a better dancer, we were voted out. Perhaps the judges and audience could see that the surprise takeover of my mind by a greater force did not always happen. But in those precious moments, it had felt like magic.The Wine-Dark Sea by Victoria Hislop is out now (Headline, £22). To support the Guardian, orderyour copyatguardianbookshop.com.
