title: Beautiful butterflies get more attention from the public – and from scientists | Butterflies | The Guardian
description: Research has shown that species considered colourful and patterned are the subject of more studies, and receive more conservation funding
Author: Kate Ravilious
Headline: Research has shown that species considered colourful and patterned are the subject of more studies, and receive more conservation funding
Content: A swallowtail butterfly: in a survey of 21,000 people, larger, more colourful and patterned butterflies were consistently rated more attractive.Photograph: Julia Hiebaum/AlamyView image in fullscreenA swallowtail butterfly: in a survey of 21,000 people, larger, more colourful and patterned butterflies were consistently rated more attractive.Photograph: Julia Hiebaum/AlamySpecieswatchButterfliesBeautiful butterflies get more attention from the public – and from scientistsResearch has shown that colourful and patterned species are the subject of more studies, and receive more conservation fundingKate RaviliousWed 7 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLarge and beautiful butterflies attract far more attention than species that are smaller and dull. Now a new study has shown that this bias towards beauty results in the boring butterflies being overlooked in conservation programmes.To understand the link between beauty and conservation, researchers surveyed more than 21,000 people from more than 100 countries, asking them to look at photos of European butterflies and rate their beauty on a scale of 1 to 10 based on their first impression. The results, which are published inCurrent Biology, reveal that larger more colourful and patterned butterflies, like the yellow swallowtail, were consistently rated more attractive than the smaller, less conspicuous brownish species, such as the alpine grayling. That bias also extended into scientific research, with more studies on attractive species, and more funding and resource going into conservation of showier species.By contrast, national and Europeanred lists, which are based on fixed measurement criteria, do not exhibit the beauty bias. In fact, the most recent lists show that many of the small, brown, less attractive species are facing the greatest threat from climate breakdown.The authors argue that nature conservation programmes need to recognise the beauty bias and give greater consideration to inconspicuous butterflies, which, while not as showy, play equally important functions within ecosystems.Explore more on these topicsButterfliesSpecieswatchWildlifeIUCN red list of endangered speciesConservationResearch fundingInsectsEndangered speciesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: A gleaming beetle that could be bad news for my garden favourites | Insects | The Guardian
description: Allendale, Northumberland: On a hot autumn day, I see rosemary beetles here for the first time. This could be a problem for many thriving plants
Author: Susie White
Headline: Allendale, Northumberland: On a hot autumn day, I see rosemary beetles here for the first time. This could be a problem for many thriving plants
Content: A mating pair of rosemary beetles on a lavender stem.Photograph: Lankowsky/AlamyView image in fullscreenA mating pair of rosemary beetles on a lavender stem.Photograph: Lankowsky/AlamyCountry diaryInsectsCountry diary: A gleaming beetle that could be bad news for my garden favouritesAllendale, Northumberland:On a hot autumn day, I see rosemary beetles here for the first time. This could be a problem for many thriving plantsSusie WhiteWed 7 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis year there have been several firsts in my garden: old lady, vestal and blood-vein moths attracted to the light trap;hummingbird hawk-moths, normally occasional, feeding summer-long from verbena and buddleia; and it’s a painted lady year –a once-a-decade event, these high-flying insects migrating from Africa through successive generations. Southerly winds and heatwaves have added to the species visiting my North Pennine garden.Now, in a herb bed, I spot something less welcome. Among the resinous leaves of rosemary is a gleaming beetle, itselytrastriped in purple and green, scintillating like lustreware. It’s not something I’ve seen before, but I immediately know what it means. Rosemary beetle,Chrysolina americana,is a Mediterranean species with no natural predators in the UK. It is shimmering and beautiful – but can reduce plants of theLamiaceaefamily to bare sticks and cause them to die back. This includes my favourites: lavender, sage, thyme – and rosemary.Country diary: Bright and bohemian, this moth could be a David Hockney | Paul EvansRead moreRosemary beetles were first discovered living outdoors in the UK in 1994 and have increased rapidly since then in our warming climate. The Royal Horticultural Society is monitoring their spread and hasasked for sightings, which I submit. The advice is to hand-pick this non-native invasive species and tolerate “where possible”, seeing them as “as a colourful addition to the garden”. I wonder how rosemary beetles made it to my borders, as they have quite short wings and can’t fly far, preferring to walk, and I’ve propagated all my own herbs.On a hot autumn day the gleaming beetles are out in force, mating at the top of branches – they particularly like lavender seedheads rather than flowers. Just touching a stem causes them to drop, a defence mechanism common to other beetles, making them hard to spot against the soil. The grubs are dull grey with longitudinal darker stripes, and both larvae and adults feed on the leaves.Studying the bushes makes me notice other things: cinnamon bugs in their smart finery, seven-spot ladybirds, a garden snail sheltering in a sage leaf, a dramatically patterned cabbage bug, a tiny froghopper. Red admirals flicker over calendulas in this unusual autumn warmth, but there are colder days to come. Rosemary beetles are only likely to survive in my frost hollow if it’s a mild winter.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsInsectsCountry diaryPlantsRural affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought the baby would change him’: the women whose pregnancies are blighted by domestic abuse | Domestic violence | The Guardian
description: An estimated 20,000 cases are disclosed to maternity services in England every year. Two survivors tell their stories
Author: Emily Retter
Headline: An estimated 20,000 cases are disclosed to maternity services in England every year. Two survivors tell their stories
Content: Composite: Guardian design; Olga Rolenko/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design; Olga Rolenko/Getty ImagesDomestic violence‘I thought the baby would change him’: the women whose pregnancies are blighted by domestic abuseAn estimated 20,000 cases are disclosed to maternity services in England every year. Two survivors tell their storiesEmily RetterWed 7 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvie bought the baby monitor with a rare flicker of enthusiasm, having become increasingly numb as her pregnancy progressed. She liked that it would send video footage to her phone. “I thought, ‘This is really good. Not only can you hear the baby – you can see the baby.’” Unfortunately, her partner appreciated the monitor too. Soon she was carrying it around the house on his orders, so he could watch her. “He used it as surveillance,” she says.By then she was worn down, and terrified. He had become more controlling since they learned she was pregnant. By the seventh month he had become physically abusive, too. “We were just lying in bed watching something,” she recalls of the first attack. “An argument broke out but it started getting overly aggressive … It just felt more threatening and he looked really agitated. So I ended up shimmying over and sitting on the edge of the bed. All of a sudden he just swung the biggest punch at my arm. Then he did it again. The impact was like whiplash.”Trauma makes her memory hazy, Evie says, but somehow she ended up lying on the bed again. “Then he climbed over me, putting his knees either side. As he put his arm down, it squashed my belly.”She shrieked. “Then he just snapped out of it.” As she cried he apologised and put his arms around the bump. “He talked to the baby, sang to the baby …” she recalls. He claimed he had lashed out due to his anxiety. “I accepted it wouldn’t happen again because he was so apologetic.”The Domestic Abuse Commissioner estimates that in England and Wales,30% of domestic abuse begins during pregnancy, but the real figure is almost certainly higher because of underreporting.New researchpublished by the For Baby’s Sake Trust, which supports young families experiencing domestic abuse, estimates that 20,000 cases of domestic abuse are disclosed to maternity services inEnglandevery year.Lauren Seager-Smith, the chief executive of For Baby’s Sake, stresses “pregnancy does not cause abuse”, but explains: “It can be a context in which we see an increased use of abusive behaviours … This could include increased monitoring, isolation from family, friends and colleagues, financial control, coercion around healthcare or reproductive rights, physical, emotional and sexual abuse, and even jealousy and resentment towards the developing baby.”Elaha Walizadeh, a senior programme manager at Refuge, the biggest specialist domestic abuse organisation in the UK, says that between 2024 and 2025 “14% of our service users reported being pregnant”, but believes this is the “tip of the iceberg”. Women may come into more contact with healthcare professionals during pregnancy, but “because not all healthcare professionals and advisers are trained in recognising the signs and having the right conversations with these survivors, survivors are being missed”.Evie became pregnant early in her relationship. She describes “lovebombing”: gifts, flowers, chocolates. She now sees signs of control were there, dressed up as love. “‘Oh, you’re going to see your mum?’ he would say. ‘I was going to get a movie night ready …’”He was “over the moon” when she became pregnant but his control intensified. “It started with tracking apps – he ‘wanted to know I was safe’,” she says. “Or he’d say: ‘I’d rather you not go there. I’ve got a bad feeling.’” He even started accompanying her to work sometimes. “He had to be with me constantly. Every midwife appointment. I couldn’t go to doctors on my own, couldn’t have my flu jab on my own.” Evie was asked routine questions concerning domestic abuse. She said everything was fine because she thought it was.Later her partner became aggressive. Arguments escalated, usually triggered by an accusation she was not paying him enough attention. Doors would slam, and the name-calling began: “slag”, “stupid bitch”. But the apologies afterwards and excuses of anxiety convinced her, until the physical attack. Even then, she felt too vulnerable to leave or seek help. “No one wants to bring a child up in a broken home,” she says. “I thought the baby would change him and make him happy.”double quotation markHe thought it was a good idea to have a child because then I couldn't leaveA month before the birth, another violent outburst led to the authorities finally becoming involved. He eventually moved out, but would “sneak back” and continued to demand Evie carry the baby monitor. Fear kept her silent. She allowed him to attend the birth and he had supervised contact with the new baby, who he bonded with, but the physical abuse against her escalated until she secured a non-molestation order, granted by courts to prevent domestic abuse. She has not had any contact for years.“I feel like I died and my body just carried on,” is how Evie describes her emotions towards the end of her pregnancy and early motherhood. There is a blankness to her voice even now. “I hold a lot of guilt,” she says, believing she “failed” her child. “I am hypervigilant, extremely jumpy …” She still ruminates on why the abuse began. “I believe at first he thought it was a good idea to have a child because then: ‘She can’t leave me.’ But then the baby was getting all the attention.”Dr Panos Vythoulkas, a lead perinatal clinical psychologist at the North London NHS foundation trust, says this is common. “The baby introduces another person whose needs must be recognised. Someone who feels entitled to control their partner may experience these changes as a threat to their position, attention or authority.” He citessurvivor accountsthat repeatedly describe “increased possessiveness”. Abusers resent “the attention given to the pregnancy or experience the baby as a rival. A woman’s need for rest, support or choice not to have sex may be interpreted as rejection or a challenge to their authority.”View image in fullscreenSome abusers have cited difficult relationships with their own fathers.Photograph: posed by model; Johner Images/Getty Images/Johner RFThe clinical psychologist Dr Jill Domoney has workedwith abuserswho have faced up to their actions. “In some of those cases there was a real tension between what they’d internalised about masculinity – needing to be strong and in control and to look after the family financially – and what was being expected of them as fathers, needing to provide in circumstances where that might not be possible,” she says. “Maybe they’re feeling quite vulnerable and scared – but not feeling they were allowed to express that.” Some had difficult relationships with their own fathers.Like Evie, Vythoulkas believes that abusers may initially desire pregnancy because it offers opportunities for control. “Financial pressures, insecure housing, isolation and increased dependence can restrict a woman’s options. An abusive partner may exploit these circumstances by withholding money, limiting contact with others or obstructing healthcare,” he says.Riley says her partner was desperate for children. Although they were in a long-distance relationship, “within a matter of weeks” he was talking about babies. She eventually agreed. However, when she rang to tell him the news, his reaction was staggering. As well as asking her to do a pregnancy test on video to prove she wasn’t lying, “He immediately said: ‘Is it mine?’” Shaken, she refused to do the test but still found herself desperately reassuring him. Vythoulkas confirms that “accusations of infidelity and doubts about the baby’s paternity” are regularly observed as part of abusers’ insecurity.double quotation markHe used to call me a rhino and said I looked disgustingThe abuse Riley then began to experience was initially a disorientating combination of lack of interest and manipulation. Her partner would look at his phone if she put his hand on her stomach to feel the baby kicking, and insisted he felt nothing. He did not want to discuss baby names. No plans were made to move in. Yet he would regularly visit unannounced. “He would turn up on my doorstep at 2am; it was like he was trying to catch me out or put fear into me,” she says.Then the verbal insults and aggression escalated, especially when Riley declined sex. “He used to call me a rhino and said I looked disgusting. If I cried he would tell me to stop turning on the waterworks and ask if I agreed it was pathetic. My self-esteem was at an all-time low.”She tried to end the relationship but he kept showing up. Her low confidence made this harder to resist. “I felt very alone. I didn’t share the things he was saying to me, partly because I felt ashamed and partly I had become so used to what was happening.”Then the physical intimidation began, stopping short of contact. “He was once boiling a pan of water and we got into an argument and he held this big pan of water in front of me and kind of lunged.” He didn’t throw it. “It creates a really confusing emotional situation because you can be genuinely frightened of someone while still desperately wanting the relationship to be OK.”Fear stopped her taking action: fear of his response and fear of having her baby removed. “He would say: ‘Don’t go and pull something where I’m not at the birth because you’ll regret it,’” she recalls. He was present, but they did not move in together afterwards. When he visited, the violent outbursts intensified, usually when Riley was holding the baby. It culminated with Riley being held hostage in her home with her baby, punched as she fed the infant, strangled and raped. She believes she could have died. Her partner was convicted and is now serving a prison sentence. “At no point did he ever beg for forgiveness,” she says. “He would talk about work stresses, money pressures, his childhood or the way he had been treated himself.”Abuse during pregnancy can be fatal. AByline Timesinvestigation based on police information found at least 223 women experienced pregnancy loss linked to domestic abuse in England and Wales between 2017 and 2021. Victims of intimate partner violence are alsotwice as likelyto forgo prenatal care, exacerbating the risk of pregnancy loss. The MBRRACE Confidential Enquiry into Maternal Deathsfound thatsuicide was the leading cause of maternal death in the first postnatal year, and that domestic abuse was documented in 43% of women who died. Evie says she felt suicidal after her child’s birth. “I drank to numb myself and I wanted to end my life because I couldn’t cope,” she says.Evie also points to another potential result of abuse: the behavioural challenges she now observes in her son. Walizadeh says Refuge sees children with brain injuries potentially caused by physical abuse during pregnancy, as well as “children who later in life go on to develop symptoms of ADHD [attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]and other forms of developmental conditions”.For Baby’s Sake and Refuge stress the need for continued training in perinatal services about domestic abuse.It needs to be spotted early. “By the time you’ve actually realised how dangerous it is, it’s too risky to leave,” says Riley.All names have been changedIn the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org.Explore more on these topicsDomestic violencePregnancyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The nurse used the torch on her phone to do the op’: hospitals stripped of resources in Ukraine’s occupied territories | World news | The Guardian
description: Clinics and hospitals in affected areas lack staff, power and medicines, with supplies redirected to the Russian military
Author: Ruchi Kumar
Headline: Clinics and hospitals in affected areas lack staff, power and medicines, with supplies redirected to the Russian military
Content: A premature baby in an incubator in a hospital in Zaporizhzhia. Organisations in Ukraine report an anecdotal rise in maternal and child mortalities.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APView image in fullscreenA premature baby in an incubator in a hospital in Zaporizhzhia. Organisations in Ukraine report an anecdotal rise in maternal and child mortalities.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APUkraine in depthWorld news‘The nurse used the torch on her phone to do the op’: hospitals stripped of resources in Ukraine’s occupied territoriesClinics and hospitals in affected areas lack staff, power and medicines, with supplies redirected to the Russian militarySupported byAbout this contentRuchi KumarWed 7 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 08.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this summer, the once bustling corridors of the district hospital in Hola Prystan, a city in the Russian-occupied Kherson region ofUkraine, were ominously quiet. At times, it was plunged into darkness during power cuts lasting hours.Much of the hospital’s medical equipment and supplies had been stolen and redirected to the military, and many experienced staff had gone.“They [the Russian forces] even took some of the furniture,” says Natalia Sergeevna, who spent more than two decades working as a nurse in the hospital before escaping to Ukrainian-held territory in July.In some ways, her hospital had been lucky, she says, with others in Russian-occupied territories repurposed for military use – as has beenhappening in regionsbordering Ukraine – or simply closed down.Despite its bare-bones infrastructure and dark corridors, people still came to the hospital, says Sergeevna, often making difficult journeys across the mine-infested landscape of occupied Kherson.View image in fullscreenA hospital damaged by Russian shelling in Kherson in July.Photograph: Global Images Ukraine/Getty Images“They came with injuries and wounds; they came looking for oncologists or endocrinologists or palliative care. Women still came with pregnancies,” she says, “but every day it was getting harder to help them.”In recent months, the situation has deteriorated further, withblockades and supply shortagesleaving some Russian-occupied territories with limited medical support.In June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine saidconditions in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, where Sergeevna worked, were becoming desperate, with thousands of people left without food, water and medicines.It said ambulances had stopped coming to people’s homes, with medical assistance only available for the most urgent cases and patients dying during attempted evacuations.Sergeevna says she had stayed in the hope of liberation, but by the summer things had become unbearable. “There is almost no available support to do any kind of surgeries; even basic procedures like removing polyps aren’t possible.View image in fullscreenA woman takes care of a baby in a shelter in the city of Sievierodonetsk, Donbas region.Photograph: Fadel Senna/AFP/Getty Images“In one case this year, we were performing a C-section, and the woman developed uterine bleeding, but there was no blood available for transfusion, because all of the supplies had been sent to the [Russian] soldiers,” she says.Another obstacle is theforced “passportisation” of the population in occupied territories, with medical services refused to people who do not have a Russian compulsory health insurance policy, which can only be obtained through a Russian passport.“They treat you very badly if you are Ukrainian. We have no rights, they tell us to our face, ‘you’re a nobody’,” says Marina*, who lives in a town occupied by Russian forces. She says she had to be taken to hospital in 2023 after she developed complications during her pregnancy and went into early labour.“The baby was coming with the backside down, and I needed an emergency C-section. I was in a lot of pain,” she says. “But it was 11.30pm, and the curfew was in place. We tried getting out, but they shot at us.”View image in fullscreenA member of an emergency medical aid team working in Kherson.Photograph: Global Images Ukraine/Getty ImagesMarina says she spent an excruciating night cared for by her husband and a neighbour, before rushing to the clinic as soon as the curfew lifted. “When we got there, there was no obstetrician, no qualified staff for pregnancy, no one to help. I eventually had a C-section with the help of my neighbour, who was a nurse, and thankfully my baby and I survived.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In a normal circumstance, we would have known about this complication, but because there were no tests or medical professionals left in our town, not even an ultrasound machine, I had no way of diagnosing this,” she says.In another case, from earlier this year, Sergeevna says her colleagues were forced to treat a patient with endometriosis without anaesthesia.“She was bleeding when she came to the hospital. So there was no anaesthesia, not even power. And the nurse at the time used the torch on her phone to do the procedure because there was no other option.”View image in fullscreenA doctor holds up a baby born by caesarean section at Zaporizhzhia’s regional perinatal centre in May.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APAccurate figures are not available; but organisations monitoring the situation in the region detect an anecdotal rise in maternal and child mortalities, as well as long-term health problems. There are also reports of difficulties in accessing contraceptives and abortion.From Ukraine and Sudan to Gaza: why have hospitals become a target of war?Read moreSergeevna says the situation is particularly acute for women, and that she had been dealing with women facing a range of mental health issues because of the lack of medical care and trauma they had suffered, including rape and sex slavery.She says one 18-year-old had come withthe letter “Z”cut into her torso with a blade. While inspecting her wound, Sergeevna discovered the girl had been raped. “But that was not why she came to us; she was too ashamed to admit that. She came only because she couldn’t tolerate the wound any more because of swelling and inflammation.”With few doctors left in her district and depleting resources, Sergeevna and her team did their best to stitch her up. “But there was nothing else we could do for her. There were no resources to check her for STDs or provide her with contraceptives. We did not even have any way to provide psychological support.”*Namehas been changedExplore more on these topicsWorld newsUkraine in depthUkraineRussiaMaternal mortalityWomen's healthEuropeInfant and child mortalityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Inquest under way into why President Lula’s success in curbing Amazon deforestation has not led to success at polls
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Inquest under way into why President Lula’s success in curbing Amazon deforestation has not led to success at polls
Content: Flavio Bolsonaro, centre, is in pole position to win the election runoff on 25 October against Brazil’s incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenFlavio Bolsonaro, centre, is in pole position to win the election runoff on 25 October against Brazil’s incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/GettyView from the AmazonBrazilFlávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaignersInquest under way into why President Lula’s success in curbing Amazon deforestation has not led to success at pollsJonathan WattsWed 7 Oct 2026 15.23 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 07.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years ifFlávio Bolsonaroholds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election.This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation.The far-right son of the former president and jailed coup-mongerJair Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote, putting him in pole position before the 25 October runoff with the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was backed by 44.2%.The result is an unnerving jolt to climate and nature campaigners. Taken out of context, this appears to be a vote against the forest. The current administration of Lula (as the veteran Brazilian president is best known) hasreduced deforestation in the Amazonby almost 50%.But that success secured little noticeable electoral traction for either Lula or pro-forest candidates in other polls held the same day. The former environment minister Marina Silva lost a bid for the Senate and Joenia Wapichana, a former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, failed to win a seat in Congress. Out of 57Indigenous candidates, only two won.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro has shown he is as willing as his father, Jair, to curb nature protections and allow Indigenous territories to be exploited.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APFlávio Bolsonaro is the heir to the political legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain whose four years in power resulted in a 59.5%increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying 2bn trees.If he wins, Bolsonaro has promised to free his father, who was imprisoned for plotting amilitary coupand attempting to annihilate democracy in Brazil. He has said that his father could have any position he wants in his administration.Election share mapFlávio Bolsonaro has shown that he will be just as willing as his father to dismantle protections for climate and nature and allow illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers to invade Indigenous territories. As a lawmaker, he backed a 2019 bill to eliminate requirements for landowners in the Amazon to conserve a proportion of native vegetation. In his manifesto, he completely ignored the climate crisis. And he has courted support from some of the most predatory landowners in the rainforest.View image in fullscreenLula’s social media campaign has not been as effective as that of the Bolsonaro team.Photograph: Evaristo Sa/AFP/GettyHe is also part of a movement – Bolsonarism – that is geared towards maximising profits for extractive industries regardless of the environmental cost. Take its victorious candidate for the Amazonian state of Pará,Daniel Santos, who was fined $275,000 (£208,000) for deforestating 280 hectares (690 acres) of his land without authorisation and is now promising to waive such penalties. As a result of Sunday’s election, Bolsonarists now control seven of the nine states in the Brazilian Amazon, and could win an eighth in the runoffs.Bolsonarist influencein the legislature, which is dominated by agribusiness interests, is also growing. Flávio’s brother, Carlos, and mother-in-law, Michelle, were elected to the Senate, while an uncle and brother won seats in the lower house of deputies.Even before the election, Congress had been pushing hard to weaken environmental protections. Now it will be almost impossible to stop, particularly given the current chaos in the supreme court, which has been a partial check on untrammelled expansion by miners, ranchers and monoculturalists. Against these forces, Lula would struggle to govern even if he wins the runoff.View image in fullscreenA Flavio Bolsonaro supporter rides in a truck decorated with campaign stickers for the far-right presidential candidate at a rally in Goiania, Goias state.Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/GettyAs a result, it is not just the Amazon that is in peril, but all of Brazil’s biomes, its traditional peoples and the stability of the global climate. The question now is why voters paid so little heed to these concerns.Far right on the march and Lula’s failures: key drivers of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Brazil surgeRead moreThat inquest is already under way. Many focus on the influence of social media, which has been used far more effectively by the far right. During the Bolsonaro administration, his sons were part of the “hate cabinet” that spread fear and disinformation via WhatsApp groups and other online channels – Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos, was indicted by federal police for leading the group. Environmentalists were often the target.Another factor is the expansion of US-style Pentecostalism, which is steadily supplanting Catholicism across Brazil, particularly in the Amazon. The political and environmental consequences of that religious shift can be seen by comparing the pro-nature treatise of the past two popes with the sermons of many evangelical preachers who encourage followers to seek wealth today as much as, if not more, than following moral creeds to ensure a good afterlife.election shareLula, 80, has been slow to adapt. Although he is arguably the most iconic and successful Latin American politician of the 21st century, his messaging seems less attuned to the people than it was in his heyday. The Workers party has struggled in an era of weaker unions and in some ways been the victim of its own success – with education and social policies that raised millions out of poverty and created greater expectations for consumption and entrepreneurism; and huge subsidies to farmers, who now support the right wing because they chafe at environmental limits.View image in fullscreenA woman looks at posters depicting the former president Jair Bolsonaro, alongside the words: ‘Remember that?’Photograph: Pilar Olivares/ReutersTied into those explanations are the geopolitics of the climate and nature crisis, which is exacerbating great power rivalrybetween the US and Chinaand amplifying extreme ideologies as much as extreme weather. In this light, the Brazil election is just the latest in a broader pattern of the far right taking control to expand extractivism despite growing evidence that the capitalist economy is breaking planetary boundaries.In the past two years, Donald Trump hasripped apart environmental regulationsin the US and treated the rest of the Americas as his sphere of influence. Argentina was already onboard. Venezuela has been invaded for its resources, while in Colombia, Peru and Chile there has been a sharp shift to the right.Will Brazil be the next domino to fall to Trumpism and its bonfire approach to nature? The Bolsonaro family certainly hope so. Jair went so far as to salute the US flag. His son Eduardo urged the US to apply tariffs on Brazilian people to “punish” the government for imprisoning his father. The Brazilian intelligence agency has warned that the US was trying to interfere in the election.That election isn’t over yet. Lula stands a small chance if he can win over the many millions of voters who chose not to mark their ballots for either candidate. But the odds are stacked against him. Most of the eliminated candidates were on the right so their supporters are more likely to switch to Bolsonaro. No first round leader has ever failed to win the runoff of a Brazilian presidential election.Voters, of course, are allowed to change their minds. Either on 25 October or, constitutionally, in four years’ time. But for how much longer will that be possible? If Bolsonaro wins, it won’t just be Lula that is finished, it could also be the Amazon and democracy itself.Explore more on these topicsBrazilView from the AmazonJair BolsonaroAmericasDeforestationLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaConservationTrees and forestsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Canada to indefinitely bar mental illness as sole reason for access to euthanasia | Canada | The Guardian
description: Legislation is an effort by ruling Liberals to address growing clash over who has access to doctor-assisted death
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Legislation is an effort by ruling Liberals to address growing clash over who has access to doctor-assisted death
Content: Sean Fraser, the justice minister, with health minister Marjorie Michel in Ottawa on Wednesday.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSean Fraser, the justice minister, with health minister Marjorie Michel in Ottawa on Wednesday.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockCanadaCanada to indefinitely bar mental illness as sole reason for access to euthanasiaLegislation is an effort by ruling Liberals to address growing clash over who has access to doctor-assisted deathLeyland Ceccoin TorontoWed 7 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada’s federal government said on Wednesday it would advance legislation to prevent people whose sole health condition is mental illness from accessing euthanasia, an effort by the ruling Liberal party to address a clash in the country over who has access to physician-assisted death.Under the current rules, people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness have been barred from accessingmedical assistance in dying(Maid) to end their lives. But that ban – due to be lifted in March – has divided lawmakers over whether to permit this expansion of the Maid program.Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the justice minister, Sean Fraser, said his government would indefinitely bar people whose sole condition is mental illness from accessing the program. He said that while there was no “perfect consensus” on this issue, upcoming legislation reflected the “correct” approach.Earlier this year, a government committee concluded the government should expand access to Maid and should “indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness from eligibility for medical assistance in dying”. That report also flagged the need for “increased and more equitable access” to mental health services.Canada’sMaid laws, drawn up after a2015 supreme court decision, initially only permitted those who are terminally ill to be eligible for the procedure. But in 2019, a Quebec judge ruled that restricting access to those who had a “reasonably foreseeable death” was unconstitutional, forcing federal lawmakers to amend and expand the existing laws.In 2021, the law was updated so adults could receive an assisted death if two doctors confirmed an irremediable physical condition causing immense suffering that cannot be relieved. Given the uncertainty surrounding mental illness, lawmakers in 2021 initially put a temporary exclusion in place for people who suffer solely from a mental illness. They renewed that pause in 2023 and 2024.According to the latest government figures, the vast majority of Maid deaths – 95.6% – involved people whose natural death was considered “reasonably foreseeable”. Only 4.4% were cases in which death was not considered reasonably foreseeable. Those include people with conditions such as multiple sclerosis and incurable neurological disease that can causes profound disability and immense suffering.The Liberal party’s legislation is also an effort to ward off a private member’s bill that would amend the section of the criminal code covering Maid so that “a mental disorder is not a grievous and irremediable medical condition”.Advocates for expanding Maid to include mental illness alone say the current rules violate their constitutional rights and access to healthcare. Fraser acknowledged to reporters that a federal case – led by the advocacy group Dying With DignityCanada– challenging the government’s previous decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness could affect the upcoming bill.Fraser said lawmakers would also work to decriminalize what are known as advanced requests, effectively giving people suffering from some illnesses such as Alzheimer’s the chance to choose Maid before their illness deprives them of the capacity to consent.At present, Quebec is the only jurisdiction that permits the use of these requests. Fraser gave no specifics on the timing of the legislation but said that provinces will decide whether to provide advance requests. While the province of Alberta has already said it will not permit advance requests, the justice minister said the bill attempts to ensure “the doctors who provide the services will not be treated as criminals for doing so”.In Canada, Crisis Services Canada can be contacted at any time on 1.833.456.4566, or via text on 45645 from 4pm-12am ET. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsCanadaAmericasAssisted dyingHuman rightsMental healthHealthDeath and dyingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil | Brazil | The Guardian
description: After a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian project
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: After a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian project
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro 45, goes into the 25 October runoff as favourite after a first-round win against Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday.Photograph: André Borges/EPAView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro 45, goes into the 25 October runoff as favourite after a first-round win against Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday.Photograph: André Borges/EPABrazil‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ BrazilAfter a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian projectFlávio’s surprise first-round win highlights rapid rise of Brazil’s House of BolsonaroTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroWed 7 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlávio Bolsonaro, the far-rightfrontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, increasing fears about a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power.Brazil was re-democratised in the 1980s after a brutal 21-year dictatorship that Flávio’s father, the disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro,has long praised.Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent LulaRead moreLast year,Jair Bolsonaro, a former soldier who served under that military regime, was jailed for 27 years for trying to engineer a coup after he lost the 2022 election to the current leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, in Sunday’s presidential election first round and goes into the runoff on 25 October as favourite. On Tuesday, the rightwinger vowed to capitalise on the hugely increased far-right presence in congress after the election to change the constitution and “re-democratise this country”.“The only thing standing in the way of Brazil becoming a barbarity is calledFlávio Bolsonaroas president,” he claimed at a campaign event in Goiânia, a city near the capital, Brasília.The incendiary comments caused outrage among historians and opponents of Bolsonaro’s radical populist movement, who have accused him of co-opting the language of democracy to disguise an illiberal shift.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro with the former presidential candidate Ronaldo Caiado (left) and the São Paulo governor, Tarcisio de Freitas, during a rally in Goiania.Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty ImagesTalíria Petrone, the leftwing congresswoman, wrote on X: “This is the announcement of a coup.”Marcelo Freixo, a newly elected congressman from Lula’s Workers’ party (PT), said: “Brazil was re-democratised in 1988. The person who tried to undo this was his father, who was convicted of an attempted coup. What they want, once again, is a coup.”Bolsonaro did not spell out what he meant by “re-democratising” Brazil, a vibrant if polarised multiparty democracy that the Sweden-based V-Dem instituteranks 28th on its liberal democracy index, two places ahead of the UK and 23 ahead of the US.But Jair Bolsonaro, who haspraised authoritarian leadersincluding Chile’s former dictator Augusto Pinochet, has long hankered for a return to military rule.Last September, the supreme court found Jair Bolsonaro guilty of trying toconvince military chiefs to help him cling to powerat the end of his 2018-22 presidency. The conspiracy culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, a far-right insurrection seemingly inspired by the 6 January 2021 storming of the US Capitol.Writing in O Globo newspaper, Míriam Leitão, a prominent political and economic journalist, warned that if Bolsonaro won, Brazil faced “theextreme and concrete dangerof … another coup d’état attempt”.“Flávio follows the same ideas as his father and has already said that an intervention in the institutions is necessary,” Leitão wrote. “If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, he will have more tools at his disposal to carry out his father’s authoritarian project: robust caucuses in the lower house and senate, a weakened supreme court, and the support of the Donald Trump administration.“Political science shows that it’s in the second term that an autocrat doubles down on their plan. Look at the case of Donald Trump. The risk isn’t of the son repeating the father, it’s that he surpasses him.”View image in fullscreenSupporters of Flávio Bolsonaro at a rally before the presidential election runoff.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersMiguel Lago, a political scientist, said Sunday’s far-right election triumph – in which Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) secured the senate’s largest caucus, with 28 of its 81 seats – would permit radical changes, including the impeachment of supreme court ministers considered enemies of the Bolsonarismo movement.Jair Bolsonaro and his jailed co-conspirators are likely to be freed if his son wins, with the former president expected to become an influential minister able to select the new heads of the armed forces.“It’s better than a coup d’état … it’s almost like a coup d’état with the support of the majority of the population,” Lago said.Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, has been accused of “killing” democracy by using control over the country’s congress and institutions to approve sweeping constitutional changes, includingscrapping presidential term limitsso he can seek indefinite re-election.Flávio Bolsonaro recently met Bukele’s security minister, Gustavo Villatoro, in São Paulo, hailing the Central American country’s hardline security policies under which thousands have been jailed during a state of exception that has lasted nearly five years.Bolsonaro told reporters that during their conversation, Villatoro “stressed the importance” of using control of congress to make the “necessary legal changes”.2:54Lula admits Brazil election result ‘unexpected’ as Bolsonaro leads first round – videoCelso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist, said he believed that by using the word “re-democratise”, Flávio Bolsonaro sought “to smuggle his authoritarian purposes into acceptable language”.Barros said Bolsonaro, unlike his father who always seemed to favour an “old school barracks uprising” to seize power, appeared to be part of “a new generation of authoritarians” who sought to dismantle democracy from within by undermining and occupying the institutions.“Then you don’t need to break any laws to achieve authoritarianism … because you are the law,” Barros added, citing Hungary’s former far-right prime minister Viktor Orbán as an example. “Clearly, Flávio’s plan is a corrosion of democracy so [Brazil] becomes a Hungary or Bukele-style system.”Danilo Araújo Marques, a historian, said the word “democracy” had been co-opted before in Brazil by undemocratic forces, when the military men and politicians behind the 1964 coup called their actions “an intervention to democratise the country”.“They all talked about democracy … [but] democracy has a different meaning in the mouth of a coup-monger,” said Marques, who is from a research unit at the Federal University of Minas Gerais called Projeto República.Marques noted that during the campaign, Bolsonaro had claimed his octogenarian opponent, Lula, represented the past while he was selling the future. “But this future means going back to what [Brazil] was before,” Marques said. “It’s a ‘future’ that is based on the order prior to the 1988 constitution, which is precisely the military dictatorship.”Asked to clarify his plans on Wednesday, Bolsonaro rejected speculation he was seeking to finish “what his father didn’t do”. “Let’s stop lying. Let’s touch down in the real world,” he told reporters, adding: “Brazil needs to go back to normal, that’s all.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilFlávio BolsonaroJair BolsonaroThe far rightAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer? | Quebec | The Guardian
description: Lack of majority for Parti Québécois puts any referendum in doubt, especially amid bruising trade war with Trump
Author: Martin Patriquin
Headline: Lack of majority for Parti Québécois puts any referendum in doubt, especially amid bruising trade war with Trump
Content: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon celebrates his victory to become the next premier of Quebec.Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPaul St-Pierre Plamondon celebrates his victory to become the next premier of Quebec.Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesQuebecAnalysisSeparatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?Martin Patriquinin MontrealLack of majority for Parti Québécois puts any referendum in doubt, especially amid bruising trade war with TrumpWed 7 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.15 EDTShareThe victory of the Parti Québécois in Monday’s election in Quebec might seem to bring its signature goal, of separating the French-speaking province fromCanada, much closer – but Canadian unity may not be nearly as threatened as may first seem.The PQ’s victory was both impressive and disappointing. The party added 56 seats to its roster and more than doubled its vote share compared with the 2022 election, giving it its first taste of power in 14 years. Crucially, however, it was left five seats short of a majority, making its promise to hold a referendum after Donald Trump leaves office in 2028 nearly impossible.It also won with barely 28% of the popular vote, the lowest percentage for any government in Canada’s electoral history, according to the polling analyst Philippe Fournier.The vast majority of Quebecers voted for parties that want nothing to do with a referendum. It’s a reflection of the province’s 30-year aversion to another bruising debate about Quebec’s place in Canada – particularly in the wake of Trump’s tariffs and threats against the country.The result not only puts another referendum in doubt, but a raft of other PQ initiatives too, including abolishing the monarchy and applying Quebec’s strict language laws to the province’s colleges. The new government will also face stiff opposition to its plans to reduce immigration levels, which haveangered farmersandthe business community.Meanwhile, the most popular politician in the province remains far and away the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, in large part because of his resistance to Trump. That has left the PQ leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, in an awkward situation for a separatist: he can’t be seen as a threat to Canadian unity. He essentially acknowledged this in his victory speech, pledging to be a “good-faith collaborator” with the rest of the country, and even addressing the crowd in English; then attempted to court the other side of the debate by announcing on Tuesday he would prevent the lieutenant governor, who represents the British crown, from swearing in his new government.“Seventy per cent of Quebecers don’t want a referendum,” said John Parisella, who served as chief of staff to two Quebec premiers and the province’s delegate general in New York and Washington.“And every time they see Trump’s picture on the screen at night, it does nothing to improve a desire for separation. For a lot of Quebecers, the link with Canada is absolutely crucial, even if it isn’t necessarily emotional.”The vote, in fact, may have less to do with embracing separatism and more about punishing the current government. The election saw the total collapse of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), which has been in power since 2018. An alliance of federalists and separatists (the party describes itself as nationalist), it didn’t win a single seat, and harvested just a third of its vote share compared to 2022. Its leader, Christine Fréchette,lost her own riding to the Parti Québécois, and on Tuesday afternoon she resigned.In a province whose political discourse has focused on the federalist-separatist divide, the election also suggested a return to normalcy of sorts – with separatists returning to the PQ’s fold, while the federalist vote dispersed to the opposition Liberal party and the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec (PCQ).The PCQ feasted on the CAQ’s support in the election, winning 19 ridings in the hinterland and in the Quebec City area, where leader Éric Duhaime won his seat for the first time. Founded in 2009, the populist party counts a prominent anti-vaxxer and a rage-bating anti-woke radio host as two of its winning candidates.The party was able to break through in part because of its promise to build an underground highway linking Quebec City to its suburbs across the St Lawrence, despite government reports saying the endeavor would cost as much as C$9.3bn (US$6.5bn) and do little to alleviate traffic.Montreal, meanwhile, went decidedly Liberal red, with leader Charles Milliard regaining seats on the island and in the traditionally English redoubt of the Eastern Townships. The staunchly federalist Liberals, who are unaffiliated with Carney’s federal Liberals, will serve as Quebec’s official opposition. Governing with but a handful of seats in the province’s biggest metropolis will be challenging enough for the PQ; as history hasshown, winning a referendum without it is somewhere near impossible.Canada faces another potential menace to its sovereignty in a little less than two weeks, when Alberta in the west holds a “referendum on a referendum” on secession. Happily for Carney, and unfortunately for Trump, polls suggest Albertans are as averse to dalliances with separation as their Quebecer brethren have now become to the east – no matter the party they just chose to govern.Explore more on these topicsQuebecCanadaAmericasanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos | China | The Guardian
description: New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’
Content: A satellite image shows what security analysts believe are Y-8 light attack fighters at a new China-Laos joint training facility in Ban Keun.Photograph: Vantor/ReutersView image in fullscreenA satellite image shows what security analysts believe are Y-8 light attack fighters at a new China-Laos joint training facility in Ban Keun.Photograph: Vantor/ReutersChinaSatellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in LaosNew ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’Oliver Holmesin BangkokWed 7 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSatellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility inLaos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion,Chinaopened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.Map of airport siteThe airport, about ⁠30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement andfirst reportedby Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.In itsannouncementlast week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.View image in fullscreenConstruction under way at the site on 2 September.Photograph: Vantor/ReutersGovernments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn ofAfrica.The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.Afteryears of speculation and denials, China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project.The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsChinaLaosAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flydubai attack investigation widens as alleged hijacker’s training in New Zealand scrutinised | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Hamam al-Hammami spent 175 days in New Zealand until May 2019, as Australian Jewish group calls for full investigation into his time in Melbourne
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Hamam al-Hammami spent 175 days in New Zealand until May 2019, as Australian Jewish group calls for full investigation into his time in Melbourne
Content: New Zealand has joined multiple countries that are trying to track the background of flydubai co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane on 30 September.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAView image in fullscreenNew Zealand has joined multiple countries that are trying to track the background of flydubai co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane on 30 September.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAFlydubai plane incidentFlydubai attack investigation widens as alleged hijacker’s training in New Zealand scrutinisedHamam al-Hammami spent 175 days in New Zealand until May 2019, as Australian Jewish group calls for full investigation into his time in MelbourneEva Corlettin Auckland andAdeshola Orein MelbourneWed 7 Oct 2026 01.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 01.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation into the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane, after police confirmed he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.Disaster wasnarrowly avertedon 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt of the co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, 29, to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard.Hammami, an Omani national, hadallegedly used a crash axein the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air, the United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said. Israeli and other officials in the region suspect heoriginally planned for such an attack in July, but postponed it.Flydubai co-pilot originally planned attack for July, investigators believeRead moreThe New Zealand police assistant commissioner, Michael Johnson, on Tuesday confirmed the man was in the country on a student visa for 175 days, from 30 November 2018 to 23 May 2019.“Police can confirm the co-pilot was in New Zealand to complete a portion of his flight training for a UK-based company, no longer operating in New Zealand,” Johnson said in a statementThe police are now investigating his time in the country, Johnson said.New Zealand joins multiple countriesscrambling to piece togetherthe background of Hammami and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted alone.Over the weekend, Australian security agencieslaunched an investigationafter it emerged Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. Heleft the country without completing his engineering degree, RMIT University in Melbourne confirmed.On a now deleted social media profile believed to belong to Hammami, the then student appears in a selfie with other teenagers in a shopping centre food court in Melbourne’s CBD.The UK’s Telegraph reported on a post on a now deleted X account that appears to be linked to Hammami that described his years studying overseas as “the golden years of my religious commitment”, and claimed he became less observant when he returned to Oman.On Wednesday, Australia’s peak Jewish body, the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, called for a thorough investigation of Hammami’s associations in the country.Flydubai co-pilot’s time in Australia being investigated by security agencies after alleged cockpit attackRead more“We have seen over the years the availability of extremist literature in religious bookstores, the presence of preachers of hate and violence and the capacity for those living in Australia to fall under the sway of recruiters and nefarious street preachers,” the council’s co-chief executive, Alex Ryvchin, said in a statement.“We have to understand who associated with this [alleged] terrorist, who influenced him and what vestiges of his murderous ideology remain.”The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, who also trained in New Zealand for a time, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.In a phone call on Saturday with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentNew ZealandAir transportMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelUnited Arab EmiratesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric cars | International trade | The Guardian
description: Mood in trade talks said to have changed as EU member states harden demands for protection against Chinese imports
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Mood in trade talks said to have changed as EU member states harden demands for protection against Chinese imports
Content: EU negotiators are hoping for a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus.Photograph: Cynthia Lee/AlamyView image in fullscreenEU negotiators are hoping for a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus.Photograph: Cynthia Lee/AlamyInternational tradeEU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric carsMood in trade talks said to have changed as EU member states harden demands for protection against Chinese importsLisa O’Carrollin BrusselsWed 7 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 04.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEU trade negotiators are heading to China for two days of crunch talks aimed at sealing a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus by curbing its exports of cheap hybrid electric cars intoEurope.Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his team fly out on Wednesday and will be negotiating up to the wire in talks scheduled to start the following day and continue late into Friday.Sources say they hope to achieve “tangible, meaningful and measurable” results before the meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Thursday next week, whereChinais high on the agenda.The main focus is on what has been described as a “proof of concept” pilot agreement involving one sector, which is expected to be cars, which could be scaled up for other sectors in the coming months.UK reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align with EURead moreDiplomatic efforts to avert a full-scale trade war started at the end of June, albeit with little hope that China could curb exports to the EU given its historic ability to pivot quickly any time trade barriers are put in its path. For example, after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in October 2024there was a boom in exports of hybrid cars, which were not subject to tariffs.Last month, the EU asked China to voluntarily restrict hybrid exports to address soaring sales, warning that if they did not restrict them, safeguards – which could include quotas – could be enacted.It is not known what China’s response was. But sources say the mood in talks has changed as EU member states have hardened demands for protection against Chinese imports that threaten their own industries.On Monday, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, agreed a “historic U-turn” on its policy on China by siding with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in authorising effective permission for EU leaders to approve a new instrument to allow them to defend trade by cutting access to the single market at short notice.In a joint paper with Emmanuel Macron, the two countries spoke of “a massive industrial shock … affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.]”.The paper called for the use of all existing trade defence tools, but also for a new diversification instrument and “possible additional” new measures to allow the bloc to react when “third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field”.Andrew Small, a former EU adviser on China, said Šefčovič’s talks will test the resolve of both Beijing and Brussels and will “determine whether China is willing to put sufficiently serious offers on the table”.Small, who is the Asia director at the European Council on Foreign Relations in Berlin, warned: “China’s most effective tactic may be to draw Europe into a ‘process trap’ offering just enough to delay action, without addressing the forces driving European deindustrialisation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU marketsRead moreSources say the Franco-German proposals for a new instrument, dubbed a “kill switch”, were born out of frustration, particularly in Paris, that a so-called“trade bazooka”available to Brussels, officially known as the anti-coercion instrument, has never been used.Paris pushed for the use of the ACI following Trump’s threat of tariffs last year but it never gained traction from others as it could take up to a year to implement.Handlesblatt, the Germany business newspaper, described Monday’s change in policy as “nothing less than an economic turning point”, with chief political reporter Martin Greive concluding in a hard-hitting column that Merz was “putting an end to years of naiveté towards Beijing”.“Merz has recognised in recent months that Germany is the epicentre of the China shock 2.0; that there might not be much left of German industry if Germany continues to stand by and watch as China gains enormous export advantages through trillions in subsidies, the unilateral siphoning off of knowhow, and a – to put it mildly – questionable monetary policy,” he wrote.Explore more on these topicsInternational tradeEuropeEuropean UnionChinaChinese economyAsia PacificGlobal economynewsShareReuse this content

title: Abortion pill access jumps almost 50% after Australia eases restrictions for pharmacies | Health | The Guardian
description: The number of pharmacies stocking the MS-2 Step medication increased from 2,228 to 4,107 after rules relaxed in 2023
Author: Melissa Davey
Headline: The number of pharmacies stocking the MS-2 Step medication increased from 2,228 to 4,107 after rules relaxed in 2023
Content: A woman prepares to take the first of two mifepristone pills for a medical abortion. Australia’s TGA has scrapped restrictions on the prescription of the pills.Photograph: Charlie Riedel/APView image in fullscreenA woman prepares to take the first of two mifepristone pills for a medical abortion. Australia’s TGA has scrapped restrictions on the prescription of the pills.Photograph: Charlie Riedel/APHealthAbortion pill access jumps almost 50% after Australia eases restrictions for pharmaciesThe number of pharmacies stocking the MS-2 Step medication increased from 2,228 to 4,107 after rules relaxed in 2023Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMelissa DaveyMedical editorWed 7 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of Australian pharmacies stocking an abortion pill increased by almost 50% when prescribing restrictions were relaxed, with researchers saying the findings suggest deregulation of abortion promotes safer and faster healthcare.A study published in the medical journal JAMA Network Open on Thursday examined the impact of changes by the Therapeutic Goods Administration in 2023 which meant the medication, MS-2 Step, could be prescribed by any GP.Prior to the changes, GPs needed additional training and registration to prescribe it. The requirement for pharmacists to be registered to dispense the drug was also scrapped, and administrative hurdles were relaxed. Appropriately trained nurse practitioners and endorsed midwives also became eligible prescribers.Women suffer more pain than men across the whole body, major global study findsRead moreBy comparing pharmacy ordering data in the two years before and after the changes, researchers led by La Trobe University found by mid-2025, 49% more pharmacies were stocking the medication. There were 2,228 pharmacies stocking it before the policy change, rising to 4,107 by mid-2025.The number of postcodes with a pharmacy stocking the medication rose from 915 to 1,292 – or nearly half of all Australian postcodes – two years after the changes. Regional coverage increased from 23% to 35% of postcodes, while the proportion of stocking pharmacies in remote areas nearly doubled, rising from 12.5% to 22%.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe lead author of the paper, Prof Kristina Edvardsson from La Trobe University’s School of Nursing and Midwifery, said it showed“Australian women who need access to this medication can access it closer to home”.“It removes the unnecessary travel and stress around getting the medication once it’s prescribed. That’s super important, particularly for women who might be more disadvantaged, women living in rural, remote areas, and women who might not have the means to travel.“If you can go to your local pharmacy and pick up this medication, it means getting care quicker.”Edvardsson saidother studies have foundimproving access to MS-2 Step is safe, and that whenaccess to the medical abortion pill increases, the need for surgical abortion decreases.“In some European countries, medical abortionaccounts for more than 90%of all abortions, and itlooks like we’re heading that wayhere as well with a steady increase in medication abortion versus surgical abortion,” she said.MS-2 Step, available under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, comprises two drugs used together,mifepristone and misoprostol. It can be takenuntil up to 63 daysof gestation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt the time of the study, MS-2 Step was the only abortion pill available, but in February an additional drug, Arzestra, comprising the same two medicines,was approved by the TGA.Dr Anna Noonan, a postdoctoral research fellow and abortion researcher with the University of Technology Sydney, said the data should be “an important signal” to countries where more restricted prescribing was still in place, such as the US.“There are still pervasive, unnecessary barriers in lots of places, and data like this is an important signal that regulation and overregulation is not the way forward,” she said.Noonan said there was still work to be done to improve rural and regional access, and that her own research suggested a lot of “invisible work” also occurred by local doctors, nurses and advocates working behind the scenes so that people can confidentially and more easily find healthcare.“Doctors and nurses are going to pharmacies in advance saying, ‘I’m going to be an abortion provider in this community, will you stock this medication?’“Overregulation creates extra work for those trying to provide timely care, and it doesn’t work out in the best interests of people seeking care,” Noonan said. “The more we encourage a deregulated environment, the easier access will be, particularly for people with less resources.”Explore more on these topicsHealthWomen's healthAbortionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Catastrophic wildfire loop’ after colonisation left parts of Australia more at risk from bushfires, study finds  | Environment | The Guardian
description: Researchers found the shift from open woodland to dense forest after 1788 led to more intense fires, consistent with loss of cultural burning practices
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: Researchers found the shift from open woodland to dense forest after 1788 led to more intense fires, consistent with loss of cultural burning practices
Content: Researchers worked with traditional owners to reconstruct 1,000 years of vegetation and fire history in Croajingolong national park in Gippsland, Victoria. Pictured: bushfires in east Gippsland in January 2020.Photograph: Darrian Traynor/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenResearchers worked with traditional owners to reconstruct 1,000 years of vegetation and fire history in Croajingolong national park in Gippsland, Victoria. Pictured: bushfires in east Gippsland in January 2020.Photograph: Darrian Traynor/Getty ImagesAustralian climate and environmental reportingEnvironment‘Catastrophic wildfire loop’ after colonisation left parts of Australia more at risk from bushfires, study findsResearchers found the shift from open woodland to dense forest after 1788 led to more intense fires, consistent with loss of cultural burning practicesSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereSupported byAbout this contentPetra StockWed 7 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe drastic land use changes wreaked by colonisation created a “catastrophic wildfire loop” that rendered south-east Australia more susceptible to climate-fuelled bushfires, experts say.A team of researchers, working with the Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation, an organisation that represents traditional owners, reconstructed 1,000 years of vegetation and fire history at Purghagoolah, a lake surrounded by forest in Croajingolong national park in Gippsland,Victoria.Bruce Pascoe’s new book may spark another culture war. He hopes for ‘decency and intellectual curiosity’ this timeRead moreThey analysed pollen and charcoal particles deposited over time in a metre-long sediment core, uncovering historical changes in the landscape and the interactions between weather, eucalypt cover and fire frequency and intensity.View image in fullscreenAerial view of Purghagoolah (Lake Elusive) in Croajingolong national park in Gippsland, Victoria.Photograph: Michael-Shawn FletcherThe results,published in Nature, revealed the shift from open woodland to dense forest after colonisation led to more intense fires, changes consistent with the loss of cultural burning practices and the removal of traditional owners, the Gunaikurnai people, from the land.Michael-Shawn Fletcher, a professor at the University of Melbourne and the study’s lead author, said prior to colonisation “this was a cared for and managed landscape”.Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter“Gunaikurnai are removed from Country and you see a change in the amount of trees and shrubs in the landscape, and that drives more fires,” he said. “It’s actually land use change, more than a century before climate changes, that has allowed shrubs to increase, fires to get hotter. Those hot fires then trigger eucalypt recruitment. And the eucalypts then increase, driving further fire.”Fletcher said the research provided scientific evidence for the value of cultural burning, and the importance of integrating Indigenous knowledge into modern fire management strategies.View image in fullscreenThe field research team carries equipment through Croajingolong national park.Photograph: Michael-Shawn FletcherCultural burning refers to the way First Nations people use low-temperature fire to maintain a safe and productive landscape.
