These practices, which are still used in parts of Australia today, are based on a responsive “right time, right place” approach that differs from mainstream prescribed burning practices undertaken by government agencies for hazard reduction.“Hopefully this opens a conversation around the possibilities, into a new future where we can actually start getting control of the catastrophic fire problem,” Fletcher said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNarooma payphone heritage-listed for connecting people when mobiles failed during black summer bushfiresRead moreProf David Bowman, a fire scientist based at the University of Tasmania, who was not an author of the paper, said the research was significant and contributed to the “growing realisation” about the legacy of landscape change resulting from the loss of Indigenous fire management.“Other factors have exacerbated these changes, [such as] the introduction of non-native animals, non-native plants in some cases. These are very complex ecological processes, but taking out traditional fire management is a very significant thing to have happened.”The long-term records were “critically important” for piecing together the historical changes in fire regimes, and how they’re responding to climate drivers, he said. “One of the big questions in wildfire science is how anomalous, or how unprecedented, is the stuff that’s happening?”Bowman described the research as “like a pipe opener”. “I really hope that it opens up a conversation that we really need to have about managing our landscapes as the fire crisis is worsening.”Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentAustralian climate and environmental reportingBushfiresIndigenous AustraliansVictoriaClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Overseas, Albanese sees ‘the very definition of climate injustice’ – but at home, he still wants coal | Cop31 | The Guardian
description: It isn’t hard to see a contradiction between the PM’s message in Fiji and his opposition to legal action to stop a NSW coalmine
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: It isn’t hard to see a contradiction between the PM’s message in Fiji and his opposition to legal action to stop a NSW coalmine
Content: Anthony Albanese visits the Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project (TCAP) during the pre-Cop31 meeting in Funafuti, Tuvalu.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese visits the Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project (TCAP) during the pre-Cop31 meeting in Funafuti, Tuvalu.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesCop31AnalysisOverseas, Albanese sees ‘the very definition of climate injustice’ – but at home, he still wants coalAdam Mortonin Nadi, FijiIt isn’t hard to see a contradiction between the PM’s message in Fiji and his opposition to legal action to stop a NSW coalmineGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 19.16 EDTShareThere are unlikely to be many bigger moments in Australian community action on the climate crisis this year than a judgment by the high court on Wednesday.In what may prove a historic victory, the courtsided with a handful of community members in the Hunter Valleyto overturn a state regulator’s approval of a coalmine expansion that allowed it to operate until 2048. This doesn’t happen every day, and the judgment could have ramifications for other coal developments in New South Wales.If comments he made in May are taken at face value, the decision won’t please Anthony Albanese.Speaking on 2HD radio in Newcastle, the prime minister said the renewable transition was needed, but the government supported “existing industries” – that is, coal. He hoped the community group would lose as the Mount Pleasant mine expansion had “been through appropriate approvals”.‘A real-life moment from The Castle’: the retired Australian couple who took on a coal giant and wonRead moreWell, not according to the high court.Critics were quick to note the contrast between Albanese’s language opposing legal action to stop a coalmine and the message he delivered over the past three days at a climate conference in Fiji in preparation for theCop31summit in Turkey next month.With Pacific island counterparts, the prime minister helped lead a delegation of about 50 dignitaries to the atoll and reef island nation of Tuvalu. Remote and tiny doesn’t do Tuvalu justice. It is described as the least visited country on the planet. Its land totals just 26 sq km, mostly narrow strips less than 2 metres above sea level. And the distance between the ocean and where most of its people live is getting smaller.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe rate of sea level rise around Tuvalu is about twice the global average, according to Nasa researchers. It means the edges of the nation are being eroded. The delegation was given a presentation illustrating the escalating threat of floods and storm surges washing through homes and infrastructure in the years ahead.They also saw an example of what the country is doing to give itself the best chance to survive, visiting a land reclamation project on the main atoll of Funafuti that is mostly funded by the Australian government. Sand and gravel dredged from the lagoon is being used to create more than 20 hectares of new, higher ground.View image in fullscreenAustralian PM Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen, who is the president of the formal negotiations.Photograph: Huang/Menders/Zuma Press Wire Service/ShutterstockIt is a project of hope, and a way to buy time. Possibly the most powerful moment on the quick trip came when the delegation was addressed by a 13-year-old, Melelusi Sokotia, who spoke powerfully about how her friends’ aspirations to be “teachers, doctors, builders” was being overridden by the basic question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.Melelusi made a plea: “Please work together to protect small islands like ours.”Later, back in Fiji, a leaders’ plenary heard from the Nepali foreign affairs minister, Shisir Khanal, who travelled for the pre-Cop meeting while his country staggers under the fallout from devastating flooding in August.double quotation markIt wasn’t hard to see a screaming internal contradiction – a case of a leader sending conflicting messages to different audiencesWhile the Pacific confronts a crisis of rising tides and more fierce cyclones, Khanal said Nepal was threatened by melting mountain ice bringing havoc from above. He pointed out the two threats were linked. Melting glaciers ultimately add to rising seas.The minister said Nepal and the Pacific had something else in common. Neither contributes much at all to the global emissions causing these catastrophes. “Yet our people pay with their lives and development gains for a crisis they had no hand in creating,” he said. “This is the very definition of climate injustice.”Albanese didn’t ignore this. He took Khanal’s message on enough to repeat part of it – that Nepal faced “extraordinarily traumatic” climate events despite running entirely on hydroelectricity – in a speech before flying out on Wednesday.He described other examples of extreme events becoming less predictable and more intense as “the science told us would occur”. Climate change wasn’t an abstract future challenge, but “a daily reality that communities are dealing with”. “We saw that first-hand yesterday in Tuvalu,” Albanese said.The point of Albanese’s speech was to argue for more international investment in the Pacific Resilience Facility, a fund designed to help people in the region cope and live that has received A$100m in Australian government support. He didn’t mention coal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut when held up against his commentary about the high court judgment, it wasn’t hard to see a screaming internal contradiction – a case of a leader sending conflicting messages to different audiences.Does Albanese disagree with the high court judgment and still support coal expansion, given its contribution to the crisis he has accurately identified? There was no chance to test this on Wednesday. He left pre-Cop without taking questions from journalists.None of this is to dismiss the work being done in Fiji. Despite the focus in Australia on the number of leaders who flew to Nadi and Funafuti for the meeting, there is little sense on the ground of it being the failure some have described.Pre-Cop meetings usually barely make a blip on the public radar. They’re not meant to. They’re a chance for diplomats and bureaucrats to gather before the big end-of-year UN climate summit to lay groundwork and hopefully give it some chance of success.This year is something else entirely. It is being held in the Pacific in an attempt to bring focus to the plight and needs of its peoples. In that, it has had at least some success. Ministers and their representatives from about 50 governments, including India and European nations, attended. So did thousands of diplomats and civil society members. They talked about Pacific needs.Australia faces summer of extreme weather, Anthony Albanese warns at pre-CopRead moreThe trip to Tuvalu included only two national leaders from outside the region – but the EU climate commissioner and the heads of the Asian Development Bank, the Green Climate Fund and the UN climate secretariat were on board. They saw and heard things people doing their jobs should see and hear.Pacific national and community leaders are not uniform in their views, but they have largely applauded the focus and Australia’s support. Some are also critical, and cynical, about what they see as Australia’s hypocrisy on fossil fuels. That issue isn’t going away.The ultimate test of this week’s success is whether it helps Cop31 pull off a meaningful agreement on issues to limit climate catastrophe and better direct finance to those that need it to survive, including in the Pacific. To describe that as a challenge in the current geopolitical climate is a spectacular understatement.One upside of this week has been that the two men responsible for trying to pull that off – the president of the formal negotiations, Australia’s Chris Bowen, and the Turkish Cop31 president, Murat Kurum – have had a few days together to build their relationship and consider how they might do that.And they have had a consistent and forceful reminder from those around them of why it matters.Adam Morton is Guardian Australia’s climate and environment editor and writes theClear Air newsletterExplore more on these topicsCop31Environmental activismPacific islandsFossil fuelsAnthony AlbaneseEnergyMininganalysisShareReuse this content

title: Rubio in Greece digs into past to tout Trump’s ‘America first’ approach | Marco Rubio | The Guardian
description: In the shadow of the Parthenon, the secretary of state gave a selective reading of history as he urged Europe to ‘awaken from its slumber’
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: In the shadow of the Parthenon, the secretary of state gave a selective reading of history as he urged Europe to ‘awaken from its slumber’
Content: Rubio speaks to assembled officials and reporters in front of the Parthenon in Athens on Wednesday.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRubio speaks to assembled officials and reporters in front of the Parthenon in Athens on Wednesday.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesMarco RubioAnalysisRubio in Greece digs into past to tout Trump’s ‘America first’ approachAndrew RothGlobal affairs correspondentIn the shadow of the Parthenon, the secretary of state gave a selective reading of history as he urged Europe to ‘awaken from its slumber’Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.24 EDTShareThe US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, delivered a classically inspired apologia for Donald Trump’s “America first” foreign policy on Wednesday, giving a sweeping speech to the backdrop of the Parthenon in Athens that appeared tailor-made for campaign ads if he runs for president in 2028.In the speech, the top US diplomat drew historical parallels from the founders, philosophers and conquerers of antiquity to the modern American spirit – as well as his family’s own journey to the United States – as he called onEuropeto “awaken from its long slumber” and reject a “future of atrophy and servitude and decline”.The highly produced speech contained a forceful rejection of the kind of globalist politics that Trump has blamed for America’s and Europe’s ills, including growing illegal immigration and the outsourcing of manufacturing. In it, Rubio warned that the western world was at an “inflection point” and defended America’s “unapologetic pursuit of national power”.EU drops sponsorship of disinformation conference at Trump officials’ requestRead more“The word nationalism became a dirty word, so we tore down our monuments,” Rubio said. “We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the country they would inherit.”Now, he said, the western world had found itself at a crossroads, where it either must “maintain its place at the head of the world or [resign] itself to a future of atrophy, servitude and decline”.“Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice,” Rubio continued. “We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialise our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.”The speech comes as relations between the US and Europe are facing numerous strains, including the US war in Iran, Washington’s scattershot support for Ukraine’s defense against Russia, disputes insideNatoincluding Trump’s recent demands for sovereignty over Greenland, and a growing ideological divide being driven by powerful officials including the US vice-president, JD Vance.The shift in the Trump administration’s use of national power has unsettled many European allies, who have continued to seek compromises in order to keep the Trump administration onside on major issues including support for Ukraine and economic cooperation through theEuropean Union.Vance, a likely contender in the 2028 elections, put European allies on notice last year in a speech at the Munich security conference, when he accused leaders of being “terrified of their own people” and warned about the “threat from within” that Europe would reject values it shared with the US.Rubio has developed a less aggressive – but nonetheless pointed – message of calling for European powers led by the US to fight against “civilisational erasure”.Rubio addressed the tensions as he invoked Abraham Lincoln’s first inaugural address in 1861 on the eve of the civil war, saying: “Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them.”“Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age,” he said, extolling the recent agreement between the US, Denmark, and Greenland that he claimed will “reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of Nato.”But the speech on Wednesday indicates that the shift in US geopolitical power may remain through a following presidency, as two of the most prominent Republican officials in the current administration have delivered forceful declarations to Europe that there will not be a return to the politics of the past.On Wednesday, speaking to a crowd of 250 invited Greek and European officials, as well as journalists, Rubio sought to rally European allies, saying they should follow the example of the current government ofGreece, to embrace a partnership with the US on everything from “everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally”.“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago,” Rubio said, pointing to positive tendencies including increases in European defense spending, expanded manufacturing and production, and a “flurry” of new partnerships and programs.To bolster his case, Rubio delivered a selective reading of history from antiquity to the present, saying that the values of the Ancient Greeks imbued those of later scientists and explorers, including some controversial choices including Christopher Columbus and the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés, whose legacies are associated with the subjugation of Latin America.But Rubio said they, as well as many others, carried a frontier spirit that was born in antiquity.“The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers – born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world,” he said.The Acropolis speech was heavily produced, with four cameras including one mounted on a crane, and was unusual for a secretary of state delivering a speech during a three-country swing through Iceland, Portugal and finally Greece.In an unusual aside for the US’s top diplomat, Rubio also linked his own journey back to Europe, and then back to the Greeks of antiquity as well.“Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now – I stand here today as the secretary of state of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish,” he said.Explore more on these topicsMarco RubioUS foreign policyRepublicansDonald TrumpGreeceEuropeNatoanalysisShareReuse this content

title: María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87 | Spain | The Guardian
description: Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis
Content: Maricarmen in Madrid in October 2025.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMaricarmen in Madrid in October 2025.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesSpainMaría del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis‘Now is the moment’: housing activists at Madrid encampment pin wary hopes on Spain’s early electionAshifa KassamandSam Jonesin MadridWed 7 Oct 2026 16.57 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaría del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died.News of her death came two weeks after Maricarmen, as she had come to be known across Spain,was evicted from the Madrid apartmentwhere she had lived for more than seven decades.The pensioner, whose apartment had been purchased by an investment firm who sought to hike her rent by 230%, swiftlybecame a symbolof the many left behind by Spain’s surging housing market.Scenes of the eviction, which saw police use rounds of teargas as they carried out the order, made headlines across Spain. The shocking images – showing Abascal being forcibly removed from her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police – swiftly crystallised into anger.About 10,000 people took to the streets of Madrid hours later, wielding signs such as “Shame” and “We’re all Maricarmen”. From Spain’s north to the south, people poured into plazas to protest the suffering wrought by rentsthat had soared80% in the span of a decade while house prices had climbed 63%.View image in fullscreenA flyer with an image of María del Carmen Abascal is seen at a vigil in Madrid on 7 October.Photograph: Thomas Coex/AFP/Getty ImagesFrom the hospital where she was being treated for severe exhaustion, Abascal cheered on the fledgling movement. “I would like to be there with you all,” she said in a video shot from her hospital bed. “But I’m not that lucky. So from here, I ask you all for courage and to fight and defend what is yours.”As encampments began springing up across the country, the investment firm that bought Abascal’s home said she could return. The deal did little to quell the anger that had boiled over in the wake of the eviction.This week the wave of outrage led the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez,to call a snap general electionafter rightwing and far-right parties voted down two emergency decrees his government had proposed to address the housing crisis.The Madrid tenants’ union said the solution had come too late for the octogenarian. “This was a completely preventable situation following an agonising ordeal,” it said in a statement announcing that Abascal had died in hospital,reportedly hoursbefore she was due to sign a new lease with the investment firm that had evicted her.“The events triggered by the injustice of her eviction undoubtedly mark a turning point in the history of this country: massive demonstrations, encampments in the squares, an early election, and the call for a general strike,” it added. “The housing debate is at the center of it all, but the cost of getting to this point has been too high.”Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”Spain’s health minister, Mónica García, said Abascal’s plight had “served to awaken awareness across all of Spain, lighting a fuse that cannot be put out”, and adding that her “dignity and courage” had shown the way.View image in fullscreenMaría del Carmen Abascal in Madrid on 2 June.Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesThe Podemos MEP and former equalities minister Irene Montero was more blunt. “This isn’t a death; it’s a murder,” she wrote on social media. “Such bloody anger. Thank you for fighting, Maricarmen.”Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP) – which voted against last week’s emergency housing measures – also offered his condolences.“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”Her death came a day after Sánchez’s cabinet approved two new housing decrees intended to “maintain the spirit” of the two previous decrees that were voted down in parliament last week by the PP, the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party.The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; regulating room rentals; imposing a new tax on seasonal rentals; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases; and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.With the lower and upper houses of parliament dissolved following the calling of the snap election, the decrees will be voted on by the permanent council of congress, a special council that operates when parliament is not in session.The body’s 69 members are distributed proportionally among the various parliamentary groups to reflect the composition of the lower chamber, meaning Sánchez will probably have enough support to get at least one of the decrees passed.In the heart of Madrid, where campaigners have set up agiant protest camp, news of Abascal’s death was met with a moment of silence. Soon after, hundreds marched from the camp to the country’s parliament chanting: “Maricarmen lives on, the fight continues.”Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropePedro SáncheznewsShareReuse this content

title: WHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia following suspected plague death | World Health Organization | The Guardian
description: ‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency says
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: ‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency says
Content: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s director general, said he wanted clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed reports of ‘a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause’.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s director general, said he wanted clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed reports of ‘a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause’.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesWorld Health OrganizationWHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia following suspected plague death‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency saysLuke HardingSenior international correspondentWed 7 Oct 2026 16.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheWorld Health Organizationhas said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia following the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia.Darya Shipilovadied two days after falling ill with cold-like symptoms. She was an employee at the anti-plague research institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, with some reports suggesting she was infected after a workplace accident.The Russian authorities have denied a connection with the institute and say Shipilovadied from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable.At the same time, officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted.What do we know about death of anti-plague institute worker in Russia and is there a wider risk?Read moreOn Wednesday the WHO director general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event and we’re not able to conduct a full risk assessment.“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.”Tedros said he also wanted more clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed media reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”.“We assess any reporting from the community,” he said. “We asked Russia to respond to that. We’re waiting for an answer.”The WHO’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, Maria Van Kerkhove, said the agency still did not know how Shipilova became infected in the first place – and with what viral disease. If pneumonic plague was ruled out, “what did she actually die from?” Kerkhove asked.In an interview with local media, Shipilova’s 64-year-old mother, Svetlana, discounted the theory that her daughter had been infected after smashing a test tube. “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid friends who believe this. A test tube is unbreakable, even if you throw it against the wall,” she said.She described her daughter as a dedicated worker and “pure person” devoted to her job.Former classmates are also sceptical she was infected at her workplace. One reportedly said: “They’ve smeared a woman without properly investigating. Knowing how hard-working and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.”The Kremlin has sought to downplay the incident and has brushed aside an offer of assistance made earlier this week by Donald Trump, the US president. The White House has pressed Moscow for more details of the case, while stressing the risk to the US is very low.On Tuesday Trump said he would speak about the plague issue “very soon” with Vladimir Putin, who celebrated his 74th birthday on Wednesday. The Kremlin said no call had been arranged but could be quickly organised.According to theBaikal Medical Journal, health officials in Irkutsk have taken extensive measures to stop a potential outbreak from spreading. Neighbours said workers in white protective suits and gas masks disinfected the two-storey brick building where Shipilova lived several times after her death last Friday.“The smell was unbearable and very pungent,” a woman in her 40s said. “A woman knocked on our door. I said: ‘What are you treating here?’ I already knew about the plague rumours.“She said: ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t even have any cockroaches in our building. I saw her packing her overalls into a bag. I was like, ‘Well, I get it.’”Explore more on these topicsWorld Health OrganizationRussiaEuropeBubonic plagueInfectious diseasesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump backs away from top aides who reportedly advised pro-Russia government | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President floats firing Chris LaCivita and James Blair over any ‘conflict’ after reports of work in Republika Srpska
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: President floats firing Chris LaCivita and James Blair over any ‘conflict’ after reports of work in Republika Srpska
Content: Donald Trump at a White House event last month.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at a White House event last month.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersDonald TrumpTrump backs away from top aides who reportedly advised pro-Russia governmentPresident floats firing Chris LaCivita and James Blair over any ‘conflict’ after reports of work in Republika SrpskaAriana BaioWed 7 Oct 2026 16.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 19.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpdistanced himselffrom two top advisers on Wednesday, claiming he did not have “any idea who else they work for”, after it was reported they spent the weekend assisting a pro-Russia government in the Balkans.On Truth Social, TrumpwrotethatChris LaCivita, the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, “are outside consultants” and “do not work for me other than as outside consultants”.“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”EU drops sponsorship of disinformation conference at Trump officials’ requestRead moreThe president’s comments came after the New York Timesreportedthat LaCivita and Blair traveled to Republika Srpska, an autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to assist the government ahead of elections over the weekend. Sources told the newspaper that each adviser was paid hundreds of thousands of dollars.LaCivita and Blair are meanwhile working withMaga Inc, the Trump-backed SuperPac assisting Republican candidates in November’s USmidterm elections.Both men havelong histories with Trump, and the US president has praised them separately on social media.LaCivitajoinedTrump’s 2024 presidential campaign in 2022, after leading a pro-Trump Super Pac called Preserve America. In 2024, Trump wrote on Truth Social that LaCivita was “THE BEST” co-campaign manager alongside Susie Wiles, who now serves as the White House chief of staff.Blair worked for Trump’s 2020 campaign in Florida and was the political director of Trump’s 2024 campaign. He joined the president at the White House as deputy chief of staff for legislative, political and public affairs.In April, Trump called Blair “one of the brightest political minds” while announcing that Blair would leave his White House position, briefly, to join Maga Inc and assist Republicans in the midterms. Trump said Blair would return to the White House after the midterms.Trump’s statement distancing himself from the two advisers comes as Maga Inc prepares to ramp up efforts to assist Republican candidates in next month’s elections.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRubio in Greece digs into past to tout Trump’s ‘America first’ approachRead morePublic polls indicate Democrats areleading Republicansin severalkey competitive races. That is largely attributed to widespread disapproval over Trump’s handling of the economy and cost of living.A spokesperson for Maga Inc told theNew York Timesthat Blair and LaCivita remained engaged with midterm efforts while traveling, saying the two “hosted a team call with race captains on Saturday morning to go over recent survey data”.The Guardian has contacted Maga Inc for comment.Despite polling showing waning voter enthusiasm for Republicans, the party has a cash advantage over Democrats.At the end of August, Maga Inc had more than$415mcash on hand. Several Super Pacs tied to Maga Inc have begun launching multimillion-dollar ad blitzes.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpRussiaBosnia and HerzegovinaTrump administrationUS politicsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: French police suspend use of stun grenades at school protests as minister rejects accusations of brutality | France | The Guardian
description: Minister says use of grenades has been stopped after a student lost a hand as protests across France continue
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Minister says use of grenades has been stopped after a student lost a hand as protests across France continue
Content: A police officer throws a dispersal grenade during a demonstration in Paris on Tuesday.Photograph: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA police officer throws a dispersal grenade during a demonstration in Paris on Tuesday.Photograph: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceFrench police suspend use of stun grenades at school protests as minister rejects accusations of brutalityMinister says use of grenades has been stopped after a student lost a hand as protests across France continueHow dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?Jon Henleyin ParisWed 7 Oct 2026 16.04 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 05.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance’s interior minister has suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations but rejected mountingaccusations of police brutalityduring two weeks of protests marred by often violent clashes that have injured hundreds.Laurent Nuñez told RTL radio on Wednesday that he had ordered a temporary halt on the use of the grenades “in the context of the high school students’ movement” after a 15-year-old boy lost a hand during a protest in Lens, northernFrance, on Monday.Authorities have not confirmed the exact circumstances – in particular, whether the boy had picked up the grenade or been struck by it – but said up to 200 protesters had been hurling projectiles at police when the riot squad intervened.Nuñez said he was suspending use of the grenades “until we know exactly what happened in this case”. But he later told MPs that accusations of “police repression” were “excessive” because officers “are not intervening if the protests are peaceful”.The injured boy’s mother said on Wednesday that her son’s hand had been amputated. She told BFMTV: “His life has been stolen. He’s a 15-year-old kid, how can children be treated like that?” She said her son had not tried to pick up the grenade.The education ministry said classes had been wholly or partially suspended in 429 of the country’s 3,700 lycées – high schools attended by pupils aged between 15 and 18 – on Wednesday, a significantly lower number than on Tuesday.However, 80 university campuses, including the prestigious Sciences Po in Paris, were blockaded in largely peaceful protests by students on Wednesday, unions said, and teachers’ and other unions said they backed further strike action on Thursday.Nuñez told parliament that 215 teenagers and 89 school staff had been injured since the start of the protests – which were triggered by chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes,dilapidated buildingsand long school days – while 761 police officers had also been wounded.He said 18 internal police investigations had been launched over allegations of brutality during the demonstrations, including one incident in which a young protester lost multiple teeth and another in which a student lost the use of an eye.View image in fullscreenProtesters encounter teargas during demonstrations in Paris on Tuesday.Photograph: Véronique de Viguerie/Getty ImagesHe said inquiries were always opened over accusations of “non-proportional” policing, but he insisted officers were there to protect the students. Rights groups and trades unions have repeatedly accused the police of using unnecessary force.On Tuesdayat least 250,000pupils, parents, teachers and unionists took to the streets in cities across France on the biggest day yet of the campaign, prompting the president, Emmanuel Macron, to hold an emergency cabinet meeting.Most marches passed off without serious incident but some, including in Paris, ended in sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, with officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters.French security forces do not have orders to “confront” protesting high school students, the prime minister said on Wednesday, as allegations of police brutality mounted following days of protests.Hundreds of students, police and teaching staff have been injured since the movement demanding better conditions in high schools began.After rights groups, unions and the students accused authorities of using disproportionate force, the government said it would suspend the use of stun grenades by police at student-led demonstrations.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said in a televised address on Wednesday night that the country could not be “indifferent” to the concerns of high school students, acknowledging that the “anger of young people does not come from nowhere”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut he too denied police had “orders to confront” the protesters. He promised the government would present an action plan focusing on replacing absent teachers, renovating school buildings and reorganising timetables by the end of October.Lecornu on Tuesday condemned the violence and told parliament it could not be tolerated, while also rejecting accusations that the government had ordered “police repression” against the protesters.Over the past two weeks, demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded using batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.View image in fullscreenPolice and students face off outside Sciences Po in Paris.Photograph: Tom Nicholson/Getty ImagesTwenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked, while more than 6,600 people have ​been arrested, almost all of them minors. More than 1,800 are being prosecuted, nearly 1,500 of them under 18, the justice ministry has said.Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty France, on Wednesday welcomed the decision to suspend police use of stun grenades as “an important first step” but said the devices should be “permanently banned from the policing of all protests”.She added: “Protests should not be battlefields. Stun grenades are designed to shock, disorient and sow panic, often among dense crowds. Some can cause permanent hearing loss as well as life-changing mutilations due to the blast and shrapnel.”The protests, months before key presidential elections to choose Macron’s successor, have rattled a government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit amid mounting investor concern over France’s ​sky-high debt and weak economic growth.They have also sparked a heated political row, with the government accusing the radical-left La France Insoumise party of encouraging and even orchestrating the movement after numerous LFI MPs attended school blockades.The party’s veteran leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has strongly supported the protests while urging non-violence.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins | Gaza | The Guardian
description: People tell of lives changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent Israeli offensive
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: People tell of lives changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent Israeli offensive
Content: Palestinians describe daily routines full of challenges including shortages of water and nourishing food, disease, unemployment and the threat of death. Photograph: Ali Jadallah/Anadolu/GettyPeople tell of lives changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent Israeli offensiveBySeham Tanteshin Gaza andJason BurkeWed 7 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAhmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are cheap and plastic and battered, but they are among the 43-year-old driver and mechanic’s most valuable possessions.Ishtaiwi lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in centralGazawith his two daughters. Their former home is far to the north, in the now ruined town of Beit Lahiya, uninhabitable and impossible to reach.View image in fullscreenAhmed Ishtaiwi, 43, from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in southern Gaza.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAhmed Ishtaiwi’s chairs are among his most valuable possessions.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian“When I sit on those chairs, I remember sitting in the garden at home, having breakfast and drinking tea. They remind me of my life there,” he said last week.Wednesday is the anniversary of the raid on 7 October 2023 by Hamas militants into southernIsraelthat killed 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and triggered a relentless Israeli military offensive that killed 73,000 Palestinians, mostly civilians, wounded many more and reduced swathes of Gaza to rubble.When Layan al-Jbour, a 15-year-old from the southern city of Khan Younis, tries to bring some order to the crowded makeshift shelter she shares with her parents, brothers and sisters in al-Mawasi, a strip of coastline at the southernmost end of Gaza, she recalls life before the war.“When I tidy the tent, I remember our home and how I used to tidy it. I remember my room and how I used to make my bed. When I put a sheet over a table and arrange the bedding, the place looks like our old home,” al-Jbour said.View image in fullscreenLayan al-Jbour, 15, from Khan Younis holds up a cardiology report from a hospital. The only item she took with her was her schoolbag.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianFormer UN food agency official claims he was fired for highlighting hunger in GazaRead more“We hardly took anything with us from our home. We left everything behind, and the only thing I took was my schoolbag. It is the most precious thing I own now. It reminds me so much of my school days. I loved going to school and meeting my friends there.”Across Gaza, Palestinians describe daily routines full of challenges that nothing in their former lives prepared them for: shortages of water and of nourishing food, minimal healthcare, disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the continuing threat of death or injury.Despite a ceasefire a year ago, Israel’s airstrikes continue. Palestinians who have approached the “yellow line” that divides Gaza into zones controlled by the Israeli military and by Hamas have been shot dead. In the last year, the overall death tollhas risenby a further 1,400 people.In recent days, Israeli attacks have intensified, killing at least two Palestinians in Gaza on Tuesday, according to health officials. The Israeli military said the strikes targeted militants.On Wednesday, Gaza medics said at ​least two Palestinians were killed and others wounded in airstrikes in Beit Lahiya and Khan Younis.View image in fullscreenPalestinians gather at the site of an Israeli airstrike that killed a Palestinian in a camp in Khan Younis on Wednesday.Photograph: Tariq Mohammad/APAImages/Shutterstock“It is what we feared … a ceasefire that just isn’t a ceasefire,” said one international aid worker now based in Amman, Jordan, who worked in Gaza throughout much of the conflict. “Daily life is horrible. People aren’t hungry any more but they are still malnourished. Our local staff are telling us that this is just the next stage of the conflict.”Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told the UN security council last month that despite the increase in supplies entering Gaza, the health situation remained critical, with “infectious diseases … widespread amid overcrowded displacement sites and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions”.Inadequate funding for relief efforts exacerbated the “shortages of medical supplies, fuel and the overall humanitarian response”, Alakbarov said, while “restrictions on the entry of critical humanitarian items imposed by Israel” were slowing preparations for cold weather.Israeli authorities deny shortages and say adequate supplies are reaching Gaza,with more than 600 trucksentering the territory each day.View image in fullscreenSaleh Kilani, 70, from Beit Lahiya, lives in a camp in Deir al-Balah in southern Gaza.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianSaleh Kilani, 70, from Beit Lahiya, used to have a farm and olive trees before the war. “Around this time of year, I used to press about 60 containers of olive oil. But I lost all of that too. If I go to my home I may die, and if I go to my farm, I may die too. This is not a life. We are exhausted and we have lost hope.”Kilani said life before the conflict seemed very distant. “We never used to think twice about seeing orange and peach trees, green fields, grapes and figs. These things were simply part of our lives. Now when we see them, we are surprised,” he said.Hamas, which swiftly reimposed its authority over the 2.3 million Palestinians who live in the third of Gaza not under the control of the Israeli military, has rebuilt a rudimentary administration which provides patchy education, some healthcare services and limited policing based on deterrence through often arbitrary punishment.Donald Trump’s plan to definitively end the war in Gaza has stalled, with little progress towards disarming Hamas, securing the withdrawal of Israeli troops and beginning the vast job of reconstruction.“My biggest fear is that this situation will continue. We are living through a period that can be described as neither war nor peace,” said Kilani.The only time Esraa Abu Taiba recalls her prewar existence is when she gets to practise her former profession: beautician.View image in fullscreenEsraa Abu Taiba, 26, from Bani Suheila to the east of Khan Younis, used to work as a beautician in her former life.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianThe 26-year-old lived in Bani Suheila, a town to the east of Khan Younis and now within the zone controlled by Israel. Of her five brothers, two were killed in the conflict, two were wounded, and one is among themore than 1,500 Palestinians from Gazain detention in Israel.“Before the war my life was quiet and good,” she said. “I could go wherever I wanted without fear or restrictions. We lived in our own home. We had a washing machine, a tap and a garden. The house belonged to us and we lived there comfortably.“Now we live in a tent. Our lives depend on carrying water and getting food from the community kitchen. A water truck comes to the end of the street and … I go to collect it because my mother cannot carry it.”Like most Palestinians in Gaza, her family was displaced multiple times during the conflict, and they have lost everything from their former home – except a house key, which her mother keeps close.“The only thing I still do from my old life is some beauty work. I cut girls’ hair in the tents around us and do their makeup for weddings,” said Abu Taiba.“It takes me back to a beautiful and happy period of our lives, when we used to celebrate weddings and other happy occasions before the war. It takes me away from the misery we are living through, even if only for a little while.”Explore more on these topicsGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineIsraelIsrael-Gaza warInternally displaced peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Houthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west Yemen | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land
Content: Several pro-Houthi men take part in a rally to recruit new fighters for the group in Sanaa on Wednesday.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSeveral pro-Houthi men take part in a rally to recruit new fighters for the group in Sanaa on Wednesday.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenHouthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west YemenGroup’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to landPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorWed 7 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-westYemen, approaching the city of Taiz and firing a missile and an explosive towards the airport in Aden, the chief international hub of the Saudi-backed government.The explosive hit the key airport moments before a plane was due to land. The British ambassador toYemen, Abda Sharif, said the attack could have endangered thousands of people. It forced the flight – from Cairo – to be diverted to Jeddah and led to a review about the safety of flights in Aden.Independent observers said there was a danger that the Houthis were on course to capture Yemen’s third city of Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure Aden. Saudi warplanes had been using their air superiority to try to hit any Houthi accumulation of forces near the city, especially to the west.View image in fullscreenA Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighter is seen purportedly firing at a Houthi position near Dhubab in Taiz.Photograph: Southern Giants Brigades/ReutersHouthi forces also claimed that they had fired missiles towards two airports in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Saudi authorities initially said the attacks had been repelled, but then said three people had been killed and 36 people wounded.The Institute for the Study of War said it was adjusting its previous assessment that Houthi forces on the coastal plain were collapsing “in light of evidence in the last 24 hours indicating that theHouthishave stopped Yemeni government-aligned advances”.Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?Read moreThere has been widespread criticism on social media of some of the claims aboutYemeni government advancesissued at the beginning of the week.Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, gave a lengthy address marking the third anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel, and singled out the Qatari-owned Al Jazeera for criticism of its coverage of the Yemen war. Trying to link the various conflicts in the Middle East, he urged Yemenis to investigate the Saudi role in the Palestinian cause, “stressing that whoever searches will only find it stabbing the nation in the back”, and said the formal positions taken by the Saudi regime did not in reality benefit the Palestinian people.The Houthi leader also stressed that the Saudi government was not content with complicity in Gaza, but played a key role in conspiring against the Islamic resistance in Lebanon, where it incited everyone against Hezbollah in a single front with the US and Israel.Southern Giants forces – a pro-government militia in Yemen – are still leading efforts to recapture the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea that had been the first target of an offensive launched by the Yemen government on Monday. The group is now positioned in the military airport sector in the Dhubab district near the Bab al-Mandab strait.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricaSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors | Israel | The Guardian
description: Forced closure marks low point in UK-Israeli relations, with reports UK is considering retaliatory expulsion of Israeli diplomats from London
Author: William Christou
Headline: Forced closure marks low point in UK-Israeli relations, with reports UK is considering retaliatory expulsion of Israeli diplomats from London
Content: The British consulate in East Jerusalem.Photograph: Amir Levy/GettyView image in fullscreenThe British consulate in East Jerusalem.Photograph: Amir Levy/GettyIsrael‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doorsForced closure marks low point in UK-Israeli relations, with reports UK is considering retaliatory expulsion of Israeli diplomats from LondonIsrael marks three years since 7 October attack – liveWilliam ChristouandSufian Tahain JerusalemWed 7 Oct 2026 11.14 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK consulate in East Jerusalem gave few signs it was at the centre of a geopolitical controversy this week, with little movement around the high-walled building save the fluttering of the union jack and the occasional car exiting the compound.The mission is to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure in response to aUK ban on trade with illegal settlementsin the occupied West Bank and sanctions on those who help build or finance them.The forced closure marked the lowest point in UK-Israeli relations for decades, with reports of the UK consideringa retaliatory expulsionof 27 Israeli diplomats from London.It would be the Palestinians who pay the price for the consulate’s closing, warned Amjad Iraqi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst on Israel andPalestine. The UK consulate in East Jerusalem is separate from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv – which remains open – and provides services to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, services they will now lose.“It’s quite telling that the Israeli government response was primarily about blocking the UK’s ability to support Palestinians, rather than the core of UK-Israeli relations themselves,” Iraqi said. “For [the Israeli] foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, the response is low-cost, in their minds it’s just Palestinians bearing the cost.”UK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats over planned East Jerusalem consulate closureRead moreIsrael has already curtailed the diplomatic activities of the Netherlands, Spain and Norway in the occupiedWest Bank.Palestinian residents of Sheikh Jarrah, the East Jerusalem neighbourhood that is home to the consulate, appeared resigned when asked about the impact the closure might have on their lives.“I mean, it was the British that were the basis of the issue, wasn’t it? They were the ones who signed the Balfour declaration?” said Abu Abdo, a 79-year-old former repairman and resident of Sheikh Jarrah, referring to a 1917 document by the British foreign secretary Arthur Balfour, which expressed support for a Jewish state in Palestine.It was a dramatic end for the consulate’s tenure in East Jerusalem, which since its move to the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood in 1967 has experienced its fair share of political upheaval.The UK government first bought the plot that would become its consulate in 1963, when East Jerusalem was still under Jordanian control. It was meant to be a direct liaison between the UK government and the Jordanian-administered West Bank and East Jerusalem. The compound took four years to build and was finally ready for the UK consul-general to move into by 1967.By the time the new consul-general moved into the premises, however, East Jerusalem was no longer under the control of the Jordanians. Just weeks before John Henry Lewen was to move into the building, the six-day war broke out and Israel captured East Jerusalem from the Jordanian forces.Lewen assumed his post at the consulate in a changed East Jerusalem under Israeli control. The consulate he oversaw occupied a unique position as the UK did not recognise Jerusalem as being under any single country’s control.As the UK foreign secretarytoldparliament in June 1967: “Our consul-general in Jerusalem is subordinate neither to the ambassador in Tel Aviv nor to the ambassador in Amman, but directly to the Foreign Office.”Lewen’s tenure was marked by the political problems that plagued Jerusalem in the aftermath of the six-day war and the birth of Israel. In 1969, a bomb wasplacedunder the window of a consul secretary, harming no one but damaging the compound.Years later, Palestinians would present their grievances to the British consulate in Sheikh Jarrah. In 2017, protesters demonstrated outside the consulate to mark the centenary of the Balfour declaration. Men placed flags in the consululate windows reading “Balfour is a crime”, while schoolgirls carried thousands of letters written by Palestinian students asking Britain to apologise for the declaration.This week, however, there was little sign of the political turmoil which the British consulate had waded through during its 60 years on the site. The neighbourhood, mostly made up of diplomatic missions and UN and other international organisations’ offices, was quiet.Residents in the area expressed disappointment over what they saw as a lack of international support for the Palestinian people in recent years.“We have seen very little but studies and words, no action from the international community,” said Abu Abdo.Explore more on these topicsIsraelWest BankPalestineForeign policyMiddle East and north AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bendy elm still standing against all odds crowned UK tree of the year | Trees and forests | The Guardian
description: Hundred-and-fifty-year-old Wych elm in Newcastle, Co Down has grown sideways owing to strong winds
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Hundred-and-fifty-year-old Wych elm in Newcastle, Co Down has grown sideways owing to strong winds
Content: The tree has somehow resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m elms.Photograph: Michael CooperView image in fullscreenThe tree has somehow resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m elms.Photograph: Michael CooperTrees and forestsBendy elm still standing against all odds crowned UK tree of the yearHundred-and-fifty-year-old Wych elm in Newcastle, Co Down has grown sideways owing to strong windsPippa NeillEnvironment reporterWed 7 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe “astonishing and bizarre” Bendy Tree inNorthern Irelandhas been crowned the winner of this year’s tree of the year competition.Half a million trees to be planted in England in three years, says governmentRead moreThe wych elm tree, located in Newcastle, County Down, owes its name to its near horizontal trunk, which has grown sideways owing to the strong seaside winds coming off the Irish Sea.The 150-year-old tree has resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m elms, making it a worthy winner of the competition’s “against the odds” theme.The tree was originally planted in the mid-19th century as part of a row of wych elms along the town’s promenade to shelter the main street from sea winds. Many of those trees were felled during redevelopments of the town, with the bendy tree now the last one standing.View image in fullscreenNewcastle’s bendy elm.Photograph:  Michael Cooper“When you look at this astonishing and bizarre tree, there’s no doubt about what it has endured,” said May Chemais, ancient tree inventory lead for the Woodland Trust, the charity that runs the annual competition.“We’ve all been through changes and hardships that have shaped who we are: I think that’s why the Bendy Tree has struck a chord with people,” she said.For John Martin, director of the Woodland Trust NI, it is the whimsical nature of the tree that makes it a worthy winner.Could you be an ‘autumn spotter’? Public asked to track changing colours of trees in EnglandRead moreHaving grown up visiting Newcastle as a child, Martin recalls seeing the tree out of the corner of his eye and being surprised to see a tree growing this way.“You expect nature to behave in a certain way and we would expect a tree, most of the time, to grow upwards, whereas this one has grown sideways,” he said. “I guess it gives people a bit of a smile on their day.”The tree’s unusual shape has also provided welcome shade to residents and visitors resting on the bench located beneath its branches.“Older trees like this one are providing our communities with so much – from shade, wellbeing and health benefits, to stories, culture and pride of place,” said Chemais.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCrowhurst Yew in Crowhurst, Surrey.Photograph: Lee CooperOther trees nominated in this year’s competition included the Crowhurst Yew in Crowhurst, Surrey, England. Villagers hollowed out the trunk in 1820 to create a parish meeting room within the tree. The roof of this room collapsed during a storm in 1845, but the tree lived on, with the wooden door to the secret room remaining to this day.Also in the top 10 shortlist was the Culmstock Yew in Culmstock, Devon, England. This tree is perched on top a 20-metre high church tower, with its existence pre-dating residents’ living memories.View image in fullscreenCulmstock Yew in Devon.Photograph: Lee CooperLast year’s honour went to a75ft ash treethat shades homes on one of Glasgow’s busiest roads.The Woodland Trust has this week launched its Igniting Innovation competition for anyone aged 16 to 25 to share their ideas for projects that could benefit nature and make life better for woods, trees and people.Three winners will receive £5,000 in funding and up to a year of expert mentoring to bring their projects to life.Explore more on these topicsTrees and forestsNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Family of student who took his own life say university ‘will be held to account’ | Universities | The Guardian
description: Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of Glasgow
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of Glasgow
Content: Ethan Scott Brown died at the age of 23 on the day he should have been graduating.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenEthan Scott Brown died at the age of 23 on the day he should have been graduating.Photograph: Family handout/PAUniversitiesFamily of student who took his own life say university ‘will be held to account’Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of GlasgowNadeem BadshahWed 7 Oct 2026 17.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe family of a student who took his own life after beingwrongly told he would not be eligible to graduatehave said the University of Glasgow “will be held to account”.Ethan Scott Brown, 23, was due to graduate in December 2024 after studying geography.However, his family said that in September that year,the universitytold him he had not been awarded a grade for one course and would therefore not be eligible to graduate with an honours degree.His family said as a result, he took his own life on 13 December 2024, the day he should have been graduating.He was found dead in his bedroom by his mother, Tracy Scott, that morning.Scott, who collected her son’s degree posthumously, has called for a fatal accident inquiry to be held into his death.The university has said it is “profoundly sorry” and is implementing a series of recommendations after a review.The university’s internal inquiry found “systemic” errors in the way Brown’s degree had been graded, and that he had enough marks for a 2:1 honours degree. It also found that although Brown had told staff that he had concerns about his mental health, they had failed to offer him support.View image in fullscreenTracy Scott, pictured after a meeting with the Scottish education secretary on Wednesday.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAOn Tuesday it was reported that the family had settled a civil court action with the university. The sum of the settlement has not been disclosed.On Wednesday, the family met the Scottish education secretary, Màiri McAllan, at St Andrew’s House in Edinburgh.Speaking after the meeting, their solicitor Aamer Anwar said they had placed “the University ofGlasgowon notice that they will be held to account”.Anwar claimed that in its drive to become a global institution, the university had “forgotten its soul”.He added: “Their failures were catastrophic and systemic. They failed not just in their duty of care to Ethan, but to many other students over the years.“Today’s meeting with the minister was important and was welcomed. The minister offered to ask the QAA [Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education], who are investigating the university, to meet with the family.“The family welcomed the apology by Ms McAllan for her predecessor’s statement in September 2025 which implied an acceptance of the university’s position that Ethan’s case was an isolated incident.”Anwar added that the university’s governance process was “not fit for purpose”.View image in fullscreenThe family’s solicitor, Aamer Anwar, claimed that the University of Glasgow had ‘forgotten its soul’.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAA spokesperson for the University of Glasgow said: “The university is profoundly sorry that Ethan tragically took his own life and fully understands the deep distress this has caused his family. We repeat our sincere apology as well as our deepest sympathy.“Following an internal investigation into assessment regulations, the university self-referred to the Scottish Funding Council.“The Quality Assurance Agency subsequently carried out a targeted peer review, which resulted in a series of recommendations for action.“The university fully accepted the recommendations and is on track to implement them.”A spokesperson for the Crown Office said the circumstances of Brown’s death were being investigated by the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service, adding that the family would be kept updated on any developments.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisiscounselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsUniversitiesGlasgowStudentsScotlandHigher educationMental healthHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour Send changes at risk as parents rush to secure support, say experts | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Overhaul of special education in England could unravel, thinktank finds, because of ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Overhaul of special education in England could unravel, thinktank finds, because of ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic
Content: The IfG says the government’s plans may take longer to complete than the 2030 timeline.Photograph: Sydney Bourne/Getty Images/Image SourceView image in fullscreenThe IfG says the government’s plans may take longer to complete than the 2030 timeline.Photograph: Sydney Bourne/Getty Images/Image SourceSpecial educational needsLabour Send changes at risk as parents rush to secure support, say expertsOverhaul of special education in England could unravel, thinktank finds, because of ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamicRichard AdamsEducation editorWed 7 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour’s flagship changes to special education inEnglandare at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing tosecure support for their childrenbefore the system changes, new analysis has found.TheInstitute for Government (IfG) thinktanksays the government’s plans to largely replace education, health and care plans (EHCPs) in England with more widespread support in mainstream schools may be too optimistic and take longer to complete than its 2030 timeline.The thinktank’s report calls on the government to review the timetable for the changes. And it suggests that if ministers do not act they “risk basing both their reforms and spending plans on assumptions that the system cannot deliver”.The news will be seen as a sign that the government’s ambitious plans to overhaul the special education system did not reckon with the scale of worry among parents, many of whom appear to have acted to ensure support and avoid uncertainty in the future.Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for supportRead moreThe Guardian recently reported that councils and schools havereported a surge in applicationsfor EHCPs, with one school describing the level as “unreal” compared with previous years. Several councils are now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.Amber Dellar, the author of the IfG report out this week, said the long rollout of the changes created a “moral hazard” that encouraged parents to apply for EHCPs now rather than wait for the new system.“There’s a ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic, as schools and parents have an incentive to secure EHCPs before they are phased out, because there’s a lot of uncertainty about what these new specialist packages of support will contain and who will be eligible for them,” she said.Dellar said the government’s plans added new resources in order to reduce the need for families to seek EHCPs, the individualised packages of support agreed between parents and local authorities that can be enforced by specialist tribunals.But Dellar said budgets for the additional resources for special educational needs and disabilities (Send) would be eroded if demands for EHCPs shot above the government’s own forecasts, with councils saying they have to keep issuing EHCPs until the existing legislation is repealed.She said: “The government has a lot riding on the reforms taking effect before they fully kick in – its spending plans for the parliament have some assumptions about savings baked in that are based in particular on them being able to slow the growth or the trajectory of numbers of pupils with EHCPs.“It has a lot politically riding on it as well, and of course in terms of the wellbeing of the children and families involved.”View image in fullscreenThe changes would see mainstream schools given greater support for pupils with special needs.Photograph: Daniel Atkin/AlamyADepartment for Education(DfE) spokesperson said: “The figures in this report are speculative and there is no evidence that proposed reforms are driving additional EHCP demand.“We inherited a Send system with record numbers of EHCPs and families waiting months for support. We are already investing to change that, backing schools to improve inclusion, widening access to specialists and rolling out training for every teacher to better support children before needs escalate.“It is vital that we take the time needed to get this right, but we are completely committed to the implementation timelines set out in the schools white paper and will announce next steps soon.”The changesannounced in Februaryunder Keir Starmer’s administration promised to overhaul a system that parents have denounced for forcing them to seek EHCPs to secure specialist support or a place in a special school.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMany parents said the EHCP application process – introduced by the Conservatives in 2014 – required lengthy waits for NHS assessments for conditions such as ADHD or autism, or great expense for those who could afford private assessments. Families then face bureaucratic delays from schools and local authorities, or legal appeals to a specialist Send tribunal to override councils’ objections.Mark Franks, the director of welfare at the Nuffield Foundation, which funded the report, said: “While there is broad agreement that the current system is under strain, uncertainty and concern remain about whether future levels of investment and the nature of reform will be sufficient to provide high-quality support for all children and young people.”The IfG said the additional costs of Send provision could erode the extra funding being offered for state schools in England, saying it could absorb “around two-thirds of the generous schools funding uplift over this parliament”.The package of changes would see mainstream schools given greater support for pupils with special needs, including the creation of specialist bases, allowing pupils to attend local schools and reduce pressure on special schools.The DfE also wants individual support plans to replace many EHCPs, which would be retained for children with the most profound needs.The IfG said: “It is not clear exactly how the reforms will slow the growth in EHCPs before the new system is fully in place.”‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provisionRead moreDellar said: “The government is making investments now, in early intervention and in specialist bases. But the whole way the government is approaching these Send reforms is deliberately to take a slow, phased approach – largely because it knows that those investments are going to take a while to have an effect.“Its investments in early assessment are going to take a little time to bear fruit. It has not yet properly set out exactly what preventative support it wants schools to put in place. So until schools have that, it’s unclear that they will actually be able to start doing the work the government wants them to do.“On top of that, the system is tightly bound by existing legislation. Local authorities [LAs] in particular have quite strict guidelines, and tribunals suggest that there are often disputes over eligibility for EHCPs but LAs are likely to be pulled towards the law as it stands until the law changes.”Explore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsSchool fundingSchoolsEducation policyChildrenDisabilityDepartment for EducationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decades | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Convicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum terms
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Convicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum terms
Content: Luke Ings (left) and Liam Bennett were jailed as teenagers.Composite: ITV MeridianView image in fullscreenLuke Ings (left) and Liam Bennett were jailed as teenagers.Composite: ITV MeridianUK criminal justiceTwo men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decadesConvicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum termsRajeev SyalHome affairs editorWed 7 Oct 2026 15.16 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men jailed with indefinite sentences for public protection (IPPs) have been freed after each serving about two decades in custody despite receiving minimum terms of two years or less.A high court judge and a magistrate hearing an appeal after a review by theCriminal Cases Review Commission(CCRC) told Luke Ings and Liam Bennett they would be freed, and also replaced an indeterminate sentence given to a third man, James Ward.Ward, who was freed in 2017 after serving 10 years more than his one-year minimum and was later recalled to prison, was also in court, sitting in the public gallery to see his original sentence replaced.Relatives of Ings and Bennett hugged in the public gallery at Wolverhampton crown court on Wednesday as Mr Justice Choudhury told them the IPPs had been “cancelled”.Choudhury said Bennett would instead be sentenced to four years and 264 days, Ward to two years, and Ings to 42 months with a 30-month extended licence.All three men’s original sentences were quashed and replaced after they argued that judges had wrongly found them to be dangerous or had not considered alternative sentences.Choudhury, sitting with the magistrate Norma Grant, told the appellants: “You have already spent considerably longer than those [replacement] sentences in custody.
