The effect is that you, Mr Bennett, and you, Mr Ings, will be entitled to release without further supervision, and you, Mr Ward, will no longer be subject to supervision.”The ruling came after the CCRC referred the cases of the three men back to the crown court to review minimum terms imposed on them by judges in Wolverhampton, Reading and Leicester respectively in 2006 and 2007.Bennett and Ings, now both 38, were 17 when they committed offences that led to them being classed as dangerous offenders and given indeterminate sentences with respective minimum terms of 24 months and 21 months in 2007 and 2006.Bennett was originally sentenced at Wolverhampton crown court in May 2007 after being found guilty of reckless arson for setting fire to items in the loft space of an empty council property, and admitting criminal damage and burglary.Ings was sentenced to detention for public protection after appearing at East Berkshire youth court in March 2006 and admitting offences including a robbery in an underpass and an assault on a teenager in a fast food outlet.Ward, now 41, was 21 when he was given a one-year minimum sentence in 2006 at Leicester crown court for arson and criminal damage. He admitted arson – after setting fire to items in his prison cell while serving time for assault – and was released in 2017, but was later recalled to prison and remained in custody until August this year.Muin Boase, representing Bennett, successfully argued that the judge who sentenced him in 2007 did not give proper weight to his youth, lack of maturity and capacity to change after a difficult childhood.In its ruling, the appeal court said there had been no proper basis for the original finding of dangerousness.Detention for public protection and imprisonment for public protection (DPP and IPP) sentences were abolished in 2012, having been made available to tackle offenders considered a significant risk to the public in 2005.The law was changed to stop courts handing out IPP sentences after warnings that they were being applied too widely, but the abolition was not retrospective, meaning many prisoners serving such sentences are still behind bars.The government has faced calls to take action on IPP jail terms, with the former justice secretary Ken Clarke saying last month that ministers should not to be too cautious.His comments came a week after the current justice secretary, Alex Norris, told MPs that the government planned to bring forward legislation to end IPP sentences “once and for all” by the end of this parliament.More than 2,000 prisoners remain held indefinitely under IPP sentences, with 99% past their original tariff and 80% having served 10 years or more.Additional reporting by the Press AssociationExplore more on these topicsUK criminal justiceCriminal Cases Review CommissionSentencingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Party hopes to win over affluent middle-class voters as leader rejects calls to ‘unite the right’ in conference speech
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Party hopes to win over affluent middle-class voters as leader rejects calls to ‘unite the right’ in conference speech
Content: Kemi Badenoch said in her speech that economic growth would be the ‘central organising principle’ of the next Conservative government.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/GettyView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch said in her speech that economic growth would be the ‘central organising principle’ of the next Conservative government.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/GettyConservativesTories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut planParty hopes to win over affluent middle-class voters as leader rejects calls to ‘unite the right’ in conference speechPippa CrerarPolitical editorWed 7 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.The Tory leader also said couples would be able to leave an additional tax-free sum of £1m to their families, as the party attempts to shore up its traditional base in southern England.The move would mean the number of families paying inheritance tax – currentlyless than 5% do so– would fall by more than a half, Badenoch said, with the £6bn cost to be paid for by cuts the party says it has identified, including to the welfare bill.“My ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it,” she told the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. “I believe the people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort. So this is my guarantee: no stamp duty when you buy your home, no mansion tax when you live in your home, and no inheritance tax on your home when you pass it to your children or grandchildren.”The Tories’ policy plans announced this week – also includingsupport with childcarefor those earning more than £100,000 and repealing the mansion tax – have been firmly focused on affluent middle-class voters, many of whom deserted the party at the last election.They have been welcomed by Conservative MPs and activists, who are relieved that Badenoch appears to be trying to shore up the party’s core support despite her natural proclivity to lean into culture wars on the right.However, the inheritance tax plans are likely to raise fears about overheating the housing market, giving elderly homeowners an incentive to stay in large family homes rather than downsize. The move also prompted accusations the party was favouring the rich over struggling families.In a statement, Tax Justice UK said: “Kemi Badenoch has just announced a massive inheritance tax giveaway to some of the wealthiest people in Britain. This is a reckless policy that will deprive public services of cash when they most need them.”Stuart Adam, a senior economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes. These will mostly be people living in London and the south-east.”Reform UK suggested Badenoch’s inheritance tax plans would affect only 2% of houses, the majority in London. Its finance spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said: “The Tory party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country.”Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair and minister for equalities, said: “The Tories haven’t changed. Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories’ choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead.”View image in fullscreenBadenoch acknowledged that the party faced a long road to recovery after its defeat at the 2024 general election.Photograph: WPA/GettyDespite the Tories appearing more united this week than they have done for years, Badenoch did acknowledge in her speech that the party, still polling lower than at the time of its catastrophic 2024 election defeat, faced a long path to recovery.She issued an appeal to Reform voters to back her. “We let them down and we want them to come back home. They deserve better than Reform politicians,” she said. “We have changed our party. There is still a lot of work to do. People are looking through the shop window. They like what they see, but let’s be honest, not enough of them are buying it. We need to fix that.”Senior Tories have been urging Badenoch to focus more on the economy, which they hope will help them to win back middle-class swing voters in their traditional heartlands, and to pivot away from culture wars and migration.Badenoch added that economic growth would be the “central organising principle” of the next Conservative government, cutting red tape in areas such as planning, building a third runway at Heathrow and implementing a new energy policy, while also creating jobs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMost of her speech, however, was devoted to attacks on her opponents, with the Tories desperate to edge ahead of Reform in the polls and be seen once again as the main opposition party on the right.Badenoch rejected calls from within her own party to “unite the right” by striking a deal with Nigel Farage’s party – reflecting warnings from her closest allies that doing so would risk toxifying the Conservative brand irrevocably.She said: “A year ago, those politicians were measuring up the curtains for No 10. Now, some of them are measuring up the curtains for their prison cells.“The circus goes on and on, and it will never stop because this is who Reform politicians are. So, to those who say ‘unite the right’, we are not uniting with that. People deserve better and we are going to give them better than that: character, conduct and standards matter.”Badenoch also drew a sharp dividing line with Reform on race, after Suella Braverman, the former Conservative home secretary who defected to Farage’s party, suggested that minority ethnic people could not be English.“I don’t want to explain to my son when we’re watching our brilliant England team play football that some people don’t think our black players are English,” she said. “I remember back in the day when Ian Wright and John Barnes were playing. Nobody was questioning whether they were English. We certainly didn’t have sitting MPs questioning whether they were English.“We must not let these people take us backwards. That is not the country we are. Reform MPs are openly questioning people’s identity.“I don’t know whether you’ve noticed, but I am black. I am British. I am proud of my country. I’m proud of our history, all that we have done, and all that we will do in the world.”Badenoch acknowledged that last year her leadership of the party had been under intense pressure. But she added: “Let me tell you, I’m not someone who gets written off, and neither is the Conservative party. There is a reason our party is still here after 200 years. We have adapted to every single challenge and every single age, and we are doing it again.”Explore more on these topicsConservativesConservative conference 2026Conservative conferenceKemi BadenochTax and spendingInheritance taxnewsShareReuse this content

title: Patricia Krenwinkel, former Manson follower, granted parole for third time | California | The Guardian
description: The 78-year-old has spent nearly six decades in prison and California governor has overturned last two parole grants
Author: Sam Levin
Headline: The 78-year-old has spent nearly six decades in prison and California governor has overturned last two parole grants
Content: Patricia Krenwinkel listens to the ruling denying her parole on 20 January 2011.Photograph: Reed Saxon/APView image in fullscreenPatricia Krenwinkel listens to the ruling denying her parole on 20 January 2011.Photograph: Reed Saxon/APCaliforniaPatricia Krenwinkel, former Manson follower, granted parole for third timeThe 78-year-old has spent nearly six decades in prison and California governor has overturned last two parole grantsSam Levinin Los AngelesWed 7 Oct 2026 19.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatricia Krenwinkel, a formerCharles Mansonfollower, was granted parole on Tuesday after nearly six decades in prison for her role in the infamous Tate-LaBianca murders in Los Angeles.This is thethird timethat Krenwinkel, 78, has been approved for release by California’s board of parole hearings. After both of her last two parole grants, Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, reversed the parole board’s decisions anddenied her freedom, and Krenwinkel’s attorneys are now urging the Democrat to allow this latest ruling to stand.Krenwinkel, who was 21 at the time of the 1969 killings, has been imprisoned longer than any other woman inCalifornia, and the parole board has repeatedly acknowledged her record of rehabilitation over 57 years in prison, concluding she would not in her elderly age be a danger to society.She was convicted in 1971 for her role in the violent crime spree over two nights that claimed the lives of actor Sharon Tate, who was eight months pregnant, and her four friends, and grocery owner Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary. The killings were gruesome and became one of the most notorious crime stories in the US.Krenwinkel was 19 years old when she “fell under Charles Manson’s control” and was exploited and psychologically abused by the cult leader, her attorneys have said.“Reaching this moment has taken decades of hard, deliberate work to confront who she was, what she did, and the devastating harm she caused,” her longtime lawyer, Keith Wattley, said in a statement after the parole grant. “She fully accepts responsibility for her actions, everything she contributed to, and every life she destroyed in 1969. Pat does not excuse or minimize that harm.”Over her decades in prison, Krenwinkel has had a clean disciplinary record, and nine consecutive psychological evaluations in the past 40 years have found her to be a low public safety risk, according to Wattley, who has represented Krenwinkel for 16 years. He said she has participated in extensive therapy and group counseling, earned a college degree and trained service dogs for people with disabilities.“I have seen the depth of her remorse and the extraordinary work she has done to change her life. I firmly believe she is ready to return home,” Wattley added.Debra Tate, Sharon Tate’s sister, has repeatedlyobjectedto the release of Krenwinkel and other Manson followers.When Newsom denied Krenwinkel parole in 2022, after the board first found her suitable for release, the governoracknowledgedthat she had been a “victim of Mr Manson’s abuse” and said she had “matured in prison and engaged in commendable rehabilitative efforts”. But he argued she had “not developed sufficient insight into the causative factors of her crime and her triggers for antisocial thinking” and was still dangerous.When Newsom again denied her parole in 2025, he also acknowledged her “serious chronic medical conditions” had diminished her strength, but concluded she “must do additional work to deepen her insight before she can be safely released”.The governor is required to consider her elderly age and that she committed the crime as a youth in his review of her case.Krenwinkel’s attorneys and advocates have repeatedly argued the governor was caving to political pressures by denying parole to people convicted in high-profile cases. Newsom previously vetoed the release of Leslie van Houten, another former Manson follower, but an appeals court sided with her andgranted her freedom in 2023. Newsom also faced scrutiny foroverturning the parole grant of Sirhan Sirhan, convicted of assassinating Robert F Kennedy, even after two of Kennedy’s sons favored his release.The push for Krenwinkel’s release comes at a time of growing concern about the increasing number ofelderly people languishing in US prisonsafter decades of incarceration. Krenwinkel’s longtime friends from inside California’s women’s prisontold the Guardianlast year that she was a mentor and support system to others in the prison.Wattley, founder of UnCommon Law, a non-profit organization that represents people at parole hearings, urged Newsom to “uphold the law” and approve Krenwinkel’s freedom: “The parole process exists because people can change, rehabilitation matters, and public safety must be grounded in evidence. Pat’s case raises a fundamental question: if three parole grants don’t lead to release, what is the point of this process?”Spokespeople for Newsom did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Wednesday.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaCharles MansonWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Leon Botstein resigns from Bard roles as key Democrat demands investigation into Epstein links | Jeffrey Epstein | The Guardian
description: Jamie Raskin says ‘startling’ email asked whether young woman was ‘for me, or are you keeping her for yourself’
Author: Stephanie Kirchgaessner
Headline: Jamie Raskin says ‘startling’ email asked whether young woman was ‘for me, or are you keeping her for yourself’
Content: Leon Botstein said he had submitted his resignation to protect Bard from any distraction.Photograph: New York Daily News/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeon Botstein said he had submitted his resignation to protect Bard from any distraction.Photograph: New York Daily News/Getty ImagesJeffrey EpsteinLeon Botstein resigns from Bard roles as key Democrat demands investigation into Epstein linksJamie Raskin says ‘startling’ email asked whether young woman was ‘for me, or are you keeping her for yourself’Stephanie KirchgaessnerWed 7 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 20.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA powerfulDemocraticlawmaker has called for a criminal investigation into former Bard College presidentLeon Botsteinafter congressional investigators uncovered an email from Botstein to accused sex traffickerJeffrey Epsteinin which he says Botstein asked if a young woman was “for me, or are you keeping her for yourself”.The latest development appears to have triggered the immediate resignation of Botstein from all Bard-affiliated positions, including his professorship and roles in Bard’s music programs. Botstein had led the college for 50 years and only recently stepped down as president.Brandon Weber, the chair of Bard College’s board of trustees, said in a statement on Wednesday evening that the college had received additional communications from Congressman Jamie Raskin, who is the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee and is leading a congressional investigation into Botstein’s relationship with Epstein.Weber said Bard was undertaking “a full review” of the allegations that have been made in Raskin’s letter, and was cooperating with the committee’s investigation. Weber also said members of the executive committee of Bard’s board of trustees voted unanimously to accept Botstein’s resignation.Botstein said in a statement that “any assertion that I knew of or was involved in Epstein’s criminal behavior is wrong”.“But I do not want to see even false allegations about me put the institution I have served for more than half a century put at any risk,” he said, saying he had submitted his resignation to protect Bard from any distraction.Botstein has faced intense scrutiny since the release earlier this year of the Epstein files, which revealed a friendly relationship between the then longtime college president and Epstein, who died in prison in 2019 while facing sex-trafficking charges. The revelations, including that Botstein had once been on Epstein’s island for a visit, contributed to his decision to step down as president.The latest controversy centers on an email that the Democratic committee members – who have access to unredacted emails in the Epstein files – said was sent by Botstein to Epstein in connection to a young foreign model and aspiring vocalist who they say was being “groomed” by Epstein throughout 2014.According to a letter sent by Democrats Jamie Raskin and Madeleine Dean to attorney general Todd Blanche and FBI director Kash Patel, records in the Epstein files indicate that Epstein was offering the young woman – referred to as Jane Doe – advice and help with her plans to attend school and develop her career in the US.View image in fullscreenJamie Raskin with Epstein survivors in Washington DC in February.Photograph: Alex Wroblewski/AFP/Getty ImagesBut instead of helping her pursue her career, the lawmakers said in their letter, Epstein pressured her to take sex education and massage courses, and “employed” her while he was sexually abusing her.“By all appearances, Epstein was trafficking this young woman across state and international lines by mid-2014,” the Democrats’ letter said. Jane Doe, they said, was sent to Europe, Canada, and multiple destinations in the US. The Democrats’ letter further alleges that the files indicate that Epstein “used his relationship with Leon Botstein to convince Jane Doe that she could have a successful musical career after modeling”.In May 2014, Epstein sent Jane Doe to meet Botstein, ostensibly for him to assess her musical talents. The Democratic lawmakers say they have reviewed one “startling” email – which had been redacted by the Department of Justice – that they said was sent from Botstein’s then Bard account, president@bard.edu.It reads: “Is [Jane Doe] for me, or are you keeping her for yourself.”The lawmakers wrote: “The evidence meets the federal standard for opening a criminal investigation, yet [the] DoJ and FBI apparently had it for at least 18 months without investigating Botstein. We are demanding they investigate Botstein and other potential co-conspirators.”In a statement, Botstein denied the Democrats’ allegations, including that he had sent the email in question.“The allegations in this letter are untrue, including an email that I did not author or send,” he said.The lawmakers said they have also heard from more than a dozen whistleblowers who have provided the committee with allegations of “decades of unpunished sexual misconduct at Bard”. In his statement, the Bard board of trustees chairman said: “When a formal complaint alleging sexual harassment or assault is filed, an independent external investigator conducts the review and submits a report to an impartial hearing chair. The college president has not had unilateral decision-making authority over title IX investigations or adjudications since the 2015-16 school year.”The Guardian reported in April, before Botstein’s resignation, that the then president told staff there was no way he could have known that Epstein – who was a convicted sex offender during their interactions – was actually “reprehensible”. At the time, he predicted he would be cleared of any hint of impropriety.The Guardian asked Bard at that time about the May 2014 email, which appeared in the redacted Epstein files as an email that Epstein appeared to have forwarded to himself, and was originally sent by an email address that only contained the name “President”. A spokesperson for Bard College told the Guardian at the time that the May 2014 message “has absolutely nothing to do with Bard College or President Botstein”.Botstein announced he was stepping down as president in May, after an independent review ofhis contacts with Jeffrey Epsteinfound the college president’s frequent interactions with Epstein “could have alerted” him to the possibility that he and Bard would be facilitating Epstein’s abuse of women.An investigation by the WilmerHale law firm, which had been commissioned by Bard’s board of trustees earlier this year to review Botstein’s interactions with Epstein, found the Bard president – who had previously claimed he was not friends with Epstein – made about 25 visits to Epstein’s townhouse, a two-day visit to Epstein’s Little St James Island, and that there were two visits by Epstein to Bard. These visits, WilmerHale reported, included “multiple women” who have since been identified as victims of Epstein.Botstein has not been charged with wrongdoing in connection with his relationship with the accused sex trafficker. They were in contact from 2012 to 2019.The Times Unionfirst reportedRaskin’s letter.Explore more on these topicsJeffrey EpsteinUS politicsUS universitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Skepticism mires Trump’s Iowa steel plant project: ‘Promises are not the same as jobs’ | Steel industry | The Guardian
description: The project has sparked doubts over whether the plant will be built and delivered as promised, given Trump’s record
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: The project has sparked doubts over whether the plant will be built and delivered as promised, given Trump’s record
Content: Rewant Ruia, chairman of Mesabi Metallics, Ravi Ruia, board member of Mesabi Metallics and director of Essar Capital, and US secretary of energy, Chris Wright, listen as Donald Trump delivers remarks at the White House on 28 September 2026.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRewant Ruia, chairman of Mesabi Metallics, Ravi Ruia, board member of Mesabi Metallics and director of Essar Capital, and US secretary of energy, Chris Wright, listen as Donald Trump delivers remarks at the White House on 28 September 2026.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesSteel industrySkepticism mires Trump’s Iowa steel plant project: ‘Promises are not the same as jobs’The project has sparked doubts over whether the plant will be built and delivered as promised, given Trump’s recordMichael SainatoWed 7 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumphas long sought to portray himself as a man of steel, from the White HousephotoshoppingTrump to look like Superman, to enacting tariffs on steel and approving the sale of US Steel to Japan’s Nippon Steel with a”golden” sharegiven to the US government.Most recently, theTrump administrationannounced plans to construct the largest steel plant in the US, a $15bn plant in Lee county, Iowa, to be built by India-based Mesabi Metallics.But the project and claims surrounding it have incited skepticism over whether the plant will be built and delivered as promised, given Trump’s record and the financial history of Mesabi Metallics’ parent company, Essar Global.The plant had originally been scheduled to be built in Minnesota, a state that usually votes for Democrats. The shift to Iowa – whereRepublicans are strugglingin the midterms – has also attracted attention.Doug May, who worked for 43 years as a steelworker at a mill in Granite City, Illinois, characterized the announcement as “political pandering” given the timing and how tariffs arehurtingIowa farmers.“He pulled the same thing in 2018, just before an election, when he announced that $10bn Foxconn project,” May said.That project, in swing state Wisconsin, failed to produce the jobs Trump and Foxconn had promised.May argued Trump was using the steel industry as a campaign strategy, while ignoring the work the United Steel Workers have done to push to save the industry, includingfilingmore than 150 trade cases over the past decades to combat unfair trade practices that harm US workers.More than 40 domestic steel producersin the US filed for bankruptcy in the late 1990s.“We, the steel workers in Granite City, served as the best foot soldiers lobbying Congress, holding rallies and campaigns, to raise awareness to the cheating of foreign steelmakers and the need for stronger trade enforcement during that era,” added May. “Arguably, we played a very important role in saving domestic steel.”Essar Global firstproposedbuilding a steel plant with a $1.65bn investment in the Mesabi iron range in north-east Minnesota when they purchased Minnesota Steel in 2007.By 2016, Essar Steel Minnesotahad filedfor bankruptcy, following construction delays and financing issues at its Nashwauk, Minnesota, project, where its iron ore mine, which is supposed to fuel the Iowa steel plant, is located.In efforts to get rid of its debt, Essar Globalsold offassets, including the completion of a sale of Essar Oil for $12.9bn to a Russia-controlled energy company.Mesabi Metallics briefly changed ownership to Virginia billionaire Thomas Clarke, before he lost control of the company in 2018, with Essar Globalregaining control, but then losing its mining leases in 2021 when the state of Minnesotarevoked themafter a missed deadline.“This plant that has been 20 years in the making,” said Mark Dayton, former governor of Minnesota whodealtwith Mesabi Metallics in the state through their bankruptcy proceedings.“I had, a decade ago, a very bad experience with Essar Steel because they started this plant, raised lots of expectations and hopes up north, and then went into default and went into bankruptcy and the like,” he said.Dayton said it did look like the plant was “actually proceeding, which is great if they’re going to actually complete building this plant”.But he added: “I’m skeptical of the announcement inIowathis close to the election. That’s going to require $15bn of investment. I’d like to see that money on the table from Essar before they start to bring a shovel.”Some, including May, see echoes of Trump’sFoxconn announcementin June 2018. Ahead of the 2018 midterm elections, Trump described plans by the Taiwanese electronics contract manufacturer to open a gargantuan site outside Milwaukee as “the Eighth Wonder of the World” andsaid the plant“will provide jobs for much more than 13,000 Wisconsin workers”.Trump’s promises came as his approval ratings with the public were low, with Democratspoisedto take advantage and regain control of the House.The site currently hasabout 1,100 employeesand became an albatross around the necks of its backers as Foxconn’s ambitious plans failed to materialise.This time around, Trump’sapproval ratings are even lowerthan they were in 2018 and Democrats areexpectedto regain control of the House and possibly the Senate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump hasclaimed“they’ve already started building” the plant, though a local NBC news affiliate in Iowa reviewed county records and disputed this claim.“The review found no major property purchases tied to the project this year. County officials say they don’t have details from the company about its plans. No permits have come before supervisors,” TV6 Investigatesreported.A site location has not been disclosed by elected officials or Mesabi Metallics, with steel productionaimedto begin in 2030. Mesabi Metallics did not respond to multiple requests for comment.In Iowa, the state’s Sierra Club chaptercriticizedthe special state legislature session called for by the Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, to expand government subsidies the state can provide to Mesabi Metallics for the project. The state government is experiencingbudget shortfalls, with more than $1bn in deficits the past two years.“Any time we step up incentive programs above and beyond what we’re giving, our revenues are going to be downgraded. And I understand there’s going to be jobs and economic activity around this, but the state is hurting financially,” said Pam Mackey Taylor, director of the Iowa chapter of the Sierra Club. “Do we need to really double the incentives that other large projects get to support this steel project?”The Iowa governor’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment.In a special session, the Iowa legislatureapproved$1.36bn in tax incentives over 10 years to Mesabi Metallics. The steel plant isprojectedto create 1,750 permanent jobs and support up to 6,000 construction jobs.The White House did not comment directly on the steel plant’s move to Iowa or on White House senior communications strategist Jason Miller’spastwork as a registered foreign lobbyist for Mesabi Metallics.Mesabi Metallicspaidat least $240,000 SHW Partners, a government relations firm led by Miller, according to lobbyist disclosure records. The government of India also paid his firm $150,000 per month for “strategic counsel, tactical planning and government relations assistance on policy matters before the US government”, with the contract beginning in April 2025.Miller said the contract with India stopped in June 2026 and claimed the lobbying for Mesabi Metallics was domestic, not foreign, and ended in July 2026.“Taking a lobbyist who’s on the payroll of a foreign government and companies with huge government contracts and putting him inside the White House will create a three-headed beast of divided loyalties,” said Jon Golinger, democracy advocate at Public Citizen, in astatementon Miller’s appointment to a White House role.In response to Miller’s lobbying work and criticisms of it, Miller said: “Public Citizen is a bunch of America-hating fake news soy boy losers who prefer new investments go to China and not the US, and respectfully, they can get rekt. Not only did I deregister from Mesabi Metallics months ago, I took the additional step of recusing myself from having anything to do with their announcement at the White House.”A White House spokesperson, Kush Desai, said in an email: “No president has done more to revive American steelmaking than President Trump, whose 50 percent Section 232 tariffs on steel is driving record investments into this key sector. Those tariffs, along with the Administration’s other pro-growth and pro-investment policies, are not going away anytime soon.”Explore more on these topicsSteel industryDonald TrumpIowaUS midterm elections 2026US politicsMinnesotafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: McDonald’s sued for allegedly using AI tool to determine pricing for franchises | McDonald's | The Guardian
description: Suit says AI tool allows independently owned franchises to exchange nonpublic price and sales information
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Suit says AI tool allows independently owned franchises to exchange nonpublic price and sales information
Content: According to the company, the average price of a McDonald’s menu item increased about 40% between 2019 and 2024.Photograph: Damian Dovarganes/APView image in fullscreenAccording to the company, the average price of a McDonald’s menu item increased about 40% between 2019 and 2024.Photograph: Damian Dovarganes/APMcDonald'sMcDonald’s sued for allegedly using AI tool to determine pricing for franchisesSuit says AI tool allows independently owned franchises to exchange nonpublic price and sales informationGaya GuptaWed 7 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 07.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMcDonald’s is facing a lawsuit in federal court over its alleged use of anAItool to determine pricing across independent franchises, which prosecutors say violates antitrust laws and has unfairly inflated menu prices for Americans.The vast majority ofMcDonald’sUS stores are independently owned and are said to individually decide on prices under company policy. Antitrust laws require businesses to set prices independently from their competitors, as coordinating prices can stifle market competition and push up costs for consumers.The lawsuit, filed on 2 October in a federal Chicago courtroom, alleges that McDonald’s AI tool is illegal because it amounts to independent franchise locationsexchanging nonpublic price and sales data.Slew of lawsuits over disability access frustrates US cafe and shop ownersRead more“This case is about McDonald’s bringing ‘optimization’ to America’s largest fast food chain,” the complaint says. “McDonald’s has built and for years deployed its own information-sharing pricing platform, which draws on data from its millions of daily transactions to set menu prices across thousands of US restaurants. The result is algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin.”In response to the lawsuit, a spokesperson for the McDonald’s corporation said that the “complaint is filled with inaccuracies and we will vigorously defend against this lawsuit”.“AI does not set menu prices at McDonald’s restaurants – McDonald’s franchisees do,” it said. “Optional tools are available to franchisees to help them make the best decisions for their businesses and customers, but these tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way.”A recent Reutersinvestigationreported that some McDonald’s franchise owners have been pressured by the company to use the AI pricing tools and record their deviations from the tool’s recommendations. McDonald’s contested that characterization, calling the Reuters reporting “speculative and uninformed”.The litigation, which has been proposed as a nationwide class-action lawsuit, was first brought forward by an Illinois man named Michael Thomas. Thomas, a McDonald’s regular who is described as “price conscious”, found that the cost of his usual order – a Quarter Pounder with cheese, fries and a Coke – varied even within his neighborhood in DeKalb, Illinois. The attorney listed as representing Thomas did not immediately reply to a request for comment.Thomas does not appear to be alone in his experience. At a McDonald’s in Manhattan’s financial district, Chukwama Okeke, 43, was finishing a mango-pineapple smoothie that he bought as part of a value meal that cost about $15 – something he only gets about once a month.Okeke said that when he orders the same meal at a McDonald’s in Brooklyn’s Crown Heights neighborhood, he ends up paying closer to $9.“McDonald’s in Manhattan is much more expensive than those in Brooklyn,” he said. “I’ve notice in some areas if they have a lot of like foot traffic, the prices tend to get higher.”Beatriz Milander, 27, who ordered a snack wrap, a small fries and an iced coffee for $11.51, hadn’t noticed a huge difference between what she pays in the financial district and what she pays in her Bronx neighborhood, but said prices overall had inched up.“In the last few months, I’ve seen them do more deals or like lower-priced things,” she said. “But it definitely was pricing up for a little bit there.”Experts say that companies using AI to set or alter pricing could exacerbate the country’s affordability crisis and make it harder for Americans to bear everyday costs. So far this year, at least 90 pieces of legislation have been filed across the country to push back against algorithmic price-fixing, according to Lindsay Owens, the head of the left-leaning thinktank Groundwork Collaborative, who recently authored abookon the topic.McDonald’s acquired an AI company, Dynamic Yield, in 2019, but has firmly denied using AI in setting menu prices. In a statement released on 1 October, the day before the lawsuit was filed, the chain denied using dynamic pricing and described its pricing tool as simply providing information that franchises are free to decide whether to adopt.The fast-food chain has been scrutinized over recent years for its elevated prices, and went viral in 2023 over an $18 Big Mac meal at a Connecticut McDonald’s. The franchise’s owner filed a lawsuit alleging that it was the AI pricing tool that suggested the $18 price to the franchise.According to a fact sheet the chain published in 2024, the average price of a McDonald’s menu item increased about 40% between 2019 and 2024.Explore more on these topicsMcDonald'sAI (artificial intelligence)Food & drink industryLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Millionaire tax no more? Rightwing groups lead effort to repeal Washington state law | Washington state | The Guardian
description: An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight?
Content: The millionaire tax is signed into law by Governor Bob Ferguson.Photograph: Office of Governor Bob FergusonView image in fullscreenThe millionaire tax is signed into law by Governor Bob Ferguson.Photograph: Office of Governor Bob FergusonWashington stateMillionaire tax no more? Rightwing groups lead effort to repeal Washington state lawAn initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight?Adam Willems in SeattleWed 7 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVoters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “millionaire tax” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that wassignedinto law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it.Aninitiativeon November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires. Acoalitionof advocacy groups and unions opposing the initiative say taxing the state’s 20,000 highest-earning households could raise approximately $3.5bn in necessary annual revenue to fund core priorities like education and healthcare, and expand tax credits and sales tax exemptions.Facingdwindlingfederal funds under the Trump administration yet home to substantial tech-industry wealth, including prominent billionaires such as Bill Gates, Steve Ballmer and,until recently, Jeff Bezos, Washington has joined other states and municipalities by turning to its wealthiest earners as a source of revenue. Massachusetts, Maine and New York already impose a unique tax rate on millionaires, and Hawaiipasseda similar measure in May.California, whose resident billionaires possess acollective net worthhovering above $2tn, will seevotersdecide on a proposed one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth. The measure is opposed by most billionaires as well as Gavin Newsom, the governor; some progressive groups also question the long-term benefits of the one-off tax.Washington’s governor, Bob Ferguson, hassaidhe would veto any effort to expand the millionaire tax to encompass lower-earning households. And, after decades of voter-rejected efforts to reform the state’s tax structure, which has historically lacked an income tax and instead levied sales taxes, property taxes and fees, Washingtonians in recent years have approved new progressive revenue streams, including a capital gains tax. Advocates claim that the millionaire tax is part of a clear mandate to better align the state’s largely regressive tax code with its progressive values.The statewide fight over an income tax really began in the 1930s, according to the Washington state senate majority leader, Jamie Pedersen, an architect of the millionaire tax. Nearly 100 years ago, the state’s supreme court ruled that income taxes constituted a property tax, hamstringing efforts to diversify beyond flat-rate excises. By 2002, a state commission led by Bill Gates Srconcludedthat Washington’s tax code was uniquely regressive, and called for a state-level income tax. But, in 2010, voters stillvoted by wide margins againsta proposed tax for those earning above $200,000; Steve Ballmer, Microsoft’s then CEO, was theleading contributorto the campaign opposing the tax, and the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, ranked fourth.A reliance on sales, property and other taxes leaves the state with “the second-worst tax code in the nation when it comes to who actually pays as a share of their income”, said Emily Vyhnanek of theWashington State Budget and Policy Center, a non-partisan research group. Those in the lowest-earning quintile spend up to 13.8% of their annual income on state taxes, while those in the top 1% currently spend about 4%, they said.In 2021, lawmakers passed a 7% tax on capital gains above $250,000, which survived a constitutional challenge and aconservative-led ballot initiativeaiming to overturn it in 2024. The initiative’s resounding defeat was “some indication that voters were willing to vote for something that the opponents labeled as an income tax”, Pedersen said. By 2025, facing a nearly $15bn shortfall over the ensuing four years, Democratic lawmakers debated new ways to tackle the state’s structural budget problem, and landed on the high earners’ income tax.Lawmakers had “99.9% certainty” that conservative groups would challenge the tax through a ballot initiative, Pedersen said.Brian Heywood, a conservative hedge fund executive and the founder ofLet’s Go Washington, a political action committee, has helped spearhead and fund initiative 645, the ballot initiative to overturn the millionaire tax. Heywood and his business moved from California to Washington state in 2010, in part drawn by the state’s lack of capital gains and income taxes. Voicing concerns about a slippery slope, Heywood said the new income tax and ensuing capital flight risked compromising Washington’s “golden goose” economy, which features Microsoft, Amazon, Boeing and others.“I can’t tell you how many people have left the state,” he said. “My business partner moved to Arizona. I probably know 50 people that are deca- or centi-millionaires that have left the state.”Academic research suggests about 2% of residents affected by the millionaire tax might leave Washington, according to Rian Watt of the Seattle-based thinktank Economic Opportunity Institute.View image in fullscreenBrian Heywood, who has opposed the millionaire tax and wants it repealed.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSince Let’s Go Washington’s founding in 2022, Heywood has spent at least $11m of his own money on 20 proposals,includinga campaign to repeal Washington’s carbon market. More than 60% of voters rejected that effort in 2024, and the campaign opposing Heywood was partially funded by Gates and Ballmer.In September, several business owners in Washington confronted public outcry and boycotts after public disclosure forms revealed they had donated to Let’s Go Washington; in both cases, business ownersclaimedthey solelysupportedLet’s Go Washington’s efforts to overturn the millionaire tax, and not its other initiatives on the 2026 ballot. Let’s Go Washington is behind two other proposals, including a campaign to ban trans girls from participating in girls’ sports at school.Opponents haveexpressed alarmat the initiative and have dubbed it “the most extreme proposal of its kind”, as it would require girls to undergo “verification of biological sex” during sports physicals, potentially through genital exams.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHeywood claimed Democratic lawmakers, and the state’selection-finance watchdog, have strategically tried to isolate him and Let’s Go Washington, and “try to make me toxic, somehow” in the eyes of donors.Aseparate campaignbacking the millionaire tax repeal was launched in July, and selected former Republican congresswoman Jaime Herrera Beutler as its spokesperson. That campaign did not return the Guardian’s request for comment.Pedersen suggested that advocates interested in overturning the millionaire tax may “have figured out Brian Heywood” and may be “trying to distance themselves from his pretty toxic brand”.The state supreme court is also slated to hear a legal challenge to the tax early next year, which will test the validity of the new income tax against state-constitutional and legal precedent.Recent polling suggests that the initiative is likely to fail. In a survey of Washington residents, research firm DHM found 57% of respondents opposed repealing the tax. Kara Krnacik, who helped lead the survey, said Washington residents may be growing more open to an income tax below the million-dollar threshold: 41% of respondents said they were in favor of an income tax that might eventually extend to those making $100,000 or more, up from 36% in November 2025.But if the tax is overturned, lawmakers face a “very stark reality”, Pedersen said, and may have to find revenue through “inferior alternatives” such as hiking the sales tax rate, or enacting a statewide payroll tax. Meanwhile, if the tax survives, Pedersen said lawmakers may begin to scrap or reform other regressive taxes in Washington, including its business taxes.“I think it’s really significant that you do not see almost any major business that is aligning itself with the initiative 645 folks,” Pedersen said.Public disclosure recordssuggestthe initiative’s opponents have outspent its supporters by more than 50%; and major labor unions in the state have contributed more than $6m to the campaign defending the tax.In addition to new legal challenges, Heywood said he had begun to consider ways to circumscribe how unions receive and disburse funds in the state.Explore more on these topicsWashington stateWest CoastUS economyEconomicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Canada’s Weston family buys Boots for $8.9bn | Boots | The Guardian
description: Former Selfridges owners buy UK high street institution from long-term backer Stefano Pessina
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Former Selfridges owners buy UK high street institution from long-term backer Stefano Pessina
Content: Wittington Investments, the holding company of the Weston family that controls the Loblaws grocery chain and Drugmart pharmacies in Canada, will own Boots’ UK and Irish retail operations and opticians chain.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWittington Investments, the holding company of the Weston family that controls the Loblaws grocery chain and Drugmart pharmacies in Canada, will own Boots’ UK and Irish retail operations and opticians chain.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Getty ImagesBootsCanada’s Weston family buys Boots for $8.9bnFormer Selfridges owners buy UK high street institution from long-term backer Stefano PessinaSarah ButlerWed 7 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Canadian family that once owned Selfridges department store has bought the UK pharmacy and beauty retailerBootsfor $8.9bn (£6.74bn).Wittington Investments, the holding company of the Weston family that controls the Loblaws grocery chain and Shoppers Drug Mart pharmacy outlets in Canada, will own Boots’ UK and Irish retail operations and opticians chain, the No7 beauty brand and a franchise arm in Thailand.The acquisition of the Nottingham-headquartered chain, which has 1,800 stores across the UK and employs 50,000 people, is also being backed by the investment firm Fairfax, which owns The Sporting Life Group and Sleep Country, Canada’s largest mattress retailer, which owns Simba Sleep in the UK.Galen Weston, the chair of Wittington, who is likely to become chair of Boots, said: “Boots is one of Britain’s most enduring businesses, with a rich heritage, a trusted name and a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland.“We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come.”The transaction, which sees the exit of Boots’ long-term backer Stefano Pessina and his latest backer, the financial firm Sycamore Partners, is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027.In 2022, the US pharmacy group Walgreens put Boots up for sale with a suggested price tag of up to £10bn, but it later dropped the plans as potential buyers, including Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, the US private equity investor Apollo Global Management and Asda’s owners TDR Capital,struggled to raise funds. Aplan to float the businessat a valuation of about £7bn was dropped in 2024.“Boots is an iconic brand and a British institution,” said Pessina, whotook Boots privatewith the backing of the investment firm KKR in 2007. He has since kept a stake under different private equity owners and merged and demerged it from Walgreens.“It has been one of the privileges of my and [my wife] Ornella’s life to have been so closely associated with Boots over the last 20 years. We are delighted to be passing on a thriving Boots to strong and reliable owners who understand the value of its great heritage.”Pessina will retain ownership of Boots’ interests in the Farmacias Benavides pharmacy chain in Mexico and the Alliance Healthcare Deutschland, a German drug distributor.The acquisition of Boots marks the return of the Weston family’s Canadian branch to the UK high street, after the family sold off the Selfridges department store chainfor £4bnin 2022.The separate UK branch of the family’s company is known for holding a majority stake in Primark through the parent company Associated British Foods, which is led by family member George Weston.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham pledges extra £210m towards regenerating boarded-up high streetsRead moreRichard Hyman, the veteran retail analyst, said the Weston family were “the most encouraging ownership of Boots for many, many years”.He said: “For years, watching Boots has been a bit like watching corporate pass the parcel. Its ownership has changed with extraordinary frequency and each owner has stripped a bit more out of it.”Hyman said Boots had an opportunity to make more of its vast loyalty scheme and to offer more services through its network of stores across the UK, many of which had seen little modernisation in recent decades.Boots has closed more than 300 outlets in recent years. It is unclear whether its new owners plan to close more shops, but they are likely to take a close look given the rising costs of high street retail, the shift of trade to online, and competition from discounters such as Savers, Lidl and Home Bargains.Hyman said: “Boots needs and deserves owners that will show it a bit of love, and history shows the Westons take a longer view.”Explore more on these topicsBootsRetail industryMergers and acquisitionsPrivate equitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Jon Rahm’s LIV exit set to trigger mass exodus of players from stricken tour | LIV Golf Series | The Guardian
description: Tyrrell Hatton and other big names are likely to follow Jon Rahm in abandoning LIV Golf, which faces a race against time if it is to continue
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Tyrrell Hatton and other big names are likely to follow Jon Rahm in abandoning LIV Golf, which faces a race against time if it is to continue
Content: Jon Rahm became LIV Golf’s highest-profile player when he joined in December 2023.Photograph: Michael Miller/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJon Rahm became LIV Golf’s highest-profile player when he joined in December 2023.Photograph: Michael Miller/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesLIV Golf SeriesJon Rahm’s LIV exit set to trigger mass exodus of players from stricken tourTyrrell Hatton and other big names likely to followTour filed for bankruptcy after Saudi funding withdrawnEwan MurrayWed 7 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConfirmation that Jon Rahm will play no part in LIVGolfin its post-Saudi Arabian form is likely to be only the start of a mass exodus from the breakaway circuit.A bankruptcy hearing on Wednesday heard Rahm’s lawyer say “unacceptable” terms proposed by LIV 2.0 mean the Spaniard will shortly walk away from a tour which has lingering hopes of continuing as a going concern. Rahm’s departure from LIV, which he joined in 2023, was inevitable, but still a significant blow and moment in time given his status in his sport.Phil Mickelson’s reps say he sought treatment for family trauma and addictionRead more“Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0,” the two-time major winner’s attorney, John Beck, said.The expectation from those with knowledge of the LIV situation is that a batch of other players including Tyrrell Hatton, Tom McKibbin, Cameron Smith, Joaquin Niemann and Adrian Meronk will also flee the scene when legalities permit. The initial habitat for those players, from the start of next season, is likely to be the DP World Tour. LIV faces a race against time to earn commitment from players of even average quality in its mission to continue with 75-man events into 2027.Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) abruptly confirmed in April it willend funding of LIV at the end of 2026. It is estimated the PIF spent more than $5bn (£3.8bn) in the project, which was intended to challenge golf’s established tours. LIVentered Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedingsin the US last month, which was always likely to facilitate the departure of big names such as Rahm. They had signed for LIV on multi-year, multi-million dollar contracts which had become unaffordable.Rahm’s representatives are “in advanced discussions for a consensual separation agreement” with LIV. Documents listing creditors had previously shown that Rahm had an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.7m).View image in fullscreenJon Rahm (left) and Sergio García both participated in the LIV Golf tour.Photograph: Erik S Lesser/EPAThe status of Bryson DeChambeau, LIV’s remaining marquee name, is unclear. DeChambeau is known to have little appetite to return to the PGA Tour in the US, with that sentiment thought to be mutual. DeChambeau’s preference has always been an elongated version of LIV but that competitive model remains open to much question.LIV Golf, along with BC Partners Credit, has been outwardly bullish about its future. “Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf’s emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season,” said Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, in a statement. An immediate winner from this mess is likely to be the DP World Tour. Golfers are expected to gravitate towards that circuit for 2027 as a means to potentially play their way back on to the PGA Tour.LIV has already cut ties with all but a skeleton staff.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLIV entered into a formal restructuring support agreement with BC Partners Credit on Tuesday. Full detail of that, including potentially $300m (£227m) financing, remains unclear. Scott O’Neil, LIV’s chief executive, said: “We believe deeply in the future of this league and in the opportunity to build something distinctive alongside our players. We’re delivering on our major milestones and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers.”Rahm withdrew from this week’s Spanish Open in Madrid in order to remain at home as his wife, Kelley, is expecting their fourth child. He previouslysettled a dispute with the DP World, formerly European, Tour which could have impacted his future Ryder Cup involvement.Explore more on these topicsLIV Golf SeriesGolfSaudi Arabia and sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mystery | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: Jorge Messi wanted his country to fall in love with his son. That ambition was fulfilled during a brilliant international career that ended this week
Author: Marcela Mora y Araujo
Headline: Jorge Messi wanted his country to fall in love with his son. That ambition was fulfilled during a brilliant international career that ended this week
Content: Lionel Messi and his Argentina teammates reflect on an emotional night against Benin.Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/ReutersView image in fullscreenLionel Messi and his Argentina teammates reflect on an emotional night against Benin.Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/ReutersLionel MessiLionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mysteryJorge Messi wanted his country to fall in love with his son. That ambition was fulfilled during a brilliant international career that ended this weekMarcela Mora y AraujoWed 7 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“What Argentina is doing in this World Cup is of a sacred order,” Brazilian writer Milly Lacombe posted at the height of the tide of anti-Argentinian sentiment during this year’s tournament. She was exploring the contradiction she felt around her support of Lionel Messi: “a player who is a God and a man who shakes Trump’s hand”.Lacombe highlighted the importance of acknowledging the complexities around Messi and the Argentinian team. How is it possible that Messi was not speaking out against the racist incidentswe all saw around the Argentina team, she asked. “That’s why it hurts so much to see someone with Messi’s power choosing to make himself small,” she wrote.Much was made of Messi’s silence at the time. Then again, much has been made of his visible discomfort with words throughout his epic career. Journalist John Carlin once said that having interviewed Messi twice, he would decline a third opportunity, such was the challenge of getting the little giant to say anything of consequence. In 2010, Juan Sebastián Verón said he had never seen Messi as nervous as when he had to address his teammates for the first time asArgentinacaptain. In terms of public speaking, perhaps Messi’s most famous outburst was at the 2022 World Cup when he told a Dutch player to “go away”.View image in fullscreenA giant number 10 shirt was displayed on the pitch before Messi’s farewell apperance.Photograph: Rodrigo Abd/APDespite this reticence, Messi has always meant something, even when he doesn’t speak. Messi and Argentina were treated as darlings when they won the World Cup in 2022. By the time the 2026 final ended in defeat to Spain, they had become villains.“That’s why it’s important to understand that when Messi, in the middle of a game that was lost, looks at the sky, and then after that he turns the game around and smashed it, there is something very mysterious there. Right? That we can’t explain. That we just feel,” Lacombe said after Argentina’s semi-final victory over England this summer. “I started supporting England but by the end of the match I was weeping, surrendered to the commitment, the passion, the love that I saw the Argentina team pour on to the pitch. It’s only in that moment of intense passion that we reach the sacred.”Not everyone surrendered to the sacred in the same way. The final against Spain lacked sublime power and opened the floodgates of vitriol from all corners of the globe. Argentinian fans were offended, hurt, defensive and aware they may have just seen Messi’s last appearance in an Argentina shirt. When he confirmed he would end his international career – his final appearance for Argentinacame against Benin on Tuesday– a wave of grief and gratitude swept the nation.View image in fullscreenAn 18 yr old Lionel Messi grapples with Hungary’s Vilmos Vanczák and is sent off after 44 seconds on his Argentina debut.Photograph: Michael Mayhew/Getty Images/AllstarMessi grew up in Barcelona’s youth system, and he was eligible to play for both Spain and Argentina. His debut for Argentina – in a youth match against Paraguay – set up a rush to ensure he pledged his allegiance to the country of his birth, before Spain could tempt him. He was already one of the Barcelona’s academy most promising stars, but he was little known in Argentina. His father, Jorge, wanted nothing more than for his son to represent Argentina, and sent videos to then-manager Marcelo Bielsa hoping to expedite the process. For years, Jorge endured an uphill struggle to consolidate the ties between Lionel and Argentina. Messi’s prowess, seemingly unstoppable in a well-oiled Barcelona system, did not come through at national level. For a long time, Jorge would ask his compatriots the same question. How can we get Argentina to love my son?Now, as we start to write Messi’s football obituary, some of the most grievous incidents against him are resurfacing. There was the time when a panel of pundits stood in a minute’s silence in protest against Messi’s performances for his country. He was criticised for not singing the national anthem. We learned that before Argentina matches he suffered bouts of vomiting and diarrhoea. Diego Maradona mocked him, saying he was no leader (although he would later make Messi Argentina’s captain). And when the campaign to win over the nation stepped up and he gave interviews, his discourse was shockingly basic and he gave little away.But Messi never gave up. He missed penalties, wept, and stood to take them again. “What characterized Messi in the national team is that he lost. He lost a lot. He’s constituted in defeat” Argentinian journalist Alejandro Wall says.View image in fullscreenAdoring fans cheer for Messi before the match against Benin.Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/ReutersBut the vitriol more often came from the press than the people. When hequit the national team in 2016, a spontaneous show of love and desire swept the nation, and he reversed his decision. From then on, the Argentinian Football Association’s main priority mirrored that of Jorge Messi: finding a coach who could adapt the entire system to Lionel. It wasn’t easy.Perhaps it was only after Maradona’s death in 2020 that the new Messi started to emerge. He walked taller, more confident and comfortable in his role as leader. In 2021, Argentina won the Copa América, and snippets of Messi’s pep talks to his teammates filtered out. He made simple statements in his unmistakable Rosario accent, aspiring the ‘s’ and not pronouncing most final consonants. His – and Argentina’s – achievements since then speak for themselves.Tuesday’s farewell at the Monumental Stadium – much like that first youth game against Paraguay – had a rushed, improvised air. The Argentinian FA struggled to secure opponents, not wanting to share box office with another footballing power. Benin were mocked by some as unworthy, and even Lionel Scaloni made reference to a desire to face bigger opponents than Bolivia and Burkina Faso, the other teams Argentina played this window. Burkina Faso ended up sending an Under-23 side who arrived a few hours before the match, and the stadium was not filled to capacity. Ticket prices were extortionate, and diehard fans refused to fall for what they called “a scam”.View image in fullscreenAn electric atmosphere at Estadio Monumental.Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/ReutersBut against Benin they turned up in numbers. Earlier, Messi had picked up an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires, in a small and shabby ceremony in a back office of the Argentinian FA. Delicately produced homages to No 10 were aired. Social media posts full of hyperbolic emotion appeared. “Like Scheherazade, he mocked destiny match by match, to gift the Argentina people another day of his magic. The thousand and one nights of Lionel Messi with the light blue and white come to their end,” read one post. “Whoah, hold it! It’s 9am. I can’t start weeping yet” came a swift reply.To paraphrase Wayne Rooney, the entertainment around the match was crap. There was a drawn out homage by Soledad Pastorutti, who sang the same number she had once performed with Maradona. A veteran of the Falklands/Malvinas War sang the national anthem, and thenclad himself in the same flagthat fell on the pitch in Atlanta. The terraces chanted against AFA president Chiqui Tapia in a beautiful chorus, which went some way to atoning for the drone show at the end, with adverts for an insurance company glittering in the sky.But football is about redemption, and the night was redeemed. Benin actually put up a fight, bookended by the team’s captain gifting Messi a statue of a Dahomey Agojie, the group of women who fought against French occupation. Messi set up three of his team’s three goals and took a penalty. He didn’t miss.View image in fullscreenLionel Messi salutes his adoring fans after his final match for Argentina.Photograph: Roberto Tuero/ZUMA/ShutterstockThe cameras zoomed in on weeping faces but the sounds from the concrete terraces were decisively celebratory, relentless, trembling. It was football through and through. And Messi loved it. You could tell. He picked up the microphone and launched into a speech so articulate and confident that it merits a dissertation studying its every word. He addressed conspiracy theories surrounding the World Cup final: “Nothing odd happened. The match against England wore us out at an emotional level”. He warned of hard times to come but said team unity is the way through.“We had the dream of fulfilling our dream,” he said, adding: “I don’t know, I’m talking more than ever. I don’t want to leave here. I love you”. And Argentina loves him back.As Lacombe said, when Messi looks at the sky, then turns a situation around and smashes it, there is mystery. There is something sacred.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiArgentina (Football)Argentina (World news)US sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Teen brilliance to Pochettino’s haters: Winners and losers from the USMNT’s perfect window | USA | The Guardian
description: The United States winning four of four benefits many that were involved, and may hurt those who were left behind
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: The United States winning four of four benefits many that were involved, and may hurt those who were left behind
Content: The US scored 12 goals in four games during this international window.Photograph: Alejandro Salazar/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe US scored 12 goals in four games during this international window.Photograph: Alejandro Salazar/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockUSATeen brilliance to Pochettino’s haters: Winners and losers from the USMNT’s perfect windowThe United States winning four of four benefits many that were involved, and may hurt those who were left behindPablo Iglesias MaurerandJeff RueterWed 7 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWinnersCavan SullivanSo much of the discourse surrounding Sullivan’s possible debut in the lead-up to this window was centered around tempering expectations. The 17-year-old’s play, though – particularly against Mexico – made it almost impossible not to fall back into old habits and anoint him as the next big thing.There’s plenty of data to unpack about Sullivan’s movement, combination play and even his defensive upside across this window but even the casual observer would be taken by his energy. Sullivan was eager – at times almost frenetic – when running at defenders and he “tries shit”, as Bruce Arena once said of Clint Dempsey. That’s an ideal palate cleanser for US fans after this summer’s World Cup crashout. I’m not going to drive the hype train anytime soon, but I’m considering buying a ticket.PIMSebastian BerhalterThe USMNT’s kids are thriving, and ‘they have a bit of swag to them’Read moreOften among the first men off the bench during the World Cup, Berhalter still looks effective in that role while faring especially well in a start against Mexico. His ability to break lines with his distribution is among the pool’s best, but the real boon is his dead-ball service. His delivery from indirect restarts and corner kicks is dependable and precise, a welcome reprieve after years of watchingChristian Pulisicsend his corners right at the first defender.JRDiego KochenWhile Matt Freese and Chris Brady floundered, Kochen calmed the game down in his debut before a composed shift in the 3-0 win over Mexico. His command of his area is already arguably the pool’s best, while his defenders spoke of inherently trusting him in possession thanks to his upbringing at Barcelona. Long touted as a goalkeeper of the future, Kochen has left many wondering whether the future is now.JRJulian HallThe scouting report on most US strikers tends to lead with their physical traits, whether it’s their considerable strength or their pace. Hall is a rare exception, with his preternatural spatial awareness and off-ball movement allowing him to get dangerous looks, while his finishing chops continue to improve as he starts for New York. Folarin Balogun still looks like a comfortable first-choice striker, but Hall is a worthy young apprentice.JRLosersView image in fullscreenMilan’s Christian Pulisic was left out of this US camp.Photograph: Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty ImagesChristian PulisicPulisic was certainly the most auspicious absentee from Mauricio Pochettino’s roster this go-around, though there were valid reasons for his exclusion. Some cited Pochettino’s need to evaluate younger players, while others pointed out the fact that Pulisic was only recently recovered from the leg injury that sidelined him at the World Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf only it were that simple. Pochettino was asked straight away to speak about Pulisic’s absence and he declined to do so, telling reporters he wouldn’t offer insight into any individual roster exclusion. A few minutes later, he spoke at length about the exclusion of Balogun, even going as far as to say he’d spoken with him personally – understandable given the drama surrounding the Monaco striker’s aborted transfer to Everton. He also offered some extended thoughts throughout the window about what he’s looking for in terms of senior leadership: players who bleed for the badge, are desperate to be in a US camp and don’t turn down call-ups. You’d be hard-pressed to get an actual mention of Pulisic out of Pochettino, but it’s not terribly hard to read between the lines.PIMPochettino: Manchester City verdicts show fans ‘lived through an era of deception’Read morePochettino non-believersPlenty of people argued against bringing Pochettino back for a second cycle, and they may well be proven right someday. That said, there is little reason to criticize the Argentinian this window. The mix of youngsters and senior players he gathered were a joy to watch and many of tham spoke glowingly about Pochettino, who pulled all the right levers throughout the window. The manager spoke openly about the “contagious” energy of his young charges and the effect it had on him was readily apparent. It would be hard to imagine engineering a stronger start to a World Cup window.PIMSergiño DestDest was woefully ineffective during the World Cup at either providing width in possession up the right – a side the US failed to activate regularly in their five games – or not becoming a liability in defense, something Belgium exploited to great success in the last-16. Pochettino had seemed to find a solution by advancing Dest away from right-back to the wing, but that’s now a prime place for Sullivan to occupy opposite a left-flank playmaker (like Reyna or Malik Tillman) or the expected return of Pulisic. That also overlooks Tim Weah, who captains Marseille and was among the team’s most consistent performers under Gregg Berhalter.Right-back is also looking like it has a new, serious contender with Alex Freeman clearly ready to be the primary option given his versatility in the role. Frankie Westfield, another debutant this window, offers a compelling alternative with his upfield passing. Dest remains ever-present for PSV, and he’s bound to stick around the pool. But now there are real questions about where he fits. Pochettino tried utilizing him as an inverted left winger in the second half against Canada, where he couldn’t change an ugly, foul-filled game. Pochettino regulars like Tyler Adams and Reyna saw regular involvement in each match, but Dest was far more peripheral than usual.JRExplore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsMauricio PochettinoChristian PulisicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Verstappen’s victory in Sepang should serve as a warning to Red Bull’s rivals | Max Verstappen | The Guardian
description: Improvements to the car are paying off as the team look to lay the groundwork for renewed success next season
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Improvements to the car are paying off as the team look to lay the groundwork for renewed success next season
Content: Max Verstappen and the Red Bull team principal, Laurent Mekies, are soaked with energy drink after victory at the Bahrian Grand Prix in Malaysia.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersView image in fullscreenMax Verstappen and the Red Bull team principal, Laurent Mekies, are soaked with energy drink after victory at the Bahrian Grand Prix in Malaysia.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersMax VerstappenAnalysisVerstappen’s victory in Sepang should serve as a warning to Red Bull’s rivalsGiles RichardsImprovements to the car are paying off as the team look to lay the groundwork for renewed success next seasonWed 7 Oct 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 14.43 EDTShareThe importance for Max Verstappen ofemerging triumphant from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysiawas writ large in the Dutchman’s pleasure at finally being able to drive a competitive car. In a ride with which he was comfortable and able to take to a dominant victory for Red Bull, Verstappen was in his element. With it came a sense of what might have been had he not been long out of the championship fight, but also what might be to come next year.The transformation was so marked because for so long this season the car has been a handful – the reason Verstappen’s title hopes faded long ago. That the team have come back to deliver a win in such emphatic fashion was no little achievement.F1 looks amateurish and incompetent after farcical scenes in Sepang | Giles RichardsRead moreIn the opening period of the season, the RB22 was nowhere, deficient in almost every department. It lacked pace, balance, even consistency, and for all his skill Verstappen seemed powerless. He described it as feeling like a passenger in the car at times.The four-time world champion wrestled it to a couple of podiums in the first half of the season but it was a sisyphean task. “At the start of the season, I really had weekends where I would turn the steering wheel and strange things would happen,” he said. Which, a rather understated critique, belies the fact that the last place a driver wants to be is in a car where he is unsure which way it is going to jump.Red Bull,under Laurent Mekies, stuck at it and brought major upgrades to Miami and Austria. Yet the scale of what needed doing across so many facets of the car remained difficult to overcome. Only a month ago Verstappen could only qualify sixth at Monza, admittedly a power track where the relative paucity of their electrical energy deployment was a hindrance. It nonetheless suggested a win was as far away as ever.View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen pulls ahead of Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli in Sepang.Photograph: Vincent Thian/APYet there were indications that each incremental development was bringing a greater understanding of the car and how to coax the best out of it. In Madrid, Verstappen qualified just over a tenth of a second off pole and had real pace in the race, which might have delivered more on a track where overtaking was possible. At the next round in Baku, Red Bull brought their final upgrade, including a development to the floor. In qualifying Verstappen was unlucky with yellow flags to start from eighth but in the race the car was rapid.
