He flew through the field,chasing the winner, Mercedes’ George Russell, to the flag right on his gearbox.The car’s speed on the straights was noted by rivals, not least Mercedes, as Verstappen closed on Russell. Red Bull’s other driver, Isack Hadjar, who had spent three races out with a wrist injury, felt as if he had been given a new ride. “I definitely feel like I jumped in a car that’s way better than when I left it in Budapest,” he said.What followed in Sepang was validation that Red Bull really had got it right. Verstappen took pole and won with a drive that exemplified his car’s improvements. The RB22 was quicker in a straight line than the Mercedes and fast in the medium and high-speed corners, its achilles heel previously.On a track punishing to the tyres, the car was well-balanced, less damaging to the rubber, allowing better energy deployment. Having addressed problems which conflated with one another, the car coalesced into a more coherent whole. Verstappen described the process as having “pushed weaknesses out of the car”. It has taken them 16 meetings but on this form Red Bull are finally up with McLaren, Ferrari and Mercedes.Their progress stands as testament to a team working collectively to tremendous effect. It is an achievement that must be acknowledged alongside building their own engine for the first time and delivering a win; a feat that is recognised across the paddock as perhaps beyond expectations and which was far from guaranteed to be successful as Honda, with more experience, have demonstrated all too clearly this season.View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen driving ahead of Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and his Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar.Photograph: Clive Mason/Getty ImagesThere may have been an element of the win in Sepang being track-specific. The fact the Mercedes upgrades deployed there did not deliver at all was a factor, and they must contend with Russell starting the Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid following an engine change after a late retirement in Malaysia. But the Red Bull is a different car now and how it performs on the streets of Singapore this weekend will be telling.Verstappen will want more wins, but it is instructive how he and the team are viewing these final meetings. They want to end strongly and feed every possible piece of information into next year’s car. Hadjar said: “We have to try all the things, make all the mistakes now and do all the learning to arrive in 2027 ready to roll and start on high.” It is an ambition which will not be lost on their rivals, who know only too well how formidable Red Bull can be if they are quick out of the blocks.Explore more on these topicsMax VerstappenRed BullFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Will Venable: the White Sox manager who used basketball tactics to transform a baseball loser | Chicago White Sox | The Guardian
description: The White Sox were one of the worst teams in MLB history. Now they are just five wins from a place in the World Series
Author: Branson Wright
Headline: The White Sox were one of the worst teams in MLB history. Now they are just five wins from a place in the World Series
Content: Will Venable played basketball at college before embarking on his MLB career.Photograph: Kenneth Richmond/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWill Venable played basketball at college before embarking on his MLB career.Photograph: Kenneth Richmond/Getty ImagesChicago White SoxWill Venable: the White Sox manager who used basketball tactics to transform a baseball loserThe White Sox were one of the worst teams in MLB history. Now they are just five wins from a place in the World SeriesBranson Wrightin ClevelandWed 7 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe postgame celebration songs pounded through the Bluetooth speakers in theChicago White Soxclubhouse on Monday night, minutes after the team’s playoff victory over the Cleveland Guardians at Progressive Field.The White Sox, who lost 121 games two seasons ago, have made a remarkable turnaround. A team who were once so abjectthat they stopped tweeting out their resultsare now just five wins from the World Series. They can seal their progress to the American League Championship Series on Wednesday if they beat the Guardians in Chicago.But amid the clubhouse excitement in Cleveland, one individual remained the same. As usual.“He’s the same guy every single day,” White Sox designated hitter Andrew Benintendi said about the club’s manager, Will Venable. “He’s even keel. … Being Steady Eddie and showing up every day as the same guy.”Venable has been the catalyst for the White Sox this year. His consistent approach and calm demeanor have helped set the tone for a team whose manager once envisioned his future on a basketball court. Long before Venable managed a major-league team, he learned about spacing, timing, preparation, trust and precision away from the baseball diamond.Venable was a shooting guard for Princeton University from 2001 to 2005. He was first team All-Ivy League, led his team to the NCAA Tournament and once scored 21 points against Duke. As a baseball player, Venable was also All-Ivy, which made him only the second Princeton athlete to accomplish that distinction in baseball and basketball.And he eventually took the Princeton concepts of basketball and used them in his baseball career.“For me, my time playing basketball, especially at Princeton, helped me understand the importance of attention to detail,” said Venable, who played eight years in the majors, mostly for the San Diego Padres. “The spacing and timing required [in the Princeton offense] helped me as a baseball player understand the importance of every little detail.”Princeton’s style of basketball taught Venable how to see baseball spatially and collectively. The basic concepts of the Princeton offense rely on constant player movement, precise passing, back-door cuts and read-and-react decisions rather than fixed set plays.The Princeton offense is about players functioning as connected pieces rather than individuals. This postseason, Chicago’s pitching philosophy has been a team effort – sharing the ball as in basketball. Instead of the traditional routine in the playoffs of leaning on a starter to throw six-plus innings followed by relief, the White Sox focus on managing matchups, not innings. It’s not about who starts but who gets the next out.Venable essentially manages his pitching staff the way a basketball coach manages a roster: through combinations, matchups, short bursts and putting players into situations where their particular skills have the greatest advantage.“That’s carried over into managing,” Venable said. “The details matter: where we position guys, the timing of their pre-pitch movements, timing at the plate, all the very fine details and the precision of the game. I learned that through my time in basketball.”And many White Sox players have learned from their manager. They learned from the unconventional style but mostly from the confidence that leaks into his players.That confidence was on display Monday when rookie Braden Montgomery’s opposite-field double in the sixth inning gave the White Sox the lead. In that same inning, Montgomery scored on a single as the White Sox held on for a 4-3 Game 2 victory. The switch-hitting outfielder had a .430 OPS in 103 plate appearances against left-handed pitchers in the regular season, the worst among qualifying hitters from the right side of the plate. And it was just his third hit in 12 postseason plate appearances.“That’s a guy that’s not going to shy away from the moment,” Venable said. “It all culminates into trusting the player and really again putting the nine best guys out there to get the job done.”Montgomery said Venable’s quote is special.“I respect him so much for having that confidence in me, and that means the world to me,” Montgomery said. “I’d run through a wall for Will.”Earlier this season catcher Kyle Teel needed a dose of confidence as he struggled at the plate after he returned to the active roster.“[Will] came up to me and told me not to do too much and stay within myself,” Teel said. “I hit a home run right after he said that. He’s a phenomenal leader. I’m grateful he’s our manager.”Shortstop Colson Montgomery said Venable’s confidence has a strong influence on the team.“When you see your manager walking around with all of the confidence in the world, why would I not walk around like that too,” Montgomery said. “There’s never a doubt wondering if he believes in me.”After losing 102 games in his first season as manager in 2025, Venable earned belief when the White Sox made a chase for a Central Division title this season and finished 84-78. They fell one game short behind the Guardians. Venable says the turnaround is a team and organizational effort.“[General manager Chris Getz] was very clear about what he thought [winning] looked like, and as he outlined his plan and his values, I was very much in line with that,” Venable said. “That’s why I ultimately thought it was a good partnership and that this was going to be a place where we could help the organization move forward. … I was on board with the vision and wanted to do my part to help him.”His part included developing a trust among his players, establishing confidence and bringing the lessons from basketball – precision, trust, interconnectedness and unselfishness – to baseball.“It’s because they’ve done it together,” Venable said. “It’s because they’ve done it for each other, and that’s something that we witness every single day in that clubhouse.”Explore more on these topicsChicago White SoxMLBBaseballUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cristiano Ronaldo: the extraordinary eight points he says Jorge Jesus agreed to make | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: Ronaldo says he ‘validated’ notes for Jorge Jesus to say at a press conference, then walked out when Portugal’s head coach did not deliver them
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Ronaldo says he ‘validated’ notes for Jorge Jesus to say at a press conference, then walked out when Portugal’s head coach did not deliver them
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo wants Jorge Jesus to say: ‘I made a mistake by putting someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game.’Photograph: Patrícia de Melo Moreira/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo wants Jorge Jesus to say: ‘I made a mistake by putting someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game.’Photograph: Patrícia de Melo Moreira/AFP/Getty ImagesCristiano RonaldoCristiano Ronaldo: the extraordinary eight points he says Jorge Jesus agreed to makeRonaldo lists notes ‘validated’ for Portugal coach to sayPelé, Maradona, loyalty and selfies get mentionsGuardian sportWed 7 Oct 2026 04.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo said in a lengthystatement on Tuesdaythat the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, had agreed to make eight points relating to him in a press conference before the team’s game in Denmark last week.Ronaldo said he had approved a document listing the points after a video meeting involving him, Jesus, his adviser Tiago Craveiro and his club Al-Nassr’s sporting director, Simão Coutinho.Cristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promisesRead moreThe meeting, according to Ronaldo, was at “the coach’s request” and he said the document was then “delivered to the coach, as he had requested”.Ronaldo said Jesus’s failure to make the points in the press conference constituted “the second time he had broken his word to me” and that he then “decided to leave the campwithout waiting for any further breach of word”.Ronaldo’s statement included reference to his failure to salute Portugal’s fans after the game in Norway during which he warmed up extensively but was not brought on. He said:“The notes I validated were the following: ‘I think it is important, also because it is the truth, to clarify a few things before talking about Denmark:1.I myself, and no one else, proposed to Cristiano a plan for him this sporting season with the national team. It was a long and very good conversation.2.I know how much he lives and loves the national team and the weight he has in the world, and even more the weight and the positive influence he has had on the national team for 24 consecutive years.3.The plan I proposed to Cristiano was accepted.4. He never questioned my options. He was exemplary, loyal and professional.5. The match in Norway was not part of the plan I drew up for him. However, I felt that he had managed to recover physically from the first match and I warned him that I might have to use him. Cristiano agreed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion6.I made a mistake by putting someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game. If it were today I would not do it.7.To close the subject: I want Cristiano in the national team. In fact I do not want him a little, I want him a lot. Fortunately he also believes in me. He believed at Al-Nassr and he does here as well.8.About not greeting the fans. We have already spoken about that. Someone who has played more than 230 matches for the national team does not receive lessons from me on love for Portugal. It was a moment of frustration that erases nothing. He is the player who gives the most autographs, takes the most selfies, and shows the most affection to the fans. Let us not invent problems where they do not exist. When we are not happy we react.”Ronaldo’s statement then said: “That was all. None of these notes, therefore, said that the coach should even apologise to me.”Reflecting on Jesus’s conduct in the press conference Ronaldo said: “I heard expressions and an aggressiveness that I do not believe I deserved, an attitude of ‘I want, I can and I command’ that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before.”Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoPortugalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Coco Gauff says online racist abuse during China Open was ‘draining’ after loss to Mertens | Coco Gauff | The Guardian
description: Coco Gauff said she had been left drained by the racist abuse she experienced during the China Open after losing in the last 16 to Elise Mertens
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Coco Gauff said she had been left drained by the racist abuse she experienced during the China Open after losing in the last 16 to Elise Mertens
Content: Coco Gauff lost in straight sets to Elise Mertens on Wednesday.Photograph: Lintao Zhang/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCoco Gauff lost in straight sets to Elise Mertens on Wednesday.Photograph: Lintao Zhang/Getty ImagesCoco GauffCoco Gauff says online racist abuse during China Open was ‘draining’ after loss to MertensAmerican involved in disputed point during tournamentGauff called out ‘insane’ amount of abuse onlineAgenciesWed 7 Oct 2026 07.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCoco Gauff said she had been left drained bythe racist abuse she experiencedduring the China Open after losing in the last 16 to Elise Mertens.The American was dismayed earlier this week after an incident during her match against Chinese teenager Sun Xinran. The 16-year-old thought she had hit a winner late in the first set but Gauff had raised her hand to stop the point because she was distracted by flickering lights on the stadium’s advertising hoardings. The move prompted some boos from the crowd. The umpire agreed to have the point replayed, and Gauff went on to win 7-5, 6-1.Coco Gauff says ‘insane’ wave of racist abuse followed disputed point at China OpenRead moreOn social media, Gauff called out the “insane” amount of racist messages she had received after the match, adding: “I’m not a cheater or a thief.”Gauff also clarified that she challenged the point before Sun had returned the ball, when she noticed the lights flicker for a second time.Asked about the incident, a spokesperson for the Women’s Tennis Association said it was “appalled by the racial abuse directed atCoco Gauffand are in contact with her to offer our full support”.Gauff was far from her best on Wednesday against Mertens, hitting eight double faults and 34 unforced errors overall in a 6-3, 6-3 defeat.Gauff, who has an excellent record in China, was asked by reporters in Beijing whether she had been affected by the abuse.“It has been kind of draining, I’m not going to lie. I just turn off my phone and move on. There’s nothing you can do,” she said. “I think today I was just a bit flat. I just didn’t play well. I think I wasn’t moving well. There were a lot of things I didn’t do well.”During the match, she told her ​team that she had “no ​energy” and felt as though she might pass out.“I ​think I just ‌didn’t play well,” ​Gauff said. “I think ​I wasn’t moving well. There were a lot of things I didn’t do well. I thought Elise played well on the big points, made me play a big ball, yeah.”Mertens will face Iga Swiatek in the quarter-finals after the eighth seed defeated American Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-3.Explore more on these topicsCoco GauffTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lionel Messi describes ending Argentina career as his ‘saddest day’ in football | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: Lionel Messi described his retirement from international football as the ‘saddest day of my career’ after playing his final game for Argentina in a 3-0 defeat of Benin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Lionel Messi described his retirement from international football as the ‘saddest day of my career’ after playing his final game for Argentina in a 3-0 defeat of Benin
Content: An emotional Lionel Messi reacts during a tribute to him after his final game for Argentina.Photograph: Gustavo Garello/APView image in fullscreenAn emotional Lionel Messi reacts during a tribute to him after his final game for Argentina.Photograph: Gustavo Garello/APLionel MessiLionel Messi describes ending Argentina career as his ‘saddest day’ in footballMessi addresses crowd after scoring in win against Benin‘Not coming any more is going to be deeply painful’Agence France-PresseWed 7 Oct 2026 03.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 06.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLionel Messi described his retirement from international football as the “saddest day of my career” after playinghis final game for Argentinain a 3-0 defeat of Benin.Messi, who scored and provided two assists in the victory at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires, took to the field after the win to express gratitude to fans and teammates as he reflected on his 21-year career withArgentina.Lionel Messi bids tearful farewell to Argentina after scoring in 3-0 win over BeninRead more“It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years,” Messi told the stadium “Even in the worst moments we went through and that I had, I never stopped fighting, never stopped being here.“Not coming any more is going to be deeply painful. I swear I’d like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you.”Messi said that returning to the Monumental – where Argentina played their first game after winning the 2022 World Cup – was bittersweet. “Now I’m here on the saddest day of my career, which is the day I have to say goodbye to the national team, goodbye to all of you. But now I’ll be on that side [with the fans], supporting all the boys, everyone who comes in. Always united.”View image in fullscreenDrones create the shape of Lionel Messi above the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires.Photograph: Tobias Skarlovnik/Getty ImagesMessi said that despite the sadness, he had no regrets about the timing of his international exit, citing the exertions of Argentina’s campaign at this year’s World Cup, where they battled through to the final only tolose to Spain.He said the emotional rollercoaster of that tournament – which includeda 2-1 defeat of Argentina’s bitter rivals Englandin the semi-final – had taken a toll. “Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We had the dream of fulfilling my dream and the dream of the whole country, of becoming world champions again. In the last World Cup we were very close, and the reality is that nothing strange happened, as people say. The match against England took a huge toll on us physically, and emotionally it was very big.“We arrived with just enough, we fought like we always did with this jersey, with all the teammates I got to be with and share things with, not only them but also those who were around in the time when we managed to win. We were very close.”Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiArgentinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Eckert’s Spygate ban may be lenient, but no sane manager will try the same trick again | Southampton | The Guardian
description: Verdict has been a long time coming and the Southampton head coach has recaptured hearts and minds at St Mary’s
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Verdict has been a long time coming and the Southampton head coach has recaptured hearts and minds at St Mary’s
Content: A Middlesbrough fan with a pair of binoculars at the height of Spygate – before the first leg of the playoff semi-final against Southampton.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Middlesbrough fan with a pair of binoculars at the height of Spygate – before the first leg of the playoff semi-final against Southampton.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersSouthamptonEckert’s Spygate ban may be lenient, but no sane manager will try the same trick againVerdict has been a long time coming and the Southampton head coach has recaptured hearts and minds at St Mary’sLouise TaylorWed 7 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Hi Tonda, are you a cheat?” That simple, succinct, question cut to the heart of a matter that has vexed the Football Association all summer. It was posed by the Northern Echo’s Dominic Shaw afterSouthampton overcame Middlesbroughin the second leg of May’s Championship playoff semi‑final and proved the cue for Tonda Eckert to walk out of his press conference at St Mary’s.Although Southampton’s manager subsequently admitted to authorising spying on opponents, England’s football authorities struggled to decide what punishment best fitted an act some regard as heinous but which others fail to take seriously. Now, in autumn, we finally have an FA verdict, withEckert given a six-week bansuspended until the end of the 2027-28 season, a £28,000 fine and a reprimand.Southampton manager Tonda Eckert given six-week suspended ban for Spygate scandalRead moreDespite the apparent leniency of the sanction, one thing is clear: Eckert’s summer in purgatory surely dictates no sane England-based coach would contemplate engaging in espionage now.Eckert may wish he could turn back time to early May and rewrite history. On the eve of the playoff semi-final first leg on Teesside, William Salt, then an intern Southampton first-team analyst, was caught lurking awkwardly beside a tree while filming a Middlesbrough training session on his iPhone. Spygate was born and an independent disciplinary commission convened by the Football League (EFL)expelled Southamptonfrom the playoff final against Hull after their win against Boro across two legs. The governing body also decreed the Saints would begin the current Championship season on minus four points.View image in fullscreenTonda Eckert on the touchline at Middlesbrough’s Riverside Stadium during the first leg of Southampton’s playoff semi-final.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersBy then Southampton had also admitted to spying on Oxford and Ipswich training. There is a certain irony that Eckert’s team won none of the three games – albeit Middlesbrough were ultimately beaten on aggregate – involving covert surveillance. Yet the EFL independent disciplinary commission panel made plain its discomfort regarding the “particularly deplorable” pressure placed on a young worker hired on a temporary contract. Salt has since been given a staff job as an analyst in Southampton’s academy and is reportedly progressing well.With the EFL empowered to sanction clubs but not individuals in such cases, it was down to the FA to punish Eckert. The 33-year-old German issued a public apology in June but wasnot charged with misconduct by the FA until late July. A further hiatus ensued before a hearing at Wembley on 24 September.This extraordinary delay afforded Eckert ample time to regret dispatching Salt to Middlesbrough’s training ground adjacent to the luxury Rockliffe Hall Hotel and golf course just south of Darlington. Salt’s primary mission was to discover whether Hayden Hackney, Middlesbrough’s star midfielder and theChampionshipplayer of the season, was fit after injury. Unfortunately, clandestine manoeuvres were evidently not his strong suit. Salt soon found himself being chased into hotel toilets, and realised that using his bank card to buy a coffee at Rockliffe had not been the smartest move. That payment facilitated a search for his name on Southampton’s website. It was swiftly identified, enabling Steve Gibson, Middlesbrough’s owner, to make a formal complaint to the EFL regarding a breach of its anti-spying regulations.It is understood that, until this point, Southampton’s manager remained unaware of the Bev Priestman precedent. The former head coach of Canada Women wasbanned from all football activity for a yearby Fifa after being found guilty of initiating spying. During the 2024 Paris Olympics her staff secretly filmed a New Zealand training session using a drone and the former England women’s assistant manager paid a high price.It is unclear whether Eckert has since been in touch with the 40-year-old, now in charge of Wellington Phoenix. Priestman met such extreme hostility in previously welcoming Canada that she relocated her family to New Zealand. During ‘Spygate’, Eckert’s wife was heavily pregnant and based in Berlin, preparing for the birth of their first child. Back in Hampshire, her husband received death threats via LinkedIn.Southamptonsupplied the manager with protection while police advised him that driving his own car was unsafe and that he should restrict his movements.Plenty of people were extremely angry, with St Mary’s regulars polarised between those who believed the manager had shamed their club and should be sacked, and others who reflected that what is euphemistically called “training observation” of opponents is commonplace and largely unpunished across tracts of Europe. The second camp remembered that, seven years ago,Leeds were fined £200,000after the club’s then manager, Marcelo Bielsa, sent an analyst to monitor a Derby training session. Frank Lampard, then in charge of Derby, complained after spotting him perched up a tree.After that incident the EFL tightened its regulations regarding espionage appreciably. Nonetheless, Eckert’s advocates claim that, given he started last season as Southampton’s under-21s coach and became the manager afterWill Still’s sacking in November, he had missed the EFL’s annual managerial summer rules refresher course.View image in fullscreen‘I would lie if I said this summer’s been easy,’ Eckert said last month.Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PAEckert, who began his career as a Germany national team analyst before moving into coaching at Cologne, RB Salzburg, RB Leipzig, Bayern Munich, Barnsley and Genoa, was only half-joking when he recently told reporters that the EFL handbook was his staple bedside summer reading. He also made contact with Gareth Southgate and visited the former England and Middlesbrough, manager, with the pair discussing English football culture and its zero tolerance for spycraft at length.“I would lie if I said this summer’s been easy,” said Eckert last month. “I’ve asked the FA for forgiveness.” He has had unwavering support from Southampton’s board who made it clear they had no desire to sack him in the face of considerable dressing room hostility on the part offrom players who felt betrayed by ‘Spygate’.With first-team hearts and minds since seemingly recaptured by the coach who led them so close to promotion last season, Southampton have won four and drawn two of their opening eight Championship games. Next up on Sunday is the visit of Portsmouth. South-coast derbies are invariably tense but Eckert’s reprieve may ensure he cuts an unusually relaxed figure in the technical area.Explore more on these topicsSouthamptonFootball LeagueFootball politicsThe FAChampionshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: All aboard the Tuchel train? England camp has clear winners and losers | England | The Guardian
description: While it’s full steam ahead for Alex Scott, Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly, others look likely to be left behind
Author: David Hytner
Headline: While it’s full steam ahead for Alex Scott, Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly, others look likely to be left behind
Content: Myles Lewis-Skelly (centre) and Lewis Hall (right) were among those who impressed.Photograph: Michael Regan/The FA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMyles Lewis-Skelly (centre) and Lewis Hall (right) were among those who impressed.Photograph: Michael Regan/The FA/Getty ImagesEnglandAll aboard the Tuchel train? England camp has clear winners and losersWhile it’s full steam ahead for Alex Scott, Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly, others look likely to be left behindDavid HytnerWed 7 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel’s original idea had been for continuity. The England manager wanted to build on the positives from the World Cup and he was minded to stand by the vast majority of the players who had been a part of the journey to the semi-finals in North America over the summer. His squad for the four-matchNations Leaguewindow and the beginning of a new international cycle would not be defined by radical change. What was it about the best-laid plans?As Tuchel prepared to name his group in mid-September, he knew that he would be without a clutch of World Cup players because of injury. He then lost another handful after the announcement. Fast forward tothe Czechia game at Wembleyon Tuesday night – the final one of the quartet – and, after further withdrawals, Tuchel could count only 12 players who were available to him during the World Cup. He knows the train moves quickly in football, stopping for nobody. That flexibility is a prerequisite in his line of work. This felt like something else.England ready to level up and embrace ‘calculated risks’, claims TuchelRead moreTuchel and his staff were resolved to road-test an updated game model as they sought to move on from the devastation ofthe World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina. Again, nothing too radical because the principles were in place. They wanted to give the players greater freedom in terms of where they could roam on the pitch; encourage them to trust their instincts and take risks, all within a framework where covering for a teammate was fundamental. Tuchel would need some new players to execute it and, as he reflects on a positive window, in whichdefeat by Spainwas followed by three wins, two against Czechia either side ofthe 7-0 dismantling of Croatiain Rijeka, he will feel he has found them.There are always winners and losers from an international camp and maybe they are more pronounced on this occasion because of the timing; the sense of a fresh start, the desire to turn the page after Argentina. It was always going to be a tone-setter for the ultimate goal of Euro 2028 glory.The biggest winners were Alex Scott and Lewis Hall, with Myles Lewis-Skelly getting an honourable mention. James Trafford pushed his claim to supplant Jordan Pickford as the first-choice goalkeeper, and then there was Trent Alexander-Arnold, ever tantalising, ever nuanced.As for the losers, well, take your pick from those who were not present, with Tuchel making it clear that it would be harder for them. “It is always like this,” he said. “Everyone should be desperate to come because the train is rolling. Full credit to the players who bought in to that. We can only put our full energy into the camp and the players who are in camp. They make the camp special.”View image in fullscreenAlex Scott (centre) caught Thomas Tuchel’s eye before being forced to withdraw with injury.Photograph: Sebastian Frej/Getty ImagesTuchel described Scott and Hall as “really excellent”. In the case of the former, Tuchel cannot contain his excitement. He does not want to. Scott did well when he came on as a 70th-minute substitute for his debut against Czechia in Prague and was very good from the start against Croatia, catching the eye with his smoothness on the half turn, his dynamic surges.It was noticeable that when Tuchel’s assistant, Anthony Barry, spoke on Monday about fluid, hard-running midfielders to fit the team’s style, he name-checked three: Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson, who are well-established, and Scott. It is such a frustration thathe aggravated a thigh problem against Croatiaand is out for two months, which will rule him out of the matches in November against Croatia and Spain. Tuchel worked with Scott in November 2025 and at the pre-World Cup camp in Florida. “Alex came in here now and was on a completely new level,” Tuchel said. “He was super-strong.”Graphic showing minutes played for England in the international breakIt was a positive window for Lewis-Skelly, who Tuchel counted on as a midfielder rather than a left-back for the first time. The 20-year-old started three of the games and came on as a 79th-minute substitute against Croatia. The worry was how he picked up bookings in both matches against Czechia; he is now suspended for the home game against Croatia. “I wasn’t aware of the yellow card,” Tuchel said of Tuesday’s one at Wembley, rather surprisingly. He knows about the need to stay out of red card territory.Kobbie Mainoo is a potential loser from the emergence of Scott and Lewis-Skelly. Tuchel was at pains to sympathise with the Manchester United midfielder over the injury that forced his withdrawal, particularly after he did not play him for a single minute at the World Cup. But with Rice certain to return after an agreed rest this time this out, and James Garner in the frame, Mainoo has work to do. Ditto Jordan Henderson, who was not up to speed fitness‑wise after his broken arm at the World Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTrent Alexander-Arnold made his mark after being brought back into the fold.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesHall has taken his chance at left-back, stepping up after Nico O’Reilly played against Spain and was then forced to withdraw. Hall started in each of the subsequent games – “three top matches from him”, Tuchel said – and if he is plainly in possession of the shirt, he deserves to keep it in November. Which is bad news for O’Reilly and Djed Spence, who has not yet played this season.Did Alexander-Arnold do enough at right-backafter his surprise recall? He could not have done much more with his starting opportunities in both Czechia games. There was the lovely cross for Anthony Gordon’s breakthough goal in Prague and a driving, attack-minded performance at Wembley. Everybody knows what Alexander-Arnold can do; he showed it again and the argument remains that he must be included for his points of difference.Total Midweek Kane: England’s icon delivers a classic on his way to footballing ultimacy | Barney RonayRead moreOn the other hand, what does Tuchel do when Reece James, Tino Livramento and Spence are available? The manager has previously made it plain he considers all three to be ahead of Alexander-Arnold. He said he might have called up Ben White if he were fit and also has Jarell Quansah, even if the Bayer Leverkusen player would rather be considered in central defence. That was where Tuchel started him against Czechia at Wembley – ahead of Trevoh Chalobah and Jarrad Branthwaite.Cole Palmer has found himself under an unforgiving spotlight after his withdrawal, particularly after Tuchel questioned whether he wanted to play forEngland. It looks a long way back for the Chelsea No 10 and the same is true of Phil Foden. Both were overlooked when Tuchel gave a late call-up to Morgan Gibbs-White, and neither looks an easy fit for this team’s aggressive style. “I don’t know [if they are],” Tuchel said. “That is the honest answer. They were not here. This team took another step and it’s always about the guys who are here.”Tuchel has plenty to ponder before the November matches. He will hope to see John Stones recover his fitness and form at Inter. There is a belief that the centre-back’s move to Serie A, where the tempo is slower, can help him find his rhythm. Marcus Rashford will be expected to return; he has credit in the bank with Tuchel, even if Gordon has nailed down the starting spot on the left wing.Can Noni Madueke stage a comeback on the right after being dropped? And what of the strikers in the Saudi Pro League, Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney, who were also dropped? Tuchel now sees Jude Bellingham as the back-up No 9 to Harry Kane. He gave Dominic Calvert-Lewin only brief substitute appearances against Spain and Czechia at Wembley. The train hurtles on.Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelNations LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Robertson rant and the wrong system? Pocognoli’s Scotland start raises questions | Scotland | The Guardian
description: There has been no new manager bounce, Ben Gannon-Doak is playing in an odd position and the wider plan looks flawed
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: There has been no new manager bounce, Ben Gannon-Doak is playing in an odd position and the wider plan looks flawed
Content: Andy Robertson has already questioned the attitude of his Scotland teammates with Sébastien Pocognoli’s era barely having started.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Robertson has already questioned the attitude of his Scotland teammates with Sébastien Pocognoli’s era barely having started.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAScotlandAnalysisRobertson rant and the wrong system? Pocognoli’s Scotland start raises questionsEwan MurrayThere has been no new manager bounce, Ben Gannon-Doak is playing in an odd position and the wider plan looks flawedWed 7 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTShareWhat is the general situation after four games?Scotland are staring at a third-place finish inGroup B1 of the Nations League, which will have repercussions for their seeding in Euro 2028 qualifying. More striking, though, was the general standard of performance over Sébastien Pocognoli’s first four games as manager.Scotland were dismal for a half in Slovenia before a decent butscorelessrecovery. They capitulated after an early sending-offagainst Switzerland, failing to register a shot on target in a meek 3-0 loss. North Macedonia were as poor an international team as Scotland have faced in recent times, rendering the2-0 win in Skopjeworthy of little more than a shoulder shrug. Pocognoli’s men rounded off this extended window by being played off the Hampden Park pitchby Slovenia. Andy Robertson, the captain, strikingly questioned the attitude of his teammates. There has been no new manager bounce.Pocognoli was given only a two-year contract, which was odd given the pedestal he was placed on by the Scottish Football Association when hired in August. The likelihood remains host-nation status will secure the Scots a place in the next Euros, but the country cannot arrive at the event under the cover of darkness. The alarming nature of the performance against Slovenia – it really had no redeeming qualities – places a huge emphasis on November’s fixtures.Are Scotland suited to the way Pocognoli wants to play?It does not look that way. The manager deploys a three-man backline as routine, with an emphasis on pressing high and wingbacks being crucial to attacking phases.Scotlanddo not have an obvious two-man central defensive pairing, meaning they most definitely struggle when the number is increased by one. Time and again, they leave far too much space in behind and look woefully exposed. Counterattacks bypass Scotland’s midfield all too easily. Pocognoli’s Scotland are a dream to play against.Success for the Scots under Steve Clarke came from being well-drilled, compact and difficult to beat. Unsexy perhaps, but effective. Playing with gay abandon is all well and good when having a level of security Scotland simply do not possess currently. Scotland allowed Slovenia to be just as menacing as Morocco and Brazil, top-quality opposition they faced at the World Cup. Pocognoli’s desired methods may be impossible to implement without day-to-day involvement with players. Ideology is fine when club football permits an overhaul of personnel.When Scotland switched to a defensive four in the closing stages of the Slovenia clash, players appeared generally confused. This was a bad look for Pocognoli, who has insisted he is “flexible” in a tactical sense and disputed the idea he had a touchline row with Robertson. Scott McTominay’s return for the next set of fixtures would provide an iota of hope, were it obvious where the Napoli man fits in. The setup as is will not maximise the abilities of McTominay, John McGinn, Ryan Christie and Billy Gilmour.View image in fullscreenSébastien Pocognoli consoles Billy Gilmour after Scotland’s feeble defeat at home against Slovenia on Tuesday.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesDidn’t fans want a revolution?A reality is Scotland have qualified for three of the last four major tournaments. Noise directed towards Clarke underappreciated the scale of his work. That said, after seven years, Clarke’s tenure had run its course.The obvious move at that point was to turn towards a coach who had succeeded in tournament football with a similarly sized nation. With the level of available talent dropping or ageing, there was also a requirement for pragmatism and realism. Instead, Scottish FA officials spoke of a data-led search for Clarke’s successor, which led them to a coach who had never managed in international football before. Trying to be too smart by half? This team was not fundamentally broken, it just needed to progress.Nobody of sane mind should insist upon Scotland morphing into the Ajax team of the 1970s. The baseline, created by Clarke, is now tournament participation. This summer’s World Cup was the latest example of how finals involvement positively alters attitudes within and outside Scottish football to an unparalleled level. That is the important thing. The rest is fluff.There were 34,000 at Hampden for Slovenia’s visit; hardly disastrous in broaderNations Leaguecontext but almost 20,000 short of capacity. The public are yet to buy into Pocognoli and the blue-sky vision sold by his employers.How does Pocognoli handle Ben Gannon-Doak?Some in Scotland would have us believe Gannon-Doak is the tartan equivalent of a young Ryan Giggs. The truth is that at 20 Gannon-Doak is a player who is lightly raced at club level and, at this point, looks unlikely to make a first-team impact at Bournemouth. He has searing pace and a directness that scares defenders, which is offset by woeful decision making. Whether these shortcomings can he improved upon very much remains to be seen.What is clear is that Gannon-Doak cannot operate as a right wingback for Scotland against credible opposition. Deploying him there also denies a start to Aaron Hickey, who is undeniably one of Scotland’s best players. Gannon-Doak is a winger (as are Josh McPake and Findlay Curtis). Pocognoli’s first-choice method does not involve wingers. Something has to give.View image in fullscreenBen Gannon-Doak, pictured holding off Slovenia’s Erik Janza, is not a wingback.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAWhat is the wider scenario that Pocognoli is part of?The Scottish FA suddenly has a chief football officer in Craig Mulholland, and a head of strategy, operations and performance in Graeme Mathie. The latter was plucked from the Scottish second tier and the former was present in the dressing room during Scotland’s Nations League fixtures. The move to insert this level of middle management carrying wishy-washy job descriptions is strange, not least when neither of the individuals in question can provide working examples of markedly improving the big picture with an equivalent nation. Meanwhile, the new Scotland Under-21s manager, Tony Docherty,who is fielding teams in the same formation as Pocognoli, last took charge of a plummeting Ross County.Scottish football in general has a reluctance to let others mark its homework. Those in high office, typically very pleased with themselves, fail to convince on umpteen levels. Scotland have to work far, far harder at finding resource for the men’s A team. Six starters against Slovenia were 30 or older. Clarke could be obstinate but there was no raft of exciting footballers he chose to ignore.There is no question of the Scottish FA becoming anxious towards Pocognoli. Indeed, as was the case with Clarke, they seem beholden to him. If this goes wrong, however, there will be significant questions to be answered about a chosen direction of travel.Explore more on these topicsScotlandNations LeagueanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘I wanted to depart in the best way possible’: Kieran McKenna on Ipswich exit and future plans | Ipswich Town | The Guardian
description: In an exclusive interview, former Ipswich manager talks of his lasting affection for the club, savouring time out with family and friends and ideas for his next move
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: In an exclusive interview, former Ipswich manager talks of his lasting affection for the club, savouring time out with family and friends and ideas for his next move
Content: Kieran McKenna: ‘I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community.’Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKieran McKenna: ‘I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community.’Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesIpswich TownInterview‘I wanted to depart in the best way possible’: Kieran McKenna on Ipswich exit and future plansNick AmesIn an exclusive interview, former Ipswich manager talks of his lasting affection for the club, savouring time out with family and friends and ideas for his next moveWed 7 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was on the Portman Road pitch, bathed in bright early May light while immersed in the relief and joy of a third promotion in five years, that Kieran McKenna realised the moment was right. The thought had flickered earlier in the season that this might be his final campaign at Ipswich, only to be pushed into the subconscious by the Championship’s remorseless grind. “But standing out there, I felt this was probably time,” he says of those moments after QPR had been swept aside and areturn to the Premier Leagueassured. “Another big victory, a full stadium, in front of my family and the fans. It was an amazing way to go out on a high.”Five months later McKenna has no regrets about electing to cut things short while the going was so good. The golf bag lying outside his garage speaks of a man enjoying the break and, more pertinently, of something bigger. His son has recently become interested in the sport and sharing those moments with loved ones, whether out on the greens or spending part of the summer travelling along the East Anglian coastline in a camper van, were among the biggest reasons to pause a soaring career. At 40, McKenna had spent two decades immersed in coaching; it was time to appreciate life’s essentials while continuing professional development at his own speed.Next Generation 2026: 20 of the best talents at Premier League clubsRead moreHe had, as usual, been linked with moves away but the idea of a voluntary career break was hard for many to fathom when the decision wasfinalised in June. “For people on the outside it’s maybe a bit more difficult,” he says. “But those who know my path and my values, the ones closest to me who know me really well, I think they understood why I wanted to step out and what the benefits were of having a period like this.”Not everyone in football saw it that way: the phone has rung with proposals for his next move but McKenna says those overtures arrived “too soon, especially given the way I left Ipswich”. Leaving through the front door, a luxury rarely afforded, made him proud and there is no desperation to leap back into the fray. “I’m certainly in no rush,” he says. “I’m enjoying the time I’m having and hopefully an opportunity will come along that’s right. I have an idea what that would feel like but football doesn’t always follow your plan.”Since early September he has dipped his toe back in. That has involved tuning back into the process of watching and assessing games, while travelling to spend time with Bayern Munich, the Wigan Warriors rugby team and Colorado Rapids, who are managed by his friend Matt Wells. He has been working on foreign languages, topping up an already competent level of Spanish. This week he is visiting clubs in Spain and, next Wednesday, he will begin work as a technical observer for Uefa when Shakhtar Donetsk play AEK Athens at Stamford Bridge. “I wanted to give myself the best possibility to learn before taking on the next challenge,” he says.View image in fullscreenMcKenna basks in Ipswich’s promotion in May. ‘All we get is people coming up telling the story of how much the last few years have meant for them,’ he says.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersMore than once McKenna repeats an assertion he made after promotion in May: that 2025-26 was the hardest of his four-and-a-half seasons at Ipswich, during which he masterminded a dizzying rise from League One to the top flight that marked him among football’s hottest managerial properties. The pressure was heightened last season: Ipswich had gone down and were expected to bounce back, even though the remarkably close-knit core who had propelled them through the divisions were drifting away. In effect, he took two different teams to the top.“You can see how it could really have gone in two distinct directions,” he says, making a comparison with the fall Luton experienced after a brief reacquaintance with the elite. “We had the feeling internally that if we didn’t work really hard to pull everyone together then it could have gone in a negative way.”McKenna pulled them over the line and reached the end of his own journey. Along the way he had come close to departing more than once but jumping ship earlier would have jarred. “I had a lot of different opportunities to leave, could have left in many different circumstances really,” he says. “But I was always aware I wanted to depart in the best way possible, with the club on a high, back in the Premier League and with a great chance to build for what will hopefully be a really successful period.”The hardest aspect of his final day, he explains, was looking down a camera and addressing the supporters with a five-minute speech in which he did not attempt to suppress his emotion. He reels off a list of coaching staff and other colleagues with whom the goodbyes were touching, meaningful, joyful. Many of the friendships, particularly with members of the “really, really special team” that he led to those successive promotions, will be lifelong. The night before this interview, he spent most of a journey back from London speaking to one of them.View image in fullscreenKieran McKenna acclimatising to the Premier League in 2024.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersHe laughs off the idea he would have relished getting his hands on the £200m summer transfer spend – not to mention a new training ground whose design he influenced – that appears to have given his successor, Gary O’Neil, a better shot at survival. If anything, he suggests, it shows the club have begun their own new chapter. McKenna also emphasises the thought of potential reputational damage from a second relegation did not factor into his decision to quit. “It wasn’t about the thought of a worst-case scenario or what could go wrong,” he says.It was about prioritising life where we meet, in the family’s home a brisk half-hour walk from Portman Road. He and his wife chose to stay in Ipswich, where their two children attend school, having become more than mere itinerants passing through. It so happens Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson kept homes nearby after moving upwards. McKenna has hero status here too, in these unassuming yet football-crazed surroundings. Although he keeps a low profile and locations for socialising are chosen judiciously, the overwhelming affection of a town and county often rear up.“Everyone is respectful; all we get is people coming up telling the story of how much the last few years have meant for them, their family and their friends, and wishing me the best,” he says. “Moving down here together, going all in, making ourselves part of this community, it’s been another of the really positive things. It’s a little bit different living in the area where you were managing but it’s the right thing for us at this time.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHas muscle memory ever taken him on an early-morning drive to the training ground? “You’d think it might, but it’s just a different life. You’re not setting the alarm for 5.30am and driving there in the dark. You’re getting up with the kids and having breakfast with them, and you’re around when they go to bed. Although the geography is the same, the life is different.”He does not think such a heady half-decade, in which a talent honed at Tottenham and Manchester United blossomed gloriously, has changed a grounded personality honed in rural County Fermanagh. “I probably feel about 20 years older,” he says. “But my friends at home were telling me in the summer that I haven’t changed since I was 10. I couldn’t have arrived at Ipswich with a better background as a coach but, on the other hand, if you’d given me a list of the things I’d have to deal with in the next five years I really wouldn’t have believed it. After going through so many things you’re wiser for the experience.”Nonetheless the fact remains: taking a breather when the world is your oyster feels vanishingly rare in football management. Maybe everyone should do it. “But what’s right for me, after two decades coaching, might be different for a manager who only stopped playing three years ago,” he says. “It’s been a massive body of work. You leave United, pick your bags up, get in the car and five-and-a-half hours later you’re in Ipswich. At 35 you’re leaving your family behind, checking into a hotel 10 days before Christmas; you absolutely throw yourself into the job for the next four and a half years and the family do the same. I want to enjoy the time we have now, take this period to reflect and be in the best position I can for the next role.”View image in fullscreenMcKenna says his two decades in coaching have taken a toll.Photograph: Nick Potts/PASo what would that next iteration of McKenna’s career look like, in a perfect world? He has been linked with any potential vacancies at Celtic and his old employers Spurs; his name will be circling once the season’s sackings start, although Ipswich will be owed a sizeable fee for any role he takes this year.“I’m always going to want to be somewhere where I can improve players, play attacking football and win games,” he says. “But beyond that I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community, trying to build something memorable. It was a really special opportunity at Ipswich and you want to do that again in your career. But you have to be ready to come in somewhere and get some short-term success as well.”The chance will surely arise soon; it does not take a giant leap to imagine McKenna in a Champions League dugout in the next few years if the stars align. Until then the self-growth will continue and there will always be dispatches from Portman Road, where his brother and children are regulars. McKenna would rather look forward and will not beat that path for now. “I think that’ll be some way down the line,” he says. “They’re cracking on with the season. There’s nothing that can lessen my pride and love for everything we’ve been through. Hopefully I’ll be back in the stadium as an old hand, and some of the people will remember the times we had.”They are unlikely to forget; McKenna’s aim is that, by then, at least one other set of supporters will have felt the magic too.Explore more on these topicsIpswich TowninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is only the beginning,’ vows Mikel Arteta after signing £80m-plus Arsenal deal | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Mikel Arteta has put pen to paper on a lucrative new contract that ties him to Arsenal until 2030
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Mikel Arteta has put pen to paper on a lucrative new contract that ties him to Arsenal until 2030
Content: Mikel Arteta – pictured with the CEO, Richard Garlick (left), and the sporting director, Andrea Berta – has extended a stay that began in December 2019.Photograph: Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta – pictured with the CEO, Richard Garlick (left), and the sporting director, Andrea Berta – has extended a stay that began in December 2019.Photograph: Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesArsenal‘This is only the beginning,’ vows Mikel Arteta after signing £80m-plus Arsenal dealFour-year-contract secures Spaniard’s futureTitle winner is Premier League’s best-paid managerEd AaronsWed 7 Oct 2026 07.13 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta has promised “this is only the beginning” of what he can achieve as Arsenal manager after signing a new long-term contract that would take his reign at the club beyond a decade if he sees it out.The Spaniard is understood to have signed a four-year deal worth more than £20m a season, making him the best-paid Premier League manager. That is a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season as Arsenalended their 22-year wait to be crowned championsafter three successive runners-up finishes.Arsenal shelve plans for major expansion of Emirates StadiumRead moreArteta, whotook over from Unai Emeryin December 2019, is the Premier League’s longest-serving manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola from Manchester City. Afterlosing the Champions League finallast season to Paris Saint-Germain in a penalty shootout, the 44-year-old is targeting more success as he seeks to build a winning dynasty at Arsenal, where he previously served as captain under Arsène Wenger.“It’s a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best forArsenal,” Arteta said. “This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue. We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.“This is such a proud moment for me and my family. I feel the love and respect from our fantastic supporters, and they have mine – and ours – in return.”Arteta’s previous contract, which was due to expire at the end of this season, was believed to be worth about £10m a season plus a £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League. The new deal, to June 2030, cements his status as one of the best-paid managers in the world. His coaching staff have also signed extended deals.“It has been an incredible journey so far and we are excited for what lies ahead in this special relationship,” said Arsenal’s co-chairs, Stan and Josh Kroenke. “Last season was an incredible moment in Arsenal’s history, a moment in which we created memories that will last a lifetime. We’re determined to create many more in the years ahead.“We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019. He has a deep understanding of Arsenal’s values and carries them in his heart. He knows what this club means to everyone connected to it and is committed to building on everything we have achieved together.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArsenal confirmed this week that they have shelved plans for a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium after Arteta is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would have been caused by any temporary move. His side face Leeds on Saturday as they attempt to bounce back from a surprise3-0 defeat at Brightonbefore the international break that ended the champions’ 100% start to the new campaign.Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Portuguese authorities took 83 days to tell Rui Pinto his witness protection was ending | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Portuguese authorities kept the Manchester City whistleblower Rui Pinto in the dark for almost three months about their decision to end his status as a protected witness
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Portuguese authorities kept the Manchester City whistleblower Rui Pinto in the dark for almost three months about their decision to end his status as a protected witness
Content: Rui Pinto entered Portugal’s protection programme after cooperating with the country’s justice authorities.Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRui Pinto entered Portugal’s protection programme after cooperating with the country’s justice authorities.Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesSoccerPortuguese authorities took 83 days to tell Rui Pinto his witness protection was endingCommission concluded in July threat level was lowManchester City whistleblower given 10 days’ noticeExclusive byEd AaronsandMiguel Dantasin PortoWed 7 Oct 2026 06.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePortuguese authorities kept Rui Pinto in the dark for almost three months about their decision toend his status as a protected witnessand notified the Manchester City whistleblower 10 days before it was due to expire, it can be revealed.According to documents seen by the Guardian, the special security programmes commission (CPES), which oversees Portugal’s witness protection programme, met on 8 and 9 July to discuss Pinto’s case. It concluded that the threat level against him was low and that the special protection measures were no longer warranted.Manchester City’s glory cannot be taken away from the players, says Kyle WalkerRead moreYet it was not until 30 September that Pinto, who has been a protected witness since 2020 after agreeing to grant Portuguese authorities access to millions of files gathered before his arrest, was informed of the decision – 83 days after it had been made.With 10 days’ notice, Pinto was left with little time to address a number of immediate issues. He needs to find somewhere safe to live and establish a way of supporting himself in a new location, while avoiding contact with family members.The Guardian contacted the CPES on two occasions seeking details of the criteria and evidence used to determine that Pinto’s protection should be withdrawn. On Wednesday, the commission was also asked to explain the 83-day gap between its decision and the notification. None of the inquiries received a response.On 30 September, the day Pinto was informed his protected-witness status was coming to an end, thePremier League’s guilty verdict against City, which had been confirmed 24 hours earlier, was dominating headlines around the world. The authorities stood by the decision reached nearly three months earlier despite protestations from Pinto and his lawyers that hefears for his life.Pinto entered Portugal’s protection programme after cooperating with the country’s justice authorities. His revelations have subsequently been used by judicial, tax and sporting authorities across Europe, including the Premier League’s investigation into City’s alleged financial irregularities. Pinto’s lawyers argue that the authorities should take into account his cooperation with the justice system and the continuing risks associated with his disclosures before ending his protection.Mounting pressure appears to have prompted a rethink. Last Saturday Portugal’s justice minister, Rita Alarcão Júdice, was questioned by journalists about the decision. She said the authorities would review Pinto’s case and promised to respond by Saturday, the date on which his protection is due to end.“I have received various requests and we are examining them very carefully,” Júdice said. “If there has been any irregularity, or if any procedure was not handled as it should have been, that will, of course, be taken into consideration.”The Guardian understands that, as it firstreported, Pinto remains willing to cooperate with British authorities in the City case and in other investigations stemming from his findings. He handed over millions of documents to investigators in France, which can now be shared with other nations – including the UK – under international cooperation and bilateral ties.Pinto’s lawyer, Francisco Teixeira da Mota, told the Guardian an appeal against the decision would be filed this week. “The most shocking thing is the fact that he wasn’t heard before the decision was made,” he said. “It’s something that goes against the European court of human rights.”In a press release last week, Pinto’s defence team called the decision “an act of state terrorism”. Their outrage has intensified after they learnedtheir client had been kept in the dark for almost three months. “It says a lot,” Da Mota added.Explore more on these topicsFootballPortugalManchester CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal and Chelsea set to miss a month of next WSL season due to Club World Cup | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: The Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to by the Club World Cup
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to by the Club World Cup
Content: Arsenal’s victory in the 2025 Champions League final has guaranteed them a place in the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028.Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/ReutersView image in fullscreenArsenal’s victory in the 2025 Champions League final has guaranteed them a place in the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028.Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/ReutersWomen's Super LeagueArsenal and Chelsea set to miss a month of next WSL season due to Club World CupBack end of 2027-28 season likely to be ‘challenging’Fixture contestion a growing area of concernExclusive byMatt HughesWed 7 Oct 2026 05.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to the Club World Cup, with Arsenal and Chelsea likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month.The Guardian revealed last week that the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup isset to be awarded to the US, with transatlantic travel to cause additional problems for European sides, while the proposed dates of 5-30 January will clash directly with the WSL.Too nice: do Arsenal lack the grit and tenacity to end WSL title drought?Read moreFifa has yet to confirm the qualification criteria for the Club World Cup but the Guardian has learned Arsenal are guaranteed to be involved as 2025 Champions League winners and Chelsea are likely to join them, although they would lose their place if Manchester City win this season’s Champions League. Based on this season’s schedule, an extended run in the Club World Cup would mean the two English clubs missing up to four WSL match weeks plus the fourth round of the FA Cup, playing havoc with the fixture list and causing major congestion at the end of the season.Uefa will be granted places for six clubs: five to qualify automatically and one to take part in a six-team qualifier before the tournament, with the three highest-ranked clubs joining 13 automatic qualifiers to form a 16-team competition. While the process has still to be ratified by the Fifa council, it is understood Uefa’s spots will be given to the Champions League winners between 2024 and 2027 – currently Barcelona as the two-time champions and Arsenal, with this season’s title still up for grabs – topped up by the highest-ranked clubs in Uefa’s Champions League coefficient table.Chelsea are third in that table for the current four-year cycle, behind Barcelona and Lyon with a 17-point lead over fourth-placed Bayern Munich, and cannot be caught. Based on the current rankings, Bayern and Wolfsburg are next in line to qualify, although the latter have not qualified for this season’s Champions League and will not accumulate additional points, so are likely to be overhauled by Real Madrid or Paris Saint-Germain. Fifa plans to cap the number of participants from each country at two, so City winning the Champions League would cost Chelsea their place.The WSL declined to comment as it has yet to be told of Fifa’s plans for the tournament, but sources conceded its impact is likely to prove challenging. The WSL has a winter break, which is scheduled for 21 December to 10 January this season, and although that could be pushed back slightly, aligning it with the Club World Cup is not viewed as practical due to the congested calendar.As well as creating a lopsided ­season, moving the winter break would result in a backlog of WSL fixtures during the period when the Champions League knockout stage begins at the beginning of February. The issue of fixture congestion is a growing area of concern in the women’s game and 2028 will be particularly problematic due to the Olympic football tournament taking place in Los Angeles in August, just before the start of the European domestic season.The International Olympic Committee has expanded women’s football to 16 nations at the 2028 Games, and unlike the men’s version which is restricted to players under 23 with three overage exceptions, senior internationals are permitted to take part.Fifa’s imposition of the Club World Cup in the middle of the European season has exacerbated the problem, and last month European Leagues, a lobby group, extended its legal complaint to the European Commission about the world governing body’s alleged “abuse of power and dominant position” to include the women’s game.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballShareReuse this content

title: Bochum ban fans from jumping in unison over sickness fears | Bochum | The Guardian
description: After an engineering report highlighted the problem of a ‘trampoline effect’ which might make some feel unwell, the German club have moved to stop synchronised jumping in one stand
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After an engineering report highlighted the problem of a ‘trampoline effect’ which might make some feel unwell, the German club have moved to stop synchronised jumping in one stand
