title: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming | Games | The Guardian
description: The launch of a collector’s box hints at a new reality: the kinds of games I grew up with are becoming a luxury item, locked behind a forbidding spending barrier
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: The launch of a collector’s box hints at a new reality: the kinds of games I grew up with are becoming a luxury item, locked behind a forbidding spending barrier
Content: An investment … Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenAn investment … Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection.Photograph: Rockstar GamesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Pushing Buttons newsletterGamesWhat the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gamingThe launch of a collector’s box hints at a new reality: the kinds of games I grew up with are becoming a luxury item, locked behind a forbidding spending barrierDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a parent (and partner) to a habitual collector, I do feel like an unwelcome portion of my life is occupied by an endless war against stuff. Surfaces in my home ceaselessly accumulate piles of random objects: a JoyCon wrist strap, a sticker sheet, an unidentifiable plastic piece of a toy or gizmo, an Xbox 360 controller with no batteries, cases for Switch cartridges lost down the side of the sofa … Stuff encroaches everywhere, especially in a gaming household. Much as I regret theimminent disappearance of physical games, I do not regret the extra space I have in my attic as a result of switching almost entirely to downloaded games over the last decade or so.Speaking of the imminent disappearance of physical games: Rockstar recently announced a £350 ($400) “collector’s box” of Grand Theft Auto 6 goodies … that doesn’t include the game itself. Not even a download code. The Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection, to give it its full and unwieldy name, contains a hat, a bag, a pair of sunglasses, a figurine, a poster and more, including a mirror and a “swizzle spoon” that looks, unambigiously, like a cocaine spoon. The game retails at £70, so if you want something to play alongside all your stuff, you’re looking at an outlay of £420.I’m not about to rag on this box of merch. People love this kind of stuff, and as a lifelong collector of Japanese gatcha and blind-box toys, I am in no position to judge how people spend their money. I have a few video game special editions that I cherish – the statue that came with my copy of The Last Guardian is still on my shelf – though I also have many more that are relegated to various cupboards. But it is unusual, however, for them to be this expensive. Usually with gaming special editions, we’re talking an extra £20-50 for a statue, or a steelbook, maybe a booklet and a keyring. 2009’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s “prestige edition”came with night vision gogglesfor $150. In 2015, Fallout 4’s $120 collector’s edition shipped with aplastic Pip Boywrist unit (I had one; alas, it was flimsy and disappointing).There have been some infamously expensive gaming special editions down the years, some of which were PR stunts (see Saints Row IV’smillion-dollar pack, which included a Lamborghini and cosmetic surgery – nobody bought it). But in the 2020s high-priced video game merchandise has become more common, from a Balenciaga PlayStation tie-in line to£580 for Pokémon Lego.View image in fullscreenPriced out … expensive video games and merch have now become a luxury item.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesWhat’s behind this is a troubling sense that video games as we once conceived of them – console games, played at home, perhaps on a nice 4K TV – have become a luxury item. People who can afford to spendup to £790for a console and games are perhaps now people who can afford an extra £350 for a box of merch.Continual price-risesfrom Xbox and PlayStation suggest that video game companies do not seem particularly worried about pricing people out. Super-expensive merch and special editions like GTA 6’s form part of the same upward trend.This stratification of the gaming world has been happening for years, ever since the first smartphones. The vast majority of the world’s players – about 80%, according toNewzoo– play for free, or at low cost, on mobile phones. The remaining 20% of players account for a disproportionate share of spending on the high-end gaming market on consoles and PC. With merch boxes like this, games companies are really going after that 20% for all they’ve got.I’m saddened by the idea of gaming becoming even more of a luxury hobby. On the one hand, games in the broadest sense are more accessible than ever – you’re three taps away from playing Monopoly Go on a phone at any moment. But the kinds of games I grew up with and love to write about, games that feel like worlds rather than temporary diversions, are now increasingly locked behind a spending barrier. With the increasing scarcity of physical discs and cartridges, you can’t even reliably buy them second hand any more.I guess there’s one advantage to the increasing cost of collector’s editions: the price has removed any lingering temptation to buy them. God knows I donotneed more stuff.What to playView image in fullscreenA game to sit back and wallow in … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17Keith has been playing Silver Pines, a neo-noir detective drama with point-and-click adventure sensibilities. “As I played, I discovered countless references to 80s and 90s neo-noir culture – from Blue Velvet to Twin Peaks,” he writesin our review.“It was a pleasure to explore every broken-down movie theatre, oily car garage and sweat-stinking interrogation room, collecting weird trinkets and working out how they’d all fit together – then exploring them again (and again) when the answers failed to show up. Silver Pines is a game to sit back and wallow in, like a private eye, kicking off his wingtip shoes and pulling that bottle of bourbon from the bottom drawer as rain trickles down the window and sodium street lights paint the walls a sickly shade of yellow.”Available on:PC, PS5, Switch 2Estimated playtime:12 hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenFarewell, Ninja Theory … Hellblade 2.Photograph: Ninja TheoryAward-winningUK studio Ninja Theoryhasreportedlybegun laying off staff. The creator of Hellblade was one of the developers affected byMicrosoft’s programme of lay-offsand studio closures in July, and according to Xbox COO Matt Booty two agreements to keep the studio running have failed. It is a sad end to one of the UK’s most interesting development houses.Meanwhile, Windows Centralobtained the transcriptto a recent in-house meeting held for Xbox staff by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. In it, Sharma refers to the next generation Xbox platform currently known asProject Helixas “a family of devices” rather than a single console. “There is not one device that fits all,” she stated. “We will certainly have a great console first, but we also know that many players will be on the go.” Could the ROG Xbox Ally, launched in partnership with Asus last year, have just been a beta test for a fully fledged handheld Xbox?The news site GamesIndustry.Biz hasan interesting featureonZach Cregger’s Resident Evil movieand how it has affected the Resident Evil games. Although the film led to a modest uptick in sales, the real value of movie and TV tie-ins, according to industry analysts, is that they keep those franchises in the minds of gamers so that subsequent titles benefit from the exposure. As game development cycles continue to widen, it looks like we can expect a lot more movies and TV shows to fill in the gaps.What to clickFrom Super Bowl champ to master architect: Mike Tomlin’s sprawling Minecraft city is magnificentGears of War: E-Day – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenGet cozy … Flame, Forest and Flood.Photograph: Fairy Mount GamesA question from my friendDavidvia email:“I keep hearing that game publishers are avoiding the whole of November because of GTA 6– will there really be NO choice for those of us who don’t want to shoot stuff and run people over?”Thankfully, it’s only the big western publishers who are staying clear of the GTA 6 launch window – lots of other developers are diving in regardless. Cozy strategy gameFlame, Forest and Flood(try saying that three times) is launching on the same day as GTA, offering a delightful tactical alternative, set in a hex-based woodland idyl. Staying on a rural theme, the purposefully rage-inducing “precision platformer”Trees Hate Youis a woodland hiking game, where you are attacked by nature. Alternatively,Football Manager 2027is arriving on 10 November, so instead of leading a gang of drug dealers into a bloody turf war, you could lead Plymouth Argyle into the Premier League. I’m not sure which scenario is more challenging.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump
Content: A very interesting impression … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenA very interesting impression … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMoviesReviewThe Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet ZuckerbergJeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions TrumpPeter BradshawWed 7 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts. Sixteen years have gone by sinceThe Social Network, written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher; this was the addictive, obsessive-compulsive movie about the birth of Facebook in Harvard’s macho-competitive cauldron of student sexism and nerdy self-pity, starring Jesse Eisenberg as the fast-talking, arrogant, not-necessarily-evil genius Mark Zuckerberg. Now Sorkin is back with a sequel of sorts, directing his own script – and now Zuckerberg is basically evil, but also weirdly slow talking, as if all the zinging, smart-alecky Sorkinesque dialogue energy of the first film has been siphoned away in early middle age and dispersed among the insurgents in the new cast.Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?Read moreSorkin’s jittery, funny, syncopated style is unmistakable, as distinctive in its way as David Mamet, although he has one joke about “spatula” being a Yiddish word that hehas borrowed from Philip Roth’s Portnoy’s Complaint. It is the story of how in 2021, Zuckerberg’s Facebook empire was challenged bycourageous whistleblower-employee Frances Haugenand Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, who were on a mission to tell the world how Zuckerberg, scared by falling revenue, changed the algorithm so that engagement was supercharged by rage bait and hate speech, malice and envy. Facebook, moreover, didn’t factcheck political ads, thus driving a huge, nationwide surge in extremist groups and teen bullying and becoming a major player in the Capitol riots. (Having said that, this film does not say aloud the word “Trump” and rather cravenly declines to specify Maga activity.)Mikey Madison sympathetically plays the unhappy, principled, supersmart Haugen, who is dismissed as a “disrupter” – and Sorkin leaves it to us to notice that this in other circumstances is what oligarchs smugly call themselves.Jeremy Allen Whitedoes a capable, unflashy, unrisky job as Horwitz, a stolid performance that perhaps, in sync with the film, tells us about the diligent professionalism of old-school print journalism. And Zuckerberg? Well, we were all hoping and expecting it would be Jesse Eisenberg again. (You’ve heard of Richard Linklater’s Boyhood; this would be Aaron Sorkin’s Techbrohood.) But no: it is Jeremy Strong, who does a very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet, modifying the torpid sadness of his Kendall Roy in TV’s Succession, making this the unhurried contempt of someone simultaneously burdened and energised by knowing he’s richer and therefore smarter than everyone else. (A famous line in The Social Network was “A million dollars isn’t cool. You know what’s cool? A billion dollars.” This film starts by telling us that Facebook is worth a trillion dollars.)Zuckerberg, though, is almost a cameo, with no equals with whom he can exchange dialogue, only employees – although the film imagines one former investor-turned-critic called Charlie (Bill Burr) who heckles Zuckerberg’s practice performance before a confessional hearing, with Zuckerberg amusingly having to be told how to smile. Charlie is the angry, unheeded voice of conscience.View image in fullscreenRattles along at an entertaining clip … Jeremy Allen White as Jeff Horwitz and Mikey Madison as Frances Haugen in The Social Reckoning.The resulting drama rattles along at an entertaining clip, although there are false notes. When Frances has secret meetings with Horwitz in a hotel, the film has her wearing a slinky evening dress, supposedly as a kind of disguise, so that if recognised it would seem like she was out on a date. Hmm, really? Or is it so that the movie’s female lead has scenes where she looks glamorous? Later, Horwitz affectionately tells her to be less “mean”. But she is not “mean”. She just speaks Sorkinspeak. So does Horwitz. The ubiquity of Sorkinspeak effaces the difference between all the characters.The most disturbing scene comes at the very beginning, showing a drunk woman livestreaming her racist abuse of traffic cops; this is the woman whom Haugen recognises as an acquaintance of hers, radicalised byFacebook. Towards the end we glimpse her again, looking ambiguously appalled by what she has become. But would she be appalled in reality? Or is this just the film-makers’ wish fulfilment? The closing-credit titles – usually the platform for a film to promote and summarise its heroes’ achievements – concedes that Facebook still isn’t checking political ads. Plus, of course, the film is set at the start of the Trump interregnum of 2020-24, when it seemed as if the Capitol riots were the ultimate wake-up call and moderation had returned. Nowadays Trump and his tech bro courtiers are more vainglorious than ever, and the values of investigative journalism have been thrown out at the Washington Post by its owner Jeff Bezos. This is a film which doesn’t reckon with the future we’re living in.The Social Reckoning is out on 8 October in Australia, and 9 October in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFacebookMark ZuckerbergWall Street JournalAaron SorkinMikey MadisonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption
Author: Arielle Pardes
Headline: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption
Content: ‘AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying … jobs in the global economy. Women are just strikingly underrepresented.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying … jobs in the global economy. Women are just strikingly underrepresented.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behindWomen hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruptionSupported byAbout this contentArielle PardesWed 7 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI.The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present.“A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.”Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching.Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared with 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recentreportfrom LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’sresearchshows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI.AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have.“AI is creating some of the fastest-growing, highest-paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.”The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said.“What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB.org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs.Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now holdabout one-thirdof tech jobs in the US. Butresearchhas found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement.‘I’ve seen so many women fall through the cracks’Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at the investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.”Putatunda said it was not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up.“If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.”Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went onmaternity leave for four months, and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare.“That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.”The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI.“Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.”When people have tried to address these tech industry problems in the past, the solutions have largely come down to giving women more mentorship and implementing diversity programs with goals around representation. But in recent years, companies have aggressively scaled back their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, largely in response to a political climate that discourages them. That has left fewer companies with institutional programs to hire and promote women.The political climate has made it more challenging to get AI companies to support initiatives focused on women, said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. Newhouse, a former technology product executive with two decades of industry experience, points to the Department of Justice targeting corporations with DEI programs, claiming the initiatives violate anti-discrimination laws. Companies such as Accenture, Deloitte, IBM and PayPal have all agreed to pay multimillion-dollar settlements under this enforcement.“It is getting harder to go into companies being called AI Powered Women,” Newhouse said. “And our advocates inside those companies are also struggling with having women-focused initiatives.”Still, she said the risk that women are left behind in the AI workforce was something that kept her up at night. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” she said. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency
Content: Supporters of James Talarico, the Democratic candidate leading the Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, in Eagle Pass on 13 July.Photograph: Bob Daemmrich/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSupporters of James Talarico, the Democratic candidate leading the Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, in Eagle Pass on 13 July.Photograph: Bob Daemmrich/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionUS midterm elections 2026The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy tooEditorialDonald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacencyWed 7 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.49 EDTShareFor once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president hasinstructed supporters. Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, theyhave reason to be upbeat. The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and thegerrymanderingof Republicans, but surveys give it a lead ofabout nine pointson the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates.Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. That wouldrequire flipping four seats, with 35 in play. Remarkably, Democrats are prospering in red states from Texas to Alaska. In Kansas – which Mr Trump carried by 16 points, and which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932 – the race is neck and neck.Even putting aside the ongoing questions about polling accuracy, there are very good reasons for caution. The first and most glaring is that the Democrats remainunpopular. Voters are being turned off the Republicans rather than drawn towards their rivals; pundits talk of ared undertowrather than a blue wave.Second, the picture is extremely patchy. Democrats’ striking progress in key races where few had favoured them is tied to standout candidates and especially unpopular opponents – notably in Texas, where the Christian pastor and economic populistJames Talaricois leading Ken Paxton, viewed unfavourably by a third of his own party’s supporters. Yet Democrats are struggling in some places where they initially had good reason for optimism, such asMaine. Third, the huge Republican spending advantage is now materialising – with$700m of advertisingbooked since the start of September.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesMr Trump, who has fared better than his party in elections, is hitting the campaign trail. He may make sure his base turns out. But candidates – including those who benefited from his endorsement – are increasinglydistancing themselvesfrom the president because he alienates others. He is visibly more energised by his construction projects than how his voters can pay their bills. His war on Iran looks not only reckless and ineffectual, but is pushing up prices. Strikingly, voters are now more likely to identify Republicans than Democrats as“elitist”. Latino voters who swung to him arechanging their minds, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement excesses contributing.Outrageously, Mr Trump has usedtaxpayer-funded advertsto laud his presidency. It goes without saying that he cannot be expected to respect the midterm results. The supreme court rejected his efforts torestrict mail-in voting– used by almost a third of the electorate – but he continues to smear it.Just as he disrupts the electoral process, in office he rejects the norms and restraints that his predecessors recognised, and relies more and more on executive orders – seeking to avoid checks on issues ranging from war to vaccines. But shouldDemocratsmanage to take both House and Senate, they would regain both legislative control and investigative powers. In these elections, most votes will be driven by economic stress rather than democratic peril. But their outcome will be critical to the defence of American democracy – or its continued erosion.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionDonald TrumpDemocratsUS politicseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego? Trump is beyond irresponsible | Ted Widmer | The Guardian
description: We appear to be entering a new era, in which political desperation at home leads to increasingly unhinged threats abroad
Author: Ted Widmer
Headline: We appear to be entering a new era, in which political desperation at home leads to increasingly unhinged threats abroad
Content: ‘We want honest,’ Trump said at one point, confusingly. Yes, we do.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘We want honest,’ Trump said at one point, confusingly. Yes, we do.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald Trump‘Take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego? Trump is beyond irresponsibleTed WidmerWe appear to be entering a new era, in which political desperation at home leads to increasingly unhinged threats abroadWed 7 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.07 EDTShareDonald Trump was in Nebraska on Monday, and though his long rally speech had elements of a performance, this was no Bruce Springsteen album. He offered another dark meditation on a world spiraling out of control, one in which the destruction of American cities is increasingly a possibility, unless Americans trust him to use the vast powers of the presidency to annihilate his foes.The president drew fury when he suggested that Iran could launch a nuclear attack and “take out”Los Angelesor San Diego. California leaders reacted with scorn at Trump’s alarmism.Governor Gavin Newsom denounced Trump as “deranged and dangerous”, while the mayors of Los Angeles andSan Diego, Karen Bass and Todd Gloria, objected strenuously to putting their cities in harm’s way, even if only in his feverish imagination.Perhaps the worst problem with Trump’s speech – and there were many – was not that it vividly daydreamed about Armageddon-on-the-Pacific. It was just so delusional that it had almost no basis in fact at all.It is inherently destabilizing when a nation’s leader cannot be trusted to make an accurate statement, and the situation is especially troubling when the nation is the United States, the defender of the rules-based order since 1945.First, the claim itself. When read inside thetranscript, the words don’t make a great deal of sense. It’s almost like scat singing as the president goes into his famous “weave”, his word for the way he lurches from one half-formed thought to another, like a rodeo clown on a bucking bronco.“[Kamala] stole a lot of things that didn’t work out too well. But I want, I wanna see, I wanna see a tremendous victory. You wanna see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did. And again, remember, with the word, it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.“They can take out a city. Let them take, let it, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s, this is a very small price to pay, and it’s gonna be over very soon. It’s essentially almost over with.”If he was talking about the war as being “almost over with”, then he’s certainly wrong, as the conflict drags into its eighth month with no sign of resolution. But if he was talking about the midterms, then he’s correct that it will end soon, and not well for him.In effect, he now has to go into the reddest part of a red state to sustain his vanishing popularity. Monday night’s rally was held at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds, in Hall county, Nebraska, which had a population of 62,895 in 2020. Even farmers are wary of this war, which has raised the price of fertilizers and diesel.The language about LA and San Diego was to be fair, quite vague. Presumably, he was worried that Iran’s nuclear program might be able to target LA or San Diego. But by saying “let them …” it almost sounded like he was encouraging them to, as when John F Kennedy, in Berlin, held up that city as a model of courage and said: “Let them come to Berlin,”in both English and German).In either case, there is no possibility of it happening, as his military advisers know, and as even he must know at some level. Irandoes not have a nuclear weapon,nor can its missiles reach the United States, on either the east or west coast.Furthermore, it is the height of irresponsibility to even discuss such an unimaginable threat. All foreign leaders understand that any attack on the United States with a nuclear weapon would result in an overwhelming counterattack. It’s called deterrence.It is that knowledge – and the cautious way in which previous American presidents have talked about nuclear weapons – that has helped to preserve the peace all these years. We appear to be entering a new era, in which political desperation at home leads to increasingly unhinged threats abroad.The rest of the speech was also a mess. There was a lot of red-baiting, despite the fact that the cold war ended in 1991. There were the usual schoolyard insults, in this case lobbed toward the Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico (“I call him Alfred E Neuman”) and Georgia senator Jon Ossoff (“he looks like Pee-wee Herman to me”).And more pot-stirring, with no basis in fact. Often, his claims undermined each other, as Trump claimed both that Iran has been rendered toothless (“we’re kicking Iran’s ass”) and that it remains a lethal threat, capable of destroying our second- and eighth-largest cities. Which one is it? Over and over, we have heard that Iran’s nuclear program has been “obliterated”. But if so, why are we still at war?The rest of the speech was the usual farrago of distortions and lies, as the most casual effort to factcheck shows. “We want honest,” Trump said at one point, confusingly. Yes, we do.But whether we are going to get it, is another question entirely.Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of AmericaExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026US-Israel war on IranSan DiegoLos AngelescommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are the Democratic Socialists of America so successful? | Akin Olla | The Guardian
description: There’s an unsung reason for the organization’s success even as other leftwing groups face a bumpy road
Author: Akin Olla
Headline: There’s an unsung reason for the organization’s success even as other leftwing groups face a bumpy road
Content: ‘The Democratic Socialists of America functions as a federation in which the national office is beholden to its constituent parts.’Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The Democratic Socialists of America functions as a federation in which the national office is beholden to its constituent parts.’Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesOpinionDemocratic socialismWhy are the Democratic Socialists of America so successful?Akin OllaThere’s an unsung reason for the organization’s success even as other leftwing groups face a bumpy roadWed 7 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTShareA lot has been written recently in an effort to understand the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and how we’ve risen to such prominence in a short time.It is clear that we reflect a growing disillusionment with theDemocratic party, and a further radicalization of the American population. But many leftwing social movement organizations, such asBlack Lives Matterand the Women’s March, have risen in the last decade or so, and many groups, from MoveOn to the Sunrise Movement, have attempted to absorb large numbers of people, influence the Democratic party and enter the public consciousness with lower levels of success.It may just be that we happened to be the organization that had the name closest to the ideology of Bernie Sanders, the man arguably most responsible for reintroducingdemocratic socialismto the popular American lexicon. But name recognition alone can’t explain both our rapid growth and the ability to sustain that growth. Sanders has also talked about the need for a “political revolution” – but his own organization, Our Revolution, is politically irrelevant.The DSA has a believability problem with older Black voters. But young people want to take more risksRead moreWhat is missing from the discussion is the DSA’s structure.Unlike all of the groups I’ve named, it is a thoroughly democratically run organization that allows its members to set its goals, elect its leaders and amend its constitution. None of the other organizations even have constitutions to be altered. Instead, they have corporate bylaws and unelected executive boards to maintain theirtax statuswith the IRS.While the DSA is primarily operated and funded by its growing membership, the other organizations rely on foundation funding and have a deeper reliance on professional staff. While local chapters of most of these groups have almost no control over the national structure, the DSA functions as a federation in which the national office is beholden to its constituent parts.The DSA is not succeeding because of a good name. It is growing because it treats its members like adults capable of managing their own affairs and that of the organization, and they reward it with monthly dues and a long commitment that supersedes the natural highs and lows of uprisings.This idea isn’t new; in fact it is foundational to the success of the American project (well, OK, success is a bit of a stretch, isn’t it?). Writing in the early 19th century, the French philosopher Alexis de Tocquevilledescribedthese kinds of membership-driven organizations as the “free schools” of democracy that serve as the bedrock of America’s political system.They prepare Americans to lead and give them the political vehicles in which they can work with their neighbors to steer the country. This model is dying, but we still see it alive through organizations like the NAACP and the US Student Association, which I was a member of in my youth.The NAACP is more than a hundred years old and the US Student Association will be 80 next year. While the DSA was created in 1982, it can trace its full history as a faction within larger organizations going back wellover a century.It is doubtful that theconflict-ridden Black Lives Global Network Foundation, the 501(c)3 organization that took the reins of the BLM movement, will survive the decade.BLM chapters have dissolved,broken awayor become relatively dormant across the country. The network helped oversee the largest protest in US history, but it is doubtful that there are more than a handful of chapters functioning in the country. The Minneapolis chapter, arguably its most successful, reconstituted itself as Black Visions, and thensunsettedafter years of misalignment and the forcing out of its original leadership.The Green New Deal-championing Sunrise Movement has fared better, but not by much. It too has faced internal power struggles between leadership, who are paid staff members, and its base.double quotation markI joined the DSA after sitting through one meeting and realizing that my voice actually matteredAccordingto one former member, the organization went from having more than 500 chapters in 2021 to probably fewer than 90 by 2023. It has made efforts to become more democratic but could only muster 700 votes for an internal decision, despite counting more than 80,000 members years prior.While some of this must be the natural attrition of social movements – the DSA’s membership also ebbs and flows – founders of the Sunrise Movement have publiclyrecognizedthe internal conflict built into their model.And this is why the DSA will continue to succeed where most groups fail. It has clear mechanisms for its membership to change the direction of the organization without engaging in backroom schemes and internal coups. Clashes still happen, but they are facilitated by clear guidelines that allow factions – called caucuses – to vie for power, and leaders have clear term limits.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI joined the US Student Association (USSA) with a desire to learn from it and steal members for my own organization, in the vein of theQuébécoisstudent unions. But the USSA was so democratic and full of meaningful deliberation that I realized I could change it from within instead of splintering it.Over a decade later, I’m a dedicated alumnus who has volunteered dozens of hours out of sheer love for the organization. There is evidence thatparticipatingin a thoughtful deliberative process increases satisfaction with the outcomes of a decision and trust of institutions.I joined the DSA after sitting through one meeting and realizing that my voice actually mattered. I did not need to become a staff member or somehow be appointed to the board of directors. I could make the DSA what I want it to be, while being transformed by it in turn.I hadn’t experienced that since my days at the USSA’s national student congress. And that is because the new model of social movement organization has long become dominant.Accordingto the Harvard sociologist Theda Skocpol, grant-funded, staff-run, low membership participation models became popular in the 1970s. They create an incentive model that I believe is deleterious to long-term social change.Foundations force organizations to become constant money-chasing machines, applying for annual grant after annual grant, and to adopt a model of centralized control that maximizes efficiency – having tens of thousands of decision-makers can be messy, after all.This model can still bring in a lot of members, but they tend to be temporary participants, or paper members, like the millions of members of MoveOn, who donate monthly but do little to operate between mobilizations, and have no clear role in determining the future of the organization as a whole.I supported the development of a new generation of organizations through my work as a trainer with the Momentum Community, but the groups I advised, many of which are named in this article, still suffered from this top-down non-profit model. These groups can absorb thousands of people in moments of public frustration, but they are structurally unable to keep them.The DSA is growing not only because it reflects frustration over the status quo; it is growing also because it gives people a voice within a vehicle that promises to change that status quo.Akin Olla is a contributing opinion writer at the Guardian USExplore more on these topicsDemocratic socialismOpinionActivismUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Badenoch made the best of it – but the Tories still have a mountain to climb before any hope of No 10  | Henry Hill | The Guardian
description: Conference announcements on inheritance tax and childcare boosted the party’s mood, but the task is still holding off Reform, rather than any realistic bid for power, says the political editor of the Critic, Henry Hill
Author: Henry Hill
Headline: Conference announcements on inheritance tax and childcare boosted the party’s mood, but the task is still holding off Reform, rather than any realistic bid for power, says the political editor of the Critic, Henry Hill
Content: Kemi Badenoch shakes hands with delegates after her speech on the final day of the Conservative conference in Birmingham, 7 October 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch shakes hands with delegates after her speech on the final day of the Conservative conference in Birmingham, 7 October 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionConservative conference 2026Badenoch made the best of it – but the Tories still have a mountain to climb before any hope of No 10Henry HillConference announcements on inheritance tax and childcare boosted the party’s mood, but the task is still holding off Reform, rather than any realistic bid for powerWed 7 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTShareOn paper, the traditional role of the journalist at a British party conference boils down to some simple questions: what was the mood of the assembled activists? Did the leader give a good speech? In practice, the changing nature of conferences and the media makes this superficially simple task more complicated than it may initially appear.Any journalist covering the leader’s speech, for instance, will have watched it in full. But it will reach the vast majority of its intended audience in fragmentary form, through clips – and speeches are increasingly written with that reality in mind. The conference hall is not really the audience, or the full speech really the product. This adds a layer of complexity to the reviewer’s task.Likewise, it is less meaningful than once it was to talk about the mood of the conference. Thirty years ago, when our political parties were much more robust social institutions than they are today, millions of Britons were party members through thick and thin, and thousands attended annual conference whether they liked the leadership or not.It was this democratic culture that gave us the spectacular showdowns at Labour conferences in the 1980s, or Tory activists cheering Norman Tebbit’s excoriation of the European Union in the 1990s. But it is unthinkable now: most people disaffected with a party – especially theConservatives– are simply not members of it; they certainly don’t take time off work and spend several hundred pounds to attend conference.Even with that caveat, however, there is no doubt that the mood inside the Conservative party is considerably improved on last year’s. Manchester proved that Kemi Badenoch can makegood use of a spotlight, even in otherwise extremely challenging conditions, and her position has improved markedly since then. Her personal ratings are up, her party’s polling has recovered (a little), her only real rival for the leadership has defected to Reform UK, and Reform has its own problems.The policy side of things is helping, too. I was very critical of Badenoch’s decision to go as slowly as she did on policy, and do think that first year of near-radio silence did the Tories serious damage. But the eventual policy announcements have, so far, been generally well-considered; if they still tend to err too much on the side of caution, it is at least better than the alternative, the wild promises of an opposition which has abandoned all hope of office.1:37Andy Burnham clashes with Kemi Badenoch at his first PMQs - videoBirmingham has also confirmed that the Conservatives have recognised the need for a strategic pivot. Badenoch has come under fire from some quarters for returning to the party’s “comfort zone” ontax cuts and deregulation, rather than trying to reassemble Boris Johnson’s 2019 coalition and go blow-for-blow with Reform.But that analysis fundamentally misunderstands the current state of play. As much as the gladiatorial spectacle of the “fight on the right” appeals to journalists, so long as the Tories and Reform are polling where they are, they are not really each other’s primary opponent. Reform’s immediate frontlies through Labour; of the 98 seats where it placed second in 2024, 89 are held by a Labour MP.The Conservatives’ front, in contrast, is much more southern, affluent and Liberal Democrat-facing. Many commentators, both inside the party and out, too quickly assume this means “liberal”, because they assume such voters should be Tory by default. This ignores the fact that, by 2024, the Conservatives did not actually have an attractive economic pitch to those voters. Badenoch’s bet is that a substantial number of these voters – both those who defected to the Lib Dems and a large share who party strategists identify as simply having stopped voting – can be wooed back with a strong economic offer on things such aschildcare and inheritance tax.It remains to be seen whether she gets the polling bounce that is the traditional marker of a successful party conference. But based on what I saw over the past few days, I would say this was broadly a positive event for the Tories.I worry, however, that the party itself is over-reading it. Yes, its situation has improved – but that is clearing the extremely low bar set by two sets of catastrophic local elections in 2025 and 2026. Yes, Badenoch’s personal ratings have improved – but she remains in truth the second least unpopular leader, rather than a particularlypopularone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKemi Badenoch is the most rightwing leader in Tory history. Isn’t it time she got some actual scrutiny? | Owen JonesRead moreTory loyalists can be perhaps forgiven, meanwhile, for playing up the “Kemi bounce”, which has lifted their party from about 17.5% to about 20% inthe current polling average, while ignoring the “Kemi slump” that preceded it (she took the leadership when the party was at 26% on that same average). But you would not guess, reading the room in Birmingham, that the Conservatives are still several points shy of their disastrous vote share at the 2024 election.Yet perhaps this is again a problem of the chimerical nature of conference. The party strategists I spoke to seemed quite realistic about their task at the next election: avoid extinction and remain the largest rightwing party. But the party leadership could hardly make that their top line: it would simply demotivate their remaining troops and be severely punished by the press.It is therefore their difficult task to consistently strike an optimistic note without entirely falling for it themselves – and ours to try to work out if, or when, they have.Henry Hill is political editor of the CriticExplore more on these topicsConservative conference 2026OpinionKemi BadenochConservativesConservative conferencecommentShareReuse this content

title: Richard Morecroft’s dulcet tones on ABC news were a virtual comfort blanket for Australians during times of crisis | Max Uechtritz | The Guardian
description: The broadcaster brought heart, soul and empathy to the job, and took new reporters – and baby flying foxes – under his wing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The broadcaster brought heart, soul and empathy to the job, and took new reporters – and baby flying foxes – under his wing
Content: ABC newsreader Richard Morecroft (right) alongside long-time weather presenter Mike Bailey (centre) and director of news and current affairs Max Uechtritz in 2002.Photograph: ABCView image in fullscreenABC newsreader Richard Morecroft (right) alongside long-time weather presenter Mike Bailey (centre) and director of news and current affairs Max Uechtritz in 2002.Photograph: ABCOpinionAustralian mediaRichard Morecroft’s dulcet tones on ABC news were a virtual comfort blanket for Australians during times of crisisMax UechtritzThe broadcaster brought heart, soul and empathy to the job, and took new reporters – and baby flying foxes – under his wingWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.51 EDTShareNo one disproved Hunter S Thompson’s infamous indictment of television more than Richard Morecroft.Richard was the antithesis of Thompson’s denunciation of the TV business as “uglier than most things … a kind of cruel and shallow money trench through the heart of the journalism industry”.Rather than ugly, Richard made the newsroom environment at Sydney’s ABC Gore Hill beautiful. Or as near to beautiful as such a den with such a remit could be. He gave it heart, soul and empathy. Made it interesting and fun. Inclusive. Newcomers – from nervous cadet reporters to production assistants and new co-hosts – would be taken aside for a warm welcome word over a hot cuppa. For a man at the top of the broadcast tree, hierarchy wasn’t in Richard’s vocabulary. Not off air anyway.Richard Morecroft, veteran ABC news presenter, dies aged 70 after cancer diagnosisRead moreYou know someone was born with natural empathy and generosity of spirit when the instinctive reaction from so many – including myself – when learning of his way-too-early death was to remember him as a gentle man and a gentleman.The prime minister has calledhim beloved and a figure of absolute trust, and so he was. Friends and strangers alike have mentioned his dulcet tones, reassuring us in our lounge rooms like a virtual comfort blanket when the news was all conflicts and crises.He’d had practice, of course, fronting the ABC kids’ program Behind the News before coming to national attention co-hosting The National with Geraldine Doogue, with chief reporters Max Walsh and Richard Carleton. A famous photograph of the 1984 ABC federal election coverage from Canberra’s national tally room features Richard Morecroft, Barrie Cassidy, Chris Clark, Jenny Magrath and pre-Antony Green guru, Dr Victor Prescott.View image in fullscreen(L to R) Jenny Magrath, Dr Victor Prescott, Barrie Cassidy, Richard Morecroft and Chris Clark at the ABC desk at the national tally room on the evening of the 1984 federal election.Photograph: National Archives AustraliaIf Richard was among a rare breed of broadcasters who fronted nightly bulletins for nearly two decades (1983–2002), he was unique in another special way. Surely no other newsreader on the planet hadrescued and raised a baby flying fox, which he sometimes kept wrapped in a hanky next to his warm heart while reading the news! It prompted a book and TV production called Raising Archie. Archie had been found clinging to his mum after she’d been electrocuted on power lines. Richard became the foster dad, washing and feeding Archie, changing his nappies and taking him to the post office to weigh. He even helped teach Archie to fly before releasing him into the wilderness.View image in fullscreenRichard Morecroft with Archie, the orphaned baby flying fox he cared for.Photograph: ABCFormer ABC sports presenter Peter Wilkins, who sat next to Richard for years, describes him as self-effacing, the perfect person on set and unflappable. He certainly needed to be, given the antics of the studio crew pulling faces and practical jokes trying to put him off his lines. That was the camaraderie of a bygone era.‘He loved that little bat’: Richard Morecroft’s passion for wildlife rescue praised in tributesRead moreRichard’s memoir, 20 Years from the Waist Up, was typical of his intellectual self-deprecating humour. He wrote of wearing board shorts, bare feet and underwear under the desk and turning the word “rank” into “wank” on air.He cared deeply for our world and environment. Richard wrote at least seven books, including tomes for children on animals and nature. Our family favourite is the gloriously illustrated and written Zoo Album he co-wrote with his wife, Alison Mackay. They kindly inscribed our copy for our children when it was launched in 2003. Our daughter Isabella was eight years old. It left a mark. She’s now a veterinary surgeon.Max Uechtritz is a former ABC news directorExplore more on these topicsAustralian mediaOpinionAustralian Broadcasting CorporationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia is building a lot of new homes. But is the datacentre boom holding us back? | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: Housing construction is at its strongest level since 2016, but it’s AI that is sucking up resources for builders
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: Housing construction is at its strongest level since 2016, but it’s AI that is sucking up resources for builders
Content: In the past year, spending on datacentre construction was 17 times higher than spending on factory construction in Australia, writes Greg JerichoPhotograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenIn the past year, spending on datacentre construction was 17 times higher than spending on factory construction in Australia, writes Greg JerichoPhotograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPGrogonomicsBusinessAustralia is building a lot of new homes. But is the datacentre boom holding us back?Greg JerichoHousing construction is at its strongest level since 2016, but it’s AI that is sucking up resources for buildersWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 18.13 EDTShareThelatest series of data on housing and building activityhas been released, showing residential building is growing strongly but also that the datacentre boom is massive and ongoing.As political parties look to keep housing on the agenda, the massive resources devoted to building datacentres is going to hit anyone wishing to increase housing supply.For a government wanting a good story, it has one in the form of housing. Not only are house prices finally showing some semblance of reality, housing construction is also doing well. In the year to June, the volume of residential building rose 8.7% – the strongest since 2016.If turbocharged petrol prices are driving up inflation, then why are Australia’s unemployed on the line? | Greg JerichoRead moreThe increase of total building was even stronger – up 10% on the year, the best since the GFC stimulus years:Click here if this graph does not displayThe government would also be extremely satisfied to see the number of new private sector house commencements rose 11.6% to 31,707 dwellings.That number is the highest recorded since 1994, excluding the boost during the Covid “homebuilder” surge and the abnormal number of commencements in March 2000 designed to beat the introduction of the GST.Click here if this graph does not displayThe government will suggest this is a sign that investors are shifting to new housing construction, given that still gives them the 50% capital gains tax discount.As the June quarter includes time before and after the budget, we will need to wait for the September quarter to get a better sense of whether or not this is a blip or a more sustained increase.But there is decidedly no blip for public sector housing, which has – for over 30 years now – been barely part of the housing equation.Click here if this graph does not displayThis was a key aspect of a report released last week by the Senate’s select committee on intergenerational housing inequality,Locked Out: The Growing Generational Housing Divide.The committee, chaired by the Greens senator Barbara Pocock and at which I gave evidence, made numerous findings of a pretty general nature. The first was unanimous across all members of the multiparty committee: “It is an indisputable fact, universally agreed by the committee, that Australia is in a housing crisis. This crisis has been long in the making.”The report highlights that while the changes to the CGT discount and negative gearing were vital to improve the housing crisis, there remains still much to be done.Public housing is a key part of that. The committeefound“the dominant message from submitters [including myself] was the need to build significantly more affordable and social housing at scale through long-term government investment and clear delivery targets”.While the committee itself made no specific recommendations, due to its multiparty nature,Senator Pocock proposed“that the Australian government commit to a national target to increase public and community housing to at least 10% of Australia’s housing stock over the next decade”.This would mark a significant shift.From 1955 to 1985, public and social housing accounted for, on average, 13% of all new residential buildings. By contrast, over the past 30 years (aside from the GFC stimulus period), public and social housing has never accounted for more than 4%.In the year to June, it was just 2.3%:Click here if this graph does not displayThe report also noted the issue of rents, and Pocock also proposed a cap on annual rent increases at the lesser of 2% or the inflation rate.What will we get out of the AI boom? The data suggests lots of noisy, energy-hungry datacentres and not much elseRead moreThe issue of rents is rather hot at the moment as the opposition tries to blame rents going up on the changes to the CGT and negative gearing (which is laughable, given anyone renting a place before May is grandfathered), and One Nation are claiming their cuts to migration will deliver falls in rents.In reality, rents essentially follow interest rates:Click here if this graph does not displayBut all housing policy around new builds always needs to deal with the issue of the available number of builders to actually do the work. And this is where the datacentre boom is truly becoming an issue, because that is accounting for stonks of work.Datacentres are covered in the Australian Bureau of Statistics survey under the “commercial building not elsewhere classified (n.e.c)” category. Usually that makes up about 1% of the value of non-residential building commencements. But in the year to June, it was 20%:Click here if this graph does not displaySo big has the surge of datacentre building been that it was worth just under three-quarters of the increase in non-residential building commencements over the past year.We are putting a heck of a lot of eggs into the datacentre basket, hoping like hell it delivers benefits to someone other than AI companies selling hopes and dreams.Usually almost double is spent building factories compared with the buildings in the “commercial n.e.c” category. But in the past year, more than 17 times the amount of money was spent building datacentres than factories:Click here if this graph does not displayThat’s a lot of resources devoted to something that, unlike a factory, will not employ many people after it is built, and unlike a house will not provide a place for people to live for the next 40 years.Right now building construction is doing well. But the question is whether we will look back and see a waste of money and work on buildings that didn’t deliver what was promised, instead of money spent building homes for people to live in or places for people to work.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsBusinessGrogonomicsHousingConstruction industryDatacentres - AustraliaAI (artificial intelligence)RentingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Halloween is looming – this year, I’m ditching my cynicism and getting busy with the pumpkins | Iman Amrani | The Guardian
description: From Day of the Dead to Samhain, celebrating autumn is centuries old. Now, I want this to be a moment of magic and connection for my kids, says writer Iman Amrani
Author: Iman Amrani
Headline: From Day of the Dead to Samhain, celebrating autumn is centuries old. Now, I want this to be a moment of magic and connection for my kids, says writer Iman Amrani
Content: The pumpkin patch at Tulleys Farm, Crawley.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe pumpkin patch at Tulleys Farm, Crawley.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionHalloweenHalloween is looming – this year, I’m ditching my cynicism and getting busy with the pumpkinsIman AmraniFrom Day of the Dead to Samhain, celebrating autumn is centuries old. Now, I want this to be a moment of magic and connection for my kidsWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTShareDarker nights are drawing in, there’s a hint of a chill in the air and the supermarket’s seasonal aisles are groaning with spooky paraphernalia. Halloween is coming. Every year about now, I tell myself I’m going to get my hands on a pumpkin andbake a pielike the ones my mum would make with us when we were little.Halloween wasn’t a huge deal in our house, and neither was baking, but I hold warm memories of helping my mum go through the steps that led us to one delicious latticed pumpkin pie and one uglyjack o’lanternthat we would display in the window with pride.As I got older, Halloween became an excuse to ride around on my bike looking for trouble or going to parties wearing risque outfits under the guise of them being “costumes”. Now, along with that proliferation of Halloween tat in the shops – mountains of plastic ghosts and witches, destined for landfill – cafe chains try to exploit my olfactory memory by lacing their products with artificialpumpkin spiceflavouring. Simple magic has been lost, life has moved on and I realise I’ve never followed through on making that pie.Now I’m a mum to twin toddlers, which means my hands are full – as strangers constantly remind me in the street – but I’m finding myself inclined to create some magic around this dark time of the year, especially at this dark time in the world. Never one to miss an educational moment, my mum would teach us that Halloween wasn’t always an American celebration of commercial excess. One of itspredecessors was Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival still celebrated by some, which marked the end of the harvest season and the beginning of winter, and during which the veil between the physical and spiritual worlds grew thin. A time for reflection and drawing your loved ones close.View image in fullscreenPeople in costume at a Day of the Dead event, Mexico City, 30 October 2025.Photograph: José Méndez/EPALast year, my mother and I took the twins to a Dia de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) community event in Margate, led by local Mexicans. There was Mexican food and music, and even an altar where people could put pictures of lost family members and pets. It was a lovely cultural exchange that felt fun, meaningful and very much in the spirit of the season. Rather than just being about consumption, the event reminded me thatHalloween, Dia de los Muertos or Samhain can also be wonderful opportunities for storytelling – something that should not be underestimated.When I was five, my mother’s father died suddenly, and it concerned me to discover she didn’t hold all the answers about where he had gone. My questions multiplied and I’d sometimes stand in the playground watching other children running around and wonder why no one was talking about the fact that, one day, we were all going to die. The silence made it feel much more scary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStores are selling Halloween stuff in August. Time has lost all meaning | Dave SchillingRead moreI have a lot of bones to pick with Disney, but our family loves thefilm Coco, which is set in Mexico during Dia de los Muertos. Miguel, the protagonist, crosses over to the Land of the Dead in search of his ancestors. Watching it as an adult makes me realise how much I needed stories like this as a child, that could have helped me make sense of terrifying unknowns such as death. We are living through scary times on so many levels and a celebration now feels like as good a time as any to build strength and resilience through imagination and the exchange of stories.The twins are still small, but they have loved the books we got from the library with themes of witches and werewolves or yetis and fairies. I have paper Halloween decorations from last year stored with the Christmas ones and the twins have worn their bat costumes again to flap around the living room. These are moments that I treasure already.They are remembering things now too, which means we are in a memory-building era. I am not going to kill myself with an unrealistic Halloween to-do list, and I don’t want to contribute to unnecessary waste, but this year I’m adamant that we will go to a pumpkin patch together, so they can connect this time of year to harvest and nature. And I’m going to make that pie, although I might have to invite my mum over to help us. I’m still getting started on all of this but I’m going to embrace the celebration in the spirit that my mother did, and try to add my own details to the story. Just don’t expect anything from me at Easter.Iman Amrani is a freelance writer and producerExplore more on these topicsHalloweenOpinionAutumnChildrenPumpkinFamilyAutumn food and drinkcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Greens may yet win in Holborn and St Pancras – but what happened to the party set to ‘replace’ Labour? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: On the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political margins, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: On the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political margins, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Zack Polanski and Green party deputy leader, Mothin Ali, with supporters in Camden, north London, during the campaign for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, 26 September 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenZack Polanski and Green party deputy leader, Mothin Ali, with supporters in Camden, north London, during the campaign for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, 26 September 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionGreen partyThe Greens may yet win in Holborn and St Pancras – but what happened to the party set to ‘replace’ Labour?Andy BeckettOn the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political marginsWed 7 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.26 EDTShareOnly a few months ago, in the spring, there was a sense of giddy possibility about the Greens. Zack Polanski’s radical new leadership felt fresh and dynamic, especially compared with those of the other parties. Former Labour supporters, in particular, were switching tothe Greens in huge numbers, Green candidateswere winningacrossthe country, and the party wassecond behind Reform UKin some national polls.Like Reform, theGreen partypresented itself as a revolt against a failed status quo. Unlike Reform, the Greens’ urgent stance on the climate crisis gave them a potent moral authority: even many people who did not support them believed that the Greens were right about the most universal issue.After an unprecedentedly hot summer, some of that authority and momentum remains. Last week, at theparty’s bustling conferencein Brighton, impressive-sounding statistics about the party’s growth this year – along with modern icons of Green success,such as Hannah Spencer, victor of February’s Gorton and Denton byelection – were presented to determinedly cheering delegates in crammed halls.This week, in the high-profile London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras, wherePolanski hopes to succeed Keir Starmerin Thursday’s byelection, the usual cheery squads of Green activists have been striding back and forth between wealthy streets and council estates, distributing thick bundles of a party newspaper with the front-page headline “Greens close in!”. Given the party’s recent election record, Polanski’s populist appeal and the possibility that some of the many local leftwing voters may see the contest as a low-risk way to warn Andy Burnham not to follow Starmer’s premiership rightwards,a Green win is not impossible.But, even if it happens, the problems the party has accumulated since the spring will not have gone away. For some voters, the novelty of Polanski’s leadership has faded. For others his style, more radical and provocative than previous Green leaders, has allowed the party to shift to extreme positions, particularly on Israel, with the Brighton conference passing a motion (which the Jewish Polanski neither supported nor opposed) that “Zionism is racism”.Zack Polanski had the chance to show real leadership. He blew it | Rafael BehrRead moreMeanwhile, Burnham’s confident, sometimes iconoclastic start as prime minister has removed Polanski’s unique selling point as a good communicator who does not accept the usually conservative terms of British political debate.In his conference speech, Polanski admitted: “Now I get asked, isn’t your job done?”The idea that one of the Greens’ main purposes is to shiftLabourleftwards and towards bolder climate policies, and that that approach is yielding results, was everywhere at Brighton, from mutually encouraging chats between activists in the queues to upbeat contributions from the main stage.It’s not a role that should be dismissed as minor. The Greens’ influence over Labour – both undermining Starmer in record time by taking so many votes from his party and creating political space for Burnham’s coup and governmental refresh – has arguably been a sign of Britain belatedly catching up with other European democracies, such as Spain, where centre-left parties have long been forced to be bolder by more leftwing ones. After decades of Labour paying most attention to forces to its right, the Greens’ important place in Labour’s calculations makes a refreshing change.And yet, being an influence rather than a definite national rival – the Greens are now about20 points behind Labourin some polls – is undeniably a comedown. During Polanski’s first months as leader, he regularly said he wanted the Greens to“replace” Labour. Partly because of that apparent possibility, the Greens attracted respected leftwing strategists such asMichael ChessumandJames Meadway, who had worked under Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership and became disillusioned by Labour under Starmer.At some leftwing gatherings last spring, those who hadn’t switched to the Greens could feel a bit over-cautious and old-fashioned. It’s possible that the rightwing media even encouraged this shift, giving Polanski plenty of coverage, in order to divide the left and prevent Labour from ever holding sole power again.With Labour’s electoral future now looking more promising, one of the Greens’ leaflets in Holborn and St Pancras modestly presents Polanski as “a strong voice … tokeep Labour in check”. In his Brighton speech, Polanski said: “Vote Green and watch Labour move.” It’s a typically pithy and clever line: explaining the mechanics of politics to voters, and treating them like grownups, in ways that party leaders rarely do.But it may not be an inspiring line for more tribal Greens who decided decades ago that Labour, and alliances with Labour, were not for them. Another Green conference theme was “Real hope. Real change.” It sounded defensive, and too similar to Labour’s conference theme the previous week: “Hope again”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Greens do still hold the initiative on some issues: advocating rent controls, wealth taxes, an end to fiscal conservatism, and more radical climate policies, with Labour expected soon to allow alimited expansion of oil and gas drillingin the North Sea. There are also signs of the Greens positioning themselves as the party of the most disadvantaged, such as asylum seekers, benefits claimants and transgender people – groups that Burnham’s less judgmental government may treat better than Starmer’s did, yet probably within limits set by Labour’s considerable number of socially conservative supporters.“We will always stand with … everyone who is under attack,” said Polanski in Brighton, a statement that could be seen as too vague, impractical and idealistic. Yet if this country is to become a more truly representative democracy – a possible upside of the current political fragmentation – why shouldn’t the most vulnerable effectively have their own party? The most privileged have had the Tories for centuries.The astute political analystRob Ford suggeststhat the Greens’ poll decline “may not matter much” if the party still campaigns effectively and attracts strong support from the dozens of relatively youthful, highly educated and diverse urban constituencies. Thursday’s byelection will test that theory.Yet either way, there is something disturbing about a party with such a crucial cause having to face a reduction in status. The Greens’ drift back towards the political margins reflects not just their own mistakes, but the reluctance of many Britons to face up to climate realities. As withExtinction Rebellion, it’s more comfortable to call them extremists and ignore what they say.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
