title: Three years on from the 7 October attacks, antisemitism has taken hold in Britain: Jews aren’t safe | Dave Rich | The Guardian
description: Britain cannot call itself a diverse democracy when communities are living with such fear. A line must be drawn. Let it be now, says Dave Rich, author and director of policy at the Community Security Trust
Author: Dave Rich
Headline: Britain cannot call itself a diverse democracy when communities are living with such fear. A line must be drawn. Let it be now, says Dave Rich, author and director of policy at the Community Security Trust
Content: Demonstrators in Whitehall, London, following a series of attacks on Jews, 10 May 2026.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenDemonstrators in Whitehall, London, following a series of attacks on Jews, 10 May 2026.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyOpinionAntisemitismThree years on from the 7 October attacks, antisemitism has taken hold in Britain: Jews aren’t safeDave RichBritain cannot call itself a diverse democracy when communities are living with such fear. A line must be drawn. Let it be nowWed 7 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 04.09 EDTShareOn another anniversary of the 7 October attacks, the lasting impact on Britain’s Jews is found in the essential daily decisions we now have to make. Beyond the simple fear that you or your children might get killed the next time you go to synagogue or visit your local kosher shop, Jews are hiding the fact they are Jewish.This has gone beyond the choice of whether to wear your Star of David necklace inside or outside your shirt. It is found in the job applicants who remove their Jewish community volunteering from their CV; the people who use false names when ordering an Uber; the parents who move their children from mainstream schools to Jewish ones.The danger for Britain runs deep, for if Jews cannot live an open Jewish life here, then modern Britain as a cohesive, diverse liberal democracy will have failed.This didn’t begin with Jews. The murder of Terence Carney, a 70-year-old man from Hartlepool, County Durham, may not seem an obvious starting point when trying to understand the impact the Hamas attack and what followed has had on Britain, but it has proved to be a chilling portent of much of what has followed since.Carney had gone for his regular morning walk in October 2023 when he was fatally stabbed by Ahmed Alid, an Islamist extremist who had arrived in the UK illegally three years earlier. Alid had already tried to kill his Iranian housemate Javed Nouri, who had converted to Christianity and whom he regarded to be an “apostate”. Nouri managed to fight him off, but Carney was not so lucky.When police asked Alid why he had committed these appalling acts, he said he wanted “Palestine to be free from the Zionists” and that he had murdered Carney, a random passerby with no connection to the Middle East, “because Israel was killing children”. This was just eight days after the 7 October attack on southern Israel – the day on which about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, were killed by Hamas – but already the ripple of that attack had washed on to British shores.People rarely speak about Terence Carney now, but he was the first victim of terrorism on British soil related to 7 October and the subsequent tragedy inGaza.As I describe in my new book, From Be’eri to Bondi: Global Antisemitism After October 7, the Hamas attack and the wars in Gaza and the wider Middle East that followed unleashed a lethal combination of terrorist violence and extremist incitement, street protests and viral campaigns, rising hate crimes and falling social cohesion, with hostile states such as Iran stoking the fire. All of this was both predictable and predicted: it was no surprise that after the atrocities by Hamas in the Be’eri kibbutz and elsewhere in southern Israel in 2023 camethe massacre of Jews on Bondi Beachtwo years later.At first, Britain largely avoided the wave of anti-Jewish violence that swept world after 7 October. In the past 12 months that has changed. Since the terror attack atHeaton Park synagogue in Manchesterlast year that killed Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby, injured others and left a community traumatised, Britain has witnessed the stabbing of Jewish men in Golders Green, arson attacks on synagogues “almost certainly directed” from Iran, and the conviction of two Islamic extremists for a terrorist plot against Manchester’s Jewish community that could have killed hundreds. Just this week, two Iranianshave been chargedwith an alleged plot, also to target Jewish people in the Manchester area. This has gone well beyond a problem for Britain’s Jewish community. In its scale and impact, it’s a threat to our national security.Why these attacks are occurring is where things get complicated. It has become impossible not to notice that the justifications anti-Jewish terrorists offer for their crimes echo the language and ideas that motivate large numbers of people to march peacefully against Israel. Alid’s desire to expel Zionists from Palestine and avenge Palestinian children’s deaths in Gaza, for example, is more widely held than ought to be comfortable, given how he acted as a result. You can even hear an echo of that desire in the recentGreen party votecondemning Zionism to be racism. I am sure most protesters who march for Palestine would never endorse Alid’s bloody methods, but the similarity of slogans is troubling nonetheless.We think of democratic protest and terrorism as two opposing categories of behaviour, but the world is not so neat. Political violence always draws sustenance from a hinterland of ideas and rhetoric shared by many more people who would never pick up a knife or a gun, but who articulate the same grievances.The belief that Israel is engaged in a “war on children” is common across the pro-Palestine movement,promoted by major NGOsand found in a thousand Instagram reels about genocidal Zionist baby-killers. Without doubt, it is deeply upsetting that thousands of Palestinian children have been killed in Gaza, and many feel that Israel could have done more to minimise civilian casualties. But to describe this not as the result of a tragic and unbearable conflict, but as a “war on children”, is to imply that killing children is the whole point: a charge that echoes the medieval blood libel. From that assumption to Jihad al-Shamie yelling: “This is what you get for killing our children” as he tried to batter down the doors of Heaton Park synagogue last Yom Kippur is not as big a leap as some might wish.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI know this reality is uncomfortable for some. It would be far more convenient if the people attacking Jews always wore swastikas rather than, as has happened, keffiyehs. The riposte that British Jews should take more care not to conflate themselves with Israel misses the point entirely. Nobody tells Russians in London not to conflate themselves with Russia, just as nobody threatens to protest outside their local Chinese takeaway about the Chinese government’s treatment of the Uyghurs, assome have protestedat Israeli-owned restaurants in Britain. It wouldn’t even occur to people to do so. The double standard, the unique demand, is the first stage of discrimination.We are in an extraordinary period. That the Home Office hashad to commit£250m to increase policing in Jewish communities across England and Wales, while also raising the national terrorist threat level, recognising the scale of anti-Jewish terrorism and far-right extremism, shows the staggering cost of failing to tackle antisemitism at its source. The government now has plenty of reviews and recommendations to implement regarding how to reduce the extremism that drives anti-Jewish hatred. Civil society, too, needs to step up: it can’t all be left to Whitehall.The history of antisemitism is marked by moments in time and place when it has been politically weaponised by dangerous actors who are able to lure millions to its toxic scent. The blending of vengeful anti-Israel sentiment with older antisemitic tropes over the past three years, all while Jews are being murdered on multiple continents, makes me fear we have entered such a phase.Antisemitismmatters once more, and we all have a role to play in addressing it.Dave Rich is director of policy at the Community Security Trust.His new book, From Be’eri to Bondi: Global Antisemitism After October 7, is published by RoutledgeDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I see what’s happening here in Paris: reasonable student demands met with awful violence  | Helen Massy-Beresford | The Guardian
description: The debate around the schools protests is angry and polarised: a foretaste of how next year’s presidential election is likely to play out, says Helen Massy-Beresford, a British journalist and editor who lives in Paris
Author: Helen Massy-Beresford
Headline: The debate around the schools protests is angry and polarised: a foretaste of how next year’s presidential election is likely to play out, says Helen Massy-Beresford, a British journalist and editor who lives in Paris
Content: Demonstrators and French police clash in Paris on Tuesday during a nationwide day of student protests over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreenDemonstrators and French police clash in Paris on Tuesday during a nationwide day of student protests over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersOpinionFranceI see what’s happening here in Paris: reasonable student demands met with awful violenceHelen Massy-BeresfordThe debate around the schools protests is angry and polarised. I fear this is a foretaste of how election tensions next year will play outHelen Massy-Beresford is a British journalist who lives in ParisWed 7 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 10.39 EDTShareIt would be tough to argue that the demands of France’s protesting high school students are not reasonable ones, worth taking to the streets for:investment in crumbling schools, replacing absent teachers, reducing class sizes and overstuffed timetables, and bridging the inequality gap between schools in different areas.Theprotests across the countryon Tuesday, which demonstrators dubbedl’acte III(Act 3), orla grande mobilisation,were billed as the most dramatic day of action yet, with more school blockades and a march through central Paris in the afternoon. More than 400 schoolsclosed preventively, including my elder daughter’s, a combined collège (for 11- to 15-year-olds) and lycée.At 11 she’s too young to be involved, and after her reports of fireworks, burning bins and smoke as she and her friends ran in through the gates one day last week, I must say I’m relieved – no matter how worthwhile the cause. It was business as usual on Friday (a few more parents picking up their children than would normally, though), while on Tuesdaymorning, with school closed, the gates were blocked with bins and about 50lycéens(one dressed as Batman) were there, wielding their banners. The atmosphere was calm, with attention shifting to the big protest march through the city due later in the day.While there have been some cases of violence from protesters,heavy-handed police methodshave been severely criticised. In one incident, in Tours, a 16-year-old boy lost sight in his right eye, an injury the city’s prosecutor said was consistent with a rubber bullet. In a particularly dark turn on Monday, and in circumstances that are not yet entirely clear,a lycée student lost his handat a demonstration in Lens, northern France. A police investigation is under way.As the protests have grown in scope, the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has promised the government will listen and try to meet the main demands – but that’s unlikely to mean suddenly freeing up billions to invest in schools that have gone underfunded for years, as thevideos posted onlineof rat-infested, flooded or crumbling classrooms testify.View image in fullscreenA protester throws a traffic cone at a member of the riot police during a demonstration of high-school students in Paris on Tuesday.Photograph: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP/Getty ImagesThe political debate surrounding the escalating social movement is angry and polarised: a foretaste of the how the country’s April 2027 presidential election is likely to play out. The high school movement comes at an already tense time, with France’s government once again trying to push through a budget full of spending cuts without a parliamentary majority.Last year, to get the budget over the line, the government had to usespecial constitutional powersto bypass the need for a parliamentary vote. This year’s budget, due for a vote in November, includes pension and healthcare cuts aimed at helping to plug the seemingly bottomless budget deficit – and is likely to be just as problematic for the government.The intensity of the protests has prompted a mudslinging match between two of the favourites for the first round of the presidential elections. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed, is vocally on the side of the protesters (many of whom will vote for his party when old enough) but rejects the narrative that his party stirred up the unrest. Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is using the protests to call foran anti-riot law. She’s clearly not following the advice of the Socialist party leader, Olivier Faure, who during apresidential primary debateamong leftwing candidates urged people not to fall into the classic rightwing trap of focusing on the violence while ignoring the cause of the protests.Faure made reference to the proverb of the wise man pointing at the moon and the fool looking at his finger: “look at the moon, not the finger,” he said – and it’s a sensible message for all the wannabe presidents. Many of thelycéensprotesting today will be voting for the first time next April.Even if Le Pen is now looking at the finger, she certainly shouldn’t be written off for next year’s election; her message seems to be resonating with a large number of French citizens and she is the clear favourite for the first round of the presidential elections. We’ve been here before: if the polls are correct, it will beLe Pen’s third second-round run-off. The difference is that in 2022 and 2017 she was up against Emmanuel Macron – a centrist candidate who voters from across the spectrum could get behind to block her, even if many reported holding their nose at the ballot box.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs things stand, that may be harder for many in 2027. Le Pen’s opposition is fragmented, with several potential candidates still in the running on the left and centre right – and because of that, Le Pen’s second-round adversary may prove easier for her to beat, to the benefit of absolutely no one.Everything stayed quiet yesterday in my north-east Paris neighbourhood. But in the centre of the city, organisers saysome 100,000 people turned out(the interior ministry estimated 56,000).Under a blazing early October sun, huge – and mainly calm – crowds gathered in Place de la République and marched to Place de la Nation to chant and wave placards. As the main crowd dispersed, some small groups clashed with police as the sun was setting.For now, themovement’s momentum seems to be building, not receding. Some politicians are realising that, six months away from a fraught election, they should listen to their future voters.Helen Massy-Beresford is a British journalist and editor who lives in ParisExplore more on these topicsFranceOpinionProtestYoung peopleSchoolsMarine Le PenParisEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Zack Polanski had the chance to show real leadership. He blew it | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: A toxic debate over anti-Zionism leaves the Green leader looking like a passenger in the movement that carried him to the top, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: A toxic debate over anti-Zionism leaves the Green leader looking like a passenger in the movement that carried him to the top, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Zack Polanski campaigning in Holborn and St Pancras, London, ahead of the byelection in the constituency on Thursday.Photograph: Neil Terry/Story Picture AgencyView image in fullscreenZack Polanski campaigning in Holborn and St Pancras, London, ahead of the byelection in the constituency on Thursday.Photograph: Neil Terry/Story Picture AgencyOpinionZack PolanskiZack Polanski had the chance to show real leadership. He blew itRafael BehrA toxic debate over anti-Zionism leaves the Green leader looking like a passenger in the movement that carried him to the topWed 7 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 04.09 EDTShareWhen Donald Trump calls someone a socialist he is not using the word in the same way that, say, Zohran Mamdani does. The mayor of New York espouses democratic socialism as a mission of equitable distribution of wealth and opportunity.The US president sayssocialism only pretends to be democratic “because it sounds so nice”; that “it’s really communism you’re talking about” and that people such as Mamdani pose “the biggest threat to our nation … since its founding”.People who despise an idea, seeing it as the manifestation of everything wicked, cannot be expected to define it accurately. As with the radical right and socialism, so it is with the left and Zionism.There are interwoven historical, biblical and intellectual strands to the belief that Jews have an ancestral homeland on the eastern border of the Mediterranean. It is a belief that has evolved across centuries. It was expressed as liturgical yearning before being crystallised in the modern era as a political ambition to be safe from persecution, given urgency by mass slaughter before achieving realisation in 1948 with the foundation of the state now calledIsrael. Since then it has been refracted through different lenses of war and contemporary Israeli politics.That process defies capture by a single word. Zionism can be left and right; moderate and extreme.It contains multitudes. Unless you want to join the Green party of England and Wales, in which case, there is only one permitted definition. Last weekend, the partyvoted for a motionthat declares Zionism “fundamentally incompatible with anti-racist principles, equality and justice” because it is based on “European settler-colonial systems of domination and oppression”. The Greens are now an “anti-Zionist” party to their constitutional core.Any objection on the basis that such a policy vilifies Jews who recognise other definitions of Zionism is dealt with in a pre-emptive clause. The only target is Zionism “as defined” in the motion and not the “religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists”.By this Orwellian formula, Jews who call themselves Zionists are still tolerable to the Greens, but only if their personal understanding of Zionism is something the party considers to be the wrong one. If they want to be loyal members, they should adopt the doctrinally correct definition. But then they would have to stop being Zionists. Jews are welcome as long as they repress undesirable features of their cultural identity and religious practice to satisfy the party line.Naturally, the drafters of the motion do not think this is antisemitism. Here is another word whose meaning is defined not with reference to the experience of Jews but to the grievance of those who don’t like to be accused of targeting them. In the radical-left lexicon, antisemitism is addressed most commonly as the charge that cannot fairly be levelled against an “anti-Zionist” – the tool that Zionists use to deflect criticism of their nefarious ways.In practice, the Greens have made themselves hostile to the vast majority of British Jews, given the density of kinship connections and emotional sympathies, past or present, that most have to the idea of Israel as a place of sanctuary.Many hate the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, are repulsed by the racist pronouncements of his far-right ministers, horrified by the atrocious conduct of the war in Gaza and prepared to condemn it without equivocation. They despair at the ultra-nationalist trend in Israeli politics but hold that feeling alongside a belief that the country itself should be allowed to exist.The Greens disagree. They reject a two-state solution in the Middle East on the basis that Israel – not just occupied Palestinian territories, but the whole country – is illegitimate in its conception. It is an aberration whose erasure from the map is a non-negotiable demand in the global struggle against racism.That position is more extreme than the one held by the Palestinian Authority. It has broughtcensure from the European Green group, to which the Green party of England and Wales is affiliated. It has issued a statement observing that fewer than 1% of members voted for the anti-Zionism motion and that Green MPs and other senior figures in the party opposed it. In light of that contradiction, they seek “clarity from the leadership”.They won’t get it from Zack Polanski. If the Green leader had wanted to make his position clear he could have stayed in Brighton for the debate, spoken his mind and cast his vote. Buthe slipped away to campaignahead of this week’s byelection in Holborn and St Pancras, the north London seatvacated by Keir Starmer.Polanski is Jewish. His stated attitude to Zionism is convoluted. He recognises that it means different things to different people. He endorsed a homeopathic “safeguarding” amendment to reassure Jewish Greens that attendance at synagogues, most of which hold to some idea of Zionism, would not lead to sanction by the party. The amendment was rejected.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolanski’s influence over the process was limited by the Green party’s rulebook, which gives the membership control over policy. It is unclear whether he could have swayed opinion by deploying the charisma that won him the leadership last year and, by viral contagion on social media,massively boosted party membership. He didn’t appear to try. Maybe he doesn’t know what he believes. Perhaps he feels more like a hostage of the movement that carried him to the top than its leader. Probably both.That is the suspicion of some Green veterans. They feel their partyhas been capturedby a well-organised, itinerant caucus of militant left activists who have been looking for a new host since Jeremy Corbyn and his acolytes lost control of Labour. Obsession with Israel, crowding out the party’s environmental message, is a tell.There is an ideological chain of association in the view that climate justice can only be realised by the defeat of oppressive capitalist systems of which Zionism is thene plus ultra. That approach can be effective for animating the passionate ideals of a young crowd that sees the horrors of Gaza as the defining moral cause of their generation. But it also alienates a wider audience of people who want aGreen partythat campaigns effectively on the climate and who don’t see why the road to a low-carbon future has to be paved with rows about antisemitism of the kind that poisoned Labour under Corbyn.Polanski is not going to resolve that tension. He is a talented communicator as long as his audience is predisposed to like the message. His authority is solar-powered, activated only when the light of an enthusiastic crowd shines directly on him. If there is a risk of no applause, he powers down. He had the opportunity at the Brighton conference to demonstrate a different kind of authority, generated from within, expressing conviction derived from a stable core of belief, made compelling by courage. It is the stuff of which leadership is made. Polanski doesn’t have it. If those are also qualities the voters of Holborn and St Pancras care for in a local MP, they will have to seek them elsewhere.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘In the wake of death, Courtney Love was giving it her all’: Hole’s Melissa auf der Maur on her best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘This is Courtney doing her makeup on the ’95 Lollapalooza tour. I was documenting my generation being hijacked by corporate greed – and destroyed following the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘This is Courtney doing her makeup on the ’95 Lollapalooza tour. I was documenting my generation being hijacked by corporate greed – and destroyed following the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain’
Content: ‘When the wild alternative freaks crossed into the mainstream’ … Self-Portrait with Hole, Lollapalooza, 1995.Photograph: Melissa Auf der Maur, courtesy DelMonico Books/AGO TorontoView image in fullscreen‘When the wild alternative freaks crossed into the mainstream’ … Self-Portrait with Hole, Lollapalooza, 1995.Photograph: Melissa Auf der Maur, courtesy DelMonico Books/AGO TorontoMy best shotArt and design‘In the wake of death, Courtney Love was giving it her all’: Hole’s Melissa auf der Maur on her best photograph‘This is Courtney doing her makeup on the ’95 Lollapalooza tour. I was documenting my generation being hijacked by corporate greed – and destroyed following the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain’Interview by Zoe WhitfieldWed 7 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was going through the archives for my rock photo book, I came across my first ever self-portrait, at Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris, in front of Jim Morrison’s grave. I am a 13-year-old on an awkward trip with my cool father. He had no respect or interest in Jim Morrison, and that photo is like every photo I’ve taken from that moment on – I’m trying to take agency over what is happening. Photography was the absolute first thing that gave me a feeling of having my own say. It became a way of creating my own universe, one that I could trust. It was absolutely my first love.I was sidetracked into music in a beautiful way by these radical women and a countercultural movement, so the subject of my photographs just changed. It was me within this environment, on stage with Hole, backstage with these luminary, wild people, travelling across the world. My photography followed and morphed with me, and my camera documented my generation being hijacked by corporate greed and destroyed in the wake of the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain. It was a generational call to document the Lollapalooza ’95 tour, where this photo was taken, for us to understand later. It was also when the wild alternative freaks crossed into the mainstream.double quotation markShe trusted me to be her bass player and right-hand woman. My camera got to just drink that inBass players are natural wallflowers and I always had a camera with me, just like everyone has a phone now. In terms of my duty as a female photographer in Hole – not a girlfriend, not an outside male photographer – I was able to glean the essence of that band through that misunderstood and wildly celebrated, but also dismantled queen, Courtney. What I love about the photos of her, and in this photo where she’s just doing her makeup, getting ready to go on stage, is she trusted me so implicitly. She either didn’t notice the camera, or she gave herself to the camera, so I was able to capture her true essence, in the same way that she trusted me to be her bass player and right-hand woman. My camera and I got to just drink that in.Courtney had been asked to do a tour diary of Lollapalooza for Spin magazine, so it was natural they asked me to take the photos. It felt really grown up for a 23-year-old. I was capturing the humanity, mystery and happiness – as much reality as possible to unpack later, understanding that time and distance would give me perspective. I had bought a new camera for the road, a Nikon point-and-shoot, because my manual camera was not cutting it on tour. It was a camera that could adapt to the subject changing quickly, and shit was happening quick. The wide-angle lens was a revelation, because my little hand could get the giant ocean of crowd, and I could also fit four people in a frame.This photo captures the spirit of the people who were central to this story in a very particular way, which is kind of how it landed on the cover of this book. It was near the end of the three-week tour; I have a whole roll that I took this day. I would always photograph us right before going on stage, unless shit was bad, so the fact I have half a roll of that moment means we were obviously feeling very strong that night. That is rare in a band that was living in the wake of death, with the struggles of addiction and with enemies on the tour. The fact I was confident enough to take our photo so much makes me think it was a very happy day on what should have been a very happy time in our band. We were at the peak of our alternative power, co-headlining with Sonic Youth, and Courtney was giving her all. Her life was an absolute nightmare – and there was a rivalry with Sonic Youth, who were the gatekeepers of cool at that moment – but she was giving her all on this tour.My life in the band was the defining role of that decade for me. Yes, I was later in the Smashing Pumpkins, and yes, I was an art photographer too, but my life in Hole defined me spiritually, emotionally, musically, and also publicly. Courtney, obviously, is infamous and misunderstood, but my portraits of her in this book are loving and true.Melissa Auf der Maur: My ’90s Rock Photographs is published byDelMonico Books. It accompanies the exhibition atArt Gallery of Ontario, until 6 June 2027.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Norman Jean Roy/Courtesy of the ArtistMelissa Auf der Maur’s CVBorn:Montreal, 1972High point:My 21st-century midlife resurrection as a photographer, out of the wild flames of the 90s rock life that defined me. It’s a very exciting way to use the past as a barometer, and as a way finder for the futureTop tip:The problem with our digital reality now is this abundance – I loved that, in the pre-digital film era, there was a limitation. So now it’s work within limitations and with intention, and then find your signature storytellingExplore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotCourtney LovefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and Niles | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: From a breathless tango to a kiss that sent fans wild, the pair crafted a sensational seven-year TV crush. The real-life best friends talk first impressions, Casablanca moments – and having hot husbands
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: From a breathless tango to a kiss that sent fans wild, the pair crafted a sensational seven-year TV crush. The real-life best friends talk first impressions, Casablanca moments – and having hot husbands
Content: ‘Our bodies must be in continuous contact!’ Daphne and Niles in the actors’ favourite scene.Photograph: NBC/NBCUniversal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Our bodies must be in continuous contact!’ Daphne and Niles in the actors’ favourite scene.Photograph: NBC/NBCUniversal/Getty ImagesMaking loveTelevision & radio‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and NilesFrom a breathless tango to a kiss that sent fans wild, the pair crafted a sensational seven-year TV crush. The real-life best friends talk first impressions, Casablanca moments – and having hot husbandsLesley Manville and Peter Mullan on their heart-melting TV romanceHollie RichardsonWed 7 Oct 2026 06.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Dr Crane, your glockenspiel has sprung to life!”It was a crush. An unexpected one. The psychiatrist Niles Crane (snooty, conflict-avoidant, married to a high-society wife with a fear of buffets) fell for his father’s physio, Daphne Moon (working class, Mancunian, reckons she’s a bit psychic)the moment he met herin his brother’s Seattle apartment.Across seven seasons of the mega-sitcomFrasier, the crush took hold. Daphne remained seemingly oblivious, but the pair built a friendship and a will-they-won’t-they story that fans loved to be teased with. It made for some cracking episodes: from the pair being holed up in Niles’ candlelit mansion during a rainstorm (with that broken glockenspiel) in the side-splitting A Mid-Winter Night’s Dream, to a passionate leg-in-the-air tango after Niles’ divorce in Moon Dance (“Oh mama, I’ve got it all!”).View image in fullscreenAnd the dish ran away with the spoon … Niles and Daphne in Frasier.Photograph: Getty ImagesDaphne finally learned the truth the night before her wedding to Donny. The next morning, in her white gown, she knocked on the Winnebago in which Niles (four days into a bad new marriage himself) was hiding and told him to drive.“Fasten your seatbelt, Daphne.”“Fasten yours, Niles.”It’s been 22 years since we last saw the pair on screen, but the stars Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce remain dear friends. Hyde Pierce attended – and had a near fatal car accident at – Leeves’ English wedding and he is godfather to her son. They are both in long-term marriages: Hyde Pierce and the writer-producer Brian Hargrove married in 2008 after 25 years together; Leeves and the TV executive Marshall Coben have been married for 30 years. In fact, John Mahoney, who played Marty Crane in Frasier, predicted Leeves’ relationship one day in the green room: “I always wanted kids and said to John: ‘I’m going to adopt,’” she remembers. “He said: ‘Do not do that now. Within a year, you will meet someone.’ And she did, at a Paramount party. “I don’t know how that happened.”View image in fullscreenIn the chair … Leeves and Hyde Pierce backstage on Frasier.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane Leeves“I love you doing this,” Leeves laughs from her Malibu kitchen, as Hyde Pierce joins from a study (which features a bookcase Niles would be proud of) in his New York home. He claims to have just had his hair done – endearingly, he’s a bit frazzled – before asking for reassurance that no one will see this video. They’re more than happy, though, to tell the story of Daphne and Niles.Do you remember meeting for the first time?Jane Leeves:I was on the set on the first day of the pilot and I saw David walking in and crossing the bleachers. I went racing up to him like a mad fan because I’d been watching [the Washington-DC-based sitcom] The Powers That Be, which was cancelled for some bizarre reason – it was brilliant and he played the most odd and fabulous character. I don’t think you really had any dialogue, did you?David Hyde Pierce:No, I played a suicidal congressman who only mumbled.JL:I thought there was a calmness, a kindness and an intellect that was devastatingly sexy, I have to say.DHP:Well, I thought: I can’t believe Paramount Studios doesn’t have security … No, I realised that I lucked out getting the best loon in the business.JL:A couple of lunatics.DHP:I knew her from Seinfeld and Murphy Brown – another show from the dark ages. And we just felt like kindred spirits. It’s safe to say that was true of the whole cast. They put a real family together.JL:It was extraordinary, because I was the only person at that first table read who had read with Kelsey [Grammer]. So the chemistry was unknown.View image in fullscreen‘You were pulling my tie and I liked it’ … David Hyde Pierce and Jane Leeves in Frasier.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyDHP:Also, we did a photoshoot before the pilot and I remember Jane saying something about how there could be just a little something between us, and we ended up leaning on each other.JL:I was pulling your tie.DHP:Yes, and I liked it.JL:The idea came into my head that they were polar opposites and it would be funny if he found her attractive – because she was also the opposite of Maris.What was your real relationship like off camera?JL:Contentious.DHP:A lot of sex.JL:I love David. He’s a true gentleman in every sense of the word and the finest human being you’ll ever meet.DHP:It was as it is now. We’re just best friends. Jane and her husband, Marshall, rented this wonderful shack near the ocean in Malibu. My husband and I, and our dog, would go over and stay. When they moved on, they talked to the landlord about us taking over the rental and we did that. We were very close.JL:John Mahoney was asking me for my parents’ address [in East Grinstead, West Sussex] one time – he wanted to send them a card – and I read it out. And David went: “Muffin-on-Poot?” and the whole room just fell apart.DHP:As a person from the US, everything is “something-upon-something” in the UK. That one just occurred to me and it seemed to stick. But it was with great affection.What do Daphne and Niles love about each other?DHP:For Niles, Daphne is far and above the most beautiful woman he’s ever seen in his life. Whatever aura she gives off just mesmerises him: her personality, the scent of her hair. He’s bewitched. He also thinks she’s completely beyond him, like a creature from another planet or from mythology or the woodlands or something. The fact that the relationship impossibly comes together is a beautiful surprise for him.JL:For Daphne, it’s the kindness and gentleness. He’s so different from any man she’s ever experienced. She came from a family with seven brothers, these brutes, so to find that a man could be kind, an intellectual … it’s the same thing for her, it’s this magical man in front of her.View image in fullscreenGroovy, baby … Daphne go-go dances her way into Niles’s dreams, wearing Donny’s mother’s old wedding dress.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane LeevesWe kept the suspense of the Niles attraction to Daphne going for years and people often ask me: “Why did she not know?” Yes, part of her thought that [he liked her], but the other part of her would say: “Oh, what are you talking about? He’s married and look where you come from and look who he is. He’s a doctor, for goodness sake.” And that voice in the back of her head is what made sense of that seven years of longing.DHP:The tango in Moon Dance was amazing.JL:We rehearsed at lightning speed for that. [The episode was written for the pair last minute as Grammer was on “blue flu” strike to negotiate his contract. Unusually, eight of the show’s writers each wrote a part of the script. Grammer returned in time to direct and appear in short scenes.] We had to rehearse with a choreographer. I remember going to David’s house, because we were loving it so much, to rehearse at the weekend. [The director] Jimmy Burrows would have been appalled.It takes two … the tango scene.DHP:Our late, great director was famous for not wanting people to rehearse because he had such a keen sense of the rehearsal timeframe of a situation comedy, which is not like rehearsing for a play that’s going to run for months. Even the dog [Moose, who played Eddie] suffered if he learned the trick too soon – it would be ruined and he wouldn’t be able to recreate it in front of the live audience. Jimmy was very big on: “Don’t think it out too much beforehand, because it will blossom at the right moment.”JL:I love the scene between us [in Mixed Doubles] when Daphne has been dating a Niles lookalike – he breaks up with her and runs off with Niles’ date – and Niles comes to tell Daphne. There’s a wonderful, sweet, gentle scene between them, like shades of Casablanca. [“If it’d been a different time in both our lives, we might actually have met. How do you suppose that would have gone?” Daphne asks him. “I would have said: ‘What are you doing for the rest of your life?’” he replies. They both, as friends, say they love each other.] It was such great writing – these writers were real romantics.Is there anything you wish Daphne and Niles had done differently?JL:Seven years is a long time and I think the audience was sort of begging to please bring this to a conclusion.DHP:I think we all felt we had played that “these two people didn’t think they deserved each other and didn’t believe that they could ever end up with each other” and there comes a point where you just stop believing that.View image in fullscreenA love story for the ages … Leeves and Hyde Pierce preparing on set.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane LeevesOne thing that the writers did very smartly: they got us together before people were tired of the suspense. I remember very well – speaking of moments that stick with me – when we kissed in front of the live audience. They lost their minds. That was the moment we finally came together. The creators also knew when to end the series; they ended it before any of us were ready. They didn’t want it to dribble off and have the network or the studio say: “Yeah, you’re done.” They wanted to be able to craft a final season. So I don’t know if there are things we wish they did, but I do think those two things were handled really well.JL:The only thing I wish had been handled differently was the hiding of my first pregnancy. But those were different times. [When Leeves came back from hiatus, she was pregnant with her first child. Her bump was hidden in the series and in later episodes she was given a weight-gain storyline and sent to a “fat camp”.] Daphne and Niles had just got together. I came back and I was pregnant – and they probably thought it was too early for Daphne to be pregnant and they wanted to explore this relationship. But then again, it might have been interesting if she was!DHP:I’ve never thought of that, Jane, that’s interesting, so off the rails: the idea that we see them run off together at the end of a season and when they come back they’re having a baby.When did you realise this was a love story for the ages?Love at first sight … Niles meets Daphne.DHP:I don’t know if I ever did think of it as a love story for the ages … love story for theagents?JL:There was an episode or two of Niles and Daphne every season. They were always such great fun. It wasn’t until season two that I realised this thing has legs. Niles’ reaction to Daphne in the room added another layer to Frasier’s apartment; there was this pushback between Niles, Frasier and their dad, and then Daphne comes in and there’s a whole other thing going on. But yeah, by season two, I realised that they were mining this.DHP:One of the cool things about it, too, was that it’s such sophisticated writing: knowing not to say anything when you have set up a dynamic between two characters. The whole audience knows, when Daphne walks into a room, exactly what Niles is thinking. And, eventually, vice versa. There could be comedy there, it could be poignant, it could be a million things – but it was not a show where it was a joke a minute, getting three jokes on the page. It was a different style. That’s between all the characters, in some ways. You got to know us so well.What does romance mean to you and how romantic are you in real life?JL:Oh my goodness. It’s friendship, it’s respect, it’s love. And admiration. I admire my husband, I admire his character. He’s my best friend. And he’s hot. That helps.DHP:Are you talking about my husband or your husband?JL:Oh, both of them, darling.‘I’m completely devoted to one person’: David Hyde Pierce on love, death and the Frasier rebootRead moreDHP:All of those things. I was thinking about both Niles and Daphne on the show, and me and Brian, or Jane and Marshall – what is romance? It’s a poetic thing. I think it’s possibility. Even having been together for ever, there’s just this air of possibility that the whole world has, because you are together.JL:I think I know what you’re saying: being with the right person seems to make everything possible.DHP:Yeah.View image in fullscreenHyde Pierce at the christening of Leeves’ son.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane LeevesJL:You’ve got a good one, too.DHP:I agree.What has been the most intense fan reaction to Daphne and Niles?JL:We’ve always had such respectful fans. I don’t know if there’s been a wild one!DHP: One of my favourite was in the States when the show first started to air. It was at a set time on a Thursday night or a Tuesday night: therefore, the people who wanted to watch Frasier watched it because they knew when it was on. But then there was a point where it went into syndication, which meant suddenly it was on reruns. I remember walking down the street in New York City. A garbage truck drove by and one of the guys hanging off the truck shouted: “Yo, Niles!” And I thought: oh, there’s a whole new audience getting to see the show.JL:I get the same thing in New York – New Yorkers are more open. But I always just get: “Hey, it’sthe virgin from Seinfeld.” It’s so bizarre. I’m like: “Not any more …”Did you keep anything from the set that reminds you of Daphne and Niles?JL:I kept Daphne’s wedding ring and engagement ring.DHP:The green room over the years became covered wall to wall with stills from every episode that our production photographer, Gail, took. At the end, we walked through and took pictures that were meaningful to us. [He turns his camera to a photo in his office.] It’s the three of us [him, Leeves and Grammer] at the piano. I’ve got a million more and they’re all around.View image in fullscreenThe famous Frasier green room.Photograph: Courtesy of Jane LeevesJL:We have millions. There’s a little gym upstairs and they cover the walls up there. That was the saddest thing for me, before the show was even over. We hadn’t even started rehearsing that week and people were taking those off the walls. I was like: “No, leave everything this way, I don’t need everything to change.”DHP: I think Marshall took a load of those [the photos in Leeves’ book]. Those are great.What can Daphne and Niles teach us about love?JL:To persevere. Don’t ever give up on the dream. It would have been so easy for Niles or Daphne to say: “Well, that’s just ridiculous.” But Niles never gave up that longing. And so many people were in his ear saying: “Niles, you fool, you’re sticking your knife in the toaster!”DHP:Love comes when you least expect it and it takes seven years.JL:But it’s worth it in the end.Daphne and Me by Jane Leeves with Isabella Kathryn Coben is published in the US on 20 October and in the UK on 5 November (HarperCollins, £22). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump
Content: A very interesting impression … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenA very interesting impression … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMoviesReviewThe Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet ZuckerbergJeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions TrumpPeter BradshawWed 7 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts. Sixteen years have gone by sinceThe Social Network, written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher; this was the addictive, obsessive-compulsive movie about the birth of Facebook in Harvard’s macho-competitive cauldron of student sexism and nerdy self-pity, starring Jesse Eisenberg as the fast-talking, arrogant, not-necessarily-evil genius Mark Zuckerberg. Now Sorkin is back with a sequel of sorts, directing his own script – and now Zuckerberg is basically evil, but also weirdly slow talking, as if all the zinging, smart-alecky Sorkinesque dialogue energy of the first film has been siphoned away in early middle age and dispersed among the insurgents in the new cast.Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?Read moreSorkin’s jittery, funny, syncopated style is unmistakable, as distinctive in its way as David Mamet, although he has one joke about “spatula” being a Yiddish word that hehas borrowed from Philip Roth’s Portnoy’s Complaint. It is the story of how in 2021, Zuckerberg’s Facebook empire was challenged bycourageous whistleblower-employee Frances Haugenand Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, who were on a mission to tell the world how Zuckerberg, scared by falling revenue, changed the algorithm so that engagement was supercharged by rage bait and hate speech, malice and envy. Facebook, moreover, didn’t factcheck political ads, thus driving a huge, nationwide surge in extremist groups and teen bullying and becoming a major player in the Capitol riots. (Having said that, this film does not say aloud the word “Trump” and rather cravenly declines to specify Maga activity.)Mikey Madison sympathetically plays the unhappy, principled, supersmart Haugen, who is dismissed as a “disrupter” – and Sorkin leaves it to us to notice that this in other circumstances is what oligarchs smugly call themselves.Jeremy Allen Whitedoes a capable, unflashy, unrisky job as Horwitz, a stolid performance that perhaps, in sync with the film, tells us about the diligent professionalism of old-school print journalism. And Zuckerberg? Well, we were all hoping and expecting it would be Jesse Eisenberg again. (You’ve heard of Richard Linklater’s Boyhood; this would be Aaron Sorkin’s Techbrohood.) But no: it is Jeremy Strong, who does a very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet, modifying the torpid sadness of his Kendall Roy in TV’s Succession, making this the unhurried contempt of someone simultaneously burdened and energised by knowing he’s richer and therefore smarter than everyone else. (A famous line in The Social Network was “A million dollars isn’t cool. You know what’s cool? A billion dollars.” This film starts by telling us that Facebook is worth a trillion dollars.)Zuckerberg, though, is almost a cameo, with no equals with whom he can exchange dialogue, only employees – although the film imagines one former investor-turned-critic called Charlie (Bill Burr) who heckles Zuckerberg’s practice performance before a confessional hearing, with Zuckerberg amusingly having to be told how to smile. Charlie is the angry, unheeded voice of conscience.View image in fullscreenRattles along at an entertaining clip … Jeremy Allen White as Jeff Horwitz and Mikey Madison as Frances Haugen in The Social Reckoning.The resulting drama rattles along at an entertaining clip, although there are false notes. When Frances has secret meetings with Horwitz in a hotel, the film has her wearing a slinky evening dress, supposedly as a kind of disguise, so that if recognised it would seem like she was out on a date. Hmm, really? Or is it so that the movie’s female lead has scenes where she looks glamorous? Later, Horwitz affectionately tells her to be less “mean”. But she is not “mean”. She just speaks Sorkinspeak. So does Horwitz. The ubiquity of Sorkinspeak effaces the difference between all the characters.The most disturbing scene comes at the very beginning, showing a drunk woman livestreaming her racist abuse of traffic cops; this is the woman whom Haugen recognises as an acquaintance of hers, radicalised byFacebook. Towards the end we glimpse her again, looking ambiguously appalled by what she has become. But would she be appalled in reality? Or is this just the film-makers’ wish fulfilment? The closing-credit titles – usually the platform for a film to promote and summarise its heroes’ achievements – concedes that Facebook still isn’t checking political ads. Plus, of course, the film is set at the start of the Trump interregnum of 2020-24, when it seemed as if the Capitol riots were the ultimate wake-up call and moderation had returned. Nowadays Trump and his tech bro courtiers are more vainglorious than ever, and the values of investigative journalism have been thrown out at the Washington Post by its owner Jeff Bezos. This is a film which doesn’t reckon with the future we’re living in.The Social Reckoning is out on 8 October in Australia, and 9 October in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFacebookMark ZuckerbergWall Street JournalAaron SorkinMikey MadisonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Abide with me: English choral music is a living part of our cultural heritage – we should cherish it | Classical music | The Guardian
description: One hundred years since the BBC first broadcast choral evensong, MP and former chorister Jonathan Davies hymns a beautiful and empowering collective experience that we should praise – and protect
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: One hundred years since the BBC first broadcast choral evensong, MP and former chorister Jonathan Davies hymns a beautiful and empowering collective experience that we should praise – and protect
Content: ‘Singing in a choir taught me that you can achieve more through collaboration than you can alone’ … St Paul's Cathedral choristers.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Singing in a choir taught me that you can achieve more through collaboration than you can alone’ … St Paul's Cathedral choristers.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesClassical musicAbide with me: English choral music is a living part of our cultural heritage – we should cherish itJonathan DaviesOne hundred years since the BBC first broadcast choral evensong, MP and former chorister Jonathan Davies hymns a beautiful and empowering collective experience that we should praise – and protectWed 7 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTShareSome sounds seem to belong to Britain. The peal of church bells. The brass band on a village green. The roar of a football crowd. And, heard from a cathedral at the end of the day, the extraordinary sound of a choir singing evensong.This year marks the centenary of choral evensong on BBC radio. On 7 October 1926, when the BBC was in its infancy, listeners heard a live service broadcast from Westminster Abbey. A century later, evensong can still be heard onRadio 3every week from cathedrals, churches, chapels and abbeys across the country. It is the BBC’s longest running outside broadcast and reaches hundreds of thousands of people every week.For the listener at home, the radio can make a distant cathedral feel remarkably close. But we should not celebrate this simply as a remarkable broadcasting survival story. We should celebrate it because it represents something much bigger: a living part of our cultural heritage.double quotation markFor some, evensong is prayer,  for others contemplation, inspiration or simply a moment of peace.You do not have to be religious or particularly musical to understand the power of evensong. You do not even need to know what a Magnificat or an anthem is. There is something profoundly human about sitting quietly in a great building, hearing young and old voices combine in astonishingly beautiful music. Being given permission for 45 minutes of detachment from the frenetic pace of modern life. For some it is prayer, for others contemplation, inspiration or simply a moment of peace.That is culture at its best: not something kept behind closed doors, but a collective experience. And that is why we should care about what happens when the ecosystems that sustain this tradition come under pressure.View image in fullscreenCultural inheritance … a choir in Westminster Abbey in 1937.Photograph: Sueddeutsche Zeitung Photo/AlamyCathedral music is not simply about preserving an old repertoire. It is a living tradition, with newly written music sitting alongside pieces that have been passed down through generations. Around 3,000 children and young people currently sing as choristers in the UK’s cathedrals, churches and chapels, with thousands more taking part in youth and school choirs led by church musicians. Through these experiences they develop exceptional musical skills alongside confidence, discipline, teamwork and a sense of belonging to something much larger than themselves. Many take these skills into careers far beyond music.double quotation markSinging in a church choir as a child opened up worlds for meThere is also an important social mobility story here.A cathedral choir can give a child access to world-class musical training, extraordinary cultural experiences and educational opportunities that might otherwise be beyond their reach. But we also need to be honest about the barriers, too: affordability, access to music tuition and the unfamiliarity of cathedral culture can all restrict who gets through the door. Preserving this tradition cannot mean simply preserving the status quo. It must mean widening access to it.View image in fullscreenA tradition renewed by the children who sing it … Coventry Cathedral choristers.Photograph: David Jensen/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsSinging in a church choir as a child opened up worlds for me. Not just through the opportunity – asThomas Cranmerput it – to “read, mark, learn and inwardly digest” the most sacred of texts, illuminated by a wealth of the most enriching music humankind has created. It instilled an appreciation of routines and hard work, and it taught me that you can achieve more through collaboration than you can alone. It also taught me that success is sometimes built on of the insights of failure. Something of which I occasionally have to remind myself as a member of parliament.The charityCathedral Music Trustis working hard to ensure the continuation of these sorts of opportunities and is leading a campaign to secure Unesco status for English sacred choral music. Their submission forLiving Heritage statusseeks recognition not for a historical artefact, but for a vibrant and thriving art form, one continually renewed by the children who sing it, the composers who add to its repertoire and the communities who participate in it. Unesco recognition would send an important message worldwide: that this is deemed worthy of recognition, investment and protection, and remains a vital part of the UK’s national cultural inheritance.The UK rightly celebrates its great theatres, galleries and museums. We should be equally confident in celebrating a cultural and religious tradition that is performed every day, in buildings at the heart of communities, by musicians of extraordinary skill. A tradition that has reached so many people through the simple miracle of radio. We have a responsibility not simply to admire this wonderful tradition, but to protect it and to make sure that the next generation can claim it as their own.Jonathan Davies is MP for Mid DerbyshireExplore more on these topicsClassical musicChoral musicBBCRadioRadio 3commentShareReuse this content

title: The Hungry Ghost review – this sexy, juicily spooky romcom is a scream | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Mei Leng Yew’s smart play veers between humour and horror as a young woman ignores her mum’s warning about big life changes during a ghost festival
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Mei Leng Yew’s smart play veers between humour and horror as a young woman ignores her mum’s warning about big life changes during a ghost festival
Content: Deliciously vile … Mei Mac as Girl in The Hungry Ghost.Photograph: Corinne CummingView image in fullscreenDeliciously vile … Mei Mac as Girl in The Hungry Ghost.Photograph: Corinne CummingTheatreReviewThe Hungry Ghost review – this sexy, juicily spooky romcom is a screamBush theatre, LondonMei Leng Yew’s play veers between humour and horror as a young woman ignores her mum’s warning about big life changes during a ghost festivalKate WyverWed 7 Oct 2026 07.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith shapeshifting performances and smart, heartfelt writing, Mei Leng Yew’s juicily spooky romcom is a seductively assured debut about second-generation family dynamics, the all-in nature of a new relationship, and the internal battles of a young woman trying to work out what she wants.You must not make any big decisions during the traditional Chinese Ghost festival, our protagonist’s mum warns, or else the hungry ghosts will get you. But Girl (My Neighbour Totoro’s Mei Mac) already has her bags packed to move in with her secret girlfriend of three months and nothing is as powerful as lesbians ready to U-Haul. Except perhaps a third-wheeling ghost with severe attachment issues, played giddily by Bridgerton’s Isabella Wei.As the excitable ghost climbs into Girl’s body, everything is new and tasty to her (except porridge, she realises with tongue-scraping disgust). Ailin Conant’s sensuous direction has Wei following then dragging Mac, manipulating Girl’s body and voice and capacity for consumption until she is a bottomless pit of need. Yimei Zhao’s sly set enables charming stage trickery as meals and shrines and escape-hatch windows appear. When food spills across the stage, it becomes a knees-on-the floor, arms-scooping, mouth-open-wide affair – but still not enough to fill up the hungry ghost.View image in fullscreenFood for thought … Mei Mac and Isabella Wei in The Hungry Ghost.Photograph: Corinne CummingMac and Wei are gorgeous together, twisting across the stage as they vie for space in Girl’s skin (movement direction by Jasmine Chiu), with Cantonese gliding alongside English as the ghost escalates Girl’s sense of being pulled in opposing directions. As the situation escalates, the show veers between bright comedy and grotesque horror. A tongue, in particular, serves up a deliciously vile moment for the squeamish to look away.‘Like swapping a Bentley for a Ferrari’: can the Harry Potter stage show survive being chopped in half?Read moreMac slips out of herself to play everyone else in the story: her bubbly girlfriend, her concerned mother, the disinterested officer called to the scene when the ghost’s hunger disrupts the fruit aisle at Sainsbury’s. The stage smells of incense sticks and oranges as the girl discovers she can collide the scattered parts of herself rather than be torn apart by them; this isn’t the kind of horror to leave everyone dead on stage. A late ghostly subplot earns less of your attention, but this dark, sexy, comic production is a treat for the taste buds.AtBush theatre, London, until 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreBush theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Celia Imrie | Celia Imrie | The Guardian
description: From Miss Babs in Acorn Antiques to Calendar Girls, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel and her infamous appearance on The Celebrity Traitors, it’s hard to know where to begin
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: From Miss Babs in Acorn Antiques to Calendar Girls, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel and her infamous appearance on The Celebrity Traitors, it’s hard to know where to begin
Content: Gift of the Babs … Celia ImriePhotograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGift of the Babs … Celia ImriePhotograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianFilm & Music reader interviewCelia ImriePost your questions for Celia ImrieFrom Miss Babs in Acorn Antiques to Calendar Girls, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel and her infamous appearance on The Celebrity Traitors, it’s hard to know where to beginRich PelleyWed 7 Oct 2026 05.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 05.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCelia Imrie has had such a varied career, it’s hard to know where you might know her best from. Maybe it’s as Miss Babs, the permanently flustered antiques-shop owner in Victoria Wood’s Acorn Antiques, or as Philippa Moorcroft, Dinnerladies’ spectacularly uptight HR manager. Perhaps it’s as Bridget Jones’s family friend Una Alconbury, or from Calendar Girls,The Best Exotic Marigold Hotelfilms, Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again.Everybody’s favourite manic pixie dream aunt: Celia Imrie’s 20 best films – ranked!Read moreMaybe you know her as Mrs Quickly, the ghastly would-be stepmother in Nanny McPhee. Or maybe you first encountered her in Upstairs, Downstairs, To the Manor Born, Bergerac, Lovejoy or The Darling Buds of May, or as Claudia Bing, the magnificently awful PR rival of Jennifer Saunders’ Edina in Absolutely Fabulous.More recently, she returned as Una in Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy; joined Helen Mirren, Pierce Brosnan and Ben Kingsley in The Thursday Murder Club; and popped up in The Diplomat. Then, of course, there was The Celebrity Traitors. Imrie entered the castle as a Faithful, survived being chained up in a wooden cabin, and accidentally farted while doing so – instantly producingthe Guardian’s No 2 TV moment of the year– and eventually got murdered in plain sight by Alan Carr.Now she’s back as in (yes, it’s nearly that time already) MerryChristmasAubrey Flint, alongside John Bradley as a Christmas-hating model-soldier painter sentenced to community service at a struggling retirement home, where he somehow ends up directing a chaotic production of A Christmas Carol. Richard E Grant and Jim Broadbent are along for the festive ride, too.So, from flogging dodgy antiques with Victoria Wood to meddling in Bridget Jones’s love life, retiring to India with Judi Dench to committing Celebrity Traitors flatulence on national television – plus the really important matter of what on earth she’s getting Richard E Grant for Christmas – what would you like to askCelia Imrie? Please get your questions in by 12pm on Tuesday 13 October and we’ll print her answers as part of our Readers Interview series.Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint is in cinemas on 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsCelia ImrieFilm & Music reader interviewTelevisionThe TraitorsThe Best Exotic Marigold HotelBridget Jones' DiaryMamma Mia!
