title: Only connect: two composers who put humans at the heart of their music, and the conductor who didn’t | Classical music | The Guardian
description: This week, from Reich to Kendall and Celibidache, three musicians who prove there is no such thing as “pure music”, whether we’re talking about a technique, a mode of musical expression or a musician’s legacy.
Author: Tom Service
Headline: This week, from Reich to Kendall and Celibidache, three musicians who prove there is no such thing as “pure music”, whether we’re talking about a technique, a mode of musical expression or a musician’s legacy.
Content: The Paraorchestra perform Steve Reich's Music for 18 Musicians in the Southbank Centre, September 2026.Photograph: Siân O’ConnorView image in fullscreenThe Paraorchestra perform Steve Reich's Music for 18 Musicians in the Southbank Centre, September 2026.Photograph: Siân O’ConnorTom Service on musicClassical musicOnly connect: two composers who put humans at the heart of their music, and the conductor who didn’tTom ServiceThis week, from Reich to Kendall and Celibidache, three musicians who prove there is no such thing as “pure music”, whether we’re talking about a technique, a mode of musical expression or a musician’s legacy.Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 09.20 EDTShareSteve Reichturned 90 on Saturday, and I’ve been thinking about his early tape pieces from the mid-1960s, It’s Gonna Rain and Come Out. They’re such vital works not only because they opened his imagination to what could happen if you made a micro-canon – playing the same material slightly faster or slower – which is what happened when one of his tape machines slipped out of sync with the other: it’s that these are human voices that Reich is setting.It’s Gonna Rainis made from the voice of Brother Walter, a Pentecostal street preacher in San Francisco, whose warning of apocalypse in 1965 Reich recorded and looped against itself, over and over, so that Brother Walter’s voice becomes a wall and wail of sound, a sonic realisation of the sublime inundation he’s announcing.Come Outwas made in 1966 with the voice of Daniel Hamm, one of theHarlem Six, six black men wrongly convicted of first-degree murder in New York. Reich’s piece was commissioned for a benefit event for their legal costs as “background music for passing the hat”.These pieces don’t just set words, Reich says they “set human beings”, using the vocal recordings not only as musical material but political inspiration and emotional expression. Techniques that are seemingly all about narrowly musical processes – looping, canon-ing, fugue-ing – are embedded in the facts of where they were made and how, and whose voices are being represented by whom.View image in fullscreenConnecting … Hannah KendallPhotograph: Chris AlexanderThat terrain of historical consciousness is essential toHannah Kendall’s music. She is inspired by the idea of the “plantation machine”, Cuban writer Antonio Benítez-Rojo’s phrase, which sums up the industrial processes and global networks of dehumanising capital that powered the slave trade, which are still echoed, for Kendall, by all of today’s machinery of capitalism, from environmental destruction to technological control.These are fascinating and provocative ideas, but it’s how Kendall turns them into visceral musical experience in the way she reworks the sound of ensembles and orchestras that counts. As Kendall puts it, she “creolises” the orchestra, putting dreadlock cuffs on the string instruments to change, mute and distort the sounds they make; her compositions includesound sources and instrumentssuch as walkie-talkies, music boxes, harmonicas and kettles. These reference historical and musical contexts, from the blues to Kendall’s imagination of the music made by enslaved people, including prayers and songs spoken and sung into kettles, to be out of earshot of the plantation owners.Listen toShouting Forever Into the Receiveror her recentBuilding a Burning House, which will be part of theBarbican’s Always, Already Therefestival later this month, followed a few days later by the world premiere of her I Have Discovered the Secret of Death with theLondon Symphony Orchestra, also at the Barbican.Kendall’s music remakes the orchestra to interrogate the histories of trade, slavery, and globalisation that were the machines that made civilisations such as ours function, and to which the instruments, halls, and institutional fabric of the western orchestra are indebted. Her compositions tangibly connect musical culture with the reality of these complex and impure histories.Sergiu Celibidache, meanwhile, is at the forefront of musical minds this week as a biopic of the conductor,The Yellow Tieopens in UK cinemas. The movie – themost watched Romanian film of 2025– tells of his pursuit of music in the face of his father’s fierce opposition, his appointment to the Berlin Philharmonic age 33 and how his single-minded and – supposedly – purist approach to music was born: his belief that any audio recording of a piece of music was a soul-stealing lie that could not represent the reality of live performance. (Although, hundreds of recordings of his work, especially in his later years, were released after his death in 1996.)But here’s another film worth watching, that tells a story about the conductor not told. Abbie Conant: A Solo Among Men.At 25, Conant was appointed Munich Philharmonic’s principal trombone in 1980 after a blind audition, but wasn’t allowed ever meaningfully to take up her job. As Celibidache, the orchestra’s principal conductor, told her: “We need a man for the solo trombone”. He couldn’t really tell her why, Conant relates, but she was demoted to second trombone and her life was made a misery. She was paid less than her male colleagues, she was openly bullied by Celibidache, and when she initiated legal proceedings against the City of Munich (the Philharmonic’s owner) alleging discrimination,she was forced to undergo humiliating medical and physical tests to prove her stamina, lung capacity and ability to play under pressure. It’s a story of multidimensional misogyny. Conant won her case even though it took her over 12 years, and left the orchestra of her own accord in 1993.View image in fullscreenPioneering and brave trombonist Abbie Conant.Photograph: www.osborne-conant.orgMuch of Celibidache’s reputation hangs on the revelations and transcendence of his performances with the Munich Philharmonic, above all, ofBruckner’s symphonies. But hisexcessively slow performances, sonically beautiful, but expressively one-dimensional, often feel to me like a Brucknerian bad joke. Calcifying these symphonies with a one-dimensional monumentalism does the expressive power and contradictions of Bruckner’s music no favours. (Even more of a nadir is Celibidache’s so-slow-it’s-barely-alive performance ofBach’s Mass in B Minor: the opening fugue is a masochistic trial of patience – try it, if you dare.)But whatever you think Celibidache did or didn’t do with the music he conducted: as Conant’s experience shows, if you lose yourself to the revelations of his performances, you have to ignore the human cost they clearly came at. “Purity”, as always, is no such thing, and comes at an inevitably impure price. Reich, like Kendall, understands this and composed and made music with empathy and understanding, rather than following an ideology that would rather pretend that the goal of transcendence is worth subjugating the human.This week, Tom has been listening to:Kristian Bezuidenhout’s latest, thrilling, volume ofMozart’s piano concertos, playing fortepiano with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra. I can’t get enough of these records, and the way that Bezuidenhout plunges you right into the cauldron of the drama he and the players make in the D minor Concerto, or the joy of the D major concerto K175.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicSteve ReichcommentShareReuse this content

title: Freddie Jackson, romantic US singer with 10 R&B chart-toppers, dies aged 70 | Music | The Guardian
description: Celebrated for his earnest, dextrous voice, Jackson crossed into the pop charts with the hits Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake) and You Are My Lady
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Celebrated for his earnest, dextrous voice, Jackson crossed into the pop charts with the hits Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake) and You Are My Lady
Content: Freddie Jackson pictured in 2016.Photograph: Evan Agostini/APView image in fullscreenFreddie Jackson pictured in 2016.Photograph: Evan Agostini/APMusicFreddie Jackson, romantic US singer with 10 R&B chart-toppers, dies aged 70Celebrated for his earnest, dextrous voice, Jackson crossed into the pop charts with the hits Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake) and You Are My LadyBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 7 Oct 2026 07.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 07.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFreddie Jackson, the US singer whose smooth and romantic take on R&B found a huge audience in the 1980s, has died aged 70.A statement from his family on social media reads: “Freddie was more than a legendary voice. He was a kind, generous soul who loved his fans, his family, his friends and his music with everything he had. For decades he gave us the songs that became the soundtrack to our love stories, our celebrations and our most treasured memories. That gift will live on for ever.” No cause of death was given.Blessed with a dextrous and technically brilliant voice that could flip from playful flirtation to earnest entreaties to crushed lamentations across the space of a single album, Jackson became a mainstay in the US R&B scene, earning 10 No 1 singles and four back to back No 1 albums on the country’s R&B charts. He also twice hit the main pop chart Top 20, with 1985’s Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake) and You Are My Lady. The latter song also earned him two Grammy nominations.Born in 1956, Jackson was raised in Harlem by a single mother, “eating collard greens and fried chicken”, he later said. “That’s not learned soul, it’s not acquired in some singing school or from copying what you hear on records. I live soul.”He was first grounded in gospel music, performing at a local Baptist church, before expanding his musical remit outwards, establishing himself in New York’s music scene before moving to Los Angeles where he became the vocalist of dancefloor-focused soul group Mystic Merlin, recording their third album, Full Moon, with them.After a spell as a backing singer for Melba Moore, eventually he was signed as a solo artist, modelling himself on “Black singers who were able to cross over to the pop market without selling out – Marvin Gaye, Sam Cooke, Al Green”. He released debut album Rock Me Tonight in 1985, which, containing the aforementioned hit singles, became a platinum seller and reached the US Top 10. Follow-up Just Like the First Time was also certified platinum, and four of its tracks – including a duet with Moore, A Little Bit More – hit R&B No 1.His unabashed sensuality meant he was marketed with a “lover man” image, but he was careful not to let it define him. “I’m fortunate that a lot of ladies have liked the record and gone out and bought it,” he said. “But didn’t go to Capitol and say, ‘I’m a ladies man and I want to make a ladies man record.’ I don’t want to stereotype myself and my music. I don’t want to alienate anybody.”Jackson was still topping at the R&B chart as late as 1991, but as the genre modernised and hip-hop emerged, Jackson’s style became less fashionable and his chart success waned. He nevertheless remained a familiar voice on R&B radio and continued to release new music, eventually putting out 15 studio albums.In 2024, he announced he was living with kidney disease. “This journey has had its challenges but I’ve decided to face it with openness and resilience,” he said.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockR&BSoulnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish film could steal The Jazz Singer’s crown as ‘world’s first talkie’ | Scotland | The Guardian
description: Scots-written Till the Bells Ring premiered a year before the Hollywood film, which featured spoken words by Al Jolson
Author: Eve Livingston
Headline: Scots-written Till the Bells Ring premiered a year before the Hollywood film, which featured spoken words by Al Jolson
Content: ‘A distinctly Scottish production’: a scene from the stage play Till the Bells Ring at the Coliseum in London. It was later turned into a film.Photograph: 1996-2004 AccuSoft Co. All rights reserved/courtesy of the British LibraryView image in fullscreen‘A distinctly Scottish production’: a scene from the stage play Till the Bells Ring at the Coliseum in London. It was later turned into a film.Photograph: 1996-2004 AccuSoft Co. All rights reserved/courtesy of the British LibraryScotlandScottish film could steal The Jazz Singer’s crown as ‘world’s first talkie’Scots-written Till the Bells Ring  premiered a year before the Hollywood film, which featured spoken words by Al JolsonEve LivingstonWed 7 Oct 2026 03.17 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor almost a century, The Jazz Singerhas been celebrated as the world’s first feature-length film to include synchronised dialogue (known as a “talkie”), and English as the first language of cinema. But a chance discovery threatens to upend film history with the news that it may have been beaten to the title by a full year – and by a film made inGlasgowand written in Scots.The breakthrough was made by the historian and self-confessed “film nerd” Marc David Jacobs, who was conducting research for a book on the first wave of British sound films when he came across the story of Till the Bells Ring.The 46-minute feature film, featuring spoken parts and synchronised sound throughout, premiered in Edinburgh in October 1926, a year before The Jazz Singer, starring Al Jolson,hit New York’s screens to widespread fanfare and took its place in the history books.“This was the start of what we would consider modern film,” Jacobs said. “It was a completely new art form at the time, and if it had been taken up in Britain there could have been a real alternative history of cinema where the Americans didn’t take over and get such a lead on things.”The creation of the Scottish playwright Graham Moffat, Till the Bells Ring is a domestic comedy set in Glasgow and performed by Moffat’s six-part touring company, including his wife, Margaret, and daughter Winifred, in what he called “lowland braid Scots”: a term for plain-language Scots dialect originating from central and southernScotland.View image in fullscreenGraham Moffat directed and starred in Till the Bells Ring alongside his wife, Maggie.Photograph: 1996-2004 AccuSoft Co. All rights reserved/courtesy of the British LibraryIt was billed at the time as a “super talking picture … of Victorian family life” and heralded upon its premiere as a cinematic milestone. The Edinburgh Evening News wrote in a review: “Even America has never attempted such a work … So perfect was the synchronisation between the image on screen and the broad Scots dialogue spoken by the image, that one might quite well have been listening to a legitimate stage version of the comedy.”But Jacobs said the film was quickly forgotten about. “This fits into a larger narrative about British cinema, which has been uniquely neglected,” he said. “I think if it had been celebrated as a distinctly Scottish production, it might have survived or been discovered by now. But it’s fallen under this rubric of British cinema and there’s no real sense that British cinema history is actually worth looking at.”View image in fullscreenThe film was billed at the time as a ‘super talking picture ... of Victorian family life’.Photograph: courtesy of the National Library of ScotlandThere is no evidence that the film was ever screened publicly again after its week-long run in Edinburgh’s Poole’s Synod Hall, where the city’s Traverse theatre stands today. Moffat died in 1951 having never made another film.Among Jacobs’ discoveries are that two of the film’s reels, comprising more than half its length, survive in the BFI National Archives in Hertfordshire but have never been screened since their acquisition more than 50 years ago. With this year marking the film’s centenary, Jacobs hopes that will change.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I hope this becomes more than just a Scottish story, and that archives around the world might be able to take a look and maybe find the missing reel,” he said. “But this is a film that had its origins as a stage play and the manuscripts have survived, so you can imagine perhaps playing those surviving reels and then performing that missing part on stage.“It would be an amazing moment to recreate this important landmark in world cinema history. But beyond that, hopefully it spurs people on to reconsider British cinema history as a whole and think: if this has been sitting around for 100 years, what else might be out there?”This article was amended on 7 October 2026. In an earlier version, a picture caption misspelled the name of the London theatre the Coliseum as the “Colosseum”.Explore more on these topicsScotlandGlasgownewsShareReuse this content

title: O2 signs record deal to keep London venue’s naming rights | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: 10-year sponsorship extension at a 50% premium on last agreement crowns bonanza year for live venue
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Exclusive: 10-year sponsorship extension at a 50% premium on last agreement crowns bonanza year for live venue
Content: The O2 Arena has proved a big success, hosting 239 events last year.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe O2 Arena has proved a big success, hosting 239 events last year.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesTravel & leisureO2 signs record deal to keep London venue’s naming rightsExclusive:10-year sponsorship extension at a 50% premium on last agreement crowns bonanza year for live venueMark SweneyWed 7 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 10.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleO2 has struck a record deal thought to be in the region of £200m to retain the naming rights to theLondonvenue the O2 in the largest renewal of its kind in UK history.The 10-year agreement will extend O2’s relationship until at least 2038. It cements the sponsorship as the second longest-running UK stadium naming rights deal after Arsenal’s partnership for the football club’s London ground,Under the deal with Anschutz Entertainment Group (AEG), which bought the site of the ill-fated Millennium Dome five years after it was shut following the millennium celebrations, O2 is thought to be paying about £20m a year in the wide-ranging partnership.This is an almost 50% increase on the annual amountunder the existing dealwhich was due to expire at the end of next year. It is more than triple the£6m a year O2 paidin its initial 10-year deal when the future success of the O2 and surrounding site was far from certain.View image in fullscreenVirgin Media O2’s Gareth Griffiths (left) and AEG’s Paul Samuels at the O2 in London.Photograph: Doug Peters/PA“Everyone thought it would never work, that it was crazy building on the site of the Millennium Dome, it was considered the biggest white elephant,” said Paul Samuels, president of global partnerships at AEG International, talking to the Guardian.“In the first deal we were talking about whether to put in clauses if the O2 couldn’t hit 100 shows a year – last year we did 239. We opened in June 2007 with Bon Jovi and the rest is history.”Newly published accounts show that the O2 enjoyed the best year in its 19-year history in 2025. Pre-tax profits surged 18% to £76.5m, while revenues climbed 14% to £148.6m, as music fans put aside cost-of-living concerns to see acts including Lady Gaga, Katy Perry, Radiohead and Usher.The record year resulted in a healthy £27.5m dividend being paid to its US parent company.“People will opt to save money on other things but still want to go out and spend money on live entertainment,” said Samuels. “And when it comes to technological change like AI, it can change the world but it won’t change the desire for a live experience, like music and sport.”Samuels said that each time the sponsorship deal nears renewal he receives a lot of interest from brands hoping to take over the naming rights.However, Gareth Griffiths, director of partnerships and sponsorships at themobile operator’s parent companyVirgin MediaO2, said the deal had worked so well that it was agreed within an exclusivity period.A key component of the deal is a 50% increase in the number of priority tickets made available to O2 customers, granting access to tickets to events 48 hours before they go on general sale.O2 sellsmore than 1.7m tickets each yearthrough its Priority Tickets programme across the 20 music venues it sponsors in the UK.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The O2 has been an amazing brand asset for us,” said Griffiths. “Two-and-a-half million people come to the [main] arena each year, and 7.5 million come to everything else that is on offer.“Music is right in the core DNA of our brand. Customer retention is absolutely crucial and driving loyalty through entertainment is a sweet spot for the business.”Last year, O2 lost more than 100,000 customers after a backlashfollowing the introduction of hefty price rises.Last month, it was reported that VMO2’s joint owners – Liberty Global and Telefonica – want to cut £600m in costs to calm investor fears over a £22bn debt pile.“Every pound we spend we do so very carefully,” said Griffiths. “This has been such a big success for the brand.“Churn is still one of the most important metrics in the business, it is about keeping hold of valuable customers. Both of our shareholders are absolutely fully committed to this.“This is a 10-year investment in the UK … a huge sign of intent. It has long been proven that growth comes from investment in your brand.”Explore more on these topicsTravel & leisureMusic industryO2Virgin MediaCorporate sponsorshipAdvertisingTelecommunications industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Carrie review – the teenage hell-raiser’s glorious return couldn’t come at a better time | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: This witty, smart remake takes bullying and telekinetic violence to new extremes. Even the shower scene is more excruciating than the original
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This witty, smart remake takes bullying and telekinetic violence to new extremes. Even the shower scene is more excruciating than the original
Content: Darker than Stephen King could ever have imagined … Summer H Howell as Carrie.Photograph: Courtesy of PrimeView image in fullscreenDarker than Stephen King could ever have imagined … Summer H Howell as Carrie.Photograph: Courtesy of PrimeTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewCarrie review – the teenage hell-raiser’s glorious return couldn’t come at a better timeThis witty, smart remake takes bullying and telekinetic violence to new extremes. Even the shower scene is more excruciating than the originalLucy ManganWed 7 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe automatic response to the news that a stone-cold classic of any genre is to be remade is: “Why?” In an accompanying letter to critics, the creator of the new TV series Carrie, Mike Flanagan, promises us that this was the first question he asked himself too when he was approached about the project. Why mess with perfection – in this case, the Brian De Palma horror film, based on and nearly eclipsing in terms of cultural currency Stephen King’s debut novel about a telekinetic teen, that has been gloriously shocking audiences for half a century?But it’s a far less necessary question than usual. Why remake Carrie, a story of teenage bullying, alienation and the vengeful violence they can fuel, for the modern age? Babe, look around! We’ve got the internet now. We’ve taken teenage bullying, alienation and the fuelling of vengeful violence to levels that De Palma and King, with all their vaunted capacity for darkness, could never have imagined! We are, to use a construction popular among the very youth of whom we are speaking, Carriemaxxing these days. The question is not why remake but quite why it has taken this long.De Palma’s masterpiece is a lean, mean thing, taking just 98 minutes to move from opening credits to high-school mass barbecue. Flanagan’s is an eight-hour series (and there are signs of seeds being sown for a second season already), so much in the way of plot and characters has been added. But the new Carrie has not fallen victim to the streamer’s curse of bloating. Almost everything and everyone is there for a reason, and if the whole plays more like a teen drama with extra bite than a straight up, blood-soaked horror event that is no matter when the former is clearly what it was designed to be. It’s also kinder than the film – perhaps intentionally, perhaps as a byproduct of having to flesh out the “baddies” who cannot remain elemental villains over such a long period if we are to stay interested in the story and their fates – but again, in an increasingly unforgiving world, this feels welcome and right.View image in fullscreenAll about the phones … from left: Alison Thornton, Summer H Howell and Siena Agudong in Carrie.Photograph: Courtesy of PrimeThe new Carrie starts by paying due homage. It opens with the high school gym on fire and frantic 911 calls playing over scenes of the inferno, as it consumes the rest of the school then spreads through the town. The calls segue into reports of 200 deaths, and the flames fade into interviews with survivors and students who knew Carrie. “Shy,” one calls her. “A bully,” says another. “A victim.” “Quiet … genuinely kind.” “A monster.”We then spool backward and get our introduction to Carrie (Summer H Howell) herself. She is found hiding in the “prayer closet” with her mother Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) as the police enter their home. Carrie’s father has been killed at work. None of his co-workers were aware he had a family. Carrie has been home-schooled and never been allowed to venture past the garden walls but she is not the terrified, damaged figure we expect. She is – heartbreakingly, given what is to come – open, curious and keen to experience whatever this new paterfamilias-free life, in which she must go to school and Margaret to work, has to offer. Howell does a wonderful job of playing an essentially good and optimistic character that could easily have become more Anne-of-Green-Gables-with-PMT than a potential hell-raiser driven beyond endurance.Nor is Margaret the religious zealot of the film or its source material. Conservative Christianity is definitely her thing, and she has evidently been influenced by her beloved husband’s controlling character and conspiracist bent, but in Flanagan’s version (and the mesmerising Sloyan brings out every note), this is mixed with real and profound love and fear for her daughter’s safety. She is forced out into the world at the same time as Carrie, and the effects it has on her are as carefully and almost tenderly explored by the series as her daughter’s are. It makes the endeavour noticeably richer and more compelling.Similarly, Carrie’s great tormentor Chris (Alison Thornton) is given reasons – not excuses – for her growing savagery, Sue (Siena Agudong) wrestles with her conscience from the beginning, and the dynamics between them, Carrie and the other friends/acolytes are nicely detailed.But the bullying is the thing. The supernatural powers it unleashes are not quite an afterthought, but they do almost take second place – especially in the early episodes – to the horrors unleashed by Chris and her gang on the new girl. The famous period-in-the-shower scene is of course filmed on mobiles and ends up online via a malevolent Gossip Girl-style account, and countless other cruelties are likewise compounded.Of course this Carrie doesn’t have the raw power of the film. But it has intelligence, wit and things to say about the fathomless potential for good and ill in the teenage heart – and how impossible it is to teach them which way to go.Carrie is on Prime Video nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

Headline: She joins Lennie James and Sheridan Smith on Sky’s Portrait Artist of the Year. Plus: reaching the bottom of Britain’s deepest cave. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Likeness or not? … Stephen Mangan with Vanessa Williams as she looks at her image in Portrait Artist of the Year 2026.Photograph: Chris Lobina/© Sky UK Limited.View image in fullscreenLikeness or not? … Stephen Mangan with Vanessa Williams as she looks at her image in Portrait Artist of the Year 2026.Photograph: Chris Lobina/© Sky UK Limited.TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Vanessa Williams sits for this wonderful portrait competitionShe joins Lennie James and Sheridan Smith on Sky’s Portrait Artist of the Year. Plus: reaching the bottom of Britain’s deepest cave. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Jack Seale,Phil HarrisonandPriya ElanWed 7 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePortrait Artist of the Year 20268pm, Sky ArtsStressful or soothing? It’s always a fine line between the two with this portrait competition. Art historian Katy Hessel joins the judging team for the show’s 13th series, with Stephen Mangan resuming hosting duties. The first three sitters are actors Lennie James, Sheridan Smith and Vanessa Williams. Who will break down in (happy) tears, telling a painter: “You’ve captured something I thought I’d lost”?Hollie RichardsonEchoes from Below: Exploring Britain’s Caves8pm, BBC FourTitan is the deepest cave shaft ever found in Britain. A gutsy scanning team head in there in an attempt to find out exactly how large it is – and it might even be too big for them to manage. The programme also looks at other cave discoveries, including the 17th-century “witches’ marks” at Creswell Crags.HRWinter9pm, ITV1Richard Armitage probes corpses for clues as maverick Bristol pathologist Dr Ethan Winter, a man troubled by the murder of his fiancee and by the similarity of this show’s premise to countless others. As a brutal murder proves not to be all it seems, Winter’s hunt for the truth gets risky.Jack SealeGrand Designs9pm, Channel 4Living in an old driving test centre felt like a good idea when Edinburgh artists Jana and Rory first had the opportunity. But the freezing winters have tempered their enthusiasm. Can they turn the site into a modern home on a limited budget? And can their kids live in a caravan while they try?Phil HarrisonCause of Death9pm, Channel 5A sad and shocking look at the unexpected death of 16-year-old Danny Nicholls, who was found unresponsive on the living room floor by his sister. A medical investigation showed a hidden reason that could have suddenly stopped his heart from beating.HRMartin Compston: Living Las Vegas10pm, Channel 4From Greenock to Vegas, baby! Line of Duty’s Martin Compston relocated to America’s playground when he married a local. In this episode, he brings his Tom Cruise-like glee to pole dancing, flying in a helicopter across the strip and meeting the “king of Vegas”, singer Wayne Newton, who at 84 is still going strong.Priya ElanExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Other Worlds Than These by Stephen King and Peter Straub review – a self-indulgent finale to the Talisman trilogy | Stephen King | The Guardian
description: There are moments of shivering joy as the protagonist of two enduring classics, Jack Sawyer, returns – but this time his journey feels endlessly repetitive
Author: Alison Flood
Headline: There are moments of shivering joy as the protagonist of two enduring classics, Jack Sawyer, returns – but this time his journey feels endlessly repetitive
Content: Moments of true horror … Stephen King.Photograph: Ulf Andersen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMoments of true horror … Stephen King.Photograph: Ulf Andersen/Getty ImagesStephen KingReviewOther Worlds Than These by Stephen King and Peter Straub review – a self-indulgent finale to the Talisman trilogyThere are moments of shivering joy as the protagonist of two enduring classics, Jack Sawyer, returns – but this time his journey feels endlessly repetitiveAlison FloodWed 7 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBear with me, because there is some backstory to get through before we can talk about the book I am actually here to review. Back in 1984, Stephen King and Peter Straub collaborated on the fantasy novel The Talisman. Like all the best King stories, it follows a young boy: in this case Jack Sawyer, 12, whose mother, Lily, is dying. Jack learns that a magical object called the Talisman might save her – if he can find it in a parallel world known as the Territories. Straub and King followed this up in 2001 withBlack House, in which an adult Jack investigates a series of child murders that turn out to have disturbing links to the Territories.The books are very different: one a coming-of-age cross-country quest, in which Jack flips back and forth between two versions of the US; the other a fantastical and horror-inflected murder mystery. Both are brilliant and enduring classics which will always have a place on my bookshelves – I reread both of them, all 1,800-odd pages, to prepare for Other Worlds Than These and was as swept away and delighted as the first time round.double quotation markI cannot recommend that anyone who is not a Constant Reader embark on this 800-plus-page tomeSo: in 2013 Straub had an idea for a final volume in the Talisman trilogy, drawing as Black House does from a real-life series of murders, and returning Jack (previously left on a bit of a cliffhanger) to the fray. King didn’t pick up on it back then, and Straubdied in 2022. Now King is 79, and, as he writes in a somewhat valedictory afterword, “it’s time to think about tidying up, as much as such things are possible for a writer whose mind is still crammed with cool ideas”. So he went back to that old idea – the original email lost, but the concept of a “series of motiveless, brutal crimes” in the Far West of the Territories, as Straub put it, at the story’s heart.Jack, “his tide … going out”, is now 57. An aimless, lonely émigré to the Territories, he is sent on a mission by the two-bit despot he now depressingly reports to. He’s to travel through the toxic Blasted Lands to gather information on the Great Gorge, a mysterious area of “growing danger” that Governor Youngblood wants to know more about. Flipping back and forth between “America-side” and the Territories, Jack learns that an old policeman friend has gone missing on the trail of a pair of “murderin’ kids” who have been leaving a swathe of bodies in their wake in Nebraska. These kids are, he’s told, “infested” by demons – and the infestation is spreading to the children of the Territories.For the true King fan (the “Constant Reader”, as he puts it), there are moments of shivering joy in Other Worlds Than These – not least in the title, which draws from a key scene in King’s The Gunslinger. I could never not find pleasure in a billy-bumbler (a dog-like creature), or in memories of Wolf, a wonderful creation from The Talisman, or in references to chief gunslinger Roland Deschain from the Dark Tower series. As befits King, there are moments of true horror too, and good ones, as the teenage infection spreads across the Territories.But I cannot recommend that anyone who is not a Constant Reader embark on this 800-plus-page tome. For one, it would be pointless to read it without previously having read The Talisman and Black House (and if I’m honest, probably the seven-volume Dark Tower sequence too). And even for the Constant Reader, this is really not vintage King. I would have said that I’d follow Jack Sawyer anywhere, but as Ole Travellin’ Jack crisscrossed his way across the dry desert land of the Territories, his journey started to feel endless, and endlessly repetitive. As Jack’s crew are gearing up to cross yet another rickety bridge over yet another gaping chasm, one character even makes this point when they spot it. “Oh God … talk about repetition.” I hear you, fella! Jack himself does it: “Another echo. They’re becoming tiresome,” he says, in a rather too on-the-nose comment about the eerie (not so eerie the nth time they’re mentioned) similarities between the US and the Territories.Is this deliberate? Yes, undoubtedly: “ka [destiny] is a wheel”, as we’ve been told (more than once); Jack, as Roland did before him, is treading the path laid out for him in an endless cycle. But this time round, it all gets a little portentous, self-referential and self-indulgent – and, dare I say it, boring.I still thinkStephen Kingis a genius. I still think The Talisman is the perfect coming-of-age dark fantasy novel. So thank you for the endless hours of reading pleasure, Mr King. But unlike its predecessors, Other Worlds Than These will not be going on my reread shelf.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Blockers by Michael Lewis review – the quiet heroes who tried to stop Doge | Politics books | The Guardian
description: The author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusade
Author: Sam Freedman
Headline: The author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusade
Content: Elon Musk at the CPAC conference in 2025.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreenElon Musk at the CPAC conference in 2025.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersBook of the dayPolitics booksReviewBlockers by Michael Lewis review – the quiet heroes who tried to stop DogeThe author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusadeSam FreedmanWed 7 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 03.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American government are slowly disintegrating.It is harder to get people to focus on the machinery of the state because the effects are often slow and hard to pin down. Outbreaks of disease – such as the recent wave ofexplosive diarrhoeaacross the US – might have happened anyway, but were probably made worse by lay-offs at the Centers for Disease Control. Likewise, Trump is not directly responsible for natural disasters, but response times in the past year may have been hampered by mass redundancies at the National Weather Service. Cuts to tax collection also seem to have reduced revenue by multiple billions, though we cannot be sure of the causal relationship.The other problem is that bureaucracies are hard to make interesting. Their work is technical and complicated, and most officials are taught to avoid saying anything engaging in public. By the time a journalist has explained what an agency does and why it is important, the reader may well have clicked on to the next thing.So there are few better suited to the challenge of telling this story than Michael Lewis, one of the world’s bestselling nonfiction writers, who has a knack for finding an angle that cuts through the complexity. After a career spent getting readers excited about credit default swaps (The Big Short) and sabermetrics (Moneyball) he has decided to try to help people understand the importance of civil servants.double quotation markMusk’s overweening arrogance, glibness and total lack of preparation have seriously harmed the case for proper reformBlockers is a loose sequel to the The Fifth Risk, in which Lewis focused on the transition from the Obama to the Trump administration and the disruption caused by the new team’s almost complete lack of interest in their jobs. It focused heavily on what different departments and agencies do and why they matter. This time around the problem is not indifference but malicious intent to destroy. The “blockers” are the dedicated officials who try to stop the wanton and often illegal destruction of their life’s work by Elon Musk’s Doge or other agents of chaos. They range from a researcher working on preventing wildfires to a security guard trying to block Musk’s goons from entering his building, and a lawyer attempting to keep personal tax data from being used to deport undocumented migrants.In truth, they don’t do much blocking – since they all either end up resigning when they’re asked to do something illegal, or are fired. The title refers more to the assumption by Musk and his fellow travellers that these are the people who are stopping progress and need removing. Much of the book is taken up with descriptions of the valuable work they did before being turfed out.It would have been good to have a bit more on the villains, whose motivations for participating in Doge are varied. They range from the addled young coders with limited social skills deployed by Musk, to turncoat bureaucrats looking for any easy life, and some very strange characters such as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, with his bizarre obsession with dead animal parts. Trump’s absurd commerce secretary Howard Lutnick also makes a brief cameo, deciding he needs to personally sign off any cheque for more than $100,000. It feels as if there is more to say about the personal journeys that lead people to behave this way.This is the particularly true of the boss baddie Russell Vought, the Republican operative central to developing the Project 2025 plans for Trump’s second term. Musk causes havoc, but quickly gets bored of Doge and heads back to Silicon Valley. Vought is the real deal, quietly and systematically deconstructing the state while keeping out of the spotlight and getting others to do his dirty work for him.He appears in one of the book’s most engaging chapters, which zooms in on Francis Collins, a scientist who helped discover a successful treatment for cystic fibrosis, allowing those with the condition to live much longer. Collins ended up at the head of the National Institutes of Health under Obama, continued through Trump’s first term and part of Biden’s, before stepping down to run an NIH research lab. After Trump’s re-election he was effectively forced out, saying that his position had become “untenable”. Lewis runs through a series of possible culprits, of which Vought’s cost-cutting is one. What makes this particularly remarkable is that Vought’s own daughter has cystic fibrosis. Ideology is a powerful drug.But perhaps the most interesting character of all is Sahil Lavingia. A successful software engineer, he bought into Musk’s vision and went to work for Doge in the Department of Veterans Affairs. He only lasted 55 days before giving an on-the-record interview in which he noted that “it’s kind of fine – because the government works. It’s not as inefficient as I was expecting, to be honest. I was hoping for more easy wins.” This was not on-message and he was shown the door.A few months later, though, once Doge had fallen apart, he was invited back by one of the few survivors, who had stayed on at the Treasury department. Lavingia was tasked with improving the Internal Revenue Service’s computer systems, and despite not needing the money, seems genuinely committed to the task of making things work better. Through Lavingia, Lewis gives us a taste of what serious work to enhance the state might have looked like.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are real problems with the way the government operates, both in the UK and the US, caused by poor resourcing, dysfunctional systems, or low pay for technical staff compared with the private sector. Alongside Lewis’s star civil servants, there are people who have checked out or become institutionalised. Lavingia’s lengthy battle to get a water cooler replaced reminded me of how difficult it was to get the lifts working when I was at the Department for Education.One of the most irritating aspects of Doge’s brief existence was the stream of op-eds from people who really should have known better celebrating that someone was finally trying to enact reform, even if was being done in a clumsy and aggressive manner. In reality, Musk’s overweening arrogance, glibness and total lack of preparation have seriously harmed the case for proper reform. Not just due to the mess he and the likes of Vought caused, but also because they brought the very idea of making the state more efficient into disrepute.Lewis is great at finding incredible civil servants and telling their stories. But agencies and departments should not have to rely on unsung heroes, battling failing systems, and doing 90-hour weeks for little money because of their intense devotion to public service. Most people employed by large organisations are not like that. Effective government needs processes that work when used by a regular person doing a nine-to-five job. Rather than trying to replicate the “blockers”, we need to understand what these superstars are doing and embed it in the fabric of our institutions.Sam Freedman is a former special adviser and author of Failed State (Macmillan).
