title: Goodbye Warner, hello Skydance: how will the major merger really impact Hollywood? | Warner Bros | The Guardian
description: After a windier road than expected, Paramount and Warners are now one, under the banner of Skydance, and the film industry is set for a shake-up
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: After a windier road than expected, Paramount and Warners are now one, under the banner of Skydance, and the film industry is set for a shake-up
Content: A billboard displaying the logos of Skydance, Warner Bros and Paramount on the Paramount Global offices in New York.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenA billboard displaying the logos of Skydance, Warner Bros and Paramount on the Paramount Global offices in New York.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersWarner BrosGoodbye Warner, hello Skydance: how will the major merger really impact Hollywood?After a windier road than expected, Paramount and Warner are now one, under the banner of Skydance, and the film industry is set for a shake-upJesse HassengerWed 7 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 07.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHollywood’s big five have officially become the big four. Following a twist-filled saga that saw the century-old studio Warner Bros nearly acquired by the streaming giant Netflix, only to be outbid by Paramount owners Skydance, the company led by billionaire scion David Ellison. After facing legal opposition that ultimately crumbled, Warner Bros and Paramount areofficially under the same corporate roof. They are divisions of Skydance, which joins Sony, Disney and Universal as the remaining major-studio players in Hollywood.Paramount completes $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros to form new media empire SkydanceRead moreThe merger goes beyond film production. Eventually, the streaming services HBO Max and Paramount+ will merge into a single entity, though a timeline has not been disclosed. The television channels HBO, Showtime, CBS, MTV, Comedy Central, Cartoon Network, Nickelodeon, TNT, TBS and CNN are among many now owned by a single corporation. The presence of CNN on that list has brought particular scrutiny, given the post-Skydance meddling with the once-respected CBS News, resulting in a rocky stewardship from Bari Weiss, who has overseen a dip in both ratings and prestige for the flagship program 60 Minutes. Weiss isn’t expected to add CNN to her purview;current chair Mark Thompson will remain in place for now, and Skydance has insisted that CNN will remain editorially independent. But given Ellison’s chumminess with Donald Trump, who has long ranted incoherently about CNN’s supposed biases, the presence of an oversight board with Ellison appointees has been cold comfort.That oversight board is one of a few concessions for a group of state attorneys general dropping their lawsuit attempting to block the merger. Many of these points amount to maintaining business as usual for certain elements of the companies: negotiations for pay TV rights and channel fees charged to cable companies, for example, will have to be negotiated separately, as if Warner and Paramount haven’t merged. And one of Hollywood’s great fears about the merger, unaddressed by the agreement – the inevitable layoffs that come with consolidation – may not make much immediate difference in casual media consumers’ lives (though the people actually working in the entertainment industry will feel plenty of impact, direct and indirect, none of it good).So what will be most noticeable from the consumer’s vantage, in the coming months and years? In terms of their wallets, streaming prices will jump again, though that’s less a change than an acceleration ofcurrent conditions. Paramount+ is one of the cheaper streaming services at the moment, but HBO Max is one of the pricier options; it’s hard to imagine a combined version would fetch much less than $25 a month, and that’s just for starters; it could easily go much higher (though, again, that fusion of services probably won’t be immediate, and will probably look like business as usual in the short term). This might eventually lead to a streaming landscape less dependent on viewers buying a seemingly infinite number of $20 monthly subscriptions. But consolidation isn’t exactly great for competition, either.View image in fullscreenDavid Ellison.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersThe bigger creative changes will eventually be seen on the movie side of the business. Skydance already nixed Warner movie studio co-chairs Pam Abdy and Mike De Luca, who noted upon their departure, with a hint of snark, that they’re leaving the studio with 39 movies – meaning that any real successes from Warner in the next few years will be owed to their development slate, not whoever at Skydance claims credit. Not all of those 39 movies are locked and loaded for release, of course, but there probably won’t be major, immediate changes to the Warner release schedule – especially not for 2026, which will probably still close out with the DC Comics-based horror movie Clayface, the animated Seuss adaptation The Cat in the Hat, and the sci-fi blockbuster-in-waiting Dune 3.Further ahead, the Warner movies already well into production for 2027 look financially and sometimes even creatively promising: new movies in the Superman, Ocean’s, Minecraft and Godzilla/Kong series, plus original projects from M Night Shyamalan (in collaboration with Nicholas Sparks) and JJ Abrams. Paramount, meanwhile, has new movies in the Sonic the Hedgehog, Paranormal Activity and Quiet Place series, plus a remake of the artier horror movie Possession and an adaptation of the bestseller Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow.But the movies that already have release dates plotted out a year or two ahead of time tend to be the bigger-budget, brand-name and/or franchise fare that defines most major studios these days. Less clear is how the combined studio will meet their self-selected benchmark for number of new releases a year, and whether that might include non-branded movies. That’s a theoretical bright spot of the merger, also owed to that mostly watered-downdecreefrom the attorney generals: Skydance must make good on its seemingly far-fetched promise that consolidating these companies would not reduce film production, and in fact would result in a total of 30 new releases a year, the equivalent of robust years for two different studios.The AG agreement codifies that number for five years: 30 each year for two years, then 32 each year for the following three. There are additional terms about how many of these need to be wide releases and/or independent films, as well as some deeply dispiriting definitions of what constitutes the latter (“independent” is defined as, essentially, a movie that’s not a big-budget IP play). The agreement also lays out some consequences of highly questionable utility. A sample wrist-slap: for failing to meet these standards, the company would be forced to divest from ... Miramax?! This seems about as punishing as insisting that Skydance misbehaves, they must absolutely, positively part ways with VH1.In theory, though, Skydance has committed to releasing 156 movies in the next five years, which should make theatrical exhibitors happy, and seems to be the main reason some Hollywood figures like Tom Cruise and James Cameron have championed the merger. As for the specifics, the combined planned Warner/Paramount output for 2027 is more or less on track to hit 30 films; 2028 would need another 10 movies or so to meet it, and Paramount’s post-Ellison sensibility hasn’t exactly been informed by the variety of genres and budgets that once defined big studios. These days, Paramount mostly makes big-budget sequels and cheaper horror movies.That’s where executives like the departed De Luca and Abdy would have come in handy. Their tenure at Warner was characterized by both risks and variety befitting one of Hollywood’s most recognizable and prestigious movie studios. They greenlit two beloved smash-hit horror movies with Sinners and Weapons. The studio won a best picture Oscar – their first in over a decade – with Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another. They let indie talents play in a big-studio sandbox with movies like Wuthering Heights and The End of Oak Street. Even their franchise films, like the Dune sequels, Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga, Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, and Superman had the clear creative imprint of individual creators.View image in fullscreenLeonardo DiCaprio in One Battle After Another.Photograph: APThis also meant that Warner released some major flops during the last few years, including The Bride!, Supergirl and the recent Digger, which may have sealed their fate in Ellison’s eyes. (As the producer of sequels to Top Gun and Days of Thunder, he likes his Tom Cruise in big, rumbly vehicles, not addressing the climate crisis!) 2026 was a particularly bleak year for Warner at the box office. More than half their titles were outgrossed by Coyote vs. Acme, a project that CEO David Zaslav wanted binned completely before it was finally sold off to a smaller distributor.A greater volume of releases should theoretically offset those kinds of big-money misses – and ensure that finished movies aren’t scrapped as tax write-offs, something that another possible penalty ($30m a movie that falls short of the benchmark) seems likely to hold off. But, again, Paramount’s current tastes for non-blockbusters only seem to extend as far as horror cheapies, with an added dose of shameless “apolitical” inspirational junk; Ellison doesn’t have a track record of delivering a diverse array of comedies, dramas and thrillers that might appeal to adults. That’s what ultimately feels so dispiriting about the merger, even as it shows a heartening bullishness over the theatrical business.Warner Bros, a corporate studio with plenty of ups and downs but an overall legacy of cinema history, is being absorbed by Skydance, a company that still treats the movie business – even one that has seen major recent hits like Obsession, The Odyssey and Project Hail Mary – like it can be tentpoled up to the moon.The nightmare scenario is a 30-movie theatrical slate that looks more like a streaming service’s lineup of assembly-line “content”, only minus the kinds of passion projects that Netflix and Apple have been known to finance as a lure, and maybe plus a whole lot of AI designed to cut costs. After all, Ellison has indicated that he wants Skydance to serve as atech companyas much as an old-fashioned media monopoly – a dystopian fusion that leaves little room for creative or consumer upside. It’s hard not to wonder if the most successful outcome at this point would be failure - which isn’t off the table with $80bn of debt that needs immediate attention. In the meantime, moviegoers might have to comfort themselves with one surprising takeaway: that the ego and greed driving endless entertainment-industry mergers still somehow includes making movies for theaters, at least for now.Explore more on these topicsWarner BrosParamount PicturesFilm industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: As You Like It review – there are no mere players in the RSC’s ravishing all-male escapade | Theatre | The Guardian
description: With a WWE-style wrestling match, playful eroticism and a fine cast including Hamilton’s Jonathan Groff, this is an exquisite production
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: With a WWE-style wrestling match, playful eroticism and a fine cast including Hamilton’s Jonathan Groff, this is an exquisite production
Content: Prowling with desire … Jonathan Groff and Elliot Barnes-Worrell in As You Like It.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenProwling with desire … Jonathan Groff and Elliot Barnes-Worrell in As You Like It.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewAs You Like It review – there are no mere players in the RSC’s ravishing all-male escapadeRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-AvonWith a WWE-style wrestling match, playful eroticism and a fine cast including Hamilton’s Jonathan Groff, this is an exquisite productionArifa AkbarWed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘To liberty, and not to banishment,” exclaims Celia to Rosalind, the exile who finds freedom in her disguise as a man. It is a key statement in Shakespeare’s transformative, gender-bending pastoral comedy, just before the usurping Duke Frederick’s court is replaced by the romance of the Forest of Arden. That big reveal brought a prolonged technical difficulty on the opening night of director Daniel Evans’ all-male production, which was paused for well over an hour so it could be fixed. The technical hitch aside, it is a ravishing staging, with stunning visual effects.There is little comedy or light in the severe court, which contains an intimidating physicality to reflect Duke Frederick’s thuggery, with slaps, shoves and a magnificently constructed WWE-style wrestling match, complete with bunny girls keeping score. It is replaced by Arden’s verdant hills on Anisha Fields’ exquisite set, so beautiful they verge on the voluptuous. The black Elizabethan gowns of the court, Puritan-like but flecked with ornament, and designed by Colin Richmond, are stunning too, as is the chequered shadow-play of the early scenes, in Ryan Day’s lighting design. The breathtaking contrast of the switch between worlds is inevitably lost, following the long wait of the technical problem, but is nonetheless beautifully envisioned.Jonathan Groff, the US screen star who is also Broadway theatre royalty thanks in part to his performance as the king in Hamilton, makes a fun Rosalind, perhaps too declamatory at the start, but more textured and subtle later on. He instantly establishes chemistry with Fisayo Akinade’s Celia who is a runaway highlight of this show, performing femininity without caricature, and bringing an added charge to their relationship – a playful, same-sex eroticism which sees Celia straddling Rosalind at one point.View image in fullscreenRibald romance … Greg Haiste and Gareth Snook in As You Like It.Photograph: Marc BrennerThe all-male casting brings depth and subtlety of meaning, proving ingenious rather than gimmicky, simultaneously nostalgic and of the moment: a nod to the Elizabethan age when boys and men played female parts, yet now more queer and transgressive. The love between Orlando (Elliot Barnes-Worrell) and Rosalind’s disguised male alter ego, Ganymede, stays rather superficial, but the homoeroticism is more effective in their quieter moments, when Groff almost prowls with desire. He is at his best when he is overtly performative – a male actor playing a woman (Rosalind) who is playing a man (Ganymede) – and makes it work without resorting to outright camp.The comedy is light and frothy on the whole. Gary Wilmot, who is both Duke Frederick and the exiled Duke Senior, never overplays his lines. A fantastically prim Phoebe (Tim Preston) brings a kind of librarian comedy with her disdain for the shepherd, Silvius (Edward Judge), and her love-at-first-sight for Ganymede whose brute, masculine scolding seduces her. The ribald romance between Touchstone (Greg Haiste) and Audrey (Gareth Snook) is played for music-hall laughs, the latter is flamboyantly big-haired and archly bawdy, little short of a pantomime dame.Arden itself is rural Wales. Could this be a personal vision of an idyll from Welsh-born Evans? There is a lung-opening splendour to the set as it rolls downstage, over the darkness of the court, and Shakespeare’s songs are replaced by Welsh folk hymns (music composed, arranged and supervised by Theo Jamieson). It is preceded by massive alarms made beautiful by sound designer Paul Groothuis, combining with lighting to conjure musical claps of thunder and lightning. The court could be Prospero’s colonised island, full of strange noises.The only (other) glitch in the production is its pacing, which feels too slow in its latter stages, perhaps due to the big technical pause of the night. Yet the big reveal of Arden is still awesome, when it finally comes. Evans has created magic here.AtRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Shakespeare CompanyAs You Like ItComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Contact review – Jonny Donahoe delivers a heated reunion at a bonfire of family photos | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Blythe Duff and Mark Barrett are excellent as two people helplessly bound to each other in this bitter two-hander
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Blythe Duff and Mark Barrett are excellent as two people helplessly bound to each other in this bitter two-hander
Content: Fractured … Mark Barrett and Blythe Duff in Contact.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenFractured … Mark Barrett and Blythe Duff in Contact.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanTheatreReviewContact review – Jonny Donahoe delivers a heated reunion at a bonfire of family photosÒran Mór, GlasgowBlythe Duff and Mark Barrett are excellent as two people helplessly bound to each other in this bitter two-handerMark FisherWed 7 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe arrival of a first baby changes everything. It is not just the upheaval of fitting the child into your life: the shift is also psychological. Children become parents. Parents become grandparents. Responsibility and accountability move down a generation.That is why, inJonny Donahoe’s knotty, bitter two-hander, a man known only as Son (Mark Barrett) has called on Mother (Blythe Duff) after an eight-month gap. She is spikily indifferent to his appearance, here in her back garden where she is burning family photographs on a bonfire. Despite the frosty reception, he must persist.Son’s wife Alice (pronounced Malice, according to Mother) is expecting a Christmas baby. With that in mind, he is eager to end the resentment harboured by the older woman since he was six. He wants their relationship to be civil. She is having none of it.The damage is not in their surface chitchat. If you did not know better you could miss it. Duff captures the sparkle of Donahoe’s hard-bitten wit and can be waspishly funny. Barrett counters with low-status calm, avoiding confrontation. It could all be quite innocent.Whaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? review – when John Home outdid Stratford’s BardRead moreBut Mother’s lack of sentiment goes deep. Incapable of empathy, she has been brutalised by her past. “Not everything you feel has to be expressed,” she scolds her son, sounding ever more the sociopath. The shadow of Son’s abusive father looms over them, but their own personalities also play a part in a trauma that has left them stressed, depressed and trapped in a destructive cycle.With its short, fractured sentences, the play is a tad slow, but in Ben Standish’s lunchtime production for A Play, a Pie and a Pint (with the Traverse and OneRen), Duff and Barrett are excellent in their depiction of two people helplessly bound to each other, inflicting pain even when they try to do the opposite.At Òran Mór, Glasgow, until 10 October. Then touring until 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreParents and parentingFamilyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Curious and circumspect creatures’: the artist making sculptures for the rats of New York City | Art | The Guardian
description: For his latest project, Asad Raza made ‘public art’ for rats with pieces designed to appeal to the city’s maligned rodents
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: For his latest project, Asad Raza made ‘public art’ for rats with pieces designed to appeal to the city’s maligned rodents
Content: Asad Raza: thigmotaxis (the rat show). Installation view at times, New York.Photograph: Photos by Izzy Leung. Courtesy of times.View image in fullscreenAsad Raza: thigmotaxis (the rat show). Installation view at times, New York.Photograph: Photos by Izzy Leung. Courtesy of times.Art‘Curious and circumspect creatures’: the artist making sculptures for the rats of New York CityFor his latest project, Asad Raza made ‘public art’ for rats with pieces designed to appeal to the city’s maligned rodentsHannah KayWed 7 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“We call this the Hell Door,” artist Asad Raza explained animatedly. It’s 10pm on a warm August evening, and we are standing outside a small enclosure at the back of a seafood restaurant under the Manhattan Bridge that to any other passersby would have been invisible. “Are you ready?” he asks and, with my OK, pulls the door open to reveal what looks like 100 rats cascading over the dumpsters stored in this small, dimly lit room and scampering away into their secret passages in the walls and floor.‘Each artist on their own terms’: why Lee Krasner was every bit the equal to husband Jackson PollockRead moreThis foul-smelling, grime-encrusted site is just one of more than 20 that Raza, and his team of three installers – fellow artists Devyn Gallindo, Kunning Huang and Jared Packard – have identified acrossNew YorkCity as prime locations for, as he calls it, “public art for rats”.In a minivan rented by Raza for much of the summer, I accompanied the team on one of their regular nightly routes, watching as they fished sculptural components made of concrete, wood and burlap out of the trunk to arrange in various configurations beside garbage cans, next to sewers and under bushes. Doing so meant “going across all of these social boundaries that the human world of New York has” Raza observed, that “this world of the rats doesn’t have”.That night alone, the team trekked from Seward Park and a public housing complex on the Lower East Side to the riverside walkways under construction beneath the Brooklyn and Manhattan Bridges, all the way to the landscaped flowerbeds in front of the Natural History Museum and the litter-filled medians of Times Square.View image in fullscreenFilm still from Asad Raza’s thigmotaxis, 2026.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and times, New York.At most locations along the way, they also zip-tied trail cams to pipes, gates and benches, so as to capture footage of the rats’ interactions with the sculptures. After retrieving an SD Card with the previous night’s documentation, Huang would stay behind in the van downloading it on to a laptop so that the crew could see what they had captured. As each rat sniffed, rubbed and scampered over or through the “public art” that had newly appeared outside their veritable front doors, everyone exclaimed.“I was interested in doing something that wouldn’t simply be fun or entertaining for rats,” Raza explains, when asked how he determined what “public art” for rats would look like, “because to me, a key part of art is that it’s not exactly for anything. It doesn’t necessarily have a clear purpose other than as an expression of its own form.”So when considering whether or not it would be “possible for the idea of art to cross the species boundary” Raza recognized that he had to “think about another species’ way of perceiving the world in a way that would allow us to create a similar kind of experience for them”. This line of inquiry lead him to consult Michael Parsons, an animal behaviorist, as well as architects Mara Jovanović and Zaynab Eltaib of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), advised by Jaffer Kolb, regarding what kinds of structures, forms, materials and textures would be most sensorially captivating for rats.“If we want to take them seriously as beings with their own preferences and ways of navigating the world,” Raza said, “I’m not going to make tiny Cartesian modernist villas.” Instead, rats particularly enjoy chaotic spaces with lots of entries, exits, and places to hide. “Think,” Parsons wrote in an email to Raza, “shattered bits of rubble.” This phrase stuck with the artist and has been clearly reflected in the resulting sculptures which could (like so much contemporary art) easily be mistaken for trash or debris.View image in fullscreenBehind-the-scenes photography during the making of Asad Raza’s thigmotaxis (the rat show).Photograph: Photos by Devyn Galindo. Courtesy of the artist and times, New York.To make the sculptural components, Raza worked with Jovanovic and Eltaib at MIT casting different objects – usually items found in urban environments, such as plastic bags, styrofoam and boxes – to create molds for concrete structures. The formal language that developed was one of textured concrete surfaces punctured by balloon forms that create navigable passageways, and augmented with wooden and burlap components that hold scents well.These material choices were largely informed by thigmotaxis, which is a keen sense that rats have of being in contact with a solid surface by rubbing alongside walls or structures. As night-time and semi-subterranean creatures, they use this sense to find their way and stay out of trouble, as they have poor vision but a good sense of smell.In learning more about rats, their needs, behaviors and desires over the last few months, Raza said he had come to “think about them much more as animals living their own independent lives, rather than something that makes me sick or that I don’t want to see”.“Once you get over the culturally indoctrinated, visceral fear of rats,” he added, he began to “see them as much less threatening, and more [as] curious and circumspect creatures”.View image in fullscreenAsad Raza: thigmotaxis (the rat show). Installation view in New York.Photograph: Photos by Izzy Leung. Courtesy of times.The project began when Raza was invited to create an exhibition for times, an alternative art space downtown. As an artist who normally produces site-specific, multi-sensory, often haptic installations – such as diverting a river through a gallery (Portikus Frankfurt, Germany), filling an exhibition space with soil created from local waste products (Carriageworks, Australia), conducting electricity through various encounters and materials in a reactivated power station (currently on view atE-WERK Luckenwalde, Germany) – Raza started by looking beyond the white cube of the exhibition space to the broader, non-human ecosystem of New York.Given that the city is not just home to nearly 9 million humans, but undoubtedly rife with countless other creatures big, small and most famously (to many New Yorkers’ displeasure) approximately 3 million rats, it is not altogether surprising that Raza began to wonder: “What would it mean to make art for rats?”Artifacts and documentation from the city-wide public art installations that resulted (ie the true exhibition which took place in August for our nocturnal neighbors) is now on view. Titled thigmotaxis (the rat show), this presentation features a selection of the sculptures arranged across the floor, a human-sized textured wall-work that visitors can rub against to experience thigmotaxis themselves, and a video of the rats’ nocturnal encounters with the sculptures throughout the city. “It’s a little bit of a love letter to New York,” Raza said.Asad Raza: Thigmotaxis (the rat show) is on view at times, New York until 12 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArtNew YorkDesignSculpturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s hard to imagine the fires of July’: a bike ride through the Cairngorms in Scotland | Travel | The Guardian
description: Wildfires raged through the national park this summer, but much of the landscape remains untouched – and autumn is the perfect time to go
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: Wildfires raged through the national park this summer, but much of the landscape remains untouched – and autumn is the perfect time to go
Content: Much of the burned area is far from the roads. All photographs: Markus StitzView image in fullscreenMuch of the burned area is far from the roads. All photographs: Markus StitzTravel‘It’s hard to imagine the fires of July’: a bike ride through the Cairngorms in ScotlandWildfires raged through the national park this summer, but much of the landscape remains untouched – and autumn is the perfect time to goAilsa SheldonWed 7 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 02.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the Cairngorms national park, the bracken is changing from dark green to russet and umber. Birch leaves are lined with gold, while the Scots pines remain proudly green. Autumn is arriving with a little sigh of relief here, after a summer few will forget.The wildfire that began near Glenmore and Abernethy on 15 July burned more than 33 sq km (13 sq miles) of moorland and forest. More than 500 firefighters were involved; homes and businesses were evacuated; and the emergency response lasted over a month. Visiting now, it’s hard to see, or even imagine, the damage. Much of the burned area is high on the hill and far from the roads. It’s a huge loss but, in a national park stretching 4,528 sq km (1,748 sq miles), surprisingly easy to miss.I have come with a gravel bike to retest new bikepacking routes with Kees Wouters and Yannick Ferbeek fromLegendary Rides, which offers self-guided tours, and Bikepacking Scotland founder Markus Stitz, who helped develop the routes.View image in fullscreenAilsa Sheldon on the trailI arrive in Aviemore from Edinburgh on an electric Ember bus, which allows bikes to be booked on board, a welcome development in Scottish public transport. Soon I’m heading out of town through heather and Scots pines, my bike bags stuffed with everything I need for the next few days.The original route would have taken us through Glenmore, past Loch Morlich and Ryvoan bothy, but there are still path closures. Instead, we take a new line towards Nethy Bridge. Sunlight falls through birch and rowan and the track is soft with pine needles. At Loch Garten, where ospreys nest in spring and summer, it is hard to imagine the smoke and helicopters of July.Graham Niven lives in Nethy Bridge with his wife, Amy, and runs the self-catering businessArbor Nethybeside the forest. He joined the local volunteer firefighting effort coordinated by the RSPB, part of a huge community response. “We see the forest as an extension of our home,” Graham says. The Abernethy forest is ecologically rich, filled with ancient Caledonian pine trees that are hundreds of years old. “It’s a unique and special habitat, and it’s very fragile. We were all just grieving for the forest,” he tells me.View image in fullscreenCycling by the River AvonThe news cycle has long moved on, but locals are still dealing with the effects of the wildfire. “Only in the last few weeks have we been able to look back on it as something that’s come to an end,” Graham says. Peat smouldered underground for months, meaning firefighters had to keep returning to hotspots.While business has largely returned to usual, Graham has noticed a dip in bookings for photography workshops and holiday lets. “What is less measurable is people’s confidence in booking or coming back. The buzzwords were ‘apocalyptic fire’ and Abernethy and Nethy Bridge, Cairngorms, and that does stick in people’s minds. People think of Abernethy and say: ‘Oh, it’s been burned down.’ I think it’s less than 10% of the old forest affected.” Nearby, Polly Cameron atThe Dell of Abernethyhas seen the same effect: “Bookings wise, we certainly experienced a dip, and October has still been much slower to fill.” That matters in a landscape where tourism is a vital part of the local economy.double quotation markThe Cairngorms change character as you head east: forests give way to sheep, grouse moors, abandoned crofts and long gravel roadsWe ride on along the Speyside Way, following the river through woods and farmland. Then the landscape opens. The Cairngorms change character as you head east: deep forests give way to sheep, grouse moors, abandoned crofts and long gravel roads. This is whisky country too, and we ride through the grounds of Glenlivet Distillery. It’s after hours, or the smell of malted barley would have tempted me to stop.By late afternoon the hills have turned heather-purple. We started late and by the time we reachHotel Squarein Tomintoul, darkness has settled. Our bikes go into a storage room and, happily, hot curry and cold beer are still available.The next day is shorter but steeper, taking us on to sections of the old military roads built in the 18th century after the Jacobite risings. I’m reminded of that history later atCorgarff, a white fortress on the crest of a hill. Built in the 16th century and later converted into a barracks, it was used to suppress Jacobite sympathisers and, later, the illicit whisky trade.View image in fullscreenCairngorm Bothies near BallaterWe spend the second night atCairngorm Bothies, off-grid cabins surrounded by Scots pines. In each, there’s a little nature journal and I leaf through pages of children’s handwriting with tales of red squirrels and deer. When the rain starts, any disappointment about missing out on seeing the dark skies is replaced by relief not to be camping.With a flexible route we stop often, for photos, snacks and whenever the fancy takes us. We walk through woodland to visit Burn O’Vat, a huge glacial pothole in the Muir of Dinnet national nature reserve. At Ballater we stop for coffee and morning rolls atThe Bothywhile one of our group gets a quick bike repair. The route is deliberately forgiving, and Legendary Rides provides shorter alternatives for challenging weather or tired legs, with prebooked accommodation, a personalised plan, GPX routes and WhatsApp support. “It allows you to relax and just enjoy the ride,” says Yannick.double quotation markAutumn is an ideal time for this kind of journey. The midges have retreated, the roads are emptier and there is still plenty of golden lightFrom Ballater we wind towards Loch Muick, through the Balmoral estate. After a long, winding ascent over Capel Mounth the riding becomes rougher, with a rocky descent. The gentle undulating roads that follow to Glen Clova are a welcome contrast as we roll to Alyth.I’ve visited the Cairngorms region often in the past, but this trip broadens my awareness of the diversity of landscapes it holds. To mountain peaks and forest trails I add river valleys, whisky country, high moorland, farmland and roads so empty that the only sound is the freewheel of a bicycle.View image in fullscreenA waterfall at Burn O’VatBut this is not untouched wilderness. We cross private estates managed for deer stalking and grouse shooting, as well as national nature reserves. Debates over the right ways to manage this land span centuries, with wildfire prevention now a key part of that conversation. Scotland’s right to responsible access allows us to pass through this landscape, provided we leave no trace, close gates and avoid disturbing livestock and wildlife.Autumn is an ideal time for this kind of journey. The midges have retreated, the roads are emptier and there is still plenty of golden light in the days.Cyclingthrough the area helps to support local cafes, shops and accommodation providers, and there’s never been a better time to do so. “We want people to know we’re still here, we’re still awesome,” says Graham.My tired legs power me to a final Pitlochry cafe stop before my Ember bus back to Edinburgh.The trip was provided byLegendary RidesandBikepacking Scotland. Legendary Rides offersfour-day bikepacking tripsfrom£759pp, including detailed route planning, accommodation, breakfastand personal support via WhatsAppExplore more on these topicsTravelUnited Kingdom holidaysScotland holidaysEurope holidaysCycling (Sport)Cycling (Life and style)Cycling holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tom Hunt’s recipe for fridge-raid minestrone, UK-style | Food | The Guardian
description: A creative way to use up the bits you already have around, all while getting in a healthy mixture of vegetables and whole grains
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: A creative way to use up the bits you already have around, all while getting in a healthy mixture of vegetables and whole grains
Content: Tom Hunt’s zero-waste fridge-raid 'minestrone'.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s zero-waste fridge-raid 'minestrone'.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodTom Hunt’s recipe for fridge-raid minestrone, UK-styleA creative way to use up the bits you already have around, all while getting in a healthy mixture of vegetables and whole grainsTom HuntWed 7 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis hearty dish is inspired by the diets ofthe Blue Zones, or those regions of the world where people live the longest, including Sardinia, where minestrone is a staple.Dan Buettner, who studied these communities, found that their diets are generally rich in beans, whole grains and seasonal vegetables. I’ve generalised ingredients into groups such as alliums, rather than simply suggesting the standard onion base, to inspire you to use up whatever you have in the house and what’s in season; I’d of course also encourage further diversification with the addition of other vegetables and subtle spices.Fridge-raid “minestrone”This is a hodge-podge minestrone-of-sorts, inspired by the Sardinian classic and adapted for the British larder. I’ve used a grain and pulse soup, or broth mix, because it’s widely available in British supermarkets, and includes a nourishing blend of split peas, lentils, barley and spelt; however, any lentils, soaked dried beans or grains will also work well, as do canned beans, though add those (and their tin liquid, or aquafaba) only towards the end of the cooking process. Instead of the fennel in Beuttner’s recipe, I’ve used leafy greens, mainly to make the most of the greens in my fridge, which in this instance featured beetroot leaves, chard and cauliflower leaves. I like to batch-cook this soup and keep the excess in the fridge for another meal.Serves44 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil150g diced alliums– onions, leeks, spring onions2 medium carrots, peeled and chopped (about 100g net)2 medium celery stalks, chopped (optional)1 tsp fennel seeds, or coriander seeds4 garlic cloves, peeled and minced1400g tin chopped tomatoes200g dried grain and pulse soup mix(pearl barley, yellow split peas, green split peas, spelt, and red lentils) or pearl barley or another grain400groot vegetables– celeriac, turnip, potatoes150g chopped greens– spinach, or beetroot or cauliflower leaves20g flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped from stalk to leaf20gbunch fresh basil100g small mixed pasta shapes– broken spaghetti, ditalini, orzo50g grated pecorino, or parmesan, to serveWarm three tablespoons of the oil in a large soup pot on a medium heat. Add the diced alliums, carrot and celery, if using, then stir in the fennel seeds and saute for five minutes, until soft but not coloured. Stir in the minced garlic and saute for 30 seconds more, until fragrant.Add the chopped tinned tomatoes, followed by the grain and pulse soup mix (or pearl barley), root vegetables, chopped greens, chopped flat-leaf parsley, and the finely chopped stalks from the bunch of basil (save the leaves to finish). Pour in enough water to submerge everything by 2½cm (you’ll need about one and a half litres), then bring to a boil. Turn down the heat and leave to simmer uncovered for an hour, adding more water as needed. Finely stir in the mixed pasta shapes, add up to 500ml more water, if need be, then simmer for 10 minutes until tender.Season to taste, then divide between four bowls and serve topped with the reserved basil leaves, grated pecorino and a generous drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteAutumn food and drinkSoupItalian food and drinkBritish food and drinkMain coursefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Roast chicken, congee and cookies: Ravinder Bhogal’s autumn squash recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Nutty in flavour and creamy in texture, autumn’s bounty of squash and pumpkin has many uses, both sweet and savoury
Author: Ravinder Bhogal
Headline: Nutty in flavour and creamy in texture, autumn’s bounty of squash and pumpkin has many uses, both sweet and savoury
Content: Ravinder Bhogal’s pumpkin and miso congee with chilli oil.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.View image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s pumpkin and miso congee with chilli oil.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex Jorge.FoodRoast chicken, congee and cookies: Ravinder Bhogal’s autumn squash recipesNutty in flavour and creamy in texture, autumn’s bounty of squash and pumpkin has many uses, both sweet and savouryRavinder BhogalWed 7 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe shops are heaving with pumpkins and squash, and though there are so many different varieties to choose from, most of them are interchangeable. My favourites are kabocha, crown prince and delicata, for their deeply nutty flavour and creamy texture, plus they hold their shape well when roasted or braised. And if you’re carving a pumpkin forHalloweenover the coming weeks, don’t waste the flesh: chop it up and throw into a risotto. It’s hard to imagine that such deliciousness could come from such a ghoulish grimace.Pumpkin and miso congee with chilli oil (pictured above)Congee is a favourite comfort food that is eaten across Asia, often for breakfast. This version isn’t particularly traditional, but it makes the most of pumpkin season. I love this with a drizzle of chilli oil as a contrast to the delicata’s natural sweetness.Prep15 minCook50 minServes6600gdelicata pumpkin, peeled and chopped into bite-size chunks, plus 6 wedges3tbsp avocado oil, or neutral oilSea salt and black pepper1 heapedtbsp white miso2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped1tbsp crushed ginger200g short-grain white rice1 piece kombu1 bunch spring onions, trimmed and sliced on the diagonalFor the garnish3tbsp toasted pumpkin seedsA few drops of sesame oilChilli oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Lay out the pumpkin on a baking sheet, drizzle over one tablespoon of oil and season. Roast for 30-40 minutes, until very soft and caramelised, then remove and leave to cool. Set aside the squash wedges, then puree the remaining chunks in a food processor with a splash of water.In a large saucepan, heat the remaining oil on a medium heat, add the miso and cook, stirring, until lightly caramelised. Add the garlic and ginger, and stir until fragrant.Add the rice, kombu and 1.8 litres of water and bring to a boil on medium-high heat. Partially cover, turn down the heat to a low simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, for 25-30 minutes, until the liquid has reduced and the rice is plump and has turned into a porridge. Stir in the pumpkin puree and half the sliced spring onions.Divide the congee between six bowls and top each portion with a wedge of roast squash. Garnish with the remaining spring onions, then finish with toasted pumpkin seeds, a drizzle of sesame oil and your favourite chilli oil.Chicken with kabocha squash and sageView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s pot-roasted chicken with kabocha squash and sage.This makes for a wonderful alternative autumnal Sunday roast, with minimal washing-up because it’s all cooked in one pan.Prep10 minCook1 hr 20 minServes4Sea salt and black pepper1 whole chicken(about 1½kg)1 whole garlic bulb, cut in half horizontally1 unwaxed lemon,halved1 bunchsage2 bay leaves2tbsp olive oil½tsp dried chilli flakes1tsp ground cinnamon1 small kabocha squash(about 750g), unpeeled and cut into wedges150ml dry white wine800ml chicken stock50mldouble creamSeason the chicken generously inside and out, then stuff the cavity with one of the garlic halves, both lemon halves, half the sage and the bay leaves.Put the oil in a large, deep casserole over a medium heat and, once it’s hot, brown the chicken all over – take your time to do this properly, because it really makes a difference to the overall taste. Once browned, set aside the chicken for the time being.In the oil left over from browning the chicken, fry the remaining garlic and sage with the chilli and cinnamon, then, once the mix is smelling fragrant, stir in the squash wedges to coat them in the aromatic oil. Cook for two minutes, then pour in the wine and leave to bubble away until reduced by half.Push the squash to the sides of the pan, then nestle the chicken in the middle. Pour in the stock,cover and leave to cook on a gentle heat for 50 minutes to an hour. Once cooked, stir in the cream, season if need be, and serve.Fudgy pumpkin pie cookiesView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s fudgy pumpkin pie cookies.No tricks, just treats. These are perfect for a little Halloween indulgence.Prep10 minChill40 minCook1 hr, plus coolingMakesAbout 20For the pumpkin puree200g red kurior kabochasquash, halved, deseeded, peeled and cut into 2cm cubes50g granulated sugar1tsp ground cinnamon½tsp ground gingerA pinch of ground clovesA good grating of nutmegFor the cookies225g plain flour1tsp cinnamon½tsp ground gingerA pinch of clovesA good grating of nutmeg½tsp baking powder½tsp bicarbonate of sodaSalt225g light brown sugar175g unsalted butter2 egg yolks1tsp vanilla extractStart by making the pumpkin puree. Put the pumpkin in a microwave-safe container and microwave on high for five minutes. Remove, toss, then microwave on high again for another five minutes. Keep repeating this process until the pumpkin is soft and mashable – the timing will depend on your microwave, but mine took 15 minutes. Once soft, puree in a food processor (or mash well with a fork) until smooth, then leave to cool.In a small bowl, mix the sugar and spices. In medium bowl, mix the flour, spices, baking powder, bicarb and half a teaspoon of salt. In a stand mixer, cream the brown sugar and butter until light and fluffy. Add the egg yolks and vanilla, whisk again until pale and fluffy, then stir in the pumpkin puree until well combined. Fold in the dry ingredients, then chill in the fridge for 40 minutes, until firm.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and line two baking sheets with greaseproof paper. Scoop out two tablespoons of the cookie mixture and roll them into loose balls. Roll these in the spiced sugar mix and place on the baking sheets spaced well apart. Repeat with the remaining cookie mix, then bake for 12 minutes, until golden brown.Remove and leave to cool on the baking sheet for five minutes, then transfer to a rack to cool completely.Explore more on these topicsFoodAutumn food and drinkMain courseVegetablesChickenMeatSnacksrecipesShareReuse this content

title: French wine industry facing historic low harvest after extreme summer heat | Wine | The Guardian
description: This year’s harvest expected to be down 2% on mediocre yield in 2025, when production was lowest in nearly 70 years
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This year’s harvest expected to be down 2% on mediocre yield in 2025, when production was lowest in nearly 70 years
Content: Grapes affected by drought at a vineyard in Douzens, south-west France, last year.Photograph: Idriss Bigou-Gilles/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGrapes affected by drought at a vineyard in Douzens, south-west France, last year.Photograph: Idriss Bigou-Gilles/AFP/Getty ImagesWineFrench wine industry facing historic low harvest after extreme summer heatThis year’s harvest expected to be down 2% on mediocre yield in 2025, when production was lowest in nearly 70 yearsAFPWed 7 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance’s wine industry is facing a historic low harvest after the country was hit by a series of summer heatwaves.At about 35m hectolitres, the total harvest would be down 2% on a mediocre 2025 yield and 14% below the 2021-2025 average, according to estimates published on Wednesday by the ministry of agriculture.The International Organisation of Vine andWine, which tracks global statistics on wine production and consumption, said that last year France had recorded its lowest production since 1957.This latest decline is a result of hot weather, slightly mitigated by recent rain, and a reduction in cultivated areas, which were pared back by 1.9% in the past year.View image in fullscreenChâteau Malartic-Lagravière in Bordeaux, where wine production has risen on last year.Photograph: Régis Duvignau/ReutersSome southern areas, already battered by the heat in 2025, have nonetheless seen production rise this year. In Bordeaux, despite a 5% decrease in cultivated areas, production is expected to increase by 10% on 2025, though this is still 11% below the 2021-2025 average.For the south-west the rise is about 12%, essentially a return to the previous four-year average.The Champagne region fared less well as growers had to harvest exceptionally early after the extreme heat sped up sugar buildup and hence natural alcohol production.The harvest there wrapped up in September for the first time, with production down by half on last year and the five-year average.Claude Mandois, a producer in Champagne, reported harvesting three-quarters of an average yield in terms of volume but added: “In terms of quality visually and in terms of taste we had an exceptional harvest.”In Burgundy and the Beaujolais region, production is projected to be 30% lower than the five-year average.“It’s a level of heterogeneity I’ve never experienced before,” said Jérôme Despey, the chair of the wine advisory board at the public agency FranceAgriMer and a winegrower in the southern Hérault department.He said vines in the south had become more resilient to the climate, with previous intense heat spells causing growers to adapt vineyard management practices such as largely leaving leaves to protect the grapes. Southern regions also benefited from May rainfall.The ministry and the industry emphasised overall the “excellent health” of the harvest, which was free of fungi and other moisture-related diseases.Explore more on these topicsWineFranceExtreme heatFoodnewsShareReuse this content
